name: Caenina
war: Wars of Romulus (after the rape of the Sabine women)
place: Caenina, a small town just east of Rome
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Plutarch and the Fasti Triumphales, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The first levy of the new city under Romulus; no numbers are given for the battle (Plutarch, Romulus 13, makes the first legion 3,000 foot and 300 horse).
greek_note: A levy of the city's Latin settlers; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Livy 1.10; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 2.33; Plutarch, Romulus 16; Fasti Triumphales; en.wikipedia Caenina (town)
note: Romulus killed King Acron in the battle, dedicated the first spolia opima to Jupiter Feretrius and took Caenina at the first assault. The Fasti Triumphales put his triumph over the Caeninenses on 1 March of the city's first year (752 BCE). Dionysius calls the Caeninenses Aborigines; Livy lists them beside the Sabines; treated here as Latins. Site uncertain.

name: Antemnae
war: Wars of Romulus (after the rape of the Sabine women)
place: Antemnae, at the confluence of the Anio and the Tiber (Monte Antenne, Rome)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Plutarch and the Fasti Triumphales, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The Roman levy under Romulus (Livy 1.11 calls it a legio); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of the city's Latin settlers; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Livy 1.11; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 2.34-35; Plutarch, Romulus 17; Fasti Triumphales; en.wikipedia The Rape of the Sabine Women
note: The Antemnates were caught scattered over the fields, raiding (Livy) or foraging (Dionysius), routed at the first charge, and their town was taken; the Fasti Triumphales record Romulus' second triumph, over the Antemnates, in the first year of the city. Dionysius calls them Aborigines; treated here as Latins.

name: Crustumerium
war: Wars of Romulus (after the rape of the Sabine women)
place: Crustumerium, on the left bank of the Tiber north of Fidenae (Marcigliana)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Plutarch, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The Roman levy under Romulus; no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of the city's Latin settlers; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Livy 1.11; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 2.36; Plutarch, Romulus 17
note: Livy says the Crustumini, disheartened by their neighbours' defeats, put up even less fight; Dionysius describes a pitched battle followed by an assault on the town. Dionysius calls Crustumerium an Alban colony. Roman colonists were sent there afterwards.

name: Forum (Sabine war)
place: The marshy valley between the Palatine and the Capitol, later the Roman Forum
commanders_a: Romulus, Hostus Hostilius (killed); Lucumo with the Etruscans
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Plutarch, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: About 20,000 foot and 800 horse, with Etruscan mercenaries under Lucumo of Solonium and Alban soldiers and engineers sent by Numitor (Dionysius 2.37); Tatius led about 25,000 foot and 1,000 horse.
greek_note: Dionysius names only Romans, Albans and Etruscans in Romulus' army; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Livy 1.11-13; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 2.37-46; Plutarch, Romulus 17-19; en.wikipedia The Rape of the Sabine Women; en.wikipedia Roman-Sabine wars
note: Tarpeia's betrayal had given the Sabines the Capitol without a fight. Livy tells one battle, in which Romulus vowed the temple of Jupiter Stator and Mettius Curtius' horse floundered in the marsh (the Lacus Curtius); Dionysius (2.41-43) and Plutarch describe several hard, indecisive battles. The Sabine women parted the armies and the two peoples united under Romulus and Tatius. Ancient dates for the rape range from the fourth month (Fabius, in Plutarch, Romulus 14) to the fourth year after the founding.

name: Cameria
war: Wars of Romulus and Titus Tatius
place: Cameria, north-east of Rome (probably Palombara Sabina)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Dionysius of Halicarnassus, written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: Not in Livy; known from Dionysius.
roman_force: The joint army of the Romans and of Tatius' Sabines under the two kings; Plutarch (Romulus 20) says the legion was raised to 6,000 foot and 600 horse after the union.
greek_note: Romans and Sabines; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Dionysius of Halicarnassus 2.50; en.wikipedia Cameria
note: The kings beat the Camerini in a pitched battle, stormed the town and took a third of its land; when the Camerini harassed the settlers they were routed again and a colony was planted. Dionysius calls Cameria an Alban colony. Site uncertain.

name: Cameria (second war)
place: Cameria, north-east of Rome (probably Palombara Sabina)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Plutarch, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: Not in Livy.
roman_force: The Roman army under Romulus, raised while a plague was raging at Rome (Plutarch, Romulus 24); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans and Sabines of the united city; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Dionysius of Halicarnassus 2.54; Plutarch, Romulus 24; en.wikipedia Cameria
note: After Tatius' death the Camerini attacked the Roman colonists; Romulus defeated them, killing 6,000 (Plutarch), retook the town, moved half the survivors to Rome, took half the remaining land and left a garrison (Dionysius). Plutarch says he brought back a bronze four-horse chariot.

name: Fidenae (Romulus)
place: Fidenae, on the Via Salaria above the Tiber, 8 km north of Rome (Villa Spada)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Plutarch, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The Roman army under Romulus, with cavalry sent ahead to raid and the infantry laid in ambush in thickets (Livy 1.14); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans and Sabines of the united city; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Livy 1.14; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 2.53; Plutarch, Romulus 23-24; en.wikipedia Fidenae
note: After the death of Titus Tatius. A feigned flight drew the Fidenates into the ambush and the Romans burst into the town with the fugitives (Livy); in Dionysius the Fidenates had seized grain boats, lost a battle and the town at the first assault. Plutarch says 2,500 colonists were sent on the Ides of April. Livy (1.15) calls the Fidenates Etruscans, Dionysius an Alban colony; treated here as Latins.

name: Veii (Romulus)
place: Near Fidenae, by the Tiber (Dionysius, Plutarch); Livy puts the battle in Veientine territory before Veii
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Plutarch, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The Roman army under Romulus, with a picked force in ambush on a height (Dionysius 2.55); no numbers for the Romans.
greek_note: Romans and Sabines of the united city; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Livy 1.15; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 2.54-55; Plutarch, Romulus 25; en.wikipedia Fidenae
note: Veii claimed Fidenae. Livy has one battle, after which the Veientes were chased to their walls; Dionysius three near Fidenae (one indecisive, an ambush that drove many into the Tiber, and a victory that took the Veientine camp); Plutarch two, with 8,000 and then 14,000 Etruscans killed. Veii ceded the Seven Districts (Septem Pagi) and the salt-works, gave fifty hostages and accepted a hundred-year truce; Plutarch dates the triumph to the Ides of October.

name: Fidenae (Tullus Hostilius)
war: War with Fidenae and Veii (Tullus Hostilius)
place: Between the confluence of the Anio and the Tiber and Fidenae (Livy 1.27); the plain before Fidenae (Dionysius)
commanders_a: Tullus Hostilius; Mettius Fufetius with the Albans
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The Roman army under Tullus Hostilius with the Alban army of Mettius Fufetius as subject allies; the Albans drew off to the hills during the battle and joined only in the pursuit (Livy 1.27; Dionysius 3.24-26).
greek_note: Romans and Albans, both Latin-speaking; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Livy 1.27-28; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 3.23-30; en.wikipedia Tullus Hostilius
note: The Fidenates had revolted and called in Veii. Tullus told his men the Albans were moving on his orders to take the enemy in the rear; the Fidenates fled to their town and the Veientes into the Tiber, where many drowned, and their camp was stormed (Dionysius). Tullus vowed shrines to Pallor and Pavor. Mettius was torn apart by chariots for his treachery and Alba was razed. Fidenates treated as Latins (Livy calls them Etruscans).

name: Fidenae (siege, Tullus Hostilius)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Dionysius of Halicarnassus, written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: Known from Dionysius only.
roman_force: The Roman army under Tullus Hostilius, now including the Albans moved to Rome; no numbers.
greek_note: The Roman levy; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Dionysius of Halicarnassus 3.31
note: Fidenae revolted again with hired troops, who sallied and fought before the walls with heavy losses on both sides; Tullus then shut the town in with a ditch and palisade and it surrendered on his terms.

name: Eretum (Tullus Hostilius)
place: Near Eretum (Grotta Marozza, by Mentana), about 30 km north-east of Rome
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Dionysius of Halicarnassus, written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: Known from Dionysius only; Livy has a single Sabine battle, at the Silva Malitiosa.
roman_force: The Roman army under Tullus Hostilius; no numbers.
greek_note: The Roman levy; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Dionysius of Halicarnassus 3.32; en.wikipedia Eretum
note: The war began over Roman merchants seized at the shrine of Feronia. After an indecisive first battle, the Romans broke the Sabine line near Eretum late in the day and took their camp; Tullus vowed festivals to Saturn and Ops and new Salii.

name: Silva Malitiosa
place: The Silva Malitiosa ('Knaves' Wood'), in Sabine territory; site unknown
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The Roman infantry and cavalry under Tullus Hostilius, the cavalry reinforced with ten new turmae of Alban equites (Livy 1.30).
greek_note: Romans and Albans; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Livy 1.30; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 3.33; en.wikipedia Roman-Sabine wars; en.wikipedia Tullus Hostilius
note: A charge of the Roman cavalry broke the Sabine ranks and the Sabines lost heavily in the rout; volunteers from Veii had joined them, though Veii itself stayed out of the war (Livy). Dionysius treats it as a second Sabine war after Eretum.

name: Politorium (siege)
place: Politorium, a Latin town south of Rome (perhaps Castel di Decima)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: A newly raised Roman army under Ancus Marcius (Livy 1.33); no numbers.
greek_note: The Roman levy; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Livy 1.32-33; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 3.37-38; en.wikipedia Politorium
note: Ancus took the town (by storm in Livy, after a siege and surrender in Dionysius) and moved its people to the Aventine; when the Latins reoccupied the empty town he took it again after a battle under the walls and razed it. Site uncertain: La Giostra, La Torretta and Castel di Decima have been proposed. Year approximate (Ancus reigned c. 640-616 BCE).

name: Tellenae
place: Tellenae, a Latin town south of Rome; site unknown
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The Roman army under Ancus Marcius; no numbers.
greek_note: The Roman levy; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Livy 1.33; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 3.38
note: Dionysius describes a pitched battle and then an assault on the walls, the prisoners being sent to Rome; Livy records only the capture of Tellenae and the settlement of its people at Rome.

name: Ficana (siege)
place: Ficana, on the Tiber at Monte Cugno near Acilia, about 11 miles from Rome on the road to Ostia
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The Roman army under Ancus Marcius; no numbers.
greek_note: The Roman levy; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Livy 1.33; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 3.38; en.wikipedia Ficana
note: Ficana had surrendered earlier; when it broke faith it was besieged a second time and razed (Dionysius). Livy records its capture and the removal of its people to Rome. Some editions of Dionysius read Fidenae for Ficana here.

name: Medullia
place: Before Medullia, a fortified Latin town north-east of Rome; site uncertain
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The full strength of the Roman army under Ancus Marcius (Livy 1.33); no numbers.
greek_note: The Roman levy; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Livy 1.33; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 3.38; en.wikipedia Medullia
note: Livy says the war centred on Medullia, strongly walled and garrisoned, with varying fortune, until Ancus won a pitched battle and came home with great booty. In Dionysius the Latins first stormed Medullia, then held by Roman colonists, and the Romans recovered it in the fourth year after many battles.

name: Fidenae (siege, Ancus Marcius)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Dionysius of Halicarnassus, written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: Known from Dionysius only.
roman_force: The Roman army under Ancus Marcius, with light-armed troops; no numbers.
greek_note: The Roman levy; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Dionysius of Halicarnassus 3.39-40
note: Ancus drove a mine under the walls while assaulting them, took the town, executed the ringleaders, let the soldiers plunder it and left a garrison.

name: Fidenae (Veientes, Ancus Marcius)
date: c. 631 BCE (traditional; about four years after the capture of Fidenae, Dionysius 3.41)
place: The Veientine camp across the Tiber near Fidenae
commanders_a: Ancus Marcius; Lucius Tarquinius (the future king Priscus) with the cavalry
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Dionysius of Halicarnassus and the Fasti Triumphales, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: Known from Dionysius only; Livy (1.33) records only that the Silva Mesia was taken from Veii.
roman_force: The Roman citizen army with allied auxiliaries; the Etruscan-born Tarquinius commanded the cavalry (Dionysius 3.41).
greek_note: The Roman levy with Latin auxiliaries; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Dionysius of Halicarnassus 3.41; Fasti Triumphales (en.wikipedia Fasti Triumphales)
note: The Roman cavalry cut the roads to the camp; the Veientes were beaten in a pitched battle and their camp taken, and Ancus triumphed. The Fasti Triumphales record his triumph over the Sabines and the Veientes.

name: Tiber salt-works
date: c. 629 BCE (traditional; two years after the battle near Fidenae, Dionysius 3.41)
place: The salt-works by the mouth of the Tiber
commanders_a: Ancus Marcius; Lucius Tarquinius with the cavalry
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: Known from Dionysius only.
roman_force: The Roman army under Ancus Marcius, the cavalry under Tarquinius (Dionysius 3.41); no numbers.
greek_note: The Roman levy; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Dionysius of Halicarnassus 3.41; Livy 1.33
note: A second and greater battle with the Veientes, in which Tarquinius distinguished himself with the horse (Dionysius). Livy says Ancus took the Silva Mesia from Veii, carried Roman rule to the sea, founded Ostia and made salt-works there. Site approximate.

name: Apiolae (siege)
place: Apiolae, a Latin town south-east of Rome near the Appian Way; site uncertain
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The Roman army under Tarquinius Priscus; no numbers.
greek_note: The Roman levy; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Livy 1.35; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 3.49; en.wikipedia Apiolae; en.wikipedia Lucius Tarquinius Priscus
note: The king's first war. After two battles before the town, Apiolae, reinforced by other Latins, was stormed by relays of troops, sacked and burnt (Dionysius); Livy says the booty paid for the first great games. The Fasti Triumphales put Tarquinius' triumph over the Latins in the 590s BC, which does not fit Livy's order.

name: Collatia (siege)
place: Collatia, by the Anio at Lunghezza, east of Rome
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: The fighting is in Dionysius only; Livy has Collatia handed over by the Sabines without a fight after the Sabine war (the deditio formula).
roman_force: The Roman army under Tarquinius Priscus; no numbers.
greek_note: The Roman levy; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Dionysius of Halicarnassus 3.50; Livy 1.38
note: The Collatines lost several sorties and the walls were assaulted at many points; they surrendered, were disarmed and fined, and the king's nephew Egerius was left in command with a garrison.

name: Corniculum (siege)
place: Corniculum, in the Monti Cornicolani near Montecelio, north-east of Rome
commanders_b: Tullius, chief of Corniculum (killed), per tradition
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The Roman army under Tarquinius Priscus; no numbers.
greek_note: The Roman levy; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Dionysius of Halicarnassus 3.50, 4.1; Livy 1.38-39
note: Corniculum held out, was stormed and burnt, its fighting men killed and the rest enslaved (Dionysius). Among the captives was Ocresia, the widow of the town's leader and mother of Servius Tullius (Livy 1.39). Livy lists Corniculum among the towns of the Prisci Latini taken after the Sabine war, so his date is later.

name: Fidenae (Latins, Tarquinius Priscus)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Dionysius of Halicarnassus, written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: Known from Dionysius only.
roman_force: The Roman army under Tarquinius Priscus; no numbers.
greek_note: The Roman levy; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Dionysius of Halicarnassus 3.50
note: The Latins were beaten in a pitched battle near Fidenae and abandoned their camp by night. Dionysius then describes two more battles of the Latin war, the second won with a cavalry charge on the Etruscan auxiliaries of the Latins, but names no place for them.

name: Fidenae (Egerius' camp)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Dionysius of Halicarnassus, written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: Known from Dionysius only; an attack on a camp and its foragers rather than a pitched battle.
roman_force: A force made up mostly of Latin allies, under the king's nephew Egerius, sent against Fidenae (Dionysius 3.57).
greek_note: Dionysius describes the force as mostly Latin allies; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Dionysius of Halicarnassus 3.57
note: The Etruscans had taken Fidenae through internal sedition. Its garrison, reinforced from Etruria, fell on the carelessly fortified camp and killed many foragers, and the army narrowly escaped destruction. The Fidenates (allies_a) fought with the Etruscan garrison.

name: Caere
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Dionysius of Halicarnassus, written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: Known from Dionysius only.
roman_force: The Roman army under Tarquinius Priscus; no numbers.
greek_note: The Roman levy with Latin allies; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Dionysius of Halicarnassus 3.58
note: After a victory over the Veientes and their Etruscan allies (no place named) and three raids on Veii, whose people kept within their walls, the army of Caere met the Romans in the field, was beaten and fell back into the city, and its land was ravaged.

name: Fidenae (siege, Tarquinius Priscus)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Dionysius of Halicarnassus, written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: Known from Dionysius only.
roman_force: The Roman army under Tarquinius Priscus; no numbers.
greek_note: The Roman levy with Latin allies; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Dionysius of Halicarnassus 3.58
note: A pitched battle before the walls with the Etruscan garrison and the Fidenates, then an assault; the town was stormed, the ringleaders executed or exiled.

name: Eretum (Tarquinius Priscus)
place: Near Eretum (Grotta Marozza, by Mentana), in Sabine territory
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Dionysius of Halicarnassus and the Fasti Triumphales, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: Not in Livy.
roman_force: The Roman army with Latin auxiliaries under Tarquinius Priscus; Dionysius (4.3) says the young Servius Tullius commanded the Latin auxiliaries in the Etruscan war and won the prize of valour near Eretum. No numbers.
greek_note: Dionysius names Romans and Latin auxiliaries; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Dionysius of Halicarnassus 3.59, 4.3; Fasti Triumphales (en.wikipedia Fasti Triumphales); en.wikipedia Eretum
note: The last battle of a nine-year war: the Etruscans, joined by Sabine volunteers, were beaten, and the twelve cities then submitted and sent Tarquinius the insignia of kingship. The Fasti Triumphales date the triumph over the Etruscans to 1 April 588 BCE, so the battle probably belongs to 589.

name: Anio
place: The Anio near its confluence with the Tiber, below Fidenae
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and the Fasti Triumphales, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The Roman army under Tarquinius Priscus, whose cavalry he had just doubled to 1,800 men in three centuries (Livy 1.36); the horse on the wings decided the battle.
greek_note: The Roman levy; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Livy 1.36-38; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 3.55-56, 3.63-66; Fasti Triumphales (en.wikipedia Fasti Triumphales); en.wikipedia Roman-Sabine wars; en.wikipedia Lucius Tarquinius Priscus
note: After an indecisive first battle near Rome, Tarquinius floated burning timber down the Anio to destroy the bridge and his cavalry routed the Sabines, many of whom drowned; a further victory in Sabine territory ended the war and Collatia was ceded (Livy). Dionysius puts the fire-rafts and the capture of two camps (Sabine and Etruscan prisoners) at the Anio-Tiber confluence in a first Sabine war, and describes a later second war won in unnamed battles. The Fasti Triumphales date the triumph over the Sabines to 585 BCE.

name: Veii (Servius Tullius)
place: Territory of Veii; no battle site is named
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and the Fasti Triumphales, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: No named battle: Livy says only that Servius routed a great army of the Veientes and other Etruscans; Dionysius describes a twenty-year war with Veii, Caere and Tarquinii fought in one pitched battle after another.
roman_force: The Roman army of Servius Tullius; no numbers (his census, which Livy puts after this war, counted 80,000 citizens, Livy 1.44).
greek_note: The Roman levy; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Livy 1.42; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 4.27; Fasti Triumphales (en.wikipedia Fasti Triumphales)
note: The Fasti Triumphales record three triumphs of Servius over the Etruscans (571 and 567 BCE, and one in the 560s); the war ended with the submission of the twelve cities, Veii, Caere and Tarquinii losing land (Dionysius).

name: Suessa Pometia (siege)
place: Suessa Pometia, a Volscian town on the edge of the Pontine plain; site unknown (near Cisterna di Latina and Satricum have been proposed)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and the Fasti Triumphales, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The Roman levy with the contingents of the Latin league (and perhaps the Hernici, who had joined the alliance, Dionysius 4.49); Dionysius (4.50) says the allied auxiliaries outnumbered the Romans, and Livy (1.52) that Tarquinius merged Latins and Romans into mixed maniples.
greek_note: The sources name Romans and Latin (and Hernican) allies; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Livy 1.53, 1.55; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 4.49-50; Fasti Triumphales (en.wikipedia Fasti Triumphales); en.wikipedia Suessa Pometia; en.wikipedia Lucius Tarquinius Superbus
note: After a battle on the frontier the town was invested and stormed, its men in arms killed (Dionysius). The booty, forty talents of silver according to Fabius Pictor (Livy 1.55), went to the Capitoline temple; Dionysius gives the god's tithe as 400 talents. The Fasti record a triumph over the Volsci. Year approximate (Tarquinius reigned 534-509 BCE).

name: Eretum (Tarquinius Superbus)
place: The Sabine camp near Eretum (Grotta Marozza, by Mentana)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Dionysius of Halicarnassus and the Fasti Triumphales, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: Not in Livy.
roman_force: The Roman army under Tarquinius Superbus, with a detachment sent round by night to fall on the Sabine rear and the Roman horse in the pursuit (Dionysius 4.51); no numbers.
greek_note: The Roman levy with Latin allies; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Dionysius of Halicarnassus 4.51-52; Fasti Triumphales (en.wikipedia Fasti Triumphales); en.wikipedia Eretum
note: The Sabines were routed when the night detachment struck their rear, and their camp was taken; a second Sabine army near Fidenae then surrendered, and the Sabine cities submitted and paid tribute. The Fasti record a triumph of Tarquinius over the Sabines.

name: Gabii (siege)
date: c. 529-522 BCE (traditional; a seven-year war in Dionysius)
place: Gabii, by the Lago di Castiglione, about 18 km east of Rome
commanders_b: The Gabine leaders, among them Antistius Petro (Dionysius); latterly Sextus Tarquinius as their sham commander
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The Roman army under Tarquinius Superbus; no numbers. Dionysius (4.53-54) describes years of battles, raids and ambushes on foragers in which the Gabines often had the better.
greek_note: The Roman levy with Latin allies; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Livy 1.53-54; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 4.53-58; en.wikipedia Lucius Tarquinius Superbus
note: An assault on the walls was beaten off and the war dragged on. Sextus Tarquinius, feigning flight from his father, won command of the Gabine troops, had the leading men killed or exiled (the tale of the poppies) and delivered the town. Scored for Rome because the town fell, by treachery rather than storm.

name: Ardea (siege)
place: Ardea, the town of the Rutuli, about 35 km south of Rome
commanders_b: Lucius Tarquinius Superbus; Sextus Tarquinius, Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus and Lucius Junius Brutus served in the camp
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: The siege was given up because of the revolution at Rome, not after a defeat; scored for the defenders by the rule for sieges.
roman_force: The Roman army of Tarquinius Superbus, wearied by a long blockade and the war taxes (Dionysius 4.64); no numbers.
greek_note: The Roman levy; the sources record no Greek contingent.
sources: Livy 1.57-60; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 4.64, 4.85; en.wikipedia Lucius Tarquinius Superbus
note: Tarquinius attacked the rich town of the Rutuli (treated here as Latins); the first assault failed and he turned to a blockade (Livy). During the siege the rape of Lucretia led to the expulsion of the king; the army went over to Brutus and the new magistrates made a fifteen-year truce with Ardea (Dionysius 4.85). Livy and en.wikipedia date it to 509 BCE, the year of the expulsion; entered under 510 because the siege had already lasted some time.

name: Silva Arsia
place: Silva Arsia (Livy), the 'Naevian Meadow' (Dionysius) or Aesuvian meadow (Plutarch), on the border between Roman and Veientine territory
commanders_a: Publius Valerius Publicola, Lucius Junius Brutus (killed)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Plutarch and the Fasti Triumphales, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The levy of the new Republic under both consuls: the citizen infantry under Valerius and the cavalry under Brutus (Livy 2.6); no numbers are given.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens from the city and its territory; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 2.6-7; Dionysius 5.14-16; Plutarch, Publicola 9; Fasti Triumphales; en.wikipedia Battle of Silva Arsia
note: Etruscan side: Veii and Tarquinii with the exiled Tarquins. Brutus and Arruns killed each other in single combat. Livy calls the fighting even; the Etruscans withdrew in the night after a voice from the wood proclaimed the Romans victors. Plutarch puts the battle on the last day of February and the Fasti Triumphales date Valerius' triumph to 1 March 509 (Roman, not Julian, calendar). Site unknown.

name: Rome (siege)
place: Rome: the Janiculum and the Sublician bridge over the Tiber, then a blockade of the city
commanders_a: Lars Porsenna of Clusium, with Lucius Tarquinius Superbus
commanders_b: Publius Valerius Publicola, Titus Lucretius Tricipitinus (consuls); Horatius Cocles, Spurius Larcius and Titus Herminius at the bridge
roman_force: The citizen levy of Rome under the two consuls, defending the city, the outpost on the Janiculum and the Sublician bridge (Livy 2.10-11); no numbers.
greek_note: The defenders were the citizens of Rome; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 2.9-15; Dionysius 5.21-35; Plutarch, Publicola 16-19; Tacitus, Histories 3.72; Pliny, Natural History 34.139; en.wikipedia Roman-Etruscan Wars
note: Etruscan side: Clusium. Porsenna took the Janiculum and drove the Romans back across the Tiber, where Horatius held the bridge, and then blockaded the city. Roman tradition says Porsenna made peace on terms (hostages; the Septem Pagi returned to Veii) and withdrew (en.wikipedia infobox: 'Peace treaty'); Tacitus and Pliny imply that Rome surrendered, which many modern historians (Cornell) accept, hence the Etruscan victory here. The war is historical; Horatius, Mucius Scaevola and Cloelia are legend.

name: Anio
place: The plain by the river Anio, north-east of Rome
commanders_a: Marcus Valerius Volusus, Publius Postumius Tubertus (consuls); Larcius (cavalry)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and the Fasti Triumphales, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: No separate Wikipedia battle article; Dionysius names the river.
roman_force: Two consular armies, Valerius' camped on the bank of the Anio and Postumius' on the heights near Rome, the cavalry crossing the river under Larcius (Dionysius 5.37-39); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 2.16; Dionysius 5.37-39; Fasti Triumphales; en.wikipedia Roman-Sabine wars
note: Night ended the battle (Dionysius 5.39); Livy says the consuls won and both triumphed. Dionysius dates the war to the fifth year after the kings (Loeb: 503 BCE); its consuls held office in 505 by Varro's reckoning.

name: Fidenae
place: The Sabine camps in the open near Fidenae and in Fidenae itself, across the Anio
commanders_a: Publius Valerius Publicola, Titus Lucretius Tricipitinus (consuls)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Plutarch, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: No separate Wikipedia battle article.
roman_force: Two consular armies, Valerius camped by the Sabine field camp and Lucretius on a nearby hill, Lucretius' cavalry leading the pursuit (Dionysius 5.41-42); no Roman numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Dionysius 5.40-43; Livy 2.16; Plutarch, Publicola 22-23; en.wikipedia Roman-Sabine wars
note: A Sabine night attack on Valerius' camp was caught between the ditch and the palisade; at dawn the Sabines fled, the force waiting in Fidenae was routed and the camp taken. Dionysius gives 13,500 Sabines and allies killed and 4,200 captured, and says Fidenae fell after a short siege. Livy (2.16) says only that the consuls ravaged Sabine land and triumphed.

name: Pometia
place: Auruncan territory and the town of Pometia (Suessa Pometia), in the Pontine plain
commanders_a: Opiter Verginius Tricostus, Spurius Cassius Vecellinus (consuls 502); in 503 Agrippa Menenius Lanatus, Publius Postumius Tubertus
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and the Fasti Triumphales, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: Consular armies of Roman citizens, with siege works (vineae) before the town (Livy 2.17); no reliable numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 2.16-17; Fasti Triumphales; en.wikipedia Battle of Pometia
note: Pometia and Cora, called Latin colonies by Livy, went over to the Aurunci in 503; the consuls beat a large Auruncan army in its own territory and the war shifted to Pometia. In 502 an Auruncan sortie with torches burned the vineae and badly wounded one consul; the Romans returned, and the town surrendered as they were about to scale the walls; its leading men were beheaded, the rest sold and the town razed. Livy (2.25) has Suessa Pometia taken again in 495, probably a doublet. The Fasti Triumphales record triumphs of 503 over the Sabines. The large numbers in the en.wikipedia infobox are not Livy's. Site unknown.

name: Lake Regillus
place: Lake Regillus, a since-drained crater lake below Tusculum (probably Pantano Secco, near Frascati)
commanders_a: Aulus Postumius Albus Regillensis (dictator), Titus Aebutius Helva (master of the horse)
commanders_b: Octavius Mamilius of Tusculum (killed), Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, Titus Tarquinius
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Plutarch, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The Roman levy under the dictator and the master of the horse, the cavalry fighting on foot at the crisis (Livy 2.20); Dionysius (6.5) gives 23,700 foot and 1,000 horse against about 40,000 Latin foot and 3,000 horse.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 2.19-20; Dionysius 6.4-13; Plutarch, Coriolanus 3; en.wikipedia Battle of Lake Regillus
note: The Latin League fought for the exiled Tarquins; a Volscian force arrived too late. Livy dates it 499 but notes authorities for 496 (Postumius' consulship), which Dionysius follows; modern suggestions include 493 and 489. Dionysius (6.13) says the victory was won on the Ides of Quintilis (15 July, Roman calendar), kept by the parade of the equites. The epiphany of Castor and Pollux is legend.

name: Suessa Pometia
place: The Roman and Volscian camps and the town of Suessa Pometia, in the Pontine plain
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: No separate Wikipedia battle article; named by the town taken after the battle.
roman_force: A consular army of Roman citizens, filled out by plebeian debtors who enlisted once Servilius' edict protected them from their creditors (Livy 2.24); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 2.24-25; en.wikipedia Roman-Volscian wars
note: A Volscian night attack on the Roman camp failed; at dawn the Volsci assaulted the rampart and were routed, their camp was taken, and Suessa Pometia fell within a few days and was given to the soldiers to plunder; Ecetra then sued for peace. Probably a doublet of the capture of Pometia in 502.

name: Aricia
place: Near Aricia (Ariccia), in the Alban Hills
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The Roman army of that year, citizen legions that had just beaten the Volsci (Livy 2.26); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 2.26; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles
note: The Aurunci demanded that Rome give up the Volscian land; their army was met not far from Aricia and one battle ended the war. Livy does not name the Roman commander; en.wikipedia gives the consul Servilius. Not the battle of Aricia of about 508/504 BCE, in which the Cumaeans under Aristodemus and the Latins beat Porsenna's son Arruns and Rome did not fight (Dionysius 5.36; excluded).

name: Velitrae
place: Before Velitrae (Velletri) and in the town
commanders_a: Aulus Verginius Tricostus Caeliomontanus (consul), under the dictator Manius Valerius Maximus
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: No separate Wikipedia battle article; described in en.wikipedia Roman-Volscian wars.
roman_force: Three legions under a consul: in 494 Rome raised ten legions, three for each consul and four for the dictator (Livy 2.30), a figure not credible for the period.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 2.30-31; en.wikipedia Roman-Volscian wars
note: The consul held his line still until the Volsci, charging in disorder, were spent, then routed them, took their camp and pursued them into Velitrae, where more were killed than in the battle; Velitrae's land was taken and colonised. Livy does not name the consul here; Verginius by elimination (his colleague Veturius fought the Aequi).

name: Corioli
place: Corioli, a Volscian town in the Alban Hills (perhaps Monte Giove near Lanuvium)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Plutarch, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The consular army of Postumus Cominius besieging Corioli, in which Gnaeus Marcius served as a young soldier commanding a picked guard (Livy 2.33); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 2.33; Dionysius book 6; Plutarch, Coriolanus 8-10; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles
note: Cominius had routed a force from Antium and taken Longula and Polusca; at Corioli the Volscian legions from Antium attacked the besiegers while the townsmen sallied; Marcius threw back the sortie, broke in through the gate and fired the houses, the Antiates were routed and Corioli taken. The Coriolanus story is legendary; the site is uncertain.

name: Antium
date: 484 BCE (en.wikipedia and the Loeb Dionysius: 482 BCE)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The consular army of Lucius Aemilius, citizen centuries with their cavalry (Dionysius 8.84-85); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Dionysius 8.83-85; Livy 2.42; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles
note: Only Dionysius describes it: after an even fight the Volsci feigned flight, drew the Romans into a disordered pursuit and turned on them; a storm and darkness saved the rest. Livy (2.42) reports instead a Roman victory over the Volsci and Aequi in this consulship, won by the cavalry pursuit. Dionysius puts it in the 270th year of the city, which the Loeb editor and en.wikipedia render 482 BCE; the consuls Lucius Aemilius and Caeso Fabius held office in 484 by Varro's reckoning.

name: Longula
date: 484 BCE (en.wikipedia and the Loeb Dionysius: 482 BCE)
place: A fortified hill near Longula, a Volscian town near Antium
commanders_a: Lucius Aemilius Mamercus (consul), reinforced by cohorts of his colleague Caeso Fabius Vibulanus
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Dionysius of Halicarnassus, written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The survivors of Aemilius' army, the cavalry fighting on foot beside the triarii, reinforced by night with picked cohorts sent by the other consul (Dionysius 8.86).
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Dionysius 8.85-86; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles
note: After the defeat before Antium Aemilius withdrew by night to a hill near Longula and held it against repeated Volscian assaults, finally sallying and driving the Volsci off with loss. Year as for Antium (484 BCE by Varro, 482 in en.wikipedia). Site of Longula unknown.

name: Veii
place: Before Veii, at and around the Roman camp
commanders_a: Marcus Fabius Vibulanus, Gnaeus Manlius Cincinnatus (consuls; Manlius killed); Quintus Fabius Vibulanus (killed), Caeso Fabius Vibulanus
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: Both consular armies; Dionysius gives four city legions, about 20,000 foot and 1,200 horse, with an equal force from the colonies and allies, the Latins and Hernici sending troops (Dionysius 9.5, 9.13). Livy has the triarii save the camp (2.47).
greek_note: Roman citizens with Latin and Hernican contingents; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 2.43-47; Dionysius 9.5-13; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles
note: Etruscan side: Veii with reinforcements from all Etruria. A costly Roman victory: Quintus Fabius and the consul Manlius fell, the Etruscans broke into the Roman camp before being cut down, and Marcus Fabius declined the triumph (Livy 2.47). Dionysius (9.13) has the Etruscans withdraw in the night, so that the Romans claimed the victory; the Loeb editor dates the consulship 479.

name: Saxa Rubra
place: Near the Fabian fort on the Cremera; the Veientine camp at Saxa Rubra, on the Via Flaminia north of Rome (near Prima Porta)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: Not in Wikipedia's lists; Livy names the Veientine camp.
roman_force: A consular army sent to support the Fabii on the Cremera; a squadron of its cavalry, striking the flank, decided the fight (Livy 2.49); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 2.49; Dionysius 9.16-17
note: Etruscan side: Veii. A Roman cavalry charge on the flank caught the Veientes before they had formed and drove them back to their camp at Saxa Rubra; Dionysius has the camp taken. Veii sued for peace, which it soon regretted.

name: Cremera
place: The Fabian fort on the Cremera (Fosso della Valchetta), between Rome and Veii
commanders_b: The gens Fabia: Caeso Fabius Vibulanus and Marcus Fabius Vibulanus (killed)
roman_force: A private force of one clan, not a state army: 306 Fabii with their clients and friends, about 4,000 men in all (Dionysius 9.15; Livy 2.49 gives the 306).
greek_note: The Fabii and their Roman clients; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 2.48-50, 6.1.11; Dionysius 9.15, 9.18-22; Ovid, Fasti 2.193-242; en.wikipedia Battle of the Cremera
note: Etruscan side: Veii. The Veientes lured the Fabii from their fort with herds into an ambush and killed them all; Livy has one boy left at Rome survive, which Dionysius rejects. Livy puts it on 18 July, the day of the Allia (dies Alliensis), Ovid on the Ides of February. The 306 are legend, but a defeat of a Fabian clan army is widely accepted as historical. The Fabii had set out in 479; afterwards the consul Titus Menenius Lanatus was also beaten and lost his camp (Dionysius 9.23), and the Veientes seized the Janiculum.

name: Temple of Hope
place: By the temple of Spes (Spes Vetus) on the Esquiline, about eight stades from the city (Dionysius)
commanders_a: Gaius Horatius Pulvillus (consul, recalled from the Volscian war)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The consular army of Horatius, recalled from the Volscian war to defend the city (Livy 2.51; Dionysius 9.24); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 2.51; Dionysius 9.24; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles
note: Etruscan side: Veii. After the Cremera the Veientes held the Janiculum and raided across the Tiber. Livy calls the battle by the temple of Spes indecisive (so en.wikipedia); Dionysius makes it a Roman victory.

name: Colline Gate
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: The consular army of Horatius defending the city (Livy 2.51; Dionysius 9.24); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 2.51; Dionysius 9.24; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles
note: Etruscan side: Veii. Livy says the Romans gained only a slight advantage, enough to restore their spirits (en.wikipedia: an indecisive victory); Dionysius has a Roman win over a larger Etruscan army.

name: Janiculum
place: The Roman camp on the left bank and the Etruscan camp on the Janiculum, across the Tiber from Rome
commanders_a: Spurius Servilius Structus, Aulus Verginius Tricostus Rutilus (consuls)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: Not in Wikipedia's lists; Livy names the place.
roman_force: Both consular armies: Servilius' troops, who attacked up the hill, and Verginius' army, which came to their rescue (Livy 2.51); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 2.51; Dionysius 9.25-26
note: Etruscan side: Veii. The Veientes crossed the Tiber by night and attacked Servilius' camp but were routed; at daybreak Servilius stormed up the Janiculum, was thrown back, and was saved when Verginius' army took the Etruscans in the rear and destroyed them. Servilius was later prosecuted for his rashness.

name: Veii
place: Before Veii: the Sabine camp in front of the walls and the Veientine sortie
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: No separate Wikipedia battle article.
roman_force: A consular army of Roman citizens with its cavalry, for which Latin and Hernican auxiliaries were summoned (Livy 2.53); no numbers.
greek_note: Roman citizens with Latin and Hernican auxiliaries; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 2.53; Dionysius 9.34-35; en.wikipedia Roman-Etruscan Wars
note: Etruscan side: Veii. Valerius forced the gate of the Sabine camp outside Veii, then held off the Veientes who sallied, and his cavalry routed them. A forty-year truce with Veii followed in 474.

name: Antium
place: Volscian territory, the Volscian camp on the hills, and the town of Antium (Anzio)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: No separate Wikipedia battle article; field battles followed by the surrender of Antium.
roman_force: The consular army of Quinctius, outnumbered, which he rallied in the first battle; a Hernican cohort held the outposts in the night attack (Livy 2.64); no numbers.
greek_note: Roman citizens with a Hernican cohort; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 2.64-65, 3.1; Dionysius book 9; en.wikipedia Roman-Volscian wars
note: A hard battle on level ground was won when the consul falsely announced that the enemy's other wing was fleeing; Volscian and Aequian reinforcements attacked the camp by night; next day the Romans drove the Volsci from a hill and took their camp, and Antium surrendered after a few days' siege. A colony followed in 467 (Livy 3.1). Modern historians doubt an early Roman hold on Antium, which was Volscian until 338.

name: Algidus
place: Mount Algidus, the pass of the Via Latina through the Alban Hills
commanders_a: Quintus Fabius Vibulanus, Titus Quinctius Capitolinus Barbatus (consuls)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: No Wikipedia battle article; Livy has the Aequi march to Mount Algidus but does not name the battlefield.
roman_force: Both consular armies of Roman citizens (Livy 3.2); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 3.2-3; en.wikipedia Algidum
note: The Aequi, who had broken the peace granted by Fabius the year before, were beaten in a hard pitched battle and fell back to their frontier, then raided Roman territory up to the city.

name: Capitol
war: Seizure of the Capitol by Appius Herdonius
commanders_a: Publius Valerius Publicola (consul, killed), Publius Volumnius; Gaius Claudius Sabinus Regillensis (consul); Lucius Mamilius, dictator of Tusculum
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: A coup by a band of exiles and slaves under a Sabine leader, not a war with the Sabine state; included as an assault with real fighting.
roman_force: The citizen levy under the consul Valerius, joined by a force from Tusculum sent by its dictator Lucius Mamilius (Livy 3.18); the enemy were some 2,500 exiles and slaves (Livy 3.15).
greek_note: Roman citizens with Latin troops from Tusculum; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 3.15-18; Dionysius 10.14-16
note: Herdonius, a Sabine, seized the Capitol and citadel by night; the tribunes held up the levy, and the hill was stormed with the Tusculans' help, Valerius falling in the temple forecourt and the ex-consul Publius Volumnius taking over. Often taken by modern historians as a raid by a private warlord, plausible in outline.

name: Tusculum
place: The citadel of Tusculum, in the Alban Hills
commanders_a: Quintus Fabius Vibulanus, Lucius Cornelius Maluginensis (consuls)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: Not in Wikipedia's lists; the siege of a citadel seized by the Aequi.
roman_force: The consular army of Fabius with the Tusculans, supplied and reinforced by Cornelius from Rome (Livy 3.23); no numbers.
greek_note: Roman citizens with Latin troops from Tusculum; no Greek speakers are attested.
note: The Aequi took the citadel of Tusculum in a night surprise; after some months' fighting hunger forced them out, they passed under the yoke, and a consul caught them on the Algidus on their way home and killed them to a man. Earlier that year Fabius had stormed the Volscian camp near Antium (Livy 3.22).

name: Mount Algidus
place: Mount Algidus, the pass of the Via Latina through the Alban Hills
commanders_a: Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus (dictator), Lucius Tarquitius (master of the horse), Lucius Minucius Esquilinus Augurinus (consul)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: Cincinnatus' emergency levy of all men of military age, each carrying stakes and five days' food, which walled in the Aequi while the trapped consular army of Minucius attacked from its camp (Livy 3.26-28).
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 3.26-29; Dionysius book 10; en.wikipedia Battle of Mount Algidus
note: The Aequi surrendered and passed under the yoke; Cincinnatus laid down the dictatorship after sixteen days. Legendary in its details.

name: Algidus
place: Mount Algidus, in the Alban Hills
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: Not in Wikipedia's lists; one of several battles Livy places on the Algidus.
roman_force: The consular army of Horatius (Livy 3.30); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 3.30
note: The Aequi had massacred the Roman garrison of Corbio in a night attack and taken Ortona; Horatius beat them on the Algidus with great slaughter, drove them from Algidus, Corbio and Ortona, and razed Corbio for betraying the garrison.

name: Algidus
place: Mount Algidus, in the Alban Hills
commanders_a: Titus Romilius Rocus Vaticanus, Gaius Veturius Cicurinus (consuls)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, all written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: Not in Wikipedia's lists; one of several battles Livy places on the Algidus.
roman_force: Both consular armies of Roman citizens, sent to help Tusculum (Livy 3.31); Dionysius gives a part to the veteran Lucius Siccius Dentatus.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 3.31; Dionysius book 10
note: The consuls found the Aequi in their usual position on the Algidus and killed over 7,000 (Livy); they sold the booty for the treasury and were condemned and fined after their year of office.

name: Eretum
place: Near Eretum, in the Sabine country north-east of Rome
commanders_b: Quintus Fabius Vibulanus, with Manius Rabuleius and Quintus Poetelius (decemvirs)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: Not in Wikipedia's lists.
roman_force: One of the two armies of the second decemvirate, citizen soldiers hostile to their commanders (Livy 3.41-42); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
note: Routed by the Sabines at Eretum, the army withdrew by night and entrenched on high ground between Fidenae and Crustumeria. After the fall of the decemvirs the consul Marcus Horatius Barbatus beat the Sabines (Livy 3.61-63), at a site Livy does not name.

name: Algidus
place: Mount Algidus, in the Alban Hills
commanders_b: Marcus Cornelius Maluginensis, with Lucius Minucius, Titus Antonius Merenda, Caeso Duillius and Marcus Sergius (decemvirs)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: Not in Wikipedia's lists.
roman_force: The second army of the decemvirate, under five decemvirs (Livy 3.41-42); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
note: A heavier defeat than at Eretum: the army lost its camp and fled to Tusculum. After the fall of the decemvirs the consul Lucius Valerius Potitus beat the Aequi and Volsci and took their camp (Livy 3.60-61), at a site Livy does not name (not counted separately).

name: Corbio
place: Before the enemy camp at Corbio, an Aequian town (site uncertain)
commanders_a: Titus Quinctius Capitolinus Barbatus, Agrippa Furius Fusus (consuls); Spurius Postumius Albus Regillensis and Publius Sulpicius (legates)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
roman_force: Both consular armies under one command, which Agrippa yielded to Quinctius: the consuls on the wings, the legate Postumius in the centre, the legate Sulpicius with the cavalry (Livy 3.70); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 3.66-70; en.wikipedia Battle of Corbio
note: After the Aequi and Volsci had raided up to the walls of Rome, the consuls followed them and fought by their camp at Corbio; Sulpicius' cavalry broke the enemy centre, the camp was stormed and the plundered property recovered. The en.wikipedia article gives 446 but mixes in Livy 3.4-5 (464 BCE: the camp of the consul Spurius Furius besieged by the Aequi and relieved by Titus Quinctius). Coordinates as in en.wikipedia; Corbio is also placed near Rocca Priora.

name: Ardea
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: Not in Wikipedia's lists.
roman_force: The consular army of Geganius, which walled in the Volscian besiegers in a night, with a covered way to the town for the Ardeate nobles inside (Livy 4.9-10); no numbers.
greek_note: Roman citizens with the Ardeates; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 4.9-10
note: A feud over a girl split Ardea; the nobles called in Rome and the plebs the Volsci, who besieged the town. Enclosed by Geganius' lines, the Volsci tried to fight, were cut down, then gave up their general and arms and passed under the yoke; survivors were attacked near Tusculum. Livy calls Cluilius an Aequian.

name: Fidenae
place: The plain between the Roman camp at the junction of the Anio and the Tiber and the Etruscan camp before Fidenae
commanders_a: Mamercus Aemilius Mamercinus (dictator), Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus (master of the horse), Titus Quinctius Capitolinus and Marcus Fabius Vibulanus (legates), Aulus Cornelius Cossus (military tribune)
borderline: No separate Wikipedia battle article.
roman_force: The dictator's army of Roman citizens; Cossus, a military tribune with the cavalry, killed Tolumnius in single combat and won the spolia opima (Livy 4.17-19); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 4.17-20; Propertius 4.10; en.wikipedia Aulus Cornelius Cossus
note: Etruscan side: Veii under Lars Tolumnius on the right, the Faliscans on the left and the revolted Fidenates in the centre; Fidenae had murdered Roman envoys in 438. Livy records Augustus' report that the inscribed linen corselet in the temple of Jupiter Feretrius called Cossus consul, which would put the battle in 428; the date is disputed. Before the dictatorship the consul Lucius Sergius Fidenas won a costly fight on this side of the Anio.

name: Fidenae
place: Not far from Nomentum, then the siege of Fidenae
commanders_a: Quintus Servilius Priscus Structus (dictator), Postumus Aebutius Helva Cornicen (master of the horse)
doubt: Early Rome: the only evidence is Livy, written down centuries later from the annalistic tradition; Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Modern historians doubt the details and often the battle itself.
borderline: Not in Wikipedia's lists; probably a doublet of the capture of Fidenae in 426.
roman_force: The dictator's levy, called out when the Fidenates and Veientes raided up to the Colline Gate; four divisions relieved one another in attacks on the walls while the tunnel was dug (Livy 4.21-22).
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
note: Etruscan side: Veii and Fidenae. The dictator beat the enemy not far from Nomentum and drove them into Fidenae, which he took by a tunnel driven through the hill to the citadel.

name: Algidus
place: Mount Algidus, in the Alban Hills
commanders_a: Aulus Postumius Tubertus (dictator), Lucius Julius Iullus (master of the horse), Titus Quinctius Poenus Cincinnatus (consul); Marcus Geganius, Fabius (cavalry)
borderline: No separate Wikipedia battle article.
roman_force: A levy under the lex sacrata with contingents ordered from the Latins and the Hernici, in two camps, the dictator's towards Tusculum and the consul's towards Lanuvium (Livy 4.26-27); no numbers.
greek_note: Roman citizens with Latin and Hernican allies; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 4.26-29; Ovid, Fasti 6.721-724; Diodorus 12.64; en.wikipedia Aulus Postumius Tubertus; en.wikipedia Algidum
note: The Aequi and Volsci attacked the consul's camp by night; picked cohorts under Marcus Geganius stormed the Volscian camp and the dictator took the enemy line in the rear; the Volscian Vettius Messius led a break-out, but the camp was taken and the prisoners sold. The other consul, Gnaeus (or Gaius) Julius Mento, held Rome. Tradition (doubted by Livy) says Postumius beheaded his son for leaving his post. Day as in en.wikipedia (the anniversary in Ovid's calendar); the battle is generally accepted as historical.

name: Fidenae
place: Before Fidenae (Castel Giubileo), north of Rome, and the town itself
commanders_a: Mamercus Aemilius Mamercinus (dictator), Aulus Cornelius Cossus (master of the horse); Quinctius
borderline: No separate Wikipedia battle article.
roman_force: The dictator's levy with its cavalry under Cossus, raised after the consular tribunes Titus Quinctius Poenus, Gaius Furius and Marcus Postumius had been beaten by the Veientes that year (Livy 4.31-33); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 4.31-34; en.wikipedia Fidenae
note: Etruscan side: Veii, with Etruscan volunteers, and Fidenae. The Fidenates charged with torches; Cossus rode his cavalry through the flames, Quinctius took the enemy in the rear from the ridge, many Veientes drowned in the Tiber, and the Romans broke into Fidenae and sacked it, enslaving the people. Some annalists, Livy says (4.34), told of a naval fight with the Veientes at Fidenae, which he rejects; it is not counted here.

name: Labici
place: The Aequian camp and the town of Labici, in the Alban Hills (near Monte Compatri)
commanders_a: Quintus Servilius Priscus Fidenas (dictator), Gaius Servilius Axilla (master of the horse)
borderline: Not in Wikipedia's lists.
roman_force: The dictator's levy, raised after the army of the consular tribunes, under Lucius Sergius Fidenas on his day of command, had been lured onto bad ground and fled its camp (Livy 4.45-46); its cavalry charge broke the Aequi.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
note: The Latin town of Labici had joined the Aequi. The dictator's cavalry broke the enemy line, the Aequian camp was stormed, and Labici was invested, taken and plundered; a colony of 1,500 settlers followed (Livy 4.47). Livy names the master of the horse as the dictator's son, with a variant giving Servilius Ahala.

name: Antium
place: Near Antium (Anzio), where the Volsci and Aequi had gathered
commanders_a: Publius Cornelius Rutilus Cossus (dictator), Gaius Servilius Ahala (master of the horse)
borderline: Not in Wikipedia's lists; a brief notice in Livy.
roman_force: The dictator's levy against the Volsci and Aequi encamped at Antium (Livy 4.56-57); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
note: The dictator won a single, easy battle with great slaughter, ravaged Volscian territory and stormed a fort by Lake Fucinus, taking 3,000 prisoners.

name: Verrugo
place: Verrugo, a Roman outpost in Volscian territory (site unknown)
commanders_b: The consular tribunes of 407 (not named for this action)
borderline: Not in Wikipedia's lists; a besieged garrison wiped out, told in a few lines.
roman_force: A Roman garrison holding Verrugo, and a relieving army sent too late (Livy 4.58); no numbers.
greek_note: A Roman garrison; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 4.58
note: The Volsci besieged the garrison and massacred it; the relieving force arrived only in time to surprise the Volsci scattered in search of plunder. Livy blames the senate's delay more than the tribunes.

name: Anxur
place: Anxur (Tarracina, modern Terracina), on the coast of southern Latium
commanders_a: Numerius Fabius Ambustus (consular tribune), Gaius Servilius Ahala; the tribunes Valerius and Cornelius covering Antium and Ecetra
borderline: Not in Wikipedia's lists.
roman_force: Three armies under the consular tribunes: Valerius at Antium and Cornelius at Ecetra kept the Volsci from relieving Anxur while Fabius attacked it, Servilius Ahala taking four cohorts round to the hill above the town (Livy 4.59); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
note: The attack from the height broke the defence; the town was taken and sacked by all three armies and about 2,500 prisoners taken. Afterwards the senate decreed pay for the soldiers from the treasury (stipendium). The Volsci recovered Anxur by surprise in 402 (Livy 5.8).

name: Artena
place: A pitched battle between Ferentinum and Ecetra, then the siege of Artena
commanders_a: The consular tribunes of 404: Gaius Valerius Potitus, Manius Sergius Fidenas, Publius Cornelius Maluginensis, Gnaeus Cornelius Cossus, Caeso Fabius Ambustus, Spurius Nautius Rutilus (Livy names none for the battle)
borderline: Not in Wikipedia's lists.
roman_force: The legions of the consular tribunes (Livy 4.61); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 4.61
note: After the victory between Ferentinum and Ecetra the Romans besieged Artena, drove a sortie back and forced their way into the town; the citadel was taken through the betrayal of a slave, and town and citadel were demolished. Livy notes that some thought Artena Veientine, confusing it with another Artena between Caere and Veii. Site unknown (modern Artena only takes the name).

name: Nepete
place: The territory of Nepete (Nepi), southern Etruria
commanders_a: Marcus Furius Camillus (dictator), Publius Cornelius Scipio (master of the horse)
borderline: Not in Wikipedia's lists; Livy names only the territory.
roman_force: Camillus' new levy, joined by Latin and Hernican volunteers (Livy 5.19), on its way to Veii; no numbers.
greek_note: Roman citizens with Latin and Hernican volunteers; no Greek speakers are attested.
note: Etruscan side: the Faliscans of Falerii and the Capenates, allies of Veii. Camillus beat them in the field, took their camp and much booty. Earlier in 396 they had ambushed the consular tribunes Lucius Titinius and Gnaeus Genucius, who was killed (Livy 5.18; site not named).

name: Veii (siege)
commanders_a: Marcus Furius Camillus (dictator 396), Publius Cornelius Scipio (master of the horse); the consular tribunes of 405-397
roman_force: The citizen army, paid from 406, kept before Veii in winter huts behind lines facing both Veii and Etruria, with volunteer cavalry on their own horses (403); in 396 Camillus' levy with Latin and Hernican volunteers, which took the city through a tunnel (Livy 4.60-61, 5.1-22).
greek_note: Roman citizens with Latin and Hernican volunteers; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 4.60-61, 5.1-22; Plutarch, Camillus 2-6; Diodorus 14.93; en.wikipedia Battle of Veii
note: Etruscan side: Veii, helped by Capena and Falerii; the Etruscan league refused help while Veii had a king. In 402 a Capenate and Faliscan attack on the siege lines beat the tribune Manius Sergius Fidenas when his colleague Lucius Verginius refused help (Livy 5.8). The ten-year length echoes Troy, but the fall of Veii in 396 is historical. en.wikipedia dates the battle about 396.

name: Falerii
war: War with Falerii and Capena (395-394 BCE)
place: Before Falerii (Falerii Veteres, modern Civita Castellana)
roman_force: Camillus' army of Roman citizens (Livy 5.26); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
sources: Livy 5.26-27; Plutarch, Camillus 9-10
note: Etruscan side: the Faliscans of Falerii (a people of Latin-like speech, listed here with the Etruscans). Camillus seized high ground by a night march, beat the Faliscans who came out against him and took their camp, then besieged the town; Falerii surrendered after he sent back the schoolmaster who had betrayed his pupils (a legend) and paid the Roman army for the year.

name: Volsinii
commanders_a: Lucius Lucretius Tricipitinus Flavus, Gaius Aemilius Mamercinus (consular tribunes)
borderline: Not in Wikipedia's lists.
roman_force: The armies of the consular tribunes, Lucretius and Gaius Aemilius against Volsinii, Agrippa Furius and Servius Sulpicius against Salpinum (Livy 5.32); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman citizens; no Greek speakers are attested.
note: Etruscan side: Volsinii, with Salpinum. The Volsinian line broke at the first shock and 8,000 men, cut off by the cavalry, surrendered; the Salpinates kept within their walls. Volsinii got a twenty-year truce on paying an indemnity and the army's pay for the year.

name: Allia
date: 18 July 390 BCE (Varronian date; c. 387/386 BCE by the Greek reckoning)
place: the Allia, a small left-bank tributary of the Tiber about 11 Roman miles north of Rome
