commanders_b: the military tribunes with consular power of 390 BC, among them Q. Sulpicius Longus and the three Fabii Ambusti (Livy 5.36-38)
roman_force: The Roman levy drawn up in a long single line with reserves on a hill to the right (Livy 5.38); Polybius (2.18.2) speaks of the Romans and those drawn up with them, so some allies may have served. Diodorus (14.114) gives about 24,000 men, Plutarch (Camillus 18) 40,000.
greek_note: The army was raised from Roman citizens of the lower Tiber valley; no Greek community was then allied to Rome.
sources: Livy 5.35-38; Diodorus 14.113-114; Plutarch Camillus 17-18; Polybius 2.18; en.wikipedia Battle of the Allia
note: Senones under Brennus. Livy puts the field on the left bank of the Tiber, Diodorus on the right. 18 July became the dies Alliensis; the year is 390 by Varro's era, c. 387/386 by Polybius and the Greek historians.

name: Rome (Gallic sack)
date: July 390 BCE to early 389 BCE (Varronian); about seven months by Polybius (2.22)
commanders_b: M. Manlius Capitolinus (defence of the Capitol); Q. Sulpicius Longus (consular tribune, who negotiated the ransom)
roman_force: The men of military age who withdrew to the Capitol with the senate after the Allia (Livy 5.39-40); numbers unknown.
greek_note: The defenders were Roman citizens; no Greek allies are recorded.
sources: Livy 5.39-48; Polybius 1.6, 2.18, 2.22; Diodorus 14.115-116; Plutarch Camillus 20-29; en.wikipedia Battle of the Allia
note: The city was taken and burned, but the Capitol threw back a night assault (M. Manlius, warned by the geese of Juno) and the Gauls left after a ransom of 1,000 pounds of gold; scored as a Gallic success because the city fell. Livy's account of the fighting on the Capitol is much embellished.

name: Via Gabina (Camillus)
place: in Rome and at the eighth milestone of the road to Gabii (Livy 5.49)
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
borderline: Probably legendary; included as the tradition gives it.
roman_force: Camillus' army gathered at Ardea and Veii from the refugees and the survivors of the Allia (Livy 5.45-49); no numbers.
greek_note: A levy of Roman refugees and survivors; no Greek allies.
sources: Livy 5.49; Plutarch Camillus 29; contra Polybius 2.18, 2.22 and Diodorus 14.116-117
note: Polybius and Diodorus know nothing of it: the Gauls left with the gold (Diodorus has them destroyed later by the Caeretans on the Trausian plain). Generally treated as patriotic invention.

name: Ad Maecium
place: ad Maecium, near Lanuvium (Livy 6.2); 'Mount Marcius' in Plutarch
commanders_a: M. Furius Camillus (dictator), C. Servilius Ahala (master of horse)
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
roman_force: A new levy that took in even the older men, split into three armies (Livy 6.2.6); Camillus led one of them against the Volsci. No numbers.
greek_note: A Roman citizen levy; the Latin allies had fallen away after 390.
sources: Livy 6.2; Plutarch Camillus 33-34; Diodorus 14.117; en.wikipedia Roman–Volscian wars
note: Part of Camillus' 'triple triumph' of 389 (Volsci, Aequi, Etruscans), much embellished; Oakley takes a victory at ad Maecium as the probable historical core.

name: Bola
place: Bola, in the land of the Aequi (site uncertain)
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
borderline: Known only from the doubtful 'triple triumph' narrative.
roman_force: Camillus' army from the Volscian campaign (Livy 6.2.14); no numbers.
greek_note: A Roman citizen levy.
sources: Livy 6.2.14; Plutarch Camillus 35; Diodorus 14.117
note: Livy says Camillus routed the Aequi at Bola and took camp and town at the first assault.

name: Sutrium
place: Sutrium (Sutri), a Roman ally besieged by the Etruscans
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
roman_force: Camillus' army from the Volscian and Aequian campaigns (Livy 6.3); no numbers.
greek_note: A Roman citizen levy.
sources: Livy 6.3; Plutarch Camillus 35; Diodorus 14.117
note: Livy has Camillus recover the town on the very day it surrendered to the Etruscans (probably Tarquinii and allies); the story is almost the same as that of 386 (Livy 6.9-10) and is usually taken as a doublet.

name: Contenebra (siege)
place: Contenebra, in the territory of Tarquinii (site unknown)
commanders_a: the military tribunes with consular power of 388 BC
borderline: Minor town storm, known from one passage of Livy.
roman_force: A Roman citizen army raiding the land of Tarquinii, which stormed the town by relays of fresh troops (Livy 6.4.8-10).
greek_note: A Roman citizen levy.
note: Tarquinii. Cortuosa was taken by surprise the same year without a fight.

name: Satricum
commanders_a: M. Furius Camillus, P. Valerius Potitus Poplicola (military tribunes with consular power)
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
roman_force: A Roman citizen army of the consular tribunes (Livy 6.6-8); no numbers.
greek_note: A Roman citizen levy.
sources: Livy 6.7-8; Plutarch Camillus 35
note: Antiates and other Volsci with Latin and Hernican volunteers. Livy's battle (Camillus hurls a standard into the enemy line) is often read as anticipating the battle of 381.

name: Sutrium
commanders_a: M. Furius Camillus, P. Valerius Potitus Poplicola (military tribunes with consular power)
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
roman_force: The army of the consular tribunes, reinforced from the city (Livy 6.9); no numbers.
greek_note: A Roman citizen levy.
sources: Livy 6.9; Plutarch Camillus 35-37 (under 389)
note: The Etruscans had taken Sutrium; Camillus recovered it at once. Livy's 389 and 386 episodes at Sutrium are doublets of one another.

name: Nepete (siege)
commanders_a: M. Furius Camillus, P. Valerius Potitus Poplicola (military tribunes with consular power)
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
roman_force: The army that had recovered Sutrium (Livy 6.10); no numbers.
greek_note: A Roman citizen levy.
sources: Livy 6.10
note: Nepete had been betrayed to the Etruscans; the Romans stormed it and executed the authors of the betrayal. Part of the Camillus narrative, of doubtful detail.

name: Pomptine territory
place: the Pomptine territory (ager Pomptinus), Volscian Latium
commanders_a: A. Cornelius Cossus (dictator), T. Quinctius Capitolinus (master of horse)
borderline: No proper place name; Livy places it in the Pomptine land.
roman_force: The dictator's army of Roman citizens with cavalry under the master of horse (Livy 6.12-13); no numbers.
greek_note: A Roman citizen levy.
sources: Livy 6.11-13, 6.16; en.wikipedia Roman–Volscian wars
note: The Volsci were joined by Latin and Hernican volunteers and by colonists of Circeii and Velitrae. A colony was sent to Satricum after the war (Livy 6.16).

name: Velitrae
commanders_a: Sp. and L. Papirius (military tribunes with consular power)
roman_force: The legions of the consular tribunes (Livy 6.22.1-3); no numbers.
greek_note: A Roman citizen levy.
note: The colonists of Velitrae with Praenestine auxiliaries were beaten in the field; the town itself was not attacked.

name: Satricum
commanders_a: M. Furius Camillus, L. Furius Medullinus (military tribunes with consular power)
roman_force: Four legions of 4,000 men levied for the war, with Camillus in command (Livy 6.22.8).
greek_note: A Roman citizen levy.
sources: Livy 6.22-24; Plutarch Camillus 37
note: Volsci with Praenestine allies. Livy's tale of L. Furius' rashness and Camillus' rescue is a literary set piece; the battle itself may be authentic.

name: Allia
commanders_a: T. Quinctius Cincinnatus Capitolinus (dictator), A. Sempronius Atratinus (master of horse)
roman_force: The dictator's army of Roman citizens, with the cavalry under the master of horse (Livy 6.28-29); no numbers.
greek_note: A Roman citizen levy.
note: Praeneste. The Praenestines chose the Allia for its ill omen and were routed; nine towns were taken and Praeneste surrendered, recorded on the dedication of the statue of Jupiter Imperator on the Capitol (Livy 6.29.9).

name: Satricum
commanders_a: P. Valerius Potitus Poplicola, L. Aemilius Mamercinus (military tribunes with consular power)
roman_force: Three armies were raised; the one under Valerius and Aemilius fought at Satricum (Livy 6.32); no numbers.
greek_note: A Roman citizen levy.
sources: Livy 6.32-33; en.wikipedia Roman–Volscian wars
note: Antium surrendered after the battle; the Latins in anger burned Satricum.

name: Tusculum
place: Tusculum, whose citadel held out against the Latins
commanders_a: L. Quinctius Cincinnatus, Ser. Sulpicius Praetextatus (military tribunes with consular power)
roman_force: A relieving army of Roman citizens (Livy 6.33.6-12); the Tusculans held the citadel; no numbers.
greek_note: Roman citizens and the newly enfranchised Tusculans.
sources: Livy 6.33
note: The Latins had seized the town; caught between the relief army and the defenders of the citadel they were destroyed.

name: Tusculum
place: Tusculum; afterwards a long siege of Velitrae
commanders_a: the military tribunes with consular power of 370 BC (Livy 6.36)
borderline: Briefly reported; the following siege of Velitrae saw little recorded fighting.
roman_force: An army of Roman citizens levied in a year of political strife (Livy 6.36); no numbers.
greek_note: A Roman citizen levy.
sources: Livy 6.36, 6.42; Plutarch Camillus 42
note: The colonists of Velitrae besieging Tusculum were driven off and themselves besieged; Velitrae submitted c. 367.

name: Alban territory
place: the Alban territory (Livy 6.42); on the Anio (Plutarch)
commanders_a: M. Furius Camillus (dictator for the fifth time), T. Quinctius Poenus (master of horse)
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
roman_force: A Roman citizen levy, armed (in Plutarch's story) with iron helmets and long pila against Gallic swords; no numbers.
greek_note: A Roman citizen levy.
sources: Livy 6.42.4-8; Plutarch Camillus 40-41; contra Polybius 2.18.6
note: Polybius says that when the Gauls came to Alba in the 30th year after the sack the Romans did not dare to face them; Camillus' victory is therefore doubted.

name: Colline Gate
place: outside the Colline Gate of Rome
commanders_a: Q. Servilius Ahala (dictator), T. Quinctius Poenus (master of horse)
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
roman_force: The dictator's levy, with even the older men called out to guard the city (Livy 7.11); no numbers.
greek_note: A Roman citizen levy.
sources: Livy 7.11.2-9; Polybius 2.18.7
note: Gauls in alliance with Tibur; the routed Gauls fled to Tibur, and the consul C. Poetelius triumphed over Gauls and Tiburtines. Polybius knows only of a Gallic invasion that withdrew by night when the Romans and their allies marched out.

name: Pedum
commanders_a: C. Sulpicius Peticus (dictator), M. Valerius Poplicola (master of horse)
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
roman_force: Roman legions with contingents of Latin allies sent under the treaty renewed that year (Livy 7.12.7); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans and Latins only.
sources: Livy 7.12.7-7.15.8; Fasti Triumphales (358 BC)
note: Sulpicius' triumph over the Gauls is in the Fasti, but Polybius records no Roman victory over the Gauls in these years and Livy's battle narrative is conventional.

name: Tarquinii
borderline: No proper place name beyond the territory of Tarquinii.
roman_force: The consular army of C. Fabius Ambustus (Livy 7.12, 7.15); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Hernican allies.
note: Tarquinii. The Tarquinians sacrificed 307 Roman prisoners after the battle (Livy 7.15.10).

name: Privernum
roman_force: The consular army of C. Marcius Rutilus (Livy 7.16); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Hernican allies.
sources: Livy 7.16.3-6; en.wikipedia Roman–Volscian wars
note: The Privernates' fortified camp was stormed and the town surrendered; Marcius triumphed.

name: Salinae
place: the salt-works (Salinae) near the mouth of the Tiber
commanders_a: C. Marcius Rutilus (dictator, the first plebeian), C. Plautius Proculus (master of horse)
roman_force: The dictator's army, ferried across the Tiber on rafts to surprise the Etruscans (Livy 7.17.6-9); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Hernican allies.
sources: Livy 7.17.2-9; Fasti Triumphales (356 BC)
note: Tarquinii and Falerii. Earlier in the year the consul M. Fabius Ambustus, at first thrown back by Etruscan priests brandishing snakes and torches, rallied and took their camp (Livy 7.17.2-5). Livy says 8,000 prisoners were taken by Marcius.

name: Pomptine territory
commanders_a: L. Furius Camillus (consul); M. Valerius Corvus (military tribune)
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
borderline: Known chiefly for the duel of M. Valerius Corvus and the raven; the battle followed it.
roman_force: Ten legions of 4,200 foot and 300 horse were raised from Roman citizens alone, the Latins having refused their contingents (Livy 7.25.5-9); Camillus took the field with part of them.
greek_note: A purely Roman citizen army; a Greek fleet was raiding the coast of Latium in the same year as an enemy.
sources: Livy 7.25-26; Gellius 9.11; Polybius 2.18.8
note: Livy has the Gauls routed after Valerius' duel; Polybius records that in this period the Gauls retreated without battle when the Romans and their allies marched against them.

name: Satricum
roman_force: The consular army of M. Valerius Corvus (Livy 7.27); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Hernican allies.
sources: Livy 7.27.5-9; en.wikipedia Roman–Volscian wars
note: Antiates and Volsci beaten in the field; Satricum was stormed and burned, all but the temple of Mater Matuta, and 4,000 prisoners were taken (Livy).

name: Mount Gaurus
roman_force: The consular army of M. Valerius Corvus, normally two legions with Latin and Hernican contingents; Livy (7.32-33) gives no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Hernican allies, fighting to protect the Oscan-speaking Campanians; no Greek contingents.
sources: Livy 7.32-33; Fasti Triumphales (343 BC); en.wikipedia Battle of Mount Gaurus
note: The first Roman battle with the Samnites. Valerius' triumph is in the Fasti, but Livy's narrative of the First Samnite War is heavily embellished and some historians doubt its details; en.wikipedia's list dates it 342.

name: Saticula
place: a wooded pass near Saticula (Sant'Agata de' Goti)
commanders_a: A. Cornelius Cossus Arvina (consul); P. Decius Mus (military tribune)
roman_force: The consular army of A. Cornelius Cossus, normally two legions with allied contingents; Decius seized a height with the hastati and principes of one legion (Livy 7.34).
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Hernican allies.
sources: Livy 7.34-37; Fasti Triumphales (343 BC); en.wikipedia Battle of Saticula
note: The army escaped a trap in the pass thanks to Decius and beat the Samnites the next morning. The story is suspiciously like other rescue tales; en.wikipedia's list dates it 342.

name: Suessula
roman_force: The consular army of M. Valerius Corvus, marching light without baggage (Livy 7.37); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Hernican allies.
sources: Livy 7.37.4-16; en.wikipedia Battle of Suessula
note: The Samnite camp was stormed while their foragers were scattered; Livy says 40,000 shields were collected. en.wikipedia's list dates it 341.

name: Satricum
roman_force: The consular army of C. Plautius (Livy 8.1); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Hernican allies.
sources: Livy 8.1.4-6; en.wikipedia Roman–Volscian wars
note: Antiates. An indecisive battle broken off by a storm; the Volsci withdrew to Antium by night leaving their wounded, so the Romans held the field. The same consul subdued Privernum.

name: Vesuvius
place: near Mount Vesuvius, by the Veseris (site unknown)
commanders_a: T. Manlius Imperiosus Torquatus, P. Decius Mus (consuls; Decius killed)
commanders_b: the Latin praetor L. Numisius of Circeii and others
roman_force: The two consular armies of Roman citizen legions in the manipular order of hastati, principes and triarii with rorarii and accensi (Livy 8.8), facing Latins armed and drilled the same way.
greek_note: The Latin allies were the enemy; the Roman force was a citizen army.
sources: Livy 8.6-10; en.wikipedia Battle of Vesuvius
note: Also called the battle of the Veseris. Before it the consul Manlius executed his son for fighting a duel against orders; in it Decius devoted himself (devotio). A Samnite allied army is said to have arrived too late (Livy 8.11). The Latin side also had Sidicini and Aurunci. Modern historians accept the battle but doubt the site and the devotio; en.wikipedia's list dates it 339.

name: Trifanum
place: Trifanum, between Minturnae and Sinuessa, near the mouth of the Liris (site unknown)
roman_force: The surviving consular armies after Vesuvius, Roman citizen legions (Livy 8.11); no numbers.
greek_note: A Roman citizen army.
sources: Livy 8.11.11-12; Diodorus 16.90.2; en.wikipedia Battle of Trifanum
note: Numisius had gathered fresh Volscian levies; both sides dropped their baggage and fought where they met, and the Latins and Campanians surrendered soon after. Diodorus records a Roman victory over the Latins and Campanians near Suessa, probably this battle. en.wikipedia's list dates it 338.

name: Fenectane plains
place: the Fenectane plains (campi Fenectani), Latium (site unknown)
borderline: Mentioned in one sentence by Livy.
roman_force: The consular army of Q. Publilius Philo (Livy 8.12); no numbers.
greek_note: A Roman citizen army.
note: The Latins had renewed the war in anger at the loss of their land. Publilius triumphed; his colleague Aemilius besieged Pedum without result.

name: Pedum
roman_force: The two consular armies of Roman citizens; Maenius came up from the Astura to join Camillus (Livy 8.13); no numbers.
greek_note: A Roman citizen army.
sources: Livy 8.13.4-8; Fasti Triumphales (338 BC); en.wikipedia Battle of Pedum (338 BC)
note: Tibur and Praeneste with the Pedani. Pedum was stormed; both consuls triumphed and received equestrian statues, and the Latin League was dissolved.

name: Astura
place: the river Astura, south-east of Antium
borderline: en.wikipedia treats it inside the Battle of Pedum (338 BCE); Livy narrates it as a separate battle.
roman_force: The consular army of C. Maenius (Livy 8.13.5); no numbers.
greek_note: A Roman citizen army.
sources: Livy 8.13.5, 8.14.12; Pliny NH 34.20; Florus 1.5.10; en.wikipedia Battle of Pedum (338 BC)
note: Maenius surprised the men of Aricia, Lanuvium and Velitrae as they joined the Volsci of Antium. The ships of Antium were taken after its surrender and their beaks set up on the Rostra; Florus turns this into a naval victory.

name: Cales (siege)
war: War with the Sidicini and Ausones
commanders_a: M. Valerius Corvus, M. Atilius Regulus (consuls)
roman_force: The consular army of M. Valerius Corvus with his colleague's support (Livy 8.16); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans, the Latin colonies and the Campanians who had stayed loyal in 340.
note: The Ausones (Aurunci) of Cales, allied with the Sidicini, were beaten in the field and the town was taken by escalade during a festival, guided by an escaped Roman prisoner; a Latin colony followed (334).

name: Privernum
commanders_a: C. Plautius Decianus, L. Aemilius Mamercinus (consuls)
roman_force: One, then two consular armies of Roman citizens and Latin allies (Livy 8.19-20); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans and Latins.
sources: Livy 8.19-21; Fasti Triumphales (329 BC); en.wikipedia Roman–Volscian wars
note: Vitruvius Vaccus was beaten in the field in 330 and besieged in Privernum, which was stormed or surrendered in 329; Plautius triumphed and Vaccus was executed.

name: Neapolis (siege)
commanders_a: Q. Publilius Philo (consul, then the first proconsul)
commanders_b: unknown (the city was handed over by Charilaus and Nymphius)
borderline: The siege ended by betrayal rather than storm.
roman_force: The consular army of Q. Publilius Philo, encamped between Palaepolis and Neapolis (Livy 8.23); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Campanian allies against a Greek city.
sources: Livy 8.22-26; Dionysius 15.5-10; Fasti Triumphales (326 BC)
note: Naples (Palaepolis) with a garrison of 4,000 Samnites and 2,000 Nolans. The two leading citizens tricked the garrison out and let the Romans in; Naples became an ally on favourable terms and Publilius triumphed.

name: Cutina and Cingilia
place: Cutina and Cingilia, towns of the Vestini (sites unknown)
borderline: A battle in the field followed by the storming of two small towns, known from Livy only.
roman_force: The consular army of D. Junius Brutus Scaeva (Livy 8.29); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Campanian allies.
note: The Vestini had sided with the Samnites.

name: Imbrinium
commanders_a: Q. Fabius Maximus Rullianus (master of horse, against the orders of the dictator L. Papirius Cursor)
roman_force: The dictator's army of Roman legions and allies, whose cavalry charged with bridles removed on the advice of the tribune L. Cominius (Livy 8.30).
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Campanian allies.
sources: Livy 8.30-35; en.wikipedia Battle of Imbrinium
note: Livy says 20,000 Samnites fell and adds that some sources reported two battles. The quarrel between Papirius and Fabius that followed is the better-known part of the story.

name: Caudine Forks
place: the Caudine Forks (Furculae Caudinae), the pass between Arpaia and Montesarchio
commanders_b: T. Veturius Calvinus, Sp. Postumius Albinus (consuls)
borderline: A trap and capitulation with little fighting; included as a universally named battle.
roman_force: Both consular armies, probably four legions with Latin and other allied contingents (Livy 9.1-6); 600 equites were handed over as hostages (Livy 9.5.5).
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Campanian allies; the Campanians of Capua received the humiliated army (Livy 9.6).
sources: Livy 9.1-12; Appian Samnitica 4; Cicero De officiis 3.109; en.wikipedia Battle of the Caudine Forks
note: The army, caught in a closed valley on the way to Luceria, surrendered and passed under the yoke; the peace was later repudiated by the senate.

name: Luceria
commanders_a: L. Papirius Cursor, Q. Publilius Philo (consuls)
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
roman_force: Two consular armies, one marching through Apulia and one through Samnium (Livy 9.12-15); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin, Campanian and Apulian allies.
sources: Livy 9.12-15; en.wikipedia Second Samnite War
note: Livy has the Samnite garrison of Luceria surrender, the 600 Caudine hostages recovered and the Samnites sent under the yoke; most historians treat this as an annalistic revenge for Caudium (Livy himself notes that his sources disagree). Luceria became a Latin colony in 314.

name: Saticula (siege)
commanders_a: L. Aemilius Mamercinus Privernas (dictator, 316); Q. Fabius Maximus Rullianus (dictator, 315)
roman_force: The dictators' armies of Roman legions and allies (Livy 9.21-22); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Campanian allies.
sources: Livy 9.21-22; Diodorus 19.72; en.wikipedia Second Samnite War
note: A sortie of the townsmen and an attack by a Samnite relief army on the Roman camp were beaten off; the town fell to Fabius in 315.

name: Lautulae
place: the pass of Lautulae between Tarracina and Fundi
commanders_b: Q. Fabius Maximus Rullianus (dictator), Q. Aulius Cerretanus (master of horse, killed)
roman_force: The dictator's army of Roman legions and allies, with a newly levied army brought up later (Livy 9.23); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Campanian allies.
sources: Livy 9.23; Diodorus 19.72.7-8; en.wikipedia Battle of Lautulae
note: Diodorus records a clear Roman defeat and flight, after which Capua and other Campanian towns wavered; Livy admits a reverse in which Aulius fell but adds a doubtful Roman victory afterwards.

name: Tarracina
commanders_a: M. Poetelius Libo, C. Sulpicius Longus (consuls)
roman_force: The two consular armies acting together, Roman legions with Latin and allied contingents (Livy 9.27); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Campanian allies.
sources: Diodorus 19.76.1-2; Livy 9.27; historyofwar.org Battle of Tarracina
note: Diodorus names Tarracina; Livy describes a great victory of both consuls over the Samnites in Campania without naming the place. The victory restored the Roman position after Lautulae.

name: Nola
commanders_a: C. Poetelius Libo Visolus (dictator) or the consul C. Junius Bubulcus Brutus (Livy reports both)
roman_force: The dictator's army of Roman legions and allies (Livy 9.28); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Campanian allies.
note: Nola, an Oscan city allied with the Samnites, was taken by assault after the buildings against its walls were burned; Atina and Calatia fell in the same campaign.

name: Bovianum
place: Bovianum (Bojano) and a nearby mountain pasture where the Samnites laid an ambush
roman_force: The consular army of C. Junius Bubulcus (Livy 9.31); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Campanian allies.
note: Junius retook Cluviae, sacked Bovianum and then fought his way out of an ambush, vowing the temple of Salus. Livy reports captures of Bovianum in 311, 305 and 298, and some historians doubt one or more of them.

name: Sutrium
roman_force: The consular army of Q. Aemilius Barbula (Livy 9.32); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and allied contingents.
sources: Livy 9.32
note: All the Etruscan peoples except Arretium besieged Sutrium; a long and bloody battle was ended by darkness without a decision.

name: Sutrium (first battle)
place: the plain before Sutrium (Sutri), below rough, stony high ground held by the Romans
borderline: A second Roman battle at Sutrium in 310, before the march through the Ciminian forest; distinct from the dawn attack on the Etruscan camp told in Livy 9.37 (entry -310-sutrium).
roman_force: The consular army of Q. Fabius Rullianus, Roman legions with Latin and allied contingents, which came down from high ground with javelins and stones and then charged with swords (Livy 9.35); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and allied contingents; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Livy 9.35; en.wikipedia Second Samnite War (narrative); en.wikipedia Samnite Wars
note: The Etruscans besieging Sutrium were routed; Roman cavalry cut them off from their camp, which was taken with 38 standards, and the survivors fled into the Ciminian forest (Livy 9.35).

name: Sutrium
roman_force: The consular army of Q. Fabius Rullianus, which had marched through the Ciminian forest (Livy 9.35-37); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and allied contingents; the Umbrian town of Camerinum offered help (Livy 9.36).
sources: Livy 9.35-37; Diodorus 20.35
note: This is the dawn attack on the Etruscan and Umbrian camp after Fabius' march through the Ciminian forest (Livy 9.37); Livy notes that some placed the battle near Perusia. Perusia, Cortona and Arretium then asked for a thirty years' truce. The earlier battle before Sutrium in the same year (Livy 9.35) is the entry 'Sutrium (first battle)'.

name: Lake Vadimo
place: Lake Vadimo (Lago di Vadimone), near Orte
commanders_a: not named by Livy; probably Q. Fabius Maximus Rullianus (often given as the dictator L. Papirius Cursor)
roman_force: A Roman consular army of legions and allies; the cavalry dismounted to break the Etruscan line (Livy 9.39); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and allied contingents.
sources: Livy 9.39.5-11; en.wikipedia Battle of Lake Vadimo (310 BC)
note: The Etruscans had raised a levy under a 'sacred law'; Livy calls it the battle that first broke the strength of the Etruscans. Some historians suspect a doublet of the battle at the same lake in 283.

name: Perusia
roman_force: The proconsular army of Q. Fabius Rullianus (Livy 9.40); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and allied contingents.
sources: Livy 9.40.18-20; Diodorus 20.35
note: Perusia had broken the truce; after its defeat it surrendered and received a garrison. Diodorus' account of these campaigns is placed under 310.

name: Mevania
roman_force: The consular army of Q. Fabius Rullianus, brought by forced marches from Samnium (Livy 9.41); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and allied contingents.
note: The Umbrians, who had threatened to march on Rome, were routed almost without a fight and their leaders surrendered.

name: Allifae
roman_force: The proconsular army of Q. Fabius Rullianus (Livy 9.42); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Campanian allies.
note: The Samnites were beaten and blockaded in their camp, which surrendered; the Samnites went under the yoke and Hernici found among the prisoners led to the Hernican war of 306.

name: Tifernum
place: near Tifernum, in the upper Biferno valley (site uncertain)
roman_force: The consular army of L. Postumius Megellus (Livy 9.44); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Campanian allies.
sources: Livy 9.44.6-8; en.wikipedia Second Samnite War
note: Livy's sources disagreed: some gave a great Roman victory, others an indecisive battle after which Postumius slipped away by night to join his colleague at Bovianum.

name: Bovianum
commanders_a: T. Minucius Augurinus, L. Postumius Megellus (consuls)
roman_force: The two consular armies united, Roman legions with Latin and allied contingents (Livy 9.44); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Campanian allies.
sources: Livy 9.44.9-15; Diodorus 20.90.3-4; en.wikipedia Battle of Bovianum
note: The decisive battle of the Second Samnite War: the Samnite general was captured and Bovianum taken; peace followed in 304.

name: Thuriae (Cleonymus)
place: Thuriae, in the Sallentine territory (site unknown)
commanders_a: M. Aemilius Paullus (consul); other annalists gave the dictator C. Junius Bubulcus Brutus
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
borderline: The clash with Rome is known only from Livy, who doubts his sources; Diodorus describes Cleonymus' Italian expedition without a Roman battle.
roman_force: The consular army of M. Aemilius Paullus (Livy 10.2); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Italian allies against a Greek mercenary army.
note: Cleonymus, a Spartan prince leading a mercenary army first hired by Tarentum, not the Spartan state. Livy says one battle drove him back to his ships; he then raided the Venetian coast and was beaten by the Patavini.

name: Rusellae
commanders_a: M. Valerius Maximus Corvus (dictator), M. Aemilius Paullus (master of horse)
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
roman_force: The dictator's army of legions and allies with a strong cavalry force (Livy 10.3-5); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and allied contingents.
sources: Livy 10.3-5
note: Arretium and other Etruscans. A foraging party under the master of horse was ambushed, then the dictator won a pitched battle; Livy adds that other sources said the war was settled without a battle worth recording (10.5.13).

name: Volaterrae
roman_force: The consular army of L. Cornelius Scipio Barbatus (Livy 10.12); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and allied contingents.
sources: Livy 10.12.4-6; en.wikipedia Roman–Etruscan wars
note: Indecisive by day; the Etruscans withdrew in the night leaving their camp, so the Romans held the field. The elogium of Scipio Barbatus speaks only of conquests in Samnium and Lucania.

name: Bovianum
roman_force: The consular army of Cn. Fulvius (Livy 10.12); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin, Campanian and Lucanian allies.
sources: Livy 10.12.9; Fasti Triumphales (298 BC); en.wikipedia Third Samnite War
note: Fulvius beat the Samnites near Bovianum and took Bovianum and Aufidena. The elogium of Scipio Barbatus (CIL I2 7) instead credits Scipio with taking Taurasia and Cisauna in Samnium.

name: Tifernum
place: a valley near Tifernum, upper Biferno (near Castropignano)
commanders_a: Q. Fabius Maximus Rullianus (consul), with L. Cornelius Scipio Barbatus (legate)
roman_force: The consular army of Q. Fabius Rullianus, legions with allied contingents and cavalry; Scipio led the hastati of one legion round to the hills behind the Samnites (Livy 10.14).
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Campanian allies.
sources: Livy 10.14; en.wikipedia Battle of Tifernum
note: The Samnites, mistaking Scipio's detachment for the second consular army of Decius, broke and fled.

name: Maleventum
roman_force: The consular army of P. Decius Mus (Livy 10.15); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Campanian allies.
sources: Livy 10.15.1-3; en.wikipedia Third Samnite War
note: An Apulian army marching to join the Samnites was routed.

name: Murgantia (siege)
place: Murgantia, a strong town of Samnium (site unidentified)
borderline: A town taken by storm, told in a few lines by Livy; no Wikipedia battle article.
roman_force: The proconsular army of P. Decius Mus, Roman legions with Latin and allied contingents, which stormed the town in a single day (Livy 10.17); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and allied Italian contingents; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Livy 10.17.1-4; en.wikipedia Third Samnite War
note: 2,100 armed men were cut off and captured (Livy 10.17). Livy notes that some annalists credited Fabius with the year's captures, others the new consuls or L. Volumnius.

name: Romulea (siege)
place: Romulea, in the land of the Hirpini, usually placed at Bisaccia
commanders_a: P. Decius Mus (proconsul); Q. Fabius Maximus Rullianus in other annalists (Livy 10.17)
borderline: A town taken by storm, told in a few lines by Livy; no Wikipedia battle article.
roman_force: The proconsular army of P. Decius Mus, Roman legions with Latin and allied contingents, which took the town by escalade without siege works (Livy 10.17); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and allied Italian contingents; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Livy 10.17.5-8; en.wikipedia Third Samnite War
note: The soldiers planted ladders and carried the walls; 2,300 were killed and 6,000 captured, and the town was sacked (Livy 10.17). The identification with Bisaccia is conventional, not certain.

name: Ferentinum (siege)
place: Ferentinum, a Samnite town (site unidentified; not the Hernican Ferentinum)
commanders_a: P. Decius Mus (proconsul); Q. Fabius Maximus Rullianus in other annalists (Livy 10.17)
borderline: A town taken by storm, told in a few lines by Livy; no Wikipedia battle article.
roman_force: The proconsular army in Samnium, Roman legions with Latin and allied contingents, which carried a strongly fortified position defended with great energy (Livy 10.17); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and allied Italian contingents; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Livy 10.17.8-10; en.wikipedia Third Samnite War
note: About 3,000 of the enemy were killed around the walls (Livy 10.17). Some annalists gave Ferentinum and Romulea to Fabius, Murgantia to Decius.

name: Volturnus
place: by the Volturnus, in the Capuan territory
roman_force: The consular army of L. Volumnius, returning from Etruria (Livy 10.20); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Campanian allies.
sources: Livy 10.20; en.wikipedia Third Samnite War
note: Samnite raiders laden with booty and captives from Campania were caught by the Volturnus; the prisoners were freed in the fighting.

name: Camerinum
place: the territory of Camerinum (Camerino) according to Polybius; near Clusium according to Livy
commanders_b: L. Cornelius Scipio (propraetor; en.wikipedia identifies him with Scipio Barbatus)
roman_force: A single legion left in camp under the propraetor L. Scipio, destroyed almost to a man (Livy 10.25.11, 10.26.7-12).
greek_note: A Roman legion, perhaps with allied cohorts.
sources: Polybius 2.19.5; Livy 10.25-26; en.wikipedia Battle of Camerinum
note: Senones. Polybius says the Samnites and Gauls together defeated the Romans in the land of Camerinum a few days before Sentinum; Livy blames the Senones alone and mentions a version that put Umbrians in their place.

name: Sentinum
place: the plain near Sentinum, by Sassoferrato (Marche)
commanders_a: Q. Fabius Maximus Rullianus, P. Decius Mus (consuls; Decius killed)
roman_force: Two consular armies, four legions with the Roman cavalry, 1,000 picked Campanian horse and a Latin and allied force larger than the Roman (Livy 10.25-29); the propraetors Cn. Fulvius and L. Postumius Megellus held reserve armies in the Faliscan and Vatican lands and raided Etruria.
greek_note: Latin and Italian allies with Campanian (Oscan) cavalry; no Greek contingents.
sources: Livy 10.24-30; Polybius 2.19.5-6; Duris FGrH 76 F 56; en.wikipedia Battle of Sentinum
note: Samnites and Senonian Gauls. The Etruscans and Umbrians of the coalition were drawn off to defend their homes by the propraetors' raid and took little or no part (Livy 10.27). Decius devoted himself like his father at Vesuvius. Livy gives 8,700 Roman dead; Duris' 100,000 enemy dead is wildly inflated.

name: Mount Tifernus
roman_force: The army of L. Volumnius in Samnium (Livy 10.30-31); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Campanian allies.
sources: Livy 10.30.6-7; en.wikipedia Third Samnite War
note: A Samnite force on the mountain was routed in the same season as Sentinum.

name: Caiatia
commanders_a: Ap. Claudius Caecus (propraetor), L. Volumnius Flamma Violens (proconsul)
borderline: The site is given as Caiatia in en.wikipedia's narrative; Livy's account is brief.
roman_force: The joined armies of Ap. Claudius and L. Volumnius (Livy 10.31); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Campanian allies.
sources: Livy 10.31.1-7; en.wikipedia Third Samnite War
note: Samnite raiders returning from Campania were cut off and defeated.

name: Milionia (siege)
borderline: A town taken by storm, told in one chapter by Livy; no Wikipedia battle article.
roman_force: The consular army of L. Postumius Megellus, mustered at Sora; after a failed direct assault it entered the town with siege sheds (vineae) and fought in the streets for some four hours (Livy 10.34); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and allied Italian contingents; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Livy 10.34.1-12; en.wikipedia Third Samnite War
note: 3,200 Samnites were killed and 4,700 captured (Livy 10.34). Feritrum was then found abandoned. Not the Marsic Milionia taken in 301 (Livy 10.3).

name: Rusellae (siege)
borderline: Folded into -294-volsinii in round 1; a separate engagement, the storm of a town about 100 km from Volsinii.
roman_force: The consular army of L. Postumius Megellus, brought from Samnium into Etruria (Livy 10.37); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and allied contingents; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Livy 10.37.1-5; en.wikipedia Third Samnite War
note: After beating the Volsinians before their walls, Postumius ravaged the land of Rusellae and took the town by storm, with more than 2,000 captured and somewhat fewer than 2,000 killed about the walls (Livy 10.37.3; the figures were not re-checked in this round). Livy notes conflicting versions of Postumius' campaigns in this year.

name: Luceria
roman_force: The consular army of M. Atilius Regulus (Livy 10.35-36); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Campanian allies.
sources: Livy 10.35-36; en.wikipedia Third Samnite War
note: A two-day battle: worsted on the first day, Atilius vowed a temple to Jupiter Stator and won on the second. Livy reports other versions of the year's campaign.

name: Interamna
borderline: A brief engagement with raiders.
roman_force: The consular army of M. Atilius Regulus (Livy 10.36); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Campanian allies.
sources: Livy 10.36.16-19; en.wikipedia Third Samnite War
note: Samnites who had attacked the Latin colony of Interamna were caught with their plunder and beaten.

name: Volsinii
place: near Volsinii (Orvieto), not far from its walls
roman_force: The consular army of L. Postumius Megellus (Livy 10.37); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and allied contingents.
sources: Livy 10.37.1-5; en.wikipedia Third Samnite War
note: The Volsinians were beaten before their walls and Rusellae was taken by storm; Volsinii, Perusia and Arretium then sought a forty-year truce.

name: Amiternum (siege)
place: Amiternum, a Samnite town (site unidentified; probably not the Sabine Amiternum near L'Aquila)
borderline: A town taken by storm, told in a few lines by Livy; no Wikipedia battle article.
roman_force: The consular army of Sp. Carvilius Maximus, the veteran legions left in Samnium the year before, with Latin and allied contingents (Livy 10.39); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and allied Italian contingents; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Livy 10.39.1-4; en.wikipedia Third Samnite War
note: Stormed: almost 2,800 killed and 4,270 captured (Livy 10.39). Carvilius then moved on to besiege Cominium.

name: Duronia (siege)
place: Duronia, Samnium (site uncertain; conventionally placed near the modern village of Duronia, Molise)
borderline: A town taken by storm, told in one sentence by Livy; no Wikipedia battle article.
roman_force: The new army raised for L. Papirius Cursor by decree of the senate, Roman legions with Latin and allied contingents (Livy 10.38-39); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and allied Italian contingents; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Livy 10.39.4; en.wikipedia Third Samnite War
note: Taken by assault, with fewer prisoners but somewhat more dead than at Amiternum (Livy 10.39); Papirius then marched on Aquilonia.

name: Aquilonia
commanders_a: L. Papirius Cursor (consul); his colleague Sp. Carvilius Maximus was besieging Cominium
roman_force: The consular army of L. Papirius Cursor, legions with allied cohorts and alae; mule-drivers raising dust on a hill were taken by the Samnites for a second army (Livy 10.38-42).
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Campanian allies.
sources: Livy 10.38-44; en.wikipedia Battle of Aquilonia
note: Livy says 40,000 Samnites gathered at Aquilonia, among them the sworn 'linen legion' of 16,000; Aquilonia was taken the same day. The site is unidentified.

name: Cominium
place: Cominium, about 20 miles from Aquilonia (site unknown)
roman_force: The consular army of Sp. Carvilius Maximus (Livy 10.39, 10.43); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Campanian allies.
sources: Livy 10.39, 10.43; en.wikipedia Third Samnite War
note: Stormed on the same day as Aquilonia; twenty Samnite cohorts sent to relieve it arrived too late.

name: Saepinum
place: Saepinum (Samnite town at Terravecchia, above Sepino)
roman_force: The consular army of L. Papirius Cursor (Livy 10.45); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Campanian allies.
sources: Livy 10.45.12-14; en.wikipedia Third Samnite War
note: After fighting outside the walls the town was stormed. Carvilius took Velia, Palumbinum and Herculaneum in the same campaign.

name: Arretium
place: before Arretium (Arezzo), besieged by the Gauls
roman_force: A relief army of Roman legions and allies under the praetor Metellus; Orosius (3.22) and Augustine (City of God 3.17) give 13,000 Roman dead.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Italian allies.
sources: Polybius 2.19.7-8; Orosius 3.22.13; Augustine City of God 3.17; Livy Periocha 12; en.wikipedia Battle of Arretium
note: Senones, possibly with other Gauls. Metellus' consulship in 284 suggests his death as praetor in 283; Polybius and Appian differ on the sequence. Rome answered by invading the land of the Senones and founding Sena Gallica.

name: Lake Vadimo
place: Lake Vadimo (Lago di Vadimone), near Orte
roman_force: The consular army of P. Cornelius Dolabella, Roman legions with Latin and Italian allies; no numbers survive.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Italian allies.
sources: Polybius 2.20.1-3; Florus 1.13; Livy Periocha 12; en.wikipedia Battle of Lake Vadimo (283 BC)
note: Boii with the Etruscans; Polybius says most of the Etruscans fell and only a few of the Boii escaped.

name: Populonia
borderline: The ancient sources give no place for this battle; the name comes from modern reconstruction.
roman_force: A Roman consular army of legions and allies; nothing is recorded of its size.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Italian allies.
sources: Polybius 2.20.4-5; en.wikipedia Battle of Populonia (after Salmon 1935 and Brice 2014)
note: Polybius records a second defeat of the Etruscans and Boii in the year after Lake Vadimo, after which they made peace; en.wikipedia places an Etruscan defeat at Populonia in 282.

name: Thurii
place: before Thurii (by Sibari), besieged by the Lucanians
commanders_b: unknown (the Lucanian Sthenius Statilius had led the attacks on Thurii)
roman_force: The consular army of C. Fabricius Luscinus, legions with Latin and Italian allies; no numbers survive.
greek_note: The army relieved the Greek city of Thurii, whose citizens may have joined the fighting; the field army itself was Roman and Italian.
sources: Valerius Maximus 1.8.6; Pliny NH 34.32; Fasti Triumphales (282 BC); en.wikipedia Pyrrhic War; en.wikipedia Battle of Thurii
note: Fabricius triumphed over the Samnites, Lucanians and Bruttii and left a garrison in Thurii. en.wikipedia's 'Battle of Thurii' article describes a naval battle between Rome and Tarentum won by Rome, apparently confusing this relief with the Tarentine attack on the Roman squadron (next entry).

name: Gulf of Tarentum
place: off Tarentum (Taranto), in the Gulf of Tarentum
commanders_a: the Tarentine fleet, roused by the demagogue Philocharis
commanders_b: L. Valerius (duumvir navalis, in Dio and Zonaras); Appian names Cornelius
borderline: A surprise attack on a squadron rather than a set battle; it is the casus belli of the war with Tarentum and Pyrrhus.
roman_force: A squadron of ten ships of the duumviri navales; four were sunk and one taken, five escaped (Appian Samnitica 7.1).
greek_note: The crews of Rome's small duumviral fleet are not recorded; Greek naval allies such as Naples may have supplied ships or rowers.
sources: Appian Samnitica 7.1; Cassius Dio fr. 39; Zonaras 8.2; Livy Periocha 12; en.wikipedia Pyrrhic War
note: The Roman ships sailed into the gulf in breach of an old treaty; the Tarentines, gathered in the theatre, manned their ships and attacked; the duumvir in command was killed (Livy Periocha 12). They then took Thurii and expelled its Roman garrison.

name: Tarentum
commanders_b: unknown (the Tarentines elected Agis as general)
borderline: No named battle: Barbula ravaged Tarentine land and fought the Tarentines and their allies; en.wikipedia's list calls it a siege of Tarentum, while its Pyrrhic War article records no battle.
roman_force: The consular army of L. Aemilius Barbula, sent from Samnium, Roman legions with Latin and Italian allies (Zonaras 8.2); no numbers.
greek_note: Romans with Latin and Italian allies against a Greek city.
sources: Zonaras 8.2; Appian Samnitica 7; Frontinus Stratagems 1.4.1; Fasti Triumphales (280 BC); en.wikipedia List of Roman battles ('Siege of Tarentum, 281 BC'); en.wikipedia Pyrrhic War
note: Barbula triumphed in 280 over the Tarentines, Samnites and Sallentini. Late in 281 Pyrrhus' first troops under Milon landed and Barbula withdrew to Venusia; on the way his column was harassed by the Tarentine fleet (Frontinus).

name: Heraclea
place: Plain of the Siris (Sinni) between Heraclea and Pandosia, Lucania
roman_force: The consular army of Publius Valerius Laevinus, one of four armies into which Rome split its eight legions with allies that year: Roman legions with their Latin and Italian allied (socii) contingents, heavy infantry, velites and cavalry; en.wikipedia's infobox gives at least 42,400 (40,000 foot, 2,400 horse), other modern estimates about 25,000-35,000; the sources give no breakdown.
greek_note: The army was levied from Romans, Latins and Italian allies; the Greek cities of the south were on Pyrrhus's side or owed Rome only ships.
sources: Plutarch, Pyrrhus 16-17; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 19.12; Livy, Periochae 13; Florus 1.13; en.wikipedia Battle of Heraclea
note: Pyrrhus fought with Epirotes, Macedonians, Thessalian cavalry, Greek mercenaries and 20 elephants, with Tarentine and other Italiot Greek troops (Thurii, Metapontum, Heraclea per en.wikipedia); Roman dead 7,000 and 1,800 captured (Hieronymus) or 15,000 (Dionysius). en.wikipedia gives July 280.

name: Asculum
commanders_b: Publius Decius Mus, Publius Sulpicius Saverrio
roman_force: Both consular armies: four Roman legions (about 20,000) with Latin, Campanian, Volscian, Sabine, Umbrian, Marrucinian, Paelignian, Frentanian and Daunian allies, over 70,000 infantry and 8,000 cavalry by Dionysius 20.1 (about 40,000 by modern estimate), with 300 anti-elephant wagons; a Daunian force from Arpi attacked and burned Pyrrhus's camp.
greek_note: Dionysius's order of battle names Latins, Campanians, Volsci, Sabines, Umbrians, other Italic peoples and Daunians, but no Greek contingents.
sources: Plutarch, Pyrrhus 21; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 20.1-3; Cassius Dio fr. 40; Zonaras 8.5; Frontinus 2.3.21; en.wikipedia Battle of Asculum
note: Plutarch (from Hieronymus and Pyrrhus's memoirs) gives a two-day battle won by Pyrrhus with 6,000 Roman and 3,505 Epirote dead; Cassius Dio and Zonaras give the victory to Rome; the origin of 'Pyrrhic victory'. Daunian speech (Messapic) is entered as 'other'.

name: Cranita hills
place: Cranita hills (wooded with cornel), Samnium; site unidentified
commanders_b: Publius Cornelius Rufinus, Gaius Junius Bubulcus Brutus
roman_force: The two consular armies of 277, Roman legions with Latin and Italian allies, attacking up wooded slopes; the sources give no figures.
greek_note: A normal consular levy of Romans, Latins and Italian allies.
sources: Zonaras 8.6 (from Cassius Dio); en.wikipedia Battle of the Cranita hills
note: Many Romans were killed or captured on the slopes; the consuls then separated, Rufinus going on to take Croton.

name: Croton
borderline: Capture of a Greek city held for Pyrrhus, taken by a ruse after a repulsed attack; not treated as a battle by en.wikipedia.
roman_force: The consular army of Publius Cornelius Rufinus, Roman legions with Latin and Italian allies; no figures.
greek_note: A consular levy of Romans, Latins and Italian allies; the Greek city was the enemy.
sources: Zonaras 8.6; Frontinus, Stratagems 3.6.4; Livy 24.3.2; attalus.org (277 BC)
note: Locri then went over to Rome.

name: Beneventum
roman_force: The consular army of Manius Curius Dentatus, two legions with Latin and Italian allies, about 20,000-25,000 by modern estimate (en.wikipedia); the other consul, Lucius Cornelius Lentulus, was in Lucania.
greek_note: A consular levy of Romans, Latins and Italian allies.
sources: Plutarch, Pyrrhus 25; Livy, Periochae 14; Florus 1.13; Orosius 4.2; Frontinus 2.2.1; en.wikipedia Battle of Beneventum (275 BC)
note: en.wikipedia calls it inconclusive and a Roman strategic victory; the ancient sources give a Roman victory in which Pyrrhus's night march on the Roman camp failed and elephants were killed and captured (2 killed, 8 taken). Orosius and Florus place it in the 'Arusinian plains'.

name: Tarentum (siege)
borderline: Ended by the surrender of the citadel by Milo after a blockade; little fighting is recorded.
roman_force: The consular army of Lucius Papirius Cursor, Roman legions with Latin and Italian allies; the sources give no figures.
greek_note: A consular levy of Romans, Latins and Italian allies against the Greek city.
sources: Zonaras 8.6; Livy, Periochae 14-15; Orosius 4.3; en.wikipedia Pyrrhic War
note: A Carthaginian fleet appeared off the harbour (Livy, Per. 14, says to help the Tarentines); Milo handed over the citadel and left for Epirus with the garrison.

name: Rhegium (siege)
war: Revolt of the Campanian legion at Rhegium
commanders_a: Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio, Gaius Genucius Clepsina
commanders_b: unknown (the legion's leader Decius Vibellius had gone blind)
borderline: A Roman army against a mutinous Roman (Campanian) legion: classed civil here; it could instead be treated as war against 'Campanians'.
roman_force: A consular army of Roman legions and allies (no figures), helped by grain and an auxiliary force sent by Hiero II of Syracuse (Zonaras 8.6), against the mutinous Campanian legion (citizens without vote from Capua) that had seized Rhegium in 280; the city was stormed, most defenders fell and the 300 or so survivors were beheaded at Rome (Polybius 1.7).
greek_note: Hiero II of Syracuse sent grain and an auxiliary force to the Roman besiegers (Zonaras 8.6); the bulk of the army was Roman and Italian.
sources: Polybius 1.7.6-13; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 20.16; Livy, Periochae 15; Orosius 4.3; Fasti Triumphales (Blasio, de Reginis); attalus.org (270 BC)
note: Sometimes dated 271. Polybius says the city was taken by storm.

name: Asculum Picenum
place: Picenum, near Asculum (Ascoli Piceno), the Picene capital
commanders_a: Publius Sempronius Sophus, Appius Claudius Russus
borderline: Unnamed in the sources; named here after Asculum, the Picene capital taken in the war (Florus 1.14).
roman_force: The two consular armies of 268, Roman legions with Latin and Italian allies; the sources give no figures.
greek_note: A consular levy of Romans, Latins and Italian allies.
sources: Florus 1.14; Orosius 4.4; Eutropius 2.16; Fasti Triumphales (268); en.wikipedia Picentes
note: The ground shook during the battle and Sempronius vowed a temple to Tellus; the revolt began in 269 and both consuls triumphed over the Picentes in 268. en.wikipedia (Picentes) also mentions a Picene defeat at Interamnia (Teramo) and a hard battle near Truentum.

name: Volsinii (siege)
place: Volsinii (Etruscan Velzna), usually identified with Orvieto
commanders_a: Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges (died of wounds), Marcus Fulvius Flaccus
roman_force: A consular army of Roman legions and allies, called in by the exiled Volsinian nobility; no figures.
greek_note: A consular levy of Romans, Latins and Italian allies.
sources: Zonaras 8.7; Livy, Periochae 16; Orosius 4.5; Fasti Triumphales (Fulvius, 264); en.wikipedia Volsinii
note: Fabius Gurges was mortally wounded in the fighting of 265; the town surrendered to Fulvius Flaccus in 264 after starvation, was razed, and its people moved to Volsinii Novi (Bolsena).

name: Messana
roman_force: The consular army of Appius Claudius Caudex, about two legions with Latin and Italian allies (about 9,000 men: en.wikipedia), ferried across the strait in pentekontors and triremes borrowed from Tarentum, Locri, Velia (Elea) and Naples (Polybius 1.20.13-14).
greek_note: The Greek naval allies of Tarentum, Locri, Velia and Naples supplied and crewed the boats that carried the army over (Polybius 1.20.14); the fighting troops were legionaries and Italian allies.
sources: Polybius 1.11-12, 1.20.13-14; Diodorus 23.3; Zonaras 8.8-9; en.wikipedia Battle of Messana
note: Polybius describes successive victories over Hiero's Syracusans and then over the Carthaginians besieging Messana; Manius Valerius Maximus took the cognomen Messalla for the relief in 263. The Mamertines were Campanian ex-mercenaries holding Messana.

name: Agrigentum
date: 262-261 BCE (siege of about seven months, ended by a battle with Hanno's relief army)
commanders_a: Lucius Postumius Megellus, Quintus Mamilius Vitulus
roman_force: Both consular armies, four Roman legions with as many Latin and Italian allied contingents, about 40,000 men (en.wikipedia), kept supplied by Hiero II of Syracuse.
greek_note: Hiero II's Syracuse supplied the besiegers and many Sicilian Greek towns had joined Rome; Greek troops in the battle are not recorded.
sources: Polybius 1.17-19; Diodorus 23.8-9; Zonaras 8.10; Orosius 4.7; en.wikipedia Battle of Agrigentum
note: en.wikipedia dates the battle to late 262; on Polybius's chronology the city fell early in 261. Hanno's army of about 50,000 with 50-60 elephants was beaten, the garrison broke out and 25,000 inhabitants were enslaved.

name: Lipari Islands
roman_force: Seventeen newly built quinqueremes under the consul Scipio, with raw crews of Roman citizens and naval allies (socii navales), all captured in harbour by 20 Carthaginian ships (Polybius 1.21).
greek_note: Rome called on the allied Greek cities of southern Italy, the socii navales, for ships, crews and the petty officers of its first fleets (en.wikipedia, Roman navy and Socii); the share is not recorded.
sources: Polybius 1.21.4-8; Zonaras 8.10; en.wikipedia Battle of the Lipari Islands
note: Scipio's capture earned him the nickname Asina.

name: Mylae
roman_force: The new Roman fleet of about 100-140 quinqueremes and triremes fitted with the corvus boarding bridge (en.wikipedia: about 103 in the text, 143 in the infobox), rowed by Roman citizens and naval allies, with legionary marines; Carthage had 130 ships.
greek_note: Socii navales from the Greek cities of southern Italy supplied part of the crews and most of the seamanship of the new fleet; Polybius gives no breakdown.
sources: Polybius 1.22-23; Zonaras 8.11; columna rostrata of Duilius (CIL I2 25); en.wikipedia Battle of Mylae
note: Rome's first naval victory; Carthage lost about 45-50 ships (31 captured and 13-14 sunk in the Duilius inscription and later epitomes).

name: Thermae
roman_force: The Italian allied (socii) contingents of the Roman army in Sicily, encamped apart from the legions after a quarrel over precedence, about 6,000 men of whom 4,000-6,000 were killed (Polybius 1.24.3-4).
greek_note: The victims were Italian allied land contingents.
sources: Polybius 1.24.3-4; Diodorus 23.9.4; en.wikipedia Battle of Thermae
note: Polybius places it in 260, soon after Mylae; en.wikipedia dates it 259.

name: Aleria
borderline: Capture of the Carthaginian-held town and of Corsica; the fighting is not described.
roman_force: The consul's fleet and landing force, Roman legions and allies carried by ships crewed partly by naval allies; no figures.
greek_note: The socii navales of the Greek cities of Italy crewed part of the fleet; the landing troops were Roman and Italian.
sources: Elogium of L. Cornelius Scipio (CIL I2 8-9: 'hec cepit Corsica Aleriaque urbe'); Livy, Periochae 17; Florus 1.18.15-16; Zonaras 8.11; en.wikipedia Lucius Cornelius Scipio (consul 259 BC)
note: Corsican natives as well as the Carthaginians were fought (Livy, Per. 17).

name: Olbia
borderline: Poorly recorded and contradictory: en.wikipedia (after Zonaras) says Scipio failed against Olbia, while Livy (Per. 17) and Valerius Maximus record a successful battle in which the Carthaginian commander Hanno fell.
roman_force: The consul's fleet and landing force from Corsica, Roman legions and allies; no figures.
greek_note: The socii navales of the Greek cities of Italy crewed part of the fleet; the landing troops were Roman and Italian.
sources: Livy, Periochae 17; Valerius Maximus 5.1.2; Florus 1.18.16; Zonaras 8.11; en.wikipedia Lucius Cornelius Scipio (consul 259 BC)
note: Outcome given as the battle with Hanno (Roman success); the town itself may not have fallen.

name: Mytistraton (siege)
date: 258 BCE (after a failed siege of seven months in 260 or 259)
place: Mytistraton (Mytistratum), central Sicily, probably Monte Castellazzo near Marianopoli
commanders_a: Aulus Atilius Calatinus, Gaius Sulpicius Paterculus (consuls)
roman_force: The consular armies of 258 in Sicily, Roman legions with Latin and Italian allies; no figures (Polybius 1.24.9-11).
greek_note: A Roman consular army; Hiero II's Syracuse supported the Roman war effort, but no Greek units are named.
sources: Polybius 1.24.11; Diodorus 23.9; Zonaras 8.10-11; en.wikipedia First Punic War
note: Polybius says the town withstood the siege for long owing to its strong position; Zonaras records an earlier Roman siege of seven months that failed. The site is not certain.

name: Hippana
place: Hippana, western Sicily, probably the Montagna dei Cavalli near Prizzi
commanders_a: Aulus Atilius Calatinus, Gaius Sulpicius Paterculus (consuls)
borderline: A storming known only from one sentence of Polybius.
roman_force: The consular armies of 258, which had offered battle before Panormus in vain and then took Hippana by assault (Polybius 1.24.10-11); no figures.
greek_note: A Roman consular army of Romans, Latins and Italian allies.
sources: Polybius 1.24.10-11; en.wikipedia First Punic War
note: The site is not certain.

name: Camarina (siege)
roman_force: The consular army of Atilius Calatinus, legions with Latin and Italian allies, which brought up a siege battery and breached the wall (Polybius 1.24.12); the engines were lent by Hiero II of Syracuse (Diodorus 23.9.5).
greek_note: Hiero II of Syracuse lent the siege engines; the assaulting troops were Romans and Italian allies.
sources: Polybius 1.24.12; Diodorus 23.9.5; en.wikipedia First Punic War
note: Camarina, a Greek city, had gone over to Carthage in 259; most of its people were sold into slavery (Diodorus). Distinct from the ambush of Atilius' army on its march to Camarina (-258-camarina-ambush).

name: Sulci
roman_force: The consul's fleet (size unknown) of quinqueremes with legionary marines, crewed by Roman citizens and naval allies (socii navales).
greek_note: Socii navales from the Greek cities of southern Italy supplied part of the crews of the Roman fleets of this war; no breakdown survives.
sources: Polybius 1.24.5-7; Zonaras 8.12; Orosius 4.8.4; en.wikipedia Battle of Sulci
note: Some date it to 259. Hannibal escaped to Sulci and was killed by his own mutinous men.

name: Camarina (ambush)
place: A defile on the march to Camarina, south-eastern Sicily
commanders_b: Aulus Atilius Calatinus; the military tribune Marcus Calpurnius Flamma (Quintus Caedicius in Cato)
borderline: Known only from Roman anecdotal tradition, not from Polybius.
roman_force: The consular army of Aulus Atilius Calatinus, legions and allies, trapped in a defile; a volunteer detachment of 300 (400 in Cato) seized a hill and drew the enemy on itself so that the army could escape.
greek_note: A consular army of Romans and Italian allies.
sources: Gellius 3.7 (Cato); Livy, Periochae 17; Frontinus 1.5.15, 4.5.10; Florus 1.18.13-14; Orosius 4.8.1-3; Zonaras 8.12; attalus.org (258 BC)
note: The detachment was cut down (its leader survived under the dead) but the army escaped and went on to take Camarina with a siege battery (Polybius 1.24.12; the engines were lent by Hiero, Diodorus 23.9.5): the siege is a separate entry.

name: Tyndaris
roman_force: The consular fleet (size unknown), whose van of ten ships was caught before the main body came up; crews of Roman citizens and naval allies with legionary marines; Rome lost 9 ships, Carthage 8 sunk and 10 captured.
greek_note: Socii navales from the Greek cities of southern Italy supplied part of the crews of the Roman fleets of this war; no breakdown survives.
sources: Polybius 1.25.1-4; Zonaras 8.12; en.wikipedia Battle of Tyndaris

name: Ecnomus
place: Off southern Sicily near Cape Ecnomus (Licata), east of Heraclea Minoa
commanders_a: Marcus Atilius Regulus, Lucius Manlius Vulso Longus
roman_force: 330 decked warships (Polybius 1.25.7), each with 300 rowers and 120 marines, about 140,000 men (1.26.7); the marines were picked legionaries (about 26,000 of the invasion army) in four squadrons named like the legions; the rowers were Roman citizens and naval allies (socii navales).
greek_note: The socii navales of the Greek cities of southern Italy (Naples, Tarentum, Rhegium, Velia, Locri and others) supplied part of the crews and much of the seamanship; Polybius gives no breakdown.
sources: Polybius 1.25-28; Zonaras 8.12; en.wikipedia Battle of Cape Ecnomus
note: Rome lost 24 ships; Carthage 30 sunk and 64 captured. 'Ecnomus' as the site is a modern convention; Zonaras places it east of Heraclea Minoa. Possibly the largest naval battle of antiquity by numbers engaged.

name: Adys
commanders_b: Bostar, Hamilcar, Hasdrubal son of Hanno
roman_force: Regulus's army left in Africa, 15,000 infantry and 500 cavalry (Polybius 1.29.9), probably two Roman legions and two allied alae (Lazenby).
greek_note: Roman legionaries and Latin and Italian allies drawn from the invasion army.
sources: Polybius 1.30; Zonaras 8.13; Orosius 4.8; en.wikipedia Battle of Adys
note: Some date it to early 255. The Romans had earlier taken Aspis (Clupea) on landing, then went on to take Tunis.

name: Tunis
place: Open plain near Tunis, towards the Bagradas (Medjerda)
roman_force: Regulus's army of about 15,000 infantry and 500 cavalry, probably two Roman and two allied legions; about 13,000 were killed, 500 captured with Regulus and 2,000 escaped to Aspis (Polybius 1.34).
greek_note: Roman legionaries and Latin and Italian allies.
sources: Polybius 1.32-34; Diodorus 23.14-15; Zonaras 8.13; en.wikipedia Battle of Tunis (255 BC)
note: Also called the battle of the Bagradas. The Carthaginian army (12,000 infantry, 4,000 cavalry, 100 elephants) was trained and led by the Spartan mercenary Xanthippus, with Greek mercenaries in its ranks.

name: Aspis (siege)
borderline: A failed Carthaginian attack on the Roman bridgehead after Tunis; briefly recorded.
roman_force: The Roman garrison of Aspis with the 2,000 survivors of Tunis (Polybius 1.34); they held out until the relief fleet arrived and sortied at Cape Hermaeum.
greek_note: Roman legionaries and Italian allies of the African army.
sources: Polybius 1.34, 1.36; Zonaras 8.14
note: The defenders' resistance made the Carthaginians give up the siege. The Romans had taken Aspis after a siege on landing in 256.

name: Cape Hermaeum
place: Off Cape Hermaeum (Cape Bon), north of Aspis
commanders_a: Servius Fulvius Paetinus Nobilior, Marcus Aemilius Paullus
roman_force: 350 quinqueremes (Polybius 1.36.10) with legionary marines, joined by the 40 ships and the sortie of the Aspis garrison; crews of Roman citizens and naval allies.
greek_note: Socii navales from the Greek cities of southern Italy supplied part of the crews of the Roman fleets of this war; no breakdown survives.
sources: Polybius 1.36-37; Diodorus 23.18; Orosius 4.9; en.wikipedia Battle of Cape Hermaeum
note: Carthage lost 114 ships captured and 16 sunk out of 200. en.wikipedia's infobox calls the result inconclusive because a storm off Camarina then sank 384 of the 464 Roman warships and over 100,000 men, most of them Italian allies.

name: Panormus (siege)
commanders_a: Aulus Atilius Calatinus, Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Asina
roman_force: Both consuls with the army in Sicily and a fleet of about 300 ships (220 newly built plus survivors: Polybius 1.38.5-6); siege engines breached the seaward wall and the legions stormed the new town (1.38.7-10).
greek_note: Socii navales, including the Greek cities of Italy, crewed part of the fleet that carried and blockaded; the assault was made by Roman and Italian troops.
sources: Polybius 1.38.6-10; Diodorus 23.18.4-5; Zonaras 8.14; en.wikipedia Battle of Panormus (background)
note: The old town then surrendered; 14,000 inhabitants ransomed themselves and 13,000 were sold.

name: Lipara (siege)
date: 252 BCE (a first siege had been begun in 258)
borderline: Briefly recorded: Polybius says only that the consuls of 252 took Thermae and Lipara.
roman_force: The consul's army and fleet with siege works; while Cotta was away the works were burned and the camp nearly taken, for which he had his kinsman Publius Aurelius Pecuniola flogged and reduced to the ranks (Valerius Maximus 2.7.4; Frontinus 4.1.31).
greek_note: The landing troops were Romans and Italian allies; the fleet's rowers included Greek socii navales.
sources: Polybius 1.24.13, 1.39.13; Valerius Maximus 2.7.4; Frontinus 4.1.31; Zonaras 8.14
note: Lipara was a Greek town held by a Carthaginian garrison. The siege begun by the consuls of 258 (Polybius 1.24.13) had not taken it.

name: Panormus
place: Before the walls of Panormus (Palermo), by the river Oreto
roman_force: Metellus's army of two Roman legions and two allied alae, about 16,000-20,000 (en.wikipedia); his light troops fought the elephants from the ditch and walls, supplied with missiles by the townspeople (Polybius 1.40).
greek_note: A Roman consular army; the people of Panormus helped bring up missiles, but no Greek units are named.
sources: Polybius 1.40; Diodorus 23.21; Zonaras 8.14; Orosius 4.9; en.wikipedia Battle of Panormus
note: Some date it to 251, Metellus's consular year. The captured elephants were shown at Rome.

name: Lilybaeum (siege)
commanders_a: Gaius Atilius Regulus Serranus, Lucius Manlius Vulso Longus, Publius Claudius Pulcher, Gaius Lutatius Catulus
roman_force: Both consular armies, four Roman legions and four allied alae, with a blockading fleet of about 200 ships: over 100,000 men with the crews (Polybius 1.41; en.wikipedia).
greek_note: Socii navales manned part of the blockading fleet and Hiero II supplied grain; the siege army itself was Roman and Italian.
sources: Polybius 1.41-55; Diodorus 24.1; Zonaras 8.15; en.wikipedia Siege of Lilybaeum (250-241 BC)
note: Never taken: the garrison (7,000 infantry and 700 cavalry, with Celtic and Greek mercenaries) beat off assaults and mines and burned the siege works in a gale (Polybius 1.48); blockade-runners such as Hannibal the Rhodian kept it supplied. It was evacuated under the peace of 241; en.wikipedia gives a Roman victory. Scored a draw: the siege was neither raised nor successful; the town was handed over at the peace of 241 BCE.

name: Drepana
roman_force: About 120 ships (93 captured, about 30 escaped), manned partly by 10,000 newly levied oarsmen, with marines picked from the legions besieging Lilybaeum (Polybius 1.49).
greek_note: Socii navales from the Greek cities of southern Italy supplied part of the crews of the Roman fleets of this war; no breakdown survives.
sources: Polybius 1.49-51; Diodorus 24.1; Cicero, De natura deorum 2.7; Suetonius, Tiberius 2; en.wikipedia Battle of Drepana
note: Carthage's greatest naval victory of the war; about 20,000 Romans killed or captured. Claudius is said to have thrown the sacred chickens into the sea before the battle.

name: Phintias
roman_force: Junius's 120 warships escorting about 800 transports with supplies for Lilybaeum, crewed by Roman citizens and naval allies (Polybius 1.52-54; Diodorus 24.1).
greek_note: Socii navales from the Greek cities of southern Italy supplied part of the crews of the Roman fleets of this war; no breakdown survives.
sources: Polybius 1.52-54; Diodorus 24.1; en.wikipedia Battle of Phintias
note: Rome lost 17 warships sunk and 13 damaged; a storm off Camarina then destroyed almost all the rest. Junius afterwards occupied Eryx.

name: Drepana (siege)
commanders_a: Lucius Junius Pullus, Gaius Lutatius Catulus
borderline: Largely a blockade overlapping the siege of Lilybaeum; counted separately because en.wikipedia has an article.
roman_force: Roman legions and allies blockading Drepana by land from 249, joined in 242 by Lutatius Catulus's fleet of about 200 quinqueremes, which seized the harbour (Polybius 1.59).
greek_note: Socii navales crewed part of the fleet of 242; the blockading army was Roman and Italian.
sources: Polybius 1.59-60; Zonaras 8.17; en.wikipedia Siege of Drepana
note: Catulus was wounded in an assault before the Aegates battle; the town was handed over under the peace of 241.

name: Heirkte (Mount Ercte)
place: Heirkte, probably Monte Pellegrino above Panormus (Palermo)
borderline: Three years of constant skirmishes and small battles, which Polybius likens to a boxing match, rather than one named battle.
roman_force: The Roman army of Panormus, legions and allies camped about five stades from Hamilcar's stronghold; no figures (Polybius 1.56-57).
greek_note: A Roman army in Sicily; Greek allied troops are not named.
sources: Polybius 1.56-57; Diodorus 24.5-6; en.wikipedia Hamilcar Barca
note: The usual identification is Monte Pellegrino; Hamilcar left in 244 for Eryx, neither side having gained.

name: Eryx (siege)
commanders_b: Gaius Fundanius Fundulus (243) and other Roman commanders
borderline: A two-year double blockade with frequent fighting rather than a single battle.
roman_force: Roman posts on the summit (the temple of Venus Erycina) and at the foot of the mountain, legions and allies, joined by Gallic mercenaries who deserted from Hamilcar and were set to guard the temple (Polybius 1.58, 2.7.7-10).
greek_note: A Roman army in Sicily; Greek allied troops are not named.
sources: Polybius 1.58, 2.7.7-10; Diodorus 24.8-9; Zonaras 8.16; en.wikipedia Hamilcar Barca
note: Hamilcar took the town of Eryx in 244, destroying its Roman garrison, and was himself hemmed in between the Roman posts; the stalemate ended with the peace of 241.

name: Aegates
place: West of Phorbantia (Levanzo), Aegates Islands, off western Sicily
commanders_a: Gaius Lutatius Catulus, Quintus Valerius Falto
roman_force: About 200 quinqueremes built on the model of a captured Rhodian blockade-runner and paid for by wealthy citizens, with well-drilled crews and marines picked from the army in Sicily (Polybius 1.59-61).
greek_note: The crews were raised, as for earlier fleets, from Roman citizens and naval allies including the Greek cities of Italy; Polybius gives no breakdown.
sources: Polybius 1.59-61; Diodorus 24.11; Eutropius 2.27; Livy, Periochae 19; en.wikipedia Battle of the Aegates
note: Carthage lost 50 ships sunk and 70 captured, with about 10,000 prisoners; Rome 30 sunk and 50 damaged. The battle ended the war (treaty of Lutatius). Catulus, wounded, left the fighting to Valerius Falto.

name: Falerii
commanders_a: Quintus Lutatius Cerco, Aulus Manlius Torquatus Atticus
roman_force: Both consular armies of 241, legions with Latin and Italian allies and their cavalry; no figures.
greek_note: A consular levy of Romans, Latins and Italian allies.
sources: Polybius 1.65.2; Zonaras 8.18; Livy, Periochae 20; Eutropius 2.28; Fasti Triumphales (241); en.wikipedia Falerii
note: Two battles (Zonaras 8.18): in the first the Roman infantry was worsted but the cavalry won, the second was a clear Roman victory; Polybius says Falerii fell within a few days. The Falisci spoke Faliscan, a language close to Latin, and are entered under 'Etruscans'; the old town was destroyed and its people moved to Falerii Novi.

name: Noutria
place: Noutria, an unidentified town on the Illyrian (Ardiaean) coast
commanders_a: Gnaeus Fulvius Centumalus, Lucius Postumius Albinus
borderline: One of several Illyrian towns taken by storm, mentioned briefly by Polybius; no en.wikipedia article. The site and the country are a guess.
roman_force: The consular fleet of 200 ships under Fulvius and the army of 20,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry under Postumius (Polybius 2.11), guided by Demetrius of Pharos; the Romans lost many men, several military tribunes and a quaestor in taking the town.
greek_note: Socii navales crewed part of the 200 ships, and the Greek cities of Corcyra, Apollonia and Epidamnus had just come over to Rome; their part in the fighting is not recorded.
sources: Polybius 2.11.13-16; en.wikipedia First Illyrian War
note: In the same operations 20 Illyrian boats laden with plunder were captured and the besiegers of Issa fled to Arbo; Corcyra, Apollonia and Epidamnus were taken over without fighting.

name: Faesulae
roman_force: The praetor's army of Sabine and Etruscan levies posted on the Etruscan frontier (Polybius 2.24.5 gives 50,000 foot and 4,000 horse for the Etruscan and Sabine levy), of whom about 6,000 fell (2.25).
greek_note: Polybius's list of the forces of 225 names no Greek contingents; this army was Etruscan and Sabine.
sources: Polybius 2.25-26; en.wikipedia Battle of Faesulae (225 BC)
note: Gauls: Boii, Insubres, Taurisci and the Transalpine Gaesatae. The site is uncertain: Polybius has the Gauls fall back from near Clusium towards Faesulae.

name: Telamon
place: Campo Regio near Telamon (Talamone), coastal Etruria
commanders_a: Lucius Aemilius Papus, Gaius Atilius Regulus (killed)
roman_force: The two consular armies, four Roman legions of 5,200 infantry and 300 cavalry with 30,000 allied infantry and 2,000 cavalry (Polybius 2.24.3-4), Regulus's army coming from Sardinia, joined by the survivors of the Etruscan and Sabine levies.
greek_note: Polybius's detailed list of the Roman and allied forces of 225 names no Greek contingents (the Greek cities owed ships, not soldiers).
sources: Polybius 2.24, 2.27-31; Diodorus 25.13; en.wikipedia Battle of Telamon
note: About 40,000 Gauls killed and 10,000 captured (Polybius 2.31). Gauls: Boii, Insubres, Taurisci and Gaesatae. The Veneti and Cenomani, Roman allies, raided the Boii but were not at Telamon.

name: Clusius
place: Insubrian territory beyond the river Clusius (probably the Chiese), north of the Po
borderline: No en.wikipedia article; Polybius describes a pitched battle, named in modern accounts after the river Clusius.
roman_force: The two consular armies of 223, legions with Latin and Italian allies, fighting with a river at their backs; the Cenomani allies were sent back across the river and the bridges broken, and the triarii's spears were given to the front line (Polybius 2.32-33).
greek_note: A consular levy of Romans, Latins and Italian allies.
sources: Polybius 2.32-33; Plutarch, Marcellus 4; Orosius 4.13.14; Zonaras 8.20; historyofwar.org (Battle of the River Clusius); attalus.org (223 BC)
note: Insubres (Gauls) about 50,000; Orosius gives 9,000 killed and 17,000 captured. Earlier that year the consuls had suffered losses crossing the Po near the Adda (Polybius 2.32.1-3).

name: Clastidium
roman_force: A flying column of about two-thirds of the consular cavalry, Roman and allied, with 600 light infantry (Plutarch, Marcellus 6); about 3,200 horse by en.wikipedia; the foot did not engage.
greek_note: Roman and Italian allied cavalry.
sources: Polybius 2.34; Plutarch, Marcellus 6-7; Florus 1.20; en.wikipedia Battle of Clastidium
note: Gauls: Gaesatae and Insubres. Marcellus killed Viridomarus in single combat and dedicated the spolia opima.

name: Mediolanum
borderline: A rearguard battle followed by the capture of the city; no en.wikipedia article.
roman_force: Scipio's consular army, legions with Latin and Italian allies, which had just taken Acerrae (Polybius 2.34-35).
greek_note: A consular levy of Romans, Latins and Italian allies.
sources: Polybius 2.34-35; en.wikipedia Battle of Clastidium (aftermath)
note: The Insubres attacked Scipio's rear as he drew off from Mediolanum and were beaten off with difficulty; he then took the city and the Insubres surrendered. Acerrae had fallen without a recorded assault after Clastidium.

name: Dimale (siege)
commanders_a: Lucius Aemilius Paullus, Marcus Livius Salinator
roman_force: The consular army of 219, legions with Latin and Italian allies carried over by a fleet crewed partly by naval allies; Dimale was stormed within seven days (Polybius 3.18).
greek_note: Socii navales, including the Greek cities of Italy, crewed the fleet; the assault was made by Roman and Italian troops.
sources: Polybius 3.16-18; Appian, Illyrian Wars 8; Zonaras 8.20; en.wikipedia Second Illyrian War
note: The neighbouring Illyrian towns then submitted to Rome.

name: Pharos
roman_force: Paullus's consular army: the main body landed by night in a wooded hollow while twenty ships drew Demetrius and his 6,000 men out to the harbour, then cut them off from the city (Polybius 3.18-19).
greek_note: Socii navales, including the Greek cities of Italy, crewed the ships; the landing force was Roman and Italian.
sources: Polybius 3.18-19; Appian, Illyrian Wars 8; Zonaras 8.20; en.wikipedia Second Illyrian War
