note: Demetrius fled to Philip V of Macedon; Pharos (a Greek colony held by his Illyrians) was taken and its walls razed. en.wikipedia says the last Illyrian forces on the island surrendered in 218.

name: Rhône (cavalry skirmish)
place: Near Hannibal's crossing of the Rhône, above its mouth
commanders_a: Publius Cornelius Scipio (consul, in overall command)
borderline: A small cavalry clash with no article of its own; the first fight between Roman and Hannibalic troops.
roman_force: 300 picked Roman cavalry, guided by Massaliots and joined by Celtic mercenaries in Massaliot service, against 500 Numidian horse (Polybius 3.41, 3.44-45).
greek_note: Massaliot (Greek) guides accompanied the Roman cavalry; the troopers were Roman and Italian.
sources: Polybius 3.44-45; Livy 21.29
note: Polybius gives about 140 Romans and Celts and over 200 Numidians killed.

name: Ticinus
place: West bank of the Ticinus, near Ticinum (Pavia)
roman_force: Scipio's cavalry, Roman, Latin-Italian and Gallic (about 3,600 by modern reckoning, some 2,000 of them Gauls), with the velites of his four legions (Polybius 3.65).
greek_note: Roman and Italian cavalry and Cisalpine Gallic horse; no Greek units are recorded.
sources: Polybius 3.64-65; Livy 21.45-46; en.wikipedia Battle of the Ticinus
note: The exact site is unknown.

name: Trebia
place: West bank of the lower Trebia, near Placentia
roman_force: The united consular armies: four legions with 16,000 Roman and 20,000 allied infantry and 4,000 cavalry (Polybius 3.72), with the loyal Cenomani Gauls (Livy 21.55).
greek_note: Romans, Latins and Italian socii with Cenomani Gauls; the Greek allies served mostly in the fleet.
sources: Polybius 3.68-74; Livy 21.52-56; en.wikipedia Battle of the Trebia
note: Wikipedia gives 22/23 December; the sources say only that it was near the winter solstice.

name: Mutina (Boian ambush)
place: Woods on the road to Mutina, between the Po and Mutina
borderline: No standard battle name: the Boii twice ambushed Manlius in woods on his march to relieve Mutina; he took refuge at Tannetum.
roman_force: The praetor's army in Cisalpine Gaul, given by Livy as two Roman legions with 10,000 allied infantry and 1,600 cavalry (Livy 21.17, 21.25).
greek_note: A normal army of Roman citizens and Latin and Italian socii; the Greek allies of southern Italy served chiefly at sea.
sources: Polybius 3.40; Livy 21.25-26
note: The Boii (with the Insubres) rose when the colonies of Placentia and Cremona were founded.

name: Lilybaeum (sea)
roman_force: About 20 quinqueremes and triremes of the Sicilian command, with legionaries put aboard as marines; Carthage lost seven ships captured out of 35 (Livy 21.49-50).
greek_note: The rowers of Roman fleets were largely socii navales, among whom the Greek cities of southern Italy and Sicily were prominent; Hiero of Syracuse had warned the praetor.
sources: Livy 21.49-50; en.wikipedia Battle of Lilybaeum

name: Cissa
roman_force: Two Roman legions and two allied contingents landed at Emporiae (modern estimates about 8,000 Roman and 14,000 allied infantry with 2,200 cavalry), with newly won Iberian auxiliaries; 20,000-25,000 in all.
greek_note: The Greek cities of Emporiae and Massalia gave the landing a base, but the line was Roman, Italian and Iberian.
sources: Polybius 3.76; Livy 21.60; en.wikipedia Battle of Cissa
note: The site of Cissa is unknown; it was near Tarraco.

name: Lake Trasimene
place: North shore of Lake Trasimene, Umbria
roman_force: Flaminius' consular army of two Roman legions and two allied contingents, about 25,000 men (Polybius 3.80-85).
greek_note: Hiero of Syracuse had sent 500 Cretan archers and 1,000 peltasts to the Romans that winter (Polybius 3.75), but it is not known which army they joined.
sources: Polybius 3.80-85; Livy 22.4-7; Ovid, Fasti 6.765-768; en.wikipedia Battle of Lake Trasimene
note: Ovid's date is in the Roman calendar; the exact site on the north shore is disputed.

name: Umbrian Lake
date: June 217 BCE (a few days after Trasimene)
roman_force: 4,000 Roman and allied cavalry sent ahead by the consul Gnaeus Servilius Geminus; half were killed, the rest captured (Polybius 3.86).
greek_note: Cavalry of a consular army, Roman and Italian.
sources: Polybius 3.86; Livy 22.8; Appian, Hannibalica 11; en.wikipedia Second Punic War
note: Appian names the Plestine lake; Livy says only Umbria, and Zonaras places it near Spoletium.

name: Ager Falernus
place: Pass by Mount Callicula, at the edge of the Ager Falernus
commanders_a: Hannibal, Hasdrubal (in charge of the oxen)
roman_force: The dictator's four legions with allies; the fighting fell on the 4,000 men holding the pass, of whom about 1,000 were killed (Livy 22.15-18).
greek_note: A normal Roman and Italian army; any Greek light troops sent by Hiero would have been a small share.
sources: Polybius 3.92-94; Livy 22.15-18; en.wikipedia Battle of Ager Falernus
note: Hannibal's ruse with burning brushwood on the horns of oxen.

name: Spoletium
borderline: An assault on a Latin colony beaten off; no standard battle name and no Roman field army.
roman_force: The settlers of the Latin colony of Spoletium (founded 241 BCE) defending their walls; no figures (Livy 22.9.1-3).
greek_note: A Latin colony in Umbria.
sources: Livy 22.9.1-3; en.wikipedia Spoleto
note: Livy says Hannibal was repulsed with heavy loss and, judging from one colony what Rome itself would be, turned away into Picenum.

name: Ebro (sea)
roman_force: 35 Roman quinqueremes with picked legionaries as marines, and Massaliot ships (Polybius 3.95 names two Massaliot scouts; Wikipedia gives 20 Massaliot triremes); 25 of 40 Carthaginian ships were taken.
greek_note: Ships of Massalia (Greek) sailed with the Roman fleet, whose rowers were largely socii navales.
sources: Polybius 3.95-96; Livy 22.19-20; en.wikipedia Battle of Ebro River
note: Massalia is the Greek ally.

name: Geronium
commanders_b: Marcus Minucius Rufus, Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus
roman_force: Minucius' half of the dictator's army, two legions with allies, rescued by Fabius with the other two (Polybius 3.103-105).
greek_note: A normal Roman and Italian army.
sources: Polybius 3.100-105; Livy 22.18-30; en.wikipedia Battle of Geronium
note: Earlier Minucius had won a skirmish against Hannibal's foragers; in the main battle he was ambushed and saved only by Fabius.

name: Cannae
commanders_b: Lucius Aemilius Paullus (killed), Gaius Terentius Varro, Gnaeus Servilius Geminus (killed)
roman_force: Eight Roman legions and as many allied (socii) contingents, about 80,000 infantry and 6,000 cavalry (Polybius 3.107, 3.113).
greek_note: Hiero's 1,000 archers and slingers, sent early in 216 (Livy 22.37), may have served; the army was overwhelmingly Latin- and Oscan-speaking.
sources: Polybius 3.107-117; Livy 22.44-50; en.wikipedia Battle of Cannae

name: Nola
roman_force: Marcellus' army, formed from the fleet's legion and survivors of Cannae, which made a sudden sortie from the gates of Nola (Livy 23.14-16).
greek_note: Roman and Italian troops in an Oscan town.
sources: Livy 23.14-16; Plutarch, Marcellus 10-11; en.wikipedia Battle of Nola (216 BC)
note: A minor Roman success; Livy's figures are probably inflated.

name: Casilinum (siege)
commanders_b: Marcus Anicius (Praenestine commander); Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus outside
roman_force: A garrison of Latin and Etruscan allies, about 570 Praenestines and 460 Perusians with a few Romans and Latins, who beat off assaults until starved into surrender (Livy 23.17-19).
greek_note: The defenders were cohorts from Praeneste (Latin) and Perusia (Etruscan).
sources: Livy 23.17-19; en.wikipedia Casilinum
note: The town fell by capitulation on terms after a long blockade with assaults and mining.

name: Silva Litana
place: Silva Litana, a forest in the territory of the Boii (Emilia)
roman_force: Two Roman legions with allied troops raised along the Adriatic coast, 25,000 men (Livy 23.24).
greek_note: Romans and Adriatic Italian allies (Picentes, Umbrians and others).
sources: Livy 23.24; Polybius 3.118; Frontinus, Stratagems 1.6.4; en.wikipedia Battle of Silva Litana
note: The Boii cut the trees to fall on the column; Postumius' skull was made into a cup.

name: Nola
place: Before the walls of Nola, Campania
roman_force: Marcellus' army at Nola, about two legions with allies, with loyal Nolans (Livy 23.42-46).
greek_note: A normal Roman and Italian army.
sources: Livy 23.42-46; Plutarch, Marcellus 12; en.wikipedia Battle of Nola (215 BC)
note: Livy claims a clear Roman victory; modern historians think his figures inflated.

name: Dertosa
place: South bank of the Ebro near Ibera (Dertosa, modern Tortosa)
commanders_a: Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus, Publius Cornelius Scipio
roman_force: The Scipios' army of two Roman legions and two allied contingents with some Iberian auxiliaries, about 25,000 by modern estimate (Livy 23.28-29 gives no figures).
greek_note: Roman, Italian and Iberian troops; Greek Emporiae and Massalia supported the Romans from the coast.
sources: Livy 23.26-29; en.wikipedia Battle of Ibera
note: Also called the battle of Ibera (the Wikipedia title). Some lists date it to 216.

name: Cumae
roman_force: Gracchus' army of volones (slave volunteers) and allied troops, with the people of Cumae; it surprised the Capuans at Hamae (over 2,000 killed) and then held Cumae against Hannibal's assault (Livy 23.35-37).
greek_note: The volones were slaves of mixed origin; Cumae, a Greek foundation, was by then largely Oscan-speaking.
sources: Livy 23.35-37; en.wikipedia Battle of Cumae (215 BC)
note: Two actions: the night attack on the Capuans at Hamae, and Hannibal's failed attack on Cumae with a siege tower.

name: Grumentum
borderline: Known only from a short notice in Livy; no Wikipedia article.
roman_force: The Roman force in Lucania under Sempronius Longus; Livy gives no strength, only that Hanno lost over 2,000 men (Livy 23.37).
greek_note: A normal Roman and Italian force.
sources: Livy 23.37

name: Decimomannu
place: Between Cornus and Caralis, southern Sardinia
commanders_b: Hasdrubal the Bald (captured), Hampsicora (suicide), Hiostus (killed), Hanno, Mago
roman_force: The Sardinian garrison legion and a new legion brought by Manlius, about 22,000 infantry and 1,200 cavalry (Livy 23.34, 23.40).
greek_note: A normal Roman and Italian army.
sources: Livy 23.32, 23.34, 23.40-41; en.wikipedia Battle of Decimomannu
note: Also called the battle of Cornus or Caralis; Wikipedia's coordinates point to Cornus, which was stormed soon after. Includes the earlier defeat of Hiostus.

name: Sardinia (sea)
place: At sea between Sardinia and Africa
commanders_b: unknown (the fleet returning from Hasdrubal's Sardinian expedition)
borderline: No standard name ('naval battle near Sardinia' in Wikipedia's list).
roman_force: The Roman fleet of Sicily under Otacilius, which took seven Carthaginian ships with their crews (Livy 23.41).
greek_note: The fleet was rowed largely by socii navales, many from the Greek cities of southern Italy and Sicily.
sources: Livy 23.41; en.wikipedia List of battles of the Second Punic War

name: Iliturgi
place: Iliturgi (Cerro Maquiz, Mengíbar), on the upper Baetis
commanders_a: Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus, Publius Cornelius Scipio
commanders_b: Hasdrubal Barca, Mago, Hamilcar son of Bomilcar
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
roman_force: The Scipios' Roman and Italian legions in Spain, perhaps with Iberian allies; Livy gives no strength (Livy 23.49).
greek_note: Roman, Italian and Iberian troops.
sources: Livy 23.49; en.wikipedia Illiturgis, Hasdrubal Barca
note: The Scipios relieved Iliturgi; most historians consider Livy's victories in Spain of 215-214 unhistorical or inflated.

name: Intibili
place: Intibili (site uncertain, perhaps near Traiguera, Castellón)
commanders_a: Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus, Publius Cornelius Scipio
commanders_b: Hasdrubal Barca, Mago, Hamilcar son of Bomilcar
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
borderline: Known only from Livy's annalistic account.
roman_force: The Scipios' Roman and Italian legions in Spain; Livy gives no strength (Livy 23.49).
greek_note: Roman, Italian and Iberian troops.
sources: Livy 23.49
note: Doubted like the other Spanish victories Livy reports for 215-214.

name: Beneventum
roman_force: Gracchus' two legions of volones, slaves enlisted after Cannae and promised freedom for victory, with allied troops (Livy 24.14-16).
greek_note: The volones were slaves of mixed origin, some perhaps Greek; the rest were Italian socii.
sources: Livy 24.14-16; en.wikipedia Battle of Beneventum (214 BC)
note: Hanno's 17,000 infantry were mostly Bruttians and Lucanians, with 1,200 Numidian and Moorish horse.

name: Nola
commanders_a: Marcus Claudius Marcellus, Gaius Claudius Nero
roman_force: Marcellus' consular army at Nola; Nero's cavalry, sent round to take Hannibal in the rear, failed to arrive (Livy 24.17).
greek_note: A normal Roman and Italian army.
sources: Livy 24.17; en.wikipedia Battle of Nola (214 BC)
note: Livy claims a Roman victory; modern lists call it inconclusive. Hannibal withdrew.

name: Casilinum (siege)
commanders_a: Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus (consul), Marcus Claudius Marcellus (consul)
borderline: A siege ending in surrender, followed by a massacre of the garrison as it marched out.
roman_force: The two consular armies of Fabius and Marcellus, who pressed costly assaults until the garrison of 2,000 Campanians and 700 Hannibalic soldiers surrendered (Livy 24.19).
greek_note: Normal Roman and Italian armies.
sources: Livy 24.19; Plutarch, Marcellus 21
note: The en.wikipedia Casilinum article dates the recapture to 215; Livy places it in 214.

name: Leontini (siege)
roman_force: Marcellus' army in Sicily, which took the town at the first assault; 2,000 Roman deserters found there were executed (Livy 24.30).
greek_note: Roman legions and Italian allies; Sicilian Greek allies of Rome supplied the army.
sources: Livy 24.30; Plutarch, Marcellus 14
note: The storming of Leontini led Syracuse to break with Rome.

name: Apollonia
place: Philip's siege camp before Apollonia, on the Aous
commanders_a: Marcus Valerius Laevinus (propraetor), Quintus Naevius Crista (prefect)
roman_force: 2,000 picked men of Laevinus' legion and fleet under Naevius Crista, who slipped into Apollonia and then stormed Philip's camp by night (Livy 24.40).
greek_note: Legionaries and marines; the townsmen of Apollonia (Greek) were allies, not part of the Roman force.
sources: Livy 24.40; en.wikipedia First Macedonian War
note: Known only from Livy; some modern historians think the scale of the rout exaggerated. Apollonia is the allied Greek city.

name: Castrum Album
commanders_b: Publius Cornelius Scipio, Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
borderline: A surprise attack on a camp rather than a battle.
roman_force: The Scipios' army; Carthaginian cavalry surprised it and killed about 2,000 men (Livy 24.41).
greek_note: Roman, Italian and Iberian troops.
sources: Livy 24.41; en.wikipedia Battle of Munda (214 BC)
note: One of Livy's Spanish episodes of 214 that most historians doubt.

name: Iliturgi
commanders_b: Hasdrubal Barca, Mago, Hasdrubal son of Gisco
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
roman_force: A legion under Gnaeus Scipio that broke through to the besieged Roman garrison of Iliturgi (Livy 24.41).
greek_note: Roman and Italian troops.
sources: Livy 24.41; en.wikipedia Battle of Munda (214 BC)
note: Livy claims 12,000 enemy killed; it may be a doublet of the relief of 215.

name: Munda
commanders_a: Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus (wounded), Publius Cornelius Scipio
commanders_b: Hasdrubal Barca, Mago, Hasdrubal son of Gisco
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
roman_force: The Scipios' Roman and Italian legions in Spain; Livy gives no Roman strength (Livy 24.42).
greek_note: Roman, Italian and Iberian troops.
sources: Livy 24.42; en.wikipedia Battle of Munda (214 BC)
note: Livy says the Romans were winning when Gnaeus was wounded and the recall sounded; most historians doubt these Spanish victories.

name: Auringis
commanders_a: Publius Cornelius Scipio, Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
roman_force: The Scipios' Roman and Italian legions in Spain (Livy 24.42).
greek_note: Roman, Italian and Iberian troops.
sources: Livy 24.42; en.wikipedia Battle of Munda (214 BC)
note: Another of Livy's doubted Spanish victories of 214, fought after the retreat from Munda.

name: Syracuse (siege)
commanders_a: Marcus Claudius Marcellus, Appius Claudius Pulcher
roman_force: The Roman army of Sicily, including the legions formed of the survivors of Cannae (perhaps 16,000-18,000 men), and a fleet of 60 quinqueremes that attacked the sea walls of Achradina (Polybius 8.3-7; Livy 24.34).
greek_note: Syracusan exiles and pro-Roman Sicilian Greeks served with Marcellus, and Greek socii navales rowed part of the fleet; the legions were Roman and Italian.
sources: Polybius 8.3-7, 8.37; Livy 24.33-34, 25.23-31; Plutarch, Marcellus 14-19; en.wikipedia Siege of Syracuse (213-212 BC)
note: Livy places the start of the siege in 214; Wikipedia and most modern accounts in 213. The city fell in 212 and Archimedes was killed.

name: Megara Hyblaea (siege)
borderline: A storming known from a single sentence of Livy.
roman_force: Part of Marcellus' army before Syracuse, which stormed and sacked the town (Livy 24.35).
greek_note: Roman legions and Italian allies.
sources: Livy 24.35

name: Acrillae
roman_force: Marcellus' marching column, which surprised Hippocrates' army of 10,000 foot and 500 horse while it was fortifying camp and killed some 8,000 (Livy 24.35).
greek_note: Roman legions and Italian allies.
note: The site of Acrillae is not securely identified.

name: Arpi
commanders_a: Quintus Fabius Maximus (consul 213, son of Verrucosus)
borderline: A recapture by night assault; no Wikipedia article.
roman_force: The consul's army, which broke in by night during a storm and fought in the streets until 1,000 Spaniards of the garrison went over to it (Livy 24.46-47).
greek_note: A normal Roman and Italian army.

name: Tarentum
roman_force: The Roman garrison of Tarentum, perhaps 5,000 men, surprised at night; the survivors held the citadel to the end of the siege (Polybius 8.24-34; Livy 25.7-11).
greek_note: A Roman and Italian garrison in a Greek city.
sources: Polybius 8.24-34; Livy 25.7-11; en.wikipedia Battle of Tarentum (212 BC)
note: Tarentine conspirators let Hannibal in; the citadel held out until 209.

name: Syracuse (relief battle)
date: 212 BCE (before the plague of that autumn)
place: The Roman siege camps before Syracuse, near the Anapus
commanders_a: Marcus Claudius Marcellus, Titus Quinctius Crispinus (in the old camp)
commanders_b: Himilco, Hippocrates (relief army), Epicydes (sally from the city)
borderline: A relief attack inside the siege of Syracuse, counted separately as in the ancient Greek battles set.
roman_force: Marcellus' army before Syracuse, divided between his own lines and the old camp under Crispinus; both beat off the simultaneous attacks of Hippocrates from outside and Epicydes from the city (Livy 25.26).
greek_note: Syracusan exiles and Sicilian Greek allies served with Marcellus, but the army was mainly the Roman and Italian legions of Sicily.
sources: Livy 25.26; en.wikipedia Siege of Syracuse (213-212 BC)
note: The Carthaginian relief army then camped by the marshes and was destroyed by plague, which killed Himilco and Hippocrates (Livy 25.26).

name: Thurii
place: Before Thurii, on the Gulf of Taranto
borderline: A garrison lured into an ambush before the town went over to Hannibal; no standard battle name.
roman_force: The small Roman garrison of Thurii under Atinius, which marched out with the young men of Thurii against Hanno's infantry and was routed when Mago's hidden cavalry charged (Livy 25.15).
greek_note: The Thurine levies that marched out with the garrison were Greek, but they fled at once and were in league with the enemy; the garrison was Roman and Italian.
note: Thurii is the Greek city on the Carthaginian side; it then received the Carthaginians, letting Atinius and the Roman survivors leave by sea.

name: Campi Veteres (death of Gracchus)
borderline: An ambush of a small party rather than a battle.
roman_force: The proconsul with his lictors and a small cavalry escort, betrayed by the Lucanian Flavus (Livy 25.16-17).
greek_note: A small Roman escort.
sources: Livy 25.16-17; Polybius 8.35; Appian, Hannibalica 35
note: Livy gives three versions of the place; Campi Veteres is the one he prefers.

name: Beneventum
roman_force: The consul Fulvius' army, which stormed Hanno's supply camp (Livy 25.13-14); Wikipedia gives 18,400 men.
greek_note: A normal Roman and Italian consular army.
sources: Livy 25.13-14; en.wikipedia Battle of Beneventum (212 BC)
note: Hanno had gathered grain there for Capua.

name: Capua
commanders_b: Quintus Fulvius Flaccus, Appius Claudius Pulcher (consuls)
roman_force: The two consular armies, four Roman legions with as many allied contingents; they lost about 1,500 men and withdrew (Livy 25.18-19).
greek_note: Normal Roman and Italian armies.
sources: Livy 25.18-19; en.wikipedia Battle of Capua (212 BC)
note: Hannibal raised the first Roman blockade of Capua.

name: Silarus
roman_force: 8,000 men given to Centenius from the regular armies and about as many volunteers he raised, 16,000 in all (Livy 25.19).
greek_note: Roman and Italian troops with volunteers from Campania, Lucania and Samnium.
sources: Livy 25.19; en.wikipedia Battle of the Silarus
note: Known only from Livy; some modern historians doubt it.

name: Herdonia
roman_force: The praetor's army of two legions with allies, about 18,000 men, of whom some 2,000 escaped (Livy 25.21).
greek_note: A normal Roman and Italian army.
sources: Livy 25.21; en.wikipedia Battle of Herdonia (212 BC)
note: Some modern historians suspect a doublet of the battle of 210.

name: Upper Baetis
place: Castulo and Ilorci, on the upper Baetis (Guadalquivir)
commanders_a: Hasdrubal Barca, Mago, Hasdrubal son of Gisco, Masinissa, Indibilis
commanders_b: Publius Cornelius Scipio (killed), Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus (killed)
roman_force: About 30,000 Romans and Italian allies of the two Scipios' armies, with 20,000 Celtiberian mercenaries who deserted Gnaeus before his battle (Livy 25.32-36).
greek_note: Roman, Italian, Celtiberian and Iberian troops.
sources: Livy 25.32-36; Appian, Iberica 16; en.wikipedia Battle of the Upper Baetis
note: A double battle a few days apart: Publius fell near Castulo, Gnaeus near Ilorci. Livy dates it to 212; most modern accounts to 211.

name: Marcius' night attack
place: Carthaginian camps south of the Ebro (site unknown)
commanders_a: Lucius Marcius Septimus (eques, elected commander by the troops)
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
borderline: No standard name; Livy cites Claudius Quadrigarius, Valerius Antias and Piso for wildly different figures.
roman_force: The survivors of the Scipios' armies, rallied by Marcius together with the garrisons left in Spain (Livy 25.37-39).
greek_note: Roman and Italian survivors of the Scipios' legions.
note: Livy says Marcius beat off an attack on his camp and then took two Carthaginian camps; modern historians doubt the scale.

name: Capua (siege)
place: Capua and the Roman siege lines around it
commanders_a: Quintus Fulvius Flaccus, Appius Claudius Pulcher (mortally wounded), Gaius Claudius Nero
roman_force: Two proconsular armies and the praetor Nero's army behind a double ring of works; their velites, carried on the cavalry's horses, beat the Capuan horse (Polybius 9.3-7; Livy 26.1-16).
greek_note: Normal Roman and Italian armies.
sources: Polybius 9.3-9; Livy 26.1-16; en.wikipedia Siege of Capua (211 BC)
note: Includes the 'Second Battle of Capua' of en.wikipedia's lists: Hannibal's attack on the siege lines failed; his march on Rome did not draw the besiegers off, and Capua surrendered. Distinct from the battle of 212 (-212-capua), in which Hannibal drove off the first blockade.

name: Himera
roman_force: Marcellus' army from Syracuse; the Numidians of Muttines, offended by Hanno, held aloof and the Carthaginians were routed (Livy 25.40-41).
greek_note: Roman legions and Italian allies, perhaps with Sicilian Greek allies.
note: Livy narrates it at the end of 212; it is usually dated 211.

name: Zacynthus (siege)
borderline: Known from one sentence of Livy; the citadel was not taken.
roman_force: Laevinus' legion and fleet, which took the town by storm except for the citadel (Livy 26.24).
greek_note: Legionaries and marines; the fleet's rowers included Greek socii navales.
sources: Livy 26.24; en.wikipedia First Macedonian War
note: Zacynthus had been Philip's since 217. Oeniadae and Nasus were also captured that year (no details).

name: Salapia
place: Salapia, Apulia, by the lagoon of Salpi near Trinitapoli
borderline: A town betrayed to the Romans, with hard fighting against the garrison; no standard battle name.
roman_force: Marcellus' consular army, let into the town by the faction of Blattius; the 500 Numidian horsemen of the garrison fought on foot to the last and only 50 were taken alive (Livy 26.38).
greek_note: A normal Roman and Italian army.
sources: Livy 26.38; Appian, Hannibalica 45-47
note: Livy calls the loss of these Numidian horsemen a heavier blow to Hannibal than the loss of the town.

name: Aegina
borderline: A capture whose fighting is not described.
roman_force: Sulpicius' fleet and its landing troops, acting with the Aetolians; the captured Aeginetans were sold or ransomed (Polybius 9.42).
greek_note: Roman legionaries and marines; the Aetolians (Greek) were a separate allied force, and Greek socii navales may have rowed part of the fleet.
sources: Polybius 9.42.5-8, 22.8.9-10; en.wikipedia First Macedonian War
note: Aegina is the Greek city. Under the Roman-Aetolian treaty the land went to the Aetolians, who sold the island to Attalus I for thirty talents.

name: Anticyra (siege)
borderline: A short siege ending in surrender.
roman_force: Laevinus' fleet attacking from the sea while the Aetolians attacked by land; the town surrendered after a few days and its people were enslaved (Livy 26.26; Polybius 9.39).
greek_note: Roman marines and fleet; the Aetolian allies (Greek) were a separate force.
sources: Livy 26.26; Polybius 9.39; en.wikipedia First Macedonian War
note: Livy says Anticyra in Locris; Polybius' Anticyra is the Phocian town, used here.

name: Echinus (siege)
place: Echinus, on the Malian Gulf, Phthiotis
roman_force: Sulpicius' fleet and its landing troops (the legion that served in Greece), attacking Philip's siege lines with the Aetolian army (Polybius 9.41-42).
greek_note: Roman legionaries and marines; the Aetolians (Greek) fought as a separate allied army.
sources: Polybius 9.41-42; en.wikipedia First Macedonian War
note: Philip beat off the relief attempt and Echinus surrendered.

name: Herdonia
roman_force: Two Roman legions with allies, drawn up in two lines; eleven of twelve military tribunes fell (Livy 27.1).
greek_note: A normal Roman and Italian army.
sources: Livy 27.1; en.wikipedia Battle of Herdonia (210 BC)

name: Numistro
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
roman_force: Marcellus' consular army: the first legion and the right ala of allies, relieved during the fighting by the third legion and the left ala (Livy 27.2).
greek_note: A normal Roman and Italian consular army.
sources: Livy 27.2; Plutarch, Marcellus 24; Frontinus 2.2.6; en.wikipedia Battle of Numistro
note: Ended at nightfall; Hannibal withdrew next day. Its historicity is doubted by some modern historians. Wikipedia's coordinates (in Calabria) are wrong; Numistro was in Lucania.

name: Sapriportis (sea)
place: Off Sapriportis, about 15 miles from Tarentum
roman_force: About 20 ships gathered at Rhegium: Roman ships with others from the allied Greek cities of Rhegium and Velia and from Paestum, partly rowed by men taken on at Croton and Thurii (Livy 26.39).
greek_note: Livy names ships of Rhegium, Velia and Paestum and rowers from Croton and Thurii, mostly Greek-speaking allies.
sources: Livy 26.39; en.wikipedia Battle of Sapriportis
note: The Tarentine fleet sought to cut supplies to the Roman citadel.

name: New Carthage (siege)
roman_force: 25,000 infantry and 2,500 cavalry of the Roman and Italian legions in Spain, with 35 ships under Laelius; 500 men waded the lagoon to scale the north wall (Polybius 10.9-15).
greek_note: Roman and Italian legions; the fleet's crews included Greek socii navales.
sources: Polybius 10.9-15; Livy 26.42-46; en.wikipedia Battle of Cartagena (209 BC)
note: Polybius dates it to 209; Livy to 210. A combined land and sea assault.

name: Canusium
roman_force: Marcellus' army of two legions with allied troops (Livy 27.12-14).
greek_note: A normal Roman and Italian army.
sources: Livy 27.12-14; Plutarch, Marcellus 25-26; en.wikipedia Battle of Asculum (209 BC)
note: Also called Asculum. Hannibal won the first day, Marcellus claimed the second; heavy losses on both sides.

name: Tarentum
commanders_a: Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus (consul), Marcus Livius (in the citadel)
roman_force: Fabius' consular army (about 20,000), which escaladed the walls where the Bruttian garrison commander let it in, with the citadel garrison and ships attacking the sea wall (Livy 27.15-16).
greek_note: A Roman and Italian army.
sources: Livy 27.15-16; Plutarch, Fabius 21-23; en.wikipedia Battle of Tarentum (209 BC)
note: Taken by assault with help from treachery; the Tarentines and the garrison were massacred and some 30,000 enslaved.

name: Lamia (first battle)
borderline: Rome was a small allied contingent, not the main army.
roman_force: About 1,000 Roman soldiers sent from the fleet by Publius Sulpicius Galba, fighting in Pyrrhias' Aetolian army with Attalus' Pergamene auxiliaries (Livy 27.30).
greek_note: The Roman contingent was legionaries from the fleet; the Aetolians and Pergamenes (Greek) were allies.
sources: Livy 27.30; en.wikipedia First Battle of Lamia
note: The Aetolians lost about 1,000 men.

name: Lamia (second battle)
borderline: Rome was a small allied contingent, not the main army.
roman_force: The same Roman contingent of about 1,000 from Sulpicius' fleet, with the Aetolians and Pergamenes (Livy 27.30).
greek_note: The Roman contingent was legionaries from the fleet; the Aetolians and Pergamenes (Greek) were allies.
sources: Livy 27.30; en.wikipedia List of battles before 301
note: The Aetolians again lost about 1,000 and withdrew inside Lamia.

name: Elis
roman_force: About 4,000 soldiers landed from Sulpicius' fleet, who sallied with the Eleans and Aetolians; Philip was unhorsed and withdrew (Livy 27.31-32).
greek_note: The Roman troops were legionaries and marines; the Eleans and Aetolians (Greek) were allies.
sources: Livy 27.31-32; en.wikipedia First Macedonian War
note: Elis is the allied Greek city. A Roman victory, against the draw of the ancient Greek battles set: Philip's attack on Elis was beaten off by the sally of Sulpicius' 4,000 Romans with the Eleans and Aetolians; the king was unhorsed and carried off on another horse, and his only gain was the fort of Phyricus, taken the next day (Livy 27.32). Livy narrates these events under 208; the modern date is 209.

name: Baecula
roman_force: About 30,000 Roman and Italian troops with some 10,000 Iberian auxiliaries (modern estimate; Polybius 10.38-40).
greek_note: Roman, Italian and Iberian troops.
sources: Polybius 10.38-40; Livy 27.18-19; en.wikipedia Battle of Baecula
note: Hasdrubal escaped with most of his army and marched for Italy.

name: Petelia
place: Below the hill of Petelia (Strongoli), Bruttium
roman_force: Part of the Roman garrison of Tarentum marching to the siege of Locri; 2,000 were killed and 1,500 captured (Livy 27.26).
greek_note: Roman and Italian garrison troops.
sources: Livy 27.26; en.wikipedia Battle of Petelia
note: An ambush with 3,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry.

name: Locri (siege)
borderline: A siege raised by a relief force, with little recorded fighting.
roman_force: Cincius' force from Sicily with siege engines and ships; it fled to the ships when Hannibal's Numidians came up (Livy 27.28).
greek_note: Roman troops from Sicily; the ships' crews may have included Greek socii navales.
sources: Livy 27.28
note: Locri (Greek) was Hannibal's ally with a Carthaginian garrison.

name: Venusia (ambush of Marcellus)
place: A wooded hill between Venusia and Bantia
commanders_b: Marcus Claudius Marcellus (consul, killed), Titus Quinctius Crispinus (consul, mortally wounded)
borderline: An ambush of a reconnoitring party, not a battle of armies.
roman_force: The consuls' escort of about 220 cavalry, most of them Etruscans with 40 from Fregellae (Livy 27.26-27).
greek_note: Livy names the escort as Etruscans and Fregellans.
sources: Polybius 10.32; Livy 27.26-27; Plutarch, Marcellus 29
note: The death of Marcellus.

name: Clupea (sea)
roman_force: Laevinus' fleet of about 100 ships from Sicily, which defeated 83 Carthaginian ships and took 18 (Livy 27.29).
greek_note: The Sicilian fleet was rowed largely by socii navales, many from the Greek cities of Sicily and southern Italy.
sources: Livy 27.29; en.wikipedia List of battles of the Second Punic War

name: Metaurus
place: On the Metaurus river, near Sena Gallica
commanders_a: Marcus Livius Salinator, Gaius Claudius Nero (consuls), Lucius Porcius Licinus (praetor)
roman_force: The armies of Livius and Porcius (four legions with allies) joined by Nero's 6,000 picked infantry and 1,000 cavalry from the south, about 37,000 in all (Polybius 11.1-3; Livy 27.43-49).
greek_note: Roman legions with Latin, Italian and Etruscan-Umbrian allies.
sources: Polybius 11.1-3; Livy 27.43-49; en.wikipedia Battle of the Metaurus
note: Wikipedia gives 22-24 June according to the version; the exact site on the river is disputed.

name: Grumentum
roman_force: Nero's consular army, given by Livy as 40,000 infantry and 2,500 cavalry (Livy 27.40-42).
greek_note: A normal Roman and Italian army.
sources: Livy 27.41-42; en.wikipedia Battle of Grumentum
note: Livy claims a Roman victory; some lists call it indecisive, since Hannibal slipped away.

name: Utica (sea)
roman_force: Laevinus' fleet of 100 ships, which met 70 Carthaginian ships, took 17 and sank 4 (Livy 28.4).
greek_note: The Sicilian fleet was rowed largely by socii navales, many from the Greek cities of Sicily and southern Italy.
sources: Livy 28.4; en.wikipedia List of battles of the Second Punic War
note: Known only from Livy.

name: Celtiberia (Silanus)
place: The camps of Mago and Hanno in Celtiberia (site unknown)
borderline: No standard name; Silanus surprised the camps of newly raised Celtiberians.
roman_force: A detachment of 10,000 infantry and 500 cavalry sent by Scipio (Livy 28.1-2).
greek_note: Roman and Italian troops.
sources: Livy 28.1-2; en.wikipedia Battle of Ilipa (background)

name: Orongis (siege)
place: Orongis, a town of the Maesesses (site uncertain, perhaps near Jaén)
borderline: A town stormed; known only from Livy.
roman_force: A detachment of Scipio's army under his brother Lucius, which stormed the town (Livy 28.3).
greek_note: Roman and Italian troops.
sources: Livy 28.3
note: Hasdrubal son of Gisco had used the town as a base.

name: Ilipa
place: East of Ilipa (Alcalá del Río), near Seville
commanders_a: Publius Cornelius Scipio (Africanus), Marcus Junius Silanus, Lucius Marcius Septimus
commanders_b: Hasdrubal son of Gisco, Mago, Masinissa
roman_force: 45,000 infantry and 3,000 cavalry (Polybius 11.20): the Roman and Italian legions on the wings and Iberian allies in the centre, among them 3,000 foot and 500 horse of the chief Culchas (Livy 28.13).
greek_note: Roman, Italian and Iberian troops.
sources: Polybius 11.20-24; Livy 28.12-16; en.wikipedia Battle of Ilipa
note: Some date it to 207; also called Silpia or Carmona in some lists.

name: Iliturgi (siege)
roman_force: Scipio's army, attacking in two divisions; the town was stormed and its people massacred for having killed Roman fugitives in 211 (Livy 28.19-20).
greek_note: Roman and Italian legions.
sources: Livy 28.19-20; Appian, Iberica 32; en.wikipedia Illiturgis

name: Astapa (siege)
roman_force: A detachment of Scipio's army under Marcius; the townsmen sallied and died fighting after killing their families (Livy 28.22-23).
greek_note: Roman and Italian troops.
sources: Livy 28.22-23; Appian, Iberica 33

name: Carteia
place: Near the mouth of the Baetis (Guadalquivir)
roman_force: Marcius' detachment of Roman and allied infantry and cavalry; Hanno had 4,000 newly hired Celtiberians among about 6,000 men.
greek_note: Roman and Italian troops.
sources: Livy 28.30; en.wikipedia Battle of Carteia
note: Also called the battle of the Guadalquivir (anachronistic). Wikipedia places it at the mouth of the river, not at Carteia itself.

name: Carteia (sea)
place: Off Carteia, in the Strait of Gibraltar
roman_force: Laelius' squadron of one large ship and seven triremes; he sank two Carthaginian triremes and disabled a third (Livy 28.30).
greek_note: Roman ships were rowed largely by socii navales, among whom the Greek cities were prominent.
sources: Livy 28.30; en.wikipedia Battle of Carteia (naval)
note: Livy calls Laelius' flagship a septireme; Wikipedia a quinquereme.

name: New Carthage
borderline: A repulsed night attack on a city.
roman_force: The Roman garrison of New Carthage, which sallied and drove Mago's landing force back to its ships (Livy 28.36).
greek_note: Roman and Italian garrison troops.
sources: Livy 28.36; en.wikipedia Battle of Carteia (naval)
note: Mago's last attempt in Spain before he sailed to the Balearics and Liguria.

name: Ilergetan revolt
place: A valley in the land of the Ilergetes, north of the Ebro (site unknown)
borderline: No standard name.
roman_force: Scipio's Roman and Italian legions, including the pardoned mutineers of Sucro (Polybius 11.31-33; Livy 28.31-34).
greek_note: Roman and Italian legions.
sources: Polybius 11.31-33; Livy 28.31-34; en.wikipedia Indibilis
note: Livy gives the rebels 20,000 infantry and 2,500 cavalry.

name: Indibilis' revolt
place: North of the Ebro, near the lands of the Ilergetes (site unknown)
commanders_a: Lucius Cornelius Lentulus, Lucius Manlius Acidinus
borderline: No standard name.
roman_force: The two Roman armies left in Spain under Lentulus and Acidinus (Livy 29.1-3).
greek_note: Roman and Italian legions.
sources: Livy 29.1-3; en.wikipedia Indibilis
note: The rebels are given 30,000 infantry and 4,000 cavalry.

name: Locri (siege)
roman_force: 3,000 men from the Rhegium garrison under Pleminius, who escaladed one citadel, and troops Scipio brought by sea from Messana, who beat off Hannibal's assault (Livy 29.6-8).
greek_note: Roman and allied troops from Rhegium, a Greek allied city, with Locrian exiles as guides.
sources: Livy 29.6-8
note: Locrians helped the Romans; the defenders were Carthaginian garrisons in the two citadels. Followed by Pleminius' notorious misrule.

name: Salaeca
place: Near the tower of Salaeca, about 15 miles from Utica
commanders_b: Hanno son of Hamilcar (killed or captured)
borderline: A cavalry ambush; no article of its own.
roman_force: Scipio's Roman and Italian cavalry in ambush, with Masinissa's Numidian horse as the lure (Livy 29.34).
greek_note: Roman and Italian cavalry with Numidian allies; the horses and arms of the 300 Roman troopers came from Sicilian (Greek) nobles.
sources: Livy 29.34; en.wikipedia Battle of Utica (203 BC)
note: Livy gives versions of 1,000 or 2,000 killed and of Hanno's death or capture.

name: Utica (siege)
roman_force: Scipio's invasion army of 25,000-30,000: the two legions of Cannae survivors raised to about 6,200 each with volunteers, two Latin allied legions, Masinissa's Numidians, and the fleet attacking the sea walls (Livy 29.24-26, 29.35).
greek_note: The army was formed in Sicily, but its soldiers were Roman and Italian; Greek socii navales rowed part of the fleet.
sources: Polybius 14.1-2; Livy 29.35; en.wikipedia Battle of Utica (204 BC)
note: After about 40 days the arrival of Hasdrubal and Syphax forced Scipio to raise the siege and winter at Castra Cornelia. Utica held out to the end of the war.

name: Crotona
place: In the territory of Croton, Bruttium
commanders_a: Publius Sempronius Tuditanus (consul), Publius Licinius Crassus (proconsul)
roman_force: Sempronius' two newly raised legions, joined for the second fight by Crassus' two legions (Livy 29.36).
greek_note: Roman and Italian legions.
sources: Livy 29.36; en.wikipedia Battle of Crotona
note: Two engagements in Livy 29.36: Hannibal beat Sempronius in a running fight (about 1,200 Romans killed), then the combined armies of Sempronius and Crassus beat Hannibal (Livy claims 4,000 killed); en.wikipedia lists it as a drawn battle. Distinct from the obscure battle of 203 under the consul Gnaeus Servilius Caepio (-203-croton, Livy 30.19).

name: Utica
place: The camps of Hasdrubal and Syphax near Utica
commanders_a: Publius Cornelius Scipio (Africanus), Gaius Laelius, Masinissa
roman_force: Scipio's four legions (two Roman, two Latin) with Masinissa's Numidians, who fired the enemy camps by night (Polybius 14.1-6; Livy 30.3-6).
greek_note: Roman and Italian legions with Numidian allies.
sources: Polybius 14.1-6; Livy 30.3-6; en.wikipedia Battle of Utica (203 BC)
note: The burning of the camps.

name: Great Plains
place: The Great Plains (Campi Magni) on the Bagradas
commanders_a: Publius Cornelius Scipio (Africanus), Gaius Laelius, Masinissa
roman_force: Two Roman legions in the centre and two Latin allied legions, about 20,000, with Laelius' Roman and Italian cavalry on the right and Masinissa's Numidians on the left (Polybius 14.8; Livy 30.8).
greek_note: Roman and Italian legions with Numidian allies.
sources: Polybius 14.7-8; Livy 30.7-8; en.wikipedia Battle of the Great Plains
note: 4,000 Celtiberian mercenaries fought to the death on the Carthaginian side.

name: Castra Cornelia (sea)
place: The Roman naval station by Utica and Castra Cornelia
roman_force: Scipio's warships behind a wall of transports lashed four deep and manned by picked soldiers; the Carthaginians towed off about 60 transports (Polybius 14.10; Livy 30.9-10).
greek_note: The fleet's rowers were largely socii navales, many from the Greek cities of Sicily and southern Italy.
sources: Polybius 14.10; Livy 30.9-10; en.wikipedia List of battles of the Second Punic War
note: A minor Carthaginian success; the Roman warships were saved. Wikipedia's list names it Castra Cornelia.

name: Cirta
roman_force: Part of Scipio's army under Laelius, with velites set among Masinissa's Numidian squadrons and the legionaries advancing behind (Livy 30.11-12).
greek_note: Roman and Italian troops with Numidian allies.
sources: Livy 30.11-12; en.wikipedia Battle of Cirta
note: Masinissa (Massylii) was a principal; Syphax led the Masaesyli. Cirta surrendered after.

name: Insubria
place: In the land of the Insubres (site unknown, perhaps near Mediolanum)
commanders_a: Publius Quinctilius Varus (praetor), Marcus Cornelius Cethegus (proconsul)
roman_force: Four legions with allies, about 35,000, two legions in the front line and two in reserve, with Varus leading the cavalry (Livy 30.18).
greek_note: Roman and Italian legions.
sources: Livy 30.18; en.wikipedia Battle of Insubria
note: Mago died of his wound on the voyage to Africa.

name: Croton
place: In the territory of Croton, Bruttium
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
borderline: Livy himself calls the report of this battle obscure.
roman_force: The consul's army in Bruttium; no details survive (Livy 30.19).
greek_note: A normal Roman and Italian army.
sources: Livy 30.19
note: Valerius Antias claimed 5,000 enemy killed; Livy doubts it.

name: Zama
commanders_a: Publius Cornelius Scipio (Africanus), Gaius Laelius, Masinissa
roman_force: Two Roman legions (the Cannae survivors with volunteers) and two Latin allied legions, about 29,000-30,000, with 1,500 Roman and Italian cavalry under Laelius, and Masinissa's 6,000 Numidian infantry and 4,000 cavalry plus 600 horse under Dacamas (Polybius 15.5-14; Livy 30.29-35).
greek_note: Roman and Italian legions with Numidian allies; no Greek units are recorded.
sources: Polybius 15.5-16; Livy 30.29-35; en.wikipedia Battle of Zama
note: The 19 October date (from Wikipedia's list) rests on an eclipse linked to the battle; many give only autumn 202. Livy's 4,000 Macedonians in Hannibal's army are doubted.

name: Vermina
date: 17 December 202 BCE (first day of the Saturnalia, Roman calendar)
place: On Vermina's line of march, inland from Carthage (site unknown)
commanders_a: Publius Cornelius Scipio (Africanus) and his officers
borderline: No standard name; known only from Livy.
roman_force: Part of Scipio's army, mainly cavalry and light troops; Livy gives no figures for the Roman side (Livy 30.36).
greek_note: Roman and Italian troops.
sources: Livy 30.36
note: Livy says 15,000 Numidians were killed and 1,200 captured; Vermina escaped. Fought after Zama, before the peace of 201.

name: Antipatrea (siege)
place: Antipatrea, a town in a narrow pass of the Apsus (probably Berat)
commanders_a: Lucius Apustius (legate of Publius Sulpicius Galba)
borderline: A storming told in a few lines of Livy; modern works do not treat it as a battle.
roman_force: A detachment of Sulpicius's consular army sent out from the camp near Apollonia under the legate Lucius Apustius; no numbers are given (Livy 31.27).
greek_note: A detachment of the Italian consular army; no Greek contingents are recorded.
sources: Livy 31.27.1-5; en.wikipedia Second Macedonian War
note: After talks with the leading men failed, Apustius took the town by force, killed the men of military age, razed the walls and burned it; the forts of Corrhagum, Gerrunium and Orgessum fell in the same raid. Antipatrea is usually placed at Berat.

name: Chalcis (raid)
commanders_b: Macedonian garrison (its commander Sopater was killed)
borderline: A night raid: the town was stormed and its arsenals burned, then abandoned.
roman_force: A raiding force from the Roman fleet at Corcyra: 20 triremes and about 1,000 soldiers (Livy 31.22-23).
greek_note: The soldiers were Roman and Italian; some crews may have come from the Greek naval allies (socii navales) of southern Italy.
sources: Livy 31.22-23; en.wikipedia Second Macedonian War
note: Guided by Chalcidian exiles, the Romans scaled the walls, killed the garrison, burned the granaries and arsenal and withdrew before Philip V arrived.

name: Cremona
roman_force: The praetor Furius's force of Latin allies joined by the consul's army sent ahead from Etruria: two legions with allied contingents, about 18,000 foot and 2,400 horse by modern estimate (Livy 31.10, 31.21).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian army; no Greek contingents are recorded.
sources: Livy 31.10, 31.21-22; en.wikipedia Battle of Cremona (200 BC)
note: Insubres, Cenomani and Boii with Ligurian tribes had sacked Placentia; Livy gives 35,000 Gauls killed or captured.

name: Eordaea Pass
place: The pass from Lyncestis into Eordaea (probably the Kirli Derven pass near Vevi), blocked by Philip with a field-work
borderline: The forcing of a fortified pass; named by its place, rarely treated as a battle of its own.
roman_force: Sulpicius's consular army of two legions with Latin and Italian allies; the light troops and legionaries forced the Macedonian position on wooded, broken ground where the phalanx could not use its pikes (Livy 31.39). No numbers are given for the battle.
greek_note: The army had crossed from Italy; no Greek contingents are recorded in the fight.
sources: Livy 31.39; Mommsen, History of Rome, book 3 ch. 8; en.wikipedia Second Macedonian War
note: Fought some days after Ottolobus: Philip blocked the pass with ditch and rampart, the Macedonians were partly turned and partly broken with heavy loss, and Sulpicius went on to ravage Eordaea, Elimea and Orestis.

name: Ottolobus
roman_force: Sulpicius Galba's consular army, two legions with Latin and Italian allies and their cavalry, invading Macedonia from Dassaretis (Livy 31.33-39); no numbers are given.
greek_note: No Greek contingents are recorded with Galba; the Aetolians, Dardanians and Illyrians fought separately.
note: A cavalry-led action in which Philip's foragers and cavalry were routed and he withdrew; the site in Lyncus is not securely identified (perhaps near Bitola).

name: Oreus (siege)
roman_force: Marines and crews of the Roman fleet under the legate Apustius with siege engines, attacking one side of the town while Attalus attacked the other (Livy 31.46).
greek_note: Pergamene and Rhodian squadrons (allies) fought beside the Roman fleet, whose crews included Greek socii navales from southern Italy.
sources: Livy 31.46; en.wikipedia Second Macedonian War
note: The town was taken after a siege of some length; type is land, with naval support.

name: Cassandreia (siege)
borderline: A failed attempt on the walls, briefly told.
roman_force: Landing parties of the Roman fleet with the Pergamene and Rhodian fleets (Livy 31.45).
greek_note: Roman fleet crews included Greek socii navales; the allied Greek squadrons are listed as allies.
sources: Livy 31.45; en.wikipedia Second Macedonian War

name: Aous
place: The Aoi Stena gorge of the Aous (Vjose), near Kelcyre
roman_force: Flamininus's consular army, the two legions and allies of Villius with 8,000 infantry and 800 cavalry of new levies; 4,000 infantry and 300 cavalry were led round the Macedonian position by a shepherd sent by the Epirote Charops (Livy 32.8-12; Plutarch, Flamininus 4).
greek_note: Epirote guides helped, but no Greek contingents are recorded in the Roman army.
sources: Livy 32.9-12; Plutarch, Flamininus 3-5; en.wikipedia Second Macedonian War
note: After some forty days of stand-off; Macedonian losses about 2,000. The gorge is usually placed at Kelcyre, some put it nearer Tepelene.

name: Phaloria (siege)
roman_force: Flamininus's consular army of two legions with Latin and Italian allies (Livy 32.15).
greek_note: The Italian army of Flamininus; no Greek units are named.
sources: Livy 32.15
note: Stormed after the Macedonian garrison of 2,000 refused terms; the town was burned.

name: Atrax (siege)
place: Atrax, on the Peneus west of Larissa
roman_force: Flamininus's legions with a siege train; the breach they made was held by a Macedonian phalanx (Livy 32.17-18).
greek_note: The Roman legions and Italian allies did the fighting; Amynander's Athamanians were allies.
sources: Livy 32.17-18; en.wikipedia Second Macedonian War
note: Flamininus abandoned the siege after the assault on the breach failed.

name: Eretria (siege)
roman_force: The Roman fleet under the legate Lucius Flamininus with its marines and siege engines, with the Pergamene and Rhodian fleets (Livy 32.16).
greek_note: Greek socii navales served in the Roman fleet; the Pergamene and Rhodian contingents were allies.
sources: Livy 32.16; en.wikipedia Second Macedonian War
note: Taken by assault after fierce fighting; Carystus then surrendered without a fight.

name: Elatia (siege)
roman_force: Flamininus's consular army of two legions with Italian allies and a siege train (Livy 32.24).
greek_note: The Italian army of Flamininus; no Greek units are named.
sources: Livy 32.18, 32.24; en.wikipedia Second Macedonian War
note: Stormed with rams and ladders; the garrison held out briefly in the citadel.

name: Corinth (siege)
roman_force: Troops and marines of the Roman fleet under Lucius Flamininus, besieging with Attalus and the newly allied Achaeans (Livy 32.23).
greek_note: The Achaean and Pergamene forces were allies; the Roman part came from the fleet.
sources: Livy 32.19-23; en.wikipedia Second Macedonian War
note: Abandoned when Philocles brought 1,500 men from Macedonian-held Argos into the city; Italian deserters fought hard among the defenders.

name: Cynoscephalae
place: The Cynoscephalae hills, between Pharsalus and Pherae
roman_force: Two legions with Latin and Italian allies and 20 elephants, about 26,000 men in all with 6,000 Aetolian foot and 400 horse, 1,200 Athamanians, and 500 Cretans of Gortyn and 300 Apolloniates (Livy 33.3; Polybius 18.19-27).
greek_note: Within the Roman army only the Cretan and Apolloniate auxiliaries were Greek; the Aetolian and Athamanian allies added about 7,600 more, roughly a quarter of the whole.
sources: Polybius 18.18-27; Livy 33.3-10; Plutarch, Flamininus 7-8; en.wikipedia Battle of Cynoscephalae
note: Macedonian losses about 8,000 killed and 5,000 captured, Roman about 700.

name: Mincius
roman_force: The consul Cethegus's army of two legions with Latin and Italian allies (Livy 32.29-30).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian consular army.
note: The Insubres were defeated after the Cenomani withdrew from their side; Livy reports 35,000 killed.

name: Leucas (siege)
roman_force: The Roman fleet under Lucius Flamininus with troops brought from Corcyra (Livy 33.16-17).
greek_note: Soldiers and marines of the Roman fleet, some crews drawn from Greek socii navales.
sources: Livy 33.16-17; en.wikipedia Second Macedonian War
note: Opponent: the Acarnanian League, Philip's ally. After repeated assaults the city was entered with the help of traitors, with fighting in the streets.

name: Turda
place: Near the town of Turda (site unknown)
roman_force: The praetor's army of Hither Spain, usually a legion with Latin and Italian allies; the sources give no details.
greek_note: A praetorian army of Romans and Italian allies; no Greek units are recorded.
sources: Livy 33.44
note: Livy reports 12,000 of the enemy killed. Turda's site is unknown; some suggest Turba in Edetania (near Teruel).

name: Comum
roman_force: The consul Marcellus's army of two legions with Latin and Italian allies (Livy 33.36-37).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian consular army.
note: Against the Insubres and the Comenses; Livy reports 40,000 killed (doubtless inflated). Earlier that year the Boii under Corolamus had ambushed Marcellus on the march, killing about 3,000 (Livy 33.36).

name: Emporiae
roman_force: Cato's consular army of two legions with Latin and Italian allies, landed with the fleet at Rhoda and Emporiae (Livy 34.8-16).
greek_note: The Greek town of Emporiae was Cato's base, but no Greek contingent is recorded in the battle.
sources: Livy 34.11-16; Appian, Iberica 40
note: Cato attacked the camp of the rebel Spaniards of the north-east (Indigetes and neighbours) at dawn and routed them.

name: Iliturgi
place: Near Iliturgi, on the upper Baetis
roman_force: An escort of 6,000 men given to the outgoing praetor Helvius by Appius Claudius Nero (Livy 34.10).
greek_note: Roman and Italian troops of the Spanish garrison.
sources: Livy 34.10
note: Helvius beat some 20,000 Celtiberians and then took Iliturgi. Livy tells it under 195; some modern accounts date it 196 or 197.

name: Gythium (siege)
commanders_a: Titus and Lucius Quinctius Flamininus, Eumenes II, Sosilas of Rhodes
roman_force: The Roman fleet of 40 ships under Lucius Flamininus with its marines, joined for the final assault by Titus Flamininus with 4,000 soldiers (Livy 34.29).
greek_note: The Rhodian (18 ships) and Pergamene (40 ships) squadrons and the Achaeans fought as allies; the Roman part was Italian with some Greek crews.
sources: Livy 34.29; en.wikipedia Battle of Gythium; en.wikipedia Roman-Spartan War
note: Gorgopas surrendered the town on terms after Dexagoridas, who had offered to betray it, was killed.

name: Sparta (siege)
roman_force: Flamininus's army of about 50,000 with its allies: the Roman legions and Italian allies, 10,000 Achaean foot and 1,000 horse, 1,500 Macedonians and 400 Thessalian horse sent by Philip V, Spartan exiles under Agesipolis, and marines from the fleets (Livy 34.26-29, 34.38-40).
greek_note: The Roman army itself was Italian; the allied Greek contingents (Achaean, Macedonian, Thessalian, exiles, Rhodian and Pergamene marines) made up perhaps a third of the whole.
sources: Livy 34.26-40; en.wikipedia Roman-Spartan War
note: The Romans beat the Spartans outside the walls, broke into the city and were driven back by fires; Nabis then accepted Roman terms. The city was not taken.

name: Litana Forest
place: The Litana forest, in the land of the Boii
roman_force: The consul Valerius Flaccus's army of two legions with Latin and Italian allies (Livy 34.22).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian consular army.
sources: Livy 34.22
note: Against the Boii; Livy gives 8,000 killed. Not the ambush in the same forest in 216 BCE; the forest's site (between Bononia and Mutina, or in the Apennines) is uncertain.

name: Mediolanum
roman_force: The proconsul Valerius Flaccus's army of legions and Latin and Italian allies (Livy 34.46).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian army.
sources: Livy 34.46
note: Against the Insubres and Boii who had crossed the Po under Dorulacus; Livy gives 10,000 killed.

name: Placentia
place: Near Placentia, on the border of the Boii
roman_force: The consul's two legions and two allied alae, about 20,000 men; a cohort of extraordinarii restored the camp (Livy 34.46-48).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian consular army.
sources: Livy 34.46-48; en.wikipedia Battle of Placentia (194 BC)
note: A hard fight at the Roman camp: Romans lost 5,000, the Boii 11,000 (Livy); the consul then withdrew to Placentia.

name: Ilipa
roman_force: The praetor's army of Further Spain, a legion with Latin and Italian allies (normal establishment; Livy 35.1 gives no details).
greek_note: A praetorian army of Romans and Italian allies.
sources: Livy 35.1
note: Scipio caught Lusitanian raiders returning laden with booty. Not the battle of Ilipa of 206 BCE.

name: Mutina
roman_force: Two Roman legions and two allied alae, with Latin and Italian cavalry (Livy 35.4-5).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian consular army.
sources: Livy 35.4-6; en.wikipedia Battle of Mutina (193 BC)
note: Against the Boii; Livy gives 14,000 Boii killed and about 5,000 Roman dead.

name: Toletum
roman_force: The praetor's army of Further Spain, legionaries with Latin and Italian allies (normal establishment; not described in Livy 35.7).
greek_note: A praetorian army of Romans and Italian allies.
sources: Livy 35.7; en.wikipedia Celtiberian Wars
note: Against a coalition of Vaccaei, Vettones and Celtiberians.

name: Licabrum (siege)
borderline: Known from one sentence of Livy; site unknown.
roman_force: The praetor's army of Hither Spain (normal establishment; not described).
greek_note: A praetorian army of Romans and Italian allies.
sources: Livy 35.22
note: Taken by siege works and assault; perhaps Igabrum (Cabra), which is uncertain.

name: Pisae
borderline: Named only by the territory of Pisae.
roman_force: The proconsul Minucius Thermus's army of legions and Latin and Italian allies, with Numidian horsemen (Livy 35.3, 35.11, 35.21).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian army.
sources: Livy 35.21; en.wikipedia Apuani
note: Ligurians had threatened Pisae since 193; Livy reports 9,000 killed.

name: Toletum (siege)
borderline: Briefly told by Livy.
roman_force: The propraetor's army of Further Spain (normal establishment; not described).
greek_note: A praetorian army of Romans and Italian allies.
sources: Livy 35.22
note: Nobilior beat a relieving army of Vettones and took Toletum by siege works.

name: Thermopylae
place: The pass of Thermopylae and the heights of Callidromus
commanders_a: Manius Acilius Glabrio, Marcus Porcius Cato, Lucius Valerius Flaccus
roman_force: Glabrio's consular army, about 20,000 infantry, 2,000 cavalry and 15 elephants of Romans and Latin and Italian allies; Cato and Flaccus led 2,000 men each against the Aetolian-held forts (Livy 36.14-19).
greek_note: The army had crossed from Italy; Philip V and the Achaeans were allies but their troops were not in the battle.
sources: Livy 36.15-19; Appian, Syriaca 17-20; Plutarch, Cato Maior 13-14; en.wikipedia Battle of Thermopylae (191 BC)
note: en.wikipedia gives 24 April 191 BCE, a modern reckoning. Aetolians held the forts of Callidromus, Teichius and Rhoduntia for Antiochus.

name: Corycus
place: Off Cape Corycus, between Teos and Erythrae
roman_force: About 81 Roman decked ships, including the ships due under treaty from Rhegium, Locri and the allied cities of the Naples coast, with six Carthaginian ships and 24 Pergamene warships (Livy 36.42-45).
greek_note: Livy names Rhegium, Locri and the Naples coast as sources of ships, so Greek socii navales manned a good part of the Roman fleet.
sources: Livy 36.42-45; Appian, Syriaca 22; en.wikipedia Battle of Corycus
note: Seleucid losses 23 ships; one Carthaginian ship lost. A Rhodian squadron of 25 arrived after the battle.

name: Heraclea Trachinia (siege)
roman_force: Glabrio's consular army of legions and Latin and Italian allies with siege works (Livy 36.22-24).
greek_note: The Italian army that had fought at Thermopylae.
sources: Livy 36.22-24; en.wikipedia Roman-Seleucid War
note: Stormed after a siege of about 24 days; the Aetolians in the citadel surrendered.

name: Naupactus (siege)
roman_force: Glabrio's consular army with siege works (Livy 36.30, 36.34-35).
greek_note: The Italian consular army.
sources: Livy 36.30, 36.34-35; en.wikipedia Roman-Seleucid War
note: After about two months of assaults the siege was lifted on a truce arranged by Flamininus when the town was near falling; the city was not taken (by the siege rule a defence, hence draw).

name: Myonessus
place: Off Cape Myonnesus, between Teos and Lebedus
commanders_a: Lucius Aemilius Regillus, Eudamus of Rhodes
roman_force: 58 Roman warships with 22 Rhodian ships under Eudamus (Livy 37.29-30).
greek_note: The Roman fleet was the one raised in 191-190 with ships and crews from the Greek allied cities of southern Italy (socii navales); the Rhodians were allies.
sources: Livy 37.27-30; Appian, Syriaca 27; en.wikipedia Battle of Myonessus
note: Seleucid losses 29 sunk and 13 captured of 89; it gave Rome control of the Aegean.

name: Magnesia
place: Plain of the Hermus, near Magnesia ad Sipylum
commanders_a: Lucius Cornelius Scipio, Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus, Eumenes II
roman_force: Two Roman legions and two of Latin allies of 5,400 men each, about 3,000 cavalry (800 of them Eumenes's), some 3,000 Achaean and Pergamene light infantry, 500 Cretans and 500 Trallians, 2,000 Macedonian and Thracian volunteers guarding the camp, and 16 African elephants, about 30,000 in all (Livy 37.39).
greek_note: Greek speakers (Achaean and Pergamene light troops, Cretans, Macedonian volunteers, Eumenes's horse) came to roughly 15% of the coalition, mostly in allied contingents.
sources: Livy 37.38-44; Appian, Syriaca 30-36; en.wikipedia Battle of Magnesia
note: December 190 or January 189 BCE. Scipio Africanus was ill and absent; Domitius had effective command. Ariarathes IV of Cappadocia sent troops to Antiochus.

name: Amphissa (siege)
place: Amphissa and its citadel, held by the Aetolians
commanders_a: Manius Acilius Glabrio, then Lucius Cornelius Scipio with Scipio Africanus
borderline: A siege broken off by a truce, not by the defence.
roman_force: Glabrio's consular army of 191, two legions with Latin and Italian allies and siege engines, relieved by Lucius Scipio's new army of two legions with some 5,000 volunteer veterans of Africanus (Livy 37.4-7).
greek_note: The Italian consular armies; no Greek contingents are recorded at the siege.
sources: Livy 37.4-7; Polybius 21.4-5
note: Glabrio's rams brought down part of the wall and the townsmen withdrew to the citadel; the Scipios then granted the Aetolians a six-month truce so that the army could march to Asia, and the siege was given up (by the siege rule a defence, hence draw, as at Naupactus).

name: Lamia (siege)
roman_force: Glabrio's proconsular army with siege works (Livy 37.4-5).
greek_note: The Italian consular army.
sources: Livy 37.4-5
note: Stormed on the day the walls were breached; Glabrio then besieged Amphissa until the Scipios arrived.

name: Lycon
place: Near the town of Lycon, in the land of the Bastetani
roman_force: The praetor's army of Further Spain (normal establishment; not described).
greek_note: A praetorian army of Romans and Italian allies.
note: Paullus lost 6,000 men and was driven back to his camp; he beat the Lusitanians the next year (Livy 37.57).

name: Phocaea (siege)
roman_force: Marines and crews of the Roman fleet after Myonessus (Livy 37.31-32).
greek_note: Fleet soldiers, some crews from Greek socii navales.
note: Phocaea had gone over to Antiochus; after failed assaults it surrendered and was sacked by the soldiers against Aemilius's orders.

name: Mount Olympus
place: Mount Olympus in Galatia (Cile Dagi or Alis Dagi)
roman_force: Manlius Vulso's army of about 10,000 legionaries with Latin and Italian allies, velites, Cretan archers, slingers, Trallian and Thracian light troops, and about 2,800 Pergamenes under Attalus and Athenaeus; some 30,000-35,000 in all by Grainger's estimate (Livy 38.12-23).
greek_note: Cretan archers and Achaean and other Greek volunteers served under Roman command; the Pergamene contingent was allied.
sources: Livy 38.18-23; Polybius 21.37; en.wikipedia Galatian War
note: The Galatians held the heights and were broken by the Roman missile troops before the legions stormed the position; Livy's 40,000 killed or captured is considered exaggerated. The mountain is uncertainly identified.

name: Ancyra (Mount Magaba)
place: Mount Magaba, east of Ancyra (probably Elmadag)
roman_force: The same army as at Mount Olympus: legions and Italian allies with light troops and Pergamene allies (Livy 38.24-27).
greek_note: Greek auxiliaries and Pergamene allies were a small part of the force.
sources: Livy 38.24-27; en.wikipedia Galatian War
note: Against the Tectosages and Trocmi; Livy gives about 8,000 killed.

name: Ambracia (siege)
roman_force: Fulvius Nobilior's consular army of two legions with Latin and Italian allies and a siege train, with Epirote support (Livy 38.3-9; Polybius 21.27-28).
greek_note: The consul's Italian army; local Epirote help is mentioned but not as a fighting unit.
sources: Polybius 21.25-30; Livy 38.3-9; en.wikipedia Roman-Seleucid War
note: Famous for the fighting in the Roman mine and the defenders' smoke counter-mine; the city surrendered on terms when the Aetolians sued for peace.

name: Same (siege)
roman_force: Fulvius Nobilior's army with siege works, supported by 100 slingers from Aegium, Patrae and Dyme (Livy 38.28-29).
greek_note: Achaean slingers from Aegium, Patrae and Dyme served with the Romans.
note: Same refused to accept terms and was stormed after a siege of four months; the inhabitants were sold.

name: Thracian ambush
place: A defile on the road beyond Cypsela, near the Hebrus
commanders_a: Gnaeus Manlius Vulso (Quintus Minucius Thermus killed)
borderline: A named ambush only by its region.
roman_force: Manlius Vulso's army returning from Asia with its baggage train (Livy 38.40-41).
greek_note: The legions and Italian allies of the Asian army.
note: The army fought its way through but lost much of its baggage and the legate Minucius Thermus.

name: Mons Auginus
place: Mons Auginus, in the northern Apennines
borderline: A mountain assault in a campaign of subjugation; Livy names the mountain, standard works hardly treat it as a battle.
roman_force: The consul Flaminius's army of two legions with Latin and Italian allies (normal establishment; Livy 39.2).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian consular army.
sources: Livy 39.2
note: Against the Friniates and Apuani; site unknown.

name: Suismontium
place: Mons Ballista and Suismontium, in the northern Apennines
borderline: A mountain assault in a campaign of subjugation, named by Livy only by the mountains.
roman_force: The consul Aemilius Lepidus's army of two legions with Latin and Italian allies (normal establishment; Livy 39.2).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian consular army.
sources: Livy 39.2
note: Against the Friniates; Ballista is sometimes put at Monte Valestra (Reggio Emilia Apennines).

name: Saltus Marcius
place: A wooded pass in the land of the Apuani, later called the Saltus Marcius (probably in the Garfagnana)
roman_force: The consul Marcius's army of legions and Latin allies; it lost 4,000 men, three standards of the second legion and eleven of the Latin allies (Livy 39.20).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian consular army.
sources: Livy 39.20; en.wikipedia Apuani; en.wikipedia Quintus Marcius Philippus (consul 186 BC)
note: A named ambush.

name: Hasta
roman_force: The praetor's army of Further Spain (normal establishment; not described).
greek_note: A praetorian army of Romans and Italian allies.
sources: Livy 39.21
note: Atinius beat the Lusitanians near Hasta (6,000 killed) and then stormed the town, but was mortally wounded in the assault.

name: Calagurris
roman_force: The praetor's army of Hither Spain (normal establishment; not described).
greek_note: A praetorian army of Romans and Italian allies.
sources: Livy 39.21
note: After an indecisive first battle the Celtiberians attacked again near Calagurris and were routed (Livy gives 12,000 killed).

name: Toletum
commanders_b: Gaius Calpurnius Piso, Lucius Quinctius Crispinus
roman_force: The combined praetorian armies of both Spanish provinces, Romans, Latin allies and Spanish auxiliaries (Livy 39.30).
greek_note: Romans, Italian allies and native auxiliaries; no Greek units.
sources: Livy 39.30; en.wikipedia Celtiberian Wars
note: A foragers' clash grew into a battle; the praetors lost about 5,000 men and were driven to their camp. Opponents: Celtiberians, Vettones and Carpetani.

name: Tagus
place: At a ford of the Tagus, near Toletum
commanders_a: Gaius Calpurnius Piso, Lucius Quinctius Crispinus
roman_force: The combined praetorian armies of both Spanish provinces, Roman legionaries, Latin allies and Spanish auxiliaries (Livy 39.30-31).
greek_note: Romans, Italian allies and native auxiliaries; no Greek units.
sources: Livy 39.30-31; en.wikipedia Celtiberian Wars
note: A decisive Roman victory a few days after the defeat near Toletum; Livy says few of the enemy escaped.

name: Urbicua (siege)
borderline: Briefly told; the relief battles are not named.
roman_force: The praetor Fulvius Flaccus's army of Hither Spain, a legion with Latin allies and Spanish auxiliaries (normal establishment).
greek_note: Romans, Italian allies and native auxiliaries.
sources: Livy 40.16; en.wikipedia Celtiberian Wars
note: Flaccus took the town after beating off Celtiberian relief attempts.

name: Aebura
roman_force: Flaccus's army of Roman legionaries, Latin allies and native Spanish auxiliaries, reinforced by 3,000 Roman and 6,000 allied infantry with 500 cavalry; it lost about 200 Romans, 830 allies and 2,400 native auxiliaries (Livy 40.30-32).
greek_note: Livy lists Romans, Latin allies and Spanish auxiliaries; no Greek units.
sources: Livy 40.30-32; en.wikipedia Celtiberian Wars
note: Livy gives 23,000 Celtiberians killed and 4,700 captured; en.wikipedia's Celtiberian Wars article dates it 182.

name: Contrebia
roman_force: Flaccus's army of Roman legionaries, Latin allies and Spanish auxiliaries (Livy 40.33).
greek_note: Romans, Italian allies and native auxiliaries.
sources: Livy 40.33; en.wikipedia Celtiberian Wars
note: The town surrendered, and a Celtiberian relief army arriving late was caught and destroyed (about 12,000 killed).

name: Albingaunum
place: Paullus's camp in the land of the Ingauni, near Albingaunum (Albenga)
borderline: The battle has no name of its own; named here for the Ingaunian town.
roman_force: The proconsul Paullus's army of legions and Latin allies, besieged for some days in its camp (Livy 40.25-28).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian army.
note: Paullus broke out of his blockaded camp and routed the Ingauni (Livy gives 15,000 killed), ending their war.

name: Manlian Pass
place: The Saltus Manlianus, in the Iberian mountains (site unknown)
roman_force: Flaccus's veteran army on its march out of the province, legions with Latin allies, Spanish auxiliaries and Roman and allied cavalry (Livy 40.39-40).
greek_note: Romans, Italian allies and native auxiliaries.
sources: Livy 40.39-40; en.wikipedia Battle of Manlian Pass
note: An ambush that Flaccus turned into a victory (17,000 Celtiberians killed, about 4,400 Roman losses). en.wikipedia's List of Roman battles gives 181, its article 180.

name: Complega
place: Near Complega, a newly fortified Celtiberian town (site unknown)
borderline: Told briefly by Appian alone.
roman_force: Gracchus's praetorian army of Hither Spain, legions with Latin allies and Spanish auxiliaries (normal establishment; Appian gives no numbers).
greek_note: Romans, Italian allies and native auxiliaries.
sources: Appian, Iberica 43; en.wikipedia Celtiberian Wars
note: Soon after the relief of Caravis the Complegans came to Gracchus's camp as suppliants with olive branches and then attacked; he abandoned the camp in feigned flight, fell on them while they plundered it, killed most of them and took Complega and the country around.

name: Caravis
borderline: A relief action told briefly by Appian.
roman_force: Gracchus's praetorian army of Hither Spain, legions with Latin allies and Spanish auxiliaries (normal establishment).
greek_note: Romans, Italian allies and native auxiliaries.
sources: Appian, Iberica 43; en.wikipedia Celtiberian Wars
note: Gracchus relieved the allied town, besieged by some 20,000 Celtiberians.

name: Alce
roman_force: Gracchus's army of legions with Latin allies and Spanish auxiliaries (Livy 40.47-49).
greek_note: Romans, Italian allies and native auxiliaries.
sources: Livy 40.48-49; en.wikipedia Celtiberian Wars
note: Gracchus stormed the Celtiberian camp before Alce (Livy: 9,000 killed, 109 Romans lost) and then took the town.

name: Mons Chaunus
roman_force: Gracchus's army of legions with Latin allies and Spanish auxiliaries (Livy 40.50).
greek_note: Romans, Italian allies and native auxiliaries.
sources: Livy 40.50; en.wikipedia Celtiberian Wars
note: A hard-fought indecisive battle, followed three days later by a second in which the Celtiberians were routed (22,000 killed per Livy).

name: Lacus Timavi
place: The Roman camp near the Timavus springs (Lacus Timavi)
roman_force: The consul Manlius Vulso's army of two legions with Latin allies, 3,000 Gallic auxiliaries under the chief Catmelus, and a supporting fleet (Livy 41.1-4).
greek_note: Romans, Latin allies and Gallic auxiliaries; no Greek units.
sources: Livy 41.1-4; en.wikipedia Histri
note: Opponent: the Histri. They surprised and took the Roman camp, then were caught feasting in it and cut down (8,000 killed) when the legions returned.

name: Nesactium (siege)
commanders_a: Gaius Claudius Pulcher, Marcus Junius Brutus, Aulus Manlius Vulso
roman_force: The consul Claudius's army with the proconsular armies of Junius and Manlius, legions with Latin allies (Livy 41.11).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian army.
sources: Livy 41.11; en.wikipedia Histri
note: Opponent: the Histri. The Romans diverted the river that supplied the town and stormed it; Mutila and Faveria were also taken by assault.

name: Scultenna
roman_force: The consul Claudius's army of legions with Latin allies (Livy 41.12).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian consular army.
sources: Livy 41.12
note: Livy gives 15,000 Ligurians killed.

name: Mutina (siege)
roman_force: The proconsul Claudius's army of legions and Latin allies (Livy 41.16).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian army.
note: The Ligurians had taken the Roman colony late in 177; Claudius stormed it back within three days (8,000 Ligurians killed).

name: Mons Letum
place: Mons Letum, in the Apennines (site unknown)
commanders_a: Quintus Petillius Spurinus (killed), Gaius Valerius Laevinus
roman_force: The consular armies of Petillius and Valerius, legions with Latin allies (Livy 41.18).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian army.
sources: Livy 41.18; Valerius Maximus 1.5.9
note: The consul Petillius was killed leading the assault on the mountain, but the Ligurians were routed (Livy gives 5,000 killed).

name: Carystus (Liguria)
place: Near Carystus, in the land of the Statellates (near Aquae Statiellae)
roman_force: The consul Popillius's army of legions with Latin allies; it lost about 3,000 men (Livy 42.7).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian consular army.
sources: Livy 42.7-9
note: Livy gives 10,000 Statellates killed; their surrender and enslavement by Popillius caused a scandal in Rome.

name: Callinicus
place: The hill Callinicus, near the Roman camp a few km north of Larissa
roman_force: Licinius's army of two legions of 6,000 with 16,000 allied infantry and 800 cavalry, joined by Eumenes's 4,000 foot and 1,000 horse; the legions stayed in camp, and the fighting fell to the Italian cavalry and light infantry on the right, the cavalry and light troops of the Greek allies (Aetolians among them) on the left, 400 Thessalian horse, and Eumenes's 200 Gauls and 300 Cretans (Livy 42.31, 42.55-60).
greek_note: Greek allied cavalry and light infantry formed the whole left wing, so Greek speakers were a large share of the troops engaged, though a minor share of the whole army.
sources: Livy 42.57-60; en.wikipedia Battle of Callinicus; en.wikipedia Third Macedonian War
note: A cavalry battle; the Romans lost about 2,000 foot and 200 horse and moved their camp across the Peneus. Cotys IV led the Odrysian Thracians for Perseus.

name: Phalanna
roman_force: A Roman foraging force, about 800 of whom were trapped on a hill, relieved by the consul with light infantry, cavalry, Numidians and elephants (Livy 42.65-66).
greek_note: Roman and Italian troops with Numidian allies.
sources: Livy 42.65-66; en.wikipedia Third Macedonian War
note: Perseus first captured about 1,000 carts and 600 men, then was driven off when the consul came up; Livy reports a second, much larger version from other sources.

name: Haliartus (siege)
roman_force: About 10,000 socii navales from the praetor Lucretius's fleet, with 2,000 Pergamene troops under Eumenes's brother Athenaeus (Livy 42.63).
greek_note: The assault was made by the fleet's socii navales, recruited largely in the Greek and Oscan coastal cities of southern Italy; the Pergamenes were allies.
sources: Livy 42.63; en.wikipedia Third Macedonian War
note: Haliartus, a Boeotian city that sided with Perseus (with some Macedonian help), was stormed and razed; 2,500 were sold.

name: Uscana
place: Uscana, in the land of the Penestae (near Kicevo)
roman_force: About 8,000 men gathered by the legate Appius Claudius in Illyria, Roman troops with local levies (Livy 43.9-10).
greek_note: Roman troops with Illyrian levies; contingents from the Greek coastal cities served in this command but are not named here.
sources: Livy 43.10; en.wikipedia Third Macedonian War
note: A night attack that failed when the garrison sallied; only about 1,000 escaped.

name: Uscana (siege)
place: Uscana, in the land of the Penestae
roman_force: A garrison of about 4,000, Roman soldiers and Illyrian troops (Livy 43.18-19).
greek_note: Livy describes the garrison as Romans and Illyrians.
sources: Livy 43.18-19; en.wikipedia Third Macedonian War
note: After an assault the garrison capitulated on terms; Perseus disarmed it and sold the townspeople. Livy dates it to Perseus's winter campaign.

name: Heracleum (siege)
place: Heracleum, on the coast below Olympus
roman_force: A detachment of the consul's army, about 2,000 men (Livy 44.8-9).
