greek_note: Roman and Italian legionaries.
sources: Livy 44.8-9; en.wikipedia Third Macedonian War
note: Livy describes the wall being scaled by a shield 'testudo' of the kind young soldiers practised in the circus games.

name: Cassandreia (siege)
roman_force: The praetor Marcius Figulus's fleet with its soldiers, joined by 20 ships of Eumenes and 5 of Prusias II (Livy 44.10-12).
greek_note: Fleet soldiers and crews, some from Greek socii navales; the Pergamene and Bithynian ships were allies.
sources: Livy 44.10-12; en.wikipedia Third Macedonian War
note: The garrison beat off the assault and Gallic auxiliaries arrived by sea from Thessalonica; the siege was given up.

name: Meliboea (siege)
place: Meliboea, on the coast below Ossa
borderline: The siege was abandoned without a battle when a relief force of 2,000 approached.
roman_force: A detachment of about 5,000 men from the consul's army (Livy 44.13).
greek_note: Roman and Italian troops.
sources: Livy 44.13; en.wikipedia Third Macedonian War
note: The Romans burned their siege works and withdrew.

name: Pydna
place: The plain south of Pydna, near Katerini
roman_force: Two legions with Latin and Italian allies (Marrucini, Paeligni, Samnite cavalry are named), Greek, Ligurian and other auxiliaries and 22 elephants: about 29,000-37,000 men (Livy 44.40-42; Plutarch, Aemilius 16-22).
greek_note: Greek allied infantry stood with the Latin and Italian allies on the flanks of the legions, a small share of the army.
sources: Livy 44.36-42; Plutarch, Aemilius 16-22; en.wikipedia Battle of Pydna
note: Dated by the lunar eclipse of the night before. Numidian elephants and troops had been sent by Masinissa; an Athenian decree also mentions Attalid troops.

name: Elpeus
place: The dry bed of the Elpeus (Enipeus) below Mount Olympus, where Perseus held a fortified line
borderline: Holding attacks to pin Perseus while Nasica marched round; Livy's text breaks off in a gap.
roman_force: Paullus's consular army, two legions with Latin and Italian allies and allied auxiliaries, less the picked force sent round by Pythium with Scipio Nasica; the fighting in the river bed fell mainly to the light troops (Livy 44.35).
greek_note: Greek allied auxiliaries (Cretans among them) served with the Italian army, a small share of it.
sources: Livy 44.35; en.wikipedia Third Macedonian War
note: Paullus attacked the Macedonian line in the river bed on successive mornings and drew off at midday; the outcome is lost in a lacuna of Livy. Nasica's success at Pythium then forced Perseus back to Pydna.

name: Pythium
place: The pass of Pythium (Petra) over Olympus
commanders_a: Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Corculum, Quintus Fabius Maximus Aemilianus
roman_force: A picked flanking force: 5,000 men by Livy; by Nasica's own letter (in Plutarch) 3,000 Italian allies and 5,000 of the left wing, with 120 horse and 200 Thracians and Cretans (Livy 44.35; Plutarch, Aemilius 15-16).
greek_note: Only the small Cretan detachment was Greek.
sources: Livy 44.35; Plutarch, Aemilius 15-16
note: Nasica's column turned the Macedonian line on the Elpeus, and Perseus fell back to Pydna.

name: Scodra
roman_force: Two legions (10,400 foot, 600 horse) with 10,000 Italian allied foot and 800 horse, a fleet, and 2,000 foot and 200 horse of the Parthini (Livy 44.21, 44.30-31).
greek_note: Romans, Italian allies and Illyrian Parthini; any Greek element came only from fleet crews.
sources: Livy 44.30-32; en.wikipedia Third Illyrian War
note: The Illyrians sallied and were beaten back at the gates; Gentius asked for a truce and surrendered three days later. The campaign lasted about thirty days.

name: Delminium (siege)
commanders_a: Gaius Marcius Figulus, Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Corculum
roman_force: The consular armies of Marcius Figulus (156) and Scipio Nasica (155), legions with Latin and Italian allies (normal establishment; Appian, Illyrica 11).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian consular army.
sources: Appian, Illyrica 11; Florus 2.25; Livy, Periochae 47
note: Opponent: the Dalmatae. Figulus burned much of the town with fire-darts in 156; Nasica completed its capture in 155.

name: Aegitna
place: Aegitna, on the coast near Antipolis (perhaps Cannes)
roman_force: The consul Opimius's army, assembled at Placentia and marched over the Apennines (Polybius 33.9-10).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian consular army; Massalia, whose colonies were threatened, is not recorded as sending troops.
sources: Polybius 33.8-11; attalus.org
note: Opimius stormed Aegitna, then defeated the Oxybii and the Deciates in the field, on behalf of Massalia's colonies Nicaea and Antipolis.

name: Vulcanalia ambush
place: A wooded defile between Segeda and the land of the Arevaci (site unknown)
roman_force: Nobilior's consular army of nearly 30,000, legions with Latin and Italian allies (Appian, Iberica 45).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian consular army.
sources: Appian, Iberica 45; en.wikipedia Second Celtiberian War
note: Unnamed in Appian; sometimes called the battle of Segeda. About 6,000 Romans fell; Carus and 6,000 of his men were then cut down by the Roman cavalry. The date is the festival of Vulcan in the Roman civil calendar, after which Romans would not fight on that day.

name: Tagus
roman_force: The praetor Mummius's army of Further Spain, Romans and Italian allies (normal establishment; Appian, Iberica 56).
greek_note: A praetorian army of Romans and Italian allies.
sources: Appian, Iberica 56; en.wikipedia Battle of the Tagus (153 BC)
note: Mummius routed the Lusitanians but lost order in the pursuit; they turned, took his camp and killed about 9,000.

name: Ocile
place: Ocile (Okile), across the strait (probably Zilil, near Asilah)
commanders_b: Caucaenus (the Lusitanians south of the Tagus)
roman_force: Mummius's rebuilt praetorian army of Further Spain (Appian, Iberica 57).
greek_note: A praetorian army of Romans and Italian allies.
sources: Appian, Iberica 57; en.wikipedia Lusitanian War
note: Lusitanian raiders who had crossed to Africa were besieging Ocile; Mummius killed many of them and raised the siege. The identification of Ocile is uncertain.

name: Numantia
roman_force: Nobilior's consular army with 300 Numidian cavalry and 10 elephants sent by Masinissa (Appian, Iberica 46).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian consular army with Numidian allies.
sources: Appian, Iberica 46; en.wikipedia Second Celtiberian War
note: The Romans drove the Numantines to their walls, then a wounded elephant panicked the others; the sortie killed about 4,000 Romans.

name: Axinium
borderline: A failed attack on a town, told in one sentence.
roman_force: Nobilior's consular army after its defeat at Numantia (Appian, Iberica 47).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian consular army.
sources: Appian, Iberica 47; en.wikipedia Second Celtiberian War
note: The attack achieved nothing and cost many men.

name: Oxthracae
place: Oxthracae, the largest town of the Lusitanians (site unknown)
borderline: Appian says only that Atilius killed about 700 Lusitanians and took the town; not treated as a battle in modern works.
roman_force: The praetor Atilius's army of Further Spain, Romans and Italian allies (normal establishment; Appian, Iberica 58).
greek_note: A praetorian army of Romans and Italian allies.
sources: Appian, Iberica 58; en.wikipedia Lusitanian War
note: The neighbouring peoples, some of the Vettones among them, then submitted, but rose again when Atilius went into winter quarters. The site is unidentified; the coordinates mark only the region.

name: Pallantia (siege)
borderline: A siege given up for want of supplies; harassing attacks rather than a pitched battle.
roman_force: Lucullus's consular army, the same that had taken Cauca and besieged Intercatia (Appian, Iberica 55).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian consular army.
sources: Appian, Iberica 55; en.wikipedia Celtiberian Wars
note: The Pallantine horsemen harassed his foragers until Lucullus, short of food, raised the siege and retreated under pursuit. Pallantia is usually placed at Palencia; some prefer Palenzuela.

name: Cauca
roman_force: The consul Lucullus's army of legions with Latin and Italian allies (Appian, Iberica 51-52).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian consular army.
sources: Appian, Iberica 51-52; en.wikipedia Second Celtiberian War
note: Opponent: the Vaccaei, not at war with Rome. About 3,000 Caucaei fell fighting at the gates; after their surrender Lucullus's troops massacred the town.

name: Intercatia (siege)
roman_force: Lucullus's consular army (Appian, Iberica 53-54).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian consular army.
sources: Appian, Iberica 53-54; en.wikipedia Second Celtiberian War
note: Roman assaults on the walls failed; Scipio Aemilianus won a single combat and the town made terms, paying cloaks, cattle and hostages. Not taken (by the siege rule a defence; terms favoured Rome).

name: Carthage (siege)
date: 149-146 BCE (the city fell in spring 146 BCE)
commanders_a: Manius Manilius, Lucius Marcius Censorinus, Lucius Calpurnius Piso, Lucius Hostilius Mancinus, Scipio Aemilianus
roman_force: Two consular armies (four legions with Latin and Italian allies) and a fleet: about 40,000-50,000 men with 4,000 cavalry by modern estimate, against Appian's 80,000 foot and 4,000 horse; Numidian cavalry under Gulussa joined later (Appian, Punica 75, 93-135).
greek_note: An Italian army; only the fleet crews (socii navales) included Greeks of southern Italy, and Polybius was present as Scipio's adviser.
sources: Appian, Punica 75-135; Polybius 38-39 (fragments); en.wikipedia Siege of Carthage (Third Punic War); en.wikipedia Third Punic War
note: One entry for the siege: the failed assaults of 149, the fire-ship attack, Mancinus's lodgement and Scipio's night attack on Megara in 147, and the six-day street fighting of spring 146 that ended at the Byrsa. The naval battle of 147 is a separate entry.

name: Nepheris
place: Hasdrubal's camp at Nepheris, south-east of Tunis
roman_force: Manilius's consular army of legions and Italian allies, with Scipio's cavalry squadrons covering the retreat (Appian, Punica 102-104).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian consular army.
sources: Appian, Punica 102-104; en.wikipedia Third Punic War
note: Manilius attacked the strong camp against Scipio's advice and suffered heavily in the withdrawal across a river; a second expedition later that year made no progress.

name: Thrace
borderline: Known only from brief notices; no site is named.
roman_force: Metellus's consular army that had won at Pydna, two legions with allies (en.wikipedia, from Zonaras).
greek_note: An Italian consular army.
sources: Zonaras 9.28; Livy, Periochae 50; en.wikipedia Fourth Macedonian War
note: After Pydna Andriscus raised a new army in Thrace; Metellus forced a battle before the levies were ready and routed it. Andriscus fled to the Thracian chief Byzes, who handed him over.

name: Defeat of Juventius Thalna
borderline: The battle has no name or known site in the sources.
roman_force: The praetor Juventius's army of one legion with allied troops, probably with Greek contingents (Livy, Periochae 50; Florus 1.30; Zonaras 9.28).
greek_note: A small Roman army that may have included Greek allied contingents.
sources: Livy, Periochae 50; Florus 1.30; Zonaras 9.28; en.wikipedia Fourth Macedonian War
note: Juventius was killed and his army almost destroyed, Rome's worst defeat so far by a Hellenistic power.

name: Hippo Diarrhytus (siege)
roman_force: The consul Piso's army of legions and Italian allies with siege engines (Appian, Punica 110).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian consular army.
sources: Appian, Punica 110; en.wikipedia Third Punic War
note: A sortie burned the Roman siege engines and Piso gave up the siege for winter quarters.

name: Aspis (siege)
commanders_b: Lucius Calpurnius Piso, Lucius Hostilius Mancinus
borderline: Briefly told: assaults by land and sea that failed.
roman_force: Piso's army with Mancinus's fleet (Appian, Punica 110).
greek_note: Legions and Italian allies, with fleet crews partly Greek socii navales.
sources: Appian, Punica 110; en.wikipedia Third Punic War

name: Pydna
roman_force: Metellus's consular army of two legions with allies, about 20,000 men by modern estimate (en.wikipedia, from Livy's Periochae and Zonaras).
greek_note: An Italian consular army; the Attalid fleet that supported the advance is not recorded in the battle.
sources: Livy, Periochae 50; Zonaras 9.28; Florus 1.30; en.wikipedia Second Battle of Pydna
note: Andriscus won a first cavalry skirmish, but his cavalry commander Telestes deserted; Metellus then routed his army. Andriscus was beaten again in Thrace and handed over by the Thracian Byzes.

name: Port of Carthage
place: Outside the harbours of Carthage, Gulf of Tunis
commanders_a: Scipio Aemilianus (en.wikipedia names Lucius Hostilius Mancinus)
roman_force: The Roman blockading fleet; its size is not given (Appian, Punica 121-123).
greek_note: Roman fleets of the period were manned largely by socii navales from the Greek and Oscan coastal cities of southern Italy.
sources: Appian, Punica 121-123; en.wikipedia Battle of the Port of Carthage; en.wikipedia Third Punic War
note: The new Carthaginian fleet of some 50 triremes sailed out through a newly cut channel; the first day was indecisive, and in the withdrawal many Carthaginian ships jammed at the quay were sunk or taken. en.wikipedia's infobox calls it a Carthaginian victory; the blockade held.

name: Nepheris
place: The Carthaginian camp and town of Nepheris
roman_force: Scipio's legions and Italian allies, with Gulussa's Numidian cavalry pursuing the fugitives (Appian, Punica 126).
greek_note: A Roman and Latin-Italian army with Numidian allies.
sources: Appian, Punica 126; en.wikipedia Third Punic War
note: The camp was stormed from several sides; Nepheris town surrendered after a siege of about three weeks. Called the Second Battle of Nepheris in en.wikipedia's list.

name: Tribola
place: A wooded pass near Tribola (site unknown, perhaps in the Serrania de Ronda)
roman_force: The praetor Vetilius's army of about 10,000, Romans and Italian allies (Appian, Iberica 63).
greek_note: A praetorian army of Romans and Italian allies.
sources: Appian, Iberica 61-63; en.wikipedia Battle of Tribola; en.wikipedia Lusitanian War
note: A named ambush; about 4,000 Romans fell and 6,000 fled to Carpessus. Afterwards 5,000 Belli and Titthi sent by the quaestor were destroyed. en.wikipedia's Lusitanian War article dates it 148.

name: Chaeronea
commanders_b: about 1,000 picked Arcadians of the Achaean army (no commander named)
borderline: The destruction of a retreating contingent, named only by the place; not in en.wikipedia's Achaean War article.
roman_force: Metellus' army of the province of Macedonia, the force that had just won at Scarpheia: legions with their Italian allies; no numbers are given (Pausanias 7.15.4).
greek_note: A Roman-Italian provincial army; Macedonian auxiliaries may have served, but no Greek contingent is recorded on Metellus' side.
sources: Pausanias 7.15.4; the ancient Greek battles set, Chaeronea 146 BC
note: After Scarpheia, Metellus overtook about a thousand picked Arcadians near Chaeronea and cut them down (Pausanias).

name: Scarpheia
place: Near Scarpheia, eastern Locris, east of Thermopylae
roman_force: Metellus's army of the province of Macedonia, which had just crushed Andriscus: about two legions with their Italian allies (numbers not given by Pausanias).
greek_note: A legionary army from Italy; any Greek-speakers would have come from allied Greek cities of southern Italy or local auxiliaries in Macedonia, none of which are attested.
sources: Pausanias 7.15.2-4; Livy Per. 52; en.wikipedia Battle of Scarpheia
note: Critolaus disappeared after the rout (drowned in the marshes or took poison). Metellus then cut down a force of 1,000 Arcadians near Chaeronea (Pausanias 7.15.4), entered as -146-chaeronea.

name: Corinth
place: Leucopetra on the Isthmus, before Corinth
roman_force: Mummius's consular army of 23,000 infantry and 3,500 cavalry, probably two legions with Italian allies, together with Cretan archers and a Pergamene contingent under Philopoemen sent by Attalus II (Pausanias 7.16.1).
greek_note: Cretan archers and Pergamene troops fought on the Roman side, but the bulk of the army was Roman and Italian.
sources: Pausanias 7.16.1-8; Livy Per. 52; Orosius 5.3; en.wikipedia Battle of Corinth (146 BC)
note: Also called the battle of Leucopetra. The Achaeans had 14,000 foot and 600 horse; a flank attack by 1,000 picked Roman infantry broke them. Corinth was then sacked and destroyed. 'Greek cities' in allies = the Cretans.

name: Mount Venus
place: The 'mountain of Venus' covered with olive trees, beyond the Tagus (probably the Sierra de San Vicente)
roman_force: The praetor's army brought from Rome, 10,000 foot and 1,300 horse (Appian, Iberica 64), with the provincial troops of Hispania Ulterior.
greek_note: Legions and Italian allies levied in Italy; Greek-speakers would have been few.
sources: Appian, Iberica 64; en.wikipedia Lusitanian War (the 'raid of Carpetania')
note: Viriathus first destroyed a detachment of 4,000 sent in pursuit, then defeated Plautius himself when he attacked the camp on the mountain. Wikipedia's Lusitanian War article calls the campaign the 'raid of Carpetania'; its list of Lusitanian wars dates its 'Battle of Mount Venus' to 143 BCE (the second fight there, entered separately).

name: Baecor
place: Pursuit of Viriathus to Baecor, in the upper Baetis region
borderline: Appian names Baecor as the place to which Fabius pursued Viriathus after defeating him, not as the name of a battle.
roman_force: The consular army of Fabius Aemilianus, about 15,000 foot and 2,000 horse, mostly newly levied men (Appian, Iberica 65).
greek_note: A freshly raised consular army of Romans and Italian allies.
sources: Appian, Iberica 65; en.wikipedia Lusitanian Wars
note: Fabius put Viriathus to flight, took two of his towns and killed many of his men in the pursuit to Baecor; site unidentified.

name: Mount Venus
place: The mountain of Venus (probably the Sierra de San Vicente)
roman_force: The praetor's provincial army of Hispania Ulterior, legions and Italian allies (no numbers given).
greek_note: A provincial army of legions and Italian allies; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, Iberica 66; en.wikipedia List of wars involving the Lusitanians (Battle of Mount Venus, 143 BC)
note: Viriathus fell back to the mountain of Venus, then turned on his pursuers, killed about 1,000 men and took some standards, driving the Romans back to their camp.

name: Itucca
borderline: Appian describes a battle followed by repeated attacks that drove the Romans back to Itucca; the name is a place-name label.
roman_force: Servilianus's consular army of about 18,000 foot and 1,600 horse, with ten elephants and 300 horsemen sent from Africa by the Numidian king Micipsa (Appian, Iberica 67).
greek_note: Legions and Italian allies with a small Numidian contingent; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, Iberica 67; en.wikipedia Lusitanian Wars
note: About 3,000 Romans were killed. Itucci is probably the site at Torreparedones near Baena, but the identification is uncertain.

name: Erisana
place: Erisana (Erisane), a town of Viriathus besieged by the Romans
roman_force: Servilianus's proconsular army, the same force of about 18,000 foot and 1,600 horse he had led the year before, with its Numidian elephants (Appian, Iberica 67-69).
greek_note: Legions and Italian allies; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, Iberica 69; Livy Per. 54; en.wikipedia Lusitanian Wars
note: Viriathus slipped into the besieged town by night, attacked the siege works at dawn and drove the Romans into a place hemmed in by cliffs, then let them go in return for a treaty recognizing him as a 'friend of the Roman people' (ratified 140). Dated 142 in Wikipedia and 140 in some popular accounts; 141 (Servilianus's proconsular year) follows Appian's sequence. Site unidentified.

name: Numantia
place: Numantia, on the Duero near Garray
roman_force: The consular army of Quintus Pompeius, given by Appian as 30,000 foot and 2,000 horse, later reinforced with raw recruits from Italy (Appian, Iberica 76-78).
greek_note: Legions and Italian allies; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, Iberica 76-79; Livy Per. 54; en.wikipedia Numantine War
note: Pompeius was beaten in an attack on Numantia in 141; his blockade of 140 failed through sorties, cold and disease, and he made a secret peace that the Senate later disowned. Entered as one siege entry.

name: Termantia
roman_force: The consular army of Quintus Pompeius (30,000 foot and 2,000 horse at the start of the campaign, according to Appian).
greek_note: Legions and Italian allies; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, Iberica 77; Diodorus 33.16-17; en.wikipedia Numantine War
note: Pompeius turned on Termantia after failing at Numantia and was beaten in several engagements, losing some 700 men in one of them (Appian).

name: Baetis
place: a crossing of the Baetis (Guadalquivir), on the Lusitanians' return from their raid on Saguntum
borderline: Appian describes a pursuit at the river crossing that wore down Tautalus' army until it surrendered, not a named battle.
roman_force: Caepio's army of Hispania Ulterior, legions with Italian allies and Spanish auxiliaries; no numbers are given (Appian, Iberica 75).
greek_note: Legions, Italian allies and Spanish auxiliaries; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, Iberica 75; en.wikipedia Lusitanian War
note: Tautalus, Viriathus' successor, had been repulsed at Saguntum; his surrender ended the Lusitanian War. 'other' in languages = Iberian.

name: Numantia
place: before the walls of Numantia, on the Duero near Garray
borderline: Not a separately named battle in en.wikipedia's Numantine War article; known from Frontinus and the Livian epitome.
roman_force: Popillius' consular army of legions and Italian allies (numbers not given), which tried to storm Numantia with scaling-ladders and was attacked in the rear by a Numantine sortie (Frontinus 3.17.9).
greek_note: Legions and Italian allies; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Frontinus, Strategemata 3.17.9; Livy, Per. 55 (not checked online)
note: The walls seemed undefended; as the Romans climbed down again, the Numantines sallied out and fell on their rear. Distinct from Pompeius' defeats (-141-numantia) and Mancinus' (-137-numantia).

name: Numantia
commanders_b: Gaius Hostilius Mancinus (with his quaestor Tiberius Gracchus)
roman_force: The consular army of Mancinus, more than 20,000 Roman soldiers besides slaves and camp followers (Plutarch, Tiberius Gracchus 5-7).
greek_note: Legions and Italian allies; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, Iberica 80; Plutarch, Tiberius Gracchus 5-7; Livy Per. 55; en.wikipedia Numantine War
note: After repeated defeats before Numantia Mancinus withdrew by night, was surrounded and capitulated; Tiberius Gracchus negotiated the treaty, which the Senate repudiated, handing Mancinus over to the Numantines. Wikipedia's Numantine War article dates it 136; Mancinus was consul in 137.

name: Pallantia (siege)
place: Pallantia, city of the Vaccaei (probably Palencia)
commanders_b: Marcus Aemilius Lepidus Porcina, Decimus Junius Brutus (Callaicus)
roman_force: The armies of the two Spanish provinces, the proconsul Lepidus's of Citerior joined by Brutus's of Ulterior: legions and Italian allies (no numbers given).
greek_note: Legions and Italian allies; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, Iberica 80-83; Livy Per. 56; en.wikipedia Decimus Junius Brutus Callaicus
note: Lepidus attacked the Vaccaei without the Senate's sanction; the siege failed for lack of supplies and the Romans lost heavily in a disorderly night retreat. Dated 137 in some accounts. 'Celtiberians' here = the Vaccaei. Pallantia may also be Palenzuela.

name: Numantia (siege)
place: Numantia, on the Duero near Garray, enclosed by Scipio's ring of seven camps and a wall
commanders_a: Publius Cornelius Scipio Aemilianus (with Jugurtha, Gaius Marius)
roman_force: About 60,000 men: some 20,000 Romans with about 40,000 allies, including Iberian contingents and the Numidian force of Jugurtha with archers, slingers and twelve elephants, plus volunteers and Scipio's band of 500 friends (Appian, Iberica 84, 89, 97).
greek_note: The army was Roman, Italian, Iberian and Numidian; no Greek contingent is attested.
sources: Appian, Iberica 84-98; Livy Per. 57-59; en.wikipedia Siege of Numantia
note: The town fell by starvation in summer 133; most survivors killed themselves and the rest were enslaved. 'Iberians' in allies = Scipio's Spanish allied contingents; 'other' in languages = Iberian.

name: Tauromenium (siege)
commanders_b: The rebel garrison of Eunus's kingdom
roman_force: A consular army of legions and Italian allies sent to Sicily, with whatever Sicilian levies the province supplied (no numbers given).
greek_note: The legions came from Italy; Greek-speaking Sicilian levies, who had fought the rebels from the start, probably served alongside them.
sources: Diodorus 34/35.2.20-21; Orosius 5.9; en.wikipedia First Servile War
note: Calpurnius Piso besieged the town without success in 133; Rupilius starved it out and took it in 132 through treachery. The rebels were mainly slaves from the Greek East (Eunus, a Syrian, styled himself King Antiochus).

name: Enna (siege)
roman_force: Rupilius's consular army of legions and Italian allies, with Sicilian levies (no numbers given).
greek_note: The legions came from Italy; Greek-speaking Sicilian levies probably served alongside them.
sources: Diodorus 34/35.2.21-23; Orosius 5.9; Valerius Maximus 2.7.9; en.wikipedia First Servile War
note: Cleon fell in a sally against the siege lines; the city was betrayed. Eunus fled, was captured and died in prison at Morgantina.

name: Leucae
place: Near Leucae, between Phocaea and Smyrna
commanders_b: Publius Licinius Crassus Dives Mucianus (captured and killed)
roman_force: The consul Crassus's army from Italy (size not recorded), with contingents of the client kings Nicomedes II of Bithynia, Mithridates V of Pontus, Ariarathes V of Cappadocia and Pylaemenes of Paphlagonia (Eutropius 4.20; Orosius 5.10).
greek_note: The war was fought largely with the levies of the Greek cities of Asia and of the Hellenistic client kingdoms, which the sources name as Crassus's helpers.
sources: Strabo 14.1.38; Justin 36.4; Eutropius 4.20; Orosius 5.10; Valerius Maximus 3.2.12; en.wikipedia Eumenes III
note: 'Pergamon' here = the rebel claimant Aristonicus (Eumenes III) and his army of Pergamenes, freed slaves and Thracian mercenaries. Crassus was captured (by Thracians, Valerius Maximus) and killed, early 130. Ariarathes V also died in this war.

name: Stratonicea
place: Stratonicea on the Caicus, where Aristonicus took refuge after his defeat
roman_force: The consul Perperna's army (size not recorded), fighting alongside the forces of the Greek cities and client kings of Asia.
greek_note: The Roman effort in Asia rested heavily on the levies of the Greek cities and Hellenistic client kings.
sources: Strabo 14.1.38; Justin 36.4; Florus 1.35; Eutropius 4.20; en.wikipedia Eumenes III
note: Perperna defeated Aristonicus in their first encounter (130), then besieged him in Stratonicea and starved him into surrender (129). The battle site is disputed; one entry for battle and siege.

name: Entremont (siege)
place: Entremont, oppidum of the Salluvii, just north of Aix-en-Provence
borderline: The sources record Sextius's defeat of the Salluvii; the capture of Entremont is known mainly from archaeology (destruction layer, siege missiles).
roman_force: A consular army of legions and Italian allies sent at the request of Massalia (no numbers given).
greek_note: Legions and Italian allies; the war was fought on behalf of Greek Massalia, but no Massaliote troops are attested in the field.
sources: Livy Per. 61; Diodorus 34/35.23; Strabo 4.1.5; en.wikipedia Battle of Vindalium (background)
note: Date 123 or 122. 'Gauls' = the Salluvii (Celto-Ligurian). Sextius founded Aquae Sextiae nearby.

name: Isere
place: Confluence of the Isere (Isara) and the Rhone, near Valence
commanders_a: Quintus Fabius Maximus (Allobrogicus), Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus
roman_force: The consular army of Fabius Maximus joined with Domitius's, fewer than 30,000 men (Strabo 4.1.11), legions and Italian allies, probably with Domitius's elephants.
greek_note: Legions and Italian allies; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Livy Per. 61; Strabo 4.1.11, 4.2.3; Orosius 5.14; Appian, Celtica 12; en.wikipedia Battle of the Isere River
note: 'Gauls' = the Arverni and Allobroges with remaining Salluvii; the ancient figures of 120,000-200,000 Gauls and huge Gallic losses are surely exaggerated. Name written without accent (Isère). Led to the annexation of the Rhone valley.

name: Vindalium
place: Vindalium, near the Rhone-Sorgue confluence (probably Mourre de Seve, Sorgues), north-east of Avignon
roman_force: The proconsul Domitius's army of legions and Italian allies with war elephants, which panicked the Allobrogian horses (Orosius 5.13; Florus 1.37).
greek_note: Legions and Italian allies; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Livy Per. 61; Orosius 5.13.2; Florus 1.37; en.wikipedia Battle of Vindalium
note: Orosius gives 20,000 Allobroges killed and 3,000 captured. 'Gauls' = the Allobroges.

name: Lete
borderline: Known from an honorific inscription; not a named battle in the literary sources.
roman_force: The garrison army of the province of Macedonia under the quaestor, after the governor Sextus Pompeius had fallen in battle (the Lete decree).
greek_note: The provincial army was Roman and Italian; Macedonian (Greek-speaking) local troops may have served, but the decree's details are uncertain.
sources: Lete decree for Marcus Annius (Syll.3 700); en.wikipedia Scordisci
note: The decree honours Annius for defeating the invading Gauls (Scordisci) after the death of the praetor Sextus Pompeius, and again in a second engagement.

name: Thrace (defeat of Cato)
borderline: No conventional name and no recorded site: the Scordisci destroyed Cato's army somewhere in Thrace.
roman_force: The consul Cato's army sent to Macedonia, legions and Italian allies with the provincial forces; it was destroyed (Livy, Per. 63; Eutropius 4.24).
greek_note: A consular army from Italy; Macedonian (Greek-speaking) provincial troops may have served, but none are recorded.
sources: Livy, Per. 63; Eutropius 4.24
note: 'Gauls' = the Scordisci. Cato escaped; he was later convicted of extortion in Macedonia (Velleius 2.8.1).

name: Noreia
roman_force: The consul Carbo's army, legions and Italian allies (size not given in the sources).
greek_note: A consular army of Romans and Italian allies; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Livy Per. 63; Strabo 5.1.8; Appian, Celtica 13; Velleius 2.12; en.wikipedia Battle of Noreia
note: Carbo tried to ambush the Cimbri after a parley and was himself routed; a storm saved part of the army. Carbo was consul in 113; the Wikipedia Cimbrian War article implies 112.

name: Suthul
place: Before the town of Suthul, where Jugurtha's treasury lay, probably near Calama (Guelma)
roman_force: The consular army of Spurius Albinus left under his brother Aulus, perhaps 40,000 men in three legions with allies, including a Ligurian cohort and two squadrons of Thracian cavalry who deserted to Jugurtha (Sallust, Jugurtha 38).
greek_note: Legions and Italian allies with Ligurian and Thracian auxiliaries; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Sallust, Jugurtha 37-39; Livy Per. 64; en.wikipedia Battle of Suthul
note: Aulus's siege of Suthul failed; Jugurtha lured him away and stormed his camp by night, and the survivors passed under the yoke. The Suthul-Calama identification is doubted by some. 'other' in languages = Ligurian.

name: Gallia Narbonensis (defeat of Silanus)
borderline: No conventional name and no recorded site: the Cimbri defeated Silanus in the Roman province beyond the Alps.
roman_force: The consul Silanus' consular army, Roman legions with Italian allies; no numbers are given.
greek_note: A consular army of Romans and Italian allies; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Livy, Per. 65; en.wikipedia Cimbrian War
note: The Cimbri had asked Rome for land to settle before the battle (Livy, Per. 65).

name: Muthul
place: Plain by the river Muthul (probably the Mellegue), near the Algerian-Tunisian border
commanders_a: Quintus Caecilius Metellus (Numidicus), Gaius Marius, Publius Rutilius Rufus
roman_force: Metellus's consular army, the remnants of Albinus's army retrained and reinforced: legions and Italian allied cohorts with cavalry, slingers and archers (Sallust, Jugurtha 43-50).
greek_note: Legions and Italian allies with light auxiliaries; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Sallust, Jugurtha 48-53; en.wikipedia Battle of the Muthul
note: Jugurtha ambushed the Roman column on the march; Metellus beat off the Numidian infantry and Rutilius routed Bomilcar's force and its 44 elephants. Jugurtha escaped and the war went on, so the Wikipedia list calls it indecisive and its infobox a Numidian strategic success; on the field the Romans won.

name: Zama (siege)
roman_force: Metellus's consular army of legions and Italian allies (Sallust gives no numbers).
greek_note: Legions and Italian allies; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Sallust, Jugurtha 56-61; en.wikipedia Jugurthine War
note: The assaults failed while Jugurtha attacked the Roman camp and Marius's force at Sicca; Metellus raised the siege and went into winter quarters.

name: Thala (siege)
commanders_b: Jugurtha (escaped), Roman deserters in the garrison
roman_force: Metellus's proconsular army of legions and Italian allies, marching across the desert with water carried on pack animals (Sallust, Jugurtha 75).
greek_note: Legions and Italian allies; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Sallust, Jugurtha 75-76; en.wikipedia Jugurthine War
note: Thala fell after a forty-day siege; Roman deserters inside burned the palace and themselves. The identification with modern Thala is uncertain.

name: Burdigala
place: In the territory of the Nitiobriges (near Agen), on the Garonne above Burdigala
commanders_b: Lucius Cassius Longinus (killed), Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus (killed), Gaius Popillius Laenas
roman_force: The consul Cassius's army, legions and Italian allies (Wikipedia gives about 40,000; the sources give no figure).
greek_note: A consular army of Romans and Italian allies; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Livy Per. 65; Caesar, Gallic War 1.7, 1.12; Orosius 5.15.23; en.wikipedia Battle of Burdigala
note: Wikipedia names it after Burdigala (Bordeaux), but Livy Per. 65 places it in the land of the Nitiobriges, hence Agen. 'Gauls' = the Tigurini, a canton of the Helvetii allied with the Cimbri. The survivors under Popillius passed under the yoke.

name: Capsa (siege)
borderline: A surprise attack at dawn after a desert march; the town surrendered almost at once, so there was little real fighting.
roman_force: Marius's consular army, Metellus's veterans with the new levies including the capite censi, and Latin and allied cavalry (Sallust, Jugurtha 84-91).
greek_note: Legions and Italian allies; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Sallust, Jugurtha 89-91; en.wikipedia Jugurthine War
note: Marius had the town burned and the adult males killed.

name: Mulucha (siege)
place: A rock fortress near the river Muluccha (probably the Moulouya), holding Jugurtha's treasure
roman_force: Marius's army of legions and Italian allies with auxiliary cohorts; a Ligurian private of the auxiliary cohorts found the path up the rock that let a picked party take the fort from behind (Sallust, Jugurtha 93-94).
greek_note: Legions and Italian allies with Ligurian auxiliaries; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Sallust, Jugurtha 92-94; en.wikipedia Jugurthine War
note: Wikipedia dates it late 107; Sulla, quaestor of 107, arrived during the siege. Whether Sallust's Muluccha is the Moulouya is disputed, so the site is only regional. 'other' in languages = Ligurian.

name: Cirta (first battle)
place: On the march towards winter quarters, on two hills in the region of Cirta
borderline: Sallust's first of two battles near Cirta; Wikipedia's 'Second Battle of Cirta' article treats it as part of one action.
roman_force: Marius's army of legions and Italian allies, with Sulla's cavalry and Manlius's slingers, archers and Ligurian cohorts (Sallust, Jugurtha 97-100).
greek_note: Legions and Italian allies with Ligurian and light auxiliaries; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Sallust, Jugurtha 97-99; Orosius 5.15; en.wikipedia Second Battle of Cirta
note: Attacked late in the day, Marius held two hills overnight and at dawn routed the Numidians and Mauretanians, who were sleeping off their celebrations. Dated 107 in Wikipedia's Jugurthine War article.

name: Cirta (second battle)
roman_force: Marius's army marching in square: legions and Italian allies, Sulla's cavalry on the right, Manlius with the slingers, archers and Ligurian cohorts on the left (Sallust, Jugurtha 100-101); Wikipedia gives 30,000-40,000.
greek_note: Legions and Italian allies with Ligurian and light auxiliaries; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Sallust, Jugurtha 100-101; Orosius 5.15; en.wikipedia Second Battle of Cirta
note: The Numidian, Gaetulian and Mauretanian army attacked the Roman column from all sides and was routed. Bocchus then opened the talks that led to Jugurtha's betrayal to Sulla (105).

name: Arausio
commanders_b: Quintus Servilius Caepio (proconsul), Gnaeus Mallius Maximus (consul)
roman_force: Two armies in separate camps, the proconsul Caepio's and the consul Mallius's, legions and Italian allies; Livy (after Valerius Antias) gives 80,000 soldiers and 40,000 servants and camp followers killed (Per. 67).
greek_note: Two consular armies of Romans and Italian allies; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Livy Per. 67; Plutarch, Lucullus 27; Orosius 5.16; Dio fr. 91; Granius Licinianus 33; en.wikipedia Battle of Arausio
note: The date is from Plutarch (Lucullus 27). Shortly before, the legate Marcus Aurelius Scaurus's force was overwhelmed and he was captured and killed (not entered separately). The casualty figures are generally thought inflated.

name: Heraclea
place: near Heraclea (Minoa), on the south coast of Sicily
commanders_a: the rebel slaves of the district of Heraclea, who soon chose Salvius (Tryphon) as king
commanders_b: a detachment of 600 soldiers sent by the praetor Publius Licinius Nerva
borderline: No conventional battle name; the place is given only as near Heraclea.
roman_force: 600 soldiers sent by the praetor Nerva from the Roman garrison of Sicily (Diodorus 36.4); their origin is not recorded.
greek_note: The detachment came from the praetor's forces in Sicily; whether its men were Italians or Greek-speaking Sicilians is not recorded.
sources: Diodorus 36.4 (Photius' epitome); en.wikipedia Second Servile War
note: The rebels held a strong position and destroyed the detachment; the victory brought in more slaves and the rising spread (en.wikipedia: 'beaten and slaughtered').

name: Morgantina
place: Before Morgantina, besieged by the rebels
roman_force: The praetor's provincial force, largely the militia of the Sicilian cities with some troops from Italy (Diodorus 36.4).
greek_note: Diodorus describes Nerva's army as raised in Sicily, whose cities were Greek-speaking.
sources: Diodorus 36.4.5-8; en.wikipedia Second Servile War
note: Salvius routed the relief force and took its camp; the fate of Morgantina itself is told differently (Wikipedia says it fell; Diodorus has the defenders hold out with the help of slaves promised their freedom).

name: Scirthaea
place: Near Scirthaea, west-central Sicily, some 12 miles from the Roman camp
roman_force: About 17,000 men: 14,000 Romans and Italians, 800 Bithynians, Thessalians and Acarnanians, 600 Lucanians under Cleptius and 600 others (Diodorus 36.8.1).
greek_note: Thessalian and Acarnanian contingents (with Bithynians, 800 in all) fought on the Roman side, a small fraction of the army.
sources: Diodorus 36.8; Florus 2.7; en.wikipedia Second Servile War
note: Athenion was wounded and feigned death; about 20,000 rebels were killed (Diodorus) and the rest fled to Triocala. 'Greek cities' in allies = the Thessalians and Acarnanians.

name: Triocala (siege)
roman_force: Lucullus's army of about 17,000 Romans, Italians, Lucanians, Bithynians, Thessalians and Acarnanians (Diodorus 36.8.1).
greek_note: The same army as at Scirthaea, with small Thessalian and Acarnanian contingents.
sources: Diodorus 36.8-9; en.wikipedia Second Servile War
note: The siege made no progress; learning he was superseded, Lucullus burned his works and disbanded his army. The site of Triocala at Caltabellotta is generally accepted.

name: Sicily (defeat of Servilius)
borderline: No conventional name: a surprise attack on the praetor's camp, site unknown.
roman_force: The praetor Servilius' provincial forces, raised after his predecessor Lucullus had burned his siege works and disbanded his army; no numbers are given.
greek_note: The sources do not say whether Servilius' army was Italian or raised from the Greek-speaking Sicilian cities.
sources: Diodorus 36.9 (Photius' epitome); en.wikipedia Second Servile War
note: Athenion surprised Servilius' camp and routed and dispersed his army; the revolt went on until the consul Aquillius arrived.

name: Aquae Sextiae
place: Near Aquae Sextiae (Aix-en-Provence), probably in the plain towards Pourrieres below Mont Sainte-Victoire
roman_force: Marius's reformed army, perhaps six legions with Italian allies and auxiliaries (modern estimates 32,000-40,000); Ligurian auxiliaries opened the first fight against the Ambrones, and Marcellus led 3,000 men in the decisive ambush (Plutarch, Marius 19-21).
greek_note: Legions, Italian allies and Ligurian auxiliaries; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Plutarch, Marius 18-21; Livy Per. 68; Velleius 2.12; Orosius 5.16; en.wikipedia Battle of Aquae Sextiae
note: Two engagements: first the clash with the Ambrones at the river, then, two days later, the main battle against the Teutones. 'Cimbri and Teutones' = the Teutones and Ambrones. 'other' in languages = Ligurian. Wikipedia's coordinates are at Aix itself.

name: Tridentum
roman_force: Catulus's consular army of legions and Italian allies, about 20,000 men (Plutarch, Marius 25, gives 20,300 the next year); the primus pilus Gnaeus Petreius of Atina won the grass crown for breaking out with his legion (Pliny, NH 22.11).
greek_note: A consular army of Romans and Italian allies; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Plutarch, Marius 23; Pliny, NH 22.11; Livy Per. 68; en.wikipedia Battle of Tridentum
note: Catulus abandoned the Adige line and fell back south of the Po; a garrison left in a fort across the river was overpowered and let go on terms by the Cimbri (Plutarch). Counted as a Cimbric success (Roman withdrawal); Wikipedia calls it a Roman tactical withdrawal.

name: Vercellae
place: The Raudine Plain (Campi Raudii), near Vercellae
commanders_a: Gaius Marius, Quintus Lutatius Catulus, Lucius Cornelius Sulla (cavalry)
roman_force: Marius's 32,000 men and Catulus's 20,300 (Plutarch, Marius 25, from Sulla's memoirs), legions and Italian allies, with cavalry under Sulla.
greek_note: Two consular armies of Romans and Italian allies; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Plutarch, Marius 24-27; Livy Per. 68; Velleius 2.12; Florus 1.38; Orosius 5.16; en.wikipedia Battle of Vercellae
note: 'Cimbri and Teutones' = the Cimbri. Site disputed (near Vercelli; Rovigo and other sites have been proposed). Marius gave citizenship to two cohorts from Camerinum for their valour in this war (Valerius Maximus 5.2.8).

name: Sicily (death of Athenion)
borderline: No conventional name: the decisive battle of the war, in which Aquillius is said to have killed Athenion with his own hand; site unknown.
roman_force: The consul Aquillius' army from Italy, legions with Italian allies; no numbers are given.
greek_note: A consular army from Italy; Sicilian (Greek-speaking) levies may have served, but none are recorded.
sources: Diodorus 36.10; Florus 2.7; en.wikipedia Second Servile War
note: The last 1,000 rebels (under Satyrus, Diodorus) surrendered in 100 BCE and were sent to fight beasts at Rome; there was no battle in 100 BCE.

name: Castulo
place: Castulo (near Linares, Jaen) and a neighbouring Oretanian town
commanders_a: Quintus Sertorius (military tribune under Titus Didius)
commanders_b: the people of Castulo and their Oretanian neighbours
borderline: A night attack on the winter quarters and a reprisal raid on the attackers' town; no conventional battle name.
roman_force: Part of Titus Didius' army wintering in Castulo, legionaries of the province of Hispania Citerior, rallied by the military tribune Sertorius after a night attack on their quarters (Plutarch, Sertorius 3).
greek_note: Legionaries of the Spanish province; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Plutarch, Sertorius 3.3-5 (Perrin's note dates it to 97 BC)
note: Plutarch calls Castulo a Celtiberian city; the attackers came from the neighbouring Oritani (Oretani). Sertorius killed those who had entered, dressed his men in their armour, took the Oretanian town by surprise and sold the survivors.

name: Colenda (siege)
date: c. 97-96 BCE (nine months; Appian gives no year)
place: Colenda, a Celtiberian town of uncertain site (Cuellar, Segovia, has been suggested)
borderline: A nine-month siege ending in the town's fall; Appian does not describe assaults or sorties, so it may fail the siege rule.
roman_force: Didius' proconsular army of Hispania Citerior, legions with Italian allies; no numbers are given (Appian, Iberica 99-100).
greek_note: Legions and Italian allies; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, Iberica 99-100; en.wikipedia Titus Didius
note: The inhabitants were sold into slavery. Didius also killed some 20,000 Arevaci in an unnamed battle and moved Termes down from its hill (Appian); neither is entered.

name: Cappadocia (Sulla)
commanders_b: Gordius (for the Pontic-backed king Ariarathes IX); an Armenian force that came to his aid
borderline: Fighting without a named battle: Plutarch says only that Sulla killed many Cappadocians and still more Armenians, drove out Gordius and restored Ariobarzanes.
roman_force: Few Roman troops of his own; Sulla relied on allied levies who joined him eagerly (Plutarch, Sulla 5.3), presumably from Cilicia and the client states and Greek cities of Asia Minor.
greek_note: Plutarch says Sulla used allies rather than his own few soldiers; in Cilicia and Asia Minor these were largely Greek-speaking.
sources: Plutarch, Sulla 5.3; the ancient Greek battles set, Cappadocia (Sulla) 96 BC
note: The date is disputed: 96 BCE (Badian) or 92 BCE. Sulla then met the Parthian envoy Orobazus on the Euphrates. 'other' in languages = the Anatolian languages of the allies.

name: Tolenus River
commanders_b: Publius Rutilius Lupus (consul, killed), Gaius Marius (legate)
roman_force: The consul Rutilius's northern army of newly raised citizen legions, crossing in two columns (Rutilius's and Marius's) on separate bridges (Appian, BC 1.43).
greek_note: Roman citizen and Latin troops; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, BC 1.43; Ovid, Fasti 6.563-566; Orosius 5.18; en.wikipedia Battle of the Tolenus River
note: Rutilius was ambushed after crossing and killed with about 8,000 men; Marius, seeing the bodies float downstream, crossed and took Scato's camp the same day. Some place the battle on the Liris.

name: Aesernia
roman_force: The consul's southern army, newly levied legions of Roman citizens with contingents of the loyal Latin colonies (no numbers given); about 2,000 were killed (Appian, BC 1.41).
greek_note: Roman citizens and Latins; the loyal Greek cities of the south contributed little to the land armies.
sources: Appian, BC 1.41; Orosius 5.18; en.wikipedia Battle of Aesernia
note: Caesar was trying to relieve the besieged Latin colony of Aesernia. Orosius says he then rebuilt his army with Gallic and African troops.

name: Aesernia (siege)
commanders_b: Lucius Cornelius Scipio, Lucius Acilius, Marcus Claudius Marcellus
roman_force: The garrison and colonists of the Latin colony of Aesernia, with the Roman troops under Marcellus (no numbers given).
greek_note: A Latin colony and its Roman garrison.
sources: Appian, BC 1.41; Livy Per. 73; Diodorus 37.19; en.wikipedia Social War (91-87 BC)
note: Scipio and Acilius escaped disguised as slaves; the town was starved into surrender late in 90 and became an Italian stronghold. Commanders of the besiegers are not securely attested.

name: Grumentum
roman_force: A Roman detachment of the southern army under the legate Crassus; about 800 were lost (Appian, BC 1.41).
greek_note: Roman and Latin troops; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, BC 1.41; en.wikipedia Social War (91-87 BC)
note: Crassus fled into Grumentum after the defeat; Wikipedia's Social War article records Grumentum's capture by the rebels.

name: Acerrae
place: Before Acerrae, besieged by the Samnites
roman_force: The consul's rebuilt army: Roman and Latin troops reinforced by 10,000 Gallic infantry and Numidian and Mauretanian horse and foot (Appian, BC 1.42); many Numidians deserted when Papius paraded Jugurtha's son Oxyntas.
greek_note: Roman, Latin, Gallic and African troops; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, BC 1.42; Orosius 5.18; en.wikipedia Battle of Acerrae
note: Papius attacked the Roman camp and was beaten off by a cavalry charge, losing about 6,000 men; the first Roman success of the war. The siege of Acerrae went on.

name: Fucine Lake
place: In the Marsic country, near the Fucine Lake
commanders_b: Marsi and Marrucini (Herius Asinius, praetor of the Marrucini, killed)
borderline: The site is given as near the Fucine Lake by Wikipedia; Appian places the fight among vineyards and walls without naming a place.
roman_force: Marius's northern army (the late Rutilius's legions) with Sulla's southern force taking the enemy in the flank (Appian, BC 1.46).
greek_note: Roman citizen and Latin troops; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, BC 1.46; Livy Per. 73; Plutarch, Marius 33; en.wikipedia Social War (91-87 BC)
note: Appian gives 6,000 Marsi killed and 7,000 disarmed.

name: Teanum Sidicinum
place: A rocky defile near Teanum Sidicinum (Teano)
roman_force: The consul's southern army, Romans and Latins with Gallic and African auxiliaries (about 30,000 foot and 5,000 horse after its reinforcement, according to historyofwar.org's reading of Appian).
greek_note: Roman, Latin, Gallic and African troops; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, BC 1.45; historyofwar.org Battle of Teanum Sidicinum
note: Caesar, ill, escaped in a litter to Teanum; most of his army was lost or threw away its arms.

name: Mons Falernus
commanders_a: Titus Lafrenius, Gaius Vidacilius, Publius Ventidius
roman_force: Pompeius Strabo's army of Picenum, Roman citizen legions raised largely from his own clients in Picenum (no numbers given).
greek_note: Roman citizen troops; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, BC 1.47; en.wikipedia Social War (91-87 BC); historyofwar.org
note: Strabo was beaten and fell back on Firmum, where he was besieged. Possibly fought before the Tolenus; the site is uncertain.

name: Firmum
commanders_a: Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo, Servius Sulpicius Galba
roman_force: Strabo's besieged army breaking out of Firmum while a relief force under Sulpicius fell on the besiegers' rear (Appian, BC 1.47).
greek_note: Roman citizen troops; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, BC 1.47; en.wikipedia Social War (91-87 BC)
note: The beaten rebels fled into Asculum. Wikipedia's Social War article names Sextus Julius Caesar for the relieving force; Appian names Sulpicius. Lafrenius is often emended to Afranius.

name: Asculum (siege)
place: Asculum (Ascoli Piceno), where the war began
commanders_a: Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo, Sextus Julius Caesar
roman_force: Pompeius Strabo's army of citizen legions, in which the young Pompey and Cicero served, with auxiliary cavalry including the turma Salluitana of Iberian horsemen from the Ebro valley, granted citizenship in the camp before Asculum on 17 November 89 (ILS 8888).
greek_note: Roman citizen legions with Spanish and other auxiliaries; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, BC 1.47-48; Orosius 5.18; Velleius 2.21; ILS 8888 (the Asculum bronze); en.wikipedia Battle of Asculum (89 BC)
note: Vidacilius forced his way into the town with eight cohorts but, failing to rouse it, killed himself. Asculum surrendered in November 89; Strabo triumphed on 25 December. 'other' in languages = Iberian.

name: Stabiae (siege)
borderline: Pliny records only that Sulla destroyed the town on this date; the fighting is not described.
roman_force: Sulla's army of citizen legions and loyal Italian troops (no numbers given).
greek_note: Roman citizen and loyal Italian troops; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Pliny, NH 3.70; en.wikipedia Social War (91-87 BC)

name: Asculum
roman_force: The consul Strabo's army of citizen legions with auxiliaries (including Iberian cavalry), the force besieging Asculum.
greek_note: Roman citizen legions with Spanish auxiliaries; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, BC 1.48; Velleius 2.21; Orosius 5.18; en.wikipedia Battle of Asculum (89 BC)
note: Strabo defeated an Italian relief army (60,000 according to Wikipedia, citing Velleius), often seen as the turning point of the war; Wikipedia's Social War article dates it January 89 and names Vettius Scato, whose men fled over snowy mountains. The relief commander is uncertain.

name: Fucine Lake
place: Near the Fucine Lake, at a camp of the Marsi
roman_force: The consul Cato's army, formerly Marius's northern army of citizen legions (no numbers given).
greek_note: Roman citizen troops; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, BC 1.50; Livy Per. 75; Orosius 5.18.24; en.wikipedia Social War (91-87 BC)
note: Cato, after earlier successes, fell while attacking the Marsic camp near the lake (Appian, Livy); Orosius blames the younger Marius. Wikipedia's Social War article counts it a Roman victory, but the sources do not say how the fight ended.

name: Pompeii (siege)
roman_force: Sulla's army of citizen legions with a legion raised among the Hirpini by Minatius Magius of Aeclanum (Velleius 2.16), and a fleet (Postumius Albinus's ships, whose crews killed him).
greek_note: Roman citizen and loyal Italian troops; naval crews may have included Greeks from the loyal cities of Campania, but none are attested here.
sources: Appian, BC 1.50; Velleius 2.16; Orosius 5.18; en.wikipedia Social War (91-87 BC)
note: Sling bullets and ballista damage from the siege survive at Pompeii. The town's fall is not explicitly recorded; Wikipedia records its capture, and it later received a Sullan colony (80 BCE).

name: Nola
place: Between Pompeii and Nola, ending at the walls of Nola
borderline: Wikipedia calls it Cluentius's relief attempt rather than a battle of Nola.
roman_force: Sulla's army besieging Pompeii, citizen legions and loyal Italian troops; Sulla won the grass crown here for saving his army (Pliny, NH 22.12).
greek_note: Roman citizen and loyal Italian troops; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, BC 1.50; Pliny, NH 22.12; en.wikipedia Social War (91-87 BC)
note: Cluentius first repulsed Sulla, then, reinforced by Gauls, was routed and pursued to Nola, where he and many of his men (Appian: about 20,000) were cut down at the gates.

name: Aeclanum (siege)
borderline: Sulla set fire to the wooden walls and the town surrendered; it was then sacked, so the fighting was brief.
roman_force: Sulla's army of citizen legions and loyal Italian troops (no numbers given).
greek_note: Roman citizen and loyal Italian troops; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, BC 1.51; en.wikipedia Social War (91-87 BC)
note: The fall of Aeclanum brought the surrender of the other Hirpini.

name: Bovianum
place: Bovianum, the rebels' capital in Samnium (Boiano), after a battle in the hills near Aesernia
roman_force: Sulla's army of citizen legions and loyal Italian troops (no numbers given).
greek_note: Roman citizen and loyal Italian troops; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, BC 1.51; en.wikipedia Social War (91-87 BC)
note: Sulla surprised and routed Papius Mutilus's army by a mountain march (Mutilus fled wounded to Aesernia), then stormed Bovianum after a three-hour fight. Which Bovianum (Vetus or Undecimanorum) is disputed.

name: Canusium
borderline: Known only from Appian's brief account; not a named battle in Wikipedia.
roman_force: The praetor Cosconius's army in Apulia, citizen legions with loyal Italian troops (no numbers given).
greek_note: Roman citizen and loyal Italian troops; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, BC 1.52
note: Cosconius, besieging Canusium, was beaten by a Samnite relief army after heavy losses on both sides and fell back to Cannae. Possibly 88.

name: Aufidus
place: On the river Aufidus (Ofanto) between Cannae and Canusium
borderline: Known only from Appian's brief account; not a named battle in Wikipedia.
roman_force: The praetor Cosconius's army in Apulia, citizen legions with loyal Italian troops (no numbers given).
greek_note: Roman citizen and loyal Italian troops; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Appian, BC 1.52
note: Trebatius crossed the river to attack and was caught and routed, his survivors fleeing to Canusium; Cosconius then overran Larinum, Venusia and Apulian Asculum. Possibly 88.

name: Protopachium
place: Near the fortress of Protopachium in eastern Bithynia, east of the Sangarius (site unknown)
commanders_a: Neoptolemus, Nemanes the Armenian (generals of Mithridates VI)
roman_force: Aquillius's army of 40,000 foot and 4,000 horse, raised mostly from Bithynia, Cappadocia, Paphlagonia and the Galatians, with very few Romans (Appian, Mithridatic Wars 17).
greek_note: The army was levied in the Hellenistic kingdoms and Greek cities of northern Anatolia, where Greek was widespread, alongside Celtic Galatians and native Anatolians.
sources: Appian, Mithridatic Wars 17-19; en.wikipedia Battle of Protopachium
note: Aquillius lost about 10,000 dead and 300 prisoners and fled to Pergamon; later handed over to Mithridates and executed. Dated 89 by Wikipedia; some modern accounts put the opening battles of the war in 88.

name: Apulia (death of Poppaedius Silo)
borderline: No conventional name: the battle in Apulia in which the Marsic leader Silo fell, ending organised Italian resistance.
roman_force: Metellus Pius' army in Apulia, Roman legions with Latin and loyal Italian contingents; no numbers are given. Silo's Marsi and Samnites numbered about 50,000 according to Diodorus.
greek_note: A Roman-Italian army; the loyal Greek cities of southern Italy (Naples, Rhegium) sided with Rome in the Social War, but no Greek contingent is recorded here.
sources: Appian, BC 1.53; Diodorus 37.2.10-11; Livy, Per. 76; en.wikipedia Social War (91-87 BC)
note: Metellus had taken Venusia in the same campaign; the exact site is not recorded.

name: Esquiline Forum
war: Sulla's first civil war (march on Rome, 88 BCE)
place: the Esquiline Gate and Esquiline Forum, Rome
commanders_a: Lucius Cornelius Sulla, Quintus Pompeius Rufus
roman_force: Sulla's six legions from the siege of Nola (Appian, BC 1.57), against the citizens and slaves whom Marius and Sulpicius armed in the city, Marius offering freedom to slaves who joined him (Plutarch, Sulla 9; Appian, BC 1.58).
greek_note: Legions raised in Campania and central Italy during the Social War; Greek speakers only among the citizens of the southern Italian cities and the freedmen and slaves of Rome.
sources: Plutarch, Sulla 9; Appian, BC 1.57-58; en.wikipedia March on Rome (88 BC); historyofwar.org, Sulla's attack on Rome or battle of the Esquiline Forum
note: Street fighting as Sulla's army entered Rome; the first time a Roman army took the city by force.

name: Rhodes (siege)
place: Rhodes, the city and its harbours
commanders_a: Lucius Cassius (proconsul of Asia); Damagoras (Rhodian admiral)
borderline: The Romans present were refugees under Cassius; the defence was essentially Rhodian.
roman_force: The Rhodian citizen army and fleet under the admiral Damagoras, with the proconsul Lucius Cassius and the Romans and Italians who had fled from Asia to the island (Appian, Mith. 24-27); no numbers are given.
greek_note: The defence was borne by the Rhodian fleet and citizens; the Roman element was the band of refugees with Cassius.
sources: Appian, Mith. 24-27; Diodorus 37.28; en.wikipedia Siege of Rhodes (88 BC)
note: Several sea fights and a failed assault with a sambuca mounted on ships; type set to sea for the main arm. Mithridates abandoned the siege.

name: Delos
commanders_b: Apellicon of Teos, sent by the Athenian tyrant Athenion
borderline: A small night action against the expedition of Mithridates' ally Athens.
roman_force: A small force under Orbius, the Roman officer guarding Delos, probably raised from the island's Roman and Italian residents; he surprised Apellicon's Athenian expedition by night (Posidonius in Athenaeus 5.214-215).
greek_note: The Italian community of Delos included many Greek-speaking southern Italians and freedmen, but the make-up of Orbius' force is not recorded.
sources: Posidonius in Athenaeus 5.214d-215b; en.wikipedia First Mithridatic War
note: Shortly afterwards Archelaus' Pontic fleet took Delos and massacred its Italians (Appian, Mith. 28).

name: Sciathus (sea)
place: the waters off Sciathus (Skiathos), northern Aegean
commanders_a: Quintus Braetius Sura (legate of the governor of Macedonia)
borderline: A minor sea fight known from brief notices; the site off Sciathus is inferred from Sura's capture of the island.
roman_force: Braetius Sura's small squadron and troops from the province of Macedonia; he sank a large ship and a hemiolia of Metrophanes and took the Pontic depot on Sciathus (Appian, Mith. 29).
greek_note: Rome had no standing fleet in the Aegean in 88 BCE; Sura's ships would have been crewed by local Greek and Macedonian sailors.
sources: Appian, Mith. 29; Plutarch, Sulla 11; en.wikipedia First Mithridatic War

name: Chaeronea
borderline: A three-day indecisive fight known only from brief notices; not usually given its own name.
roman_force: Braetius Sura's small force from the garrison of the province of Macedonia; no numbers are given (Appian, Mith. 29; Plutarch, Sulla 11).
greek_note: The Macedonian garrison was a small Roman force with local Macedonian, Greek and Thracian auxiliaries; their proportion is unknown.
sources: Appian, Mith. 29; Plutarch, Sulla 11; en.wikipedia First Mithridatic War
note: Archelaus and the Athenian Aristion against Sura; Spartan and Achaean contingents then joined the Pontic side and Sura fell back. Plutarch (Sulla 11.4) claims Sura won three battles and drove Archelaus back to the sea; Appian (Mith. 29) has an indecisive three-day fight, kept here as a draw.

name: Janiculum
roman_force: The consul Octavius' troops in the city with Pompeius Strabo's army from Picenum, against Marius' men, who had seized the Janiculum through the treachery of the tribune Appius Claudius (Appian, BC 1.68).
greek_note: Italian armies on both sides, Marius' partly raised in Etruria; no Greek contingents are recorded.
sources: Appian, BC 1.68; Orosius 5.19; en.wikipedia Bellum Octavianum
note: Octavius drove the Marians off the hill, but Strabo held back from a pursuit; the siege of Rome ended soon after in the city's surrender.

name: Rome (siege)
place: Rome and its approaches (the Janiculum, the Colline Gate, Ostia)
commanders_a: Lucius Cornelius Cinna, Gaius Marius, Quintus Sertorius, Gnaeus Papirius Carbo
commanders_b: Gnaeus Octavius, Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo, Lucius Cornelius Merula
roman_force: Cinna's army, the legion left at Nola that he won over and levies of the new Italian citizens, with about 6,000 men Marius raised in Etruria (Appian, BC 1.65-67), against Octavius' troops in the city and Pompeius Strabo's army; Brunt estimated the two sides at about 120,000 and 60,000.
greek_note: Italian armies on both sides; Marius also enrolled slaves, but no Greek units are recorded.
sources: Appian, BC 1.64-71; Plutarch, Marius 41-43; Orosius 5.19; en.wikipedia Bellum Octavianum; historyofwar.org, Siege of Rome, 87 BC
note: A blockade with real fighting (the Janiculum, an indecisive battle of Strabo against Sertorius near the Colline Gate, Marius' capture of Ostia); the Senate surrendered the city and Octavius was killed.

name: Athens and Piraeus (siege)
date: autumn 87 BCE to spring 86 BCE (Athens stormed on 1 March 86 BCE)
place: Athens and its port Piraeus, Attica
commanders_a: Lucius Cornelius Sulla; Gaius Scribonius Curio (Acropolis)
roman_force: Sulla's five legions with some cohorts and cavalry brought from Italy, reinforced with soldiers, money and supplies from Aetolia and Thessaly (Appian, Mith. 30); en.wikipedia gives 37,000-44,000 in all, about 20,000 of them auxiliaries.
greek_note: Appian says Sulla raised troops in Aetolia and Thessaly, and the auxiliaries of his army were largely Greek and Macedonian.
sources: Plutarch, Sulla 12-14; Appian, Mith. 30-41; Pausanias 1.20.4-7; en.wikipedia Siege of Athens and Piraeus (87-86 BC)
note: Athens under the tyrant Aristion fell first; Archelaus then abandoned Piraeus by sea and Sulla burned it. Some give 12 February rather than 1 March for the storm of Athens.

name: Chaeronea
commanders_a: Lucius Cornelius Sulla; Lucius Licinius Murena; Lucius Hortensius; Servius Sulpicius Galba; Aulus Gabinius
roman_force: Sulla's veteran legions, fewer than 15,000 foot and 1,500 horse by Plutarch's count (Sulla 16), with Macedonian and Greek allies, the troops Hortensius brought down from Thessaly, and men of Chaeronea who seized Mount Thurium for him; modern estimates about 30,000 in all.
greek_note: Beyond a Roman core of under 17,000 the army was made up of Macedonian and Greek allies, and Chaeronean volunteers led the attack on Thurium (Plutarch, Sulla 17-18).
sources: Plutarch, Sulla 15-19; Appian, Mith. 41-45; Memnon of Heraclea; en.wikipedia Battle of Chaeronea (86 BC)
note: Pontic strength 60,000 (Memnon) to 120,000 (Appian); Sulla's claim of 12 or 14 Roman dead is doubted.

name: Orchomenus
place: the plain and marshes by Orchomenus, Boeotia (Lake Copais)
roman_force: Sulla's army of about 30,000 (Delbrück), the same legions and Greek and Macedonian allies as at Chaeronea, much weaker in cavalry than the 80,000 Pontic troops; Sulla dug ditches across the marshy plain against the Pontic horse (Plutarch, Sulla 20-21).
greek_note: The same Roman-Greek army as at Chaeronea; no separate figures for the Greek allies are given for this battle.
sources: Plutarch, Sulla 20-21; Appian, Mith. 49-50; Frontinus, Strat. 2.3.17; en.wikipedia Battle of Orchomenus
note: en.wikipedia dates it autumn 86 BCE; many works give 85 BCE.

name: Lectum
place: off Cape Lectum (Babakale), the south-western tip of the Troad
roman_force: The fleet Lucullus had gathered from Rome's eastern allies, ships and crews from Rhodes, Cyprus, Phoenicia and Pamphylia, joined by Cos and Cnidus (Plutarch, Lucullus 2-3; Appian, Mith. 56).
greek_note: Rome had no fleet of its own in the East; the ships and crews were lent by Greek allies, with some Phoenician ships.
sources: Plutarch, Lucullus 3.8; the ancient Greek battles set, Lectum 85 BC
note: Fought after Lucullus had let Mithridates escape from Pitane (85 BCE), shortly before the larger victory over Neoptolemus off Tenedos. 'other' in languages = Phoenician.

name: Tenedos (sea)
commanders_a: Lucius Licinius Lucullus; Damagoras of Rhodes
roman_force: A fleet Lucullus assembled from Rome's eastern allies, ships and crews from Rhodes, Cyprus, Phoenicia and Pamphylia (Appian, Mith. 56), joined by Cos and Cnidus (Plutarch, Lucullus 3); Lucullus sailed in a Rhodian ship under Damagoras.
greek_note: Rome had no fleet of its own; the ships and crews were lent by Greek allies (Rhodes, Cyprus, Pamphylia, Cos, Cnidus) with some Phoenician ships, and a Rhodian commanded the flagship.
sources: Plutarch, Lucullus 2-3; Appian, Mith. 56; en.wikipedia Battle of Tenedos (86 BC)
note: Fought after Lucullus' smaller victory off Lectum (-85-lectum) and after Mithridates' escape from Pitane, so in 85 BCE; en.wikipedia dates it 86 BCE.

name: Rhyndacus
place: on the Rhyndacus river near Miletopolis, Mysia
commanders_b: Mithridates the Younger (son of Mithridates VI)
roman_force: The two legions Valerius Flaccus had brought from Italy (the later Fimbriani or Valeriani), led by Fimbria after Flaccus' murder; Fimbria killed 6,000 Pontic horse and then stormed the Pontic camp by night (Memnon 34).
greek_note: Two Italian legions; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Memnon of Heraclea 34; Appian, Mith. 52; en.wikipedia First Mithridatic War
note: Also called the battle of Miletopolis. Fimbria served the Cinnan government, not Sulla, but the battle was against Pontus.

name: Ilium (siege)
borderline: Ilium had declared for Sulla against the Cinnan government Fimbria served, so this is partly an episode of the Roman civil strife.
roman_force: Fimbria's two Valerian legions; the Ilians shut their gates and appealed to Sulla, and Fimbria took the city after eleven days, then sacked and burned it (Appian, Mith. 53).
greek_note: Two Italian legions; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Appian, Mith. 53; Strabo 13.1.27; Livy, Per. 83; en.wikipedia First Mithridatic War

name: Mount Tifata
place: the foot of Mount Tifata near Capua, by the Volturnus
commanders_a: Lucius Cornelius Sulla, Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius
roman_force: Sulla's army from the East, five legions of Italians and 6,000 cavalry with further troops from the Peloponnese and Macedonia, about 40,000 men (Appian, BC 1.79), against the consul Norbanus' newly levied legions.
greek_note: Appian says Sulla added troops raised in the Peloponnese and Macedonia to his five Italian legions, a small share of the whole.
sources: Velleius 2.25; Appian, BC 1.79, 1.84; Plutarch, Sulla 27; en.wikipedia Battle of Mount Tifata
note: Also called the battle of Casilinum; Appian places Sulla's first victory near Canusium. en.wikipedia gives November 83 BCE.

name: Colline Gate
place: before the Colline Gate (Porta Collina), Rome
commanders_a: Lucius Cornelius Sulla; Marcus Licinius Crassus (right wing)
commanders_b: Pontius Telesinus, Marcus Lamponius, Gaius Carrinas, Gaius Marcius Censorinus, Lucius Junius Brutus Damasippus
roman_force: Sulla's veteran legions of the Mithridatic war, Crassus commanding the right wing, against about 70,000 Samnites, Lucanians and Marians under Telesinus and the Marian generals (Appian, BC 1.93; en.wikipedia).
greek_note: Sulla's legions were Italian; the Samnite and Lucanian army opposing him spoke Oscan; no Greek contingents are recorded.
sources: Appian, BC 1.93; Plutarch, Sulla 29-30; Velleius 2.27; en.wikipedia Battle of the Colline Gate (82 BC)
note: Sulla's own left wing was routed; Crassus' victory on the right decided the battle. About 50,000 dead are reported; Carrinas and Censorinus were executed the next day.

name: Sacriportus
roman_force: Sulla's veterans (about 40,000 by en.wikipedia's figure) against Marius' army of 85 cohorts (Appian, BC 1.87), of which five cohorts of foot and two of horse deserted to Sulla on the field.
greek_note: Italian armies on both sides; Greek speakers at most a handful among the eastern levies Sulla had brought.
sources: Appian, BC 1.87; Plutarch, Sulla 28; Velleius 2.26; en.wikipedia Battle of Sacriportus
note: Marius lost some 28,000 men killed, captured or deserted, and fled to Praeneste.

name: Praeneste (siege)
place: Praeneste (Palestrina) and the passes leading to it
commanders_a: Quintus Lucretius Afella (Ofella); Lucius Cornelius Sulla; Pompey
commanders_b: Gaius Marius the Younger; relief armies of Gaius Marcius Censorinus, Lucius Junius Brutus Damasippus and Pontius Telesinus
roman_force: Afella's blockading army and the forces Sulla posted on the passes, against Marius' garrison of the survivors of Sacriportus; relief armies (Censorinus' eight legions, ambushed by Pompey, Damasippus' two legions, and the Samnites and Lucanians of Telesinus and Lamponius) failed to break in (Appian, BC 1.88-92).
greek_note: Italian armies on both sides; the Samnite and Lucanian relief forces spoke Oscan.
sources: Appian, BC 1.87-94; Plutarch, Sulla 28-32; Velleius 2.26-27; en.wikipedia Sulla's civil war
note: The town surrendered after the Colline Gate; Marius the Younger killed himself and the defenders were massacred.

name: Aesis
roman_force: Metellus Pius' Sullan army in Picenum against Carrinas' Marian legions; numbers not given (Appian, BC 1.87).
greek_note: Italian armies on both sides; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Appian, BC 1.87; en.wikipedia Sulla's civil war

name: Sena Gallica
roman_force: Pompey's legions raised in Picenum from his father's clients and veterans, against Censorinus' Marian army; Pompey's men then sacked the town (Appian, BC 1.88).
greek_note: Italian armies on both sides; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Appian, BC 1.88; en.wikipedia Sulla's civil war

name: Spoletium
commanders_a: Pompey, Marcus Licinius Crassus; Lucius Cornelius Sulla
roman_force: Pompey's and Crassus' legions, who killed about 3,000 of Carrinas' men and shut him up in Spoletium; Sulla ambushed the relief Carbo sent, killing about 2,000 (Appian, BC 1.90).
greek_note: Italian armies on both sides; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Appian, BC 1.90; en.wikipedia Sulla's civil war
note: Carrinas escaped from Spoletium by night during a storm.

name: Saturnia
borderline: Known only from a single sentence in Appian.
roman_force: A Sullan division against Marian troops in Etruria; no numbers are given (Appian, BC 1.89).
greek_note: Italian armies on both sides; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Appian, BC 1.89; en.wikipedia Sulla's civil war

name: First Clusium
roman_force: Sulla's main army against Carbo's consular army, fighting all day until darkness without result (Appian, BC 1.89).
greek_note: Italian armies on both sides; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Appian, BC 1.89; Velleius 2.28; en.wikipedia First Battle of Clusium
note: Indecisive; Sulla then withdrew.

name: Fidentia
date: 82 BCE (the war article puts it at the end of 83 BCE)
place: near Fidentia (Fidenza), between Placentia and Parma
commanders_b: a Marian commander not named by Plutarch
roman_force: Lucullus' detachment of 16 cohorts against 50 Marian cohorts (Plutarch, Sulla 27).
greek_note: Italian and Cisalpine troops on both sides; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Plutarch, Sulla 27; Appian, BC 1.92; en.wikipedia Battle of Fidentia (82 BC); en.wikipedia Sulla's civil war
note: Lucullus' victory near Placentia in Appian (BC 1.92) may be the same action or a second one; the main war article dates Fidentia to the end of 83 BCE.

name: Faventia
roman_force: Metellus Pius' army (about 20,000 by en.wikipedia's figure), attacked late in the day by Carbo's and Norbanus' tired troops; the Marians lost about 10,000 dead and 6,000 deserters, and only 1,000 got back in order to Arretium (Appian, BC 1.91).
greek_note: Italian and Cisalpine armies on both sides; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Appian, BC 1.91; Velleius 2.28; en.wikipedia Battle of Faventia (82 BC)
note: After the defeat a Lucanian legion under Albinovanus went over to Sulla.

name: Second Clusium
commanders_b: the commanders of Carbo's army after his flight to Africa
roman_force: Pompey's army against the army Carbo left at Clusium when he fled after Faventia; Appian puts the Marian dead at about 20,000 (BC 1.92).
greek_note: Italian armies on both sides; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Appian, BC 1.92; en.wikipedia Second Battle of Clusium
note: The survivors under Carrinas, Censorinus and Damasippus joined Telesinus for the march on Rome that ended at the Colline Gate.

name: Halys
place: a crossing of the Halys (Kızılırmak) river, Pontus
roman_force: Murena's army in Asia, built on the two Fimbrian (Valerian) legions Sulla had left there (Appian, Mith. 64-65).
greek_note: Two Italian legions; Murena may also have used Asian levies, but none are recorded.
sources: Appian, Mith. 64-66; Memnon of Heraclea 36; en.wikipedia Battle of Halys
note: Mithridates forced the river against Murena, who retreated into Phrygia; Sulla then ordered an end to the war.

name: Pityussa (sea)
borderline: A brief notice in Plutarch; the storm rather than the fight decided it.
roman_force: Annius' fleet carrying about 5,000 heavy infantry, against Sertorius' light craft and the Cilician pirate ships allied to him; a storm scattered Sertorius' ships (Plutarch, Sertorius 7).
greek_note: The Cilician pirate crews with Sertorius were largely Greek-speaking; the Roman forces on both sides were Italian.
sources: Plutarch, Sertorius 7; en.wikipedia Sertorian War
note: Sertorius had first landed and overpowered Annius' garrison on the island.

name: Tingis
borderline: Known from Plutarch's brief account; no conventional battle name.
roman_force: Sertorius' band of Roman exiles with the Maurusian rebels against Ascalis, against the force Sulla sent under Paccianus to support Ascalis; Sertorius won, took Paccianus' men into his service and then took Tingis (Plutarch, Sertorius 9).
greek_note: Roman exiles and Moorish tribesmen; the Cilician pirates had left Sertorius to serve Ascalis.
sources: Plutarch, Sertorius 9; en.wikipedia Sertorian War

name: Utica
commanders_b: Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus (killed), Hiarbas of Numidia
roman_force: Pompey's six legions, brought from Sicily in 120 warships and 800 transports (Plutarch, Pompey 11), against Domitius' Marians and the Numidians of King Hiarbas, about 20,000 in all.
greek_note: Italian legions; the transports and crews gathered in Sicily may have been partly Greek-manned, but no Greek units are recorded.
sources: Plutarch, Pompey 11-12; Livy, Per. 89; Orosius 5.21; en.wikipedia Sulla's civil war
note: Pompey stormed Domitius' camp in a rainstorm; he then hunted down Hiarbas and restored Hiempsal to the Numidian throne.

name: Volaterrae (siege)
commanders_a: Lucius Cornelius Sulla (began the siege) and his legates
borderline: A long blockade ending in surrender (79 BCE); actual fighting is not well attested.
roman_force: Sullan legions blockading the hill town, held by proscribed Marians and the Etruscan townsmen, for about two years (Strabo 5.2.6).
greek_note: Italian forces on both sides; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Strabo 5.2.6; Cicero, Pro Caecina 18; Granius Licinianus 36; en.wikipedia Volterra
note: The start may be late 82 BCE.

name: Mellaria (sea)
place: in the strait off Mellaria, near Tarifa
roman_force: Sertorius' small fleet carrying his invasion force from Africa, which Plutarch counts as 2,600 men he called Romans and 700 Libyans (Sertorius 12), against Cotta's Sullan squadron.
greek_note: Roman exiles and North Africans on Sertorius' side and a provincial squadron on Cotta's; no Greek contingents are recorded.
sources: Plutarch, Sertorius 12; en.wikipedia Sertorian War

name: Baetis River
