roman_force: Sertorius' army of about 2,600 Roman exiles, 700 Libyans, 4,000 Lusitanian light infantry and 700 horse (Plutarch, Sertorius 12), against the governor Fufidius' provincial army, of whom Plutarch says 2,000 Romans fell.
greek_note: Italian legions against Roman exiles with Lusitanian and North African allies; no Greek contingents.
sources: Plutarch, Sertorius 12; Sallust, Histories 1; en.wikipedia Battle of the Baetis River
note: The exact site on the river is unknown.

name: Anas
roman_force: Hirtuleius' Sertorian army, largely Lusitanian, against the army of Hispania Citerior under its governor Domitius Calvinus; numbers not given.
greek_note: Italian provincial legions against Sertorian Roman and Lusitanian troops; no Greek contingents.
sources: Livy, Per. 90; Plutarch, Sertorius 12; Orosius 5.23; en.wikipedia Sertorian War
note: Sertorius himself killed Metellus' legate Thorius Balbus in another, unnamed engagement about the same time.

name: Ilerda
roman_force: Manlius' army from Transalpine Gaul, three legions and 1,500 horse (Orosius 5.23), against Hirtuleius' Sertorian army of Roman exiles and Iberian levies.
greek_note: Italian legions with Gallic and Iberian auxiliaries; no Greek contingent is recorded (Massalia's allies are not mentioned).
sources: Orosius 5.23; Livy, Per. 90; Plutarch, Sertorius 12; Caesar, BG 3.20; en.wikipedia Sertorian War
note: Manlius was driven into Ilerda, escaped and lost his baggage to the Aquitani on the way back to Gaul.

name: Lacobriga (siege)
place: Lacobriga (Plutarch's Langobritae), western Hispania; identification uncertain (often Lagos, Algarve)
commanders_b: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius; Aquinius (commander of the ambushed foragers)
roman_force: Metellus' proconsular army besieging a Lusitanian town allied to Sertorius; Sertorius ran water into the town and ambushed a whole legion (6,000 men) sent to forage, forcing Metellus to raise the siege (Plutarch, Sertorius 13).
greek_note: Italian legions against Sertorius' Roman and Lusitanian troops; no Greek contingents.
sources: Plutarch, Sertorius 13; en.wikipedia Sertorian War
note: The site is disputed; Lagos in the Algarve is the usual identification.

name: Salona (siege)
borderline: Known only from brief notices ('Salonas cepit'); whether there was an assault is not recorded.
roman_force: The proconsul Cosconius' army in Illyricum; Eutropius says only that he subdued much of Dalmatia and took Salona in a two-year war (Eutropius 6.4).
greek_note: An Italian provincial army; the Greek towns of the Dalmatian coast (Issa, Tragurium) were Roman allies but no contingent is recorded.
sources: Eutropius 6.4; Orosius 5.23; Cicero, Pro Cluentio 97

name: Milvian Bridge
place: near the Milvian Bridge and the Campus Martius, Rome
roman_force: Catulus' army raised at Rome under the senatus consultum ultimum, against Lepidus' army raised in Etruria and Cisalpine Gaul from dispossessed farmers and old Marians (Appian, BC 1.107; Florus 2.11).
greek_note: Italian armies on both sides; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Appian, BC 1.107; Florus 2.11; Plutarch, Pompey 16; en.wikipedia Marcus Aemilius Lepidus (consul 78 BC)

name: Mutina (siege)
borderline: Brutus surrendered after a long siege and was later killed; fighting is not described.
roman_force: The army Pompey raised quickly from his veterans as legate pro praetore, against Brutus' Lepidan forces in Cisalpine Gaul (Plutarch, Pompey 16).
greek_note: Italian and Cisalpine troops on both sides; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Plutarch, Pompey 16; Livy, Per. 90; en.wikipedia Marcus Aemilius Lepidus (consul 78 BC)

name: Cosa
roman_force: Catulus' and Pompey's armies against the remains of Lepidus' Etrurian army, part of which Lepidus took off to Sardinia (Plutarch, Pompey 16; Exuperantius 6).
greek_note: Italian armies on both sides; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Plutarch, Pompey 16; Exuperantius 6; en.wikipedia Marcus Aemilius Lepidus (consul 78 BC)
note: Lepidus died in Sardinia soon after; Perperna took his troops to join Sertorius in Spain.

name: Olympus (siege)
war: Servilius' war against the pirates (78-74 BCE)
place: Mount Olympus and the town of Olympus, eastern Lycia
borderline: The sources record the capture of Olympus, Phaselis and Corycus without describing the fighting.
roman_force: The proconsul Servilius' army and fleet in Cilicia and Lycia, its size not recorded; he took Olympus, where the pirate chief Zenicetes burned himself with his household (Strabo 14.5.7).
greek_note: Roman commands against the pirates drew their ships and crews from the Greek maritime allies of the East; the legionary core was Italian.
sources: Strabo 14.5.7; Florus 1.41; Eutropius 6.3; Orosius 5.23
note: Servilius had first won a sea battle against the pirates off the coast (Florus 1.41).

name: Contrebia (siege)
place: Contrebia Leucade (near Aguilar del Rio Alhama, La Rioja)
borderline: Sertorius' rebel army against a Celtiberian town; counted as a Roman force although outside the civil fighting proper.
roman_force: Sertorius' army of Roman exiles and Iberian allies; he took the town after a siege of 44 days by undermining a tower, and demanded the deserters sheltering there (Livy, fr. of book 91).
greek_note: Sertorius' army was Roman and Iberian; no Greek speakers are recorded.
sources: Livy, Histories fr. book 91; en.wikipedia Contrebia Leucade

name: Lauron
commanders_a: Quintus Sertorius; Octavius Graecinus; Tarquitius Priscus
roman_force: Pompey's army of about 30,000 foot and 1,000 horse, against Sertorius' besieging army, which ambushed his foragers with ten heavy and ten light cohorts and 2,000 horse (Frontinus, Strat. 2.5.31; Orosius 5.23).
greek_note: Italian legions against Sertorius' Roman and Iberian army; no Greek contingents.
sources: Plutarch, Sertorius 18; Plutarch, Pompey 18; Frontinus, Strat. 2.5.31; Appian, BC 1.109; en.wikipedia Battle of Lauron
note: Sertorius then took and burned Lauron before Pompey's eyes; Frontinus puts Pompey's loss at 10,000.

name: Valentia
place: between the Turia and the walls of Valentia (Valencia)
roman_force: Pompey's army against the Sertorian army of Perperna and Herennius, largely the Roman cohorts Perperna had brought from Italy; Herennius and about 10,000 of his men fell (Plutarch, Pompey 18; Sallust, Histories 2).
greek_note: Italian armies with Iberian auxiliaries on both sides; no Greek contingents.
sources: Plutarch, Pompey 18; Sallust, Histories 2; en.wikipedia Sertorian War
note: Valentia was taken and sacked.

name: Italica
roman_force: Metellus' four understrength legions with auxiliaries and allied troops, against Hirtuleius' army of similar size, which lost about 20,000 men (Frontinus, Strat. 2.1.2; Orosius 5.23).
greek_note: Italian legions with Spanish auxiliaries against Sertorian Romans and Lusitanians; no Greek contingents.
sources: Frontinus, Strat. 2.1.2; Orosius 5.23; Livy, Per. 91; en.wikipedia Battle of Italica
note: Metellus waited out the midday heat, held his centre and enveloped Hirtuleius from the wings.

name: Segovia
place: near Segovia (or a Segontia; identification uncertain)
commanders_b: Lucius Hirtuleius and his brother (both killed)
borderline: Only late sources place Hirtuleius' last defeat 'at Segovia'; some scholars merge it with the battle of Seguntia/Saguntum.
roman_force: Metellus' army against the remains of Hirtuleius' Sertorian army after Italica; no numbers are given (Orosius 5.23; Frontinus, Strat. 2.7.5).
greek_note: Italian legions against Sertorian Romans and Iberians; no Greek contingents.
sources: Orosius 5.23; Frontinus, Strat. 2.7.5; Florus 2.10

name: Sucro
place: on the Sucro (Jucar) river near its mouth
roman_force: Sertorius' army against Pompey's; Sertorius routed Pompey's wing and Pompey was wounded, while Afranius broke the other Sertorian wing and plundered the camp (Plutarch, Sertorius 19; Pompey 19).
greek_note: Italian legions against Sertorius' Roman and Celtiberian army; no Greek contingents.
sources: Plutarch, Sertorius 19; Plutarch, Pompey 19; Appian, BC 1.110; en.wikipedia Battle of Sucro
note: Sertorius withdrew when Metellus approached the next day.

name: Saguntum
commanders_a: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius, Pompey; Gaius Memmius (killed)
roman_force: The combined armies of Metellus and Pompey against Sertorius, whose own men forced him to give battle; heavy losses on both sides (Plutarch, Sertorius 21; Appian, BC 1.110).
greek_note: Italian legions against Sertorius' Roman and Celtiberian army; no Greek contingents.
sources: Plutarch, Sertorius 21; Plutarch, Pompey 19; Appian, BC 1.110; en.wikipedia Sertorian War
note: Plutarch makes it a Sertorian defeat; Appian has Sertorius beating Pompey while Metellus beat Perperna; en.wikipedia calls it inconclusive, the last pitched battle of the war.

name: Clunia (siege)
roman_force: Pompey and Metellus besieging Sertorius in Clunia, who made frequent and costly sorties and then slipped away to rebuild his army (Livy, Per. 92; Plutarch, Sertorius 21).
greek_note: Italian legions against Sertorian Romans and Celtiberians; no Greek contingents.
sources: Livy, Per. 92; Plutarch, Sertorius 21; en.wikipedia Sertorian War
note: The place did not fall; Sertorius escaped and the besiegers withdrew to winter quarters.

name: Isaura (siege)
war: Servilius' war against the pirates (78-74 BCE)
borderline: The town surrendered after its water was cut; fighting is not described.
roman_force: Servilius' proconsular army; he diverted the river that supplied Isaura and forced it to surrender by thirst (Frontinus, Strat. 3.7.1), earning the name Isauricus.
greek_note: An Italian proconsular army, probably with auxiliaries from the Greek cities of Pamphylia and Lycia; none recorded.
sources: Frontinus, Strat. 3.7.1; Eutropius 6.3; Orosius 5.23; Strabo 12.6.2

name: Pallantia (siege)
borderline: Siege works and a withdrawal before the relief army; real fighting is not described.
roman_force: Pompey's proconsular army, which undermined the walls on timber props and set them alight as it withdrew before Sertorius' relief army (Appian, BC 1.112); Sertorius led Roman exiles and Spanish allies.
greek_note: Italian legions against Sertorian Romans and Spaniards; no Greek contingents.
sources: Appian, BC 1.112; en.wikipedia Sertorian War
note: 'Celtiberians' in allies = the Pallantini (Vaccaei). Sertorius repaired the walls and then fell on the Romans before Calagurris (-74-calagurris-siege).

name: Chalcedon
place: before the walls and in the harbour of Chalcedon (Kadikoy)
commanders_b: Marcus Aurelius Cotta; Publius Rutilius Nudus (naval prefect)
roman_force: Cotta's consular army of Roman and allied troops, among them Cyzicene auxiliaries, and the 64 ships of the Roman fleet in the harbour under the prefect Nudus (Appian, Mith. 71; Memnon 27).
greek_note: The Cyzicenes lost heavily before the walls (about 3,000 allied dead), and the fleet destroyed in the harbour was drawn from the allied Greek cities of Asia and the Propontis.
sources: Appian, Mith. 71; Plutarch, Lucullus 8; Memnon of Heraclea 27; en.wikipedia Battle of Chalcedon (74 BC)
note: Combined battle: the Pontic army routed Cotta's troops outside the walls, then broke the harbour chain and took or burned the 64 Roman ships; type set to land.

name: Calagurris (siege)
roman_force: Pompey and Metellus besieging the town were surprised by Sertorius' relief army, which killed about 3,000 of them and raised the siege (Appian, BC 1.112).
greek_note: Italian legions against Sertorian Romans and Celtiberians; no Greek contingents.
sources: Appian, BC 1.112; Livy, Per. 93; en.wikipedia Sertorian War
note: Calagurris fell to Afranius in 72 BCE after a famine in which the defenders ate their dead (Valerius Maximus 7.6 ext. 3).

name: Mount Vesuvius
place: the slopes of Mount Vesuvius, Campania
roman_force: About 3,000 militia hastily raised by the praetor Gaius Claudius Glaber, not regular legions (Plutarch, Crassus 9; Appian, BC 1.116).
greek_note: Levies of Campania, where Greek was still spoken at Naples and in the coastal towns.
sources: Plutarch, Crassus 9; Appian, BC 1.116; Florus 2.8; Frontinus, Strat. 1.5.21; en.wikipedia Battle of Mount Vesuvius
note: The rebels climbed down the cliffs on vine ropes and fell on Glaber's camp from behind.

name: Salinae
place: Salinae, the salt works on the Campanian coast near Herculaneum and Pompeii, and nearby
commanders_b: Publius Varinius; his legates Lucius Furius and Lucius Cossinius (killed)
borderline: A series of defeats of Varinius' forces in 73 BCE; no conventional battle name.
roman_force: The praetor Varinius' levies: his legate Furius with about 2,000 men and his colleague Cossinius with another force were beaten in turn, Cossinius being surprised and killed at Salinae, and then Varinius himself was defeated (Plutarch, Crassus 9; Sallust, Histories 3).
greek_note: Levies of Campania and central Italy; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Plutarch, Crassus 9; Sallust, Histories 3; Appian, BC 1.116; en.wikipedia Third Servile War

name: Cyzicus (siege)
roman_force: Lucullus' five legions (one from Italy, the two Fimbrian legions and two more), 30,000 foot and 1,600 horse by Appian's count (Mith. 72; Plutarch says 2,500 horse), besieging the besiegers, while the Cyzicene citizens defended the city.
greek_note: The city itself was held by its Greek citizens, who repulsed the Pontic assaults; Lucullus' field army was Italian.
sources: Appian, Mith. 72-76; Plutarch, Lucullus 9-11; Memnon of Heraclea 28; en.wikipedia Battle of Cyzicus (73 BC)
note: Mithridates' army, said to be 300,000 with camp followers, was starved out and broke up.

name: Rhyndacus
roman_force: Ten cohorts and the cavalry under Lucullus, marching through a snowstorm, against the Pontic cavalry and baggage sent away from Cyzicus; 15,000 men and 6,000 horses were captured (Plutarch, Lucullus 11; Appian, Mith. 75).
greek_note: Italian legionary cohorts and cavalry; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Plutarch, Lucullus 11; Appian, Mith. 75; en.wikipedia Battle of the Rhyndacus (73 BC)
note: Some chronologies put it in 72 BCE.

name: Granicus
place: at the crossings of the Aesepus and Granicus rivers
commanders_b: Hermaeus, Marius (Pontic generals of the retreating army)
roman_force: Lucullus' army caught the Pontic land forces retreating from Cyzicus toward Lampsacus as they crossed the flooded Aesepus and Granicus, killing about 20,000 (Plutarch, Lucullus 11; Appian, Mith. 76).
greek_note: Lucullus' Italian legions; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Plutarch, Lucullus 11; Appian, Mith. 76; en.wikipedia Third Mithridatic War
note: Also called the battle of the Aesepus; often dated 72 BCE.

name: Lemnos (sea)
place: off the Achaean harbour (Troad) and at Lemnos or a nearby islet (Neae)
commanders_b: Marcus Marius (Varius), Alexander the Paphlagonian, Dionysius the eunuch; Isidorus
roman_force: A fleet Lucullus raised from the allied cities of the Troad and Hellespont, with legionaries landed on the island to take the beached Pontic ships from behind; 13 ships were taken first off the Achaean harbour and then 32 royal ships at Lemnos (Plutarch, Lucullus 12; Appian, Mith. 77).
greek_note: The ships and crews came from the Greek cities of the Troad and Hellespont; the legionaries were the Roman element.
sources: Plutarch, Lucullus 12; Appian, Mith. 77; Orosius 6.2; en.wikipedia Battle of Lemnos (73 BC)
note: The Roman renegade Marius, Sertorius' envoy to Mithridates, was captured and executed. This entry includes the capture of 13 Pontic ships off the Achaean harbour near Tenedos under Isidorus (Plutarch, Lucullus 12), which the ancient Greek battles set lists as 'Tenedos 73'; en.wikipedia redirects 'Battle of Tenedos (73 BCE)' here. Triarius' later victory near Tenedos is -72-tenedos-sea.

name: Tenedos
commanders_b: the Pontic squadron returning from Crete and Spain (commanders not named)
borderline: Known only from Memnon; it may overlap with Lucullus' Aegean victories of 73/72 (the Achaean harbour and Neae near Lemnos, entered as -73-lemnos-sea).
roman_force: Triarius' fleet of about 70 triremes, which sailed from Nicomedia, against just under 80 Pontic ships (Memnon 33).
greek_note: Rome's fleets in the East were drawn from the allied Greek cities; Memnon does not say whose ships these were.
sources: Memnon 33 (Photius, Bibliotheca codex 224); the ancient Greek battles set, Tenedos 72 BC
note: The Pontic ships had been sent to Crete and to Spain (to Sertorius); Memnon says the rout completed the destruction of the fleet Mithridates had brought to Asia.

name: Mount Garganus
roman_force: The consul Gellius' consular army with the praetor Arrius, against Crixus' 30,000, two thirds of whom fell (Appian, BC 1.117; Livy, Per. 96 gives 20,000 killed).
greek_note: Newly levied Italian legions; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Appian, BC 1.117; Livy, Per. 96; Plutarch, Crassus 9; en.wikipedia Third Servile War

name: Picenum
commanders_b: Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus Clodianus, Lucius Gellius Publicola
roman_force: The two consular armies of Lentulus and Gellius, beaten first separately and then together (Appian, BC 1.117; Plutarch, Crassus 9).
greek_note: Newly levied Italian legions; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Appian, BC 1.117; Plutarch, Crassus 9; Livy, Per. 96; en.wikipedia Battle of Picenum
note: Only Appian places the combined defeat in Picenum; Plutarch records Lentulus' defeat and then Gellius'.

name: Mutina
commanders_b: Gaius Cassius Longinus (proconsul of Cisalpine Gaul); Gnaeus Manlius (praetor)
roman_force: The governor of Cisalpine Gaul Gaius Cassius Longinus with about 10,000 men (Plutarch, Crassus 9).
greek_note: The provincial army of Cisalpine Gaul, Italians and Cisalpine provincials; no Greek contingent.
sources: Plutarch, Crassus 9; Livy, Per. 96; Orosius 5.24; en.wikipedia Battle of Mutina (72 BC)

name: Mount Haemus
commanders_a: Marcus Terentius Varro Lucullus (proconsul of Macedonia)
borderline: Known only from a sentence in the epitomators.
roman_force: The proconsul of Macedonia's army; Eutropius says only that Lucullus beat the Bessi 'in a great battle on Mount Haemus' (Eutropius 6.10).
greek_note: The army of Macedonia combined Italian legions with Macedonian and Thracian auxiliaries; no figures.
sources: Eutropius 6.10; Festus, Breviarium 9; Appian, Illyrica 30
note: Lucullus then took the Greek cities of the western Black Sea coast (Apollonia, Callatis, Tomis, Histria) which had sided with Mithridates.

name: Heraclea Pontica (siege)
commanders_a: Marcus Aurelius Cotta; Gaius Valerius Triarius (fleet)
roman_force: Cotta's army, Roman legions with allied levies, whose assaults and siege engines failed, and the fleet of Triarius blockading the harbour; the city fell when the Pontic garrison betrayed it (Memnon 27-35).
greek_note: Cotta's army was Roman with Bithynian and Asian levies; Triarius' blockading ships were largely provided by Greek allies; no figures.
sources: Memnon of Heraclea 27-35; en.wikipedia Third Mithridatic War
note: Cotta sacked the city; the start date is given as 73 or 72 BCE.

name: Themiscyra (siege)
roman_force: Lucullus' army with siege towers and mines; the defenders broke into the mines and loosed bears, wild beasts and swarms of bees on the sappers (Appian, Mith. 78).
greek_note: Lucullus' Italian legions; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Appian, Mith. 78; en.wikipedia Third Mithridatic War
note: Appian does not say whether the town fell; Lucullus moved on against Mithridates at Cabira.

name: Amisus (siege)
commanders_a: Lucius Licinius Lucullus; Lucius Licinius Murena
roman_force: Lucullus' army, left under Murena while Lucullus marched on Cabira; Lucullus stormed the walls when the guards relaxed, and Callimachus set the Greek city on fire as he fled (Plutarch, Lucullus 14-19; Appian, Mith. 78, 83).
greek_note: Lucullus' Italian legions; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Plutarch, Lucullus 14-19; Appian, Mith. 78, 83; Memnon of Heraclea 30; en.wikipedia Third Mithridatic War
note: Amisus was an Athenian colony; Lucullus restored the surviving citizens.

name: Cabira
commanders_a: Lucius Licinius Lucullus; Sornatius; Marcus Fabius Hadrianus
roman_force: Lucullus' army, three legions with auxiliaries, about 20,000 foot and 1,600-2,500 horse (en.wikipedia), with 30,000 Galatians carrying grain behind it (Plutarch, Lucullus 14); the convoy escorts of ten cohorts under Sornatius and Hadrianus won the decisive actions.
greek_note: Italian legions with Galatian porters and auxiliaries; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Plutarch, Lucullus 14-17; Appian, Mith. 78-82; Memnon of Heraclea 29; en.wikipedia Battle of Cabira
note: A panic in the Pontic camp turned the convoy fights into a rout; Mithridates fled to Armenia.

name: Osca
roman_force: Pompey's army, which baited Perperna with ten cohorts and ambushed him, against the Sertorian army Perperna took over after murdering Sertorius (Appian, BC 1.115; Frontinus, Strat. 2.5.32).
greek_note: Italian legions against Roman and Iberian Sertorians; no Greek contingents.
sources: Appian, BC 1.115; Plutarch, Pompey 20; Plutarch, Sertorius 27; Frontinus, Strat. 2.5.32; en.wikipedia Sertorian War
note: en.wikipedia 'Battle near Osca'; Appian and Plutarch name no site. Date 72 BCE (some 73 BCE), soon after Perperna murdered Sertorius.

name: Rhegium (Crassus' wall)
place: Crassus' ditch and wall across the isthmus of the Rhegium peninsula, Bruttium
borderline: A siege line and repeated attacks on it rather than a named battle.
roman_force: Crassus' army, six new legions with the two former consular legions (Appian, BC 1.118), holding a ditch and wall some 300 stades long across the peninsula (Plutarch, Crassus 10).
greek_note: Italian legions; the Greek cities of Bruttium (Rhegium) lay behind the line but no contingent is recorded.
sources: Plutarch, Crassus 10-11; Appian, BC 1.118-119; en.wikipedia Third Servile War
note: Spartacus broke through on a snowy night, filling the ditch, but with heavy losses; result taken as the rebels' escape.

name: Crete (sea)
place: off northern Crete (perhaps near Cydonia); site uncertain
borderline: Antonius' defeat is recorded only summarily; site and date uncertain.
roman_force: Antonius' fleet of his extraordinary command against the pirates, with ships, crews and supplies requisitioned from the Greek cities; the Cretans took many ships and hanged prisoners from the rigging (Florus 1.42).
greek_note: Antonius' command levied ships and money on the Greek cities of the East (the Gytheum decree), so his crews were largely Greek; no figures.
sources: Florus 1.42; Livy, Per. 97; Diodorus 40.1; en.wikipedia Marcus Antonius Creticus; en.wikipedia 71 BC; attalus.org, events of 71 BC
note: Antonius died in Crete soon after; the mocking surname Creticus followed.

name: Cantenna
place: near Mount Cantenna (Camalatrum) and the Lucanian lake, near Giungano
commanders_a: Marcus Licinius Crassus; Quintus Marcius Rufus and Pomptinus (legates)
roman_force: Crassus' army of eight legions with auxiliaries, about 45,000 men (en.wikipedia; Appian, BC 1.118), against the Celtic and German rebels who had broken away under Gannicus and Castus; 12,300 rebels fell (Plutarch, Crassus 11).
greek_note: Italian legions; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Plutarch, Crassus 11; Livy, Per. 97; Frontinus, Strat. 2.4.7, 2.5.34; en.wikipedia Battle of Cantenna

name: Silarius River
place: near the upper Silarus (Sele) river, on the borders of Lucania
roman_force: Crassus' eight legions; the Livian tradition puts the rebel dead at 60,000 and the captives at 6,000 (Orosius 5.24).
greek_note: Italian legions; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Plutarch, Crassus 11; Appian, BC 1.120; Livy, Per. 97; Orosius 5.24; en.wikipedia Battle of the Silarius River
note: The exact site is uncertain. Spartacus died fighting and his body was not found; 6,000 captives were crucified along the Via Appia.

name: Sinope (sea)
borderline: A sea fight during the siege of Sinope, known only from Memnon.
roman_force: Censorinus' squadron of 15 triremes escorting grain ships from the Bosporus to Lucullus' army (Memnon 37).
greek_note: Roman squadrons in the Black Sea were supplied by the allied Greek cities; Memnon does not say whose ships these were.
sources: Memnon 37 (Photius, Bibliotheca codex 224); the ancient Greek battles set, Sinope 70 BC
note: The defenders' fleet under Cleochares beat Censorinus and seized the transports; Lucullus later took the city after Cleochares and Seleucus burned their ships and fled (-70-sinope-siege).

name: Sinope (siege)
roman_force: Lucullus' army and fleet besieging the Pontic capital, held by a Pontic and Cilician garrison; the garrison burned its heavy ships and escaped in light craft, and Lucullus freed the Greek city (Plutarch, Lucullus 23; Appian, Mith. 83; Memnon 37).
greek_note: Italian legions; Lucullus' ships were probably provided by the allied Greek cities of the Black Sea and Propontis, but no figures are given.
sources: Plutarch, Lucullus 23; Appian, Mith. 83; Memnon of Heraclea 37; en.wikipedia Third Mithridatic War

name: Tigranocerta
place: by the river before Tigranocerta (probably Arzan, near Batman; Silvan has also been proposed)
roman_force: Lucullus' striking force of 24 cohorts, not more than 10,000 legionaries, with all his cavalry and about 1,000 slingers and archers (Plutarch, Lucullus 27); his Thracian and Galatian horse attacked the flank of the Armenian cataphracts (Plutarch, Lucullus 28).
greek_note: Italian legions with Thracian and Galatian cavalry; the light troops may have included Cretan or Asian archers, but none are named.
sources: Plutarch, Lucullus 26-28; Appian, Mith. 84-85; Memnon of Heraclea 38; Frontinus, Strat. 2.1.14; en.wikipedia Battle of Tigranocerta
note: Plutarch dates it to the day before the Nones of October, the anniversary of Arausio. Tigranes' host is put at over 100,000 (Plutarch: 150,000 foot, 55,000 horse), certainly exaggerated.

name: Armenia (defeat of Mithrobarzanes)
place: at Lucullus' camp on his march from the Euphrates to Tigranocerta, site unknown
borderline: No conventional name: an Armenian cavalry attack on the Roman camp, beaten off.
roman_force: Sextilius' detachment of about 1,600 cavalry and not many more infantry, about 3,500 men in all, left to guard the camp being built (Plutarch, Lucullus 25; en.wikipedia).
greek_note: Part of Lucullus' legions and cavalry; the cavalry may have included Galatian and Thracian horse; no Greek units are recorded.
sources: Plutarch, Lucullus 25; en.wikipedia Third Mithridatic War
note: Tigranes had sent Mithrobarzanes to stop Lucullus; he fell in the fight and most of his men were killed in flight.

name: Cydonia
roman_force: Metellus' proconsular army, landed near Cydonia; its size is not reliably recorded (Phlegon of Tralles fr. 12; Livy, Per. 98).
greek_note: An Italian consular army; no Greek allied contingent is recorded.
sources: Phlegon of Tralles fr. 12; Livy, Per. 98-99; Florus 1.42; Velleius 2.34; en.wikipedia Quintus Caecilius Metellus Creticus
note: Lasthenes fled to Knossos; Panares surrendered Cydonia after a siege.

name: Tigranocerta (siege)
place: Tigranocerta, the new Armenian capital (probably Arzan, near Batman; Silvan has also been proposed)
commanders_a: Lucius Licinius Lucullus; Lucius Licinius Murena
borderline: Usually treated together with the relief battle; counted separately under the siege rule.
roman_force: Lucullus' army, left under Murena with 6,000 men before the walls during the relief battle; after the battle the Greek mercenaries in the city turned on the Armenian garrison and let the Romans in (Plutarch, Lucullus 26-29; Appian, Mith. 84-86).
greek_note: Italian legions; inside the city the Greek mercenaries and settlers Tigranes had deported there sided with the Romans.
sources: Plutarch, Lucullus 26-29; Appian, Mith. 84-86; Memnon of Heraclea 38; en.wikipedia Third Mithridatic War
note: Lucullus sent the deported Greeks home to their cities.

name: Pontus (Fabius' defeat)
place: Pontus, near Cabira (Niksar), where Fabius was afterwards besieged; site not recorded
borderline: No conventional name: Mithridates' victory over Lucullus' legate on his return to Pontus; site not recorded.
roman_force: The force Lucullus had left to hold Pontus under his legate Fabius (numbers not given); Appian says Fabius freed and armed the slaves in his camp (Mith. 88).
greek_note: Detachments of Lucullus' Italian legions; local auxiliaries from the Pontic cities may have served, but none are recorded.
sources: Dio 36.9-10; Appian, Mith. 88; Plutarch, Lucullus 35; the ancient Greek battles set, Pontus (Fabius' defeat) 68 BC
note: Fabius was then shut up in Cabira and rescued by Triarius (Dio 36.10.1).

name: Comana
place: near Comana Pontica (Gumenek, near Tokat), on the Iris
roman_force: Triarius' relief force, the troops he brought up to rescue Fabius at Cabira, with Fabius' men (Dio 36.10); no numbers are given.
greek_note: Detachments of Lucullus' Italian legions; Triarius had commanded in Asia and may have brought Greek allied troops, but none are recorded.
sources: Dio 36.10.2; attalus.org, events of 68 BC ('Triarius defeats Mithridates at Comana'); the ancient Greek battles set, Comana 68 BC
note: Mithridates retired to Comana and was beaten there; in the next year he destroyed Triarius' army at Zela (Gaziura) (-67-zela).

name: Knossos (siege)
date: 68 BCE (en.wikipedia lists the siege as 72-69 BCE)
roman_force: Metellus' proconsular army besieging the chief Cretan city; Lasthenes burned his house and escaped before it fell (Dio 36.17a-19; Livy, Per. 99).
greek_note: An Italian consular army; no Greek allied contingent is recorded.
sources: Dio 36.17a-19; Livy, Per. 99; Florus 1.42; en.wikipedia Quintus Caecilius Metellus Creticus
note: Metellus went on to take Lyctus and Eleutherna, the latter by treachery.

name: Arsanias
place: on the Arsanias (Murat) river, on Lucullus' march toward Artaxata
roman_force: Lucullus' army, the legions and cavalry of the Tigranocerta campaign, increasingly mutinous; it routed the Armenian and Pontic cavalry and archers but then refused to go on to Artaxata (Plutarch, Lucullus 31-32; Appian, Mith. 87).
greek_note: The same Italian legions with Galatian and Thracian horse; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Plutarch, Lucullus 31-32; Appian, Mith. 87; Dio 36.5; en.wikipedia Battle of Artaxata
note: Also called the battle of Artaxata (en.wikipedia's title), after Lucullus' objective; the fighting was on the upper Arsanias (Murat), north of Lake Van, and the army then refused to march on to Artaxata.

name: Nisibis (siege)
roman_force: Lucullus' army, which stormed the walls on a stormy night when the defenders had relaxed their guard (Plutarch, Lucullus 32; Dio 36.6-7).
greek_note: Italian legions; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Plutarch, Lucullus 32; Dio 36.6-7; en.wikipedia Third Mithridatic War

name: Zela
roman_force: Triarius' army, the troops Lucullus had left in Pontus, at least two legions; 7,000 Romans fell, among them 24 tribunes and 150 centurions (Plutarch, Lucullus 35; Appian, Mith. 89).
greek_note: Italian legions; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Plutarch, Lucullus 35; Appian, Mith. 89; Dio 36.12-13; en.wikipedia Battle of Zela (67 BC)
note: Mithridates recovered most of Pontus; he was wounded in the battle.

name: Lappa (siege)
commanders_b: Cretan defenders; Lucius Octavius (Pompey's legate) was present
borderline: Known from Dio's brief account of the quarrel between Metellus and Pompey's legates.
roman_force: Metellus' army stormed Lappa although Pompey's legate Octavius had come there to receive the Cretans' surrender; Metellus dismissed Octavius and executed the Cilicians with him (Dio 36.18-19).
greek_note: An Italian consular army; no Greek allied contingent is recorded.
sources: Dio 36.18-19; Florus 1.42; en.wikipedia Quintus Caecilius Metellus Creticus
note: Octavius later joined the Cretans at Hierapytna with troops taken from Sisenna's army, but withdrew without a battle.

name: Korakesion (sea)
roman_force: Pompey's eastern squadron of the Lex Gabinia command, which gave him up to 500 ships, 120,000 foot and 5,000 horse in all (Plutarch, Pompey 25-26); about 200 ships by the Roman figure at Korakesion.
greek_note: The Gabinian fleets were raised largely from the Greek maritime allies of the East (Rhodes and the cities of Asia), whose crews manned most ships; the infantry was Italian.
sources: Plutarch, Pompey 24-28; Appian, Mith. 94-96; Dio 36.37; en.wikipedia Battle of Korakesion
note: The pirates were beaten at sea, then besieged and surrendered; about 20,000 prisoners were resettled at Soli (Pompeiopolis), Dyme and elsewhere.

name: Cyrus River
place: Pompey's winter camps on the Cyrnus (Kura) river
commanders_a: Pompey; Quintus Caecilius Metellus Celer; Lucius Valerius Flaccus
borderline: Repulse of a surprise attack on the winter camps; no conventional battle name.
roman_force: Pompey's army in three winter camps, attacked by the Albanians during the Saturnalia and beating them off (Dio 36.54; Plutarch, Pompey 34).
greek_note: Italian legions with eastern auxiliaries; no Greek contingent is named.
sources: Dio 36.54; Plutarch, Pompey 34; en.wikipedia Caucasian campaign of Pompey

name: Lycus
place: near the Lycus, where Pompey later founded Nicopolis (near Susehri)
roman_force: Pompey's army of the Lex Manilia, the legions taken over from Lucullus and Glabrio with his own troops, in a night attack on Mithridates' 30,000 foot and 2,000-3,000 horse (Appian, Mith. 97-100; Plutarch, Pompey 32; Dio 36.48-49).
greek_note: Italian legions with auxiliaries of the eastern provinces; no Greek contingent is named.
sources: Appian, Mith. 97-100; Plutarch, Pompey 32; Dio 36.48-49; en.wikipedia Battle of the Lycus
note: Also called the battle of Nicopolis; Mithridates fled through Colchis to the Bosporus.

name: Pelorus
place: on the river Pelorus, Iberia (eastern Georgia); site unidentified
roman_force: Pompey's legions, which charged at the run to close with the Iberian archers; about 9,000 Iberians fell and over 10,000 were captured (Plutarch, Pompey 34; Dio 37.2).
greek_note: Italian legions with eastern auxiliaries; no Greek contingent is named.
sources: Plutarch, Pompey 34; Dio 37.1-2; Appian, Mith. 103; en.wikipedia Caucasian campaign of Pompey
note: Artoces submitted and gave his children as hostages.

name: Abas
place: on the river Abas (perhaps the Alazani), Caucasian Albania
roman_force: Pompey's army, with the cavalry placed in front and the legionaries kneeling hidden behind it, against 60,000 Albanian foot and 12,000 horse by Plutarch's count (Pompey 35; Strabo gives 22,000 horse; Dio 37.4).
greek_note: Italian legions with eastern auxiliary cavalry; no Greek contingent is named.
sources: Plutarch, Pompey 35; Dio 37.3-5; Strabo 11.4.5; en.wikipedia Battle of the Abas
note: The Albanian numbers are probably exaggerated.

name: Jerusalem (siege)
date: 63 BCE (three-month siege of the Temple, ending on a fast day)
commanders_a: Pompey; Faustus Cornelius Sulla (first over the wall)
roman_force: Pompey's legions from Syria with siege engines brought from Tyre, supported by the partisans of Hyrcanus II who opened the city to him; the Temple, held by Aristobulus' men, was stormed after three months and about 12,000 Jews were killed (Josephus, BJ 1.141-151; AJ 14.54-73).
greek_note: Italian legions with auxiliaries raised in the eastern provinces, including the Greek cities of Syria; no figures.
sources: Josephus, BJ 1.141-154, AJ 14.54-79; Dio 37.15-16; Strabo 16.2.40; en.wikipedia Siege of Jerusalem (63 BC)
note: Side 'Judea' is the Hasmonean faction of Aristobulus II; Josephus' 'fast day' is variously read as the Day of Atonement or a Sabbath, so month unknown.

name: Pistoria
place: in the hills near Pistoria (Pistoia), Etruria
commanders_a: Marcus Petreius (for the consul Gaius Antonius Hybrida)
roman_force: The consular army of Gaius Antonius Hybrida, led in battle by his legate Marcus Petreius with a cohort of veterans in front, against Catiline's two legions, no more than about a quarter of whom were properly armed (Sallust, Cat. 56-61).
greek_note: Italian armies on both sides; Catiline's men were Sullan veterans and the poor of Etruria; no Greek speakers recorded.
sources: Sallust, Catiline 56-61; Dio 37.39-40; Plutarch, Cicero 22; en.wikipedia Battle of Pistoria
note: Metellus Celer blocked Catiline's escape over the Apennines into Gaul; Catiline and about 3,000 of his men died fighting.

name: Ventia
place: near Ventia, a town of the Segovellauni in the Rhone valley; site unidentified
roman_force: A part of the army of Transalpine Gaul under Pomptinus' legate Lentinus, which fought the Allobroges near Ventia and in the end took the town (Dio 37.47-48).
greek_note: An Italian provincial army with Gallic auxiliaries; Massalia was an ally but no Massiliot contingent is recorded.
sources: Dio 37.47-48; Livy, Per. 103; en.wikipedia Allobroges
note: Lentinus was at first driven back by a sudden attack of Catugnatus.

name: Solonium (siege)
place: Solonium (Solonion), chief town of the Allobroges; perhaps Salagnon or Montmiral
commanders_a: Gaius Pomptinus; his legates Lucius Marius and Servius Sulpicius Galba
roman_force: The army of Transalpine Gaul under the propraetor Pomptinus; his legates Marius and Galba crossed the Rhone and burned part of the town but were driven off by Catugnatus' relief, and Pomptinus then besieged and took it with his whole army (Dio 37.48).
greek_note: An Italian provincial army with Gallic auxiliaries; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Dio 37.48; Livy, Per. 103; Cicero, De provinciis consularibus 32; en.wikipedia Allobroges
note: Some date the campaign to late 62 BCE.

name: Histria
war: Campaigns of Gaius Antonius Hybrida in Macedonia
place: near the Greek city of Histria, Scythia Minor (Dobruja)
commanders_a: a king of the Bastarnae (not named)
roman_force: The proconsul of Macedonia's army of infantry and cavalry; Antonius fled with his cavalry and the infantry was cut down (Dio 38.10).
greek_note: The army of Macedonia combined Italian legions with Macedonian and Thracian auxiliaries; no figures.
sources: Dio 38.10; Livy, Per. 103; en.wikipedia Battle of Histria
note: The victors were the Bastarnae, whom Dio calls Scythians (their ethnicity is disputed), who came to the help of the Greek cities of the coast; the Dardani had beaten Antonius earlier in an unnamed battle.

name: Mons Herminius
place: Mons Herminius (Serra da Estrela) and the coast beyond
commanders_a: Gaius Julius Caesar (propraetor of Hispania Ulterior)
commanders_b: the hill tribes of Mons Herminius
borderline: A campaign of several actions (the mountain, an island off the coast, Brigantium) rather than one named battle.
roman_force: Caesar's provincial army of twenty cohorts, to which he added ten newly raised (Plutarch, Caesar 12), against the Lusitanian hill peoples, whom he pursued to the Ocean (Dio 37.52-53).
greek_note: Roman legions of Further Spain, partly raised in the province, with Spanish auxiliaries; no Greek speakers recorded.
sources: Dio 37.52-53; Plutarch, Caesar 12; Suetonius, Julius 54; en.wikipedia Gaius Julius Caesar
note: Caesar then fetched ships from Gades and took Brigantium among the Callaeci without a fight.

name: Thurii
place: the territory of Thurii, on the Gulf of Taranto
commanders_a: Gaius Octavius (praetor 61, on his way to Macedonia)
commanders_b: runaway slaves, remnants of the bands of Spartacus and Catiline
borderline: A mopping-up action against runaway slaves; no conventional battle name.
roman_force: The troops Octavius was taking to his province of Macedonia, with which the Senate charged him to clear the runaway slaves from the land of Thurii (Suetonius, Augustus 3.1); no numbers.
greek_note: Troops raised in Italy; no Greek units are attested.
sources: Suetonius, Augustus 3.1, 7.1; en.wikipedia Gaius Octavius (praetor 61 BC)
note: Suetonius says the infant future Augustus was surnamed Thurinus in memory of his father's success at Thurii.

name: Thrace (Octavius against the Bessi)
place: the land of the Bessi (upper Hebrus), site unknown
borderline: No conventional name and no recorded site: 'a great battle' against the Bessi and Thracians.
roman_force: The proconsul's army of Macedonia, legions with provincial auxiliaries; no numbers are given (Suetonius, Augustus 3.2: 'a great battle').
greek_note: The army of Macedonia was Roman-Italian; Macedonian and Greek auxiliaries are likely but not recorded.
sources: Suetonius, Augustus 3.2; Velleius 2.59.2; en.wikipedia Gaius Octavius (praetor 61 BC)
note: Octavius was saluted imperator for it (Broughton, MRR 2.191).

name: Arar
place: The crossing of the Arar (Saone), probably near Trevoux or Macon
commanders_b: the Tigurini canton of the Helvetii (no leader named)
roman_force: Three of Caesar's six legions (VII-XII) caught the Tigurini, the last quarter of the Helvetii still on the near bank; the legions were raised in Cisalpine Gaul and Narbonensis.
greek_note: Caesar's legions of 58 BCE were raised in Cisalpine Gaul and the Province; no Greek units are named in this action.
sources: Caesar BG 1.12-13; Plutarch Caesar 18; en.wikipedia Battle of the Arar
note: Helvetii (Tigurini canton). The exact crossing point is unknown.

name: Bibracte
place: About 18 Roman miles from Bibracte (Mont Beuvray), Saone-et-Loire
commanders_b: Helvetian chiefs (Divico in some modern accounts)
roman_force: Six legions (VII-XII), the two newest guarding the baggage, with auxiliary light infantry and about 4,000 Gallic (mostly Aeduan) allied cavalry.
greek_note: Caesar's auxiliaries included a few hundred Cretan archers (named in 57 BCE, BG 2.7); the legions and cavalry were Latin- and Celtic-speaking.
sources: Caesar BG 1.23-26; Plutarch Caesar 18; en.wikipedia Battle of Bibracte
note: Helvetii with the Boii and Tulingi. Battlefield sites proposed include Montmort and Armecy; Caesar's figure of 368,000 migrants is doubted.

name: Vosges
place: Upper Rhine plain of Alsace, probably near Cernay or Mulhouse (also called the battle of Vesontio)
commanders_a: Gaius Julius Caesar, Publius Licinius Crassus (cavalry)
roman_force: Six legions (VII-XII), about 25,000-30,000 men, with auxiliary light infantry and allied Gallic cavalry.
greek_note: Only the small Cretan archer contingent among the auxiliaries spoke Greek.
sources: Caesar BG 1.48-53; Cassius Dio 38.47-50; en.wikipedia Battle of Vosges (58 BC)
note: Suebi with the Harudes, Marcomanni, Triboci, Vangiones, Nemetes and Sedusii. The day is a modern reckoning; the site is uncertain.

name: Sabis
place: River Sabis, the Sambre (traditionally) or the Selle near Saulzoir
roman_force: Eight legions (VII-XIV, 30,000-45,000 men) caught building their camp, with Numidian, Cretan and Balearic light troops, Gallic cavalry and Treveran horse (who fled).
greek_note: The Cretan archers named at Bibrax were with the army; all else was Latin- and Celtic-speaking.
sources: Caesar BG 2.16-28; Plutarch Caesar 20; en.wikipedia Battle of the Sabis
note: Nervii with the Atrebates and Viromandui; the Atuatuci came too late. The river is traditionally the Sambre; Turquin (1955) argued for the Selle.

name: Axona
place: Caesar's camp on the Aisne near Berry-au-Bac (Mauchamp), after the Belgic attack on Bibrax
commanders_a: Gaius Julius Caesar, Quintus Titurius Sabinus
roman_force: Eight legions (VII-XIV, about 40,000 men), six in line and two in camp, with Numidian light troops, Cretan archers and Balearic slingers sent to Bibrax, and Gallic cavalry.
greek_note: Caesar names Cretan archers among the troops sent to relieve Bibrax (BG 2.7), a few hundred men at most.
sources: Caesar BG 2.5-11; Cassius Dio 39.1-2; en.wikipedia Battle of the Axona
note: Belgic coalition (Suessiones, Bellovaci, Nervii and others); allies the Remi, whose oppidum Bibrax the Belgae had assaulted. Wikipedia's infobox coordinates (49.43, 2.85) disagree with the usual site at Berry-au-Bac.

name: Alexandreion
place: Battle near Jerusalem, then the siege of the fortress of Alexandreion (Sartaba) above the Jordan valley
borderline: Known only from Josephus; not given a battle name in most modern works.
roman_force: Gabinius' Syrian army (the legions left by Pompey), with Antony leading the advance and the cavalry, and Jewish troops of Hyrcanus II under Peitholaus and Malichus.
greek_note: The Syrian legions had served in the East since Pompey's war and may have taken local recruits; Gabinius' horse included Gauls and Germans (the later Gabiniani).
sources: Josephus BJ 1.160-168, AJ 14.82-91; en.wikipedia Alexander of Judaea
note: Josephus reports 3,000 of Alexander's men killed near Jerusalem; Alexandreion later surrendered.

name: Atuatuci (siege)
place: The chief oppidum of the Atuatuci, perhaps the citadel of Namur or Thuin
roman_force: Caesar's army of eight legions with a siege tower; the town surrendered, then made a night sortie in which 4,000 were killed, and 53,000 were sold.
greek_note: As in the rest of the 57 BCE campaign, only the Cretan archers spoke Greek.
sources: Caesar BG 2.29-33; en.wikipedia Siege of the Atuatuci
note: Atuatuci (Belgae). The site is disputed (Namur, Thuin, Montaigle, Hastedon).

name: Octodurus
place: Octodurus (Martigny), Valais, below the Great St Bernard pass
roman_force: Legio XII, understrength (perhaps 5,000 men or fewer), with some cavalry, in its winter camp.
greek_note: A single legion raised in Cisalpine Gaul or Narbonensis.
sources: Caesar BG 3.1-6; en.wikipedia Battle of Octodurus
note: Seduni and Veragri. Galba broke out and won, but then withdrew from the Alps.

name: Machaerus
place: A battle in the field, then the two-day siege of the fortress of Machaerus east of the Dead Sea
commanders_a: Sisenna (son of Gabinius), Mark Antony, Servianus
borderline: Known only from Josephus; not given a battle name in most modern works.
roman_force: A detachment of Gabinius' Syrian army under his legates; Josephus says 5,000 of Aristobulus' men fell before the siege.
greek_note: The Roman army of Syria, Latin-speaking with possible local recruits.
sources: Josephus BJ 1.171-174, AJ 14.92-97; en.wikipedia Aristobulus II
note: Aristobulus, escaped from Rome, was captured and sent back.

name: Sotiates
place: Territory of the Sotiates and their oppidum, probably Sos (Lot-et-Garonne)
borderline: Described by Caesar but rarely given a battle name in modern works.
roman_force: Twelve legionary cohorts and a large cavalry force, reinforced by auxiliaries and cavalry from Tolosa, Carcaso and Narbo.
greek_note: Legionaries of Caesar's army and Gallic levies of the Province.
sources: Caesar BG 3.20-22; en.wikipedia Sotiates
note: Sotiates (Aquitani). A field battle after an ambush, then the siege of their town, which surrendered after a failed sortie by Adiatuanus' 600 devoted followers.

name: Morbihan (sea)
place: Off the coast of the Veneti, probably Quiberon Bay or the mouth of the Gulf of Morbihan
commanders_a: Decimus Junius Brutus Albinus (fleet), Gaius Julius Caesar (watching from the shore)
roman_force: Galleys built on the Loire and ships levied from the Pictones, Santones and other pacified states, with rowers and seamen from the Province and legionaries on board.
greek_note: Rowers and seamen were raised in the Province (Narbonensis), where some may have been Greeks of the Massiliot coast; the allied ships were Gallic.
sources: Caesar BG 3.7-16; Cassius Dio 39.40-43; en.wikipedia Battle of Morbihan
note: Veneti, about 220 ships, destroyed after the Romans cut their halyards with hooked poles; also called the battle of Quiberon Bay.

name: Sabinus against the Venelli
place: Sabinus' camp in the territory of the Venelli (Unelli), Cotentin, perhaps Le Petit-Celland
borderline: Described by Caesar but rarely given a battle name in modern works.
roman_force: Three legions under Sabinus, who feigned fear and charged the Gauls as they climbed to his hill camp.
greek_note: Legions of Caesar's Gallic army; no Greek units named.
sources: Caesar BG 3.17-19; Cassius Dio 39.45
note: Venelli with the Lexovii and Aulerci Eburovices.

name: Vocates and Tarusates
place: The Aquitanian camp in the lands of the Vocates and Tarusates (Landes or Gers)
borderline: Described by Caesar but rarely given a battle name in modern works.
roman_force: Crassus' twelve cohorts with cavalry and auxiliaries from the Province; four cohorts broke into the rear of the enemy camp.
greek_note: Legionaries and Gallic levies of the Province.
sources: Caesar BG 3.23-27
note: Aquitani (Vocates, Tarusates and others), with help from Hither Spain (Cantabri); Caesar claims 50,000 men, of whom a quarter escaped.

name: Landing in Britain
place: The open beach of east Kent, probably between Walmer and Deal
borderline: No fixed name in standard works.
roman_force: Legions VII and X, landed from about 80 transports with warships firing slings, arrows and artillery; the cavalry transports failed to arrive.
greek_note: Two legions of Caesar's Gallic army; no Greek units named.
sources: Caesar BG 4.20-36; Cassius Dio 39.51-53; en.wikipedia Caesar's invasions of Britain
note: Britons of Kent (Cantiaci). Includes the later attack on the foraging Seventh legion and the defeat of the Britons before the camp.

name: Nile
place: On and beside a branch of the Nile in the Delta (site unknown)
borderline: Known from short notices: Dio describes a second victory, on the river and on land, after the battle beyond Pelusium.
roman_force: Gabinius' army of Syria (the legions Pompey had left there, with Gallic and German horse), fighting on land and with boats on the river; Dio gives no numbers (Dio 39.58).
greek_note: The army was the Italian legions of Syria with western cavalry; any Greek speakers came from local recruits and the Jewish and Syrian helpers of the march.
sources: Cassius Dio 39.58; Strabo 12.3.34, 17.1.11; Plutarch Antony 3
note: Archelaus, husband of Berenice IV, fell (Strabo 17.1.11; Dio 39.58) and Ptolemy XII was restored. Set 12 has this battle as Nile 55 BCE.

name: Pelusium
place: Pelusium, the eastern gate of Egypt, and the battle beyond it in the eastern Delta
borderline: A capture and an unnamed field battle; grouped under the name of Pelusium.
roman_force: Gabinius' Syrian army; Antony with the cavalry seized Pelusium, and Antipater brought Jewish troops and supplies.
greek_note: Gabinius' force was the Roman army of Syria with Gallic and German horse (some of whom stayed in Egypt as the Gabiniani).
sources: Plutarch Antony 3; Cassius Dio 39.58; Josephus AJ 14.98-99; Strabo 12.3.34
note: The Ptolemaic army of Berenice IV. Dio says Gabinius reached Pelusium without opposition and defeated the Egyptians beyond it the same day; the later river battle in which Archelaus fell is entered as Nile (55 BCE).

name: Usipetes and Tencteri
place: Near the confluence of the Meuse and the Rhine, perhaps at Kessel
borderline: Largely a massacre of a migrating people after a cavalry clash; included because it began with a battle.
roman_force: Caesar's army of eight legions and about 5,000 Gallic allied cavalry; 800 German horsemen first routed the Gallic cavalry, then the legions stormed the German camp.
greek_note: Only the Cretan archers among the auxiliaries would have spoken Greek.
sources: Caesar BG 4.1-15; Plutarch Caesar 22; Appian Celtica 18
note: Usipetes (Usipi) and Tencteri. The site is disputed: Kessel (Netherlands) or near Koblenz (Moselle confluence).

name: Mount Tabor
borderline: Known only from Josephus.
roman_force: Gabinius' Syrian army back from Egypt, with Antipater's Jewish supporters; Josephus says 10,000 of Alexander's 30,000 fell.
greek_note: The Roman army of Syria; no Greek units are named.
sources: Josephus BJ 1.176-178, AJ 14.100-102; attalus.org (Tabor)

name: Bigbury
place: A river crossing (the Stour) and a forest stronghold beyond it, probably Bigbury Wood near Canterbury
borderline: The identification and the name Bigbury are modern.
roman_force: Five legions and 2,000 (mostly Gallic) cavalry; the Seventh legion stormed the stronghold under a testudo and earth ramp.
greek_note: Legions of Caesar's Gallic army and Gallic cavalry.
sources: Caesar BG 5.8-9; en.wikipedia Caesar's invasions of Britain
note: Britons of Kent (Cantiaci).

name: Thames crossing
place: The only ford of the Thames in Cassivellaunus' territory, location unknown (Brentford and Westminster are proposed)
borderline: A forced river crossing, not a pitched battle.
roman_force: Caesar's cavalry and legions (five legions in Britain) forced the staked ford, the infantry wading neck-deep.
greek_note: Legions of Caesar's Gallic army and Gallic cavalry.
sources: Caesar BG 5.18; Cassius Dio 40.3; Polyaenus 8.23.5
note: Catuvellauni under Cassivellaunus. Polyaenus' elephant story is probably a confusion with Claudius' campaign.

name: Cassivellaunus' stronghold
place: Cassivellaunus' oppidum, possibly Wheathampstead (Devil's Dyke), Hertfordshire
borderline: A short assault on a stronghold; the site is unknown.
roman_force: Caesar's legions assaulted the stronghold from two sides; guided by the Trinovantes and the other tribes that had submitted.
greek_note: Legions of Caesar's Gallic army.
sources: Caesar BG 5.21-22; en.wikipedia Caesar's invasions of Britain
note: Catuvellauni. At the same time the four kings of Kent (Cingetorix, Carvilius, Taximagulus, Segovax) attacked Caesar's naval camp and were repulsed.

name: Atuatuca
place: A defile two miles from the winter camp at Atuatuca, among the Eburones, probably near Tongeren
commanders_b: Quintus Titurius Sabinus, Lucius Aurunculeius Cotta
roman_force: One legion recently raised north of the Po and five further cohorts (fifteen cohorts in all), destroyed on the march after leaving camp.
greek_note: A new legion levied in Transpadane Gaul.
sources: Caesar BG 5.26-37; Cassius Dio 40.5-6; Suetonius Caesar 25; en.wikipedia Ambiorix's revolt
note: Eburones (Belgae). The site of Atuatuca is disputed; Tongeren is the usual identification.

name: Cicero's camp (siege)
place: Quintus Cicero's winter camp among the Nervii (site unknown, Hainaut) and Caesar's relief battle nearby
commanders_a: Quintus Tullius Cicero, Gaius Julius Caesar
roman_force: Cicero's single legion held the camp; Caesar relieved it with two legions (about 7,000 men) and 400 cavalry and routed some 60,000 Gauls.
greek_note: Legions of Caesar's Gallic army.
sources: Caesar BG 5.38-52; Cassius Dio 40.7-10; en.wikipedia Ambiorix's revolt
note: Nervii with the Eburones, Atuatuci and smaller Belgic tribes.

name: Ichnae
place: Near Ichnae, on the Balikh south of Carrhae
borderline: A skirmish with a satrap's cavalry; no Wikipedia battle article.
roman_force: Part of Crassus' army of Syria (legions levied in Italy in 55 BCE and the Syrian garrison) on its first crossing of the Euphrates.
greek_note: The legions were levied in Italy; any light troops raised in Syria would have included Greek-speakers.
sources: Cassius Dio 40.12; Plutarch Crassus 17; en.wikipedia Silaces, Ichnae (Mesopotamia)
note: Silaces was wounded and fled to report to the king.

name: Zenodotium (siege)
place: Zenodotium, a Macedonian-Greek town of Osroene near Nicephorium
borderline: A small storming of a town.
roman_force: Crassus' army, after the town's tyrant had killed about 100 Roman soldiers sent into it; the town was stormed and its people sold.
greek_note: As at Ichnae: Italian legions with possible Syrian light troops.
sources: Plutarch Crassus 17; Cassius Dio 40.13
note: Greek city: Zenodotium. Crassus was hailed imperator for it.

name: Labienus against Indutiomarus
place: Labienus' winter camp among the Remi on the border of the Treveri (southern Ardennes)
borderline: A camp sortie rather than a named battle.
roman_force: One legion and cavalry summoned secretly from neighbouring states, which made a sudden sortie and killed Indutiomarus.
greek_note: A legion of Caesar's Gallic army with Gallic allied cavalry.
sources: Caesar BG 5.53-58; Cassius Dio 40.11
note: Treveri. Dated to the winter after Atuatuca; some chronologies put it in early 53 BCE.

name: Carrhae
place: The plain south of Carrhae (Harran), near the Balikh
commanders_b: Marcus Licinius Crassus, Publius Licinius Crassus, Gaius Cassius Longinus
roman_force: Seven legions (about 35,000 heavy infantry), nearly 4,000 cavalry including 1,000 Gallic horsemen brought by Publius Crassus from Caesar, and about 4,000 light infantry (Plutarch Crassus 20).
greek_note: The legions were levied in Italy; the light infantry and some cavalry were probably raised in Syria and the Greek towns of Mesopotamia.
sources: Plutarch Crassus 20-31; Cassius Dio 40.16-27; Ovid Fasti 6.465-468; en.wikipedia Battle of Carrhae
note: The date is Ovid's (fifth day before the Ides of June); some modern works give May 53 BCE. The Osroenian chief Abgar (Ariamnes in Plutarch) misled the army and deserted before the battle.

name: Labienus against the Treveri
place: A river crossing on the borders of the Treveri (perhaps the Alzette or the Ourthe)
borderline: Described by Caesar but rarely given a battle name.
roman_force: Twenty-five cohorts and a large cavalry force; Labienus feigned retreat to draw the Treveri across the river.
greek_note: Legions of Caesar's Gallic army and Gallic cavalry.
sources: Caesar BG 6.7-8; Cassius Dio 40.31
note: Treveri, before their German allies arrived.

name: Atuatuca
place: The baggage camp at Atuatuca among the Eburones, probably near Tongeren
borderline: A raid on a camp by 2,000 German horsemen.
roman_force: Legio XIV (a new legion) guarding the army's baggage, with some 200 cavalry and the sick; two cohorts of foragers were cut off and destroyed.
greek_note: A recently levied legion from Cisalpine Gaul.
sources: Caesar BG 6.35-42
note: Sugambri. They failed to take the camp and withdrew, but destroyed two cohorts; Caesar presents it as a setback.

name: Cenabum (siege)
place: Cenabum (Orleans), town of the Carnutes on the Loire
borderline: More a sack after a short siege than a battle.
roman_force: Caesar's legions (at least eight) stormed the gates when the townsmen tried to escape over the Loire bridge by night; the town was sacked and burned.
greek_note: Legions of Caesar's Gallic army.
sources: Caesar BG 7.11; en.wikipedia Battle of Alesia (background)
note: Carnutes, in revenge for their massacre of Roman traders at Cenabum that began the revolt.

name: Noviodunum
place: Noviodunum of the Bituriges, perhaps Neuvy-sur-Barangeon
borderline: A surrender interrupted by a cavalry engagement.
roman_force: Caesar's army; about 400 German horsemen decided the cavalry fight with Vercingetorix's vanguard, after which the town surrendered again.
greek_note: Legions of Caesar's Gallic army with Gallic and German cavalry.
sources: Caesar BG 7.12-13
note: Bituriges and Vercingetorix's cavalry. Site uncertain.

name: Avaricum (siege)
roman_force: Eight (probably understrength) legions, about 25,000-30,000 legionaries, with auxiliaries; the town was taken by assault from a siege terrace.
greek_note: Legions of Caesar's Gallic army.
sources: Caesar BG 7.13-28; en.wikipedia Siege of Avaricum
note: Bituriges and the confederation under Vercingetorix. Caesar says of 40,000 inhabitants only 800 escaped.

name: Vingeanne
place: Probably the Vingeanne valley near Montsaugeon, on Caesar's march through the land of the Lingones
roman_force: Caesar's army of ten or more legions on the march; German horsemen and light infantry hired from beyond the Rhine broke the Gallic cavalry.
greek_note: Legions of Caesar's Gallic army with German cavalry.
sources: Caesar BG 7.66-68; Plutarch Caesar 26; en.wikipedia Battle of the Vingeanne
note: The cavalry battle that drove Vercingetorix into Alesia. The site is a modern identification (Wikipedia's infobox coordinates are wrong).

name: Alesia
date: September 52 BCE (siege of about six weeks)
place: Alesia, Mont Auxois above Alise-Sainte-Reine, Cote-d'Or
commanders_a: Gaius Julius Caesar, Titus Labienus, Mark Antony, Gaius Trebonius, Decimus Brutus, Gaius Fabius
roman_force: Ten or eleven legions (I, V, VII-XV; 30,000-50,000 legionaries) with about 10,000 auxiliaries, among them German cavalry and light infantry, behind double lines of circumvallation.
greek_note: Archers and slingers among the auxiliaries may have included Cretans; the army was overwhelmingly Latin-, Celtic- and Germanic-speaking.
sources: Caesar BG 7.68-90; Plutarch Caesar 27; Cassius Dio 40.39-41; en.wikipedia Battle of Alesia
note: Gallic confederation under Vercingetorix and the relief army (Caesar claims 250,000). Vercingetorix surrendered.

name: Gergovia
place: Gergovia, chief oppidum of the Arverni (plateau of Gergovie, near Clermont-Ferrand)
roman_force: Six legions (V, VI, VIII, X, XI, XIII among them), 15,000-30,000 legionaries, with Aeduan allied troops (10,000 Aeduan infantry joined during the siege).
greek_note: Legions of Caesar's Gallic army with Aeduan allies.
sources: Caesar BG 7.34-53; Plutarch Caesar 26; en.wikipedia Battle of Gergovia
note: Arverni and allies. Caesar's failed assault cost 46 centurions and about 700 men; he raised the siege.

name: Lutetia
place: Left bank of the Seine near Lutetia (Paris), perhaps the plain of Grenelle
roman_force: Four legions (Caesar names VII and XII) and the cavalry, after a night crossing of the Seine from Metlosedum.
greek_note: Legions of Caesar's Gallic army.
sources: Caesar BG 7.57-62; en.wikipedia Battle of Lutetia
note: Parisii, Senones and Aulerci; Camulogenus was killed. The battlefield is disputed (Grenelle, Issy, or upstream near Melun).

name: Tarichaea (siege)
place: Tarichaea (Magdala), on the Sea of Galilee
borderline: Known only from Josephus as a capture; the fighting is not described.
roman_force: The remnant of Crassus' army that Cassius had brought back to Syria (about two legions' worth).
greek_note: Survivors of the Italian legions of Carrhae with whatever was raised in Syria.
sources: Josephus AJ 14.119-120, BJ 1.180
note: Josephus says 30,000 were enslaved; Peitholaus was put to death at Antipater's urging.

name: Antioch (siege)
place: Antioch on the Orontes, and the ambush of the retreating Parthians near Antigonea
roman_force: The two weak legions of Syria, formed from the survivors of Carrhae, with local levies; Cassius held Antioch and ambushed the Parthians on their retreat, mortally wounding Osaces.
greek_note: Italian legionaries with Syrian levies from a Greek-speaking province.
sources: Cassius Dio 40.28-29; Cicero Att. 5.20-21, Fam. 2.10; en.wikipedia Siege of Antioch (51 BC)
note: The ambush near Antigonea is sometimes counted as a separate battle.

name: Pindenissus (siege)
place: Pindenissus, hill town of the free Cilicians in the Amanus range
commanders_a: Marcus Tullius Cicero, Quintus Tullius Cicero, Gaius Pomptinus
borderline: A provincial siege known from Cicero's letters.
roman_force: Cicero's provincial army of two understrength legions with auxiliary infantry and cavalry; the town fell to towers, a terrace and archers after 57 days.
greek_note: The Cilician legions had long served in the East and Cicero raised auxiliaries locally, from a Greek-speaking province.
sources: Cicero Att. 5.20, Fam. 15.4; Plutarch Cicero 36
note: The Eleutherocilices (free Cilicians). It surrendered on the morning of the Saturnalia; Cicero had earlier taken forts on Mount Amanus and been hailed imperator.

name: Bellovaci
place: Country of the Bellovaci, near the Bellovacian camp on a hill by the Aisne-Oise woods (forest of Compiegne)
borderline: A campaign with an ambush-battle, not usually given a battle name.
roman_force: Four legions (VII, VIII, IX and XI), with Remi and Lingones cavalry and German horse; Correus' ambush of the foragers was turned and he was killed.
greek_note: Legions of Caesar's Gallic army with Gallic and German cavalry.
sources: Caesar BG 8.6-22 (Hirtius); Cassius Dio 40.43
note: Bellovaci with Atrebates, Ambiani, Aulerci, Caleti and Veliocasses.

name: Lemonum (siege)
roman_force: Two understrength legions under Caninius, whose camp Dumnacus attacked for several days, then 25 cohorts under Fabius; Dumnacus raised the siege.
greek_note: Legions of Caesar's Gallic army.
sources: Caesar BG 8.26-27 (Hirtius); historyofwar.org Gallic War
note: Andes under Dumnacus besieged the pro-Roman Pictonian Duratius in Lemonum (also spelled Limonum).

name: Loire
place: Near a bridge over the Loire, in the country of the Andes (perhaps Les Ponts-de-Ce)
borderline: Not usually given a battle name.
roman_force: Fabius' cavalry caught Dumnacus' column and held it until the legions came up; Hirtius reports 12,000 Gauls killed.
greek_note: Legions of Caesar's Gallic army with Gallic cavalry.
sources: Caesar BG 8.27-29 (Hirtius)
note: Andes; the pursuit after Lemonum.

name: Uxellodunum (siege)
place: Uxellodunum, probably the Puy d'Issolud, Lot
commanders_a: Gaius Caninius Rebilus, Gaius Fabius, Gaius Julius Caesar
roman_force: Two legions under Caninius and 25 cohorts under Fabius, then Caesar with his cavalry; the spring was cut by mining.
greek_note: Legions of Caesar's Gallic army.
sources: Caesar BG 8.32-44 (Hirtius); en.wikipedia Siege of Uxellodunum
note: Cadurci and Senones. Caesar had the hands of the defenders cut off.

name: Corfinium (siege)
place: Corfinium (Corfinio), town of the Paeligni, Abruzzo
commanders_a: Gaius Julius Caesar, Mark Antony, Gaius Scribonius Curio
commanders_b: Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus, Publius Cornelius Lentulus Spinther
borderline: Little fighting: a skirmish for the bridge three miles out, then encirclement and surrender.
roman_force: Caesar: legions XIII and XII, then VIII, 22 new cohorts from Gaul and 300 Norican horse; Domitius: 33 cohorts (about 16,000) of fresh levies from the Marsi, Paeligni and Picenum.
greek_note: Both armies were raised in Italy and Cisalpine Gaul.
sources: Caesar BC 1.15-23; Appian BC 2.38; Plutarch Caesar 34; en.wikipedia Siege of Corfinium
note: Domitius' cohorts went over to Caesar.

name: Brundisium (siege)
commanders_a: Gaius Julius Caesar, Mark Antony, Gaius Caninius Rebilus
commanders_b: Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus, Lucius Scribonius Libo
borderline: Mostly missile exchanges at the harbour works; Pompey evacuated by sea.
roman_force: Caesar: six legions (VIII, XII, XIII and three new); Pompey: about twenty cohorts in the town, with transports fitted with towers against Caesar's harbour moles.
greek_note: Both armies were Italian levies and Caesar's Gallic veterans.
sources: Caesar BC 1.24-28; Plutarch Pompey 62; en.wikipedia Siege of Brundisium
note: Caesar took the town and two ships, but Pompey's army escaped to Dyrrachium.

name: Massilia (siege)
commanders_a: Gaius Trebonius, Decimus Junius Brutus Albinus, Gaius Julius Caesar
roman_force: Caesar: three legions under Trebonius (about 15,000) with siege terraces and towers, and twelve warships built at Arelate; Pompeian: Domitius with his tenants and slaves from Igilium and Cosa, beside the Massiliot citizens and Albici highlanders.
greek_note: The Roman forces on both sides were Latin-speaking; the Greeks were the Massiliot defenders, counted as the enemy.
sources: Caesar BC 1.34-36, 2.1-16, 2.22; Cassius Dio 41.19, 41.25; Lucan 3.298-762; en.wikipedia Siege of Massilia
note: Greek city: Massilia, a principal belligerent with Domitius' Pompeians; allies the Albici. Domitius escaped; the city lost most of its territory.

name: Ilerda
place: Ilerda (Lleida) on the Sicoris (Segre), and the retreat towards the Ebro
roman_force: Caesar: six legions (VI, VII, IX, X, XI, XIV) with 5,000 auxiliary infantry and 3,000 Gallic cavalry, later 6,000 more Gauls; Pompeians: five legions with about 80 cohorts of Spanish auxiliaries (scutati and caetrati) and 5,000 cavalry.
greek_note: Italian and Spanish legions, Gallic cavalry and Iberian-speaking auxiliaries.
sources: Caesar BC 1.37-87; Appian BC 2.42; Cassius Dio 41.20-23; en.wikipedia Battle of Ilerda
note: A campaign of manoeuvre; the Pompeian army, cut off from water, surrendered (2 August in the Fasti). 'other' = Iberian.

name: Massilia (sea)
place: Off Massilia, near the islands in front of the harbour
roman_force: Brutus' twelve warships built at Arelate, manned with picked legionaries and centurions; against 17 Massiliot warships carrying Albici and Domitius' men.
greek_note: The rowers of Brutus' new fleet are not described; the fighting men were legionaries.
sources: Caesar BC 1.56-58; en.wikipedia Siege of Massilia
note: Greek city: Massilia. The Massiliots lost nine ships.

name: Tauroento (sea)
place: Off Tauroentum (Le Brusc), east of Massilia
roman_force: Brutus' 18 ships (12 built at Arelate and 6 taken from Massilia), with legionaries aboard; against Nasidius' Pompeian squadron of 16-17 ships and 17 Massiliot ships.
greek_note: The crews of Nasidius' squadron, raised in Italy and Sicily, are not described.
sources: Caesar BC 2.3-7; en.wikipedia Battle of Tauroento
note: Greek city: Massilia. The Massiliots lost nine ships (five sunk, four taken); Nasidius withdrew to Spain. The Massilia article puts it in early September.

name: Bagradas
place: The plain of the Bagradas (Medjerda) near Utica
borderline: Fought in Caesar's civil war against the Pompeians' ally Juba, but no Pompeian Roman force took part, so not counted as civil.
roman_force: Most of Curio's two legions (five cohorts left in camp) and his few hundred cavalry; nearly all were killed with Curio.
greek_note: Italian legionaries and Gallic horse.
sources: Caesar BC 2.37-44; Appian BC 2.45-46; Cassius Dio 41.42; en.wikipedia Battle of the Bagradas River (49 BC)
note: Juba's army included his guard of 2,000 Spanish and Gallic horsemen.

name: Utica
place: Before the Pompeian camp at Utica
commanders_a: Gaius Scribonius Curio, Gaius Caninius Rebilus
roman_force: Curio: two legions (Domitius' former cohorts from Corfinium) and 500 cavalry; Varus: legions raised in Africa, with Numidian horse and light infantry sent by Juba.
greek_note: Italian and African-Roman legions with Numidian allies.
sources: Caesar BC 2.23-36; en.wikipedia Battle of Utica (49 BC)
note: Varus' men fled into the town.

name: Curicta (siege)
place: The island of Curicta (Krk) and the strait off the Illyrian coast
roman_force: Caesarians: Gaius Antonius' fifteen cohorts on the island and Dolabella's fleet, defeated at sea; Pompeians: the squadrons of Octavius and Libo. One Opitergian cohort under Vulteius fought to the death on rafts.
greek_note: Octavius and Libo commanded Pompey's Liburnian and Achaean squadrons (Caesar BC 3.5); the Achaean ships were Greek-manned.
sources: Cassius Dio 41.40; Florus 2.13.31-33; Lucan 4.402-581; Livy Periochae 110; Orosius 6.15.8; en.wikipedia Siege of Curicta
note: A naval defeat followed by the blockade of Antonius' army, which surrendered. Combined land and sea action.

name: Salona (siege)
roman_force: Caesarians: the community of Roman citizens of Salona, who armed their freed slaves and stormed Octavius' five camps in turn; Pompeians: Octavius' squadron and troops with Dalmatian allies.
greek_note: Octavius' squadron included Pompey's Achaean ships (Caesar BC 3.5).
sources: Caesar BC 3.9; en.wikipedia Siege of Salona; historyofwar.org Siege of Salonae
note: Octavius withdrew to Pompey at Dyrrachium. historyofwar dates it to 49 BCE; Caesar tells it at the opening of 48.

name: Dyrrhachium
date: April - July 48 BCE (main battle about 10 July)
place: The lines of Petra south of Dyrrachium (Durres)
commanders_b: Gaius Julius Caesar, Mark Antony, Publius Cornelius Sulla
roman_force: Pompey: nine citizen legions (five from Italy, one of Cilician veterans, one from Crete and Macedonia, two raised in Asia), filled with recruits from Thessaly, Boeotia, Achaea and Epirus, about 7,000 cavalry and allied archers and slingers; Caesar: seven, then eleven understrength legions with Gallic and German cavalry.
greek_note: Caesar says Pompey filled his legions with men of Thessaly, Boeotia, Achaea and Epirus and raised two legions in Asia; his archers came from Crete, Lacedaemon and Pontus (BC 3.4). Share given for both armies together.
sources: Caesar BC 3.41-72; Appian BC 2.60-62; Plutarch Caesar 39; en.wikipedia Battle of Dyrrhachium (48 BC)
note: Pompey broke Caesar's lines of circumvallation; Caesar withdrew to Thessaly.

name: Gomphi (siege)
roman_force: Caesar's army after Dyrrhachium (nine much-reduced legions with Gallic and German cavalry) stormed the walls between mid-afternoon and sunset.
greek_note: A few Greek light troops from Aetolia and Acarnania served with Caesar in this campaign.
sources: Caesar BC 3.80; Appian BC 2.64; Cassius Dio 41.51; en.wikipedia Siege of Gomphi
note: Greek city: Gomphi, which shut its gates to Caesar on Pompey's side; sacked.

name: Pharsalus
place: The plain of the Enipeus near Palaepharsalus, Thessaly
commanders_a: Gaius Julius Caesar, Mark Antony, Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus, Publius Cornelius Sulla
commanders_b: Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus, Metellus Scipio, Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus, Titus Labienus, Lucius Afranius
roman_force: Caesar: eight understrength legions (VI-XIII, about 22,000), 1,000 Gallic and German cavalry and Greek light troops from Aetolia, Acarnania and Dolopia; Pompey: eleven legions (45,000 by Caesar's count) filled with Greek recruits, 7,000 cavalry (many from Galatia, Cappadocia, Thrace and Macedonia) and archers and slingers from Crete, Sparta, Pontus and Syria.
greek_note: Pompey's legions included two raised in Asia and were made up with men from Thessaly, Boeotia, Achaea and Epirus (Caesar BC 3.4); Caesar had Greek light infantry. Share given for both armies together.
sources: Caesar BC 3.82-99; Plutarch Pompey 68-72, Caesar 42-46; Appian BC 2.68-82; en.wikipedia Battle of Pharsalus
note: The Republican date corresponds to about June 48 BCE in the Julian reckoning. Allied kings: Deiotarus (Galatia), Ariobarzanes (Cappadocia), Sadala (Thrace) and others.

name: Messana and Vibo (sea)
place: The harbours of Messana (Messina) and Vibo (Vibo Valentia)
borderline: Two fireship raids on fleets at anchor; not usually named as a battle.
roman_force: Pompeian: Cassius' fleet of Syrian, Phoenician and Cilician ships with fireships; Caesarian: Pomponius' 35 ships at Messana and Sulpicius' ships at Vibo, defended by convalescent veterans who manned ships and counter-attacked.
greek_note: Cassius' squadron was the Syrian, Phoenician and Cilician fleet (Caesar BC 3.5, 3.101). Share given for both sides together.
sources: Caesar BC 3.101
note: Cassius burned 35 ships at Messana and 5 at Vibo, but at Vibo the veterans took two of his ships, his own among them; news of Pharsalus ended the raid.

name: Nicopolis
war: Caesar's civil war (war with Pharnaces II)
roman_force: Legio XXXVI (former Pompeians), a legion of raw recruits levied in Pontus, and two Galatian legions of King Deiotarus armed in the Roman fashion, with Galatian and Cappadocian cavalry.
greek_note: The Pontic legion was levied in the Greek-speaking province of Pontus (Bellum Alexandrinum 34).
sources: Bellum Alexandrinum 34-40; Cassius Dio 42.46; en.wikipedia Battle of Nicopolis (48 BC)
note: Pharnaces II, king of the Bosporus, invading his father's kingdom of Pontus.

name: Alexandria (siege)
place: The palace quarter, harbours and island of Pharos at Alexandria
commanders_b: Achillas, Ganymedes, Arsinoe IV, Ptolemy XIII
roman_force: Legio VI and Legio XXVII, 3,200 infantry and 800 Gallic and German cavalry, later Legio XXXVII (former Pompeians) and warships from Rhodes, Pontus, Lycia and Asia.
greek_note: The fleet was Rhodian, Pontic, Lycian and Asian (Bellum Alexandrinum 13), manned by Greek-speakers.
sources: Caesar BC 3.106-112; Bellum Alexandrinum 1-33; Plutarch Caesar 48-49; Cassius Dio 42.7-43; en.wikipedia Siege of Alexandria (47 BC)
note: Achillas' army included the Gabiniani, Roman soldiers left in Egypt in 55 BCE with Gallic and German horse; Romans in foreign service, so not counted as civil.

name: Synodium
place: A defile in inland Dalmatia, on Gabinius' march to Salona
borderline: The place-name comes from Appian's account of Octavian's later campaign.
roman_force: Fifteen cohorts of new recruits raised in Italy and 3,000 cavalry; Gabinius lost over 2,000 men, 38 centurions and 4 tribunes.
greek_note: New Italian levies.
sources: Bellum Alexandrinum 42-43; Appian Illyrica 12, 25
note: Dalmatae. Gabinius died at Salona soon after.

name: Tauris (sea)
place: Off the island of Tauris, probably Sipan, near Epidaurum (Cavtat)
roman_force: Vatinius' improvised fleet of light ships and one quinquereme from Brundisium, carrying veteran legionaries who boarded the enemy; Octavius' larger Pompeian squadron.
greek_note: The crews of both squadrons are not described.
sources: Bellum Alexandrinum 44-47; Cassius Dio 42.11; en.wikipedia Battle of Tauris
note: Octavius' flagship sank and he escaped to Africa.

name: Zela
war: Caesar's civil war (war with Pharnaces II)
roman_force: Legio VI (under 1,000 veterans), Legio XXXVI, Deiotarus' Galatian legion (later XXII Deiotariana) and the Pontic legion from Domitius' army, with a small cavalry force: about 15,000.
greek_note: The Pontic legion levied for Domitius fought in the line (Bellum Alexandrinum 69, 76).
sources: Bellum Alexandrinum 69-77; Plutarch Caesar 50; Suetonius Caesar 35, 37; Appian BC 2.91; en.wikipedia Battle of Zela
note: 'Veni, vidi, vici'. The Fasti give 2 August, the anniversary of Ilerda.

name: Chersonesus
place: Off Chersonesus, on the coast west of Alexandria
borderline: A small sea fight, not separately named in standard works; the ancient Greek battles set names it Chersonesus.
roman_force: Caesar's fleet of Rhodian, Pontic, Lycian and Asian warships, sailing without embarked soldiers to meet the transports of Legio XXXVII; a single Rhodian ship bore the brunt of the fight (Bellum Alexandrinum 9-11).
greek_note: The ship that fought was Rhodian and the whole squadron came from Rhodes, Pontus, Lycia and Asia; Caesar had no legionaries aboard.
sources: Bellum Alexandrinum 9-11 (classics.mit.edu translation)
note: The Alexandrians lost one ship taken, one sunk and a third disabled; Caesar lost none and towed the legion's transports to Alexandria.

name: Pharos
date: Winter 48/47 BCE (the day before the fight on the Heptastadion)
place: The island and town of Pharos, Alexandria
borderline: A distinct amphibious action inside the siege of Alexandria; not separately named in most modern works (the ancient Greek battles set names it Pharos).
roman_force: Ten cohorts, picked light troops and Gallic cavalry landed from small boats while the fleet attacked the island from the sea; about 600 defenders were taken (Bellum Alexandrinum 17-19).
greek_note: The landing force was legionary and Gallic, but the fleet that attacked from the sea was manned by Rhodians, Pontians, Lycians and Asian Greeks.
sources: Bellum Alexandrinum 17-19; en.wikipedia Siege of Alexandria (47 BC)
note: Caesar kept Pharos after his defeat on the mole the next day (entered as Heptastadion).

name: Canopus
place: Off Canopus (Abu Qir), east of Alexandria
commanders_a: Tiberius Claudius Nero, Euphranor of Rhodes (killed)
borderline: A small sea fight not separately named in standard works; the ancient Greek battles set names it Canopus.
roman_force: Caesar's squadron under Tiberius Claudius Nero, with the Rhodian ships under Euphranor, sent to cover the supply convoys that the Alexandrian fleet at Canopus threatened (Bellum Alexandrinum 25).
