greek_note: The Rhodian ships led the fight, and Caesar's fleet was drawn from Rhodes, Pontus, Lycia and Asia.
sources: Bellum Alexandrinum 25; Suetonius Tiberius 4
note: Euphranor pursued too far, was surrounded without support and died with his ship; the Bellum gives no overall result, so scored as indecisive (the ancient Greek battles set scores a Roman victory).

name: Alexandria harbour (sea)
place: The shoals and channel between Pharos and the Eunostos harbour, Alexandria
commanders_a: Gaius Julius Caesar, Euphranor of Rhodes
borderline: A distinct naval battle within the siege, not separately named in standard works.
roman_force: Caesar's fleet of 9 Rhodian, 8 Pontic, 5 Lycian and 12 Asian warships, Euphranor's Rhodians leading, with legionaries on board.
greek_note: All the warships came from Rhodes and the Greek-speaking provinces of Asia, Lycia and Pontus (Bellum Alexandrinum 13).
sources: Bellum Alexandrinum 12-16; en.wikipedia Siege of Alexandria (47 BC)
note: Two Egyptian ships captured and three sunk, with no loss to Caesar. Euphranor was killed later in a second sea fight off Canopus (entered as Canopus); an earlier small fight off Chersonesus is entered as Chersonesus.

name: Heptastadion
place: The Heptastadion mole between Pharos and the city, Alexandria
borderline: A distinct battle within the siege, not separately named in standard works.
roman_force: Three cohorts on the mole, with rowers and sailors from the fleet, broke when Alexandrians landed behind them; Caesar lost about 400 legionaries and as many seamen, and swam to safety (Bellum Alexandrinum 19-21).
greek_note: The sailors and rowers of the Rhodian and Asian fleet fought and died beside the legionaries (Bellum Alexandrinum 20-21).
sources: Bellum Alexandrinum 19-21; Plutarch Caesar 49; Suetonius Caesar 64; Cassius Dio 42.40; en.wikipedia Siege of Alexandria (47 BC)
note: The fight for the mole on the day after the capture of Pharos (entered separately as Pharos); Caesar kept Pharos.

name: Nile
place: The Ptolemaic camp by a branch of the Nile in the western Delta
commanders_a: Gaius Julius Caesar, Mithridates of Pergamon, Antipater
roman_force: Caesar's legions (VI, XXVII, XXXVII) and his Gallic and German cavalry, joined with the relief army of Mithridates of Pergamon (raised in Syria and Cilicia) and Antipater's Jewish troops, about 20,000 in all.
greek_note: The Greek- and Aramaic-speaking troops were the allied army of Mithridates; Caesar's own force was Latin-speaking with Gallic and German cavalry.
sources: Bellum Alexandrinum 26-32; Josephus AJ 14.127-136; Cassius Dio 42.43; en.wikipedia Battle of the Nile (47 BC)
note: Ptolemy XIII drowned in the flight. Wikipedia gives February 47 BCE; Alexandria was recovered on 27 March by the Fasti.

name: Ruspina
commanders_a: Titus Labienus, Marcus Petreius, Gnaeus Calpurnius Piso
roman_force: Caesar: 30 cohorts of recently landed legionaries, 400 cavalry and 150 archers; Labienus: about 8,000 Numidian horse, 1,600 Gallic and German cavalry and many light infantry, joined by Petreius and Piso with 1,600 more cavalry.
greek_note: Italian legionaries, Gallic and German cavalry and Numidian allies.
sources: Bellum Africum 11-18; Cassius Dio 43.2; en.wikipedia Battle of Ruspina
note: Caesar, surrounded, broke out and regained his camp; Wikipedia counts a Pompeian victory, others call it indecisive. About October 47 BCE in the Julian reckoning.

name: Uzitta
place: The ridges and plain round Uzitta, west of Ruspina
commanders_b: Metellus Scipio, Titus Labienus, Juba I
borderline: A series of skirmishes, cavalry fights and set-piece stand-offs rather than one battle.
roman_force: Caesar: his army growing to about eight legions, with Gallic and German cavalry and Gaetulian deserters; Scipio: ten Roman legions raised largely in Africa, Labienus' cavalry, and Juba's Numidians and elephants.
greek_note: Italian and African-Roman legions with Numidian, Gaetulian, Gallic and German horse.
sources: Bellum Africum 37-66

name: Thapsus
commanders_b: Metellus Scipio, Lucius Afranius, Marcus Petreius, Titus Labienus, Juba I
roman_force: Caesar: ten or more legions (veteran V, VII-X, XIII, XIV and new XXV-XXX) with Gallic, German and Gaetulian cavalry; Scipio: eight legions (many raised in Africa), large cavalry and light infantry forces, Juba's Numidians and 60 elephants.
greek_note: Italian and African-Roman legions with Numidian, Gallic and German allies.
sources: Bellum Africum 79-86; Plutarch Caesar 53; Appian BC 2.97; Cassius Dio 43.7-9; en.wikipedia Battle of Thapsus
note: About 7 February 46 BCE in the Julian reckoning. Caesar's veterans massacred surrendering Pompeians.

name: Hippo Regius (sea)
borderline: Publius Sittius' ships were manned by his private army of Italian and Spanish soldiers serving King Bocchus II; they fought for Caesar's side, so coded as a Caesarian Roman force (civil).
roman_force: Publius Sittius' larger ships, manned by his band of Italian and Spanish soldiers in the service of Bocchus II; Scipio's few small ships carrying the fleeing Pompeian leaders.
greek_note: Sittius' mercenaries were Italians and Spaniards.
sources: Bellum Africum 96; Livy Periochae 114; en.wikipedia Battle of Hippo Regius
note: Scipio killed himself.

name: Ulia (siege)
borderline: A siege raised largely by manoeuvre after a night break-in.
roman_force: The Caesarian town and a relief of cohorts and cavalry under Paciaecus, which broke through the siege lines in a storm; the Pompeian besiegers (Roman and Spanish legions).
greek_note: Roman and Hispano-Roman troops of Baetica.
sources: Bellum Hispaniense 3-4; Cassius Dio 43.31-32; en.wikipedia Battle of Munda (background)
note: Gnaeus lifted the siege when Caesar marched on Corduba.

name: Carteia (sea)
roman_force: Didius' small fleet brought from Sardinia; Varus' Pompeian fleet escaped from Africa.
greek_note: The crews are not described.
sources: Cassius Dio, book 43; en.wikipedia Battle of Carteia (46 BC); historyofwar.org Battle of Carteia
note: Wikipedia dates it 46 BCE; some put it early in 45 BCE.

name: Corduba (January 45 BC)
place: The bridges over the Baetis at Corduba (Cordoba)
borderline: A failed attempt on the town with heavy bridge fighting.
roman_force: Caesar's army of about eight legions with Spanish and Gallic cavalry, fighting for a temporary bridge; Sextus' garrison and Gnaeus' relieving army.
greek_note: Italian legions and Hispano-Roman and Iberian troops.
sources: Bellum Hispaniense 4-6; Cassius Dio 43.32; en.wikipedia Battle of Munda (background)
note: Caesar broke off and turned to Ategua.

name: Ategua (siege)
place: Ategua (Teba la Vieja, near Santa Cruz, Cordoba)
roman_force: Caesar's army with siege works and towers against the Pompeian garrison, with Gnaeus' army failing to relieve it; sorties and assaults throughout.
greek_note: Italian legions and Hispano-Roman troops.
sources: Bellum Hispaniense 6-19; Cassius Dio 43.33-34
note: The town surrendered on 19 February 45 BCE after the garrison massacred Caesar's partisans.

name: Soricaria
place: Near Soricaria, between Ucubi and Aspavia (Baetica)
borderline: A skirmish before Munda.
roman_force: Caesar's legions and cavalry against part of Gnaeus' army (Roman and Spanish legions).
greek_note: Italian and Hispano-Roman troops.
sources: Bellum Hispaniense 24-27; en.wikipedia Battle of Munda (background)

name: Munda
place: The plain below Munda, probably near La Lantejuela or Osuna, Andalusia
commanders_a: Gaius Julius Caesar, Quintus Fabius Maximus, Quintus Pedius, Bogud of Mauretania
commanders_b: Gnaeus Pompeius (the younger), Titus Labienus, Publius Attius Varus
roman_force: Caesar: eight legions (II, III, V, VI, X, XXI, XXVIII, XXX), about 8,000 cavalry and Bogud's Mauretanians; Gnaeus Pompeius: thirteen legions (survivors of Thapsus, deserters, legions of Spanish provincials and colonists), 6,000 cavalry and 6,000 light infantry.
greek_note: Italian and Hispano-Roman legions with Iberian, Gallic and Mauretanian troops.
sources: Bellum Hispaniense 27-31; Plutarch Caesar 56; Appian BC 2.103-105; Cassius Dio 43.36-40; en.wikipedia Battle of Munda
note: The site is disputed (La Lantejuela/Osuna, Montilla, Ronda). Labienus and Varus fell; the town of Munda was then besieged and surrendered.

name: Corduba (March 45 BC)
borderline: The storming of a town divided between the factions; the Bellum Hispaniense claims 22,000 killed.
roman_force: Caesar's army after Munda, against Pompeian legionaries, slaves and freedmen who held part of the divided town.
greek_note: Italian and Hispano-Roman troops.
sources: Bellum Hispaniense 32-34; Cassius Dio 43.39
note: Sextus Pompeius had already fled; Scapula killed himself.

name: Hispalis
borderline: A small siege and ambush.
roman_force: Caesar's army, which let a Lusitanian force that had seized the town by night sally out and then destroyed it.
greek_note: Italian legions; the enemy were Pompeian partisans and Lusitanians.
sources: Bellum Hispaniense 35-36; Cassius Dio 43.39

name: Lauro
place: Near Lauro in Hispania Ulterior (possibly Lora de Estepa)
roman_force: Caesennius Lento's pursuit force of infantry and cavalry, with Didius' fleet blocking the coast; Gnaeus' remnant of Munda survivors and Lusitanians.
greek_note: Italian legions and Hispano-Roman troops.
sources: Bellum Hispaniense 37-39; Appian BC 2.105; Florus 2.13.86; en.wikipedia Battle of Lauro
note: Gnaeus Pompeius was wounded, caught and beheaded; his head was shown at Hispalis on 12 April. The site of Lauro is disputed.

name: Apamea (siege)
war: Caesar's civil war (revolt of Caecilius Bassus)
commanders_b: Gaius Antistius Vetus; later Lucius Staius Murcus and Quintus Marcius Crispus
borderline: A long blockade with little recorded fighting.
roman_force: Bassus: the Syrian legion that had murdered Sextus Caesar, with new levies and Arab and Parthian help; besiegers: Antistius Vetus' forces, later six legions under Murcus and Crispus.
greek_note: Bassus enrolled men in Syria, where the cities were Greek-speaking; the besiegers' legions came from Italy and the East.
sources: Cassius Dio 47.26-28; Appian BC 3.77, 4.58; Strabo 16.2.10; Cicero Att. 14.9; en.wikipedia Siege of Apamea
note: Pacorus' Parthians and Alchaudonius' Arabs forced Antistius Vetus to lift the first siege; the second ended in 43 BCE when both armies went over to Cassius.

name: Forum Gallorum
place: Forum Gallorum, on the Via Aemilia between Bononia and Mutina (near Castelfranco Emilia)
commanders_a: Gaius Vibius Pansa (mortally wounded), Aulus Hirtius, Octavian
roman_force: Senate: Pansa's four legions of recruits with the veteran Legio Martia, Hirtius with the veteran Legio IV and the praetorian cohorts of Hirtius and Octavian; Antony: the veteran legions II and XXXV, praetorian cohorts and a strong cavalry (Galba in Cicero, Ad Fam. 10.30; Appian BC 3.66-70).
greek_note: Both armies were legions raised in Italy and Cisalpine Gaul; Antony's cavalry included Gauls.
sources: Cicero, Ad Fam. 10.30; Appian BC 3.66-70; Cassius Dio 46.37-38; en.wikipedia Battle of Forum Gallorum
note: Antony first routed Pansa's column; Hirtius then fell on Antony's tired troops and drove them back to their siege lines, so the day ended as a Senatorial victory.

name: Mutina
commanders_a: Aulus Hirtius (killed), Octavian, Decimus Junius Brutus Albinus
roman_force: Hirtius and Octavian with the veteran legions IV and Martia and new levies, Decimus Brutus' garrison sallying from the town; Antony held his camps with veteran legions including V Alaudae (Appian BC 3.71-72; Dio 46.38-39).
greek_note: Italian and Cisalpine legions on both sides; Antony's Legio V Alaudae had been raised by Caesar in Transalpine Gaul.
sources: Appian BC 3.71-72; Cassius Dio 46.38-39; Suetonius Aug. 10; en.wikipedia Battle of Mutina
note: Antony had besieged Decimus Brutus in Mutina since December 44 BCE. The battle itself was nearly even and Hirtius fell in Antony's camp, but Antony lifted the siege on 22 April and retreated west; Pansa died of his Forum Gallorum wounds.

name: Laodicea (siege)
borderline: No separate Wikipedia article; Appian and Dio describe a siege with two sea fights off the harbour.
roman_force: Cassius had about twelve legions taken over in Syria, among them the four legions Allienus brought from Egypt, and fleets from the Phoenician cities and Cyprus; Dolabella had two legions, the support of the Laodiceans, and ships from Rhodes, Lycia, Pamphylia and Cilicia (Appian BC 4.60-62).
greek_note: The legions of Syria had been in the East since the 50s BC and filled their ranks locally, and both fleets were crewed from the Greek and Phoenician coastal cities.
sources: Appian BC 4.60-62; Cassius Dio 47.30; Cicero, Ad Fam. 12.13-15
note: Cassius beat Dolabella's fleet twice and the city was betrayed to him; Dolabella had himself killed. The Laodiceans (allies_b) had taken Dolabella's side.

name: Ionian Sea
commanders_a: Lucius Staius Murcus, Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus
borderline: Described in the sources as a sea fight on the day of the first battle of Philippi, without its own name.
roman_force: Liberators: about 130 warships; Triumvirs: transports carrying two legions, among them the Martia, a praetorian cohort and cavalry, with few escorts (Appian BC 4.115-116).
greek_note: The Liberators' fleet had been raised and crewed in the Greek East; the soldiers lost were Italian legionaries.
sources: Appian BC 4.115-116; Plutarch Brutus 47; en.wikipedia Battle of Philippi
note: Most of the convoy and the two legions were destroyed.

name: Philippi (first battle)
place: plain west of Philippi, on the Via Egnatia
commanders_b: Gaius Cassius Longinus (suicide), Marcus Junius Brutus
roman_force: Triumvirs: 19 legions and 13,000 cavalry; Liberators: 19 legions (17 on the field, about 80,000 infantry) and about 17,000-20,000 cavalry, among them Gauls, Lusitanians, Thracians, Illyrians and Parthian and Arab horse archers (Appian BC 4.88, 4.108).
greek_note: The legions were mostly Italian, but Brutus and Cassius had filled theirs in Macedonia, Asia and Syria and brought eastern allied contingents.
sources: Appian BC 4.105-114; Plutarch Brutus 38-44, Antony 22; Cassius Dio 47.42-46; en.wikipedia Battle of Philippi
note: Brutus took Octavian's camp while Antony stormed Cassius' camp; Cassius killed himself believing all lost. Thracian princes served on both sides (Rhascus with the triumvirs, Rhascuporis with the Liberators).

name: Philippi (second battle)
roman_force: The same armies: the triumvirs' 19 legions against Brutus' combined army; about 14,000 of the defeated were taken into the triumvirs' legions afterwards (Appian BC 4.128-135).
greek_note: As in the first battle: mostly Italian legionaries, with eastern recruits and allies on the Liberators' side.
sources: Appian BC 4.128-135; Plutarch Brutus 49-52; Cassius Dio 47.47-49; en.wikipedia Battle of Philippi

name: Utica
borderline: Not usually given a battle name; Appian describes a pitched battle before Cornificius' camp near Utica.
roman_force: Sextius: the legions of Africa Nova with Arabio's Numidian horsemen and the Sittians (Publius Sittius' former soldiers settled at Cirta); Cornificius: the larger army of Africa Vetus with Laelius' force (Appian BC 4.53-56). No numbers are given.
greek_note: Both armies were raised in the African provinces and Numidia; no Greek contingent is recorded.
sources: Appian BC 4.53-56; Cassius Dio 48.21; en.wikipedia Quintus Cornificius
note: Arabio's men climbed a cliff into Cornificius' camp; Cornificius was killed by Arabio's horsemen and Laelius killed himself. Appian also tells of an earlier sortie in which Sextius killed Cornificius' legate Ventidius (no place given).

name: Myndus
roman_force: Cassius' fleet of about 80 heavy warships with legionaries embarked, against 33 Rhodian ships (Appian BC 4.71).
greek_note: Cassius' ships came from the coastal cities of Asia, Cilicia and Phoenicia and were rowed largely by Greek- and Phoenician-speaking crews.
sources: Appian BC 4.65-71; Cassius Dio 47.33; Plutarch Brutus 30
note: Opponent: the city of Rhodes, which refused to support the Liberators.

name: Rhodes (siege)
roman_force: Cassius' fleet and the legions he ferried from Loryma, who invested the city by land and sea (Appian BC 4.72-74).
greek_note: The fleet was crewed from the eastern coastal cities; the legions were mostly Syrian legions filled with local recruits.
sources: Appian BC 4.72-74; Cassius Dio 47.33; Plutarch Brutus 32
note: After a second sea fight before the harbour and a short siege, the city was opened to Cassius, who fined it heavily; land and sea operations combined (type set to sea).

name: Xanthos (siege)
roman_force: Brutus' army of Macedonia, legions taken over from Gaius Antonius, Vatinius and others, with new levies raised in Macedonia (Appian BC 4.75-80).
greek_note: Most of Brutus' legionaries were Italians from the Caesarian and Pompeian legions of the Balkans, with some Macedonian recruits.
sources: Appian BC 4.76-80; Plutarch Brutus 30-31; Cassius Dio 47.34
note: Brutus first beat the Lycians in the field; the city was stormed and most Xanthians killed themselves and burned the town. Opponent: Xanthos, a city of the Hellenised Lycian League.

name: Scyllaeum
place: off Scyllaeum (Scilla) at the entrance of the strait
borderline: A sea fight known from Appian and Dio but not usually given a name.
roman_force: Sextus' fleet of light, well-handled ships against Salvidienus' hastily built larger ships (Appian BC 4.85; Dio 48.18).
greek_note: Sextus' admirals were Greek freedmen and his crews were drawn from slaves, refugees and eastern seamen.
sources: Appian BC 4.85; Cassius Dio 48.18
note: Indecisive; both fleets withdrew, Salvidienus to the harbour of Balarus.

name: Perusia (siege)
commanders_a: Octavian, Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, Quintus Salvidienus Rufus
roman_force: Octavian's veteran legions and new levies encircled the town; Lucius Antonius held it with the legions he had raised in Italy, while Antony's generals in Gaul failed to relieve him (Appian BC 5.32-49).
greek_note: An Italian civil war fought with Italian legions on both sides.
sources: Appian BC 5.32-49; Cassius Dio 48.14; Suetonius Aug. 14-15; en.wikipedia Perusine War
note: The besieged's great sortie on the last night of 41 BCE failed; the town surrendered from hunger and was burned.

name: Decidius Saxa's defeat
borderline: Dio describes Saxa's defeat in battle, but it has no conventional name.
roman_force: Saxa's army of Syria, legions that included former soldiers of Brutus and Cassius, many of whom went over to Labienus (Cassius Dio 48.25).
greek_note: The Syrian legions had long been in the East and took local recruits.
sources: Cassius Dio 48.24-26; Plutarch Antony 30; Livy Per. 127; en.wikipedia Pompeian–Parthian invasion of 40 BC
note: Labienus, a Roman Pompeian in Parthian service, led the invasion with Pacorus; Saxa fled and was killed in Cilicia.

name: Brundisium (siege)
borderline: A blockade with skirmishes that ended in the Treaty of Brundisium rather than a decision.
roman_force: Antony's army from the East and Ahenobarbus' fleet blockaded Brundisium; Octavian's garrison held out, and Antony's cavalry beat a larger force of Octavian's horse at Hyria (Appian BC 5.56-58; Dio 48.27-28).
greek_note: Antony's army had been recruited partly in the East; Octavian's was Italian.
sources: Appian BC 5.56-64; Cassius Dio 48.27-28
note: The soldiers of both sides forced the reconciliation (Treaty of Brundisium, autumn 40 BCE).

name: Cilician Gates
roman_force: Ventidius' legions sent from Italy by Antony, with slingers; Wikipedia gives two legions with cavalry and slingers, Dio gives no numbers (Dio 48.39-40).
greek_note: Ventidius' army was mostly Italian legions newly brought from the West.
sources: Cassius Dio 48.39-40; Frontinus Strat. 2.5.36; Plutarch Antony 33; en.wikipedia Pompeian–Parthian invasion of 40 BC
note: The Parthian cavalry charged Ventidius' hill camp and was routed; Labienus' army dispersed and he was caught and killed.

name: Amanus Pass
place: Amanus pass (Belen pass), between Cilicia and Syria
roman_force: Silo's advance guard of Ventidius' army, rescued by Ventidius with the main body of his legions (Dio 48.41).
greek_note: The same Italian legions as at the Cilician Gates.
sources: Cassius Dio 48.41; Strabo 16.2.8; en.wikipedia Pompeian–Parthian invasion of 40 BC

name: Mount Gindarus
roman_force: Ventidius' legions (eleven, by Wikipedia's count) with many slingers and archers, fighting from a hill camp (Dio 49.19-20; Frontinus Strat. 1.1.6).
greek_note: Ventidius had added the Syrian garrison legions, partly eastern recruits, to the Italian legions he brought.
sources: Cassius Dio 49.19-21; Plutarch Antony 34; Frontinus Strat. 1.1.6; en.wikipedia Battle of Mount Gindarus
note: Dio says it was fought on the anniversary of Carrhae (traditionally 9 June).

name: Cumae
roman_force: Octavian's Tyrrhenian squadron under Calvisius with Menodorus, who had deserted Sextus with his ships; Sextus' fleet under Menecrates (Appian BC 5.81-83).
greek_note: Menecrates, Menodorus and Demochares were Greek freedmen, and both fleets drew rowers from slaves and eastern seamen.
sources: Appian BC 5.81-83; Cassius Dio 48.46; en.wikipedia Battle of Mylae (36 BC)
note: Menecrates was killed and Demochares withdrew, but Calvisius' fleet was badly damaged.

name: Messana
place: in the strait near Messana and Scyllaeum
roman_force: Octavian's main fleet from Tarentum and Brundisium against Sextus' fleet under Demochares and Apollophanes (Appian BC 5.84-90).
greek_note: Sextus' squadrons were led by Greek freedmen and largely rowed by eastern and servile crews.
sources: Appian BC 5.84-92; Cassius Dio 48.47-48; en.wikipedia Sextus Pompey
note: Octavian was beaten off Scyllaeum and a storm next day wrecked much of his fleet; Wikipedia's article on Sextus Pompey dates it to 37 BCE.

name: Samosata (siege)
roman_force: Ventidius' army, then Antony's, with siege works; Herod brought troops to Antony (Josephus BJ 1.321-322); no numbers are given.
greek_note: Antony's legions were largely Italian, with Syrian legions and eastern allies.
sources: Plutarch Antony 34; Cassius Dio 49.20-22; Josephus BJ 1.321-322, AJ 14.439-447
note: The assaults failed and Antony withdrew on terms, taking 300 talents (Plutarch). Commagene was a Hellenistic kingdom with a Greek-speaking court under an Iranian (Orontid) dynasty.

name: Jerusalem (siege)
roman_force: Sosius with eleven legions and 6,000 cavalry besides Syrian auxiliaries (Josephus BJ 1.345-346), joined by Herod's army of about 30,000.
greek_note: The Syrian auxiliaries came from the Greek cities of Syria, and Herod's army included Greek-speaking mercenaries, but most of the force was Roman legionaries and Jewish and Idumaean troops.
sources: Josephus BJ 1.343-357, AJ 14.465-491; Cassius Dio 49.22; en.wikipedia Siege of Jerusalem (37 BC)
note: Some modern scholars date it to 36 BCE. The walls fell after 40 and 15 days; Antigonus surrendered to Sosius and was executed at Antioch.

name: Mylae
place: off Mylae (Milazzo), north coast of Sicily
roman_force: Half of Agrippa's new heavy fleet built at Portus Julius against Papias' larger squadron (Appian BC 5.105-108); Papias lost 30 ships, Agrippa 5.
greek_note: Agrippa trained 20,000 freed slaves as rowers; Sextus' fleet was crewed largely by eastern seamen and slaves.
sources: Appian BC 5.105-108; Cassius Dio 49.2-4; en.wikipedia Battle of Mylae (36 BC)
note: Wikipedia gives 11 August 36 BCE.

name: Tauromenium
place: off Tauromenium (Taormina), east coast of Sicily
roman_force: Octavian landed three legions, 500 horse and light troops under Cornificius and was then caught at sea by Sextus' fleet; he lost over 60 ships and barely escaped (Appian BC 5.109-112).
greek_note: The fleets were rowed largely by eastern and servile crews; the troops were Italian legions.
sources: Appian BC 5.109-112; Cassius Dio 49.5; en.wikipedia War between Sextus Pompey and the Second Triumvirate

name: Naulochus
place: off Naulochus, between Mylae and Cape Pelorus
roman_force: About 300 ships on each side; Agrippa's heavier ships carried the harpax grapnel, while the land armies of Octavian and Sextus watched from the shore (Appian BC 5.118-121).
greek_note: Rowers on both sides were largely freedmen, slaves and eastern seamen; Antony's 120 ships lent to Octavian came from the East.
sources: Appian BC 5.118-122; Cassius Dio 49.8-11; Suetonius Aug. 16; en.wikipedia Battle of Naulochus
note: Sextus lost 28 ships sunk and most of the rest burned or taken; Agrippa lost 3.

name: Statianus' convoy (ambush)
place: on the road to Phraaspa, Media Atropatene
commanders_a: Phraates IV (or Monaeses), Artavasdes I of Media Atropatene
commanders_b: Oppius Statianus (killed), Polemon I of Pontus (captured)
borderline: A named ambush known by its commander, not by a place.
roman_force: Two legions escorting the siege train, with Polemon's Pontic troops; Artavasdes II's Armenian cavalry rode off without fighting (Plutarch Antony 38; Dio 49.25).
greek_note: Italian legionaries with Pontic and Armenian allies.
sources: Plutarch Antony 38; Cassius Dio 49.25; en.wikipedia Antony's Atropatene campaign
note: About 10,000 Romans were killed and the siege engines destroyed.

name: Phraaspa (siege)
place: Phraaspa (Praaspa), royal city of Media Atropatene
commanders_a: Phraates IV, Artavasdes I of Media Atropatene, Monaeses
roman_force: Sixteen legions (about 60,000 Roman infantry), 10,000 Spanish and Gallic cavalry and about 30,000 allied troops from Armenia, Galatia, Cappadocia and Pontus (Plutarch Antony 37).
greek_note: The legions were largely Italian; some allied contingents from Pontus, Cappadocia and Galatia spoke Greek.
sources: Plutarch Antony 38-51; Cassius Dio 49.25-31; Velleius 2.82; en.wikipedia Antony's Atropatene campaign
note: Site identified with Maragheh or Takht-e Soleyman. Antony abandoned the siege and lost about 24,000-32,000 men in the retreat to Armenia.

name: Metulum (siege)
place: Metulum, chief town of the Iapydes (near Ogulin)
roman_force: Octavian's army of Italian legions (perhaps XIII, XIV and XV) with siege works and assault bridges, against about 3,000 Iapydes (Appian Ill. 19-21).
greek_note: Italian legions recruited in Italy and Cisalpine Gaul.
sources: Appian Illyrica 19-21; Cassius Dio 49.35; en.wikipedia Octavian's military campaigns in Illyricum
note: Opponent: the Iapydes. Octavian was hurt when an assault bridge collapsed; the defenders burned their town and died.

name: Siscia (siege)
place: Segesta/Siscia (Sisak), at the confluence of the Sava and Kupa
roman_force: Octavian's legions with a river fleet on the Sava under Menodorus; 25 cohorts were left as garrison under Fufius Geminus (Appian Ill. 22-24; Dio 49.37-38).
greek_note: Italian legions; the river flotilla was led by the Greek freedman Menodorus.
sources: Appian Illyrica 22-24; Cassius Dio 49.37-38; en.wikipedia Octavian's military campaigns in Illyricum
note: Opponent: the Pannonian Segestani. The town fell after about 30 days and a relief army was beaten off.

name: Promona (siege)
roman_force: Octavian's legions, who seized the surrounding heights and built a wall of about 7.5 km round the town; a relief army under Testimus was defeated (Appian Ill. 25-26).
greek_note: Italian legions.
sources: Appian Illyrica 25-26; Cassius Dio 49.38; en.wikipedia Octavian's military campaigns in Illyricum
note: Opponent: the Dalmatae. A cohort that broke was decimated.

name: Setovia (siege)
place: Setovia, Dalmatia (site uncertain, perhaps near Sinj)
roman_force: Octavian's legions, left under Statilius Taurus to complete the blockade (Appian Ill. 27; Dio 49.38).
greek_note: Italian legions.
sources: Appian Illyrica 27-28; Cassius Dio 49.38; Suetonius Aug. 20; en.wikipedia Setovia
note: Opponent: the Dalmatae. Octavian was struck on the knee by a stone; the Dalmatians submitted and gave 700 hostages.

name: Actium
war: War of Actium (Final war of the Roman Republic)
place: mouth of the Ambracian Gulf off Actium
commanders_a: Octavian, Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, Lucius Arruntius, Marcus Lurius
commanders_b: Mark Antony, Gaius Sosius, Lucius Gellius Poplicola, Cleopatra VII
roman_force: Octavian: about 400 lighter ships with eight legions and five praetorian cohorts embarked, his land army under Statilius Taurus ashore; Antony: about 230 large ships plus Cleopatra's 60, with 20,000 legionaries and 2,000 archers aboard, his 19 legions and 12,000 cavalry ashore (Plutarch Antony 61-65; Orosius 6.19).
greek_note: Plutarch (Antony 62) says Antony's trierarchs pressed wayfarers, muleteers, harvesters and youths in Greece to fill the crews, and many of his legionaries had been raised in the East.
sources: Plutarch Antony 61-68; Cassius Dio 50.11-35; Velleius 2.84-85; Orosius 6.19; en.wikipedia Battle of Actium
note: Officially a war against Cleopatra, but Roman legions and fleets fought on both sides, hence civil; greek_opponent is true for the Ptolemaic squadron, the only allied force engaged (allies_b). The client kings with Antony (Plutarch Antony 61: Bocchus, Tarcondemus, Archelaus of Cappadocia, Philadelphus, Mithridates of Commagene, Sadalas of Thrace) were with the land army, which did not fight; the ancient Greek battles set codes the battle as Rome against Ptolemaic Egypt with these kings and Antony's legions as allies. Antony's land army surrendered a week later.

name: Patrae
war: War of Actium (Final war of the Roman Republic)
borderline: Known only from one sentence of Dio; not separately named in modern works.
roman_force: Agrippa's fleet of Octavian's heavy warships with marines against an Antonian squadron under Quintus Nasidius; Dio gives no numbers (Dio 50.13.5).
greek_note: Antony's crews were largely pressed in Greece and the East (Plutarch Antony 62); share for both fleets together.
sources: Cassius Dio 50.13.5; en.wikipedia Quintus Nasidius
note: Agrippa took Patrae after the sea fight, having seized Leucas and its ships; he later took Corinth.

name: Sosius' sea fight
war: War of Actium (Final war of the Roman Republic)
place: Near the mouth of the Ambracian Gulf, off Actium
commanders_a: Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, Lucius Tarius Rufus
borderline: A sea fight known by its commander, not by a place.
roman_force: Tarius' small squadron, then Agrippa with Octavian's main fleet, against an Antonian squadron under Sosius that sailed out in a mist before dawn (Dio 50.14.1-2).
greek_note: Antony's crews were largely pressed in Greece and the East (Plutarch Antony 62); share for both fleets together.
sources: Cassius Dio 50.14.1-2; en.wikipedia Final war of the Roman Republic
note: Sosius routed Tarius' squadron but met Agrippa and was beaten; Tarcondimotus, king in Cilicia, was killed. Wikipedia names Lucius Arruntius in place of Tarius. Sosius escaped and commanded Antony's left at Actium.

name: Methone
borderline: A storming of a base, known from short notices; no separate article.
roman_force: Agrippa's fleet with marines stormed the Antonian base held by Bogud (Dio 50.11; Orosius 6.19.6).
greek_note: Agrippa's crews included many freedmen and eastern rowers; the marines were Italian.
sources: Cassius Dio 50.11; Orosius 6.19.6; Strabo 8.4.3; en.wikipedia Battle of Actium

name: Alexandria
war: War of Actium (Final war of the Roman Republic)
place: Alexandria, by the hippodrome and the eastern approaches
roman_force: Octavian's legions advancing from Pelusium and Gallus' army from the west; Antony's remaining legions, cavalry and fleet, with Ptolemaic troops (Plutarch Antony 74-76; Dio 51.10).
greek_note: Mostly Roman legionaries on both sides; Antony also had Ptolemaic (Greek and Egyptian) troops.
sources: Plutarch Antony 74-77; Cassius Dio 51.10; Suetonius Aug. 17; en.wikipedia Battle of Alexandria (30 BC)
note: Antony's cavalry won a skirmish near the hippodrome on 31 July; on 1 August his fleet and cavalry went over to Octavian and his infantry was beaten, and he killed himself. Wikipedia dates the fighting to July 30 BCE.

name: Paraetonium
war: War of Actium (Final war of the Roman Republic)
borderline: A minor action known from Dio; no separate article.
roman_force: Gallus with the four legions of Cyrenaica that had gone over from Antony's general Pinarius Scarpus; Antony attacked by land and sea and his ships were trapped by chains in the harbour (Dio 51.9; Orosius 6.19.15).
greek_note: The Cyrenaican legions were Antony's, partly raised in the East.
sources: Cassius Dio 51.9; Orosius 6.19.15; Plutarch Antony 69
note: Land and sea fighting; type set to land.

name: Crassus' victory over the Bastarnae
place: Moesia, south of the lower Danube (site unknown)
borderline: A pitched battle known from Dio without a place name.
roman_force: The proconsul of Macedonia's legions and auxiliaries, helped by the Getic king Rholes (Dio 51.23-24); no numbers are given.
greek_note: The army of Macedonia had long recruited locally in Macedonia and Thrace, but its legionaries were mostly Italian.
sources: Cassius Dio 51.23-24; Livy Per. 134; en.wikipedia Marcus Licinius Crassus (consul 30 BC)
note: Opponent: the Bastarnae. Crassus killed their king Deldo with his own hand and claimed the spolia opima, which Octavian refused.

name: Genucla (siege)
place: Genucla, fortress of the Getic king Zyraxes near the Danube (site unknown, perhaps in the Dobruja)
borderline: A siege known only from Dio.
roman_force: Crassus' army of Macedonia, attacking by land and from the river (Dio 51.26.5-6).
greek_note: As for Crassus' army in 29 BCE.
sources: Cassius Dio 51.26.5-6
note: Opponent: the Getae. Crassus recovered the standards lost by Gaius Antonius Hybrida in 61 BCE.

name: Eudaemon (siege)
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
borderline: Known only from one sentence of the Periplus ('Caesar' destroyed the town 'not long before our time'); whether there was fighting, and who led it, is unknown.
roman_force: A Roman force from Egypt, by the Periplus' brief notice; nothing is known of its composition.
greek_note: Any fleet from Egypt's Red Sea ports was crewed from Egypt, where Greek was the language of command and trade.
sources: Periplus Maris Erythraei 26; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles (Siege of Eudaemon)
note: en.wikipedia's List of Roman battles dates it to 25 BCE with Aelius Gallus; other scholars think of Gaius Caesar (1 BCE) or Claudius, or emend the text. Marked traditional as doubtful.

name: Vellica
place: Vellica, near Monte Cildá, Olleros de Pisuerga (Palencia)
roman_force: Augustus' army mustered at Segisama, with Legio IV Macedonica and probably IX Hispana; the whole Cantabrian army had seven or eight legions with auxiliaries and a fleet from Aquitania (Florus 2.33.48; Orosius 6.21).
greek_note: Western legions recruited in Italy, Gaul and Spain, with Gallic auxiliaries.
sources: Florus 2.33.48; Orosius 6.21.3; Cassius Dio 53.25; en.wikipedia Battle of Vellica
note: Opponent: the Cantabri. Florus' first fight 'under the walls of Bergida' may be the same battle. Many modern authors date Augustus' campaign to 26 BCE.

name: Aracillum (siege)
place: Aracillum, Cantabria (traditionally Aradillos, Campoo de Enmedio)
roman_force: Five legions with auxiliaries, who encircled the hill fort with more than 20 km of works (en.wikipedia; Florus 2.33.50; Orosius 6.21).
greek_note: Western legions and Gallic and Spanish auxiliaries.
sources: Florus 2.33.50; Orosius 6.21.5; en.wikipedia Siege of Aracillum
note: Opponent: the Cantabri. The site has not been securely identified.

name: Mons Vindius (siege)
place: Mons Vindius, Cantabrian mountains (perhaps the Picos de Europa)
borderline: A blockade in which, Florus says, the Cantabri were starved out; little fighting is recorded.
roman_force: Part of the Cantabrian army of seven or eight legions with auxiliaries (Florus 2.33.49; Orosius 6.21.5).
greek_note: Western legions and auxiliaries.
sources: Florus 2.33.49; Orosius 6.21.5
note: Opponent: the Cantabri.

name: Astura
borderline: Named after the river by modern writers.
roman_force: Carisius' army of three legions in their winter camps, warned by the Brigaecini (Florus 2.33.54-57; Orosius 6.21.9).
greek_note: Western legions and auxiliaries.
sources: Florus 2.33.54-57; Orosius 6.21.9-10; en.wikipedia Cantabrian Wars
note: Opponent: the Astures, who came down in three columns to attack the Roman camps and were beaten in a bloody battle; the survivors fled to Lancia.

name: Lancia (siege)
roman_force: Carisius' legions, who stormed the strongest town of the Astures (Florus 2.33.57-58; Orosius 6.21.10).
greek_note: Western legions and auxiliaries.
sources: Florus 2.33.57-58; Orosius 6.21.10; Cassius Dio 53.25; en.wikipedia Cantabrian Wars
note: Opponent: the Astures. Carisius kept the soldiers from burning the town.

name: Mons Medullius (siege)
place: Mons Medullius, above the river Minius (site uncertain; Las Médulas has been proposed)
roman_force: Legions who ringed the mountain with a ditch of fifteen miles (Florus 2.33.50; Orosius 6.21.7-8).
greek_note: Western legions and auxiliaries.
sources: Florus 2.33.50; Orosius 6.21.7-8; en.wikipedia Cantabrian Wars
note: Opponents: Gallaeci, Astures and Cantabri; the besieged killed themselves rather than surrender.

name: Marib (siege)
war: Aelius Gallus' expedition to Arabia Felix
roman_force: About 10,000 Roman and allied infantry from the army of Egypt, with 500 Jews sent by Herod and 1,000 Nabataeans under Syllaeus (Strabo 16.4.23).
greek_note: The army of Egypt included Greek-speaking soldiers from Egypt and Galatia, but the sources do not say how many.
sources: Strabo 16.4.22-24; Cassius Dio 53.29; Res Gestae 26; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles
note: Opponent: the Sabaeans. Gallus besieged the city for six days and withdrew for lack of water.

name: Pselchis
roman_force: Fewer than 10,000 infantry and 800 cavalry from the army of Egypt, against about 30,000 Kushites (Strabo 17.1.54).
greek_note: The legions of Egypt (III Cyrenaica, XXII Deiotariana) and their auxiliaries were beginning to recruit in Egypt and Galatia.
sources: Strabo 17.1.54; Cassius Dio 54.5; Pliny NH 6.181-182; en.wikipedia Gaius Petronius
note: The site is now under Lake Nasser. Dio puts the campaign under 22 BCE.

name: Primis (siege)
borderline: Strabo says only that Petronius took the strong town by assault.
roman_force: Petronius' army of Egypt, as at Pselchis (Strabo 17.1.54).
greek_note: As at Pselchis.
sources: Strabo 17.1.54; Pliny NH 6.181
note: Petronius went on to sack Napata. In 22 BCE he returned to relieve the Roman garrison of Primis against Amanirenas, without a recorded battle.

name: Clades Lolliana
place: west of the lower Rhine, in Gaul (site unknown)
roman_force: Lollius' army of Gaul, including Legio V Alaudae, whose eagle was lost; the Germans first ambushed his cavalry (Cassius Dio 54.20; Velleius 2.97).
greek_note: Legions and Gallic auxiliaries of the Rhine army.
sources: Cassius Dio 54.20; Velleius 2.97; Suetonius Aug. 23; en.wikipedia Clades Lolliana
note: Opponents: Sugambri, Usipetes and Tencteri. Suetonius ranks it with the Varian disaster as Augustus' two great defeats.

name: Lake Constance
place: Lacus Brigantinus (Lake Constance), from an island used as a base
borderline: A lake fight known from one sentence of Strabo (Tiberius used the island as a base 'in his naval battle with the Vindelici').
roman_force: Tiberius' army advancing from Gaul, with boats on the lake; the legions and auxilia are not named (Strabo 7.1.5; Dio 54.22).
greek_note: An army of the western provinces, recruited in Italy, Gaul and Spain.
sources: Strabo 7.1.5; Cassius Dio 54.22; Velleius 2.95
note: Opponent: the Vindelici (Celtic). The island is not securely identified. Drusus fought the Raeti in the Alps in the same campaign, without a named battle.

name: Amisia
borderline: A river fight recorded in one line by Strabo.
roman_force: Drusus' Rhine fleet with legionaries embarked, sailing through his canal and along the coast with the Frisii as allies (Strabo 7.1.3; Dio 54.32).
greek_note: Rhine legions with Gallic and Germanic auxiliaries.
sources: Strabo 7.1.3; Cassius Dio 54.32
note: Opponent: the Bructeri. A river battle (type set to sea).

name: Arbalo
place: Arbalo, on Drusus' return from the Weser (perhaps near Hildesheim or Hamelin)
roman_force: Drusus' legions and auxiliaries of the Rhine army returning from the Weser; Wikipedia estimates 19,000-42,000 men (Pliny NH 11.55; Dio 54.33).
greek_note: Rhine legions with Gallic and Germanic auxiliaries.
sources: Pliny NH 11.55; Julius Obsequens 72; Cassius Dio 54.33; en.wikipedia Battle of Arbalo
note: Opponents: Cherusci and allies. The Germans trapped the army in a narrow valley and were beaten off.

name: Lupia River
borderline: Listed by Wikipedia; the ancient sources describe Drusus' campaign against the Sugambri on the Lippe without a named battle.
roman_force: Part of Drusus' Rhine army (Wikipedia gives about 2,000 men; Dio 54.33 gives no figures).
greek_note: Rhine legions and auxiliaries.
sources: Cassius Dio 54.33; en.wikipedia Battle of the Lupia River
note: Opponent: the Sugambri.

name: Jerusalem (siege)
place: Jerusalem, the Temple courts and Herod's palace
borderline: A siege of the Roman garrison, usually told as part of the War of Varus, not a named battle.
roman_force: The legion Varus had left in Jerusalem with Sabinus and about 3,000 Sebastenian royal troops under Rufus and Gratus; relieved by Varus with two legions, four alae and auxiliaries of the kings and cities, including Aretas' Nabataeans (Josephus BJ 2.39-79).
greek_note: Josephus names the Sebastenians, from the Greek-speaking city of Sebaste, and the auxiliaries of the Syrian cities.
sources: Josephus BJ 2.39-79, AJ 17.250-298; en.wikipedia War of Varus
note: The besieged legion fought in the Temple courts and burned the porticoes; Varus relieved it and crucified 2,000 rebels.

name: Artagira (siege)
roman_force: Gaius Caesar's eastern army, the legions and auxiliaries of Syria with allied contingents; no numbers are given (Velleius 2.102; Dio 55.10a).
greek_note: The Syrian legions and auxiliaries were recruited largely in the Greek-speaking and Aramaic-speaking East.
sources: Velleius 2.102; Cassius Dio 55.10a.6-8; Florus 2.32; Strabo 11.14.6
note: Gaius was treacherously wounded by Addon at a parley and died of the wound in 4 CE; the town was taken after a long siege. Wikipedia dates the wounding to 9 September 2 CE; the usual date is 3 CE.

name: Salona
roman_force: The defenders of Salona, the capital of Dalmatia; Dio gives no details (Dio 55.29.4).
greek_note: Salona had Italian settlers and some Greek traders; the garrison is unknown.
sources: Cassius Dio 55.29.4; en.wikipedia Bellum Batonianum
note: Opponent: the Daesitiates. Bato was hit by a stone and his attack failed; his men then raided the coast as far as Apollonia.

name: Sirmium
place: near Sirmium (Sremska Mitrovica), towards the Drava
roman_force: Caecina Severus' army of Moesia, legions and auxiliaries (Dio 55.29.3).
greek_note: The Moesian army drew some recruits from Macedonia and Thrace.
sources: Cassius Dio 55.29.3; Velleius 2.110; en.wikipedia Bellum Batonianum
note: Opponent: the Breuci (Pannonians). Dio places the fight near the Drava; it saved Sirmium, at heavy cost.

name: Mons Alma
place: Mons Alma (Fruška Gora), north of Sirmium
commanders_a: Rhoemetalces I of Thrace, Aulus Caecina Severus
commanders_b: Bato the Daesitiate, Bato the Breucian
roman_force: Rhoemetalces' Thracian cavalry sent ahead by Caecina, followed by Caecina's Moesian legions (Dio 55.30.3-4).
greek_note: The Thracian royal army was Thracian-speaking, with Greek at court.
sources: Cassius Dio 55.30.3-4; en.wikipedia Bellum Batonianum
note: Opponents: Daesitiates and Breuci.

name: Volcaean Marshes
commanders_a: Aulus Caecina Severus, Marcus Plautius Silvanus
commanders_b: Bato the Daesitiate, Bato the Breucian
roman_force: Five legions (by Wikipedia's reconstruction VII, VIII and XI from Moesia with IV Scythica and V Macedonica), some 70 cohorts in all with auxiliaries, and Rhoemetalces' Thracian cavalry, which was routed early (Velleius 2.112; Dio 55.32.3-4).
greek_note: Some of the legions came from the East, but their legionaries were still largely Italian and western; the Thracian allies spoke Thracian.
sources: Velleius 2.112; Cassius Dio 55.32.3-4; en.wikipedia Battle of the Volcaean Marshes
note: The Roman columns were surprised while making camp; the legions rallied and won after heavy losses.

name: Teutoburg Forest
place: Teutoburg Forest; the main battlefield is generally placed at Kalkriese, near Osnabrück
roman_force: Three legions (XVII, XVIII and XIX), three alae and six auxiliary cohorts (Velleius 2.117), perhaps 15,000-20,000 soldiers with camp followers.
greek_note: The Rhine legions were recruited in Italy, Narbonensis and Gaul; the auxiliaries were Gallic and Germanic.
sources: Velleius 2.117-120; Cassius Dio 56.18-24; Tacitus Ann. 1.60-62; Florus 2.30; en.wikipedia Battle of the Teutoburg Forest
note: Opponents: Cherusci, Marsi, Chatti, Bructeri and others. The fighting lasted several days on the march.

name: Splonum (siege)
place: Splonum, Dalmatia (site uncertain; perhaps near Pljevlja)
roman_force: Germanicus' division of the army of Illyricum, legions and auxiliaries including German cavalry (Dio 56.11.2-3).
greek_note: The army of Illyricum was reinforced from the East as well as from Italy.
sources: Cassius Dio 56.11.2-3; en.wikipedia Bellum Batonianum
note: Opponents: Dalmatians. The assaults failed until a section of wall collapsed, after which the garrison surrendered.

name: Raetinum (siege)
place: Raetinum, Dalmatia (site uncertain; perhaps Golubić near Bihać)
roman_force: Germanicus' division of the army of Illyricum (Dio 56.11.4-7).
greek_note: As at Splonum.
sources: Cassius Dio 56.11.4-7; en.wikipedia Bellum Batonianum
note: Opponents: Dalmatians. The defenders fired their own town and many Romans were trapped in the flames; the survivors held out in the citadel, and Dio does not say clearly how it ended.

name: Seretium (siege)
roman_force: Germanicus' division of the army of Illyricum (Dio 56.12.1).
greek_note: As at Splonum.
sources: Cassius Dio 56.12.1; en.wikipedia Bellum Batonianum
note: Opponents: Dalmatians. Germanicus took the town, against which Tiberius had failed earlier.

name: Andetrium (siege)
roman_force: Tiberius' division of the army of Illyricum, while Plautius Silvanus and Lepidus led the other columns (Dio 56.12-14).
greek_note: As at Splonum.
sources: Cassius Dio 56.12-14; en.wikipedia Bellum Batonianum
note: Opponents: Daesitiates. The rock fortress was stormed after Bato slipped away; Bato surrendered soon after.

name: Arduba (siege)
place: Arduba, a town above a river (site uncertain; perhaps Vranduk)
roman_force: Germanicus' division of the army of Illyricum (Dio 56.15).
greek_note: As at Splonum.
sources: Cassius Dio 56.15; en.wikipedia Bellum Batonianum
note: Opponents: Dalmatian deserters and townspeople. The deserters were beaten and the women threw themselves and their children into the fire or the river.

name: Aliso (siege)
place: the fort of Aliso on the Lippe (perhaps Haltern)
borderline: The identification of the fort is uncertain.
roman_force: The fort's garrison with archers and survivors of Varus' army (Velleius 2.120; Dio 56.22; Frontinus Strat. 4.7.8).
greek_note: Rhine army troops.
sources: Velleius 2.120; Cassius Dio 56.22; Frontinus Strat. 3.15.4, 4.7.8
note: The Germans' assaults were beaten off, but the garrison finally abandoned the fort and broke out to the Rhine.

name: Pontes Longi
place: the 'long bridges' causeway through the marshes (Wikipedia: near Bramsche)
roman_force: Caecina's four legions (I Germanica, V Alaudae, XX Valeria Victrix and XXI Rapax) with auxiliaries, 28,000-30,000 men (Tacitus Ann. 1.60-68).
greek_note: Rhine legions and western auxiliaries.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 1.63-68; en.wikipedia Battle at Pontes Longi
note: Opponent: the Cherusci and allies. Caecina's army was nearly overwhelmed in the marsh but beat off the assault on its camp and escaped; Tacitus presents it as a Roman victory, modern historians (and Wikipedia) as inconclusive.

name: Idistaviso
place: Idistaviso plain on the right bank of the Weser, between Minden and Hamelin
roman_force: Eight legions, Gallic and German auxiliary cohorts including the Batavians of Chariovalda and the Chauci, Raetian and Vindelician cohorts, two praetorian cohorts, archers and cavalry, at least 60,000 men (Tacitus Ann. 2.11-18; Wikipedia).
greek_note: Rhine legions and western auxiliaries; the archers may have included a few eastern units.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 2.14-18; en.wikipedia Battle of the Weser River
note: Opponent: the Cherusci and allies. Wikipedia titles it the Battle of the Weser River.

name: Angrivarian Wall
place: the earthwork between the Cherusci and the Angrivarii, east of the Weser (near Leese)
roman_force: The same army as at Idistaviso: eight legions with praetorian cohorts, slingers, artillery and auxiliaries (Tacitus Ann. 2.19-22).
greek_note: Rhine legions and western auxiliaries.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 2.19-22; en.wikipedia Battle of the Angrivarian Wall
note: Some modern writers think Tacitus overstates the victory.

name: Furius Camillus' victory
borderline: A pitched battle without a recorded site or name.
roman_force: One legion (III Augusta) with the allied auxiliaries, a small force against Tacfarinas' larger Numidian and Musulamian host (Tacitus Ann. 2.52).
greek_note: The African legion and local auxilia, Latin- and Berber-speaking.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 2.52; en.wikipedia Tacfarinas
note: Opponents: Musulamii and Moors under Tacfarinas. Camillus received triumphal ornaments.

name: Pagyda
place: a fort on the river Pagyda (site unknown)
roman_force: A cohort of Legio III Augusta under the centurion Decrius (Tacitus Ann. 3.20).
greek_note: The African legion was recruited in Italy and the Latin-speaking western provinces.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 3.20; en.wikipedia Tacfarinas
note: Opponent: the Musulamii under Tacfarinas. The cohort sallied and fled; the proconsul Lucius Apronius decimated it.

name: Thala
roman_force: About 500 veterans holding the fort (Tacitus Ann. 3.21).
greek_note: Veterans of Legio III Augusta.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 3.21; en.wikipedia Tacfarinas
note: Opponent: the Musulamii. The common soldier Rufus Helvius won the civic crown here.

name: Augustodunum
place: open plain twelve miles from Augustodunum (Autun)
borderline: A pitched battle near the town, not usually given its own name.
roman_force: Two legions of the Upper German army with auxiliaries and cavalry (Tacitus Ann. 3.43-46).
greek_note: Rhine legions and western auxiliaries.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 3.40-46; Velleius 2.129
note: Opponents: Aedui and Sequani; Sacrovir's 40,000 included armoured gladiators (crupellarii). Sacrovir killed himself.

name: Thubursicum
roman_force: Dolabella's Legio III Augusta and auxiliaries (Tacitus Ann. 4.24).
greek_note: The African legion and Numidian auxiliaries.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 4.24; en.wikipedia Tacfarinas
note: Dolabella's arrival broke the siege; the Numidians fled at the first charge.

name: Auzea
place: Tacfarinas' camp by the fort of Auzea (near Sour El-Ghozlane)
roman_force: Light infantry and cavalry of Legio III Augusta's army in four columns, with Mauretanian horse sent by King Ptolemy (Tacitus Ann. 4.24-25).
greek_note: The African legion with Numidian and Moorish cavalry.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 4.24-25; en.wikipedia Tacfarinas
note: A dawn surprise attack on the camp; Tacfarinas died fighting and the revolt ended.

name: Baduhenna Wood
place: the grove of Baduhenna in Frisia (perhaps near Heiloo)
roman_force: Vexillations of the Upper German legions, picked auxiliary infantry and cavalry, Legio V Alaudae, and the cavalry of the Canninefates with German infantry in Roman service (Tacitus Ann. 4.72-73).
greek_note: Rhine legions with Germanic and Gallic auxiliaries.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 4.72-74; en.wikipedia Battle of Baduhenna Wood
note: Opponent: the Frisii. Apronius relieved the besieged fort (Flevum) but his units were beaten piecemeal; 900 fell in the grove and 400 more killed themselves at Cruptorix's villa. Wikipedia's infobox calls it a Pyrrhic Roman victory.

name: Medway
place: crossing of the river Medway, probably near Rochester
commanders_a: Aulus Plautius, Vespasian, Titus Flavius Sabinus, Gnaeus Hosidius Geta
roman_force: Four legions (II Augusta, IX Hispana, XIV Gemina, XX) with auxiliaries, about 40,000 men (Wikipedia's infobox gives 60,000); Dio's 'Celtic' auxiliaries, probably Batavians, swam the river in armour (Dio 60.20).
greek_note: Rhine and Danube legions with Gallic and Batavian auxiliaries.
sources: Cassius Dio 60.19-21; Suetonius Vesp. 4; en.wikipedia Battle of the Medway
note: Opponents: the Catuvellauni and allies. A two-day battle; Dio does not name the river, which is inferred.

name: Thames
place: the Thames near its estuary marshes
borderline: Dio describes a second battle at the Thames, but it is seldom treated as a named battle.
roman_force: Plautius' army, with Batavian auxiliaries swimming the river and other troops crossing by a bridge upstream (Dio 60.20.5-6).
greek_note: As at the Medway.
sources: Cassius Dio 60.20.5-6; en.wikipedia Roman conquest of Britain
note: The Romans lost men pursuing the Britons into the marshes.

name: Ostorius' victory over the Iceni
place: a rustic earthwork in the lands of the Iceni (site unknown; Stonea Camp has been suggested)
commanders_a: Publius Ostorius Scapula, Marcus Ostorius Scapula
borderline: Unnamed; the site is not recorded.
roman_force: Auxiliary infantry and dismounted cavalry, without the legions, who stormed the earthwork (Tacitus Ann. 12.31).
greek_note: Auxilia of the British garrison, recruited in Gaul, the Rhineland and Thrace.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 12.31; en.wikipedia Iceni
note: The first revolt of the Iceni and their neighbours, against Ostorius' disarmament; his son won the civic crown.

name: Uspe (siege)
place: Uspe, town of the Siraces beyond the river Panda (site unknown, Kuban region)
commanders_a: Gaius Julius Aquila, Cotys I, Eunones
roman_force: A few Roman cohorts under Julius Aquila with Cotys' Bosporan troops armed in the Roman manner and the cavalry of the Aorsi under Eunones (Tacitus Ann. 12.15-17).
greek_note: Tacitus names Cotys' Bosporan forces, from a largely Greek-speaking kingdom, beside the Sarmatian Aorsi and a few Roman cohorts.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 12.15-17; en.wikipedia Roman–Bosporan War
note: Opponent: the Siraces, allies of the deposed Mithridates of the Bosporus; allies_a Sarmatians = the Aorsi. The town was stormed after its offer of 10,000 slaves was refused, and Zorsines submitted.

name: Caer Caradoc
place: a fortified hill by a river in the territory of the Ordovices (site unknown; Caer Caradog near Chapel Lawn, Shropshire, is the most favoured candidate)
roman_force: Ostorius' legions and auxiliaries, who stormed the stone ramparts in testudo (Tacitus Ann. 12.33-35).
greek_note: Legions of Britain with Gallic and Germanic auxiliaries.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 12.33-36; en.wikipedia Battle of Caer Caradoc
note: Opponents: Ordovices and Silures. Caratacus fled to Cartimandua of the Brigantes, who handed him over.

name: Artaxata
borderline: Tiridates harassed the column and offered battle but withdrew; the city then surrendered without a siege and was burned. The fighting was skirmishing on the march.
roman_force: III Gallica on the right, VI Ferrata on the left and picked men of X Fretensis in the centre, with auxiliary horse and archers on the flanks (Tacitus Ann. 13.40).
greek_note: Corbulo filled his Syrian legions with levies from Galatia and Cappadocia (Tacitus Ann. 13.35).
sources: Tacitus Ann. 13.39-41; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles (Sack of Artaxata)
note: The en.wikipedia list calls it the Sack of Artaxata. Its 'Capture of Tigranocerta' (59) was a surrender without fighting and is not entered; the resistance of Legerda is entered separately.

name: Volandum (siege)
roman_force: Corbulo's army of III Gallica and VI Ferrata with a vexillation of X Fretensis and auxiliaries, while allied kings attacked elsewhere (Tacitus Ann. 13.35, 13.39).
greek_note: Tacitus (Ann. 13.35) says Corbulo filled his Syrian legions with levies from Galatia and Cappadocia.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 13.39; en.wikipedia Roman–Parthian War of 58–63
note: Stormed within a day, with three smaller forts; Artaxata surrendered soon after.

name: Legerda (siege)
borderline: A siege known from one sentence of Tacitus.
roman_force: Corbulo's Syrian legions and auxiliaries (Tacitus Ann. 14.25).
greek_note: As at Volandum: Syrian legions filled with Galatian and Cappadocian levies.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 14.25
note: A band of defenders held the fort until it was stormed.

name: Mona
place: Menai Strait and the island of Mona (Anglesey)
roman_force: Legio XIV Gemina and detachments of XX ferried in flat-bottomed boats, with auxiliary cavalry swimming beside their horses (Tacitus Ann. 14.29-30).
greek_note: Legions of Britain with Batavian and Gallic auxiliaries.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 14.29-30, Agricola 14; en.wikipedia Roman conquest of Anglesey
note: Tacitus puts the revolt of Boudica, which broke out during this campaign, under 61 CE; many modern historians prefer 60 CE.

name: Camulodunum (siege)
place: the colonia of Camulodunum (Colchester) and its temple of Claudius
borderline: A sack, but the defenders fought in the temple for two days.
roman_force: The veteran colonists and about 200 poorly armed men sent by the procurator Catus Decianus, holding the temple for two days (Tacitus Ann. 14.31-32).
greek_note: Legionary veterans settled in the colony.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 14.31-32; Cassius Dio 62.1-2; en.wikipedia Boudican revolt
note: Opponents: Iceni and Trinovantes.

name: Ninth Legion's defeat
place: on the road to Camulodunum (site unknown)
borderline: An ambush or rout without a place name.
roman_force: A vexillation of Legio IX Hispana with cavalry; the infantry was destroyed and Cerialis escaped with the horse (Tacitus Ann. 14.32).
greek_note: A western legion.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 14.32; en.wikipedia Boudican revolt
note: Opponents: Iceni and Trinovantes.

name: Watling Street
place: a defile with a wood behind, probably on Watling Street in the Midlands (Mancetter is one candidate)
roman_force: Legio XIV Gemina, vexillations of XX Valeria Victrix and the nearest auxiliaries, about 10,000 men (Tacitus Ann. 14.34); II Augusta failed to come.
greek_note: Legions of Britain with Gallic and Germanic auxiliaries.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 14.34-37, Agricola 16; Cassius Dio 62.8-12; en.wikipedia Battle of Watling Street
note: Opponents: Iceni, Trinovantes and other Britons. Tacitus' 80,000 British dead and Dio's 230,000 Britons are not credited by modern historians.

name: Tigranocerta (siege)
commanders_a: Tigranes VI of Armenia, Verulanus Severus
roman_force: Tigranes VI's Armenians with a Roman garrison; Corbulo had sent two legions under Verulanus Severus and Vettius Bolanus to support Tigranes (Tacitus Ann. 15.3-6).
greek_note: The Romans were Syrian legionaries partly levied in Galatia and Cappadocia, but most of the defenders were Armenians.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 15.4-6; Cassius Dio 62.20; en.wikipedia Roman–Parthian War of 58–63
note: The Adiabenians did most of the siege work; a sally drove them back and Vologases withdrew Monaeses.

name: Rhandeia
place: Paetus' winter camp at Rhandeia, on the Arsanias near Arsamosata
roman_force: Paetus with Legio IV Scythica and XII Fulminata, auxiliaries and allied horse, V Macedonica being in Pontus; Corbulo came too late with half the Syrian army (Tacitus Ann. 15.6-17).
greek_note: The eastern legions recruited heavily in Galatia, Cappadocia and Syria.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 15.6-17; Cassius Dio 62.21-22; en.wikipedia Battle of Rhandeia
note: Paetus' outlying detachments were beaten in detail and he capitulated after a short siege of his camp; the Romans left Armenia. The site is not securely located; Wikipedia's coordinates (39.40, 43.80) lie much further east.

name: Jerusalem garrison (siege)
place: Jerusalem: the upper city, the Antonia and Herod's palace
commanders_a: Eleazar ben Hananiah, Menahem ben Judah
borderline: A siege of the garrison, usually told as the start of the revolt rather than as a named battle.
roman_force: A Roman auxiliary cohort under Metilius, with 2,000-3,000 cavalry sent by Agrippa II from Auranitis, Batanaea and Trachonitis (Josephus BJ 2.421-456).
greek_note: Josephus says the auxiliaries of Judaea were recruited at Caesarea and Sebaste (AJ 19.365), Greek-speaking cities.
sources: Josephus BJ 2.405-456; en.wikipedia First Jewish–Roman War
note: Agrippa's troops left under truce; the Romans surrendered in the towers and were massacred, except Metilius.

name: Ascalon
commanders_b: Niger the Perean, Silas the Babylonian (killed), John the Essene (killed)
roman_force: The garrison of Ascalon, one cohort of infantry and one ala of cavalry (Josephus BJ 3.12).
greek_note: The auxiliary units of Judaea and the coast were raised largely in the Greek cities of the region.
sources: Josephus BJ 3.9-28; en.wikipedia First Jewish–Roman War
note: Two attacks were beaten off by the cavalry, with heavy Jewish losses (Josephus' 10,000 and 8,000).

name: Beth Horon
place: the Beth Horon ascent on the road from Jerusalem to the coast
commanders_a: Eleazar ben Simon, Simon bar Giora, Niger the Perean
roman_force: Legio XII Fulminata with 2,000 men from each of the other Syrian legions, six cohorts and four alae, troops of Antiochus IV of Commagene, Agrippa II and Sohaemus of Emesa, and levies from the Syrian cities (Josephus BJ 2.499-502), perhaps 30,000 men.
greek_note: Josephus lists large levies from the Greek cities of Syria and the troops of the client kings beside the legions.
sources: Josephus BJ 2.499-555; Suetonius Vesp. 4; Tacitus Hist. 5.10; en.wikipedia Battle of Beth Horon (66)
note: Cestius had attacked Jerusalem and withdrawn; he lost 5,300 infantry, 480 cavalry and the eagle of XII Fulminata in the pass. Wikipedia puts the army at 20,000 (infobox) to 29,000-36,000 (text).

name: Jotapata (siege)
roman_force: Legions V Macedonica, X Fretensis and XV Apollinaris, 23 auxiliary cohorts and six alae, with archers and horse from Antiochus IV, Agrippa II, Sohaemus and the Nabataean Malchus II, about 60,000 men (Josephus BJ 3.64-69).
greek_note: Josephus names the Caesarean and Sebastenian auxiliaries and the eastern royal contingents; X Fretensis and the Syrian auxiliaries were recruited in the Greek East.
sources: Josephus BJ 3.141-339; en.wikipedia Siege of Yodfat
note: The town fell after 47 days and Josephus surrendered to Vespasian.

name: Tarichaea
place: Tarichaea (Magdala), on the Sea of Galilee
roman_force: Titus with 600 picked horse, reinforced by Trajan with 400 horse and 2,000 archers, who rode into the town from the lake shore (Josephus BJ 3.462-502).
greek_note: The cavalry and archers were largely Syrian and eastern auxiliaries.
sources: Josephus BJ 3.462-542; en.wikipedia Siege of Tarichaea

name: Sea of Galilee
roman_force: Legionaries and auxiliaries embarked on rafts built for the purpose (Josephus BJ 3.522-531).
greek_note: Vespasian's army was recruited largely in Syria and the Greek East.
sources: Josephus BJ 3.522-531; en.wikipedia First Jewish–Roman War
note: The fugitives from Tarichaea in fishing boats were destroyed; Josephus gives 6,700 dead in town and lake.

name: Gamla (siege)
place: Gamla, on a ridge in the Golan
commanders_b: Joseph son of a midwife, Chares
roman_force: Legions V Macedonica, X Fretensis and XV Apollinaris with auxiliaries and artillery (Josephus BJ 4.1-83).
greek_note: X Fretensis and the Syrian auxiliaries were recruited in the Greek East.
sources: Josephus BJ 4.1-83; en.wikipedia Siege of Gamla
note: Golan Heights, internationally recognised as Syria and administered by Israel. The first assault was repulsed with heavy loss; the town was taken about a month later.

name: Mount Gerizim
borderline: The Samaritans, surrounded on the mountain and short of water, were attacked when they refused to surrender (11,600 dead, by Josephus); more a massacre than a battle.
roman_force: 600 cavalry and 3,000 infantry, chiefly of legio V Macedonica, under its legate Cerialis, sent by Vespasian (Josephus BJ 3.307-315).
greek_note: V Macedonica, long stationed in Macedonia and Moesia, drew many recruits from the Balkan and eastern provinces.
sources: Josephus BJ 3.307-315; en.wikipedia First Jewish–Roman War
note: Samaritans, not Jewish rebels: a new side name.

name: Japha (siege)
roman_force: Trajan (legate of X Fretensis) with 1,000 horse and 2,000 foot, reinforced by Titus with 500 horse and 1,000 foot (Josephus BJ 3.289-306).
greek_note: Detachments of Vespasian's army, recruited largely in Syria and the Greek East.
sources: Josephus BJ 3.289-306; en.wikipedia First Jewish–Roman War
note: The town was stormed; Josephus says 15,000 were killed.

name: Mount Tabor
roman_force: Placidus with 600 horse, who feigned flight to draw the defenders into the plain (Josephus BJ 4.54-61).
greek_note: Auxiliary cavalry recruited largely in Syria and the Greek East.
sources: Josephus BJ 4.54-61; en.wikipedia First Jewish–Roman War
note: The garrison of the summit surrendered for lack of water.

name: Bethennabris
place: Bethennabris (Beth Nimrah, Tell Nimrin) and the Jordan crossing
borderline: A field battle known only from Josephus and not usually given a name.
roman_force: Placidus with 500 horse and 3,000 foot (Josephus BJ 4.419-437).
greek_note: A detachment of Vespasian's eastern army.
sources: Josephus BJ 4.413-439
note: The fugitives from Gadara were routed and driven into the flooded Jordan; Josephus gives 15,000 dead.

name: Vesontio
borderline: Vindex was a Roman governor but his army was Gallic levies; counted as civil.
roman_force: The legions of Upper Germany (IV Macedonica, XXII Primigenia and others) with Belgic and Germanic auxiliaries; Vindex led some 20,000 Gallic levies of the Aedui, Sequani and Arverni (Dio 63.24; Plutarch Galba 6).
greek_note: Rhine legions and Gallic provincials.
sources: Cassius Dio 63.24-25; Plutarch Galba 6; Tacitus Hist. 1.51; en.wikipedia Battle of Vesontio (68)
note: Fought against the wishes of the two commanders, who had been negotiating; Vindex killed himself.

name: Alpes Maritimae
place: Coast of the Maritime Alps between Albintimilium and Antipolis
commanders_a: Suedius Clemens, Antonius Novellus, Aemilius Pacensis
borderline: Tacitus describes the fighting but names no site.
roman_force: Othonian: marines of the Misenum fleet with urban and praetorian cohorts landed on the Ligurian coast; Vitellian: two Tungrian cohorts, four troops of horse and the ala Treverorum under Julius Classicus sent by Fabius Valens, with Ligurian auxiliaries and local levies (Tacitus, Hist. 2.12-15).
greek_note: The Misenum fleet's marines were provincials from Egypt, Thrace, Asia Minor and Syria as well as the West; the Vitellian side was Gallic and Germanic.
sources: Tacitus, Histories 2.12-15; en.wikipedia Battle of Locus Castorum (Otho's early success in the Alps)
note: The Othonians held the field; afterwards the Vitellians fell back on Antipolis and the Othonians on Albingaunum.

name: First Bedriacum
place: On the Via Postumia between Bedriacum and Cremona
commanders_b: Salvius Titianus, Licinius Proculus, Gaius Suetonius Paulinus, Marius Celsus
roman_force: Vitellian: the Rhine armies of Caecina and Valens, legions XXI Rapax, V Alaudae and I Italica with vexillations of the other Rhine legions and Batavian, Gallic and German auxilia; Othonian: I Adiutrix, XIII Gemina and a vexillation of XIV Gemina, praetorian cohorts and 2,000 gladiators, about 50,000 against 70,000 (Tacitus, Hist. 2.11, 2.41-45).
greek_note: Only I Adiutrix, raised from the Misenum fleet, had many eastern recruits; the Vitellian army was Rhenish and Gallic.
sources: Tacitus, Histories 2.39-45; Plutarch, Otho 8-14; Suetonius, Otho 9; en.wikipedia First Battle of Bedriacum
note: Vitellius was still in Gaul; Otho, at Brixellum, killed himself two days later.

name: Locus Castorum
place: Locus Castorum (Ad Castores), about 12 Roman miles east of Cremona on the Via Postumia
roman_force: Othonian: legionaries of I Adiutrix and a vexillation of XIII Gemina, praetorian cohorts, auxiliary cohorts and cavalry under Paulinus and Celsus; Vitellian: Caecina's auxiliary infantry and cavalry, whose ambush was turned and routed (Tacitus, Hist. 2.24-26).
greek_note: I Adiutrix had been raised in 68 from marines of the Misenum fleet, many of them easterners; the rest were Italians, Danubian legionaries and Rhine auxilia.
sources: Tacitus, Histories 2.24-26; Suetonius, Otho 9; en.wikipedia Battle of Locus Castorum
note: Paulinus was blamed for not pursuing.

name: Aquilius' defeat
place: On the Rhine at the eastern end of the island of the Batavians, probably south of modern Arnhem
borderline: No conventional name (en.wikipedia calls it an unnamed battle near Arnhem).
roman_force: The auxiliary garrisons of the Rhine delta rallied under the senior centurion Aquilius, with ships of the Rhine fleet; a Tungrian cohort went over to Civilis and the Batavian rowers ran the ships aground (Tacitus, Hist. 4.15-16).
greek_note: The Rhine-delta auxilia and fleet crews were raised in Gaul and Germany.
sources: Tacitus, Histories 4.15-16; livius.org, Batavian Revolt (4); en.wikipedia Revolt of the Batavi
note: Batavi, Cananefates and Frisii.

name: Lupercus' defeat
place: Near the Rhine, probably near Noviomagus (Nijmegen)
borderline: No conventional name (en.wikipedia calls it an unnamed battle near Nijmegen).
roman_force: Detachments of V Alaudae and XV Primigenia from Vetera with Ubian and Treviran auxiliaries and a Batavian ala under Claudius Labeo, which deserted in the battle; the auxiliaries fled and the legions fell back to Vetera (Tacitus, Hist. 4.18).
greek_note: Rhine legions and Ubian, Treviran and Batavian auxilia.
sources: Tacitus, Histories 4.18; livius.org, Batavian Revolt (4); en.wikipedia Revolt of the Batavi
note: Batavi with Cananefates and Frisii.

name: Bonna
place: Before the legionary fortress of Bonna (Bonn)
roman_force: Legio I Germanica under Herennius Gallus, about 3,000 legionaries with hastily raised Belgic cohorts and camp followers, tried to stop the eight veteran Batavian cohorts marching north to join Civilis and was routed (Tacitus, Hist. 4.19-20).
greek_note: A Rhine legion with Belgic levies.
sources: Tacitus, Histories 4.19-20
note: The Batavian cohorts had been recalled from Mogontiacum by Civilis.

name: Vetera (first siege)
place: Castra Vetera, on the Fürstenberg near Xanten
commanders_a: Munius Lupercus; relieved by Dillius Vocula
roman_force: The remnants of V Alaudae and XV Primigenia, no more than 5,000 legionaries with camp followers, under Munius Lupercus, who threw back repeated assaults; relieved in December by Vocula's army (Tacitus, Hist. 4.21-23, 4.28-30, 4.34-35).
greek_note: Rhine legions recruited in Gaul, northern Italy and the Rhineland.
sources: Tacitus, Histories 4.21-23, 4.28-30, 4.34-35; livius.org, Batavian Revolt chronology; en.wikipedia Revolt of the Batavi
note: Batavi with Bructeri, Tencteri and other Germans from across the Rhine.

name: Second Bedriacum
place: On the Via Postumia between Bedriacum and Cremona, near Cremona
commanders_b: Fabius Fabullus and the other legionary legates (Caecina had been arrested by his men)
roman_force: Flavian: the Danubian legions III Gallica, VII Claudia and VIII Augusta from Moesia and VII Galbiana and XIII Gemina from Pannonia, with the praetorians cashiered by Vitellius, Pannonian and Moesian auxilia and Suebian allies under Sido and Italicus; Vitellian: IV Macedonica, V Alaudae, XV Primigenia, XVI Gallica, XXII Primigenia and I Germanica, with XXI Rapax and I Italica mixed through the line and vexillations of the British legions II, IX and XX (Tacitus, Hist. 3.21-22).
greek_note: III Gallica, a Syrian legion until 68, turned to salute the rising sun 'as is the custom in Syria' (Hist. 3.24); the rest of both armies was Danubian, Rhenish and British.
sources: Tacitus, Histories 3.15-25; Cassius Dio 65.10-15; en.wikipedia Second Battle of Bedriacum
note: A night battle; also called the second battle of Cremona. Suebi under Sido and Italicus fought for the Flavians.

name: Cremona (siege)
place: The Vitellian camp and the walls of Cremona
borderline: The storming followed the battle at once and is often counted as part of Second Bedriacum.
roman_force: The victorious Flavian legions (III Gallica, VII Claudia, VIII Augusta, VII Galbiana, XIII Gemina) stormed the fortified Vitellian camp and assaulted the walls held by the beaten Vitellian legions; the city surrendered and was sacked and burned for four days (Tacitus, Hist. 3.26-34).
greek_note: As at Second Bedriacum: only III Gallica had many eastern recruits.
sources: Tacitus, Histories 3.26-34; Cassius Dio 65.15; en.wikipedia Second Battle of Bedriacum

name: Forum Alieni
place: Forum Alieni, on the Adige (probably Legnago)
borderline: A small engagement at the start of Antonius Primus' invasion of Italy.
roman_force: Flavian: Antonius Primus and Arrius Varus with picked auxiliary cohorts and part of the cavalry of the Pannonian army; Vitellian: cohorts and cavalry posted at Forum Alieni, which were surprised and routed (Tacitus, Hist. 3.6).
greek_note: Pannonian auxilia against Rhine troops.
sources: Tacitus, Histories 3.6
note: The identification of Forum Alieni with Legnago is probable, not certain.

name: Capitol (siege)
commanders_b: Titus Flavius Sabinus (city prefect, killed), Domitian
borderline: Street fighting rather than a field battle; known as the burning of the Capitol.
roman_force: Vitellian soldiers of the German army in Rome stormed the Capitol; it was held by Flavius Sabinus with a small mixed force of soldiers, senators and knights and the young Domitian; the temple of Jupiter burned and Sabinus was killed (Tacitus, Hist. 3.69-73).
greek_note: Rhine troops against Sabinus' urban soldiers and civilians of Rome.
sources: Tacitus, Histories 3.69-73; Suetonius, Vitellius 15, Domitian 1

name: Rome
place: Rome: the Campus Martius, the Colline Gate and the praetorian camp
commanders_a: Marcus Antonius Primus, Quintus Petillius Cerialis, Arrius Varus
borderline: No en.wikipedia article; the fighting is narrated by Tacitus as a battle for the city.
roman_force: Flavian: the Danubian army of Antonius Primus entering in three columns by the Via Flaminia, along the Tiber and by the Via Salaria to the Colline Gate; Vitellian: the praetorian cohorts and remnants of the German army, who fought in the streets and the Campus Martius and to the last in the praetorian camp (Tacitus, Hist. 3.79-84).
greek_note: Only the Syrian-recruited III Gallica among the Flavian legions had many Greek speakers.
sources: Tacitus, Histories 3.79-84; Cassius Dio 65.19-21; Suetonius, Vitellius 16-17
note: Cerialis' cavalry had been beaten outside the city two days earlier.

name: Gelduba
place: The Roman camp at Gelduba (Krefeld-Gellep), on the Rhine
roman_force: Vocula's relief army of vexillations of the Upper and Lower German legions with Gallic auxilia, near defeat until the Vascon cohorts levied by Galba fell on the enemy's rear (Tacitus, Hist. 4.33).
greek_note: Rhine legionaries, Gallic auxilia and Spanish Vascones (an early Basque speech, 'other').
sources: Tacitus, Histories 4.26, 4.32-33; livius.org, Batavian Revolt chronology ('battle of Krefeld')
note: The Batavian veteran cohorts were cut to pieces, but Roman losses were heavy. Called the battle of Krefeld by livius.org and en.wikipedia.

name: Mogontiacum (siege)
borderline: Little detail of the fighting survives.
roman_force: The depleted garrison of Mogontiacum (IV Macedonica and XXII Primigenia), relieved by Vocula's army (Tacitus, Hist. 4.37).
greek_note: Upper German legions recruited in Gaul, the Rhineland and northern Italy.
sources: Tacitus, Histories 4.37; livius.org, Batavian Revolt chronology
note: Chatti, Usipi and Mattiaci.

name: Tarracina (siege)
roman_force: Vitellian: Lucius Vitellius with the cohorts and cavalry sent to Campania (six cohorts and 500 horse, Hist. 3.58); Flavian defenders: marines of the Misenum fleet who had declared for Vespasian and a band of gladiators; the town fell to a night attack (Tacitus, Hist. 3.57, 3.76-77).
greek_note: The Misenum marines included many recruits from Egypt, Thrace and the Greek East; the Vitellian cohorts came from the Rhine army.
sources: Tacitus, Histories 3.57-58, 3.76-77
note: It fell just as the Flavians took Rome.

name: Vetera (second siege)
borderline: A blockade renewed after Vocula's relief of the first siege (Tacitus Hist. 4.36); it ended in surrender through starvation (March 70) and little fighting is recorded.
roman_force: The starving remnant of V Alaudae and XV Primigenia under Munius Lupercus, who surrendered in March 70 and were massacred on the march by Civilis' German allies (Tacitus, Hist. 4.59-60).
greek_note: Rhine legions.
sources: Tacitus, Histories 4.36, 4.57-60; livius.org, Batavian Revolt chronology; en.wikipedia Revolt of the Batavi
note: Lupercus was sent as a gift to the prophetess Veleda; the surrendered legions were ambushed and massacred a few miles from the camp. Distinct from the first siege (September-December 69) and from Cerialis' battle at Vetera (summer 70).

name: Moesia
place: Moesia, south of the lower Danube (site not given)
borderline: No conventional name; a distinct victory for which Otho gave Aponius triumphal honours, but the site is not recorded.
roman_force: Legio III Gallica, transferred from Syria to Moesia in 68, with the auxilia of Moesia; they caught some 9,000 Roxolani horsemen laden with plunder on thawing ground and destroyed them (Tacitus, Hist. 1.79).
greek_note: III Gallica had recruited for a century in the Greek- and Aramaic-speaking East (Tacitus notes its Syrian custom of saluting the rising sun, Hist. 3.24); the Moesian auxilia were mostly Thracian and Danubian.
sources: Tacitus, Histories 1.79
note: Roxolani (Sarmatians).

name: Placentia (siege)
roman_force: Othonian garrison: three praetorian cohorts, a vexillation of about 1,000 legionaries and a few cavalry under Spurinna; Vitellian: Caecina's army from Upper Germany, legio XXI Rapax with German, Gallic and other auxilia, whose assaults on the walls failed (Tacitus, Hist. 2.17-22).
greek_note: The praetorians were Italians and Caecina's army came from the Rhine.
sources: Tacitus, Histories 2.17-22; Plutarch, Otho 6

name: Jerusalem (siege)
commanders_b: Simon bar Giora, John of Gischala, Eleazar ben Simon
roman_force: Legions V Macedonica, X Fretensis, XII Fulminata and XV Apollinaris, 2,000 men of III Cyrenaica and XXII Deiotariana from Egypt and 3,000 from the Euphrates garrisons, 20 auxiliary cohorts and 8 alae, troops of the client kings Agrippa II, Antiochus IV of Commagene, Sohaemus of Emesa and Malchus II of Nabataea, and Syrian levies; at least 48,000 men (Josephus, BJ 5.40-46; Tacitus, Hist. 5.1).
greek_note: Josephus names auxiliaries from the Greek cities of Caesarea and Sebaste and the 'Macedonians' of Antiochus Epiphanes of Commagene, and the Syrian legions X and XII were recruited in the Greek and Aramaic East; V and XV came from the Balkans and Pannonia.
sources: Josephus, Jewish War 5-6; Tacitus, Histories 5.1, 5.11-13; Cassius Dio 66.4-7; en.wikipedia Siege of Jerusalem (70 CE)
