note: The Temple burned on 10 Ab (about 30 August); the upper city fell on 8 September.

name: Augusta Treverorum
place: The Roman camp and the Moselle bridge at Augusta Treverorum (Trier)
commanders_b: Gaius Julius Civilis, Julius Classicus, Julius Tutor
roman_force: Cerialis' legions in their camp by the city (livius.org names II Adiutrix, XIII Gemina and XXI Rapax), with legions I Germanica and XVI Gallica lately returned to their allegiance and auxiliary cavalry; the rebels broke into the camp at dawn and were driven out (Tacitus, Hist. 4.75-78).
greek_note: II Adiutrix had just been raised from the marines of the Ravenna fleet, recruited in Dalmatia, Pannonia, Thrace and the Greek East; the other legions were western.
sources: Tacitus, Histories 4.75-78; livius.org, Batavian Revolt (9) and chronology
note: Batavi and other Germans under Civilis, Treveri and Lingones under Classicus and Tutor. Livius calls it the decisive battle of the war; the day is uncertain.

name: Grinnes and Vada
place: Roman posts on the Waal and Rhine: Arenacum, Batavodurum, Grinnes and Vada (sites not identified)
commanders_b: Gaius Julius Civilis, Julius Classicus, Julius Verax
roman_force: X Gemina at Arenacum, II Adiutrix at Batavodurum and auxiliary cohorts and cavalry at Grinnes and Vada held off simultaneous attacks until Cerialis came up with cavalry and drove the enemy into the river; the loyal Batavian officer Briganticus fell (Tacitus, Hist. 5.19-21).
greek_note: II Adiutrix had eastern recruits from the Ravenna fleet; the rest were western legions and Gallic and German auxilia.
sources: Tacitus, Histories 5.19-21; livius.org, Batavian Revolt (9)
note: Civilis escaped by swimming the Rhine. The revolt ended in a settlement in September 70.

name: Rigodulum
place: Rigodulum (Riol), on the heights above the Moselle below Trier
roman_force: Cerialis with the legions and cavalry he had brought from Italy and Upper Germany (XXI Rapax among them), who stormed the Treveran position on the slopes above the river (Tacitus, Hist. 4.71).
greek_note: Western legions and Gallic and German auxilia.
sources: Tacitus, Histories 4.71; livius.org, Batavian Revolt (9)
note: Treveri. Cerialis entered Trier the next day.

name: Vetera
place: The flooded plain by the ruined camp of Vetera, near Xanten
roman_force: Cerialis with legions II Adiutrix, VI Victrix, XIV Gemina and XXI Rapax, auxiliary infantry and cavalry; on the second day a Batavian deserter led cavalry round the enemy flank (Tacitus, Hist. 5.14-18).
greek_note: II Adiutrix, raised from the Ravenna fleet, included eastern recruits; VI Victrix came from Spain and XIV Gemina from Britain.
sources: Tacitus, Histories 5.14-18; livius.org, Batavian Revolt (9)
note: Batavi, Cugerni, Bructeri, Tencteri and Chauci. Rain stopped the Roman pursuit.

name: Machaerus (siege)
place: The fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea
roman_force: Lucilius Bassus, legate of Judaea, with legio X Fretensis and the auxilia of the province; after siege works and sorties the garrison surrendered on terms when the young fighter Eleazar was captured (Josephus, BJ 7.163-209).
greek_note: X Fretensis had long recruited in Syria and the Greek East, and the auxilia of Judaea were raised in the Greek cities of Caesarea and Sebaste.
sources: Josephus, Jewish War 7.163-209; en.wikipedia Machaerus
note: en.wikipedia dates it 71; many give 72. Bassus had first taken Herodium.

name: Forest of Jardes
place: The forest of Jardes (site unknown, perhaps near the Jordan valley)
roman_force: Bassus with his cavalry and the infantry of X Fretensis surrounded the wood and killed some 3,000 fugitives from Jerusalem and Machaerus, losing twelve men (Josephus, BJ 7.210-215).
greek_note: The army of Judaea: X Fretensis and auxilia from Caesarea and Sebaste.
sources: Josephus, Jewish War 7.210-215
note: The site of Jardes is unknown; the country is a guess.

name: Commagene
place: Commagene, near Samosata on the Euphrates
commanders_b: Epiphanes and Callinicus, sons of Antiochus IV
borderline: No conventional name; Josephus describes a pitched battle.
roman_force: Caesennius Paetus, governor of Syria, with legio VI Ferrata, some auxiliary cohorts and alae, and the troops of the client kings Aristobulus of Chalcis and Sohaemus of Emesa (Josephus, BJ 7.219-243).
greek_note: VI Ferrata and the auxilia of Syria were recruited in the Greek- and Aramaic-speaking cities of Syria.
sources: Josephus, Jewish War 7.219-243
note: The battle lasted a whole day without decision; the princes then fled to Parthia and Commagene, a Hellenistic kingdom with a Greek court, was annexed.

name: Masada (siege)
roman_force: Legio X Fretensis (about 4,800 men) with auxiliary units and thousands of Jewish prisoners as labourers, in eight camps behind a circumvallation; a ramp and ram breached the wall and the defenders killed themselves (Josephus, BJ 7.252-406).
greek_note: The army of Judaea: X Fretensis, long recruited in the East, and auxilia raised in Caesarea, Sebaste and Syria.
sources: Josephus, Jewish War 7.252-406; en.wikipedia Siege of Masada
note: Sicarii. Traditionally dated to spring 73 (wall breached about 16 April); Campbell and Cotton argue for 73/74.

name: Mons Graupius
place: Mons Graupius, north-east Scotland (perhaps Bennachie, Aberdeenshire)
roman_force: 8,000 auxiliary infantry in the centre, with four Batavian and two Tungrian cohorts leading the attack, 3,000 cavalry on the wings and four alae in reserve; the legions (detachments of II Augusta, II Adiutrix, IX Hispana and XX) stood before the camp and did not fight; Britons served in the auxilia (Tacitus, Agricola 29, 35-37).
greek_note: The fighting was done by Germanic and Gallic auxilia; only II Adiutrix, raised from the Ravenna fleet in 69 and probably among the reserve, had a few eastern recruits.
sources: Tacitus, Agricola 29-38; en.wikipedia Battle of Mons Graupius
note: Caledonii and other northern tribes; Tacitus claims 10,000 enemy and 360 Roman dead. The site is disputed (Bennachie, Raedykes, the Gask Ridge and others).

name: Oppius Sabinus' defeat
place: Moesia, south of the lower Danube (site unknown)
commanders_b: Gaius Oppius Sabinus (governor of Moesia, killed)
borderline: An unnamed defeat whose site is unknown; the governor was killed.
roman_force: The army of Moesia under its governor; the units lost are not recorded (V Alaudae has been suggested, though many put its destruction with Fuscus).
greek_note: The Moesian army recruited in Italy, the Balkans and the Greek cities of the Black Sea coast; Greek speakers were few.
sources: Suetonius, Domitian 6; Jordanes, Getica 76; Eutropius 7.23; en.wikipedia Domitian's Dacian War
note: The Dacians crossed the frozen Danube; Domitian came to Moesia in person and the war of 86-88 followed.

name: First Tapae
place: Dacia, north of the Danube (site unknown; traditionally at Tapae, by the Iron Gates of Transylvania)
roman_force: Cornelius Fuscus crossed the Danube on a pontoon bridge with an army of five or six legions and praetorian cohorts; the army was destroyed and a standard lost, and V Alaudae is often thought to have perished here (Suetonius, Domitian 6; Cassius Dio 68.9.3; Jordanes, Getica 76-78).
greek_note: The Moesian army recruited along the Danube and in Thrace and Macedonia, with some men from the Greek cities of the Black Sea; most were Latin-speakers.
sources: Suetonius, Domitian 6; Cassius Dio 67.6, 68.9; Jordanes, Getica 76-78; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles; en.wikipedia Domitian's Dacian War
note: Dated 86 or 87 (the en.wikipedia list gives 87); the site and the name 'First Tapae' are modern conjectures. In the winter of 85/86 the governor Oppius Sabinus had already been defeated and killed in Moesia.

name: Second Tapae
place: Tapae, in the plain of Caransebes before the Iron Gates of Transylvania
roman_force: The reinforced army of Moesia under Tettius Julianus, with legions brought from Pannonia and the Rhine (among them IV Flavia Felix, I Adiutrix and II Adiutrix) and auxilia; Julianus had the soldiers write their names and units on their shields (Cassius Dio 67.10).
greek_note: A Danubian army recruited mainly in the Latin-speaking provinces and the Balkans.
sources: Cassius Dio 67.10; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles; en.wikipedia Second Battle of Tapae
note: Julianus did not march on Sarmizegetusa; peace followed in 89.

name: Saturninus' revolt
place: Upper Germany, on the Rhine (site unknown)
borderline: The battlefield has no name; a single decisive battle is attested.
roman_force: Loyalist: the army of Lower Germany under Lappius Maximus (the legions I Minervia, VI Victrix, X Gemina and XXII Primigenia were later honoured for loyalty), helped by the procurator of Raetia; rebel: Saturninus' two legions at Mogontiacum, XIV Gemina and XXI Rapax, whose Chattan allies were cut off by a sudden thaw of the Rhine (Suetonius, Domitian 6-7; Cassius Dio 67.11).
greek_note: Rhine legions recruited in Gaul, the Rhineland and northern Italy.
sources: Suetonius, Domitian 6-7; Cassius Dio 67.11; Plutarch, Aemilius Paullus 25

name: Third Tapae
place: Tapae, by the Iron Gates of Transylvania
roman_force: Trajan's invasion army: the legions of the Danube with vexillations from other provinces, praetorian cohorts and many auxilia, including the Germanic irregulars, Moorish horsemen under Lusius Quietus and eastern archers shown on Trajan's Column; Roman losses were so heavy that Trajan gave his own clothes for bandages (Cassius Dio 68.8).
greek_note: Eastern archer cohorts and recruits from Macedonia, Thrace and the Greek cities of Moesia served, but the army was mainly Danubian and western.
sources: Cassius Dio 68.8; Trajan's Column; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles; en.wikipedia Trajan's Dacian Wars

name: Nicopolis ad Istrum
place: Near the later city of Nicopolis ad Istrum, on the Yantra
borderline: Reconstructed from Trajan's Column and Jordanes (Trajan founded Nicopolis after defeating the Sarmatians); often treated as a phase of the Adamclisi campaign.
roman_force: Trajan with the army of Lower Moesia and troops brought down the Danube by ship, legionaries, auxiliary infantry and cavalry; Trajan's Column shows a night battle against Dacians and Roxolani cataphracts.
greek_note: Lower Moesia's army recruited along the Danube and in Thrace, near the Greek cities of the Black Sea coast.
sources: Trajan's Column; Jordanes, Getica 101; en.wikipedia Trajan's Dacian Wars; en.wikipedia Battle of Adamclisi
note: en.wikipedia's Adamclisi article calls the night battle near Nicopolis indecisive; its Dacian Wars article calls it a Roman victory.

name: Adamclisi
roman_force: Trajan with the legions of Lower Moesia (such as I Italica, V Macedonica and XI Claudia) and auxilia, reinforced from the main army; losses were heavy on both sides, and the funerary altar at Adamclisi, listing some 3,800 Roman dead, may belong to this battle.
greek_note: Lower Moesia's legions recruited along the Danube and in Thrace; the Greek cities of the Pontic coast (Tomis, Callatis, Histria) lay close by.
sources: Trajan's Column; Tropaeum Traiani; en.wikipedia Battle of Adamclisi; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles
note: Dacians with Roxolani (Sarmatians) and Bastarnae. The Tropaeum Traiani (109) commemorates the victory; the altar may instead commemorate Fuscus' or Oppius Sabinus' dead.

name: Sarmizegetusa (siege)
place: Sarmizegetusa Regia, the Dacian capital in the Orastie Mountains
roman_force: Trajan's army converging on the capital, with legions II Adiutrix and IV Flavia Felix and a vexillation of VI Ferrata attested at the site, many auxilia and Moorish and eastern units; the Romans cut the water pipes, stormed the city and razed it, and Decebalus killed himself.
greek_note: The vexillation of VI Ferrata came from the Judaean-Syrian army, recruited in the East; the main body was Danubian.
sources: Cassius Dio 68.14; Trajan's Column; en.wikipedia Battle of Sarmisegetusa

name: Maximus' defeat
borderline: An unnamed defeat known from one sentence of Dio.
roman_force: A Roman force of Trajan's eastern army under the general Maximus; its size and units are not recorded (Cassius Dio 68.30.1).
greek_note: Trajan's eastern army drew many recruits from Syria and Asia Minor.
sources: Cassius Dio 68.30.1; en.wikipedia Trajan's Parthian campaign
note: Part of the general revolt of the conquered lands in 116; Lusius Quietus then retook Nisibis and sacked Edessa.

name: Ctesiphon
borderline: The Parthian capital fell with little recorded fighting.
roman_force: Trajan's eastern expeditionary army: the legions of Syria, Cappadocia, Judaea, Arabia and Egypt (by vexillations) with Danubian reinforcements and a river fleet brought down the Euphrates and hauled across to the Tigris; Trajan was hailed imperator and took the title Parthicus (Cassius Dio 68.28).
greek_note: The eastern legions and auxilia were recruited mainly in Syria, Asia Minor and Egypt; Danubian vexillations and Moorish cavalry added non-Greek elements.
sources: Cassius Dio 68.28; en.wikipedia Trajan's Parthian campaign

name: Edessa (siege)
borderline: Little detail of the siege survives.
roman_force: Lusius Quietus with his Moorish cavalry and detachments of the eastern army, sent to crush the revolt of northern Mesopotamia; he recovered Nisibis and besieged, sacked and burned Edessa (Cassius Dio 68.30).
greek_note: Eastern legionary detachments recruited in Syria and Asia Minor alongside Quietus' Moors.
sources: Cassius Dio 68.30; en.wikipedia Trajan's Parthian campaign; en.wikipedia Kitos War
note: Osrhoene under Abgar VII had submitted in 115 and rose in 116; Eusebius links the Mesopotamian revolt with the Jews.

name: Seleucia (siege)
commanders_a: Erucius Clarus, Tiberius Julius Alexander Julianus
borderline: Little detail of the fighting survives.
roman_force: Detachments of Trajan's eastern army under the legates Erucius Clarus and Julius Alexander, who recaptured the rebel city and burned it (Cassius Dio 68.30).
greek_note: Eastern legionary and auxiliary detachments recruited in Syria and Asia Minor.
sources: Cassius Dio 68.30; en.wikipedia Trajan's Parthian campaign
note: Seleucia, a Macedonian foundation with a Greek council and a mixed Greek, Syrian, Babylonian and Jewish population, joined the Mesopotamian revolt of 116.

name: Hatra (siege)
place: Hatra, in the desert west of the Tigris
roman_force: Trajan's eastern field army; he sent cavalry against the wall, which was thrown back, and was nearly hit himself; heat, lack of water and swarms of flies forced the withdrawal (Cassius Dio 68.31).
greek_note: The eastern legions and auxilia were recruited mainly in Syria and Asia Minor.
sources: Cassius Dio 68.31; en.wikipedia Siege of Hatra (116-117); en.wikipedia Trajan's Parthian campaign
note: Hatra, an Arab-ruled Aramaic-speaking city allied to Parthia.

name: Lydda (siege)
borderline: Known mainly from rabbinic tradition; date, commander and course are uncertain.
roman_force: Probably the army of Judaea under Lusius Quietus, governor after his Mesopotamian campaign: X Fretensis with auxilia and perhaps his Moorish horsemen; the sources say nothing of its composition.
greek_note: Inferred from the usual recruitment of the army of Judaea in Syria and the Greek cities of the coast.
sources: Rabbinic tradition (the 'slain of Lydda'); Syriac chronicles; en.wikipedia Kitos War
note: The only named siege of the Kitos War; the fighting in Cyrenaica, Egypt and Cyprus has no named battles.

name: Tel Shalem
place: Tel Shalem, in the Beth Shean valley
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
borderline: Hypothetical battle inferred from the Tel Shalem arch.
roman_force: Unknown; a vexillation of VI Ferrata had a camp at Tel Shalem, where a triumphal arch for Hadrian was set up about 135-136.
greek_note: By Hadrian's time the legions of Judaea and Syria were recruited mainly in the East.
sources: Tel Shalem arch inscription; W. Eck; en.wikipedia Bar Kokhba revolt
note: Werner Eck reads the arch as commemorating a victory over rebels in the north; Menahem Mor and others doubt that any battle was fought there.

name: Betar (siege)
commanders_a: Sextus Julius Severus (Hadrian in overall command)
roman_force: The army of the war under Julius Severus: X Fretensis and VI Ferrata with detachments of the eastern legions (III Cyrenaica, III Gallica and others), auxilia and siege artillery; inscriptions at Betar name vexillations of V Macedonica and XI Claudia from Lower Moesia. A siege wall and two camps cut the town off before it was stormed.
greek_note: By Hadrian's time the eastern legions were recruited mainly in Syria, Asia Minor and Egypt; the Moesian vexillations were Latin- and Thracian-speaking.
sources: Cassius Dio 69.12-14; Eusebius, Church History 4.6; en.wikipedia Bar Kokhba revolt
note: The revolt's last stronghold; mopping-up in the Judaean Desert caves went on into 136.

name: Elegeia
place: Elegeia, beyond the Cappadocian frontier near the headwaters of the Euphrates (probably Ilica, near Erzurum)
roman_force: The governor of Cappadocia with one legion (perhaps IX Hispana or XXII Deiotariana; disputed) and auxilia; it was surrounded and destroyed in three days and Severianus killed himself (Cassius Dio 71.2.1; Lucian, How to Write History 21, 25; Alexander 27).
greek_note: The Cappadocian army was recruited mainly in Asia Minor, but the identity of the destroyed legion is unknown.
sources: Cassius Dio 71.2.1; Lucian, How to Write History; en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 161-166
note: About 5,000-6,000 Romans are thought to have died.

name: Artaxata
place: Artaxata, the Armenian capital on the Araxes
roman_force: Statius Priscus with the reinforcing legions I Minervia (from Bonn) and V Macedonica (from Troesmis), the Cappadocian army and auxilia; the Armenian capital was taken and destroyed (HA Marcus 9; HA Verus 7).
greek_note: Two legions from the Rhine and lower Danube fought beside the Cappadocian army, which was recruited mainly in Asia Minor.
sources: Historia Augusta, Marcus 9 and Verus 7; Fronto; en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 161-166
note: The Parthian nominee Pacorus held Armenia; a new capital, Kaine Polis, replaced Artaxata in 164.

name: Sura
place: Sura, on the right bank of the Euphrates
borderline: Known only from a passing mention in Lucian.
roman_force: Not recorded; presumably detachments of the Syrian army (legions such as III Gallica and IV Scythica) with auxilia.
greek_note: The Syrian army was recruited mainly in Syria, among Greek- and Aramaic-speakers.
sources: Lucian, How to Write History; en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 161-166
note: It shows the Parthians still on the Roman bank of the Euphrates in 163; probably a Roman success in the counter-offensive.

name: Ctesiphon
place: Ctesiphon and Seleucia, on the Tigris
borderline: Little recorded fighting.
roman_force: Avidius Cassius with III Gallica and the Syrian army reinforced from the Danube; Seleucia opened its gates and was sacked, and the royal palace at Ctesiphon was burned (Cassius Dio 71.2.3; HA Verus 8).
greek_note: The Syrian army, recruited mainly in the East, with Danubian vexillations.
sources: Cassius Dio 71.2.3; Historia Augusta, Verus 8; en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 161-166
note: Plague broke out in the army on its return; the sack of Seleucia (which surrendered) is not a separate entry.

name: Dura-Europos
roman_force: Avidius Cassius with the Syrian army marching down the Euphrates, III Gallica and other legions with vexillations and auxilia; Lucian mocks a historian who claimed 70,236 Parthian dead against two Roman.
greek_note: The Syrian legions and auxilia were recruited in Syria, largely among Greek- and Aramaic-speakers.
sources: Lucian, How to Write History 20, 28; en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 161-166
note: Lucian's 'great battle of Europus'; the city passed to Rome.

name: Nisibis (siege)
borderline: Few details survive.
roman_force: Detachments of the eastern army and the reinforcing legions advancing into northern Mesopotamia (Martius Verus with V Macedonica operated in the region).
greek_note: Eastern legions recruited in Syria and Asia Minor, with the Moesian V Macedonica.
sources: Lucian, How to Write History; en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 161-166
note: The retreating Parthian army was besieged and the city taken.

name: Defeat of the Langobardi and Obii
place: Pannonia, south of the Danube (site not recorded)
borderline: Unnamed; the site is not recorded.
roman_force: Cavalry under Macrinius Vindex (the ala I Ulpia contariorum) and infantry under Candidus (a detachment of I Adiutrix, by the inscriptions) routed some 6,000 invaders (Cassius Dio 72.1a).
greek_note: The Pannonian frontier army, recruited locally.
sources: Cassius Dio 72.1a (fragment preserved by Petrus Patricius); en.wikipedia Marcomannic Wars
note: Langobardi and Obii; afterwards Ballomar and ten other tribes sent envoys to the governor Iallius Bassus.

name: Carnuntum
roman_force: A Roman army of the Pannonian frontier, perhaps with the newly raised legions II and III Italica; Lucian reports a disaster of about this time in which nearly 20,000 Romans died (Alexander 48).
greek_note: The Pannonian army was recruited along the middle Danube and in Italy; few Greek-speakers served.
sources: Lucian, Alexander 48; Ammianus 29.6.1; en.wikipedia Battle of Carnuntum; en.wikipedia Marcomannic Wars
note: Marcomanni and Quadi. The battle's place and date are reconstructed from the course of the invasion that followed.

name: Aquileia (siege)
commanders_a: Tiberius Claudius Pompeianus, Publius Helvius Pertinax (relief); Titus Furius Victorinus (killed)
roman_force: The defenders of Aquileia, the troops of the praetentura Italiae et Alpium (the new legions II and III Italica) and praetorians under the prefect Furius Victorinus, who fell; the city was relieved by Pompeianus and Pertinax (Ammianus 29.6.1; HA Marcus 14).
greek_note: II and III Italica and the praetorians were raised in Italy.
sources: Ammianus 29.6.1; Historia Augusta, Marcus 14; en.wikipedia Marcomannic Wars
note: Marcomanni and Quadi; Opitergium (Oderzo) was destroyed. McLynn dates the invasion to 167.

name: Elatea
borderline: A civic militia of a provincial city, not the imperial army.
roman_force: The citizen levy of Elatea, a city of the province of Achaea, led by the Olympic victor Mnesibulus, who killed many of the raiders and fell in the fight (Pausanias 10.34.5).
greek_note: A Greek civic militia of Phocis.
sources: Pausanias 10.34.5; en.wikipedia Marcomannic Wars (the Costoboci raid)
note: The Costoboci, a Carpathian people akin to the Dacians, raided Thrace, Macedonia and Greece as far as Eleusis.

name: Rain Miracle
place: In the territory of the Quadi, north of the middle Danube (site unknown)
commanders_a: Marcus Aurelius (perhaps Pertinax in the field)
roman_force: A Roman army surrounded by the Quadi and dying of thirst until a sudden storm refreshed it and routed the enemy; Christian writers (Apollinaris, Tertullian, Eusebius) name legio XII Fulminata from Melitene in Cappadocia (Cassius Dio 71.8-10).
greek_note: If the tradition is right, a vexillation of the eastern XII Fulminata, recruited in Cappadocia, fought; the rest were Danubian troops.
sources: Cassius Dio 71.8-10; Column of Marcus Aurelius; Eusebius, Church History 5.5; en.wikipedia Marcomannic Wars
note: Quadi. Dio credits an Egyptian magician, Christians their prayers.

name: Frozen Danube
place: On the frozen middle Danube (site unknown)
roman_force: Roman legionaries who followed the Iazyges onto the ice, stood on their shields to keep their footing and dragged the riders from their horses (Cassius Dio 71.7).
greek_note: Pannonian and Moesian legions recruited mainly in the Danube provinces.
sources: Cassius Dio 71.7
note: Iazyges (Sarmatians).

name: Singilia Barba (siege)
commanders_a: Gaius Vallius Maximianus (procurator of Mauretania Tingitana)
borderline: Known only from an honorific inscription.
roman_force: Auxiliary troops of Mauretania Tingitana brought across the straits by the procurator Vallius Maximianus, who broke a long siege of the town by the Mauri (CIL II 2015).
greek_note: The auxilia of Tingitana were raised in the West and in Africa.
sources: CIL II 2015; Historia Augusta, Marcus 21
note: Moorish raiders crossed into Baetica in 171/172 and again about 177; Italica was also attacked.

name: Laugaricio
borderline: The Trencin inscription records the winter quarters of the army and a dedication to the emperors' victory; the battle itself is inferred.
roman_force: A detachment of 855 men of legio II Adiutrix under Valerius Maximianus, part of the army of occupation in Quadic territory (Trencin inscription).
greek_note: II Adiutrix was by then recruited in Pannonia.
sources: Trencin rock inscription (CIL III 13439); en.wikipedia List of Roman battles; en.wikipedia Marcomannic Wars
note: Quadi.

name: Paternus' victory
place: Beyond the Danube, in the lands of the Quadi or Marcomanni (site unknown)
borderline: Unnamed (listed without a name in en.wikipedia's List of Roman battles); site unknown.
roman_force: The imperial expeditionary army of the second Marcomannic war under the praetorian prefect Paternus, which fought for a whole day and cut the enemy down (Cassius Dio 71.33.3-4).
greek_note: Danubian legions and praetorians, with eastern auxiliary units in small numbers.
sources: Cassius Dio 71.33.3-4; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles
note: Dio calls the enemy 'Scythians'; probably Quadi or Marcomanni.

name: Byzantium (siege)
war: Severan civil wars (Severus against Pescennius Niger)
commanders_a: Lucius Marius Maximus (commander of the Moesian army at the siege)
commanders_b: the citizens of Byzantium and Niger's partisans (no commander named by Dio)
roman_force: Besiegers: the army of Moesia (exercitus Mysiacus) under Marius Maximus, with a fleet; defenders: the citizens of Byzantium and Niger's troops, with a fleet of some 500 ships and the engines of the engineer Priscus (Dio 75.10-12).
greek_note: The defenders were the Greek citizens of Byzantium with Niger's eastern troops; the besiegers were the Latin- and Thracian-speaking Moesian army.
sources: Cassius Dio 75.10-14; Herodian 3.6.9; ILS 2935 (Marius Maximus); en.wikipedia Battle of Issus (194)
note: Dio says the siege lasted three years; the city fell after Niger's death, probably late 195. There was naval fighting in the Bosporus as well as assaults on the walls.

name: Cyzicus
war: Severan civil wars (Severus against Pescennius Niger)
roman_force: Severans: Danubian (Illyrian) legionary vexillations sent ahead into Asia; Nigrians: an army of the eastern provinces under Asellius Aemilianus.
greek_note: Niger's army drew on Syria and Asia Minor, where Greek was the common language; Severus' advance guard came from the Danube.
sources: Cassius Dio 75.6.4; Herodian 3.2.2; en.wikipedia Battle of Cyzicus (193)
note: Dio names only 'Severus' generals'; the attribution to Candidus is modern. Aemilianus was killed after the defeat.

name: Nicaea
war: Severan civil wars (Severus against Pescennius Niger)
place: in the narrows between Nicaea and Cius, Bithynia
roman_force: Severans: the Danubian (Illyrian) advance army under Candidus; Nigrians: the eastern legions and auxilia of Syria and Asia Minor led by Niger.
greek_note: Niger's army was raised in Syria and Asia Minor; the Severan army was Danubian.
sources: Cassius Dio 75.6.4-6; en.wikipedia Battle of Nicaea (193)
note: Dio describes a hard-fought battle in the defiles between Nicaea and Cius; Niger then fell back on the Taurus passes.

name: Issus
war: Severan civil wars (Severus against Pescennius Niger)
place: near Issus, at the head of the Gulf of Issus
roman_force: Severans: the Danubian (Illyrian) legions and their cavalry under Anullinus; Nigrians: the legions of Syria and the East with eastern auxilia and levies raised at Antioch (Herodian 3.1, 3.4). Dio gives 20,000 dead on Niger's side.
greek_note: Niger's army was raised in Syria and Asia Minor, with Antiochene volunteers; Severus' Danubian army was Latin- and Illyrian-speaking.
sources: Cassius Dio 75.7-8; Herodian 3.4; en.wikipedia Battle of Issus (194)
note: No month in the sources; modern accounts put it in spring (Wikipedia: May) 194. Niger fled from Antioch towards the Euphrates and was caught and killed.

name: Lugdunum
war: Severan civil wars (Severus against Clodius Albinus)
commanders_b: Decimus Clodius Albinus (suicide), Lucius Novius Rufus (killed)
roman_force: Severus: the legions of Pannonia, Moesia, Dacia and the Danube with Rhine troops, strong in cavalry; Albinus: the three British legions (II Augusta, VI Victrix, XX Valeria Victrix) and VII Gemina from Spain under Novius Rufus. Dio's figure of 150,000 is read by some as each side, by others as the total.
greek_note: Both armies were raised in the West and on the Danube; Greek speakers were few.
sources: Cassius Dio 76.6-7; Herodian 3.7; Historia Augusta, Severus 11; en.wikipedia Battle of Lugdunum
note: Fought over two days; Laetus' cavalry, held back until late in the battle, decided it (Dio). Albinus killed himself in Lugdunum.

name: Tinurtium
war: Severan civil wars (Severus against Clodius Albinus)
borderline: A preliminary engagement known from a brief notice; the result was not decisive.
roman_force: As at Lugdunum: Severus' Danubian and Rhine legions against Albinus' British legions and troops from Spain.
greek_note: Both armies were raised in the western and Danubian provinces; Greek speakers were very few.
sources: Historia Augusta, Severus 11.1; en.wikipedia Battle of Lugdunum
note: Severus had the better of the fighting but did not win the decisive victory he needed.

name: Nisibis (siege)
borderline: Known only from a brief notice in Dio; no Wikipedia battle article.
roman_force: The Roman garrison of the new province of Mesopotamia under Julius Laetus; the sources name no units, and the normal eastern garrison of legions and auxilia is assumed.
greek_note: The garrisons of Syria and Mesopotamia were recruited largely in the Greek- and Aramaic-speaking East.
sources: Cassius Dio 76.9.1
note: The Parthians withdrew when Severus arrived with his army.

name: Ctesiphon
roman_force: Severus' expeditionary army: the new legions I, II and III Parthica, the praetorian guard, Danubian and eastern legions with auxilia, carried down the Euphrates by a river fleet (Dio 76.9).
greek_note: The eastern legions, recruited in Syria and Asia Minor, marched with Severus' Danubian army and guard.
sources: Cassius Dio 76.9; Herodian 3.9.9-12; Historia Augusta, Severus 16; en.wikipedia Battle of Ctesiphon (198)
note: Severus took the title Parthicus Maximus on 28 January 198; the city was sacked and many inhabitants taken captive.

name: Hatra (siege)
roman_force: Severus' eastern expeditionary army with siege engines; Dio says the European troops refused to make the last assault and the Syrian troops sent in their place were cut down (Dio 76.12).
greek_note: Dio names Syrian troops beside the European ones; the Syrian legions were Greek- and Aramaic-speaking.
sources: Cassius Dio 76.10-12; Herodian 3.9.3-7; en.wikipedia Siege of Hatra (197-198)
note: Dio describes two sieges (198 and 199); Wikipedia dates the siege 197-198 and Herodian puts it before Ctesiphon. Hatra was an Arab-ruled, Aramaic-speaking kingdom allied to Parthia.

name: Main
borderline: Named only by Aurelius Victor ('prope Moenum amnem'); no Wikipedia battle article.
roman_force: Caracalla's field army entering from Raetia: the praetorian guard, his German bodyguard and vexillations of the Rhine and Danube legions (the sources name no units; the usual composition is assumed).
greek_note: The Rhine and Danube armies were recruited in the western and Danubian provinces.
sources: Aurelius Victor 21.2; Cassius Dio 78.13-14; en.wikipedia Caracalla
note: Against the Alamanni (their first mention); Dio also names the Cenni. The victory was celebrated at Rome in October 213.

name: Nisibis
roman_force: The eastern expeditionary army assembled by Caracalla: legions in the centre (among them II Parthica and the Syrian legions), cavalry and light troops including Moorish javelin-men on the wings (Herodian 4.15).
greek_note: The army combined Italian and Danubian units (II Parthica, the guard) with the eastern legions raised in Syria.
sources: Herodian 4.15; Cassius Dio 79.26-27; en.wikipedia Battle of Nisibis (217)
note: Three days of fighting with heavy losses on both sides; some treat it as indecisive (Wikipedia's List of Roman battles calls it a stalemate). Macrinus then bought peace.

name: Raphanea
place: the camp of legio III Gallica at Raphanea
commanders_b: Ulpius Julianus (praetorian prefect, killed by his own men)
borderline: An assault on a legionary camp that ended when the attackers deserted; not usually named as a battle.
roman_force: Defenders: legio III Gallica in its fortress; attackers: a force under the prefect Ulpius Julianus, who assaulted the walls, then killed their officers and went over (Cassius Dio 79.32; Herodian 5.4.3-4).
greek_note: III Gallica was by then recruited in Syria, where Greek and Aramaic were spoken.
sources: Cassius Dio 79.32; Herodian 5.4; en.wikipedia Battle of Antioch (218)
note: Elagabalus had been proclaimed in the camp on 16 May 218; the decisive battle followed near Antioch on 8 June.

name: Antioch
place: outside a village some 180 stades from Antioch (perhaps Immae)
roman_force: Elagabalus: legio III Gallica from Raphanea with deserters, probably including legio II Parthica; Macrinus: the praetorian guard (in lighter equipment) and other troops (Dio 79.37).
greek_note: III Gallica had long been recruited in Syria; the guard had been Danubian since Severus.
sources: Cassius Dio 79.37-38; Herodian 5.4; en.wikipedia Battle of Antioch (218)
note: Herodian places the battle near the border of Syria Phoenice; Downey proposes two engagements. Macrinus fled and was caught and killed.

name: Nisibis (siege)
war: First Mesopotamian campaign of Ardashir I
borderline: A failed siege known from brief notices; the fighting is not described.
roman_force: The garrison of Nisibis, chief city of Roman Mesopotamia; no details survive.
greek_note: The Mesopotamian garrisons were recruited in Syria and Mesopotamia.
sources: Zonaras 12.15; George Syncellus; Herodian 6.2; en.wikipedia Sasanian campaign of Severus Alexander
note: Ardashir then raided Syria and Cappadocia, which brought on Severus Alexander's campaign.

name: Severus Alexander's southern column
place: lower Mesopotamia, on the march towards Ctesiphon (site unknown)
borderline: Unnamed; known only from Herodian, whose account many modern historians doubt.
roman_force: The southern of Alexander's three columns, of eastern legions and auxilia with Danubian vexillations, advancing down the Euphrates; Herodian says it was surrounded and shot down by Ardashir's archers and cavalry (Herodian 6.5.9-10).
greek_note: An eastern field army recruited largely in Syria and Asia Minor, with western vexillations.
sources: Herodian 6.5-6; Historia Augusta, Severus Alexander 55-57; en.wikipedia Sasanian campaign of Severus Alexander
note: The Historia Augusta claims instead a great Roman victory over Ardashir; Herodian also reports heavy Persian losses, and the war ended without a change of frontier.

name: Harzhorn
place: the Harzhorn hill, between Kalefeld and Bad Gandersheim, Lower Saxony
borderline: Known from archaeology only; the link with Maximinus' campaign and the date are inferred from coins.
roman_force: Legionaries with artillery (scorpio and cheiroballistra bolts) and auxiliaries (about 1,500 Roman finds). Herodian (7.2.1) says Maximinus' army included Moorish javelin-men and Osroenian and Armenian archers.
greek_note: A Rhine-Danube army with eastern archers who spoke Aramaic or Armenian rather than Greek.
sources: Excavations since 2008; Herodian 7.2; en.wikipedia Battle at the Harzhorn
note: Germanic tribe unknown. The Roman army seems to have forced a blocked pass on its way back south.

name: Nisibis (siege)
war: Second Mesopotamian campaign of Ardashir I
borderline: A capture known from brief notices; whether there was a siege with fighting is not recorded.
roman_force: The garrison of Nisibis; no details survive.
greek_note: The Mesopotamian garrisons were recruited in Syria and Mesopotamia.
sources: George Syncellus p. 681; Zonaras 12.18; en.wikipedia Second Mesopotamian campaign of Ardashir I
note: Gordian III's army retook the city in 243.

name: Carrhae (siege)
war: Second Mesopotamian campaign of Ardashir I
borderline: A capture known from brief notices; whether there was a siege with fighting is not recorded.
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Carrhae; no details survive.
greek_note: Carrhae was a Greek-founded colonia in an Aramaic-speaking land.
sources: George Syncellus p. 681; Zonaras 12.18; en.wikipedia Second Mesopotamian campaign of Ardashir I
note: Retaken under Gordian III before Resaena.

name: Carthage
roman_force: Capelianus: legio III Augusta and the auxiliary troops of Numidia, veterans of the Moorish frontier; the Gordians: a large untrained militia of Carthage and the province (Herodian 7.9).
greek_note: Both sides were raised in Africa; the militia spoke Latin and Punic.
sources: Herodian 7.9; Historia Augusta, Gordians 15-16; en.wikipedia Battle of Carthage (238)
note: Gordian I hanged himself on hearing of his son's death. The month depends on the disputed chronology of 238 (January to April).

name: Aquileia (siege)
roman_force: Maximinus: the Pannonian and Rhine army, legio II Parthica and the praetorians, with German auxiliaries (Herodian 8.1); defenders: the citizens of Aquileia under the senatorial commissioners.
greek_note: Danubian besiegers and Latin-speaking townsmen; at most a few Greek-speaking traders in the city.
sources: Herodian 8.2-5; Historia Augusta, Maximini duo 21-23; en.wikipedia Siege of Aquileia (238)
note: Maximinus and his son were killed by soldiers of II Parthica during a lull in the siege (perhaps May 238), and the siege ended.

name: Hatra (siege)
war: Roman-Sasanian wars (Ardashir I and Shapur I)
borderline: The principal defender was the allied kingdom of Hatra; the Roman garrison is probable, not certain.
roman_force: The army of the kingdom of Hatra, a Roman ally, with a probable small Roman garrison (Latin dedications of 235; a Hatra inscription names cohors IX Maurorum Gordiana).
greek_note: The defenders were Aramaic-speaking Hatrenes with, probably, a garrison of Moorish auxiliaries.
sources: Cologne Mani Codex; al-Tabari; Hatra inscriptions; en.wikipedia Fall of Hatra
note: The siege lasted one or two years; the city was destroyed and abandoned. Its fall probably provoked Gordian III's Persian war.

name: Resaena
roman_force: Gordian's expeditionary army: the praetorian guard, vexillations of the Danubian and Rhine legions, the eastern legions and, by Shapur's account, Gothic and German contingents.
greek_note: The eastern legions, recruited in Syria and Asia Minor, formed a large part of the army.
sources: Ammianus Marcellinus 23.5.17; Historia Augusta, Gordians 26-27; en.wikipedia Battle of Resaena
note: Carrhae and Nisibis were retaken. The site lies on the Turkish-Syrian border (Ceylanpinar / Ras al-Ayn).

name: Misiche
commanders_b: Gordian III (killed or died soon after), Philip the Arab, Gaius Julius Priscus
roman_force: By Shapur's inscription, a force raised 'from the Roman Empire and the lands of the Goths and Germans': the guard, Danubian and Rhine vexillations, eastern legions and Gothic and German allies.
greek_note: As at Resaena, the eastern legions of Syria and Asia Minor were a large part of the army.
sources: Shapur's inscription (SKZ); Zonaras 12.17; en.wikipedia Battle of Misiche
note: Roman sources never admit the defeat and make Gordian's death a plot by Philip or an accident; whether he died in the battle, and the exact site, are disputed.

name: Marcianopolis (siege)
borderline: A siege ended by a payment; known chiefly from Jordanes.
roman_force: The citizens and local garrison of Marcianopolis defending their walls; no field army was present.
greek_note: Marcianopolis was a Greek-speaking city of Moesia Inferior with Thracian and Latin-speaking neighbours.
sources: Jordanes, Getica 92; en.wikipedia Gothic War (248-253)
note: After a long siege the townsmen paid the Goths to withdraw.

name: Verona
war: Civil war of 249 (Decius against Philip the Arab)
roman_force: Decius: the Danubian (Pannonian and Moesian) legions that had proclaimed him; Philip: the forces of Italy, including the praetorian guard, said to have been weaker in quality.
greek_note: Both armies were Danubian or Italian.
sources: Aurelius Victor 28.10; Epitome de Caesaribus 28.2; Zosimus 1.22; Zonaras 12.19; en.wikipedia Battle of Verona (249)
note: The Latin sources put Philip's death at Verona; some modern scholars prefer Beroea in Macedonia. Philip's son was killed at Rome.

name: Novae
borderline: A repulse of Cniva's attack known from a brief notice in Jordanes.
roman_force: The Danube frontier troops under Trebonianus Gallus, based on the legionary fortress of Novae (legio I Italica).
greek_note: The lower Danube garrison was recruited locally in Moesia and Thrace.
sources: Jordanes, Getica 101-102; en.wikipedia Gothic War (248-253); en.wikipedia Battle of Nicopolis ad Istrum
note: Cniva then moved on to Nicopolis ad Istrum.

name: Nicopolis ad Istrum
roman_force: Decius' field army: Danubian legions with vexillations and auxiliaries (no units named).
greek_note: A Danubian army, recruited in Pannonia, Moesia and Thrace.
sources: Jordanes, Getica 102; en.wikipedia Battle of Nicopolis ad Istrum
note: A surprise attack on the Goths near the city; not decisive, as Cniva withdrew in good order over the Haemus.

name: Beroe
roman_force: Decius' Danubian field army, surprised in camp.
greek_note: A Danubian army, recruited in Pannonia, Moesia and Thrace.
sources: Jordanes, Getica 102-103; en.wikipedia Battle of Beroe
note: Heavy Roman losses; Decius withdrew over the Balkan range into Moesia and Philippopolis was left to its fate.

name: Philippopolis (siege)
commanders_b: Titus Julius Priscus, governor of Thrace
roman_force: The citizens of Philippopolis and the provincial troops of Thrace under the governor Priscus.
greek_note: Philippopolis was the Greek-speaking metropolis of Thrace, and its citizens bore the defence.
sources: Jordanes, Getica 103; Dexippus, Scythica (fragments); Ammianus Marcellinus 31.5.17; en.wikipedia Siege of Philippopolis (250)
note: The city fell by treachery after a long siege; Ammianus reports 100,000 dead, surely exaggerated. Priscus then claimed the throne with Gothic backing. Wikipedia's List of Roman battles calls it the Battle of Philippopolis.

name: Abritus
place: near Abritus (Razgrad), probably in the Beli Lom valley near Dryanovets
roman_force: Decius' field army, probably built on three Danubian legions (XIV Gemina, IV Flavia Felix and VII Claudia) with vexillations and auxiliaries; Dexippus gives 80,000 for his reorganized army.
greek_note: The legions came from Pannonia and Moesia Superior, Latin- and Illyrian-speaking regions.
sources: Dexippus; Zosimus 1.23; Jordanes, Getica 103; Aurelius Victor 29; en.wikipedia Battle of Abritus
note: Fought in marshy ground; Decius was the first emperor killed in battle by a foreign enemy.

name: Interamna
war: Civil war of 253 (Aemilian against Trebonianus Gallus)
commanders_b: Trebonianus Gallus, Volusianus (both killed by their own troops)
borderline: The sources disagree whether a battle was fought: by some accounts Gallus' troops killed him after an initial defeat, by others they went over without fighting.
roman_force: Aemilian: the Moesian army that had just beaten the Goths; Gallus: the troops in Italy, including the praetorian guard.
greek_note: A Danubian army against the Italian garrison.
sources: Aurelius Victor 31; Eutropius 9.5; Zosimus 1.28; Zonaras 12.21; en.wikipedia Trebonianus Gallus
note: Aemilian was himself killed by his troops near Spoletium a few months later, as Valerian approached.

name: Barbalissos
roman_force: By Shapur's inscription, a Roman force of 60,000: the field army of Syria and the East, legionaries, archers and cavalry.
greek_note: The army of Syria was recruited in Syria and the neighbouring eastern provinces.
sources: Shapur's inscription (SKZ); en.wikipedia Battle of Barbalissos; en.wikipedia Roman-Persian Wars
note: The Roman army was destroyed and Antioch was taken soon after. Wikipedia's battle article gives 252.

name: Emesa
borderline: Known from Malalas' anecdotal account; the identification of the priest with the usurper Uranius Antoninus is uncertain.
roman_force: Local forces of Emesa raised by its priest; Malalas speaks of a band of slingers.
greek_note: Emesa was a bilingual Greek- and Aramaic-speaking city.
sources: John Malalas 12.296; coins of Uranius Antoninus; en.wikipedia Crisis of the Third Century
note: Uranius Antoninus was a local usurper; counted here as Roman against the Sasanians. Some date it 253/254.

name: Thessalonica (siege)
borderline: Known from a brief notice in Zosimus; the date (254, or 256-257 in some accounts) is uncertain.
roman_force: The citizens of Thessalonica manning the walls; Zosimus adds that the Greeks guarded Thermopylae and the Athenians rebuilt their wall.
greek_note: The defenders were the Greek citizens of Thessalonica.
sources: Zosimus 1.29.2; en.wikipedia Gothic War (248-253)
note: Zosimus' 'Scythians', probably Goths and their allies, failed to take the city.

name: Pityus (siege)
war: Gothic invasions of the 250s (Black Sea raids)
place: Pityus (Pitsunda), on the eastern Black Sea coast
borderline: Known only from Zosimus; no battle article. The raiders took Pityus in a second raid after Successianus had left.
roman_force: The garrison of the fortress of Pityus under Successianus; the forts of this coast were held by auxiliary units of the army of Cappadocia.
greek_note: The units of the Pontic forts in this period are not known.
sources: Zosimus 1.32
note: The raiders' identity (Zosimus' Boranoi, part of the 'Scythian' raids by sea) is uncertain; the date is 254 or 255.

name: Dura-Europos (siege)
roman_force: A mixed garrison: cohors XX Palmyrenorum, vexillations of legions IV Scythica, III Cyrenaica and XVI Flavia Firma, and other cohorts (II Paphlagonum).
greek_note: The garrison held Palmyrene and Syrian units in a Greek-speaking town, with a cohort raised in Paphlagonia in Greek-speaking Anatolia.
sources: Excavations at Dura-Europos; en.wikipedia Siege of Dura-Europos (256)
note: The mines and countermines survive; a Persian gas attack killed about twenty Roman soldiers in a countermine. The town was then abandoned.

name: Mediolanum
roman_force: Gallienus' field army brought from the Rhine, strong in cavalry; Zonaras makes the Alamanni 300,000, surely an exaggeration.
greek_note: A Rhine and Danube army.
sources: Zonaras 12.24; en.wikipedia Battle of Mediolanum
note: The invaders (Alamanni; perhaps the Juthungi or Semnones of the Augsburg altar) were caught on their way back from Italy. Afterwards Gallienus based his mobile cavalry at Milan.

name: Augusta Vindelicum
place: near Augusta Vindelicum (Augsburg), by the Lech
commanders_a: Marcus Simplicinius Genialis, acting governor of Raetia
borderline: Known only from the altar (found 1992); not in the literary sources.
roman_force: Soldiers of the province of Raetia, Germaniciani (troops from the Germanies) and populares (local levies), as listed on the Augsburg victory altar.
greek_note: Provincial troops and local levies of Raetia and the Germanies.
sources: Augsburg victory altar (AE 1993, 1231); en.wikipedia Augsburg Victory Altar
note: The Semnones or Juthungi were returning from Italy with thousands of Italian captives, who were freed.

name: Edessa
roman_force: By Shapur's inscription, 70,000 men from provinces across the empire: Germania, Raetia, Noricum, Dacia, Moesia, Istria, Thrace, Spain, Africa, Mauretania, Bithynia, Asia, Pamphylia, Isauria, Lycaonia, Galatia, Cilicia, Cappadocia, Phrygia, Syria, Phoenicia, Judaea, Arabia, Osroene, Mesopotamia and Rhodes.
greek_note: Shapur's list names many Greek-speaking provinces (Asia, Bithynia, Galatia, Cappadocia, Cilicia, Pamphylia, Phrygia, Rhodes) beside Syria and the Danube.
sources: Shapur's inscription (SKZ); Zosimus 1.36; Zonaras 12.23; Aurelius Victor 32.5; en.wikipedia Battle of Edessa
note: Valerian was taken during or after negotiations; the course of the battle is obscure. The army had been weakened by plague.

name: Mursa
roman_force: Gallienus: his new mobile cavalry under Aureolus and troops brought from the Rhine; Ingenuus: the legions of Moesia and Pannonia.
greek_note: Rhine and Danube armies on both sides.
sources: Zonaras 12.24; Aurelius Victor 33.2; Historia Augusta, Tyranni triginta 9; en.wikipedia Ingenuus; en.wikipedia Aureolus
note: The date is disputed (258 or 260). Ingenuus drowned himself or was killed after the defeat.

name: Caesarea (siege)
borderline: No Wikipedia battle article; the defence is known from Zonaras.
roman_force: The citizens of Caesarea under Demosthenes, who held the walls until the city was betrayed (Zonaras).
greek_note: Caesarea was the Greek-speaking capital of Cappadocia.
sources: Zonaras 12.23; Shapur's inscription (SKZ); en.wikipedia Shapur I; en.wikipedia Battle of Edessa
note: Many inhabitants were deported to Persia.

name: Pompeiopolis
roman_force: Remnants of the eastern army gathered by Ballista and Macrianus after Edessa, with ships that landed troops on the Cilician coast.
greek_note: The surviving eastern units were recruited in Syria, Cilicia and Asia Minor.
sources: Zonaras 12.23; George Syncellus; en.wikipedia Battle of Edessa; en.wikipedia Balista
note: About 3,000 Persians were killed; Ballista also seized Shapur's harem and treasure in these operations.

name: Cologne (siege)
borderline: Ended when the defenders surrendered Saloninus and Silvanus; the fighting is not described.
roman_force: Postumus: the Rhine army of Germania Inferior; defenders: the garrison and court of Saloninus at Cologne.
greek_note: Rhine troops on both sides.
sources: Zosimus 1.38.2; Zonaras 12.24; en.wikipedia Crisis of the Third Century; en.wikipedia Gallienus
note: Saloninus was proclaimed Augustus during the siege.

name: Defeat of the Macriani
place: in Illyricum or on the borders of Thrace (site unknown)
borderline: Unnamed; the sources disagree on the commander, and part of the army seems to have surrendered without fighting.
roman_force: Gallienus' Danubian forces under Aureolus against the eastern field army that the Macriani led west from Syria; much of it surrendered (Historia Augusta, Gallienus 2.6-7; Zonaras 12.24).
greek_note: The Macriani's army was the field army of the East, recruited largely in Syria and Asia Minor.
sources: Historia Augusta, Gallienus 2.6-7, Tyranni Triginta 12-13; Zonaras 12.24; en.wikipedia Macrianus Major
note: Quietus, left in the East, was then besieged at Emesa by Odaenathus and killed by the citizens (not entered: little fighting is recorded).

name: Ctesiphon (siege)
borderline: Fought by Odaenathus, a Roman client and officer (corrector totius Orientis), with Roman troops in his army; Palmyra is in allies. Wikipedia's infobox lists Palmyra and the Roman Empire together.
roman_force: The Palmyrene army of Odaenathus (heavy cavalry and horse-archers, desert nomads and Syrian levies) with Roman soldiers of the eastern army in its ranks.
greek_note: The army was mostly Palmyrene and Arab, with Greek-speaking Syrian and Roman elements.
sources: Historia Augusta, Gallienus 10, 12; Zosimus 1.39; en.wikipedia Siege of Ctesiphon (263); en.wikipedia Odaenathus
note: The siege was raised for want of supplies after several battles near the city; strategically the campaign restored Mesopotamia to Rome. A second march on Ctesiphon (266?) is reported only by Zosimus.

name: Gallienus against Postumus
place: Gaul (site unknown); Gallienus then besieged Postumus in an unnamed city
borderline: Unnamed; neither the battlefield nor the besieged city is named.
roman_force: Gallienus' field army, with Aureolus' cavalry, against Postumus' Rhine army and Gallic forces; Aureolus' slack pursuit let Postumus escape (Zonaras 12.24; Historia Augusta, Gallienus 4.4-6, 7.1).
greek_note: Both armies were raised in the western and Danubian provinces; Greek speakers were few.
sources: Zonaras 12.24; Historia Augusta, Gallienus 4.4-6, 7.1, Tyranni Triginta 3.5; en.wikipedia Postumus
note: Gallienus won the field battle but was wounded by an arrow during the siege and broke it off; Postumus kept Gaul, Britain and Spain.

name: Venerianus' naval victory
place: the waters near Byzantium (Bosporus or Propontis)
commanders_a: Venerianus (killed); Cleodamus and Athenaeus at Byzantium
borderline: Not given a name in the sources; the Historia Augusta credits Venerianus, Syncellus the citizens of Byzantium.
roman_force: An imperial fleet under the general Venerianus, with the forces of Byzantium, against a Herulian fleet said to number 500 ships (Historia Augusta, Gallienus 13.6-7; George Syncellus).
greek_note: The citizens of Byzantium fought under their own commanders, and the eastern fleets were manned from the Greek coastal cities.
sources: Historia Augusta, Gallienus 13.6-7; George Syncellus p. 717; en.wikipedia 267
note: Heruli. The survivors broke into the Aegean and raided Lemnos, Skyros and Athens.

name: Athens
borderline: The Heruli took and sacked the city; the recorded fighting is the defence and Dexippus' counterattack.
roman_force: The Athenian militia, some 2,000 men under Dexippus by his own account, who fought on from the woods after the city fell.
greek_note: The defenders were Athenian citizens led by the historian Dexippus.
sources: Dexippus (fragment of his speech to the Athenians); Historia Augusta, Gallienus 13.8; Zonaras 12.26; George Syncellus; en.wikipedia Heruli; en.wikipedia Dexippus
note: The Heruli then left Attica; the Historia Augusta credits Dexippus and a Roman fleet with driving them out.

name: Tomis (siege)
place: Tomis, on the Black Sea coast
borderline: An attack repulsed, known from one sentence of Zosimus.
roman_force: The citizens and garrison of the walled city, who repulsed the attack; no details survive (Zosimus 1.42.1).
greek_note: Tomis was a Greek city whose citizens manned the walls with the garrison.
sources: Zosimus 1.42.1; livius.org, Zosimus New History 1.42
note: Goths with Heruli, Peucini and others, gathered at the mouth of the Tyras; Zosimus' 6,000 ships and 320,000 men are surely exaggerated.

name: Marcianopolis (siege)
borderline: An attack repulsed, known from one sentence of Zosimus.
roman_force: The citizens and garrison of Marcianopolis, who beat off the attack; no details survive (Zosimus 1.42.1).
greek_note: Marcianopolis was a Greek-speaking city of Lower Moesia.
sources: Zosimus 1.42.1; livius.org, Zosimus New History 1.42
note: Distinct from the siege of 248 (or 250) already entered.

name: Cassandreia (siege)
place: Cassandreia (Potidaea), on the isthmus of Pallene
borderline: A siege known from one sentence of Zosimus; the fighting is not described.
roman_force: The citizens of Cassandreia; the besiegers left when they heard that the emperor was approaching (Zosimus 1.43.1).
greek_note: A Greek city of Macedonia defended by its citizens.
sources: Zosimus 1.43.1; livius.org, Zosimus New History 1.43
note: Besieged at the same time as Thessalonica.

name: Doberus and Pelagonia
place: near Doberus and Pelagonia, in Paeonia and Upper Macedonia
borderline: A cavalry action before Naissus, not usually given its own name.
roman_force: The Dalmatian cavalry, which killed some 3,000 of the invaders as they moved inland from Thessalonica (Zosimus 1.43.2).
greek_note: Dalmatian horsemen from the western Balkans.
sources: Zosimus 1.43.2; livius.org, Zosimus New History 1.43

name: Nestus
place: on the river Nestus (Nessos, Nestos), Thrace
roman_force: Gallienus' field army with its new mobile cavalry, including Dalmatian horsemen.
greek_note: A Danubian field army.
sources: George Syncellus; Historia Augusta, Gallienus 13.9; en.wikipedia Heruli; en.wikipedia Naulobatus; en.wikipedia Battle of Naissus
note: Against the Heruli; about 3,000 were killed and Naulobatus submitted, receiving the consular insignia.

name: Pons Aureoli
place: Pons Aureoli (Pontirolo Nuovo), on the Adda east of Milan
roman_force: Gallienus: his field army back from the Balkans with the mobile cavalry; Aureolus: the cavalry corps and garrison he commanded at Mediolanum.
greek_note: Danubian and Italian troops on both sides.
sources: Aurelius Victor 33.17-18; Zosimus 1.40; en.wikipedia Gallienus; en.wikipedia Aureolus
note: Aureolus was driven back into Milan. The bridge took its name from Aureolus, who was buried there.

name: Mediolanum (siege)
commanders_a: Gallienus (murdered during the siege), Claudius II
roman_force: Gallienus' field army and mobile cavalry besieging Aureolus' troops in the city.
greek_note: Danubian and Italian troops on both sides.
sources: Zosimus 1.40-41; Aurelius Victor 33; Historia Augusta, Gallienus 14; en.wikipedia Gallienus; en.wikipedia Claudius Gothicus
note: Gallienus was killed by his officers during the siege (September 268?); Claudius received Aureolus' surrender, and Aureolus was then killed by the soldiers.

name: Lake Benacus
roman_force: Claudius' field army, joined by Aureolus' former troops.
greek_note: A Danubian and Italian field army.
sources: Epitome de Caesaribus 34.2; en.wikipedia Battle of Lake Benacus
note: Against the Alamanni; the Epitome says barely half of them survived. Claudius took the title Germanicus Maximus.

name: Thessalonica (siege)
commanders_a: the citizens of Thessalonica (relieved by Claudius II)
roman_force: The citizens and garrison of Thessalonica; the invaders raised the siege when Claudius' army approached.
greek_note: The defenders were the Greek citizens of Thessalonica.
sources: Zosimus 1.43; en.wikipedia Heruli
note: The invaders (Goths with Heruli and others) also attacked Cassandreia before moving inland towards Naissus.

name: Naissus
commanders_b: unknown (Cniva and Cannabaudes have been suggested)
roman_force: The Danubian field army, with the cavalry under Aurelian (including Dalmatian horse) delivering the decisive attack.
greek_note: A Danubian field army recruited in Illyricum and Thrace.
sources: Zosimus 1.45; Historia Augusta, Claudius 6-8; en.wikipedia Battle of Naissus
note: Goths (Greuthungi and Thervingi) with Heruli, Gepids and Peucini. Most scholars credit Claudius, and many date it 269; Zosimus claims 50,000 enemy killed or captured.

name: Mount Haemus
borderline: An engagement in the pursuit after Naissus without a site name.
roman_force: Claudius' Danubian field army, which surrounded the survivors of Naissus in the Haemus; the infantry, quarrelling with the cavalry, attacked alone and was beaten until the cavalry came to its aid (Zosimus 1.45).
greek_note: A Danubian field army; Greek speakers were few.
sources: Zosimus 1.45; tertullian.org, Zosimus book 1 (1814 translation)
note: The Goths were then worn down by hunger and plague; many were settled or enrolled in the army.

name: Mogontiacum (siege)
roman_force: Postumus: the Gallic field army; Laelianus: legio XXII Primigenia at Mainz, perhaps with VIII Augusta.
greek_note: Rhine and Gallic troops on both sides.
sources: Aurelius Victor 33.8; Eutropius 9.9; en.wikipedia Laelianus
note: Postumus was killed by his own troops after refusing them the sack of the city.

name: Bostra
commanders_b: Trassus (killed), commander of legio III Cyrenaica
borderline: Palmyrene Empire of Zenobia: a foreign opponent here by the project's rule, though Zenobia still claimed to act within the empire.
roman_force: Legio III Cyrenaica, the garrison of Arabia, under Trassus.
greek_note: III Cyrenaica was recruited locally in Arabia and Syria, a Greek-, Aramaic- and Arabic-speaking region.
sources: Bostra inscriptions (temple of Jupiter Hammon); en.wikipedia Zenobia
note: Zabdas sacked Bostra and destroyed the legion's temple of Jupiter Hammon.

name: Augustodunum (siege)
roman_force: Victorinus: the Gallic army; defenders: the citizens of Augustodunum, who had declared for Claudius and received no help.
greek_note: Gallic troops and townsmen.
sources: Panegyrici Latini (Eumenius); en.wikipedia Claudius Gothicus
note: The city fell after a siege of many weeks and was sacked.

name: Babylon Fortress
place: the fortress of Babylon, near Memphis (Old Cairo)
borderline: Palmyrene Empire of Zenobia: a foreign opponent here by the project's rule.
roman_force: The army of Egypt under the prefect Tenagino Probus: legio II Traiana, auxiliary units and levies; Zosimus gives 50,000 for the Roman army beaten by Zabdas earlier in the campaign.
greek_note: The army of Egypt was recruited in Egypt, where its soldiers wrote and spoke Greek.
sources: Zosimus 1.44; Historia Augusta, Claudius 11; en.wikipedia Palmyrene invasion of Egypt
note: The last of several actions in Egypt in 270: Zabdas beat the Roman army (Zosimus: 70,000 against 50,000), Probus briefly retook Alexandria, and Timagenes then ambushed him near Babylon.

name: Placentia
roman_force: Aurelian's field army, marched from Pannonia after the Vandal war: Danubian legions and cavalry.
greek_note: A Danubian field army.
sources: Epitome de Caesaribus 35.2; Historia Augusta, Aurelian 21; Zosimus 1.49; en.wikipedia Battle of Placentia (271)
note: The Juthungi (the Historia Augusta says Marcomanni) ambushed the tired army in woods near Placentia; there was panic at Rome.

name: Fano
place: on the Metaurus, near Fanum Fortunae (Fano)
roman_force: Aurelian's Danubian field army.
greek_note: A Danubian field army.
sources: Epitome de Caesaribus 35.2; Historia Augusta, Aurelian 18; en.wikipedia Battle of Fano
note: Against the Juthungi; many were driven into the river.

name: Pavia
roman_force: Aurelian's Danubian field army.
greek_note: A Danubian field army.
sources: Epitome de Caesaribus 35.2; en.wikipedia Battle of Pavia (271)
note: Against the Juthungi; it ended their invasion of Italy.

name: Mint workers' revolt
place: Rome, on the Caelian Hill by the mint
borderline: An urban revolt rather than a battle between armies; included because the sources record heavy fighting, with 7,000 soldiers killed (Victor, Eutropius).
roman_force: Aurelian's troops in Rome, against the mint workers and those who joined them in the city.
greek_note: Aurelian's soldiers were mainly Danubian; the rebels were the workers of the Roman mint.
sources: Aurelius Victor 35.6; Eutropius 9.14; Historia Augusta, Aurelian 38
note: The revolt followed Aurelian's attempt to stop the debasement of the coinage.

name: Immae
borderline: Palmyrene Empire of Zenobia: a foreign opponent here by the project's rule.
roman_force: Aurelian's cavalry (Dalmatian and Moorish horse) drew the Palmyrene clibanarii into a long pursuit in the heat and then turned on them; the legions formed the infantry core.
greek_note: Aurelian's army was mainly Danubian; eastern levies joined it in Asia Minor and Syria.
sources: Zosimus 1.50; Festus 24; Historia Augusta, Aurelian 25; en.wikipedia Battle of Immae
note: Antioch opened its gates after the battle.

name: Daphne
place: the hill above Daphne, south of Antioch
borderline: A rearguard action known only from Zosimus; Palmyra counted as foreign by the project's rule.
roman_force: Aurelian's infantry, who stormed the steep hill in close order under their shields (Zosimus 1.52).
greek_note: Aurelian's army was mainly Danubian.
sources: Zosimus 1.52.1-2

name: Emesa
borderline: Palmyrene Empire of Zenobia: a foreign opponent here by the project's rule.
roman_force: By Zosimus' list: Dalmatian cavalry, Moesian and Pannonian legions, Norican and Raetian (Celtic) legions, the praetorian guard, Moorish horse, troops from Tyana and Mesopotamia, Syrians, Phoenicians, and Palestinians armed with clubs and maces.
greek_note: The eastern contingents named by Zosimus (Tyaneans, Mesopotamians, Syrians, Phoenicians, Palestinians) were largely Greek-speaking; the core was Danubian and Latin-speaking.
sources: Zosimus 1.52-53; Historia Augusta, Aurelian 25; en.wikipedia Battle of Emesa
note: Zosimus gives the Palmyrene army 70,000 men. The Palmyrene cavalry again pursued too far and was destroyed by the infantry and the Palestinian clubmen.

name: Palmyra (siege)
borderline: Palmyrene Empire of Zenobia: a foreign opponent here by the project's rule.
roman_force: Aurelian's army from Emesa, supplied by the Syrian cities; the Palmyrenes repulsed several assaults.
greek_note: The same mainly Danubian army as at Emesa, with eastern contingents.
sources: Zosimus 1.54-56; Historia Augusta, Aurelian 26-28; en.wikipedia Battle of Emesa
note: Zenobia fled towards Persia and was captured at the Euphrates; the city then surrendered. A revolt in 273 led to its sack.

name: Châlons
roman_force: Aurelian: his field army of Danubian veterans, with eastern contingents from the Palmyrene war; Tetricus: the Gallic army of the Rhine legions and Gaul.
greek_note: Western and Danubian armies; any Greek speakers came with Aurelian's eastern contingents.
sources: Aurelius Victor 35.3-5; Eutropius 9.13; Orosius 7.23.5; Historia Augusta, Aurelian 32; en.wikipedia Battle of Châlons (274)
note: The sources say Tetricus betrayed his army and went over to Aurelian at the start of the battle; modern scholars suspect propaganda. The Gallic army suffered heavy losses.

name: Probus' victory over the Burgundians and Vandals
place: an unnamed river on the frontier (site unknown)
borderline: Unnamed; Zosimus does not name the river.
roman_force: Probus' field army, smaller than the enemy; it provoked part of them to cross the river and destroyed them, then beat the rest when they broke the truce (Zosimus 1.68).
greek_note: A field army of the Danubian and western provinces.
sources: Zosimus 1.68; tertullian.org, Zosimus book 1 (1814 translation)
note: Burgundians and Vandals; the captives were sent to Britain.

name: Cremna (siege)
borderline: Against a brigand band holding a Roman city; not counted as civil, as the Isaurians were not a Roman army.
roman_force: Provincial troops of Lycia and Pamphylia, who built a siege wall and an assault mound against the city (Zosimus 1.69-70; the works survive).
greek_note: The troops of southern Anatolia were recruited in a Greek-speaking region.
sources: Zosimus 1.69-70; excavations at Cremna (S. Mitchell); en.wikipedia Cremna
note: Lydius was shot from the Roman lines by a deserter from his own band. The date (276-278) is uncertain.

name: Bonosus' revolt
place: the Rhine frontier, perhaps near Colonia Agrippina (site unknown)
borderline: Known only from the Historia Augusta; the site is not given.
roman_force: Probus' field army against the Rhine troops raised by Bonosus at Cologne; the Historia Augusta calls it a long and hard-fought battle.
greek_note: Both armies were raised in the western and Danubian provinces.
sources: Historia Augusta, Quadrigae Tyrannorum 14-15; Historia Augusta, Probus 18
note: Proculus, who rose at Lugdunum at about the same time, was also put down (no battle described).

name: Carus' victory over the Sarmatians
borderline: Unnamed; the site is unknown and the figures come from the Historia Augusta.
roman_force: Carus' field army of the Danubian provinces; the Historia Augusta claims 16,000 enemies killed and 20,000 captured.
greek_note: A Danubian field army; Greek speakers were few.
sources: Historia Augusta, Carus 9.4; Eutropius 9.18
note: Carus then marched against the Persians.

name: Meinas Sabatha
place: Meinas Sabatha, on the Royal Canal near Seleucia
borderline: Known only from later notices of a city destroyed by Carus; the fighting is not described.
roman_force: Carus' expeditionary army (see Ctesiphon, 283).
greek_note: Danubian detachments marched with the eastern legions of Syria and Mesopotamia.
sources: Ammianus Marcellinus 24.5.3; Zosimus 3.23; en.wikipedia Carus' Sasanian campaign
note: Described as the most serious resistance the Romans met before Seleucia.

name: Ctesiphon
place: Ctesiphon and Seleucia (Coche), on the Tigris
borderline: Little fighting is recorded: Bahram II was occupied in the east and the cities were taken quickly.
roman_force: Carus' expeditionary army: detachments of the Danubian and perhaps Rhine legions, the field cavalry, the guard, and the eastern legions and auxiliaries, perhaps with a supply fleet on the Euphrates (modern reconstruction; the sources name no units).
greek_note: Danubian detachments marched with the eastern legions of Syria and Mesopotamia.
sources: Historia Augusta, Carus 8; Eutropius 9.18; Aurelius Victor 38; Zonaras 12.30; en.wikipedia Carus' Sasanian campaign
note: Zonaras tells of a Persian attempt to flood the Roman camp, beaten off by Carus. Carus died soon after, reportedly struck by lightning.

name: Margus
war: Civil war of Diocletian and Carinus
place: valley of the Margus (Great Morava), near Margum, Moesia Superior
commanders_b: Carinus (killed); his praetorian prefect Aristobulus went over to Diocletian
roman_force: Diocletian led the army of Carus' Persian expedition, an eastern field force with an Illyrian core, which had proclaimed him at Nicomedia; Carinus led the larger army of the West and Illyricum with which he had just beaten Julianus. No numbers survive.
greek_note: The core of both armies was Danubian and western; Greek speakers came only with the eastern units of Carus' expedition.
sources: Eutropius 9.20; Aurelius Victor 39.11-12; Epitome de Caesaribus 38.8; Zonaras 12.30; en.wikipedia Battle of the Margus
note: Carinus was killed by his own officers, perhaps when his army was winning; some date the battle to spring 285.

name: Verona
place: the plains of Verona (campi Veronenses), Venetia; Aurelius Victor places it in Illyricum
borderline: Known only as Carinus' defeat of Julianus; rarely treated as a named battle, and the site is disputed.
roman_force: Carinus' western field army against the usurper Julianus, corrector of Venetia (Epitome) or a commander in Pannonia (Aurelius Victor), with the troops of his provinces; no numbers survive.
greek_note: Both armies were raised in Italy and the Latin-speaking Danube provinces.
sources: Epitome de Caesaribus 38.6; Aurelius Victor 39.10; Zosimus 1.73; en.wikipedia Sabinus Julianus
note: Some scholars think there were two usurpers named Julianus, one beaten in Illyricum and one near Verona.

name: Gesoriacum (siege)
borderline: A blockade that ended in the garrison's surrender; little fighting is recorded.
roman_force: Constantius' field army of Gaul blockaded Carausius' garrison, drawn from the troops he had seized in northern Gaul and Britain, and closed the harbour with a mole; Constantius also cleared Carausius' Frankish allies from the Rhine delta.
greek_note: Both forces were raised in Gaul, Britain and among Germanic recruits.
sources: Panegyrici Latini 8(5).6-7, 6(7).5.2; en.wikipedia Carausian revolt
note: Carausius was murdered by Allectus later in 293.

name: Calleva
place: southern Britain, probably near Calleva Atrebatum (Silchester), after a landing near Southampton
borderline: No conventional name: the panegyric does not name the site; Silchester is a modern suggestion from archaeology.
roman_force: Asclepiodotus' division of Constantius' invasion fleet and army of Gaul, landed in fog past Allectus' fleet off the Isle of Wight, against Allectus' army of Britain, much of it Frankish mercenaries (Panegyrici Latini 8(5).16).
greek_note: The invaders were the army of Gaul; Allectus had British troops and Frankish mercenaries.
sources: Panegyrici Latini 8(5).14-17; Eutropius 9.22; Aurelius Victor 39.42; en.wikipedia Carausian revolt
note: Constantius' soldiers who reached London after losing their way in the fog killed the remnants of Allectus' Franks there (not counted separately).

name: Carrhae
commanders_b: Galerius, Caesar; Tiridates III of Armenia
roman_force: Galerius' relatively small army of the eastern frontier provinces, with Tiridates III's Armenians; no numbers or units survive.
greek_note: The eastern frontier legions were recruited in Syria, Mesopotamia and Asia Minor, beside Danubian detachments.
sources: Eutropius 9.24; Festus 25; Aurelius Victor 39.34; Ammianus 14.11.10; en.wikipedia Battle of Carrhae (296)
note: Also called Callinicum (296): Eutropius puts it between Callinicum and Carrhae; dated 296 or 297.

name: Alexandria (siege)
roman_force: Diocletian's imperial field army with eastern and Danubian detachments besieged the rebel garrison and people of Alexandria, who had the Egyptian army behind them.
greek_note: The defenders were the Greek-speaking city and the army of Egypt; the besiegers came from the Danube and the East.
sources: Eutropius 9.22-23; Aurelius Victor 39.38; en.wikipedia Domitius Domitianus
note: Eutropius gives an eight-month siege; the city fell in March 298 (older chronologies 297).

name: Satala
place: Armenia, probably the district of Basean east of Erzurum; Satala was the Roman base
commanders_a: Galerius, Caesar; Tiridates III of Armenia
roman_force: Galerius' new army, raised in Illyricum and Moesia (Eutropius 9.25), about 25,000 by the usual figure, with Tiridates III's Armenians; it surprised Narseh's camp.
greek_note: Eutropius says the army was gathered in Illyricum and Moesia, Latin- and Thracian-speaking provinces.
sources: Eutropius 9.25; Festus 25; Aurelius Victor 39.34-35; en.wikipedia Battle of Satala (298)
note: Site uncertain: Armenian tradition places it at Osxay in Basean. Some date it 297. Narseh's family and treasury were taken; the peace of Nisibis followed.

name: Lingones
roman_force: Constantius' field army of Gaul: surprised and wounded, Constantius was hauled up the town wall by rope, and his army arrived within hours and routed the Alamanni (Eutropius 9.23).
greek_note: The army of Gaul and the Rhine was raised in Gaul and among Germanic recruits.
sources: Eutropius 9.23; Panegyrici Latini 6(7).6.3; en.wikipedia Battle of Lingones
note: Eutropius claims 60,000 Alamanni killed. Dated 298 (some c. 300-302).

name: Vindonissa
place: the plains of Vindonissa (Windisch), Maxima Sequanorum
roman_force: Constantius' field army of Gaul and the Rhine; the sources give no details.
greek_note: The army of Gaul and the Rhine was raised in Gaul and among Germanic recruits.
sources: Panegyrici Latini 6(7).6.4; en.wikipedia Battle of Vindonissa
note: Known from a passing mention in the panegyric of 310; dated 298 or 302.

name: Massilia (siege)
war: Civil wars of the Tetrarchy (revolt of Maximian)
borderline: A short siege with one failed assault; the city was opened by its citizens.
roman_force: Constantine's army of the Rhine, brought south by forced marches, against the troops in southern Gaul whom Maximian had won over with largesse; an assault failed because the ladders were too short, and then citizens opened a gate.
greek_note: Both forces belonged to the army of Gaul and the Rhine.
sources: Lactantius, De mortibus persecutorum 29-30; Panegyrici Latini 6(7).18-20; en.wikipedia Civil wars of the Tetrarchy
note: Maximian was captured and soon hanged himself (c. July 310).

name: Milvian Bridge
war: Civil wars of the Tetrarchy (Constantine against Maxentius)
place: Saxa Rubra and the Milvian Bridge on the Tiber, north of Rome
roman_force: Constantine's army of Gaul (Zosimus 2.15: 90,000 foot and 8,000 horse of Germans, other Celts and Britons; modern estimates about 40,000) against Maxentius' army (Zosimus: 170,000 foot and 18,000 horse of Romans, Italians, Etruscans, Africans and Sicilians), with the praetorian guard and the horse guard (equites singulares).
greek_note: Zosimus counts Sicilians, some of them Greek speakers, among Maxentius' troops; Constantine's army of Gaul had almost none.
sources: Lactantius, De mortibus persecutorum 44; Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 9.9 and Life of Constantine 1.37-38; Panegyrici Latini 12(9).16-18, 4(10).28-30; Zosimus 2.15-16; en.wikipedia Battle of the Milvian Bridge
note: Zosimus' numbers are much exaggerated. The praetorians were disbanded after the battle.

name: Segusium (siege)
war: Civil wars of the Tetrarchy (Constantine against Maxentius)
place: Segusium (Susa), at the foot of the Cottian Alps
borderline: A storming of a fortified town, counted as a siege with fighting.
roman_force: Constantine's invasion army, about 40,000 by modern estimate (the panegyric of 313 says barely a quarter of his forces), drawn from the armies of Gaul, the Rhine and Britain with Germanic recruits; it burned the gates and scaled the walls.
greek_note: Constantine's army came from Gaul, Britain and the Rhine; the defenders were a north Italian garrison.
sources: Panegyrici Latini 12(9).5.4-6, 4(10).21; en.wikipedia Battle of Turin (312)

name: Turin
war: Civil wars of the Tetrarchy (Constantine against Maxentius)
roman_force: Constantine's army of Gaul (about 40,000) against a Maxentian army whose core was heavily armoured cavalry (clibanarii or cataphractarii) in a wedge; Constantine's cavalry broke them with iron-shod clubs (Panegyrici Latini 4(10).22-24).
greek_note: The armies were raised in Gaul, Britain, the Rhine and northern Italy.
sources: Panegyrici Latini 12(9).6, 4(10).22-24; en.wikipedia Battle of Turin (312)
note: The people of Turin shut the gates on the fleeing Maxentians.

name: Brescia
war: Civil wars of the Tetrarchy (Constantine against Maxentius)
borderline: A minor cavalry action known only from Nazarius' panegyric of 321.
roman_force: Constantine's advancing army routed a large Maxentian cavalry force camped near Brixia.
greek_note: The armies were raised in Gaul, Britain, the Rhine and northern Italy.
sources: Panegyrici Latini 4(10).25.1; en.wikipedia Civil wars of the Tetrarchy

name: Verona
war: Civil wars of the Tetrarchy (Constantine against Maxentius)
place: Verona, in the loop of the Adige, and the field to the east
roman_force: Constantine's army of Gaul besieged Verona; Pompeianus' large army of Venetia sallied, then came back as a relief army, and Constantine fought it on a second front while part of his force held the siege lines.
greek_note: The armies were raised in Gaul, Britain, the Rhine and northern Italy.
sources: Panegyrici Latini 12(9).8-10, 4(10).25-26; en.wikipedia Battle of Verona (312)
note: Siege, sortie and relief battle counted as one entry; the garrison surrendered and the prisoners were fettered with their own swords.

name: Tzirallum
war: Civil wars of the Tetrarchy (Licinius against Maximinus Daia)
place: the Campus Ergenus (Lactantius' Campus Serenus), near Tzirallum (Corlu), between Heraclea and Adrianople
roman_force: Licinius' army of about 30,000, hastily gathered in Illyricum and Thrace, against Maximinus' 70,000 from the East (Lactantius, De mortibus persecutorum 45-47).
greek_note: Maximinus' larger army came from the Greek- and Aramaic-speaking East; Licinius' from the Latin- and Thracian-speaking Danube lands.
sources: Lactantius, De mortibus persecutorum 45-47; Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 9.10; en.wikipedia Battle of Tzirallum
note: Also called the battle of the Campus Ergenus.

name: Byzantium (siege)
war: Civil wars of the Tetrarchy (Licinius against Maximinus Daia)
borderline: A short siege: Maximinus tried bribes before force, and the garrison yielded after eleven days.
roman_force: Maximinus' eastern army, 70,000 by Lactantius' figure, from Syria, Asia Minor and Egypt, against Licinius' garrison, which held out for eleven days.
