greek_note: Maximinus' army was raised in the Greek- and Aramaic-speaking East.
sources: Lactantius, De mortibus persecutorum 45; en.wikipedia Civil wars of the Tetrarchy

name: Heraclea (siege)
war: Civil wars of the Tetrarchy (Licinius against Maximinus Daia)
place: Heraclea Perinthus (Marmara Ereglisi), on the Propontis
borderline: A siege of a few days with little recorded fighting.
roman_force: Maximinus' eastern army took the town after a siege of a few days, while Licinius was gathering his army at Adrianople.
greek_note: Maximinus' army was raised in the Greek- and Aramaic-speaking East.
sources: Lactantius, De mortibus persecutorum 45; en.wikipedia Civil wars of the Tetrarchy

name: Cilician Gates
war: Civil wars of the Tetrarchy (Licinius against Maximinus Daia)
place: the Cilician Gates pass in the Taurus
borderline: Forcing of a fortified pass, told in one sentence by Lactantius; not usually treated as a named battle.
roman_force: Licinius' army forced the fortified lines Maximinus had built in the pass; Maximinus fell back to Tarsus and died there.
greek_note: Maximinus' remaining troops were eastern; Licinius' were mainly Danubian.
sources: Lactantius, De mortibus persecutorum 49; en.wikipedia Civil wars of the Tetrarchy

name: Cibalae
war: Civil wars of the Tetrarchy (first war of Constantine and Licinius)
place: near Cibalae (Vinkovci), between the Save and the Drave, Pannonia Secunda
roman_force: Constantine's 20,000, from the armies of Gaul and the western Danube, against Licinius' 35,000 of the Illyrian and Thracian armies (Zosimus 2.18); Licinius lost some 20,000.
greek_note: Both armies were drawn mainly from the Latin-speaking West and the Danube provinces.
sources: Origo Constantini (Anonymus Valesianus) 5.16; Zosimus 2.18; Eutropius 10.5; en.wikipedia Battle of Cibalae
note: Dated 8 October 316 by the consensus; some (from Hydatius' consular list) prefer 314.

name: Mardia
war: Civil wars of the Tetrarchy (first war of Constantine and Licinius)
place: the Campus Ardiensis (Mardia), probably near Harmanli, west of Adrianople
roman_force: The bulk of Constantine's army against Licinius' survivors of Cibalae and a second army raised at Adrianople under Valens from the Thracian and eastern forces.
greek_note: Licinius' Thracian and eastern reinforcements brought some Greek speakers; the rest were Latin-speaking western and Danubian troops.
sources: Origo Constantini 5.17-18; Zosimus 2.19; en.wikipedia Battle of Mardia
note: Constantine held the field but the result was not decisive: fighting ended at nightfall and Licinius withdrew in order; the peace of Serdica followed on 1 March 317.

name: Adrianople
war: Civil wars of the Tetrarchy (second war of Constantine and Licinius)
roman_force: Zosimus 2.22: Constantine 120,000 foot and 10,000 horse and sailors from the West and Illyricum; Licinius 150,000 foot and 15,000 horse, the cavalry from Phrygia and Cappadocia.
greek_note: Licinius' army was raised in Asia Minor and the East (Zosimus names Phrygia and Cappadocia); Constantine's in the Latin West and Illyricum.
sources: Origo Constantini 5.24; Zosimus 2.22; Eusebius, Life of Constantine 2.6-10; en.wikipedia Battle of Adrianople (324)
note: Zosimus' numbers are inflated; he says 34,000 of Licinius' men fell.

name: Hellespont
war: Civil wars of the Tetrarchy (second war of Constantine and Licinius)
place: the Hellespont (Dardanelles), off Elaious and Kallipolis
roman_force: Crispus with 80 thirty-oared ships, picked from Constantine's 200 assembled at Piraeus, against Abantus' 200 from Licinius' 350 triremes, furnished by Egypt (80), Phoenicia (80), the Ionians and Dorians of Asia (60), Cyprus (30), Caria (20), Bithynia (30) and Africa (50) (Zosimus 2.22-24).
greek_note: Constantine's fleet was gathered at Piraeus from Greek waters and Licinius' came from Egypt, Phoenicia and the Greek coasts of Asia Minor and Cyprus; most crews on both sides spoke Greek.
sources: Zosimus 2.22-24; Origo Constantini 5.23, 5.26; en.wikipedia Battle of the Hellespont
note: Two days of fighting; on the second day a storm wrecked most of Licinius' fleet, and only four ships escaped. Both sides were Roman, so greek_opponent is false although Licinius' fleet was largely Greek-crewed.

name: Byzantium (siege)
war: Civil wars of the Tetrarchy (second war of Constantine and Licinius)
borderline: Usually told only as part of the Hellespont and Chrysopolis campaign.
roman_force: Constantine's army besieged the city with mounds and siege towers (Zosimus 2.25) while Licinius' strong garrison held it; Licinius crossed to Chalcedon after his fleet was lost, and the city surrendered after Chrysopolis.
greek_note: The garrison belonged to Licinius' eastern army; the besiegers to Constantine's western and Illyrian army.
sources: Zosimus 2.25; Origo Constantini 5.25-26; en.wikipedia Battle of the Hellespont

name: Chrysopolis
war: Civil wars of the Tetrarchy (second war of Constantine and Licinius)
place: Chrysopolis (Uskudar), on the Asian shore of the Bosporus
commanders_b: Licinius; Martinianus, his co-emperor; Alica with the Goths
roman_force: Constantine's army, ferried across the Bosporus, against Licinius' eastern army reinforced by Martinianus' corps and Gothic auxiliaries under Alica (Origo Constantini 5.27); about 25,000 of Licinius' men fell (Origo).
greek_note: Licinius' army was recruited in Asia Minor and the East; Constantine's in the West and Illyricum.
sources: Origo Constantini 5.27; Zosimus 2.26; Eusebius, Life of Constantine 2.16-18; en.wikipedia Battle of Chrysopolis
note: Zosimus' figure of 100,000 dead is considered exaggerated. Licinius surrendered at Nicomedia and was executed in 325.

name: Narasara
place: Narasara, in upper Mesopotamia; perhaps Nehar Harre east of Amida, or near Nineveh or Singara
borderline: Roman commander and date uncertain.
roman_force: A local Roman force of Mesopotamia; the sources give no composition.
greek_note: The frontier troops of Mesopotamia were largely recruited locally among Aramaic speakers, with some Greek speakers from Syria and Asia Minor.
sources: Festus 27; Libanius, Oration 59; Theophanes, Chronographia; en.wikipedia Battle of Narasara
note: Dated 337 (traditional), 335, 341 or October 343; site disputed. Festus makes Narseh Shapur's son.

name: Nisibis (siege)
commanders_a: Bishop Jacob (James) of Nisibis; perhaps Count Lucillianus
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Nisibis, led in Christian tradition by Bishop Jacob; units and numbers unknown.
greek_note: Nisibis was a Syriac-speaking city whose defence relied on local troops and citizens.
sources: Jerome, Chronicle; Theophanes, Chronographia; Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History 2.30; en.wikipedia Siege of Nisibis (338)
note: About 60-70 days, probably mid-June to August 338 (some date it 337). Theodoret's account may conflate it with the siege of 350.

name: Aquileia
war: Civil war of Constantine II and Constans
place: near Aquileia, by the river Alsa (Ausa)
borderline: An ambush rather than a pitched battle; no standard name.
roman_force: An advance force of Constans' army of Illyricum and Italy, sent from Naissus, ambushed Constantine II's army of Gaul, which had invaded Italy; Constantine was killed and his body thrown into the Alsa.
greek_note: Both armies were western; Constans' Illyrian troops may have included a few Greek speakers from Macedonia and Achaea.
sources: Epitome de Caesaribus 41.21; Zosimus 2.41; Eutropius 10.9; en.wikipedia Constantine II (emperor)

name: Singara
roman_force: Constantius II's eastern field army, with heavy cavalry; the Romans stormed the Persian camp but, fighting on into the night in disorder against orders, were driven out (Julian, Oration 1).
greek_note: The eastern comitatenses of Constantius were recruited in Thrace, Illyricum, Asia Minor and Syria.
sources: Julian, Oration 1; Libanius, Oration 59; Festus 27; Eutropius 10.10; Ammianus 18.5.7; en.wikipedia Battle of Singara
note: The night battle of Singara. Modern scholars variously call it a Persian victory, a Roman victory or indecisive; both sides claimed it.

name: Nisibis (siege)
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Nisibis; nothing is known of their composition.
greek_note: Nisibis was a Syriac-speaking city whose defence relied on local troops and citizens.
sources: Jerome, Chronicle; Theophanes, Chronographia; en.wikipedia Perso-Roman wars of 337-361
note: Known only from brief chronicle notices; the Persians withdrew.

name: Nisibis (siege)
roman_force: The garrison under Lucillianus and the citizens of Nisibis; Shapur dammed the Mygdonius, flooded the plain, breached the wall and attacked with elephants and boats, but the defenders rebuilt the breach overnight.
greek_note: Nisibis was a Syriac-speaking city; its siege is told in Ephrem's Syriac hymns.
sources: Julian, Orations 1 and 2; Ephrem, Carmina Nisibena; Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History 2.30; Zonaras 13.7; en.wikipedia Siege of Nisibis (350)
note: Lasted 100 days or more; Shapur withdrew because of nomad invasions in the east.

name: Mursa
place: the plain north-west of Mursa (Osijek), on the Drave
roman_force: Constantius' eastern and Illyrian armies, about 80,000, strong in cataphracts and mounted archers, against Magnentius' 36,000 (Zonaras 13.8) of the Gallic field army with Frankish and Saxon recruits (Julian, Oration 1); the officer Silvanus deserted to Constantius with his men before the battle.
greek_note: Greek speakers served only in Constantius' eastern units; Magnentius' western army had almost none.
sources: Zosimus 2.45-53; Julian, Orations 1 and 2; Zonaras 13.8; Eutropius 10.12; Ammianus 15.5.33; en.wikipedia Battle of Mursa Major
note: Also called Mursa Major. Zonaras gives losses of 24,000 for Magnentius and 30,000 for Constantius; a ruinous victory.

name: Mons Seleucus
roman_force: Constantius' army, advancing from Italy into Gaul, against what was left of Magnentius' western army; no details survive.
greek_note: Greek speakers served only in Constantius' eastern units.
sources: Socrates, Ecclesiastical History 2.32; Sozomen 4.7; Zonaras 13.9; en.wikipedia Battle of Mons Seleucus
note: Magnentius fled to Lugdunum and killed himself on 10 or 11 August 353.

name: Reims
place: near Decem Pagi (Dieuze), on Julian's march from Reims (Durocortorum) towards the Rhine
roman_force: Julian's army of Gaul, mustered at Reims; in fog the Alamanni fell on the two legions of the rearguard, which were saved by auxiliary troops (Ammianus 16.2.10).
greek_note: Julian's army of Gaul was raised in Gaul and among Germanic recruits.
sources: Ammianus 16.2.8-10; en.wikipedia Battle of Reims (356)
note: Wikipedia calls it the battle of Reims (Durocortorum), but Ammianus places the attack at Decem Pagi; the rearguard was rescued, so it was a check rather than a rout.

name: Brumath
roman_force: Julian's army of Gaul, drawn up with two wings in a crescent, enveloped an Alamannic war band (Ammianus 16.2.12-13).
greek_note: Julian's army of Gaul was raised in Gaul and among Germanic recruits.
sources: Ammianus 16.2.12-13; en.wikipedia Battle of Brumath

name: Sens (siege)
borderline: A month-long blockade with little recorded fighting.
roman_force: Julian with a weak garrison, his scutarii and gentiles being quartered in other towns; he held the walls for thirty days until the Alamanni withdrew, while the magister equitum Marcellus failed to help (Ammianus 16.4, 16.7.1).
greek_note: The garrison and guard units in Gaul were western and Germanic.
sources: Ammianus 16.4.1-3, 16.7.1; en.wikipedia Battle of Strasbourg

name: Argentoratum
roman_force: Julian's 13,000 (Ammianus 16.12.2) of the field army of Gaul: the auxilia palatina Cornuti, Bracchiati, Batavi and Reges, the legion of the Primani, and cataphract cavalry; perhaps a third to a half of the auxilia palatina were Germanic-born.
greek_note: The units Ammianus names (Cornuti, Bracchiati, Batavi, Reges, Primani) were western regiments recruited in Gaul and among Germanic peoples.
sources: Ammianus 16.12; Libanius, Oration 18.53-62; Julian, Letter to the Athenians; en.wikipedia Battle of Strasbourg
note: Also called the battle of Strasbourg. Ammianus: 243 Romans and about 6,000 Alamanni killed, many more drowned in the Rhine; 35,000 Alamanni.

name: Acimincum
place: Acimincum (Stari Slankamen), on the Danube, Pannonia Secunda
borderline: A parley that turned into a slaughter; Ammianus describes real fighting, but it is rarely treated as a named battle.
roman_force: Constantius II's escort and the army of Pannonia; the Limigantes, admitted to a parley, rushed the emperor's tribunal and were cut down by the troops (Ammianus 19.11.8-15).
greek_note: The army of Pannonia was Latin-speaking; the emperor's escort included eastern palatine units.
sources: Ammianus 19.11.1-16
note: The Limigantes were the former subject people of the Sarmatians.

name: Amida (siege)
commanders_a: Shapur II; Grumbates, king of the Chionitae
commanders_b: Count Aelianus (crucified); Ursicinus outside the city
roman_force: Seven legions (Ammianus 18.9.3-4): V Parthica, the garrison; the Magnentiaci and Decentiaci, Gauls of Magnentius' former army; XXX Ulpia; a detachment of X Fretensis; the Superventores and Praeventores; with the comites sagittarii, a native cavalry unit and the citizens (120,000 people in all, 19.2.14).
greek_note: Ammianus names western and frontier units, two of them Gallic legions; the citizens spoke mainly Aramaic.
sources: Ammianus 18.9-19.8; en.wikipedia Siege of Amida (359)
note: Ammianus was among the defenders and escaped. The Gauls' night sortie cost 400 of them.

name: Singara (siege)
roman_force: Legions I Flavia and I Parthica with many local troops and cavalry (Ammianus 20.6.8); the wall was breached by a ram and the garrison taken to Persia.
greek_note: Ammianus names two frontier legions and local troops of an Aramaic-speaking district.
sources: Ammianus 20.6; en.wikipedia Perso-Roman wars of 337-361

name: Bezabde (siege)
roman_force: Legions II Flavia, II Armeniaca and II Parthica with many Zabdicene archers (Ammianus 20.7.1); the city was stormed and its defenders killed or taken.
greek_note: Ammianus names three frontier legions and local Zabdicene archers.
sources: Ammianus 20.7.1-16; en.wikipedia Perso-Roman wars of 337-361
note: Usually identified with Eski Hendek near Cizre.

name: Virta (siege)
place: the fortress of Virta (Birtha), on the edge of the Mesopotamian desert
roman_force: The garrison of Virta, a fortress said to have been founded by Alexander (Ammianus 20.7.17-18); units not named.
greek_note: Frontier garrisons in Mesopotamia were largely recruited locally.
sources: Ammianus 20.7.17-18; en.wikipedia Perso-Roman wars of 337-361
note: Site uncertain; often identified with Tikrit.

name: Bezabde (Roman siege)
roman_force: Constantius' eastern field army with rams and artillery; Persian sorties burned the siege engines and the autumn rains ended the siege (Ammianus 20.11.6-31).
greek_note: The eastern comitatenses were recruited in Thrace, Illyricum, Asia Minor and Syria.
sources: Ammianus 20.11.6-31; en.wikipedia Perso-Roman wars of 337-361
note: Constantius withdrew to winter at Antioch.

name: Aquileia (siege)
war: Civil war of Julian and Constantius II
roman_force: Julian's troops besieged two legions and a cohort of archers of Constantius' army, sent from Sirmium towards Gaul, which had mutinied at Aquileia with the citizens' support; assaults by land and from the river failed (Ammianus 21.11-12).
greek_note: Both forces were western and Danubian units.
sources: Ammianus 21.11-12; Zosimus 3.10
note: The defenders gave in only after news of Constantius' death (3 November 361).

name: Pirisabora (siege)
roman_force: Julian's main army, about 65,000 (Zosimus 3.13): Gallic and Germanic regiments he had brought from the West (Celtae, Petulantes, Heruli, Batavi), the eastern comitatenses, Gothic auxiliaries and Saracen allies, with a river fleet of 1,100 supply ships and 50 warships (Ammianus 23.3.9).
greek_note: Julian joined his western regiments to Constantius' eastern field army, which was recruited partly in Greek-speaking Thrace and Asia Minor.
sources: Ammianus 24.2.9-22; Zosimus 3.17-18; Libanius, Oration 18; en.wikipedia Siege of Pirisabora
note: The garrison of 2,500 surrendered after the outer works were stormed; the city was burned.

name: Ctesiphon
place: the east bank of the Tigris before Ctesiphon
commanders_b: the Surena and other Persian generals
roman_force: Julian's army crossed the Tigris at night in the fleet's ships, stormed the bank and routed the Persian cataphracts and elephants into Ctesiphon (Ammianus 24.6.4-16); about 2,500 Persians and 70 Romans fell.
greek_note: Julian joined his western regiments to Constantius' eastern field army, which was recruited partly in Greek-speaking Thrace and Asia Minor.
sources: Ammianus 24.6; Zosimus 3.25; Libanius, Oration 18; en.wikipedia Battle of Ctesiphon (363)
note: Julian did not besiege the city and burned his fleet before turning back.

name: Maiozamalcha (siege)
roman_force: Julian's army of the Persian expedition (as at Pirisabora); the city was taken by a mine driven under the walls while the rest of the army assaulted (Ammianus 24.4).
greek_note: Julian joined his western regiments to Constantius' eastern field army, which was recruited partly in Greek-speaking Thrace and Asia Minor.
sources: Ammianus 24.4.2-30; Zosimus 3.20-22; Libanius, Oration 18; en.wikipedia Julian's Persian War
note: Site not identified.

name: Maranga
place: Maranga, on the Tigris north of Ctesiphon
commanders_b: Merena, master of the cavalry, and two sons of Shapur
roman_force: Julian's retreating army, drawn up in a crescent, charged at the run to cut short the Persian archery and drove off the cataphracts and elephants (Ammianus 25.1.11-19).
greek_note: Julian joined his western regiments to Constantius' eastern field army, which was recruited partly in Greek-speaking Thrace and Asia Minor.
sources: Ammianus 25.1.11-19; Zosimus 3.28; en.wikipedia Battle of Maranga
note: Site not identified.

name: Samarra
place: on the Tigris south of Samarra
roman_force: Julian's army on the march, attacked in rear and flank by Persian cavalry and elephants; Julian, riding without his cuirass, was struck by a cavalry spear and died that night (Ammianus 25.3).
greek_note: Julian joined his western regiments to Constantius' eastern field army, which was recruited partly in Greek-speaking Thrace and Asia Minor.
sources: Ammianus 25.3; Zosimus 3.28-29; Libanius, Oration 18; en.wikipedia Battle of Samarra
note: Ammianus reports heavy Persian losses, including Merena, Nohodares and fifty nobles and satraps, and the Romans held the field; but the emperor's death made it a strategic defeat, and it is usually rated indecisive. Jovian's peace followed.

name: Cyzicus (siege)
borderline: A minor siege of the revolt of Procopius.
roman_force: Procopius' troops under Marcellus stormed Cyzicus, held for Valens by Serenianus, after the tribune Aliso broke the chain across the harbour mouth (Ammianus 26.8.6-11).
greek_note: The defenders included the citizens of a Greek city; both forces belonged to the eastern army.
sources: Ammianus 26.8.6-11; en.wikipedia Procopius (usurper)

name: Nacolia
borderline: Decided by desertion more than by fighting.
roman_force: Valens' eastern field army against Procopius' last army; Agilo and his men deserted as the lines met, and Procopius fled (Ammianus 26.9.7-9).
greek_note: Both armies were drawn from the eastern field forces, recruited partly in Greek-speaking Asia Minor and Thrace.
sources: Ammianus 26.9.7-10; Zosimus 4.8; en.wikipedia Battle of Nacolia
note: Procopius was betrayed and beheaded on 27 May 366.

name: Thyatira
roman_force: Valens' eastern field army against Procopius' army, whose core were the Divitenses and Tungricani iuniores (western regiments passing through Thrace) and other troops he had won over; many of Procopius' men went over to their old commanders.
greek_note: Both armies were drawn from the eastern field forces, recruited partly in Greek-speaking Asia Minor and Thrace.
sources: Ammianus 26.9.4-6; Zosimus 4.8; en.wikipedia Battle of Thyatira

name: Scarponna
borderline: A surprise attack on an unprepared war band.
roman_force: Jovinus with the field army of Gaul surprised a large Alamannic band near Scarponna before it could arm, and destroyed it (Ammianus 27.2.1-2).
greek_note: The army of Gaul was raised in Gaul and among Germanic recruits.
sources: Ammianus 27.2.1-2
note: Jovinus then surprised a second band bathing by the river, and fought the third at Chalons.

name: Chalons
commanders_a: Jovinus, magister equitum; Balchobaudes, tribune of the armaturae
roman_force: Jovinus' army of Gaul, with the armaturae and the Ascarii among its units; Ammianus gives 6,000 Alamanni killed and 4,000 wounded against 1,200 Romans killed and 200 wounded (Ammianus 27.2.4-9).
greek_note: The army of Gaul was raised in Gaul and among Germanic recruits.
sources: Ammianus 27.2.4-9; en.wikipedia Battle of Solicinium
note: Ammianus' Catelauni. Usually dated 366 (some 367). Jovinus was rewarded with the consulship of 367.

name: Solicinium
place: Solicinium, a wooded height in the Alamannic lands beyond the Rhine (site unknown)
commanders_a: Valentinian I; Gratian; Count Sebastianus; Jovinus and Severus
roman_force: Valentinian's field army of Gaul, with the Joviani and other palatine units held in reserve by Gratian, and Count Sebastianus with the Illyrian and Italian troops, who climbed the hill and took the Alamanni from behind (Ammianus 27.10).
greek_note: The western field armies of Gaul, Italy and Illyricum were Latin- and Germanic-speaking.
sources: Ammianus 27.10; Ausonius, Mosella; en.wikipedia Battle of Solicinium
note: Site unknown: Hechingen, Sulz am Neckar, Rottenburg, Heidelberg and Schwetzingen have been proposed; coordinates are a placeholder near Hechingen.

name: Deuso
place: Deuso, in the land of the Franks on the lower Rhine (site unknown)
borderline: A treacherous ambush; the name Deuso comes only from Jerome's Chronicle, and the site is unknown.
roman_force: Severus' infantry and cavalry of the army of Gaul ambushed a Saxon raiding force that had been granted a truce; the Saxons fought back hard before they were destroyed (Ammianus 28.5.1-7).
greek_note: The army of Gaul was raised in Gaul and among Germanic recruits.
sources: Ammianus 28.5.1-7; Jerome, Chronicle; Orosius 7.32.10
note: Jerome dates it a few years later than Ammianus; Deutz has been suggested for the site.

name: Bagavan
place: near Bagavan, in Bagrevand, at the foot of Mount Npat near the source of the Arsanias
commanders_a: Traianus and Vadomarius; Mushegh Mamikonian, sparapet of Armenia
commanders_b: generals of Shapur II; Urnayr, king of Albania (wounded)
roman_force: A large Roman army sent by Valens under Traianus and the Alamannic prince Vadomarius, fighting beside the Armenian army of Mushegh Mamikonian (the Epic Histories give 90,000 Armenians).
greek_note: The eastern comitatenses were recruited partly in Greek-speaking Asia Minor and Thrace; the allied Armenians are counted separately.
sources: Ammianus 29.1.3; Epic Histories (Buzandaran) 5.4; en.wikipedia Battle of Bagavan
note: Armenian tradition (Movses Khorenatsi) calls it the battle of Dzirav. Caucasian Albanians fought on the Persian side.

name: Adrianople (siege)
commanders_a: the chief magistrate of the city (unnamed)
borderline: The defenders were townspeople, not an army; the first clash, in which the Goths of Sueridus and Colias routed the armed citizens, is counted with the siege.
roman_force: The townspeople of Hadrianopolis and the workers of the state arms factory (fabricenses), armed by the city's chief magistrate; no regular troops are mentioned (Ammianus 31.6).
greek_note: Hadrianopolis lay in the Greek-speaking south of Thrace, and its defenders were its own citizens and factory workers.
sources: Ammianus Marcellinus 31.6; en.wikipedia Gothic War (376-382)
note: Sueridus and Colias, Gothic officers in Roman service wintering at Hadrianopolis, were provoked by the magistrate, routed the armed citizens and joined Fritigern; the Goths lost heavily before the walls, and Fritigern left a force behind and went off to plunder, saying that he 'kept peace with walls'. Wikipedia dates it 376; it follows Marcianople in Ammianus.

name: Marcianople
place: about nine miles from Marcianople (Devnya), Moesia Secunda
roman_force: Lupicinus with the troops he could gather in Thrace and Moesia, about 5,000 by modern estimate; most were killed and the standards lost (Ammianus 31.5.8-9).
greek_note: The army of Thrace and Moesia was recruited in provinces mainly Latin- and Thracian-speaking, with Greek in the coastal cities.
sources: Ammianus 31.5.4-9; Jordanes, Getica 26; en.wikipedia Battle of Marcianople
note: Also Marcianopolis.

name: Ad Salices
place: Ad Salices (the Willows), in the Dobruja; site not identified
roman_force: Legions brought from Armenia under Traianus and Profuturus, and part of Gratian's palatine troops under Richomeres; Frigeridus with Pannonian and transalpine auxilia was sent but kept away by gout (Ammianus 31.7.2-5); perhaps 5,000-6,000 men.
greek_note: The Armenian-front legions were eastern units, but the western palatine troops of Gratian were Latin and Germanic speakers.
sources: Ammianus 31.7-8.1; en.wikipedia Battle of the Willows
note: Also the battle of the Willows. A bloody draw: the Goths stayed in their wagon laager for a week. Wikipedia places the site in Bulgaria near Marcianople; the itineraries put Salices in the northern Dobruja.

name: Dibaltum
place: outside Dibaltum (Deultum, Debelt), near the Black Sea coast of Thrace
roman_force: Barzimeres with a unit of scutarii cavalry, the Cornuti and other infantry (Ammianus 31.8.9-10); they were surrounded by a late-arriving cavalry force and mostly destroyed.
greek_note: The Cornuti and scutarii were palatine units of western and Germanic origin.
sources: Ammianus 31.8.9-10; en.wikipedia Battle of Dibaltum

name: Argentovaria
war: Gratian's war with the Lentienses (Roman-Alamannic wars)
commanders_a: Nannienus; Mallobaudes, comes domesticorum and king of the Franks (for Gratian)
roman_force: The army of Gaul under Nannienus and the Frankish king Mallobaudes, with units recalled from the march to Illyricum (Ammianus 31.10.6-10).
greek_note: The western field army of Gaul was Latin- and Germanic-speaking.
sources: Ammianus 31.10; Orosius 7.33.8; Epitome de Caesaribus 47.2; en.wikipedia Battle of Argentovaria
note: Ammianus gives the Lentienses 40,000 (or 70,000, as some boasted); later writers claim about 30,000 killed. Gratian then campaigned beyond the Rhine.

name: Adrianople
place: north of Adrianople (Edirne), at the Gothic wagon laager
roman_force: Valens' eastern field army, perhaps 15,000-30,000 by modern estimates, including the Lanciarii and Mattiarii, the Batavi in reserve, the scutarii under Cassio and the sagittarii under Bacurius the Iberian (Ammianus 31.12-13); about two-thirds fell.
greek_note: The eastern field army was recruited largely in Thrace, Illyricum and Asia Minor, with many Germanic soldiers; Greek speakers were a large minority.
sources: Ammianus 31.12-13; Zosimus 4.24; Orosius 7.33; Socrates, Ecclesiastical History 4.38; en.wikipedia Battle of Adrianople
note: Valens' body was never found. The Greuthungi and Alans under Alatheus and Saphrax decided the battle.

name: Adrianople (siege)
roman_force: The garrison, survivors of the battle who had taken refuge, the palace officials and the townspeople; they beat off the assaults with artillery and stones and foiled a ruse by deserters (Ammianus 31.15).
greek_note: The defence relied on the people of a Greek-speaking Thracian city as well as on soldiers of the eastern army.
sources: Ammianus 31.15; en.wikipedia Gothic War (376-382)

name: Hebrus
place: on the river Hebrus (Maritsa), near Hadrianopolis
borderline: No standard name: a night ambush of Gothic plunderers, called Sebastianus's ambush in Wikipedia's article on the war.
roman_force: A picked force drawn from the units of Valens' eastern army at Hadrianopolis, about 2,000 men (Zosimus 4.23), under Sebastianus, who surprised the Goths at night.
greek_note: Valens' eastern field army was recruited in Thrace, Anatolia and Syria as well as among Germanic volunteers.
sources: Ammianus Marcellinus 31.11; Zosimus 4.23; en.wikipedia Gothic War (376-382)
note: Ammianus says Sebastianus hid his men behind mounds and thickets until nightfall and destroyed nearly all the sleeping Goths; the success encouraged Valens to seek battle at Adrianople.

name: Constantinople
commanders_a: unknown; the empress Dominica paid volunteers (Socrates)
borderline: A sortie before the walls rather than a pitched battle.
roman_force: The city garrison with a band of Saracen (Arab) auxiliaries and armed citizens (Ammianus 31.16.4-7; Socrates, Ecclesiastical History 5.1).
greek_note: Socrates says the people of Constantinople took up arms with the Saracens.
sources: Ammianus 31.16.4-7; Socrates, Ecclesiastical History 5.1; Sozomen 7.1; Zosimus 4.22; en.wikipedia Gothic War (376-382)
note: Ammianus tells of a Saracen who drank the blood of a slain Goth, which unnerved the Goths.

name: Thessalonica
roman_force: Theodosius' rebuilt eastern army of new recruits and barbarian, largely Gothic, enlistments, with Egyptian units brought to Macedonia in exchange for Goths sent to Egypt; the barbarian recruits went over to the enemy (Zosimus 4.30-31).
greek_note: Zosimus says Theodosius recruited heavily in the East and brought Egyptian troops to Macedonia.
sources: Zosimus 4.30-31; en.wikipedia Battle of Thessalonica (380)
note: Zosimus does not name the site precisely.

name: Danube
place: the lower Danube, Scythia Minor or Moesia
borderline: No standard name.
roman_force: Promotus with the army of Thrace and the Danube river fleet, whose warships rammed and sank the Greuthungi's dugout boats as they crossed at night (Zosimus 4.38-39).
greek_note: The army of Thrace and the Danube flotilla were recruited in the Latin- and Thracian-speaking Danube provinces, with Greek in the coastal cities.
sources: Zosimus 4.35, 4.38-39; Claudian, Fourth Consulship of Honorius; Consularia Constantinopolitana s.a. 386; en.wikipedia Odotheus
note: A river battle fought by the Roman Danube fleet. Zosimus tells the story twice; survivors were settled in Phrygia.

name: Save
war: Civil war of Theodosius I and Magnus Maximus
place: on the Save near Siscia (Sisak), Pannonia Savia
roman_force: Theodosius' eastern army with barbarian cavalry of Goths, Huns and Alans (Pacatus, Panegyrici Latini 2(12).32), which swam the Save and routed Maximus' troops of the western army.
greek_note: Greek speakers served in Theodosius' eastern regiments; Maximus' army of Gaul and Britain had almost none, and much of Theodosius' cavalry was barbarian.
sources: Panegyrici Latini 2(12).32-34; Orosius 7.35.3-4; Zosimus 4.46; en.wikipedia Battle of Poetovio
note: Also called the battle of Siscia.

name: Poetovio
war: Civil war of Theodosius I and Magnus Maximus
roman_force: Theodosius' eastern army with its Gothic, Hunnic and Alan contingents against Maximus' main western army under Marcellinus, which fought hard before breaking (Pacatus, Panegyrici Latini 2(12).35-36).
greek_note: Greek speakers served in Theodosius' eastern regiments; Maximus' army of Gaul and Britain had almost none.
sources: Panegyrici Latini 2(12).35-36; Orosius 7.35.4; Zosimus 4.46; en.wikipedia Battle of Poetovio
note: Maximus was handed over at Aquileia and executed on 28 August 388.

name: Hebrus
place: the Hebrus (Maritsa) valley, southern Thrace; Zosimus places the attack on Theodosius in the marshes of Macedonia
borderline: No standard name; known from Claudian's praise of Stilicho and from Zosimus, whose accounts differ.
roman_force: Theodosius' eastern army with Stilicho; Zosimus says barbarians hiding in the marshes nearly captured the emperor, and Claudian that Stilicho trapped Alaric's Goths by the Hebrus but was ordered to let them go.
greek_note: Theodosius' eastern army was recruited partly in Greek-speaking Thrace and Asia Minor, beside many Goths.
sources: Claudian, Against Rufinus 1 and On the Consulship of Stilicho 1; Zosimus 4.48-49; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles; en.wikipedia Alaric I
note: Outcome unclear: Wikipedia's list gives a Roman victory under Stilicho; Zosimus describes a near-disaster for Theodosius.

name: Frigidus
war: Civil war of Theodosius I and Eugenius
place: the valley of the Frigidus (Vipava), in the Julian Alps
commanders_a: Theodosius I; Timasius and Stilicho; Gainas, Alaric, Saul and Bacurius (barbarian contingents)
roman_force: Theodosius' eastern field army under Timasius and Stilicho, with about 20,000 Gothic foederati under Gainas and Alaric and other barbarians under Saul and Bacurius (Zosimus 4.57-58), against the western field army of Arbogast and Eugenius, with Frankish and Alamannic contingents; about 10,000 Goths fell on the first day (Orosius 7.35).
greek_note: Greek speakers served only in Theodosius' eastern regiments; most troops on both sides were Latin or Germanic speakers.
sources: Zosimus 4.54-58; Orosius 7.35; Rufinus, Ecclesiastical History 11.33; Socrates 5.25; Theodoret 5.24; Claudian, Third Consulship of Honorius; en.wikipedia Battle of the Frigidus
note: On the second day the bora wind blew into the westerners' faces, as Christian writers stressed. Bacurius fell; Arbogast killed himself.

name: Pholoe
place: Mount Pholoe, between Elis and Arcadia
borderline: A blockade of the Goths on the mountain with little recorded fighting; rarely treated as a named battle.
roman_force: Stilicho's western field army, shipped to the Peloponnese, with barbarian federates whose reliability was later blamed for Alaric's escape (Zosimus 5.7; Claudian).
greek_note: The field army of Italy and Gaul had few Greek speakers; a few eastern-recruited units kept since 395 are possible.
sources: Zosimus 5.7; Claudian, De IV consulatu Honorii 459-483; en.wikipedia Stilicho
note: Stilicho surrounded the Goths on Mount Pholoe but let Alaric escape to Epirus; Claudian claims a victory. Wikipedia's Stilicho article speaks of a victory 'in Macedonia' in 397.

name: Ardalio
place: On the river Ardalio, between Theveste and Ammaedara, Africa Proconsularis
roman_force: Mascezel led about 5,000 veterans of the Gallic field army (Claudian names the Ioviani, Herculiani, Augustei, Nervii and other units); Gildo had the regular garrison of Africa and a great Moorish and Gaetulian cavalry, put at 70,000 (Orosius 7.36).
greek_note: Both armies came from Gaul and Latin-speaking Africa; no Greek units are recorded.
sources: Orosius 7.36; Claudian, De bello Gildonico; Zosimus 5.11; en.wikipedia Gildonic revolt
note: The site on the Ardalio between Theveste (Tebessa) and Ammaedara (Haidra) is not precisely located. Most of Gildo's regulars went over to Mascezel and the Moorish cavalry fled, so the victory was almost bloodless; Gildo was caught at Tabraca and killed himself (31 July 398).

name: Hellespont
place: The Hellespont, off the Thracian Chersonese
borderline: Gainas was a Roman magister militum in revolt with Gothic soldiers of the imperial army; the battle could be classed as civil.
roman_force: Fravitta's liburnian warships of the eastern navy with imperial troops, against the rafts on which Gainas's Goths tried to cross from Thrace to Asia (Zosimus 5.21).
greek_note: The eastern fleet was crewed from the Aegean and Asian coasts; its commander and some of the soldiers were Goths.
sources: Zosimus 5.21; Socrates 6.6; Sozomen 8.4; en.wikipedia Gainas
note: Gainas escaped across the Danube and was killed by the Huns of Uldin, who sent his head to Arcadius (January 401). The massacre of his Goths in Constantinople (12 July 400) is excluded as a massacre.

name: Pollentia
roman_force: Stilicho's field army of Italy, reinforced by units withdrawn from Raetia, the Rhine and perhaps Britain, with Alan federate cavalry (under Saul, per Orosius 7.37) whose leader fell; modern estimates are 10,000-15,000 on each side.
greek_note: The western army was recruited in Italy, Gaul and among Germanic and Alan federates; no Greek units are recorded.
sources: Claudian, De bello Getico; Orosius 7.37; Prudentius, Contra Symmachum 2; Jordanes, Getica 154-155; en.wikipedia Battle of Pollentia
note: Result disputed: Roman sources claim a clear victory (the Gothic camp, with Alaric's wife, was taken), Jordanes a Gothic one; Alaric withdrew in good order.

name: Asti (siege)
borderline: A blockade of the emperor's refuge; no assault is recorded.
roman_force: The emperor's escort in the town, relieved by Stilicho with the field army of Italy, strengthened by units recalled from Raetia and the Rhine and by Alan federates (Claudian, De bello Getico).
greek_note: The western field army was Latin- and Germanic-speaking; Greek speakers were at most a handful.
sources: Claudian, De bello Getico; Claudian, De VI consulatu Honorii; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles; en.wikipedia Battle of Pollentia
note: Alaric withdrew west when Stilicho arrived. Claudian is vague about the town, usually identified as Hasta; some put Alaric's siege of Honorius at Milan instead.

name: Verona
roman_force: Stilicho's field army of Italy with federate troops; many of Alaric's own Gothic chiefs deserted to Stilicho (Claudian, De VI consulatu Honorii).
greek_note: As at Pollentia, a Latin- and Germanic-speaking western army.
sources: Claudian, De VI consulatu Honorii 201-330; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles; en.wikipedia Battle of Pollentia
note: Wikipedia dates it June 402; many historians prefer 403. Alaric escaped and left Italy for Illyricum.

name: Faesulae
place: The hills of Faesulae (Fiesole), above Florence
roman_force: Thirty numeri of the western field army with Hunnic federates under Uldin, Gothic under Sarus, and Alans (Zosimus 5.26).
greek_note: A western army with steppe and Germanic federates; no Greek units recorded.
sources: Zosimus 5.26; Orosius 7.37; Augustine, De civitate Dei 5.23; Olympiodorus fr. 9; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles
note: Radagaisus' host (Goths with others) was surrounded and starved rather than beaten in a pitched battle; 12,000 of his best men were taken into Roman service. Radagaisus was executed on 23 August 406.

name: Florence (siege)
borderline: No assault or relief battle is described: the city was close to surrender when Stilicho's approach ended the siege; the fighting that followed is the Faesulae entry.
roman_force: The townspeople, relieved by Stilicho's army gathered at Ticinum: thirty numeri of Roman troops with Alan and Hunnic federates under Uldin and Goths under Sarus, perhaps 15,000-20,000 men; slaves were enrolled (Zosimus 5.26; Orosius 7.37).
greek_note: The thirty numeri came from the western field army; the federates were Huns, Alans and Goths.
sources: Zosimus 5.26; Orosius 7.37; Paulinus, Vita Ambrosii 50; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles; en.wikipedia Stilicho
note: Stilicho's arrival ended the siege and drove Radagaisus onto the hills of Faesulae (next entry); Florence was nearly lost.

name: Valence (siege)
roman_force: Sarus led a small, largely Gothic army of Honorius, which had beaten and killed Constantine's general Justinianus; Constantine held Valence with the army of Britain and Gaul and was relieved by Gerontius and Edobichus with newly raised Franks and Alamanni (Zosimus 6.2).
greek_note: Both sides were western armies of Britain, Gaul and Italy with Germanic recruits.
sources: Zosimus 6.2; Olympiodorus fr. 13; Sozomen 9.11-13; en.wikipedia Constantine III (Western Roman emperor)
note: Before the siege Sarus defeated and killed Justinianus and treacherously killed Nebiogastes; he gave up after seven days and had to buy his way over the Alps from the Bagaudae.

name: Pisa
borderline: A small action known only from Zosimus; no standard battle name.
roman_force: 300 Huns sent from Ravenna under Olympius; they killed 1,100 Goths and lost 17 men (Zosimus 5.45.6).
greek_note: The force was entirely Hunnic.
sources: Zosimus 5.45.6; livius.org Zosimus, New History 5.45
note: The Goths were the reinforcements Athaulf was bringing from Pannonia to Alaric; Zosimus does not name Athaulf in the sentence. Olympius fell from power soon after.

name: Ostia
place: Portus, the harbour of Rome at Ostia
borderline: Treated as a battle only in Jaques's dictionary; the ancient sources describe Alaric's seizure of Portus, which forced the Senate to accept Attalus as emperor.
roman_force: The garrison of Portus, Rome's grain harbour; no units are recorded.
greek_note: Rome's harbour town had eastern traders, but the garrison is unknown.
sources: Zosimus 6.6; Olympiodorus fr. 13; en.wikipedia Battle of Ostia (409) (after Jaques, Dictionary of Battles and Sieges)

name: Arles (siege)
place: Arelate (Arles), and the Rhone crossing nearby
roman_force: Constantius led Honorius's field army of Italy and took over the siege that the rebel Gerontius had begun; Edobichus's relief army of Franks and Alamanni with Gallic troops was ambushed by Ulfilas's cavalry across the Rhone (Sozomen 9.14; Zosimus 6.13; Olympiodorus).
greek_note: All the armies involved were western, from Italy, Gaul and the Rhine.
sources: Sozomen 9.13-15; Olympiodorus fr. 17; Gregory of Tours 2.9 (Frigeridus); en.wikipedia Constantine III (Western Roman emperor)
note: Gerontius besieged Constantine in Arles first; most of his troops deserted to Constantius and he fled to Spain. The defeat of Edobichus is sometimes listed as a separate battle. Constantine surrendered and was executed in August or September 411.

name: Utriculum
place: Utriculum, probably Ocriculum (Otricoli) on the Via Flaminia
borderline: Only Hydatius reports a battle; Orosius and Marcellinus say Heraclian fled when Marinus approached.
roman_force: Heraclian, comes Africae, landed with the army of Africa (Orosius 7.42 gives an incredible 3,700 ships) and was met by Honorius's forces of Italy under the comes Marinus; Hydatius claims 50,000 dead.
greek_note: Both armies were western, from Africa and Italy.
sources: Hydatius 51, 56; Orosius 7.42; Marcellinus Comes s.a. 413; en.wikipedia Heraclianus
note: Heraclian fled to Carthage and was put to death there.

name: Massilia (siege)
roman_force: The defenders of Massilia under Bonifacius, who wounded Athaulf himself (Olympiodorus fr. 22).
greek_note: Massilia was a Greek foundation, but by the fifth century its people spoke Latin; Greek survived only marginally.
sources: Olympiodorus fr. 22; en.wikipedia Siege of Massilia (413)
note: The Goths were Visigoths. Athaulf withdrew and later married Galla Placidia at Narbo (414).

name: Nervasos Mountains
place: The Nervasian mountains (Nerbasii montes), Gallaecia; site unknown
roman_force: The field troops of Spain under the comes Hispaniarum Asterius with forces of the vicarius Maurocellus, coming to relieve the Suebi of Hermeric (Hydatius 71).
greek_note: The Roman troops in Spain were western and locally raised.
sources: Hydatius 71, 74; en.wikipedia Battle of the Nervasos Mountains
note: The Vandals lifted their siege of the Suebi when Asterius approached, but on their retreat they killed some of Maurocellus's men at Bracara (Braga); the usurper Maximus, backed by barbarians, was put down at the same time.

name: Arzanene
borderline: Not a separately named battle in most works; recorded as Ardabur's victory over Narses after his raid into Arzanene.
roman_force: The field army of the East under Ardabur, an Alan; no units are named (Socrates 7.18).
greek_note: The army of the East was recruited in Anatolia, Syria and Armenia, with Gothic and other federates.
sources: Socrates 7.18; en.wikipedia Roman-Sasanian War of 421-422
note: Narses retreated to Nisibis.

name: Nisibis (siege)
roman_force: Ardabur's field army of the East, reinforced and equipped with siege engines (Socrates 7.18).
greek_note: As at Arzanene, the eastern field army of Anatolia, Syria and Armenia.
sources: Socrates 7.18; Malalas 14.23; en.wikipedia Roman-Sasanian War of 421-422
note: Ardabur burned his engines and withdrew on the approach of Bahram V and his Lakhmid allies under al-Mundhir; Socrates then tells how the Lakhmids were routed and drowned in the Euphrates, a story of miraculous tone.

name: Theodosiopolis (siege)
place: Theodosiopolis, probably in Armenia (Erzurum); possibly Resaina in Osroene
roman_force: The townspeople and garrison led by Bishop Eunomius; no relief army came (Theodoret, Historia ecclesiastica 5.37).
greek_note: A frontier town of Armenia (or Osroene) whose people spoke Armenian or Syriac; Greek was the language of the officials and clergy.
sources: Theodoret, Historia ecclesiastica 5.37; en.wikipedia Roman-Sasanian War of 421-422
note: The Persians gave up after 30 days when a stone from a catapult (said to be blessed by the bishop) killed a subject king; the account is hagiographic and the town's identity disputed.

name: Tarraco
roman_force: Castinus, magister utriusque militiae, led palatine units of the field army of Italy with Gothic federates from Aquitaine, perhaps 10,000-15,000 men in all (Heather); the Goths deserted him (Hydatius 77).
greek_note: A western army of Italian palatini and Gothic federates.
sources: Hydatius 77; Prosper s.a. 422; Salvian 7.11; en.wikipedia Battle of Tarraco
note: The battle was fought in Baetica; the name Tarraco comes from a modern addition to an online translation of Hydatius (Castinus may have retreated to Tarraco). The Vandals kept Baetica.

name: Ravenna
commanders_a: Aspar; Ardabur (a prisoner in the city)
borderline: The city fell to Aspar's men, led through the marshes by a shepherd (Socrates) or by treachery of the garrison; whether there was real fighting is unclear.
roman_force: Aspar led the cavalry of the eastern army sent by Theodosius II from Thessalonica and Aquileia (the fleet under Ardabur had been wrecked and he captured); Joannes held Ravenna with the palace troops of Italy.
greek_note: The attackers were an eastern field army raised in Thrace and Anatolia with Gothic and Alan officers; the defenders were Latin-speaking Italians.
sources: Socrates 7.23; Philostorgius 12.13-14; Procopius, Wars 3.3.8-9; Olympiodorus fr. 43; en.wikipedia Joannes
note: Here roman_state marks the eastern army fighting for the western throne. Aetius arrived three days after Joannes's execution with a large Hunnic army and skirmished with Aspar's troops before a settlement (Philostorgius).

name: Arles (siege)
roman_force: Aetius with the troops of Gaul and the Huns he had brought to Italy for the usurper Joannes; the Goths left 'not unpunished' when he approached (Prosper s.a. 425).
greek_note: A Gallic army with Hunnic auxiliaries.
sources: Prosper s.a. 425; en.wikipedia Siege of Arles (425)
note: The Goths were Visigoths. Theodoric made peace and his Goths were later sent against the Vandals.

name: Arles
borderline: Known from one line of Hydatius.
roman_force: The army of Gaul under Aetius; the sources give no units or numbers. In these years it combined the Gallic comitatenses with Hunnic and other federates (assumed from the period, not stated).
greek_note: The Gallic field army was raised in Gaul and among Germanic and Hunnic federates.
sources: Hydatius, Chronicle s.a. 430; en.wikipedia Flavius Aetius; en.wikipedia Battle of Arles (435)
note: Hydatius: the Goths were beaten by Aetius in a fight not far from Arles and their noble Anaolsus was captured. Wikipedia's 'Battle of Arles (435)', sourced only to Jaques, describes a Gothic siege of Arles broken by Aetius and his Huns that is not in the ancient sources; it is probably this battle (or the siege of 425) misdated, and is not entered separately.

name: Hippo Regius (siege)
roman_force: Bonifacius with what remained of the army of Africa, his bucellarii and Gothic federates, in a city crowded with refugees (Possidius, Vita Augustini 28-29; Procopius, Wars 3.3).
greek_note: The African army and Gothic federates were Latin- and Germanic-speaking.
sources: Possidius, Vita Augustini 28-29; Procopius, Wars 3.3.30-36; en.wikipedia Siege of Hippo Regius
note: Augustine died in the besieged city on 28 August 430. The Vandals raised the siege after about 14 months (a technical Roman success), but occupied the abandoned city after the battle of 431/432.

name: Hippo Regius
roman_force: Bonifacius's African army joined by an eastern expeditionary army under Aspar sent by Theodosius II (Procopius, Wars 3.3.35-36).
greek_note: The eastern army, raised in Thrace and Anatolia, may have made up a large part of the force.
sources: Procopius, Wars 3.3.35-36; en.wikipedia Siege of Hippo Regius
note: A joint western and eastern army; roman_state gives the western command. The future emperor Marcian, then Aspar's officer, was said to have been captured here.

name: Rimini
war: Civil war of Aetius and Bonifacius
roman_force: Bonifacius brought part of his African troops, mainly his bucellarii, with Italian forces; Aetius came with troops from Gaul; modern estimates put both armies together below 7,000 men.
greek_note: Both armies were western, from Africa, Italy and Gaul.
sources: Hydatius 99; Prosper s.a. 432; Marcellinus Comes s.a. 432; en.wikipedia Battle of Ravenna (432)
note: Also called the Battle of Ravenna. Bonifacius won but died of his wounds; Aetius returned to power with Hunnic help in 433.

name: Narbonne
roman_force: Litorius led Hunnic auxiliaries and the field army of Gaul; each horseman carried two measures of wheat for the starving city (Prosper s.a. 436; Sidonius, Carm. 7.246-248).
greek_note: A Gallic army with Hunnic cavalry.
sources: Prosper s.a. 436; Sidonius, Carmen 7.246-248; en.wikipedia Battle of Narbonne (436)
note: The Visigoths besieging Narbonne were routed before they could form a line, and the siege was relieved (437).

name: Mons Colubrarius
place: Mons Colubrarius, perhaps the Roc de la Garde Roland near Olonzac
roman_force: Aetius with the field army of Gaul and probably Hunnic auxiliaries; no units are recorded. Hydatius says 8,000 Goths were killed.
greek_note: A Gallic army; no Greek units recorded.
sources: Merobaudes, Panegyric 1 fr. IIA; Hydatius 112; en.wikipedia Battle of Mons Colubrarius
note: Site uncertain; the panegyric may exaggerate.

name: Toulouse
roman_force: Litorius's army was largely Hunnic auxiliaries with Gallic troops (Prosper s.a. 439; Salvian, De gubernatione Dei 7.39).
greek_note: A Gallic army whose core was Hunnic.
sources: Prosper s.a. 439; Hydatius 117; Salvian 7.39-40; en.wikipedia Battle of Toulouse (439)
note: The Goths also lost heavily; Avitus then made peace with Theodoric.

name: Panormus (siege)
borderline: No fighting is described: Gaiseric besieged the city and failed to take it.
roman_force: Unknown: the garrison and citizens of Panormus; no commander is named, and the western field army under Sigisvult was guarding the coasts of Italy.
greek_note: Sicily was bilingual; Panormus, a Roman colony, was mainly Latin-speaking with a Greek-speaking population.
sources: Hydatius, Chronicle s.a. 440; Cassiodorus, Chronica s.a. 440; en.wikipedia Vandal War (439-442)
note: Gaiseric then ravaged Sicily and may have occupied Lilybaeum; an eastern fleet reached Sicily in 441 but was recalled.

name: Naissus (siege)
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Naissus, who fought the Huns' rams and wheeled towers with stones from the walls (Priscus fr. 6).
greek_note: Naissus lay in the Latin-speaking part of the Balkans.
sources: Priscus fr. 6 (Blockley); en.wikipedia Attila
note: Thompson dates the fall to 443; others to 442. Priscus found the riverbank still full of bones years later.

name: Utus
place: On the river Utus (Vit), Dacia Ripensis
roman_force: The praesental army and the field armies of Thrace and Illyricum under the magister militum Arnegisclus, a Goth; their paper strength has been estimated at about 71,000.
greek_note: The Balkan field armies drew on Thrace, Illyricum and Anatolia (and Gothic federates); Latin and Greek speakers both served.
sources: Marcellinus Comes s.a. 447; Jordanes, Romana 331; Chronicon Paschale s.a. 447; en.wikipedia Battle of the Utus
note: The Roman field armies were destroyed, but the Huns also lost heavily; Marcianopolis fell soon after.

name: Chersonesus
roman_force: A second eastern army, apparently the troops left around Constantinople and in Thrace; no units are recorded (Priscus fr. 9.3).
greek_note: Troops gathered near the capital were drawn from Thrace and Anatolia, with Gothic and Isaurian soldiers.
sources: Priscus fr. 9.3 (Blockley); en.wikipedia Battle of the Utus; en.wikipedia Attila
note: Dated 447 by Maenchen-Helfen, Blockley and the Wikipedia Utus article; Thompson and Wikipedia's Attila article put it in 443, after an unnamed defeat outside Constantinople. Peace was made by Anatolius 'after the battle in the Chersonese'.

name: Asemus
place: Asemus (Asamus), a fort near the mouth of the Osam on the Danube
borderline: A local resistance by sorties, described only by Priscus; not a named battle in most works.
roman_force: The citizen militia of the fortified town of Asemus, who sallied out, killed many Huns and freed captives (Priscus fr. 9.3).
greek_note: A Danube town of Latin-speaking Moesia.
sources: Priscus fr. 9.3 (Blockley)
note: Attila later demanded the return of the Hunnic prisoners the Asemuntians held.

name: Vicus Helena
place: Vicus Helena, in the territory of the Atrebates (Artois); site unidentified
roman_force: Aetius's army of Gaul, with the young Majorian leading the cavalry that surprised a Frankish wedding feast (Sidonius, Carm. 5.210-218).
greek_note: A Gallic army.
sources: Sidonius, Carmen 5.210-218; Gregory of Tours 2.9; en.wikipedia Battle of Vicus Helena
note: The Franks were Salian Franks. Proposed sites include Lens, Hélesmes, Évin and Allaines.

name: Catalaunian Plains
place: The Catalaunian Plains (Campus Mauriacus), Champagne; site unknown
commanders_a: Flavius Aetius; Theodoric I (killed); Thorismund; Sangiban
roman_force: Aetius's Roman field army of Gaul (modern estimate about 20,000 comitatenses, with limitanei) and federates: the Visigoths under Theodoric I, Sangiban's Alans, Salian and Ripuarian Franks, Burgundians, Saxons, Sarmatians, Armoricans, Liticiani and Olibriones (Jordanes, Getica 191).
greek_note: The army of Gaul and its federates spoke Latin, Germanic, Iranian (Alan) and Celtic (Armorican) tongues; no eastern units are recorded.
sources: Jordanes, Getica 190-218; Hydatius 150; Prosper s.a. 451; en.wikipedia Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
note: Wikipedia's infobox calls it inconclusive; Attila was driven back to his laager and then withdrew from Gaul. Date 20 June after Bury (others: early July or 27 September). Proposed sites: Montgueux near Troyes, Méry-sur-Seine, La Cheppe. Attila's allies included Ostrogoths and Gepids.

name: Orléans (siege)
commanders_a: Bishop Anianus (in the city); Flavius Aetius and Theodoric I (relief)
roman_force: The citizens and the Alans settled there, relieved by Aetius's coalition of the Roman army of Gaul with the Visigoths and other federates (Jordanes, Getica 194-195; Vita Aniani).
greek_note: A Gallic army and Germanic and Alan federates.
sources: Jordanes, Getica 194-195; Gregory of Tours 2.7; Vita Aniani; en.wikipedia Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
note: Attila broke off his final assault when the relief army approached; some historians see the defence of Orléans as the real turning point of 451.

name: Mediolanum (siege)
borderline: A capture with no fighting recorded; included because Wikipedia's list of Roman battles names a siege of Mediolanum (452). Round 1 excluded it with Ticinum and Patavium.
roman_force: Unknown: the garrison and citizens of Mediolanum; Aetius' field army did not defend the cities of the Po valley.
greek_note: A Latin-speaking city of northern Italy.
sources: Jordanes, Getica 222; Prosper s.a. 452; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles
note: After Aquileia fell the Huns took the cities of Venetia, then Mediolanum and Ticinum; the sources describe no resistance.

name: Aquileia (siege)
date: 452 (fell after about three months; sack traditionally 18 July)
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Aquileia, strongly walled and held without relief by a field army (Jordanes, Getica 219-221; Procopius, Wars 3.4.30-35).
greek_note: Aquileia was a Latin city with an eastern merchant community.
sources: Jordanes, Getica 219-221; Procopius, Wars 3.4.30-35; Prosper s.a. 452; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles
note: The city was razed. The Huns then took Mediolanum, Ticinum and Patavium, apparently without battles (excluded).

name: Placentia
roman_force: Ricimer and Majorian had most of the comitatenses of Italy with Germanic federates; Avitus had part of the Gallic army, without his Visigothic allies, who were in Spain.
greek_note: Both armies were western, from Italy and Gaul.
sources: Hydatius 183; John of Antioch fr. 202; Fasti Vindobonenses priores s.a. 456; en.wikipedia Battle of Placentia (456)
note: Avitus was deposed and made bishop of Piacenza, and died soon after.

name: Agrigentum
roman_force: Ricimer, then comes, with Roman troops, auxiliaries and Germanic federates of the army of Italy (Sidonius, Carm. 2.367; Hydatius 177).
greek_note: Fought in Sicily, where Greek was still widely spoken, but the army was the Latin- and Germanic-speaking army of Italy.
sources: Sidonius, Carmen 2.367; Hydatius 176-177; Priscus fr. 31; en.wikipedia Battle of Agrigentum (456)
note: The Vandals came with sixty ships; the victory gave only brief relief from their raids.

name: Corsica
roman_force: Ricimer's ships and troops of the army of Italy, which 'by a ruse' destroyed a Vandal force of sixty ships bound for Gaul or Italy (Hydatius 176).
greek_note: A western force; the crews may have included Greek-speaking sailors from southern Italy and Sicily.
sources: Hydatius 176; en.wikipedia Battle of Agrigentum (456)
note: Hydatius places the destruction of the Vandals 'in Corsica'; it may have been partly a land action. Ricimer had pursued the Vandal survivors north after Agrigentum.

name: Campi Cannini
place: Campi Canini, usually placed on the Magadino plain near Bellinzona, north of Lake Maggiore
roman_force: A detachment under the comes Burco sent by Majorian, then magister militum, against about 900 Alamannic raiders (Sidonius, Carm. 5.373-385).
greek_note: A small detachment of the army of Italy.
sources: Sidonius, Carmen 5.373-385; en.wikipedia Battle of Campi Cannini; en.wikipedia Majorian
note: Wikipedia places it 'near Lake Maggiore, Italy'; Gregory of Tours puts the Canini campi near Bellinzona.

name: Garigliano
place: Mouth of the Liris (Garigliano), near Sinuessa
roman_force: Majorian led the field army of Italy against a raiding force of Vandals and Moors, many of whom were killed before reaching their ships (Sidonius, Carm. 5.385-440).
greek_note: The army of Italy; no Greek units recorded.
sources: Sidonius, Carmen 5.385-440; en.wikipedia Battle of Garigliano (457); en.wikipedia Majorian

name: Arelate
roman_force: Majorian's army, a host of federates that Sidonius lists poetically (Huns, Alans, Rugians, Burgundians, Ostrogoths, Suebi, Bastarnae, Sarmatians and others), with Aegidius's army of Gaul, which held Arles (Sidonius, Carm. 5.470-477).
greek_note: An army of Italy and Gaul largely made up of barbarian federates.
sources: Sidonius, Carmen 5; Hydatius 197; Gregory of Tours 2.11; en.wikipedia Battle of Arelate; en.wikipedia Majorian
note: Also called the Battle of Arles (458). Theodoric II had been besieging Aegidius in Arles; after the defeat the Visigoths returned to federate status and gave up Septimania.

name: Toulouse
borderline: Probably a doublet of Arelate (458); the ancient sources describe no battle at Toulouse in that campaign.
roman_force: Majorian's army of federates and the army of Gaul (as at Arelate).
greek_note: As at Arelate.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Toulouse (458) (after Jaques, Dictionary of Battles and Sieges)

name: Lugdunum (siege)
borderline: Little is known of the fighting; some treat it only as an occupation of the city.
roman_force: Majorian's army of federates with the troops of Gaul (Sidonius, Carm. 5 and 13).
greek_note: As at Arelate.
sources: Sidonius, Carmina 5 and 13; en.wikipedia Majorian
note: The Burgundians, perhaps with Gallo-Roman supporters of Avitus, held Lyon; the city was heavily fined, and Sidonius pleaded for tax relief.

name: Cartagena
place: Portus Ilicitanus (Santa Pola), bay of Alicante
roman_force: The invasion fleet of about 300 ships that Majorian had built for Africa, surprised at anchor after some of its captains had been bribed (Hydatius 200; Marius of Avenches s.a. 460).
greek_note: A western fleet built in Italy and Spain.
sources: Hydatius 200; Marius of Avenches s.a. 460; en.wikipedia Battle of Cartagena (461)
note: Despite the name it was fought near Elche (Ilici), not at Cartagena; 13 May 460 is sometimes given. Majorian made peace and was deposed and killed in 461.

name: Orléans
roman_force: Aegidius's army of northern Gaul, the remnant of the Gallic field army, probably with Salian Franks under Childeric (Hydatius 218; Gregory of Tours 2.18).
greek_note: A Gallic army with Frankish allies.
sources: Hydatius 218; Chronica Gallica 511; Marius of Avenches s.a. 463; Gregory of Tours 2.18; en.wikipedia Battle of Orleans (463)
note: Aegidius, magister militum per Gallias, had broken with Ricimer and Libius Severus and held northern Gaul on his own; he is counted here as a Roman commander. Frederic was the brother of Theodoric II.

name: Bergamo
roman_force: Ricimer with the army of Italy, largely Germanic federates (Fasti Vindobonenses priores s.a. 464; Jordanes, Getica 236).
greek_note: The army of Italy, by now mostly Germanic federates.
sources: Fasti Vindobonenses priores s.a. 464; Marcellinus Comes s.a. 464; Jordanes, Getica 236; en.wikipedia Battle of Bergamo
note: The day is flagged as uncertain on Wikipedia.

name: Serdica
borderline: Known only from Sidonius's panegyric of Anthemius; rarely named as a battle.
roman_force: Anthemius with an eastern army; its cavalry commander, perhaps a barbarian, deserted to the Huns before the battle, and the infantry won alone (Sidonius, Carm. 2.269-298).
greek_note: The Balkan armies drew on Thrace, Illyricum and Anatolia; Latin and Greek speakers both served.
sources: Sidonius, Carmen 2.269-298; en.wikipedia Hormidac
note: Hormidac had taken Serdica by surprise after crossing the frozen Danube; the date is uncertain (Wikipedia: winter 466/467).

name: Cap Bon
commanders_b: Basiliscus (Marcellinus and Heraclius of Edessa led other columns)
roman_force: A joint expedition of Leo I and Anthemius: 1,113 ships (Cedrenus) carrying perhaps 30,000 soldiers, about 50,000 men in all with the crews and the western and Dalmatian forces of Marcellinus and Heraclius's column (Heather).
greek_note: The eastern fleet was crewed from the Aegean, Asia Minor and Egypt and carried eastern field troops; the western contingent was Latin-speaking.
sources: Procopius, Wars 3.6; Priscus fr. 53; Candidus fr. 2; Theophanes AM 5961; en.wikipedia Battle of Cap Bon (468)
note: A joint East-West operation; roman_state gives the eastern command. During a truce Gaiseric sent fireships against the anchored fleet; over 100 ships and about 10,000 men were lost.

name: Arles
place: East of the Rhone near Arelate (Arles)
roman_force: Anthemius's army of Italy under his son Anthemiolus, perhaps 10,000 men or more by modern estimate (Chronica Gallica 511 s.a. 471).
greek_note: Anthemius had brought eastern officers and some troops from Constantinople in 467; the army was otherwise western.
sources: Chronica Gallica 511 s.a. 471; Gregory of Tours 2.18; en.wikipedia Battle of Arles (471)
note: The Goths were Visigoths. The Western Empire lost control of the Rhone corridor; Arles fell to Euric about 476.

name: Rome (siege)
war: Civil war of Ricimer and Anthemius
roman_force: Ricimer's army of Italy, largely Germanic federates, with Burgundians and Odoacer's men; Anthemius held Rome with the city's people and his own troops, and Bilimer's relief force from Gaul was beaten at the bridge before Hadrian's mausoleum (Paul the Deacon; John of Antioch fr. 209).
greek_note: Anthemius, an easterner, had some eastern followers; both armies were otherwise western.
sources: John of Antioch fr. 209; Paul the Deacon, Historia Romana 15.3-4; Cassiodorus, Chronicle s.a. 472; en.wikipedia Siege of Rome (472)
note: The city fell after five months; Anthemius was beheaded (by Gundobad, per John of Antioch) on 11 July, and Ricimer died on 19 August 472.

name: Clermont (siege)
date: 474 (the Goths besieged Clermont each season from 471)
roman_force: The citizens of Clermont and Ecdicius's private force of horsemen, with 18 of whom (Sidonius, Ep. 3.3; 10 in Gregory of Tours 2.24) he rode through the besiegers.
greek_note: Sidonius (Ep. 3.3) says the Arvernian nobility was only then shedding 'the scurf of Celtic speech'; no Greek speakers are recorded.
sources: Sidonius, Epistulae 3.3, 7.7; Gregory of Tours 2.24; en.wikipedia Ecdicius
note: The Goths were Visigoths. Clermont never fell; Julius Nepos gave the Auvergne to Euric by treaty in 475.

name: Ravenna
place: Ravenna (Paulus was killed in the pine wood outside Classis)
borderline: Odoacer's Heruli, Sciri and Turcilingi were the federate soldiers of the army of Italy in mutiny; the battle could be classed as civil.
roman_force: The remnant of the army of Italy loyal to Orestes, under his brother Paulus (Anonymus Valesianus 8.37-38).
greek_note: A western army; no Greek units recorded.
sources: Anonymus Valesianus 8.37-38; Fasti Vindobonenses priores s.a. 476; Jordanes, Getica 242; en.wikipedia Battle of Ravenna (476)
note: Orestes was captured and executed at Placentia on 28 August; Paulus fell on 4 September and Romulus Augustulus was deposed.

name: Candavia
place: The Candavian mountains, on the Via Egnatia west of Lychnidus
borderline: A named ambush known only from Malchus; not usually treated as a battle.
roman_force: Sabinianus with the Illyrian field army and local troops, who surprised the Gothic rearguard and took 2,000 wagons and 5,000 prisoners (Malchus fr. 20).
greek_note: The army of Illyricum was recruited mostly in Latin-speaking provinces.
sources: Malchus fr. 20 (Blockley)
note: The Goths were Theodoric the Amal's (Ostrogoths); Theodimund was his brother.

name: Constantinople
borderline: Street fighting in a palace revolt; may count as a riot rather than a battle.
roman_force: Marcian and his brothers led their followers and the city crowd and beat the palace troops; Illus brought Isaurian soldiers over from Chalcedon by night and bought off the rebels (John of Antioch fr. 211; Malchus).
greek_note: The capital's guards and crowd were largely Greek-speaking; Zeno's Isaurians spoke Isaurian and Greek.
sources: John of Antioch fr. 211; Malchus fr. 22; Theophanes AM 5971; en.wikipedia Illus
note: Marcian was captured and sent to Cappadocia (or Papurius).

name: Seleucia
roman_force: Zeno's army of 'Macedonians and Scythians' (perhaps including Goths) under John the Scythian, with Theodoric the Amal named as co-commander; Illus and Leontius had Isaurians and troops of the East who had joined them (Theophanes AM 5976; John of Antioch fr. 214).
greek_note: Both armies came from the eastern provinces, Isauria and the Balkans; Greek was widely spoken in all of them.
sources: Theophanes AM 5976-5977; John of Antioch fr. 214; Malalas 15.13-14; en.wikipedia Illus
note: Wikipedia's Illus article also mentions an earlier rebel victory near Antioch; Seleucia may be the Isaurian city or Seleucia Pieria. The rebels fled to the fort of Papurius.

name: Papurius (siege)
place: The fortress of Papurius (Cherris), Isauria; site unidentified
borderline: A four-year blockade ended by treachery; how much fighting took place is not recorded.
roman_force: John the Scythian's blockading army; the rebels held the Isaurian fortress with Isaurian followers (John of Antioch fr. 214; Theophanes AM 5977-5980).
greek_note: Imperial troops of the East and Isaurians, a largely Hellenized people.
sources: John of Antioch fr. 214; Theophanes AM 5977-5980; Malalas 15.14; en.wikipedia Illus
note: Trocundes was caught trying to break out for help; the fort fell in 488 through the treachery of his brother-in-law, and Illus and Leontius were beheaded.

name: Cotyaeum
commanders_a: John the Scythian; John the Hunchback; Justin
commanders_b: Lilingis (killed); Longinus of Cardala; Conon; Longinus of Selinus
roman_force: The field armies under John the Scythian (magister militum per Orientem) and John the Hunchback (praesentalis), with Gothic and Hunnic contingents under officers such as Apsikal and Sigizan (Theophanes AM 5985); sizes are not given.
greek_note: The imperial army drew on Thrace, Illyricum and Anatolia, with Gothic and Hunnic federates; the rebels were Isaurian highlanders, largely Hellenized.
sources: Theophanes AM 5985; John of Antioch fr. 214b; Evagrius 3.35; en.wikipedia Battle of Cotyaeum; en.wikipedia Isaurian War
note: Counted as civil because the rebels were Roman provincials led by Zeno's brother Longinus and former imperial officers; Wikipedia's infobox treats the Isaurians as a separate belligerent.

name: Claudiopolis (siege)
roman_force: Diogenianus's force besieged in Claudiopolis and the relief army of John the Hunchback, which forced the Taurus passes; a sortie from the town completed the rout (Theophanes AM 5986).
greek_note: As at Cotyaeum.
sources: Theophanes AM 5986; en.wikipedia Isaurian War
note: A siege with a relief battle. The war ended with the deaths or capture of the rebel leaders in 497-498, without further named battles.

name: Bithrapsa
war: Arab raids on the eastern frontier
borderline: Known from one sentence of Theophanes; the site is unidentified.
roman_force: The frontier troops of Euphratensis under their dux Eugenius (Theophanes AM 5990).
greek_note: Frontier troops of northern Syria were raised locally among Syriac and Greek speakers.
sources: Theophanes AM 5990
note: The raiders were Arabs from the Persian side (probably Lakhmids).

name: Tzurta
place: The river Tzurta in Thrace, probably near Tzurulum (Corlu)
commanders_b: Aristus (magister militum per Illyricum); comites Nicostratus, Innocentius, Tancus, Aquilinus (killed)
roman_force: Aristus led 15,000 men of the Illyrian army with 520 wagons of arms; more than 4,000 were killed in flight or over the steep river bank (Marcellinus Comes s.a. 499).
greek_note: The army of Illyricum was recruited mostly in Latin-speaking provinces.
sources: Marcellinus Comes s.a. 499
note: The identification of the Tzurta is uncertain.

name: Amida (siege)
roman_force: The citizens of Amida, with monks and no regular garrison, defended the walls for three months (Joshua the Stylite 50-53; Procopius, Wars 1.7; Zacharias 7.3-4).
greek_note: Amida's people spoke Syriac; Greek was used by officials and the educated.
sources: Joshua the Stylite 50-53; Procopius, Wars 1.7; Zacharias Rhetor 7.3-4; en.wikipedia Anastasian War
note: The city fell by night in January 503 and many of its people were deported to Persia. Martyropolis, which surrendered in 502, is excluded.

name: Edessa (siege)
roman_force: Areobindus with the garrison and the citizens of Edessa, who repulsed the Persian attacks on the gates and walls (Joshua the Stylite 58-62).
greek_note: Edessa was Syriac-speaking, but Areobindus's field troops came largely from Greek-speaking provinces.
sources: Joshua the Stylite 58-62; Procopius, Wars 2.13; en.wikipedia Anastasian War
note: Kavad had demanded 10,000 pounds of gold for peace; the Persians and Lakhmids overran much of Osroene but failed before the city.

name: Constantia (siege)
date: 503 (before the attack on Edessa in September)
borderline: Little fighting is recorded: Kavad stayed only a short time, a plot to betray the city was uncovered, and he moved on to Edessa after receiving supplies from the inhabitants.
roman_force: The garrison and townspeople of Constantia; no commander is recorded.
greek_note: A Syriac-speaking frontier city whose officials and part of the garrison spoke Greek.
sources: Joshua the Stylite, Chronicle; en.wikipedia Anastasian War
note: Wikipedia spells the city Constantia; also called Constantina or Tella.

name: Nisibis
commanders_b: Areobindus (magister militum per Orientem); Romanus; Asouades (Arab phylarch)
roman_force: Areobindus's division of the 52,000-man army sent by Anastasius, with the Arab phylarch Asouades and Gothic officers such as Godidisklus and Bessas (Joshua the Stylite 54-56; Procopius, Wars 1.8).
greek_note: The army of the East was raised in Anatolia, Syria and Armenia, with Goths and Arab allies; Greek and Syriac speakers were numerous.
sources: Joshua the Stylite 54-56; Procopius, Wars 1.8.1-4; en.wikipedia Anastasian War
note: Areobindus first beat a Persian force near Nisibis, then fled west when Kavad came up and his camp at Apadna was plundered.

name: Tell Beshme
place: Between Apadna and Tell Beshme, between Amida and Nisibis
roman_force: The divisions of Patricius and Hypatius, part of the 52,000-man expeditionary army; their cavalry suffered heavily on the retreat to Samosata (Joshua the Stylite 56; Zacharias 7.4; Procopius, Wars 1.8).
greek_note: As at Nisibis (503).
sources: Joshua the Stylite 56; Zacharias Rhetor 7.4; Procopius, Wars 1.8.10-19; en.wikipedia Anastasian War
note: Name after Wikipedia's 'between Apadna and Tell Beshme'; the sources place the defeat differently, and Procopius tells it as a surprise attack on the Roman camp.

name: Amida (siege)
roman_force: Patricius and Celer with the army of the East; the Colchian Pharesmanes killed the Persian commander Glones in an ambush, and Patricius beat a relief force; the Persian garrison numbered 3,000 (Procopius, Wars 1.9; Joshua the Stylite 66-80).
greek_note: As at Nisibis (503), with Colchian and Armenian officers.
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.9; Joshua the Stylite 66-80; en.wikipedia Anastasian War
note: The starving Persian garrison finally gave the city back for a payment in gold (Procopius); the Roman recovery is scored as the besieger's success.

name: Horreum Margi
roman_force: Sabinianus led 10,000 men of the Illyrian army with wagons of arms and supplies (Marcellinus Comes s.a. 505), with a large force of Bulgar allies (Ennodius, Panegyric of Theoderic 12).
greek_note: The Illyrian army came from Latin-speaking provinces, and its Bulgar allies spoke a Turkic tongue.
sources: Marcellinus Comes s.a. 505; Ennodius, Panegyricus 12; Jordanes, Getica 300-301; en.wikipedia Battle of Horreum Margi
note: Sabinianus fled to the fort of Nato. Mundo was a Hunnic-Gepid chief in Ostrogothic service.

name: Acris
roman_force: Hypatius and Alathar led an imperial army put at 80,000; Vitalian had the federate troops of Scythia and Moesia with Huns, Bulgars and Thracian peasants, 50,000-60,000 strong at Constantinople earlier in 513 (John of Antioch fr. 214e; Marcellinus Comes s.a. 514).
greek_note: The imperial army came from the East and Thrace; the rebels from the Latin-speaking Danube provinces with steppe allies.
sources: John of Antioch fr. 214e; Marcellinus Comes s.a. 514; Malalas 16.16; en.wikipedia Vitalian (general)
note: After an initial imperial success, Vitalian's men attacked the imperial laager at night and destroyed most of the army; Hypatius was ransomed only a year later.

name: Golden Horn
place: The entrance of the Golden Horn, and the shore of Sycae (Galata) where Marinus then landed
roman_force: Marinus commanded the imperial ships and the troops he then landed at Sycae, against Vitalian's fleet (some 200 vessels from the Black Sea ports in 514) and his army of Danubian federates with Hunnic and Bulgar allies; Malalas says he used a sulphur-based incendiary devised by the philosopher Proclus of Athens (Malalas 16.16).
greek_note: The capital's ships and the Black Sea ports' vessels were crewed largely by Greek speakers; Vitalian's soldiers came from the Danube provinces.
sources: Malalas 16.16; John of Antioch fr. 214e; en.wikipedia Vitalian (general)
note: Marinus defeated the rebel fleet at the entrance of the Golden Horn, then landed at Sycae and routed the rebels there; counted as one engagement (type sea, with the landing). Vitalian fled north by night; Anastasius gave thanks at the Michaelion of Sosthenion.

name: Persarmenia
borderline: An unnamed defeat on a raid, recorded only by Procopius.
roman_force: Sittas and Belisarius, young officers of Justinian's guard, led a raiding force into Persarmenia; on their second inroad they were beaten by the Armenian brothers Narses and Aratius (Procopius, Wars 1.12.20-22).
greek_note: The forces of Roman Armenia and the guard were raised in Armenia, Anatolia and the Balkans.
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.12.20-22; en.wikipedia Iberian War
note: Greatrex dates the raids to 526; some put the second in 527.

name: Thebetha (siege)
place: Nisibis, then the Persian fortress of Thebetha, fifteen parasangs from Dara
borderline: No standard name; the site of Thebetha is not securely identified (the coordinates are those of Nisibis).
roman_force: The army of the eastern frontier, infantry and cavalry mustered at Dara under the magister militum and dux (Zacharias 9.1); no units or numbers survive.
greek_note: The eastern field army of the 520s was recruited largely in Anatolia, Thrace and Syria.
sources: Zacharias Rhetor, Chronicle 9.1; Procopius, Wars 1.12; en.wikipedia Iberian War
note: Zacharias: the Romans fought at Nisibis but could not take it, then breached the wall of Thebetha but failed to take it in the summer heat; many infantry died of thirst on the march back to Dara. Wikipedia: 'a Roman offensive against Nisibis and Thebetha in that year failed'. Procopius gives the command to Libelarius.

name: Thannuris
place: Thannuris (Tell Tuneinir), on the Khabur, south of Dara
commanders_b: Belisarius, Coutzes, Bouzes, Proclianus, Basil, Sebastian, Vincentius, Jabalah IV
roman_force: The duces and comites of the Mesopotamian frontier under Belisarius (dux of Mesopotamia), Coutzes and Bouzes, with Isaurian infantry and the Ghassanid Arabs of Jabalah IV; no reliable total is given.
greek_note: Isaurian infantry (by then largely Greek-speaking) and frontier troops of Mesopotamia and Syria, beside Latin-speaking Balkan officers and Ghassanid allies.
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.13.1-8; Pseudo-Zachariah of Mytilene, Chronicle 9.2; en.wikipedia Battle of Thannuris
note: The Persians drew the Roman cavalry into concealed ditches; much of the infantry was killed or captured and the unfinished fort was razed. Procopius may compress Thannuris and the fight at Mindouos into one encounter.

name: Mindouos
place: Mindouos (Melebasa, modern Ogunduk), north of Nisibis
borderline: Possibly the same engagement as Thannuris; English Wikipedia keeps a separate short article.
roman_force: Belisarius' frontier army of Mesopotamia, guarding the building of a fort at Mindouos; no numbers given.
greek_note: The eastern frontier army was recruited in Anatolia, Isauria, Syria and the Balkans.
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.13.1-8; en.wikipedia Battle of Mindouos
note: The Romans were routed on the hill near the fort site.

name: Dara
commanders_a: Belisarius, Hermogenes, John son of Nicetas, Bouzes, Pharas, Sunicas, Aigan, Simmas, Ascan
