roman_force: About 25,000 of the eastern field army: cavalry on the wings behind a system of ditches, infantry in the centre, Belisarius' bucellarii in reserve, 600 Hun horse under Sunicas and Aigan, 600 more under Simmas and Ascan, and 300 Heruls under Pharas in ambush (Procopius 1.13).
greek_note: The eastern field army of the 520s-540s drew on Anatolia, Isauria, Thrace, Illyricum and Armenia; Greek speakers were a large part, beside Latin-speaking Balkan soldiers, Armenians and Hun and Herul foederati.
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.13-14; en.wikipedia Battle of Dara
note: The allies are the Hun (Massagete) horse and the Heruls (Germanic peoples) of Pharas. Persian strength about 40,000 plus 10,000 from Nisibis (Procopius).

name: Satala
roman_force: About 15,000 of the new army of the magister militum per Armeniam: Dorotheus held the main body in Satala while Sittas struck from the hills with 1,000 horse; Florentius the Thracian captured the Persian standard (Procopius 1.15).
greek_note: The army of Armenia, created in 528, combined regiments transferred from the East and Thrace with Armenian recruits.
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.15.9-17; en.wikipedia Battle of Satala (530)
note: The Persian army of about 30,000 included Persarmenians, Sunitae and Sabir Huns (allies_b).

name: Callinicum
commanders_b: Belisarius, Hermogenes, Ascan, Sunicas, Simmas, Longinus, Stephanacius, Peter, al-Harith ibn Jabalah
roman_force: About 20,000 (Procopius 1.18): the eastern field army reinforced by Hermogenes, cavalry under Belisarius and Ascan, Isaurian and Lycaonian infantry, Hun horse under Sunicas and Simmas, and some 5,000 Ghassanid cavalry under al-Harith on the right.
greek_note: Procopius names Isaurian and Lycaonian infantry (Anatolian, largely Greek-speaking) beside the Balkan-recruited cavalry and the Ghassanid Arabs.
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.18; John Malalas 18.60; en.wikipedia Battle of Callinicum
note: The Ghassanid wing broke; the Roman infantry held with its back to the river and escaped to Callinicum at night. A costly Persian victory; Malalas gives a different account.

name: Martyropolis (siege)
roman_force: The garrison of Martyropolis under Bouzes and Bessas, with a relief army of the East and Armenia under Sittas and Hermogenes gathering nearby (Procopius 1.21).
greek_note: Garrison and relief army came from the eastern and Armenian field armies.
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.21.4-27; en.wikipedia Iberian War
note: The Persians mined the walls but raised the siege on news of Kavadh I's death (13 September 531) and the approach of the relief army.

name: Ad Decimum
place: the tenth milestone south of Carthage, on the coast road
roman_force: Belisarius' expedition: 10,000 infantry and 5,000 cavalry (regulars and foederati), 600 Huns, 400 Heruls and his own bucellarii, carried on 500 transports with 92 dromons (Procopius 3.11).
greek_note: The expedition combined Thracian and Illyrian (largely Latin-speaking) cavalry, eastern and Isaurian infantry and Hun and Herul foederati; Greek speakers were a large minority.
sources: Procopius, Wars 3.11, 3.17-19; en.wikipedia Battle of Ad Decimum
note: Allies: 600 Hun (Massagete) horse and 400 Heruls (Germanic peoples). Ammatas and Gibamundus were defeated in separate encounters before Belisarius routed Gelimer.

name: Tricamarum
roman_force: About 8,000 of Belisarius' army: the cavalry, led by John the Armenian with the bucellarii, decided the battle before the infantry came up; the Huns held back until the issue was clear (Procopius 4.2-3).
greek_note: The same expeditionary army as at Ad Decimum.
sources: Procopius, Wars 4.2-3; en.wikipedia Battle of Tricamarum
note: Site unidentified. Tzazon, Gelimer's brother, was killed and the Vandal camp taken.

name: Mount Papua (siege)
place: Mount Papua, on the edge of Numidia, near the town of Medeus
borderline: A blockade with one assault, ending in surrender.
roman_force: Pharas with his Heruls and other troops; 110 of them fell in a failed assault on the mountain, after which Pharas blockaded it (Procopius 4.4, 4.6-7).
greek_note: The force was built round Pharas' Herul foederati.
sources: Procopius, Wars 4.4.26-31, 4.6-7; en.wikipedia Vandalic War
note: Gelimer sheltered with the Moors of the mountain (allies_b). Site uncertain (perhaps the Edough massif).

name: Mammes
roman_force: About 18,000 after reinforcements: the regiments left in Africa and most of Belisarius' bucellarii, cavalry and infantry (cavalry dismounted to fight); Solomon broke the camel ring with 500 men (Procopius 4.11).
greek_note: The army of Africa was still the eastern expeditionary army of 533, with Thracian, Illyrian, Isaurian and Anatolian soldiers.
sources: Procopius, Wars 4.11; en.wikipedia Battle of Mammes
note: Procopius gives 10,000 Moorish dead.

name: Mount Bourgaon
roman_force: Solomon's army of about 18,000; Theodorus led some 1,000 excubitors up the mountain to take the Moors from above (Procopius 4.12).
greek_note: The same army as at Mammes, recruited in the eastern and Balkan provinces.
sources: Procopius, Wars 4.12; en.wikipedia Battle of Mount Bourgaon
note: Esdilasas was captured; Procopius' 50,000 Moorish dead is not credible.

name: Panormus (siege)
borderline: The Gothic garrison surrendered once the fleet's archers commanded the walls; little fighting.
roman_force: Belisarius' expedition of 4,000 regulars and foederati, 3,000 Isaurians, 200 Hun foederati and 300 Moors with his bucellarii; archers hoisted in boats to the mastheads shot down into the town (Procopius 5.5).
greek_note: Procopius names 3,000 Isaurians (largely Greek-speaking by then) among some 7,500 men.
sources: Procopius, Wars 5.5.12-16; en.wikipedia Gothic War (535-554)
note: The only real resistance in Sicily.

name: Bagradas River (Membresa)
roman_force: Belisarius, back from Sicily with about 100 guards, rallied some 2,000 loyal troops at Carthage; Stotzas led about 8,000 mutineers of the army of Africa, with Vandal ex-soldiers and runaway slaves (Procopius 4.14-15).
greek_note: Both sides came from the eastern expeditionary army of 533; the Arian Heruls were among the mutineers.
sources: Procopius, Wars 4.14-15; en.wikipedia Battle of the River Bagradas (536)
note: Stotzas had lifted the siege of Carthage on Belisarius' arrival; he fled into Numidia after the defeat.

name: Naples (siege)
roman_force: Belisarius' expeditionary army (about 7,500 with his bucellarii); 400 men under Magnus and the Isaurian Ennes entered through the aqueduct (Procopius 5.8-10).
greek_note: Isaurians led the entry by the aqueduct; the army was the eastern expedition of 535.
sources: Procopius, Wars 5.8-10; en.wikipedia Siege of Naples (536)
note: After about twenty days; the city, defended by its Gothic garrison and many citizens, was sacked.

name: Salona
roman_force: Mundus, magister militum per Illyricum, with the Illyrian field army and his own followers; no numbers.
greek_note: The army of Illyricum was recruited in the Latin-speaking Danubian provinces.
sources: Procopius, Wars 5.7.1-10; en.wikipedia Gothic War (535-554)
note: Mauricius, Mundus' son, fell in a skirmish; Mundus routed the Goths but was killed in the pursuit, and the Roman army withdrew.

name: Rome (siege)
commanders_a: Belisarius, Bessas, Constantinus, Peranius, Martin, Valerian, John nephew of Vitalian
roman_force: About 5,000 of Belisarius' army at first, with armed Roman citizens; then 1,600 horse, mostly Huns, Sclaveni and Antae, under Martin and Valerian, and later 3,000 Isaurians, 800 Thracian horse under John and further detachments (Procopius 5.22-6.5).
greek_note: Procopius names 3,000 Isaurians among the reinforcements beside Thracian cavalry, Huns and Slavs; the citizen militia spoke Latin.
sources: Procopius, Wars 5.18-6.10; en.wikipedia Siege of Rome (537-538)
note: Vitiges withdrew after one year and nine days, when John took Ariminum; the siege included several pitched fights before the walls.

name: Scardon
borderline: A minor engagement known only from Procopius; no standard article.
roman_force: Part of the army of Illyricum that Constantianus had brought by sea from Dyrrachium to recover Dalmatia in 536 (Procopius 5.7, 5.16).
greek_note: The army of Illyricum was raised largely in the Latin-speaking western Balkans, with some men from Epirus.
sources: Procopius, Wars 5.16.12-13 (LacusCurtius)
note: Uligisalus was beaten and fell back to Burnus, where Asinarius joined him before the siege of Salona.

name: Scalas Veteres
roman_force: Germanus' loyal troops, swollen by mutineers he had won back with arrears of pay, against Stotzas' remaining mutineers; Moors under Iaudas and Ortaias waited to join the winner (Procopius 4.17).
greek_note: Both armies came from the eastern regiments sent to Africa in 533.
sources: Procopius, Wars 4.17; en.wikipedia Battle of Scalas Veteres
note: Site unidentified. Stotzas fled with a few followers to Mauretania.

name: Salona (siege)
roman_force: Constantianus' Illyrian troops holding Salona, with a squadron of ships that defeated the Gothic fleet (Procopius 5.16).
greek_note: Constantianus' army came from Illyricum; the ships' crews may have been eastern.
sources: Procopius, Wars 5.16.8-18; en.wikipedia, the list of battles of the Roman Empire (East)
note: Land and sea siege; the Goths withdrew. Uligisalus had earlier been beaten at Scardon.

name: Urbinum (siege)
borderline: The garrison surrendered when its spring failed, as the Romans prepared an assault; little fighting.
roman_force: Belisarius' own army, after Narses and John had marched off (Procopius 6.19).
greek_note: Belisarius' eastern expeditionary army, with its Isaurian infantry.
sources: Procopius, Wars 6.19; en.wikipedia Gothic War (535-554)

name: Petra Pertusa (siege)
place: Petra (Petra Pertusa), the fort closing the Furlo gorge on the Via Flaminia
borderline: A short assault ending in surrender; no standard article.
roman_force: 1,000 horsemen sent by Belisarius under Martin and Ildiger toward Ariminum; after an attack on the gate failed they climbed the cliff and dropped rocks on the fort until the garrison surrendered (Procopius 6.11.4-20).
greek_note: Belisarius' eastern expeditionary cavalry, with Thracian and Hun horsemen.
sources: Procopius, Wars 6.11.1-20 (LacusCurtius)
note: The Goths surrendered on terms; most were taken along by Martin and Ildiger and a small Roman garrison was left.

name: Ariminum (siege)
commanders_a: John nephew of Vitalian; Belisarius, Narses, Ildiger, Martin (relief)
roman_force: John's 2,000 horse in the town; relieved by Belisarius and Narses, who had brought 5,000 regulars and 2,000 Heruls from the East (Procopius 6.13, 6.16-17).
greek_note: John's cavalry was Thracian; Narses' reinforcements were eastern regiments and Herul foederati.
sources: Procopius, Wars 6.11-17; en.wikipedia Gothic War (535-554)
note: The Goths stormed with a siege tower and then blockaded; they withdrew as the relief approached.

name: Mediolanum (siege)
roman_force: Mundilas with about 300 of Belisarius' guards and the armed citizens; the relief army of Martin and Uliaris stayed on the Po (Procopius 6.12, 6.21).
greek_note: The defence rested on the Latin-speaking citizens with a small eastern garrison.
sources: Procopius, Wars 6.12, 6.21; en.wikipedia Gothic War (535-554)
note: 10,000 Burgundians (allies_a) joined the Goths. The garrison was spared; the city was razed and its men killed (Procopius gives 300,000, an impossible figure).

name: Urbs Vetus (siege)
borderline: The garrison surrendered from hunger; the rock was judged unassailable.
roman_force: Belisarius' army (Procopius 6.20).
greek_note: Belisarius' eastern expeditionary army.
sources: Procopius, Wars 6.20; en.wikipedia, the list of battles of the Roman Empire (East)

name: Babosis
place: Babosis, near Bagai at the foot of the Aurasium (Aures)
borderline: Known only from Procopius; the site is unidentified; no standard article.
roman_force: Solomon's army of Africa, re-formed after the mutinies with reinforcements from the East; the vanguard under his guardsman Gontharis had been beaten on the Abigas before Solomon came up (Procopius 4.19.6-17).
greek_note: The army of Africa still rested on the eastern regiments of 533-536 and the reinforcements sent with Solomon in 539.
sources: Procopius, Wars 4.19.6-17 (LacusCurtius)
note: Solomon 'defeated them decisively'; Iaudas withdrew to Zerboule on the Aurasium (Procopius 4.19.17-19).

name: Auximus (siege)
roman_force: Belisarius' main army; five Isaurians broke the masonry of the garrison's cistern (Procopius 6.23-27).
greek_note: Isaurian infantry named in the siege; the army was the eastern expedition.
sources: Procopius, Wars 6.23-27; en.wikipedia Gothic War (535-554)
note: Many sorties and fights for the grass outside the walls; the garrison capitulated from starvation.

name: Faesulae (siege)
roman_force: Cyprian and Justin with their own troops, Isaurians and 500 men of Demetrius' infantry (Procopius 6.23).
greek_note: Isaurians are named among the besiegers.
sources: Procopius, Wars 6.23-27; en.wikipedia Gothic War (535-554)
note: Sorties were beaten back; the garrison capitulated from starvation, about the same time as Auximus.

name: Po
war: Gothic War (Frankish invasion of Theudebert I)
place: the Po crossing at Ticinum (Pavia) and the Roman camp near Dertona
roman_force: The Roman army of Martin and John posted near Dertona to watch the Goths (Procopius 6.25).
greek_note: Detachments of the eastern expeditionary army and Thracian cavalry.
sources: Procopius, Wars 6.25; en.wikipedia Gothic War (535-554)
note: Franks under Theudebert I. They routed first the Goths at the bridge of Ticinum and then the Romans, then withdrew when dysentery struck.

name: Ravenna (siege)
roman_force: Belisarius' whole army in Italy, with Vitalius' Illyrian troops guarding the Po and a fleet in the Adriatic (Procopius 6.28-29).
greek_note: The eastern expeditionary army and its reinforcements, with the Latin-speaking Illyrian army of Vitalius.
sources: Procopius, Wars 6.28-29; en.wikipedia Siege of Ravenna (539-540)
note: A blockade; the Gothic granaries were burned and Vitiges surrendered in May 540.

name: Antioch
war: Roman-Persian war of 540-562 (Khosrow I's invasion of Syria)
roman_force: 6,000 soldiers from Phoenice Libanensis under Theoctistus and Molatzes, who fled when the wall was breached, and the young men of the circus factions, who fought on in the streets (Procopius 2.8).
greek_note: Most of the fighting was done by the Antiochene faction youths, citizens of a Greek-speaking city.
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.8; en.wikipedia Lazic War
note: The city was sacked and its people deported to Weh Antiok Khusrau near Ctesiphon.

name: Toumar (siege)
place: Toumar, Iaudas' fortified camp on the Aurasium (Aures)
borderline: Known only from Procopius; the site is unidentified; no standard article.
roman_force: Solomon's army of Africa, short of water, whose soldiers attacked the Moorish position on the heights and carried it (Procopius 4.20.1-22).
greek_note: The army of Africa still rested on the eastern regiments of 533-536 and the reinforcements of 539.
sources: Procopius, Wars 4.20.1-22 (LacusCurtius)
note: Iaudas, struck by a javelin in the thigh, escaped to Mauretania; the Romans then took the Rock of Geminianus with his treasure.

name: Sura (siege)
war: Roman-Persian war of 540-562 (Khosrow I's invasion of Syria)
place: Sura, on the Euphrates west of Callinicum
roman_force: The small garrison of Sura under the Armenian Arsaces, who fell on the wall, and the citizens (Procopius 2.5).
greek_note: A frontier garrison and a Syrian town; Greek beside Syriac.
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.5.8-33; en.wikipedia Lazic War
note: After a day of fighting the bishop sought terms; the Persians forced the gate during the parley and sacked the town.

name: Dara (siege)
war: Roman-Persian war of 540-562 (Khosrow I's invasion of Syria)
borderline: A short siege on Khosrow's homeward march; he withdrew for 1,000 pounds of silver.
roman_force: The garrison of Dara under Martin, who countermined the Persian tunnel (Procopius 2.13).
greek_note: A garrison of the eastern army.
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.13.16-28; en.wikipedia Lazic War

name: Petra (siege)
place: Petra (Tsikhisdziri), on the Black Sea coast
roman_force: The Roman garrison of Petra under John Tzibus, killed by an arrow during the assaults (Procopius 2.17).
greek_note: A garrison drawn from the army of Armenia.
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.17; en.wikipedia Lazic War
note: The Lazi under Gubazes had called in the Persians (allies_a). A mined tower collapsed and the garrison capitulated.

name: Nisibis
roman_force: Belisarius' army of the East, with Gothic prisoners from Italy enrolled as a unit and al-Harith's Ghassanids; Peter's camp was routed by a sally until Belisarius' Goths drove the Persians back (Procopius 2.18).
greek_note: The eastern field army, with Ostrogothic and Ghassanid contingents.
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.18; en.wikipedia Battle of Nisibis (541)
note: Wikipedia's article calls it a Persian victory, its list of battles a Roman one: the sally was beaten back (about 150 Persian and 50 Roman dead) but Nisibis was not taken.

name: Sisauranon (siege)
roman_force: Belisarius' army of the East; a first assault failed with heavy loss and the fort was blockaded (Procopius 2.19).
greek_note: The eastern field army.
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.19; en.wikipedia, the list of battles of the Roman Empire (East)
note: The garrison of 800 Persian horsemen surrendered and was sent to fight in Italy.

name: Treviso
roman_force: Vitalius, magister militum of Illyricum, with his Illyrian army and a large body of Heruls under Visandus, most of whom fell (Procopius 7.1).
greek_note: The Illyrian army was recruited in the Latin-speaking Danubian provinces.
sources: Procopius, Wars 7.1.34-36; en.wikipedia Gothic War (535-554)
note: Allies_b are the Herul foederati.

name: Verona
roman_force: About 12,000 under eleven commanders led by Constantianus and Alexander; the Persarmenian Artabazes, sent west with the Persian prisoners of Sisauranon, seized a gate at night with 100 men, but the army hesitated and the Goths retook it (Procopius 7.3).
greek_note: The army of Italy was the eastern expeditionary army with eastern reinforcements.
sources: Procopius, Wars 7.3; en.wikipedia, the list of battles of the Roman Empire (East)
note: A failed surprise attack on the city.

name: Faventia
roman_force: The same army of about 12,000 under eleven commanders, against about 5,000 Goths (Procopius 7.4).
greek_note: The eastern regiments of the army of Italy.
sources: Procopius, Wars 7.4; en.wikipedia Battle of Faventia
note: 300 Goths sent round to the Roman rear caused the rout; the standards were lost.

name: Mucellium
commanders_b: John nephew of Vitalian, Bessas, Cyprian
roman_force: The armies of John, Bessas and Cyprian, gathered to relieve Justin in Florence (Procopius 7.5).
greek_note: The eastern regiments of the army of Italy.
sources: Procopius, Wars 7.5; en.wikipedia Gothic War (535-554)
note: The Goths lifted the siege of Florence to meet the relief army, which broke on a false report of John's death.

name: Naples (siege)
place: Neapolis (Naples) and the sea off it
roman_force: Conon's garrison of 1,000 Romans and Isaurians; relief fleets under Demetrius and Maximinus (Thracians, Armenians under Herodian, Phazas the Iberian and Huns) were scattered by storm and Gothic attack (Procopius 7.6-7).
greek_note: Isaurians in the garrison and eastern troops in the relief fleets.
sources: Procopius, Wars 7.6-7; en.wikipedia Siege of Naples (542-543)
note: The relief expeditions were defeated at sea; Conon surrendered on terms.

name: Anglon
commanders_b: Martin, Peter, Valerian, Narses (killed), Isaac, Adolius (killed), Philemuth, Verus
roman_force: About 30,000 of the armies of the East and of Armenia, with a Herul regiment under Philemuth and Verus and Armenian officers under the Persarmenian Narses, against about 4,000 Persians (Procopius 2.24-25).
greek_note: The armies of the East and Armenia, with many Armenians and Herul foederati.
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.24-25; en.wikipedia Battle of Anglon
note: The Roman columns, without a single commander, attacked the fortified village piecemeal and fled.

name: Edessa (siege)
roman_force: The garrison under Martin, Peter and Peranius, with the citizens, peasants and even women and children on the walls; the Persian mound was burned (Procopius 2.26-27).
greek_note: A garrison of the eastern army in a Syriac-speaking city.
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.26-27; en.wikipedia Siege of Edessa (544)
note: Khosrow withdrew after a final assault failed; the Edessans paid 500 pounds of gold. A five-year truce followed in 545.

name: Cillium
roman_force: Solomon's field army of Africa, with his nephews; part of it under Guntharis gave way (Procopius 4.21).
greek_note: The army of Africa still rested on the eastern regiments of 533-536.
sources: Procopius, Wars 4.21.19-28; en.wikipedia Battle of Cillium
note: Solomon's horse fell into a ravine and he was killed.

name: Thacia
roman_force: The outnumbered field army of Africa under John, with Armenian contingents newly arrived with Areobindus (Procopius 4.22, 4.24).
greek_note: Eastern regiments of Africa and Armenian reinforcements.
sources: Procopius, Wars 4.24; en.wikipedia Battle of Thacia
note: Stotzas fought with the Moors at the head of Roman deserters; John killed him and was killed in turn. Wikipedia's infobox also names Areobindus and Artabanes.

name: Rome (siege)
date: blockade from late 545; city taken 17 December 546
place: Rome and the Tiber below it (Portus)
roman_force: Bessas' garrison of 3,000; Belisarius' relief force from Portus (his bucellarii and the 4,000 recruits raised in Thrace and Illyricum) broke the Gothic boom on the Tiber but turned back when Isaac the Armenian was captured (Procopius 7.13-20).
greek_note: The garrison included Isaurians, who betrayed the Asinarian gate; the new recruits were Balkan and largely Latin-speaking.
sources: Procopius, Wars 7.13-20; en.wikipedia Sack of Rome (546)
note: Often called the sack of Rome (546).

name: Sufetula
roman_force: John Troglita's regiments brought from Constantinople and the army of Africa, with Moorish allies (Corippus, Iohannis 4-5).
greek_note: John's new regiments came from the eastern armies; the Moorish allies grew larger in later campaigns.
sources: Corippus, Iohannis 4-5; Procopius, Wars 4.28.45-47; en.wikipedia John Troglita
note: The standards lost at Cillium were recovered. The site and date are not precise in Corippus.

name: Rome
borderline: Usually treated as an episode of the Gothic War, not a named siege.
roman_force: Belisarius' troops, who reoccupied the empty city and beat off Totila's assaults on the half-repaired walls (Procopius 7.24).
greek_note: Belisarius' bucellarii and Balkan recruits.
sources: Procopius, Wars 7.24; en.wikipedia Gothic War (535-554)
note: Totila's three assaults in a few weeks failed.

name: Marta
roman_force: John Troglita's army (three of his regiments had been sent to Italy) with Moorish allies, who panicked first (Corippus, Iohannis 6).
greek_note: The Moorish allies of Cutzinas and Ifisdaias made up much of the army.
sources: Corippus, Iohannis 6; en.wikipedia John Troglita
note: Carcasan was king of the Ifuraces of Tripolitania.

name: Fields of Cato
place: the Fields of Cato (Campi Catonis), Byzacena
roman_force: John Troglita's regulars, horse archers and cataphracts, with large Moorish allied contingents under Cutzinas and Ifisdaias, who outnumbered the regulars (Corippus, Iohannis 7-8).
greek_note: Moorish allies formed most of the army; the regulars were eastern regiments.
sources: Corippus, Iohannis 7-8; Procopius, Wars 4.28.47-52; en.wikipedia John Troglita
note: Site unidentified. Ended the Moorish revolt; seventeen chiefs fell.

name: Petra (siege)
place: Petra (Tsikhisdziri) and the passes into Lazica
roman_force: 7,000 Romans and 1,000 Tzani under Dagisthaeus, with the Lazi of king Gubazes; the small force guarding the passes was overwhelmed by the Persian relief army (Procopius 2.29-30).
greek_note: Regiments of the army of Armenia with Tzani auxiliaries and Lazic allies.
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.29-30; en.wikipedia Lazic War
note: The walls were breached but Dagisthaeus delayed the assault and the relief arrived. Often dated 549.

name: Tzurullum
date: 549 or 550 (the 15th year of the Gothic War)
borderline: Known only from Procopius; no standard article.
roman_force: The cavalry stationed in the fortress of Tzurullum under Asbadus, a candidatus of Justinian's guard; most were killed in a disorderly flight (Procopius 7.38.5-6).
greek_note: Cavalry of the Thracian command, recruited in Thrace and Illyricum.
sources: Procopius, Wars 7.38.1-6 (LacusCurtius)
note: Asbadus was captured and later burned alive; the same Sclaveni then stormed Topirus.

name: Phasis River
roman_force: Dagisthaeus' Romans with the Lazi, against 5,000 Persians left by Mihr-Mihroe to supply Petra (Procopius 2.30).
greek_note: The army of Armenia with Lazic allies.
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.30.29-48; en.wikipedia Lazic War
note: The Persian force was destroyed.

name: Hippis
roman_force: Dagisthaeus' Romans and the Lazi, who insisted on charging first; the Roman infantry steadied the line (Procopius 8.1).
greek_note: The army of Armenia with Lazic allies.
sources: Procopius, Wars 8.1.3-11; en.wikipedia Lazic War
note: Chorianes' invasion of Lazica failed.

name: Rome (siege)
roman_force: Diogenes' garrison of 3,000 picked men; Isaurian sentries opened the Gate of St Paul (Procopius 7.36).
greek_note: Isaurians of the garrison are named; the rest were Belisarius' former troops.
sources: Procopius, Wars 7.36; en.wikipedia Gothic War (535-554)

name: Topirus (siege)
borderline: Known only from Procopius; no standard article.
roman_force: The garrison of Topirus, drawn out by a feigned flight and cut down in an ambush, and the citizens who then held the walls (Procopius 7.38).
greek_note: A Greek-speaking coastal town of the Rhodope defended largely by its own citizens.
sources: Procopius, Wars 7.38.9-18
note: The Sclaveni stormed the walls under a cloud of arrows; 15,000 men were killed (Procopius).

name: Petra (siege)
commanders_a: Bessas (wounded), John the Armenian (killed; not Belisarius' officer of that name, who died in 533)
roman_force: Bessas' army of Armenia, about 6,000; Sabir Hun allies built light rams; the old Bessas led the escalade himself (Procopius 8.11-12).
greek_note: Regiments of the army of Armenia, with many Armenians.
sources: Procopius, Wars 8.11-12; en.wikipedia Siege of Petra (550-551)
note: The garrison of about 2,300 (Procopius) was destroyed or captured and the walls razed.

name: Archaeopolis
roman_force: The Roman garrison of about 3,000 under Odonachus and Babas, which sallied against the Persian assault; the Persian elephants panicked (Procopius 8.13-14).
greek_note: A garrison of the army of Armenia.
sources: Procopius, Wars 8.13-14; en.wikipedia Lazic War

name: Adrianople
commanders_b: Constantianus, Aratius, Nazares, Justin son of Germanus, John Phagas
borderline: Known only from Procopius; no standard article.
roman_force: The army gathered for Germanus' Italian expedition, under Constantianus, Aratius, Nazares, Justin and John (Procopius 7.40).
greek_note: Troops raised in Thrace and Illyricum with eastern regiments.
sources: Procopius, Wars 7.40.34-45
note: The soldiers forced their generals to attack and were beaten; the Sclaveni took the standard of Constantianus.

name: Sena Gallica
roman_force: 50 warships from Salona and Ravenna with picked soldiers of John's and Valerian's armies, against 47 Gothic ships (Procopius 8.23).
greek_note: John's Illyrian veterans from Salona and Valerian's troops from Ravenna fought aboard; the article on the battle says the crews were mostly Greek sailors.
sources: Procopius, Wars 8.23; en.wikipedia Battle of Sena Gallica
note: 36 Gothic ships were lost and the siege of Ancona was raised.

name: Taginae (Busta Gallorum)
commanders_a: Narses, John nephew of Vitalian, Valerian, Dagisthaeus, Philemuth, Asbad
roman_force: Narses' army, perhaps 20,000-30,000: Roman regulars from Thrace, Illyricum and the East, 2,500 Lombard warriors with 3,000 followers, over 3,000 Heruls under Philemuth, 400 Gepids under Asbad, Huns and Persian deserters under Kabades; 8,000 foot archers on the wings and dismounted Germanic foederati in the centre (Procopius 8.26, 8.31).
greek_note: Barbarian contingents were a large part; the regulars came from Thrace, Illyricum and the eastern armies, so Greek speakers were perhaps a fifth to a third.
sources: Procopius, Wars 8.26, 8.29-32; en.wikipedia Battle of Taginae
note: Allies: Lombards, Heruls and Gepids (Germanic peoples), Huns.

name: Mons Lactarius
place: the Sarno valley below Mons Lactarius, near Nuceria
roman_force: Narses' army, without the Lombards sent home after Taginae, fighting on foot in a two-day battle (Procopius 8.35).
greek_note: Narses' regulars from Thrace, Illyricum and the East, with Herul foederati.
sources: Procopius, Wars 8.35; Agathias 1.1; en.wikipedia Battle of Mons Lactarius
note: The last stand of the Ostrogothic kingdom.

name: Asfeld
borderline: Roman participation was a small allied detachment.
roman_force: Only Amalafrid's contingent joined the Lombards; the main imperial army was held back by a riot at Ulpiana (Procopius 8.25, 8.27).
greek_note: A small Balkan detachment.
sources: Procopius, Wars 8.25.10-15, 8.27; Paul the Deacon 1.23-24; en.wikipedia Battle of Asfeld
note: Side B are the Gepids.

name: Rome
borderline: Usually treated as an episode, not a named siege.
roman_force: Narses' army after Taginae; Dagisthaeus scaled an unguarded stretch of the wall while the rest attacked at several points (Procopius 8.33).
greek_note: Narses' regulars and foederati, without the Lombards.
sources: Procopius, Wars 8.33
note: The Goths retreated to Hadrian's mausoleum and surrendered.

name: Cumae (siege)
roman_force: Narses' army, then a blockading detachment; a mine under the Sibyl's cave brought down part of the wall (Agathias 1.8-10, 1.20).
greek_note: Narses' regulars.
sources: Agathias 1.8-10, 1.20; en.wikipedia Gothic War (535-554)
note: Aligern, Teia's brother, surrendered after about a year.

name: Lucca (siege)
borderline: Known mainly from Agathias.
roman_force: Narses' army; the town surrendered after about three months of siege and assaults (Agathias 1.12-18).
greek_note: Narses' regulars and Herul foederati.
sources: Agathias 1.12-18
note: The garrison expected Frankish relief.

name: Parma
borderline: Known only from Agathias; no standard article.
roman_force: Fulcaris with his Heruls, ambushed by the Franks near the amphitheatre; the other generals fell back to Faventia (Agathias 1.14-15).
greek_note: The force was Fulcaris' Herul foederati.
sources: Agathias 1.14-15
note: Franks and Alamanni under Butilin; allies_b are the Heruls.

name: Volturnus (Casilinum)
roman_force: About 18,000: heavy infantry in the centre, cavalry and horse archers on the wings, and Heruls under Sindual who joined late (Agathias 2.4-10).
greek_note: Narses' regulars from the Balkans and the East, with Herul foederati.
sources: Agathias 2.4-10; en.wikipedia Battle of the Volturnus (554)
note: Franks and Alamanni under Butilin, nearly annihilated; allies_a are the Heruls.

name: Telephis-Ollaria
place: Telephis and Ollaria, on the Phasis, Lazica
commanders_b: Martin, Bessas, Bouzes, Justin son of Germanus
roman_force: The large Roman army of Lazica, Martin at Telephis, Bessas and Justin at Ollaria, with the Lazi; it fell back to Nesos (Agathias 2.19-22).
greek_note: The army of Armenia and eastern regiments with Lazic allies.
sources: Agathias 2.19-22; en.wikipedia Mihr-Mihroe's campaign of 554
note: Mihr-Mihroe feigned illness, then stormed Telephis; the Romans abandoned Ollaria.

name: Compsa (siege)
borderline: Mostly a blockade.
roman_force: Narses' army; the 7,000 Goths surrendered after Ragnaris was shot while treacherously attacking Narses at a parley (Agathias 2.13-14).
greek_note: Narses' regulars.
sources: Agathias 2.13-14; en.wikipedia Gothic War (535-554)

name: Onoguris (siege)
roman_force: A large army (Agathias' 50,000 fighting men is surely too high) with Heruls under Uligagus, Usigardus and the Antian Dabragezas; it broke when a 3,000-strong Persian cavalry relief struck (Agathias 3.6-8).
greek_note: The army of Armenia and eastern regiments with Herul and Slav officers.
sources: Agathias 3.5-8; en.wikipedia Siege of Onoguris
note: The Romans then lost Archaeopolis for a time.

name: Phasis (siege)
place: Phasis (Poti), at the mouth of the Rioni
commanders_a: Martin, Justin son of Germanus, Angilas, Theodore, Philomathius, Gibrus, Valerian, Dabragezas, Elmingir
roman_force: Perhaps 20,000: Moorish peltasts and spearmen under Angilas, Tzani heavy infantry under Theodore, Isaurian slingers and javelin men under Philomathius, Heruls and Lombards under Gibrus, eastern troops under Valerian, and the ships guarded by the Antian Dabragezas and the Hun Elmingir (Agathias 3.19-28).
greek_note: Isaurians and eastern regiments are named beside Moors, Tzani, Heruls, Lombards and Slavs.
sources: Agathias 3.19-28; en.wikipedia Siege of Phasis
note: A large sally routed the Persian assault; Agathias gives about 10,000 Persian dead.

name: Melantias
place: Melantias, about 30 km west of Constantinople
roman_force: About 300 of Belisarius' veteran bucellarii with a mass of armed peasants and refugees, used to raise dust and noise, against 2,000 Kutrigur horsemen (Agathias 5.15-20).
greek_note: Most of the force were peasants and townsmen of the Greek-speaking hinterland of Constantinople.
sources: Agathias 5.15-20; en.wikipedia Battle of Melantias
note: Kutrigur Huns. Belisarius' last battle.

name: Thracian Chersonese
place: the Long Wall across the isthmus of the Thracian Chersonese (near Bolayir) and the sea off it
commanders_b: a Kutrigur division sent by Zabergan
borderline: No standalone article; known from Agathias. Not checked against an online text of Agathias (October 2026).
roman_force: The garrison of the Chersonese wall under the young Germanus, son of Dorotheus, with light boats that sank the Kutrigur reed rafts, and a sortie that routed the attackers (Agathias 5.21-23).
greek_note: A garrison of the long-Greek Chersonese, raised in Thrace and around the capital.
sources: Agathias, Histories 5.21-23
note: Assaults on the wall and an attempt to turn it by sea on rafts of reeds both failed; Germanus was wounded in the sortie.

name: Verona and Brixia
roman_force: Narses' army of Italy, which defeated Widin's Goths and the Frankish duke Amingus and took the last Gothic strongholds (Menander fr. 3; Paul the Deacon 2.2; Malalas 18.140).
greek_note: The army of Italy still contained many eastern regiments.
sources: Malalas 18.140; Theophanes AM 6055; Paul the Deacon 2.2; en.wikipedia Gothic War (535-554)
note: Allies_b are the Franks of Amingus.

name: Pavia (siege)
roman_force: The imperial garrison and the citizens of Ticinum, who held out for three years (Paul the Deacon 2.26-27).
greek_note: An Italian city defended largely by its Latin-speaking inhabitants.
sources: Paul the Deacon, Historia Langobardorum 2.26-27; en.wikipedia Alboin
note: Also called the siege of Pavia; the city became the Lombard capital.

name: Dvin
commanders_a: Vardan II Mamikonian (Armenians); Roman commander unnamed
borderline: The Roman share in the capture is not detailed in the sources.
roman_force: Roman troops of the army of Armenia with the rebel Armenians of Vardan Mamikonian (Sebeos; John of Ephesus).
greek_note: The Armenian rebels made up most of the force.
sources: Sebeos 8; John of Ephesus 2.20-23; en.wikipedia, the article on the Roman-Sasanian war of 572-591
note: Vardan first took Dvin after killing the marzban Suren; the Persians retook it and the Armenians with Roman help captured it again.

name: Sargathon
roman_force: Marcian's army of the East, advancing on Nisibis (John of Epiphania; Theophylact 3.10).
greek_note: The eastern field army of the 570s was recruited in Anatolia, Syria, Armenia and the Balkans.
sources: Theophylact Simocatta 3.10; en.wikipedia, the article on the Roman-Sasanian war of 572-591

name: Nisibis (siege)
roman_force: Marcian's army of the East; when Justin II dismissed Marcian and Khosrow approached, the army broke up and fled (Evagrius 5.8-9).
greek_note: The eastern field army.
sources: Evagrius 5.8-9; John of Ephesus 6.2-3; Theophylact 3.10-11; en.wikipedia, the list of battles of the Roman Empire (East)
note: The siege was abandoned in disorder.

name: Dara (siege)
roman_force: The garrison of Dara and its citizens (Evagrius 5.9-10; John of Ephesus 6.5).
greek_note: A garrison of the eastern army in a Syriac-speaking district.
sources: Evagrius 5.9-10; John of Ephesus 6.5; en.wikipedia Siege of Dara (573)
note: After about four to six months; its loss reportedly drove Justin II out of his mind. A Persian force under Adarmahan meanwhile sacked Apamea (not entered: no battle).

name: Melitene
roman_force: The armies of the East and Armenia under Justinian, perhaps 30,000, with Kours' wing of perhaps 20,000 (modern estimates), including Tiberius' new recruits from the Balkans, Isauria and beyond the frontiers (Evagrius 5.14; Theophylact 3.14).
greek_note: Anatolian, Isaurian and Armenian regiments beside Balkan and foreign recruits.
sources: Evagrius 5.14; Theophylact 3.14; John of Ephesus 6.8-9; en.wikipedia Battle of Melitene (576)
note: Khosrow's camp was taken and many Persians drowned crossing the Euphrates.

name: Sirmium (siege)
borderline: A blockade ended by a negotiated surrender; little recorded fighting.
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Sirmium, with a small relief force under Theognis on the Save (Menander fr. 25, 27; John of Ephesus 6.30-32).
greek_note: A Latin-speaking city of Pannonia with a small garrison.
sources: Menander Protector fr. 25, 27; John of Ephesus 6.30-32; en.wikipedia Maurice's Balkan campaigns

name: Constantina
roman_force: Maurice's army of the East (Theophylact 3.18; John of Ephesus 6.26-27).
greek_note: The eastern field army.
sources: Theophylact 3.18; John of Ephesus 6.26-27; en.wikipedia Battle of Constantina
note: Also called the battle of Monocarton; four Persian generals fell.

name: Nymphius
place: on the river Nymphius (Batman Su), near Martyropolis
roman_force: John Mystacon's army of the East; Kours, jealous of John, held his wing back (Theophylact 1.9).
greek_note: The eastern field army.
sources: Theophylact 1.9.4-11; en.wikipedia, the article on the Roman-Sasanian war of 572-591

name: Singidunum (siege)
roman_force: The garrison and townspeople, surprised while gathering the harvest outside the walls (Theophylact 1.4).
greek_note: A Latin-speaking Danube town.
sources: Theophylact 1.4.1-4; en.wikipedia Maurice's Balkan campaigns
note: Viminacium and Augustae fell in the same campaign.

name: Adrianople
roman_force: Comentiolus' Thracian army, built round the praesental regiments; it had first beaten a Slav band on the river Erginia (Theophylact 1.7).
greek_note: The Thracian armies of the 580s spoke Latin and Greek; Theophylact records soldiers calling out in Latin in 587.
sources: Theophylact 1.7; en.wikipedia Maurice's Balkan campaigns

name: Thessalonica (siege)
commanders_a: the citizens (St Demetrius in the Miracula)
roman_force: The citizens of Thessalonica, with few regular troops, manning the walls for seven days against Avar siege engines (Miracula S. Demetrii 2.1).
greek_note: The Miracula describe the defence by the Greek-speaking townsmen.
sources: Miracula S. Demetrii 2.1; en.wikipedia Siege of Thessalonica (617)
note: The besiegers withdrew after a week.

name: Chlomaron (siege)
borderline: A siege broken off in panic; no standalone article.
roman_force: Philippicus' army of the East, the victors of Solachon, raiding Arzanene; at the approach of the Persian relief army it broke off the siege and fled in disorder (Theophylact 2.7-9).
greek_note: The eastern field army.
sources: Theophylact Simocatta 2.7-9; en.wikipedia Philippicus (comes excubitorum)
note: Philippicus, possibly ill, then handed the command to Heraclius the Elder.

name: Solachon
place: the plain of Solachon, south of Dara
commanders_a: Philippicus, Heraclius the Elder, Vitalius, Eiliphredas, Apsich
roman_force: Philippicus' army of the East, all cavalry, lancers and horse archers in three divisions, with Hun horse archers under Apsich on the left and Arab foederati as scouts (Theophylact 2.2-4).
greek_note: The eastern field army of the 580s, recruited largely in Anatolia, Armenia and Syria.
sources: Theophylact 2.2-4; en.wikipedia Battle of Solachon
note: Theophylact calls the Arab foederati Saracens; the Ghassanid federation had broken up after 584.

name: Adrianople
borderline: No standalone article; the Wikipedia article on Maurice's Balkan campaigns does not single it out. Not confirmed in an online source when checked (October 2026).
roman_force: A field army under John Mystacon with the Lombard Drocton, a former Lombard duke in imperial service, which relieved the besieged city (Theophylact 2.17).
greek_note: Thracian and eastern troops, with Lombard volunteers under Drocton.
sources: Theophylact Simocatta 2.17
note: The Avars had overrun towns of Moesia and Thrace in 587 before besieging Adrianople.

name: Tsalkajur
borderline: Known only in outline; site and commanders uncertain.
roman_force: Roman troops of the eastern or Armenian command during the army mutiny of 588; no details.
greek_note: The eastern and Armenian armies.
sources: Sebeos; en.wikipedia, the article on the Roman-Sasanian war of 572-591

name: Martyropolis
roman_force: The mutinous army of the East under its elected commander Germanus, who had gathered about 4,000 men for a raid (Theophylact 3.4).
greek_note: The eastern field army.
sources: Theophylact 3.4; en.wikipedia Battle of Martyropolis (588)
note: About 3,000 Persians were captured.

name: Martyropolis (siege)
roman_force: The army of the East under Philippicus, then Comentiolus, besieging the city the Persians had taken through the treachery of the officer Sittas; a Persian relief army beat the besiegers (Theophylact 3.5-6).
greek_note: The eastern field army.
sources: Theophylact 3.5-6, 4.13; Evagrius 6.14; en.wikipedia, the article on the Roman-Sasanian war of 572-591
note: The city was returned by Khosrow II in 591.

name: Sisauranon
roman_force: Comentiolus' army of the East; when Comentiolus fled, Heraclius the Elder rallied the troops and won (Theophylact 3.6).
greek_note: The eastern field army.
sources: Theophylact 3.6.1-4; en.wikipedia, the article on the Roman-Sasanian war of 572-591
note: Also called Sisarbanon.

name: Araxes
place: on the Araxes, in Caucasian Albania
roman_force: Romanus' army of the Caucasus front, raised from the army of Armenia (Theophylact 3.7-8).
greek_note: The army of Armenia, with many Armenians.
sources: Theophylact 3.7-8; en.wikipedia Battle of the Araxes (589)
note: The defeat led Hormizd IV to dismiss Bahram, who rebelled.

name: Blarathon
war: Roman-Persian War of 572-591 (restoration of Khosrow II)
place: on the Blarathon river near Ganzak
commanders_a: Narses, John Mystacon, Musel II Mamikonian; Khosrow II, Bindoe, Bistam
roman_force: About 60,000 in all: some 40,000 Roman troops of the armies of the East (Narses) and Armenia (John Mystacon), 12,000 Armenian cavalry under Musel Mamikonian and 8,000 Persians loyal to Khosrow II (modern figures after Sebeos and Theophylact 5.9-11).
greek_note: The eastern field army with a strong Armenian element.
sources: Theophylact 5.9-11; Sebeos 11; en.wikipedia Battle of Blarathon
note: Allies_a are Khosrow II's Persian loyalists; side B is the army of the usurper Bahram VI Chobin. Khosrow was restored and ceded Dara, Martyropolis and much of Armenia.

name: Marcianopolis
borderline: An encounter with a returning raiding party.
roman_force: The vanguard of Peter's Thracian army, which overcame some 600 Slavs behind their wagon laager after a first setback (Theophylact 7.2).
greek_note: The Thracian field army of the 590s, recruited in the Balkans and Anatolia.
sources: Theophylact 7.2.1-10; en.wikipedia Maurice's Balkan campaigns

name: Helibacia
place: the river Helibacia (probably the Ialomita), Wallachia
roman_force: Peter's army, which had crossed the Danube near Securisca and killed the chief Peiragastus, then, short of water, forced a crossing of the Helibacia on rafts and was beaten back (Theophylact 7.4-5).
greek_note: The Thracian field army.
sources: Theophylact 7.4-5; en.wikipedia Maurice's Balkan campaigns
note: The campaign began with a success (Peiragastus' death); the outcome given is that of the fight at the river.

name: Tomis (siege)
roman_force: Priscus' Thracian field army wintering in Tomis (Theophylact 7.13).
greek_note: The Thracian field army.
sources: Theophylact 7.13.1-8; en.wikipedia Maurice's Balkan campaigns
note: The khagan sent food at Easter; the siege was lifted on Comentiolus' approach.

name: Iatrus
roman_force: Comentiolus' army, which broke when its commander fled (Theophylact 7.13-14).
greek_note: The Thracian field army.
sources: Theophylact 7.13.9-7.14; en.wikipedia Maurice's Balkan campaigns
note: The Avars later killed some 12,000 Roman prisoners when Maurice refused a ransom.

name: Viminacium
place: Viminacium (Kostolac) and the north bank of the Danube
roman_force: The combined armies of Priscus and Comentiolus under Priscus, ferried across the Danube by the river fleet (Theophylact 8.2).
greek_note: The Thracian field army with eastern regiments.
sources: Theophylact 8.2; en.wikipedia Battle of Viminacium
note: A series of engagements in which several sons of Bayan fell.

name: Tisza
roman_force: Priscus' army; a detachment of 4,000 crossed the Tisza against the Gepid settlements before the battles with the khagan's army (Theophylact 8.3).
greek_note: The Thracian field army.
sources: Theophylact 8.3; en.wikipedia Battle of Viminacium
note: Allies_b include the Gepids (Germanic peoples) under Avar rule. A series of battles, grouped here as one entry.

name: Padua (siege)
borderline: Known chiefly from Paul the Deacon; the fighting is not described in detail.
roman_force: The imperial garrison of Padua, long cut off from Ravenna, which had resisted 'very bravely' and was allowed to withdraw to Ravenna when the city was set on fire (Paul the Deacon 4.23).
greek_note: A garrison of the exarchate of Ravenna, mostly locally raised Latin-speaking soldiers with some eastern troops.
sources: Paul the Deacon, Historia Langobardorum 4.23; en.wikipedia Agilulf
note: The Lombards burned the city and razed it to the ground.

name: Cremona (siege)
borderline: Known only from Paul the Deacon, who records the siege and capture but no details of the fighting.
roman_force: The imperial garrison and citizens of Cremona (Paul the Deacon 4.28); no details.
greek_note: A garrison of the exarchate of Ravenna, mostly locally raised Latin-speaking soldiers.
sources: Paul the Deacon, Historia Langobardorum 4.28
note: Agilulf besieged it with Slavs sent by the Avar khagan, took it on 21 August and razed it.

name: Mantua (siege)
date: late August - 13 September 603 (fall on the Ides of September)
borderline: Known chiefly from Paul the Deacon; no standard article.
roman_force: The imperial garrison of Mantua, allowed to withdraw to Ravenna after the walls were breached with battering rams (Paul the Deacon 4.28).
greek_note: A garrison of the exarchate of Ravenna, mostly locally raised Latin-speaking soldiers.
sources: Paul the Deacon, Historia Langobardorum 4.28; en.wikipedia Agilulf
note: Wikipedia (Agilulf) puts the fall of Mantua in 602; Paul the Deacon gives the day, the Ides of September, after Cremona.

name: Constantina
borderline: No standard name; the site is given as near Dara or Constantina.
roman_force: Germanus' army of the East, sent by Phocas against the rebel Narses in Edessa and turned against Khosrow's invasion (Theophanes AM 6095).
greek_note: The eastern field army of c. 600 was recruited largely in Anatolia, Syria and Armenia.
sources: Theophanes AM 6095; Sebeos 31; en.wikipedia, the article on the Roman-Sasanian war of 602-628
note: Germanus died of his wounds eleven days later at Constantina.

name: Dara (siege)
roman_force: The garrison of Dara (Theophanes AM 6096; Chronicle of 1234).
greek_note: A garrison of the eastern army.
sources: Theophanes AM 6096; Sebeos 31-32; en.wikipedia, the article on the Roman-Sasanian war of 602-628
note: Dates vary from 604 to 605 for the fall.

name: Arxamoun
place: Arxamoun, between Dara and Edessa (site uncertain)
borderline: Known only from Theophanes; no standard article.
roman_force: The eunuch Leontius' army of the East; Khosrow used elephants and took many prisoners (Theophanes AM 6096).
greek_note: The eastern field army.
sources: Theophanes AM 6096

name: Thessalonica
borderline: A single night attack.
roman_force: The citizens and garrison of Thessalonica, who beat off a night escalade by about 5,000 Slavs (Miracula S. Demetrii 1.12).
greek_note: The defence was by the Greek-speaking townsmen.
sources: Miracula S. Demetrii 1.12; en.wikipedia Siege of Thessalonica (617)

name: Alexandria
borderline: No standard name; known chiefly from John of Nikiu.
roman_force: Nicetas' army from Africa, with local supporters (the Greens of Alexandria), against the comes Orientis Bonosus' troops from Syria and the Blues (John of Nikiu 107-109).
greek_note: Bonosus' eastern troops and the Alexandrian factions spoke Greek; Nicetas' African troops largely Latin and Berber.
sources: John of Nikiu 107-109; en.wikipedia Heraclian revolt; Kaegi, Heraclius (2003) 38-46
note: Nicetas then held Egypt for Heraclius.

name: Caesarea (siege)
roman_force: Priscus' army blockading Shahin's Persians in the captured city; Heraclius joined briefly (Sebeos 34; Nicephorus 2).
greek_note: Anatolian and Armenian regiments.
sources: Sebeos 34; Nicephorus, Short History 2; en.wikipedia, the article on the Roman-Sasanian war of 602-628
note: The Persians broke out after a year and burned the city.

name: Cilician Gates
place: the Cilician Gates (Gulek pass) in the Taurus
commanders_b: Roman army (commanders not named; Heraclius and Theodore had organised the defence)
borderline: No standalone article; named only in modern narratives.
roman_force: What remained of the army beaten at Antioch, trying to hold the Taurus passes; no details of its make-up survive.
greek_note: The field armies of the East, recruited in Anatolia and Armenia.
sources: en.wikipedia, the article on the Roman-Sasanian war of 602-628; en.wikipedia Battle of Antioch (613)
note: The Persians then took Tarsus and the Cilician plain.

name: Antioch
roman_force: The field armies that Heraclius, his brother Theodore and Nicetas could gather in the East (Sebeos 34; Theophanes AM 6104).
greek_note: The eastern armies of Heraclius were recruited mainly in Anatolia and Armenia.
sources: Sebeos 34; Theophanes AM 6104; en.wikipedia Battle of Antioch (613)
note: The retreat was followed by a further defeat near the Cilician Gates; the Persians cut the empire in two.

name: Adhri'at
borderline: Named only in modern accounts; the battle is linked to the 'nearest land' of Quran 30:2-3.
roman_force: Nicetas' army (no details).
greek_note: The eastern field army.
sources: en.wikipedia, the article on the Roman-Sasanian war of 602-628

name: Emesa
borderline: Named only by place in modern accounts.
roman_force: Nicetas' army; a small victory with heavy losses on both sides, about 20,000 dead in all (Sebeos).
greek_note: The eastern field army.
sources: Sebeos 34; en.wikipedia, the article on the Roman-Sasanian war of 602-628

name: Jerusalem (siege)
roman_force: The citizens of Jerusalem, who had expelled the Persian garrison after a first surrender, with a few soldiers; a relief force from Jericho fled (Antiochus Strategos; Sebeos 34).
greek_note: The Christian population of Jerusalem spoke Greek and Palestinian Aramaic.
sources: Antiochus Strategos, Capture of Jerusalem; Sebeos 34; Chronicon Paschale s.a. 614; en.wikipedia Sasanian conquest of Jerusalem
note: The city was stormed and the True Cross carried off; the death toll in the sources (57,000 or 66,500) is not reliable.

name: Thessalonica
roman_force: The citizens of Thessalonica, attacked by land and from the sea in monoxyla by a Slav coalition (Drougoubitai, Sagoudatai, Belegezitai, Baiounetai, Berzetai) (Miracula S. Demetrii 2.1).
greek_note: The defence was by the Greek-speaking townsmen.
sources: Miracula S. Demetrii 2.1; en.wikipedia Siege of Thessalonica (617)
note: Dates of the sieges of 615 and 617/618 are approximate.

name: Thessalonica (siege)
roman_force: The citizens of Thessalonica without imperial help (Miracula S. Demetrii 2.2).
greek_note: The defence was by the Greek-speaking townsmen.
sources: Miracula S. Demetrii 2.2; en.wikipedia Siege of Thessalonica (617)
note: The khagan withdrew after receiving gold.

name: Alexandria (siege)
roman_force: Nicetas' army of Egypt and the citizens of Alexandria (Chronicle of Khuzistan; Severus ibn al-Muqaffa).
greek_note: The army of Egypt was locally recruited, Greek- and Coptic-speaking; Alexandria was a Greek-speaking city.
sources: Chronicle of Khuzistan; History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria; en.wikipedia Sasanian conquest of Egypt
note: The Persians entered by an unused canal shown them by a traitor; Nicetas fled to Cyprus.

name: Cappadocia
borderline: No agreed battle name.
roman_force: Heraclius' army, gathered in Bithynia from the remnants of the eastern armies and troops brought over from Thrace and drilled through the summer; the Optimatoi led the decisive charge (George of Pisidia, Expeditio Persica).
greek_note: Heraclius' army was raised in Anatolia and Thrace, with many Armenians.
sources: George of Pisidia, Expeditio Persica; Theophanes AM 6113; en.wikipedia Heraclius' campaign of 622
note: Wikipedia titles it 'Heraclius' campaign of 622'; it is sometimes wrongly called the battle of Issus, and some lists call it Ophlimus.

name: Heraclea
borderline: An ambush at a parley ('the Avar surprise'); little organised fighting.
roman_force: Heraclius' court and escort, come to a parley with the khagan; the emperor fled to Constantinople and the Avars ravaged the suburbs (Chronicon Paschale; Nicephorus 10).
greek_note: The court and the people of the Thracian hinterland of Constantinople spoke Greek.
sources: Chronicon Paschale s.a. 623; Nicephorus, Short History 10; Theophanes AM 6110; en.wikipedia Maurice's Balkan campaigns

name: Ganzak
roman_force: Heraclius' expeditionary army, perhaps 20,000-24,000 (Kaegi), against Khosrow's 40,000; the king's guard was overrun and his army scattered (Theophanes AM 6114).
greek_note: Heraclius' army was raised in Anatolia and Armenia.
sources: Theophanes AM 6114; Sebeos 38; en.wikipedia, the article on the Roman-Sasanian war of 602-628
note: Heraclius then sacked Ganzak and destroyed the fire temple at Takht-i Suleiman. Ganzak is placed at Leylan or Takht-i Suleiman.

name: Sarus
place: the bridge over the Sarus (Seyhan), near Adana
roman_force: Heraclius' army; its vanguard was cut up after crossing, and Heraclius' own charge at the bridge restored the fight (Theophanes AM 6115).
greek_note: Heraclius' Anatolian and Armenian regiments.
sources: Theophanes AM 6115; en.wikipedia Battle of Sarus
note: A nominal Roman victory: Shahrbaraz withdrew in good order and marched on to Chalcedon.

name: Tigranakert
roman_force: Heraclius' army with Lazic, Abasgian and Iberian allies, who joined him in Albania and soon after deserted (Theophanes AM 6115; Movses Daskhurantsi 2.10).
greek_note: Heraclius' Anatolian and Armenian regiments with Caucasian allies.
sources: Theophanes AM 6115; Movses Daskhurantsi 2.10; en.wikipedia, the article on the Roman-Sasanian war of 602-628
note: Heraclius routed Shahraplakan and then Shahin in turn. Which Tigranakert is meant is disputed.

name: Aliovit (Archesh)
place: Archesh (Ercis), in the district of Aliovit, north of Lake Van
roman_force: Heraclius' army, in a night attack on Shahrbaraz's camp (Theophanes AM 6115).
greek_note: Heraclius' Anatolian and Armenian regiments.
sources: Theophanes AM 6115; en.wikipedia, the article on the Roman-Sasanian war of 602-628
note: Shahrbaraz barely escaped; listed as 'Archesh' in some lists.

name: Constantinople (siege)
place: Constantinople, the Golden Horn and the Bosporus
roman_force: About 12,000 cavalry sent by Heraclius, the citizens on the walls and the fleet, which destroyed the Slav monoxyla in the Golden Horn and kept the Persians on the Asian shore (Chronicon Paschale; Theodore Synkellos; George of Pisidia, Bellum Avaricum).
greek_note: The defence was carried by the people and garrison of the Greek-speaking capital.
sources: Chronicon Paschale s.a. 626; Theodore Synkellos, Homily; George of Pisidia, Bellum Avaricum; en.wikipedia Siege of Constantinople (626)
note: Combined land and sea siege; the naval victory of 7 August decided it. Bulgar and Gepid contingents served with the Avars.

name: Lycus
roman_force: The army detached under Theodore when Heraclius divided his forces in 626 (Theophanes AM 6117 tells of a hailstorm striking the Persians); smaller than Shahin's army, given as over 50,000.
greek_note: Heraclius' Anatolian and Armenian regiments.
sources: Theophanes AM 6117; en.wikipedia Battle of the Lycus (626)
note: Shahin's army was virtually destroyed; he died soon after. Exact site on the Lycus unknown.

name: Nineveh
place: near the ruins of Nineveh, by the Tigris
roman_force: Heraclius' army, given as 25,000-50,000 by modern estimates; the Turkish allies had gone home before the battle (Theophanes AM 6118).
greek_note: Heraclius' army was recruited in Anatolia and Armenia; Greek speakers and Armenians made up most of it.
sources: Theophanes AM 6118; Chronicon Paschale s.a. 628; en.wikipedia Battle of Nineveh (627)
note: Fought in fog; Rhahzadh fell in single combat with Heraclius, according to Theophanes.

name: Tiflis (siege)
commanders_b: Shahraplakan's officers, Stephen I of Iberia
roman_force: Heraclius' army with a Western Turkish (Khazar) host given as 40,000, using traction trebuchets (Movses Daskhurantsi 2.11-14; Theophanes AM 6117).
greek_note: Heraclius' Anatolian and Armenian regiments; the Turkish allies outnumbered them.
sources: Movses Daskhurantsi 2.11-14; Theophanes AM 6117; en.wikipedia Third Perso-Turkic War
note: Allies_a: the Western Turks, called Khazars by Theophanes. Heraclius left in 627; the Turks took the city in 628. The pro-Persian Iberian prince Stephen I held it (allies_b).

name: Mu'tah
commanders_b: Zayd ibn Haritha, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, Abd Allah ibn Rawaha (all killed), Khalid ibn al-Walid
roman_force: Roman troops under Theodore with Arab allies of the Lakhm, Judham, Bali and Bahra and the Ghassanids, probably not more than 10,000 (Kaegi), against about 3,000 Muslims (Theophanes AM 6123; al-Waqidi).
greek_note: Most of the force were Christian Arab tribesmen; the Roman regulars were few.
sources: Theophanes AM 6123; al-Waqidi, Kitab al-Maghazi; Ibn Ishaq; en.wikipedia Battle of Mu'tah
note: Muslim side: the Islamic state of Medina. Later Muslim tradition presents the retreat as a success.

name: Firaz
war: Arab conquest of the Levant (Rashidun Caliphate)
place: Firaz, on the Euphrates between al-Qa'im and Abu Kamal
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
borderline: Roman and Persian participation and even the result are questioned by modern historians.
roman_force: A Roman frontier garrison on the Euphrates with Christian Arab allies (Taghlib, Iyad, Namir) and Persian remnants, as told by al-Tabari; no reliable numbers.
greek_note: A small frontier garrison among Arab allies.
sources: al-Tabari, History 11; en.wikipedia Battle of Firaz
note: Traditional accounts give 100,000 enemy dead, an impossible figure; some argue Khalid may have been repulsed.

name: Dathin
war: Arab conquest of the Levant (Rashidun Caliphate)
commanders_a: Amr ibn al-As (or Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan)
roman_force: A small force sent from Caesarea under Sergius, governor of Palestine; about 300 soldiers fell (Thomas the Presbyter; Doctrina Jacobi; Theophanes AM 6124).
greek_note: Garrison troops of Palestine, Greek- and Aramaic-speaking.
sources: Thomas the Presbyter, Chronicle s.a. 945 (Seleucid); Doctrina Jacobi 5.16; Theophanes AM 6124; en.wikipedia Battle of Dathin
note: Probably the same as the Arab sources' battle of al-Araba or Dathin; the villagers of the Gaza district also suffered heavy losses.

name: Ajnadayn
war: Arab conquest of the Levant (Rashidun Caliphate)
place: Ajnadayn, near Bayt Jibrin (perhaps the Wadi al-Samt)
commanders_a: Khalid ibn al-Walid, Amr ibn al-As
commanders_b: Theodore (Heraclius' brother), Vardan (Wardan, probably killed), Aretion
roman_force: Perhaps 10,000-20,000 (modern estimates): the forces of Palestine and Syria under Theodore and the commander the Arab sources call Wardan, probably an Armenian Vardan leading fresh troops from the north (al-Tabari; al-Baladhuri).
greek_note: The army of the East in 634-636 combined Greek-speaking regulars from Syria and Anatolia with Armenians.
sources: al-Tabari; al-Baladhuri; en.wikipedia Battle of Ajnadayn
note: Some date it to January 635.

name: Damascus (siege)
war: Arab conquest of the Levant (Rashidun Caliphate)
commanders_a: Khalid ibn al-Walid, Abu Ubayda, Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan, Amr ibn al-As, Shurahbil
roman_force: The garrison of Damascus under Thomas and the citizens; a relief force from Emesa was turned back (al-Tabari; al-Baladhuri).
greek_note: Syrian regulars and a Greek- and Aramaic-speaking city.
sources: al-Tabari; al-Baladhuri; en.wikipedia Siege of Damascus (634)
note: The city capitulated on terms; many modern historians date the surrender to 635.

name: Marj al-Dibaj
war: Arab conquest of the Levant (Rashidun Caliphate)
place: Marj al-Dibaj, beyond the Jabal Ansariya, towards Antioch
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
borderline: Known only from the late, largely legendary Futuh al-Sham attributed to al-Waqidi.
roman_force: The garrison of Damascus and refugees marching north under the truce, overtaken by Khalid's cavalry (pseudo-al-Waqidi).
greek_note: Syrian regulars and townspeople of Damascus.
sources: pseudo-al-Waqidi, Futuh al-Sham; en.wikipedia Battle of Maraj-al-Debaj
note: Thomas is said to have fallen in single combat with Khalid; other sources have him survive.

name: Sanita al-Uqab
war: Arab conquest of the Levant (Rashidun Caliphate)
place: the Eagle Pass (Thaniyat al-Uqab), near al-Qutayfah, Qalamoun
borderline: Known only from later Arab tradition; a minor clash on Khalid's march from Iraq.
roman_force: Local Roman troops guarding the approach to Damascus; no details.
greek_note: Syrian garrison troops.
sources: al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Battle of Sanita-al-Uqab

name: Bosra (siege)
war: Arab conquest of the Levant (Rashidun Caliphate)
commanders_a: Khalid ibn al-Walid, Shurahbil ibn Hasana, Abu Ubayda, Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan
roman_force: The garrison of Bostra, given as 4,000, under Romanus, which fought outside the walls before withdrawing into the fort; the city then surrendered on terms (al-Baladhuri; al-Waqidi).
greek_note: A Greek-speaking provincial capital with a large Arab population.
sources: al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; en.wikipedia Battle of Bosra

name: Marj al-Saffar
war: Arab conquest of the Levant (Rashidun Caliphate)
roman_force: The Roman force sent out from Damascus to stop the Arab advance (al-Baladhuri).
greek_note: Syrian regulars of the army of the East.
sources: al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; en.wikipedia Battle of Marj al-Saffar (634)
note: The Muslims also suffered heavy losses. Wikipedia's infobox dates it 23 January 635 (its lead and other articles say 634); distinct from Marj ar-Rum (west of Damascus, March or late 635, against Theodore and Shannash).

name: Fahl (Pella)
war: Arab conquest of the Levant (Rashidun Caliphate)
place: Fahl (Pella) and Baysan (Scythopolis), in the Jordan valley
commanders_a: Abu Ubayda, Khalid ibn al-Walid, Amr ibn al-As, Shurahbil ibn Hasana
roman_force: The Roman forces of Palestine, with survivors of Ajnadayn, under the sakellarios Theodore; they flooded the fields round Baysan (al-Tabari; al-Baladhuri).
greek_note: Syrian and Anatolian regulars with Armenians.
sources: al-Tabari; al-Baladhuri; en.wikipedia Battle of Fahl
note: Pella fell; Baysan and Tiberias surrendered. The Arab figure of 80,000-100,000 Roman dead is fantasy.

name: Emesa (siege)
war: Arab conquest of the Levant (Rashidun Caliphate)
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Emesa, through a winter siege with sorties (al-Baladhuri; al-Tabari).
greek_note: Syrian regulars and a Greek- and Aramaic-speaking city.
sources: al-Baladhuri; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Siege of Emesa
note: The city surrendered on terms and was abandoned when Heraclius' great army advanced, then retaken after the Yarmouk.

name: Marj ar-Rum
war: Arab conquest of the Levant (Rashidun Caliphate)
place: Marj ar-Rum, the plain west of Damascus
commanders_a: Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan, Abu Ubayda, Khalid ibn al-Walid
roman_force: A Roman force with a strong cavalry element sent against Damascus from the north (al-Tabari).
greek_note: Regulars of the army of the East.
sources: al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Battle of Marj ar-Rum

name: Yarmouk
war: Arab conquest of the Levant (Rashidun Caliphate)
place: the plains above the Yarmouk and its tributary the Wadi al-Ruqqad, southeast of the Sea of Galilee
commanders_a: Abu Ubayda, Khalid ibn al-Walid, Amr ibn al-As, Shurahbil, Yazid, Dhirar ibn al-Azwar
commanders_b: Vahan, Theodore Trithyrius (killed), Qanatir (Buccinator), Jabala ibn al-Ayham, Gregory, Dairjan
roman_force: The army Heraclius gathered from Antioch in five corps: Armenians under Vahan, the army of the East under the sakellarios Theodore Trithyrius, a corps under Qanatir (said to be Slavs or Rus), the Christian Arabs of Jabala ibn al-Ayham, and troops under Gregory and Dairjan; perhaps 15,000-50,000 by modern estimates, against Theophanes' 80,000 plus 60,000 Ghassanids.
greek_note: Armenians and Christian Arabs were large contingents beside the Greek-speaking regulars of the eastern armies.
sources: Theophanes AM 6126; al-Baladhuri; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Battle of the Yarmuk
note: Exact site and dates are debated; Treadgold puts the Roman army at 80,000-100,000.

name: Jerusalem (siege)
war: Arab conquest of the Levant (Rashidun Caliphate)
commanders_a: Abu Ubayda, Amr ibn al-As; Caliph Umar (terms)
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Jerusalem under Patriarch Sophronius (al-Tabari; Theophanes AM 6127).
greek_note: The Christian population of Jerusalem spoke Greek and Palestinian Aramaic.
sources: al-Tabari; Theophanes AM 6127; en.wikipedia Siege of Jerusalem (636-637)
note: The city surrendered to Umar in person.

name: Hazir
war: Arab conquest of the Levant (Rashidun Caliphate)
place: Hadir (Hazir), about 5 km east of Qinnasrin (Chalcis)
roman_force: Menas' force from Chalcis, perhaps about 7,000 (modern estimate; Arab sources say 70,000) (al-Tabari).
greek_note: Regulars of the army of the East in northern Syria.
sources: al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Battle of Hazir
note: Qinnasrin surrendered soon after.

name: Iron Bridge
war: Arab conquest of the Levant (Rashidun Caliphate)
place: the Iron Bridge over the Orontes, about 20 km from Antioch
roman_force: Roman troops defending Antioch with Christian Arab allies, given as 15,000-20,000 (Arab tradition).
greek_note: Regulars of the army of the East with Christian Arab allies.
sources: al-Waqidi; al-Baladhuri; en.wikipedia Battle of the Iron Bridge
note: Antioch surrendered on 30 October 637.

name: Aleppo (siege)
war: Arab conquest of the Levant (Rashidun Caliphate)
roman_force: The garrison of Aleppo under the commander the Arab sources call Yuqinna (al-Baladhuri).
greek_note: Syrian regulars.
sources: al-Baladhuri; en.wikipedia Siege of Aleppo (637)
note: The city capitulated after a siege of some months.

name: Emesa (siege)
war: Arab conquest of the Levant (Rashidun Caliphate)
borderline: The share of Roman regulars in the attack is uncertain.
roman_force: A Roman force swollen by Christian Arab levies of the Jazira, besieging the Muslim garrison of Emesa (al-Tabari).
greek_note: The besiegers were mostly Christian Arabs of the Jazira.
sources: al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of the Levant
note: The siege broke up when Muslim forces raided the Jazira and Khalid sallied.

name: Germanicia (siege)
war: Arab conquest of the Levant (Rashidun Caliphate)
borderline: Captured with little bloodshed.
roman_force: The garrison of Germanicia (al-Baladhuri).
greek_note: A frontier garrison of the army of the East.
sources: al-Baladhuri; en.wikipedia Siege of Germanicia

name: Pelusium (siege)
roman_force: The garrison of Pelusium, the eastern gate of Egypt, holding out for about two months with heavy losses on both sides (Ibn Abd al-Hakam).
greek_note: The army of Egypt was recruited locally and spoke Greek and Coptic.
sources: Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr; John of Nikiu 111; en.wikipedia Siege of Pelusium (640)
note: Amr began with about 4,000 men.

name: Belbeis (siege)
roman_force: The Roman troops gathered at Belbeis under Aretion, who fell in a battle before the walls (Ibn Abd al-Hakam).
greek_note: The army of Egypt, Greek- and Coptic-speaking.
sources: Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Egypt

name: Heliopolis
place: Heliopolis, about 15 km northeast of Babylon
commanders_a: Amr ibn al-As, al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam
roman_force: The field army of Egypt under Theodore, with cavalry under Anastasius and Theodosius, perhaps over 20,000 (modern estimate), against Amr's army raised by reinforcements to about 12,000-15,000; the fight at Umm Dunayn preceded it (John of Nikiu 111; Ibn Abd al-Hakam).
greek_note: The army of Egypt was locally recruited, Greek- and Coptic-speaking.
sources: John of Nikiu 111; Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr; en.wikipedia Battle of Heliopolis
note: The cavalry clash near Abbaseya and the storming of Heliopolis are one battle here; the earlier siege of Umm Dunayn (Tendunias) is now a separate entry.

name: Babylon Fortress (siege)
commanders_a: Amr ibn al-As, al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, Ubada ibn al-Samit
roman_force: The garrison of Babylon, about 4,000 men, supplied by river until the Nile fell (John of Nikiu; Ibn Abd al-Hakam).
greek_note: The army of Egypt, Greek- and Coptic-speaking.
sources: John of Nikiu 111-117; Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr; en.wikipedia Siege of Babylon Fortress
note: The garrison capitulated after the assault of Good Friday, 6 April 641, and withdrew to Rauda island.

name: Umm Dunayn (siege)
place: Umm Dunayn (Tendunias), a fortified river port on the Nile north of Babylon, in today's central Cairo
borderline: The identification of John of Nikiu's Tendunias with Umm Dunayn (Butler) and the date are uncertain.
roman_force: The garrison of Tendunias (Umm Dunayn); John of Nikiu says that only 300 of its men escaped to the fortress of Babylon (John of Nikiu 111).
greek_note: Egyptian garrison troops of the army of Egypt.
sources: John of Nikiu 111; Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr; en.wikipedia Battle of Heliopolis
note: Amr took it with difficulty, lacking siege engines, before his reinforcements arrived and before the battle of Heliopolis.

name: Bahnasa
place: Bahnasa (Oxyrhynchus) and the edge of the Fayum
borderline: A raid and a small action, known from John of Nikiu.
roman_force: A small Roman detachment of about 50 men under the general John, betrayed and killed, and the townspeople of Bahnasa (John of Nikiu 111).
greek_note: Egyptian troops and townsmen.
sources: John of Nikiu 111; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Egypt
note: The Arabs failed to take the Fayum but sacked Bahnasa.

name: Caesarea Maritima (siege)
date: 640 (fell 640 or 641; other dates 638-639; blockaded on and off since 634)
war: Arab conquest of the Levant (Rashidun Caliphate)
roman_force: The garrison of the provincial capital, supplied by sea, and its Greek, Samaritan and Jewish townspeople (al-Baladhuri).
greek_note: A Greek-speaking capital with Samaritan and Jewish communities.
sources: al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of the Levant
note: Taken by storm according to al-Baladhuri, through a traitor who showed an entrance.

name: Tarnut
date: 641 (February-March in Wikipedia; after Nikiou, May 641, in Butler)
place: Tarnut (Terenuthis), on the western edge of the Nile Delta, on the road to Alexandria
commanders_b: unknown (a detachment of the army of Egypt)
borderline: A delaying action against the Arab vanguard, known mainly from Arabic accounts.
roman_force: A detachment of the Roman army of Egypt falling back on Alexandria; the sources give no numbers.
greek_note: The army of Egypt in 641 joined Greek-speaking imperial troops with locally raised Coptic-speaking soldiers.
sources: Ibn Abd al-Hakam; Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Egypt; en.wikipedia Siege of Alexandria (641)
note: The Romans failed to inflict heavy losses but held up the advance for a full day, then fell back and joined the force that fought at Kom Sharik (Wikipedia).

name: Kom Sharik
place: Kom Sharik, western Nile Delta, on the road from Nikiou to Alexandria
commanders_a: unknown (detachments of the army of Egypt)
commanders_b: Arab cavalry vanguard of Amr ibn al-As (the place is named after Sharik ibn Sumayy)
borderline: A minor clash on the march to Alexandria, known mainly from Arabic accounts.
roman_force: Two Roman detachments of the army of Egypt falling back on Alexandria; the sources give no numbers.
greek_note: The imperial army in Egypt combined Greek-speaking officers and eastern units with locally raised, largely Coptic-speaking garrison troops.
sources: John of Nikiu 118-120 (in part); Ibn Abd al-Hakam; Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Egypt; en.wikipedia Siege of Alexandria (641)
note: The Romans routed the Arab cavalry vanguard, then withdrew when Amr's main army came up. Wikipedia dates the clashes at Tarnut, Kom Sharik, Sultais and Kiryun to Feb-Mar 641; Butler puts them after the fall of Babylon (April) and Nikiou (May 641).

name: Sultais
place: Sultais (Sulteis), western Nile Delta, on the road to Alexandria
borderline: A minor clash on the march to Alexandria, known mainly from Arabic accounts.
roman_force: A Roman detachment of the army of Egypt retreating on Alexandria; no numbers are given.
greek_note: The imperial army in Egypt combined Greek-speaking officers and eastern units with locally raised, largely Coptic-speaking garrison troops.
sources: Ibn Abd al-Hakam; Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Egypt; en.wikipedia Siege of Alexandria (641)
note: After hard fighting the Romans withdrew to Alexandria. Site not identified; dating as for Kom Sharik.

name: Kiryun
place: Kiryun (Kariun, Kirayun), on the canal about 20 km south-east of Alexandria
commanders_b: unknown (the commanders of the Alexandrian army)
borderline: Known mainly from Arabic accounts; sometimes treated as part of the siege of Alexandria.
roman_force: About 20,000 men of the Roman army of Egypt (Arab accounts) blocking the road to Alexandria.
greek_note: The field force covering Alexandria was drawn from the Greek-speaking city and garrison and from Coptic-speaking Egypt.
sources: Ibn Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Egypt; en.wikipedia Siege of Alexandria (641)
note: Ten days of indecisive fighting; on the tenth day the Arabs attacked and drove the Romans back into Alexandria.

name: Alexandria (siege)
date: 641 (from about March or June; treaty November 641; Arab entry 29 September 642)
commanders_a: Amr ibn al-As, Ubada ibn al-Samit
commanders_b: Cyrus (patriarch and prefect), Theodore, Menas, Domentianus, Constantine
borderline: Most fighting was in the field before the walls; the city was surrendered by treaty rather than stormed.
roman_force: The garrison of Alexandria and the remnants of the field army of Egypt under Theodore, with circus-faction militias (Blues and Greens) enlisted by Domentianus and Menas; the city was supplied by sea.
greek_note: Alexandria was a Greek-speaking city; its garrison and faction militias were largely Greek-speaking, with Coptic-speaking Egyptians from the countryside.
sources: John of Nikiu 119-121; Ibn Abd al-Hakam; Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt; en.wikipedia Siege of Alexandria (641)
note: Cyrus agreed the capitulation with Amr at Babylon (November 641); the last Roman troops sailed on 17 September 642 and Amr entered on 29 September 642.

name: Scultenna
place: on the river Scultenna (Panaro), in Aemilia, between Modena and Bologna (site unknown)
commanders_b: Isaac (exarch of Ravenna, perhaps killed); Wikipedia's article on Rothari names the exarch Plato
roman_force: The army of the exarchate of Ravenna ('the Romans of Ravenna' in Paul the Deacon), of whom 8,000 fell; no units are named.
greek_note: The exarchate's army was raised by now mostly from Latin-speaking Italians, under eastern (Greek and Armenian) officers.
sources: Paul the Deacon, Historia Langobardorum 4.45; Bury, A History of the Later Roman Empire; en.wikipedia Rothari; en.wikipedia Isaac (exarch)
note: Paul says 8,000 Romans fell and the rest fled. Bury thinks Isaac died fighting the Lombards, while the Liber Pontificalis says he died of a stroke; the battle followed Rothari's conquest of Liguria and of Oderzo.

name: Tripoli (siege)
war: Arab conquest of North Africa (Rashidun Caliphate)
roman_force: The Roman garrison of Tripoli, supported by Christian Berbers of the Nafusa (Arab accounts); no numbers are given.
greek_note: Tripolitania belonged to the Latin-speaking African command; Greek speakers were mostly officers and officials.
sources: al-Baladhuri; Ibn Abd al-Hakam; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of the Maghreb
note: The city held out about a month; the Arabs got in along the shore where the wall did not reach the sea (Arab tradition). Sabratha and Leptis fell about the same time.

name: Alexandria
borderline: A surprise amphibious recapture with little fighting.
roman_force: An expeditionary army sent by Constans II under Manuel, carried by a fleet of about 300 ships.
greek_note: A fleet and army sent from Constantinople, raised mainly in the Greek-speaking provinces of the empire.
sources: Ibn Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Egypt; en.wikipedia Battle of Nikiou
note: The small Arab garrison was overwhelmed; the Alexandrians welcomed the imperial troops.

name: Nikiou
place: Nikiou (Zawyat Razin, Monufia), on the Nile between Alexandria and Fustat
roman_force: Manuel's expeditionary army from Constantinople, perhaps 20,000 men (modern estimate), joined by some Alexandrians.
greek_note: The army was shipped from Constantinople and raised in the Greek-speaking East, with local Alexandrian support.
sources: Ibn Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; en.wikipedia Battle of Nikiou
note: The Romans retreated in disorder to Alexandria.

name: Alexandria (siege)
roman_force: The remains of Manuel's expeditionary army and the Alexandrians who had joined it.
greek_note: Manuel's army came from the Greek-speaking East; the city itself was Greek-speaking.
