sources: Ibn Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Egypt; en.wikipedia Battle of Nikiou
note: The Arabs stormed the city; Wikipedia says Manuel was killed (some accounts have him escape by sea). The last imperial attempt on Egypt for about 500 years.

name: Sufetula
war: Arab conquest of North Africa (Rashidun Caliphate)
commanders_a: Abdallah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh, Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr
commanders_b: Gregory the Patrician (exarch of Africa, killed)
borderline: Gregory had proclaimed himself emperor against Constans II; his army is counted as Roman.
roman_force: The army of the exarchate of Africa under the exarch Gregory, with Berber allies (Zenata, Maghrawa); the Arab figure of 120,000 is impossible.
greek_note: The African army was raised in Latin-speaking Africa with Berber allies; Greek speakers were mostly among the officers and eastern units.
sources: Ibn Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; Theophanes AM 6139; en.wikipedia Battle of Sufetula (647)
note: Gregory was killed; the Arabs sacked Sufetula and withdrew after the Africans paid a large tribute.

name: Arwad (siege)
place: the island city of Arwad (Aradus), off the Syrian coast
borderline: The fighting is known only in outline; the city surrendered at the second attempt.
roman_force: The garrison and townspeople of the fortified island city; the sources give no numbers or units.
greek_note: Aradus was a Hellenized Phoenician island city with an imperial garrison; its people spoke Greek and Aramaic.
sources: Theophanes (the envoy Thomarichos); PBE Thomarichos 1; en.wikipedia Conquest of Arwad (649-650)
note: A first attack by Mu'awiya's fleet with siege engines in winter 649 failed, and the defenders held his envoy, the bishop Thomarichos; in spring 650 he returned for a long siege and the defenders surrendered for safe passage. The fortifications were razed. Wikipedia's title calls it a conquest.

name: The Masts (Phoenix)
commanders_a: Abdallah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh (fleet of Egypt), Abu al-A'war; for Mu'awiya
roman_force: The imperial fleet led by Constans II in person, about 500 ships (Theophanes says 1,000), against about 200 Arab ships.
greek_note: The fleet was manned from the Aegean and southern Anatolian coasts, the later Karabisianoi, which were Greek-speaking.
sources: Theophanes AM 6146; Sebeos 50; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Battle of the Masts
note: Dated 654 or 655. Constans escaped by changing clothes with one of his men; heavy losses on both sides.

name: Benevento (siege)
war: Constans II's war with the Lombards
commanders_a: Romuald I of Benevento; Grimoald I (relief)
roman_force: The expeditionary army Constans II brought from the East (landed at Taranto), with Italian garrison troops; no numbers are given.
greek_note: The army Constans brought from Constantinople was raised in the Greek-speaking East, with Armenians; Latin-speaking Italian troops joined it.
sources: Paul the Deacon, Historia Langobardorum 5.6-10; Liber Pontificalis (Vitalian); en.wikipedia Constans II
note: Constans raised the siege on news of Grimoald's approach and withdrew to Naples.

name: Luceria
war: Constans II's war with the Lombards
borderline: A storming of a town mentioned briefly by Paul the Deacon.
roman_force: Constans II's expeditionary army from the East; no numbers are given.
greek_note: The expeditionary army was raised in the Greek-speaking East.
sources: Paul the Deacon, Historia Langobardorum 5.7; en.wikipedia Constans II
note: Paul says Constans took Luceria by force and destroyed it; Acerenza resisted him.

name: Pugna (Calore)
war: Constans II's war with the Lombards
place: on the river Calore, at the place called Pugna, between Benevento and Naples
borderline: A rearguard action known only from Paul the Deacon.
roman_force: Constans II's army retreating from Benevento to Naples; no numbers are given.
greek_note: The expeditionary army was raised in the Greek-speaking East.
sources: Paul the Deacon, Historia Langobardorum 5.9; en.wikipedia Constans II
note: Paul says the place was still called Pugna ('battle') in his day.

name: Forino
war: Constans II's war with the Lombards
roman_force: About 20,000 men of Constans II's army given to Saburrus (Paul the Deacon).
greek_note: The force came from the army Constans brought from the Greek-speaking East.
sources: Paul the Deacon, Historia Langobardorum 5.10; en.wikipedia Constans II
note: Saburrus, who had promised to beat the Lombards, was routed; Constans then went to Rome and Sicily.

name: Hadrumetum
war: Arab conquest of North Africa (Umayyad Caliphate)
commanders_a: Mu'awiya ibn Hudayj, Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr
borderline: Known only from Arab accounts.
roman_force: An imperial force under the patrikios Nikephoros, landed by sea to defend Byzacena (Arab accounts); no numbers are given.
greek_note: A force sent by sea from the East would have been largely Greek-speaking, joined by Latin-speaking African troops.
sources: al-Baladhuri; Ibn Abd al-Hakam; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of the Maghreb
note: Ibn al-Zubayr defeated Nikephoros and took Hadrumetum; in the same campaign Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan besieged Cululis (Jalula).

name: Amorion
commanders_b: unknown (Arab garrison left by Fadala ibn Ubayd and Yazid)
borderline: A night recapture of a town, known from Theophanes.
roman_force: Troops sent by Constantine IV under the chamberlain Andrew, who scaled the walls in the snow (Theophanes); no numbers are given for the Romans.
greek_note: The troops came from the Anatolian themes, Greek-speaking with Armenian elements.
sources: Theophanes AM 6160; en.wikipedia Siege of Constantinople (674-678)
note: Theophanes says the Arab garrison of 5,000 was slaughtered. Part of the campaign that Jankowiak dates as the first Arab siege of Constantinople (667-669).

name: Constantinople (siege)
place: Constantinople and the Sea of Marmara (Arab base at Cyzicus)
commanders_a: Constantine IV; Phloros, Petron and Cyprian (land army in Anatolia)
commanders_b: Mu'awiya I; Yazid ibn Mu'awiya, Fadala ibn Ubayd, Junada ibn Abi Umayya, Sufyan ibn Awf (land army)
roman_force: The garrison of the capital and the imperial fleet with siphon-ships using Greek fire (attributed to Kallinikos, a refugee from Heliopolis in Syria); in Anatolia a field army under Phloros, Petron and Cyprian defeated the Arab land army.
greek_note: The capital's garrison, the fleet and the Anatolian field army were drawn from the Greek-speaking core of the empire.
sources: Theophanes AM 6164-6170; Nikephoros 34; en.wikipedia Siege of Constantinople (674-678)
note: A series of blockades from a base at Cyzicus rather than a close siege. The Arab fleet was routed (late 677/early 678) and the retreating fleet wrecked by a storm off Syllaion; Theophanes gives 30,000 Arab dead in the Anatolian defeat. Jankowiak redates the main attack to 667-669.

name: Thessalonica (siege)
commanders_b: unknown (the Rhynchinoi, Strymonitai and Sagoudatai, joined by the Drougoubitai)
roman_force: The citizens, council and garrison of Thessalonica; the emperor, at war with the Arabs, could spare only ten armed transports, later a grain fleet under escort, and in 678 an expedition against the Strymonitai (Miracles of St Demetrius).
greek_note: Thessalonica was a Greek-speaking city defended chiefly by its own militia and garrison.
sources: Miracles of St Demetrius II.4; Lemerle, Les plus anciens recueils des Miracles de saint Demetrius; en.wikipedia Siege of Thessalonica (676-678)
note: The decisive assault of 25 July 677 failed and the Slavs left their siege engines; the siege was lifted in 678 (Lemerle's chronology). The Belegezitai stayed loyal and supplied grain (in allies_a as Slavs). The rising followed the execution of Perbundos, king of the Rhynchinoi.

name: Ongal
place: the Onglos, near the Danube delta (exact site unknown)
roman_force: All the themes brought over from Anatolia to Thrace (Theophanes), with a fleet sent to the Danube mouths (Nikephoros); modern estimates 15,000-25,000.
greek_note: Theophanes says the emperor brought 'all the themes' across to Thrace; the Anatolian thematic armies were largely Greek-speaking, with Armenian elements.
sources: Theophanes AM 6171; Nikephoros 36; en.wikipedia Battle of Ongal
note: The army panicked after Constantine IV left for medical treatment and was cut down in the retreat; the defeat led to the Bulgar state south of the Danube (treaty of 681).

name: Vescera
war: Arab conquest of North Africa (Umayyad Caliphate)
commanders_b: Uqba ibn Nafi (killed), Abu al-Muhajir Dinar (killed)
borderline: The Roman contingent is known only from Arab accounts; Kusaila's Berbers were the main force.
roman_force: Roman troops of the exarchate of Africa allied with the Romano-Berber army of Kusaila (Arab accounts speak of the Rum with the Berbers); no numbers are given.
greek_note: The coalition was Berber and Latin-speaking African; any Greek speakers would have been among the imperial officers.
sources: Ibn Abd al-Hakam; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Battle of Vescera
note: Uqba was ambushed on his return from his march to the Atlantic and killed with his army; Kusaila then took Kairouan.

name: Barca
war: Arab conquest of North Africa (Umayyad Caliphate)
place: coast of Cyrenaica near Barca (Zuhayr's tomb is at Derna)
borderline: Known only from Arab accounts; site uncertain.
roman_force: A Roman fleet and landing force that raided Cyrenaica (Arab accounts); no numbers are given.
greek_note: A seaborne force from the imperial fleet, manned mainly from the Greek-speaking coasts.
sources: Ibn Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of the Maghreb
note: Zuhayr, returning east after his victory at Mamma, met the landing party with a small escort and was killed with his men.

name: Sebastopolis
commanders_b: Justinian II; Leontios (strategos of the Anatolikon); Neboulos (archon of the Slavs, defected)
roman_force: The field army under Leontios with the 'chosen people' (laos periousios), a corps of 30,000 Slavs settled in the Opsikion in 688/689, of whom about 20,000 deserted to the Arabs under Neboulos.
greek_note: Theophanes and Nikephoros name a Slavic corps of 30,000 beside the Greek-speaking thematic troops, so the Slavs may have been the largest single part.
sources: Theophanes AM 6184; Nikephoros 38; en.wikipedia Battle of Sebastopolis
note: The Romans were winning until the Slavs deserted, allegedly bribed; Justinian later had the remaining Slavs' families massacred (Theophanes).

name: Marash
commanders_a: Aban ibn al-Walid ibn Uqba (governor of Qinnasrin), Dinar ibn Dinar
roman_force: An imperial army operating on the Syrian frontier; the sources give no units or numbers (Arab claims of 40,000 Roman dead are exaggerated).
greek_note: The eastern field forces of the 690s were the Anatolian themes, mostly Greek-speaking, with Armenians.
sources: al-Baladhuri; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Battle of Marash (694)
note: The Romans were pursued with heavy losses and abandoned Marash.

name: Carthage
war: Arab conquest of North Africa (Umayyad Caliphate)
commanders_b: unknown (garrison left by Hassan ibn al-Nu'man)
roman_force: The whole imperial fleet sent by Leontios (Theophanes), including the Kibyrrhaiot squadron whose droungarios Apsimar was later proclaimed emperor, with troops from Sicily.
greek_note: The fleet, with the Kibyrrhaiot sailors of the southern Anatolian coast named by Theophanes, was Greek-speaking; Sicilian troops were partly Latin-speaking.
sources: Theophanes AM 6190; Nikephoros 41; en.wikipedia Battle of Carthage (698)
note: An amphibious assault: the fleet broke the chain across the harbour, landed and defeated the Arab garrison; John then retook nearby towns.

name: Constantinople (siege)
place: Constantinople (the rebels landed at Sykai on the Golden Horn)
faction_a: Tiberios III (Apsimar; the fleet from Africa)
commanders_a: Apsimar (Tiberios III), droungarios of the Kibyrrhaiots
borderline: A civil siege known only in outline; no assaults are described and the city fell by treachery.
roman_force: Tiberios: the fleet back from Carthage, including the Kibyrrhaiot squadron, which had mutinied on Crete; Leontios: the garrison and citizens of a capital struck by plague.
greek_note: The Kibyrrhaiot fleet was raised on the Greek-speaking southern coasts of Anatolia and the islands, and the capital's garrison was Greek-speaking.
sources: Theophanes AM 6190; Nikephoros 41; en.wikipedia Tiberios III
note: After several months members of the Green faction opened the gates; the troops plundered the city. Leontios' nose was slit and he was confined to a monastery.

name: Carthage
war: Arab conquest of North Africa (Umayyad Caliphate)
roman_force: John the Patrician's expeditionary force from the imperial fleet (with the Kibyrrhaiots) and troops from Sicily; the Arabs are said to have had about 40,000.
greek_note: The expedition was carried and largely manned by the Greek-speaking imperial fleet, including the Kibyrrhaiots named by Theophanes.
sources: Theophanes AM 6190; Nikephoros 41; en.wikipedia Battle of Carthage (698)
note: Hassan besieged the city; the sorties failed and, as an Arab fleet arrived, John evacuated by sea. Hassan razed Carthage. The fleet then mutinied on Crete and proclaimed Apsimar (Tiberios III).

name: Utica
war: Arab conquest of North Africa (Umayyad Caliphate)
borderline: A last engagement mentioned only briefly; details unknown.
roman_force: John the Patrician's force after the evacuation of Carthage; no numbers are given.
greek_note: The force was the Greek-speaking expeditionary army and fleet sent from Constantinople.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Carthage (698)
note: After it John withdrew by sea to Crete.

name: Sisium
commanders_a: Heraclius (brother of Tiberios III, monostrategos of the cavalry themes)
roman_force: The army of the cavalry themes of Anatolia under Heraclius, the emperor's brother; no numbers are given for the Romans.
greek_note: Heraclius commanded the Anatolian cavalry themes (Theophanes), recruited mainly among Greek speakers.
sources: Theophanes AM 6196; en.wikipedia Heraclius (brother of Tiberius III)
note: Most of the Arab army of 10,000-12,000 was killed and the rest taken in chains to Constantinople.

name: Anchialus
roman_force: The cavalry themes sent to Thrace and a fleet that carried Justinian II to Anchialus (Theophanes); no numbers are given.
greek_note: Theophanes names the cavalry themes, i.e. the largely Greek-speaking thematic armies of Anatolia, brought across to Thrace.
sources: Theophanes AM 6200; Nikephoros 44; en.wikipedia Battle of Anchialus (708)
note: The troops scattered to forage were surprised by the Bulgars; Justinian shut himself in Anchialus for three days and escaped by sea.

name: Tyana (siege)
commanders_a: Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik, al-Abbas ibn al-Walid
roman_force: The garrison of Tyana and a relief army sent by Justinian II under two quarrelling generals, made up of regular troops and a large levy of untrained armed peasants (Theophanes).
greek_note: Garrison and relief army were raised in Cappadocia and the Anatolian themes, Greek-speaking with Armenian elements.
sources: Theophanes AM 6201; Nikephoros 44; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Siege of Tyana
note: The relief army was routed in a disorderly attack and the city surrendered; it was then sacked. Arab sources date the siege 706/707-707/708, Theophanes 708/709.

name: Cherson (siege)
commanders_a: Bardanes (Philippikos), with a Khazar relief force
borderline: A civil siege ended by the arrival of the Khazars, after which the besiegers joined the rebels.
roman_force: Justinian II's second expedition, a fleet with siege engines under the patrikios Maurus; against the Chersonites, the exiled Bardanes and a Khazar relief army.
greek_note: Cherson was a Greek city, and the expedition was raised from the Greek-speaking capital and fleet.
sources: Theophanes AM 6203; Nikephoros 45; en.wikipedia Justinian II
note: The siege engines brought down two towers before the Khazars arrived; the expedition then went over to Bardanes, proclaimed him emperor as Philippikos and sailed for Constantinople. Justinian II was killed in November 711.

name: Constantinople (siege)
borderline: A civil siege known only in outline; no assaults are described in detail.
roman_force: The Opsikion troops and the fleet that had mutinied on their way to Rhodes and Phoenix (killing their commander John the Deacon) and proclaimed Theodosios at Adramyttion, besieging the capital from Chrysopolis; against the garrison and citizens loyal to Anastasios II, who held Nicaea with his army.
greek_note: The Opsikion and the fleet, named by Theophanes, were raised in Greek-speaking north-western Anatolia and the coasts, with settled Slavs and Gothograeci in the Opsikion.
sources: Theophanes AM 6207; Nikephoros 50; en.wikipedia Theodosios III; en.wikipedia Anastasios II
note: Supporters inside the city opened the gates in November 715; Anastasios stayed in Nicaea for some months before abdicating and becoming a monk. Theophanes speaks of six months of fighting.

name: Constantinople (siege)
place: Constantinople, the Bosporus and the Sea of Marmara
commanders_b: Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik, Umar ibn Hubayra, Sulayman (fleet)
roman_force: The garrison of the capital (probably no more than 15,000) on the repaired Theodosian walls and the imperial fleet with Greek fire, which destroyed the Egyptian and African reinforcement fleets; Tervel's Bulgars attacked the Arab camp in Thrace.
greek_note: The defenders were the capital's garrison and the fleet, raised in the Greek-speaking core of the empire; the Bulgars were separate allies.
sources: Theophanes AM 6209-6210; Nikephoros 54-56; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Siege of Constantinople (717-718)
note: Christian Egyptian crews of the Arab fleet deserted in spring 718; Theophanes says the Bulgars killed 22,000 Arabs; storms destroyed much of the retreating fleet.

name: Cumae
war: Wars with the Lombards (Duchy of Naples)
place: the fortress of Cumae, west of Naples
commanders_a: John I, duke of Naples; Theodimus (subdeacon, rector of the papal patrimony)
commanders_b: the Lombard commander of Cumae (killed), for Romuald II of Benevento
borderline: A night recapture of a fortress by the ducal army of Naples, known from the Liber Pontificalis.
roman_force: The forces of the duchy of Naples under its duke John, an imperial officer, raised at the call of Pope Gregory II, who gave 70 pounds of gold to the undertaking; no numbers are given.
greek_note: Naples was a bilingual city under an imperial duke, but its militia was mostly local and Latin-speaking.
sources: Liber Pontificalis 91.7 (Gregory II); Paul the Deacon, Historia Langobardorum 6.40; PBE Ioannes 231; en.wikipedia John I of Naples
note: The Lombards of Benevento had seized Cumae by stealth; the Neapolitans entered the fortress by night, killed the Lombard commander and about 300 of his men and took about 500 prisoners (Liber Pontificalis; Paul the Deacon mentions the night attack). The fort had been occupied in 716.

name: Sophon
place: the hills of Sophon, south-east of Nicomedia
borderline: A named ambush within the siege of 717-718.
roman_force: A Roman force sent across to Bithynia from the besieged capital, which laid an ambush (Theophanes); no numbers are given.
greek_note: Troops from the capital's garrison and Bithynia, both Greek-speaking.
sources: Theophanes AM 6209; en.wikipedia Siege of Constantinople (717-718)
note: The Arab foraging army under Mardasan was destroyed.

name: Constantinople (sea)
commanders_b: Agallianos Kontoskeles (tourmarches of the Helladikoi), Stephen; Kosmas (proclaimed emperor)
roman_force: Leo III's imperial fleet with Greek fire against the fleet of the Helladikoi and the Cyclades.
greek_note: Both sides were Greek-speaking: the rebels were the men of the theme of Hellas and the islands (Theophanes), the loyalists the capital's fleet.
sources: Theophanes AM 6218; Nikephoros 60; en.wikipedia Leo III the Isaurian
note: Theophanes links the revolt to Leo's first moves against images. The rebel fleet was burned; Agallianos threw himself into the sea and Kosmas and Stephen were beheaded.

name: Nicaea (siege)
roman_force: The garrison of Nicaea, capital of the Opsikion theme; the sources do not describe it, and the Romans did not meet the Arabs in the field.
greek_note: Nicaea was a Greek-speaking city and the seat of the Opsikion, recruited in north-western Anatolia.
sources: Theophanes AM 6218; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Siege of Nicaea (727)
note: Theophanes' figures (15,000 vanguard, 100,000 in all) are much inflated; the Arabs withdrew with captives and booty.

name: Akroinon
roman_force: The field army led by Leo III and Constantine V in person; the sources do not name the units, which were presumably the thematic armies of western and central Anatolia (Opsikion, Anatolikon).
greek_note: The Anatolian thematic armies of the 8th century were recruited mainly among Greek-speaking peasants, with Armenian elements.
sources: Theophanes AM 6231; Michael the Syrian; en.wikipedia Battle of Akroinon
note: Of 20,000 Arabs about 6,800 escaped to Synnada (Theophanes).

name: Krasos
place: the plain of Krasos, Phrygia (Nikephoros; Theophanes puts the attack near Dorylaion)
borderline: An attack at a meeting rather than a pitched battle; the only named casualty is Beser.
roman_force: Artabasdos: the army of the Opsikion; Constantine V: his retinue and the troops marching with him against the Arabs, who fled to Amorion and the Anatolikon.
greek_note: The Opsikion and Anatolikon armies were raised in Greek-speaking north-western and central Anatolia; Artabasdos was an Armenian.
sources: Nikephoros, Short History 64; Theophanes AM 6233; PBE Artabasdos 1; en.wikipedia Constantine V; en.wikipedia Artabasdos
note: Constantine had called Artabasdos to a meeting in the plain of Krasos before a campaign against the Arabs; Artabasdos killed Beser and attacked, Constantine fled to Amorion, and Artabasdos took Constantinople. Wikipedia (after Treadgold) dates the start of the revolt to June 741, the PBE to June 742.

name: Sardis
roman_force: Constantine V had the Anatolikon and Thrakesion themes; Artabasdos the Opsikion and troops from Thrace.
greek_note: The themes named by Theophanes (Anatolikon, Thrakesion, Opsikion) were recruited mainly in Greek-speaking western and central Anatolia.
sources: Theophanes AM 6235; Nikephoros 64; en.wikipedia Artabasdos; en.wikipedia Constantine V
note: Artabasdos had seized the throne after attacking Constantine on the march against the Arabs (June 741 or 742); the dating of the whole revolt (741-743 or 742-743) is disputed. Artabasdos supported the icons.

name: Modrine
commanders_b: Niketas (son of Artabasdos, strategos of the Armeniakon)
roman_force: Constantine V's Anatolikon and Thrakesion troops against Niketas and the Armeniakon army.
greek_note: The themes named are Anatolian; the Armeniakon had a strong Armenian element beside its Greek-speaking majority.
sources: Theophanes AM 6235; Nikephoros 64; en.wikipedia Constantine V
note: About three months after Sardis; Constantine then marched on Constantinople.

name: Constantinople (siege)
roman_force: Constantine V's Anatolian themes with the Kibyrrhaiot fleet blockading by sea, against Artabasdos' garrison of the capital and his remaining Opsikion and Thracian troops.
greek_note: The Anatolikon, Thrakesion and Kibyrrhaiot forces were Greek-speaking, as was the capital.
sources: Theophanes AM 6235; Nikephoros 66; en.wikipedia Constantine V; en.wikipedia Artabasdos
note: A blockade with famine in the city and a failed sortie; Constantine entered on 2 November 743, and Artabasdos fled to Pouzanes, was captured and blinded.

name: Keramaia
place: the harbour of Keramaia, Cyprus (site unknown)
commanders_a: the strategos of the Kibyrrhaiots (not named)
roman_force: The fleet of the Kibyrrhaiot theme under its strategos (Theophanes); no numbers are given.
greek_note: The Kibyrrhaiot fleet, named by Theophanes, was manned from the Greek-speaking southern coast of Anatolia and the Aegean islands.
sources: Theophanes AM 6238; en.wikipedia Battle of Keramaia
note: Theophanes' 1,000 Arab dromons is an exaggeration (perhaps about 30 ships); he says only three escaped.

name: Marcellae
roman_force: Constantine V's field army marching into Thrace while a fleet of 500 ships raided the Danube delta (Theophanes); the units are not named.
greek_note: Constantine V's armies were the tagmata and thematic forces of Anatolia and Thrace, mostly Greek-speaking, with Armenians.
sources: Theophanes AM 6247; Nikephoros 73; en.wikipedia Battle of Marcellae (756)
note: The first of Constantine V's Bulgarian campaigns; the Bulgars sued for peace and gave hostages.

name: Rishki Pass
place: the Rishki Pass (Veregava), Balkan Mountains (identification tentative)
commanders_b: Constantine V; Leo, strategos of Thrace (killed)
roman_force: Constantine V's invading army, including the Thracian theme under its strategos Leo, who was killed with the logothete Leo (Theophanes).
greek_note: The theme of Thrace, named by Theophanes, was mostly Greek-speaking, with Syrians and Armenians that Constantine V had settled in Thrace.
sources: Theophanes AM 6251; en.wikipedia Battle of the Rishki Pass
note: The army was ambushed in the pass; the Bulgars did not follow up the victory.

name: Anchialus
roman_force: A fleet of 800 chelandia carrying 9,600 cavalry (twelve horses a ship) and the emperor's army marching by land (Theophanes).
greek_note: The cavalry and the fleet came from the tagmata, the themes and the naval themes, mostly Greek-speaking.
sources: Theophanes AM 6254; Nikephoros 79; en.wikipedia Battle of Anchialus (763)
note: A hard-fought battle from morning to evening; Constantine held a triumph and executed the prisoners. Telets was murdered soon after.

name: Kamacha (siege)
commanders_b: al-Abbas ibn Muhammad, al-Hasan ibn Qahtaba
roman_force: The fortress garrison of Kamacha, and a Roman force of about 12,000 that, reinforced, routed an Arab raiding force by night (Chronicle of Zuqnin).
greek_note: Kamacha lay in the Armenian borderland and its garrison was Armenian when it surrendered in 793; the field force came from the eastern themes.
sources: Chronicle of Zuqnin; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Siege of Kamacha
note: The siege was given up as winter came on.

name: Berzitia (Lithosoria)
place: Lithosoria, in the border region of Zagora (site unknown)
roman_force: A large army hastily gathered by Constantine V (Theophanes gives a round 80,000), against a Bulgar raiding force of 12,000 sent to carry off the Slavic Berzitai.
greek_note: Constantine V's army was drawn from the tagmata and the themes of Thrace and Anatolia, mostly Greek-speaking.
sources: Theophanes AM 6265; en.wikipedia Battle of Berzitia
note: The Bulgars were surprised and beaten after a long fight; the site is put north of the line Kirklareli-Vize, but may lie in Bulgaria.

name: Germanikeia
commanders_a: Michael Lachanodrakon (Thrakesion), with the strategoi Artabasdos (Anatolikon), Tatzates (Boukellarion), Karisterotzes (Armeniakon), Gregory (Opsikion)
borderline: Wikipedia treats it as a campaign; the battle with Thumama's relief army has no separate name.
roman_force: The armies of five themes, Thrakesion, Anatolikon, Boukellarion, Armeniakon and Opsikion, under their strategoi (Theophanes gives an inflated 100,000).
greek_note: Theophanes names the five Anatolian themes, recruited mainly among Greek speakers, with Armenians prominent among the officers (Artabasdos, Tatzates).
sources: Theophanes AM 6270; Lewond; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Germanikeia Campaign (778)
note: The city was nearly taken and ransomed itself with a large tribute; the army ravaged Cilicia, and Theophanes records a rout of Thumama's relief forces with 2,000 Arabs and five emirs lost. Syrian Jacobite captives were settled in Thrace.

name: Dorylaion (siege)
roman_force: The garrison of Dorylaion, reinforced with men and supplies, while Leo IV's thematic troops (about 15,000, in detachments of some 3,000) shadowed the invaders and the countryside was evacuated.
greek_note: The thematic troops named in the sources belonged to the Opsikion and neighbouring Anatolian themes, recruited mainly among Greek speakers.
sources: Theophanes AM 6271; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Abbasid invasion of Asia Minor (779)
note: Hasan raised the siege when supplies ran out; on the way back an Arab attack on Amorion was also repulsed. The Romans had taken and demolished Hadath the same year.

name: Semaluos (siege)
place: the fortress of Semaluos, Armeniakon theme (site unknown)
borderline: A minor fortress siege; site unknown.
roman_force: The fortress garrison; no units or numbers are recorded.
greek_note: Garrisons of the Armeniakon were drawn from a theme with a Greek-speaking majority and a strong Armenian element.
sources: al-Tabari; Theophanes AM 6272; en.wikipedia Abbasid invasion of Asia Minor (779)
note: Arab sources say the fortress fell after a siege of 38 days. The same year Michael Lachanodrakon heavily defeated Thumama's raid into the Thrakesion.

name: Caesarea
commanders_a: Michael Lachanodrakon (Thrakesion); Tatzates (Boukellarion); John the sakellarios
roman_force: The armies of all the Asian themes assembled at Caesarea, among them the Thrakesion under Michael Lachanodrakon and the Boukellarion under Tatzates (modern estimates 40,000-50,000; al-Tabari's 90,000 is inflated).
greek_note: The sources name the Asian themes, including Thrakesion and Boukellarion, recruited mainly among Greek speakers; Tatzates and other officers were Armenians.
sources: Theophanes AM 6273; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Battle of Caesarea (781)
note: The Abbasids withdrew with heavy losses and the caliph al-Mahdi imprisoned Abd al-Kabir.

name: Nakoleia (siege)
borderline: Sources disagree whether the town fell.
roman_force: The garrison of Nakoleia in the Opsikion; no numbers are given.
greek_note: Nakoleia lay in Greek-speaking Phrygia; its garrison came from the Opsikion.
sources: Theophanes AM 6274; Michael the Syrian; en.wikipedia Abbasid invasion of Asia Minor (782)
note: Michael the Syrian and hagiographic sources say the Arabs failed with heavy losses; Theophanes may imply the town fell. Treadgold thinks al-Rabi was beaten.

name: Darenos
roman_force: The army of the Thrakesion theme under Michael Lachanodrakon (Theophanes), facing about 30,000 Arabs; no Roman numbers are given.
greek_note: The Thrakesion, named by Theophanes, was recruited in Greek-speaking western Asia Minor.
sources: Theophanes AM 6274; Michael the Syrian; en.wikipedia Abbasid invasion of Asia Minor (782)
note: Theophanes gives 15,000 Roman dead, Michael the Syrian 10,000. In the same campaign Yazid ibn Mazyad worsted Niketas, count of the Opsikion, near Nicaea, and Harun, trapped on the Sangarios, escaped through Tatzates' defection.

name: Kopidnadon
place: Kopidnadon (Podandos, Pozanti), at the northern exit of the Cilician Gates
commanders_b: unknown; Diogenes, tourmarches of the Anatolikon (killed)
roman_force: The Anatolikon and Opsikion thematic armies, with men of the Scholai tagma whom Irene had banished to the provinces (Theophanes).
greek_note: Theophanes names the Anatolikon and Opsikion, the two largest Anatolian themes, recruited mainly among Greek speakers.
sources: Theophanes AM 6281; en.wikipedia Battle of Kopidnadon
note: A bloody defeat with many officers killed; it reopened large-scale frontier warfare.

name: Calabria
war: War with the Franks and Lombards in southern Italy
commanders_a: Grimoald III of Benevento, Hildeprand of Spoleto; Winigis (Franks)
commanders_b: John (sakellarios and logothete of the army, killed); Theodore (patrikios of Sicily); the Lombard pretender Adelchis
borderline: No battle name or site is recorded.
roman_force: An expedition sent by Irene with troops of the theme of Sicily under its strategos Theodore and the Lombard pretender Adelchis (Theophanes; Frankish annals); no numbers are given.
greek_note: The army of the theme of Sicily and Calabria was largely Greek-speaking by the late 8th century, with Latin-speaking Italians.
sources: Theophanes AM 6281; Royal Frankish Annals 788; en.wikipedia Constantine VI
note: Sent after Irene broke off the betrothal of Constantine VI to Charlemagne's daughter; the Franks are in allies (as Germanic peoples).

name: Attaleia
commanders_a: unknown (Abbasid fleet from Egypt and Syria)
borderline: A naval defeat recorded briefly by Theophanes.
roman_force: The imperial fleet with the Kibyrrhaiot squadron under its strategos Theophilos (Theophanes).
greek_note: The Kibyrrhaiot fleet named by Theophanes was manned from the Greek-speaking southern Anatolian coast and islands.
sources: Theophanes AM 6282; Pryor and Jeffreys, The Age of the Dromon
note: Theophilos was taken to Harun al-Rashid and executed when he refused to convert.

name: Probaton
place: near the fortress of Probaton, about 20 km east of Adrianople
borderline: An indecisive skirmish rather than a battle.
roman_force: Constantine VI's field army, the tagmata and the Thracian themes; the sources give no detail.
greek_note: The emperor's army in Thrace was made up of the tagmata and the European themes, mostly Greek-speaking.
sources: Theophanes AM 6283; en.wikipedia Battle of Marcellae (792)
note: After a skirmish both armies withdrew by night (Theophanes); some accounts treat it as a minor Roman defeat.

name: Marcellae
roman_force: Constantine VI's field army with the tagmata and thematic contingents; many senior officers fell, among them Michael Lachanodrakon (Theophanes).
greek_note: The army was the tagmata and the themes of Thrace and Anatolia, mostly Greek-speaking, with many Armenian officers.
sources: Theophanes AM 6284; en.wikipedia Battle of Marcellae (792)
note: The Bulgars took the baggage, the treasury and the emperor's tent; a peace with tribute followed.

name: Krasos
roman_force: The imperial field army led by Nikephoros I; the sources give no units.
greek_note: The field army of 804 consisted of the tagmata and Anatolian themes, mostly Greek-speaking.
sources: Theophanes AM 6297; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Battle of Krasos
note: Al-Tabari's 40,700 Roman dead is not credible; Nikephoros was saved by his officers. A truce and exchange of prisoners followed.

name: Patras (siege)
commanders_a: unknown (the citizens; the strategos of the Peloponnese at Corinth arrived afterwards)
roman_force: The citizens and garrison of Patras, who broke the siege with a sortie before the strategos arrived from Corinth (De administrando imperio 49).
greek_note: The defence was made by the citizens of a Greek-speaking city, as Constantine VII tells it.
sources: Constantine VII, De administrando imperio 49; Chronicle of Monemvasia; en.wikipedia Patras
note: Constantine VII says African Saracens helped the Slavs and that the victory was credited to St Andrew; the Slavs were made dependants of the church of Patras.

name: Herakleia (siege)
roman_force: The garrison of Herakleia; Nikephoros I did not risk a field battle against Harun's very large army.
greek_note: Frontier garrisons in Cappadocia came from the Anatolian themes, mostly Greek-speaking with Armenians.
sources: Theophanes AM 6298; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Abbasid invasion of Asia Minor (806)
note: The city fell after about a month and was sacked; Tyana, Thebasa and other forts were also taken. Nikephoros bought peace with tribute.

name: Comacchio
war: War with the Franks over Venice and Dalmatia
borderline: A small attack on a garrison.
roman_force: The imperial fleet sent to the Adriatic under Paul, commander of Kephalonia (Royal Frankish Annals).
greek_note: The squadron of Kephalonia, named in the Frankish annals, was manned from the Greek-speaking Ionian islands and western Greece.
sources: Royal Frankish Annals 809; en.wikipedia Pepin of Italy
note: The Franks of the garrison drove the landing off; the opponents were the Franks of Pepin of Italy.

name: Strymon
roman_force: The army stationed on the Strymon while it was being paid; the Bulgars killed the strategos and many officers and took 1,100 pounds of gold (Theophanes).
greek_note: The European themes were mostly Greek-speaking, with Slavs and settlers from Anatolia.
sources: Theophanes AM 6301; en.wikipedia, the article on the Bulgarian wars of the empire
note: The site is unknown and may lie in Bulgaria; Theophanes puts it in AM 6301 (808/809).

name: Serdica (siege)
roman_force: The garrison of Serdica, 6,000 men, killed with many civilians after surrendering (Theophanes).
greek_note: The garrison came from the themes, mostly Greek-speaking; the city's own population was mixed.
sources: Theophanes AM 6301; en.wikipedia Siege of Serdica (809)
note: Krum took the city by a ruse and massacred the garrison despite a promise of safe conduct.

name: Pliska
place: a pass of the Balkan Mountains (probably the Varbitsa pass), after the sack of Pliska
roman_force: The armies of the themes of Asia and of Thrace and the tagmata, with poorly armed levies of the poor (Theophanes); perhaps 25,000-30,000 men (Wikipedia gives 22,000).
greek_note: Theophanes names the themes of the East (Anatolia) and of Thrace and the tagmata, recruited mainly among Greek speakers.
sources: Theophanes AM 6303; Chronicle of 811 (Scriptor incertus); en.wikipedia Battle of Pliska
note: Nikephoros had beaten two Bulgar forces and sacked Pliska on 20 July; on the way back the army was trapped behind palisades in a pass and destroyed. Krum made a drinking cup of the emperor's skull.

name: Mesembria (siege)
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Mesembria; Michael I's relief army did not arrive in time.
greek_note: Mesembria was an old Greek city; its garrison came from the theme of Thrace.
sources: Theophanes AM 6305; en.wikipedia, the article on the Bulgarian wars of the empire
note: Krum took the city with siege engines, said to have been built for him by an Arab engineer, and seized a stock of Greek fire; Develtos had fallen earlier in 812.

name: Versinikia
place: near the fortress of Versinikia, north of Adrianople (near Malomirovo)
commanders_b: Michael I; Leo the Armenian (strategos of the Anatolikon); John Aplakes (strategos of Macedonia, killed)
roman_force: An army summoned from all the themes, even the guards of the Syrian passes, with the tagmata; the Anatolikon under Leo the Armenian fled first, while the Macedonians under John Aplakes attacked on the right (Theophanes).
greek_note: Theophanes names the Anatolikon and the Macedonian theme and the eastern themes, recruited mainly among Greek speakers, with many Armenians.
sources: Theophanes AM 6305; Scriptor incertus; en.wikipedia Battle of Versinikia
note: Wikipedia's figures: Romans 20,000-36,000, Bulgars 6,000-12,000. Leo's flight was seen as treachery; Michael abdicated and Leo V took the throne on 11 July 813.

name: Constantinople (siege)
borderline: A blockade and ravaging of the suburbs with little fighting at the walls.
roman_force: The garrison of the capital and the tagmata under Leo V; an ambush laid for Krum at a parley wounded him but failed.
greek_note: The capital's garrison and the tagmata were recruited mainly in the Greek-speaking provinces.
sources: Theophanes AM 6305; Scriptor incertus; en.wikipedia, the article on the Bulgarian wars of the empire
note: Krum ravaged the suburbs and withdrew to besiege Adrianople.

name: Adrianople (siege)
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Adrianople, the seat of the theme of Macedonia.
greek_note: Adrianople and its theme were mostly Greek-speaking, with Armenian settlers (the family of the future Basil I was among the captives).
sources: Theophanes AM 6305; Scriptor incertus; en.wikipedia, the article on the Bulgarian wars of the empire
note: The city surrendered from hunger after a siege with engines; its people were deported beyond the Danube.

name: Mesembria
date: 813/814 (the article on Leo V dates it spring 816)
borderline: Reported only by the later chronicles (Genesios, Theophanes Continuatus); some modern historians doubt the story or its date.
roman_force: Leo V's field army of the tagmata and themes, which surprised the Bulgars in a night attack; the sources give no units or numbers.
greek_note: Leo V's army was drawn from the tagmata and the themes of Thrace and Anatolia, mostly Greek-speaking.
sources: Genesios 1; Theophanes Continuatus 1.14; en.wikipedia Battle of Mesembria
note: According to the later tradition Leo feigned flight, then fell on the pursuing Bulgars by night and almost destroyed them before raiding Bulgaria; the 30-year peace with Omurtag followed (815 or 816).

name: Constantinople (siege)
place: Constantinople (land walls, Blachernae, the sea walls and the Golden Horn)
commanders_b: Thomas the Slav; Anastasios; Gregory Pterotos
roman_force: Michael II: the tagmata, reinforced by the Opsikion and Armeniakon themes, and the imperial fleet with Greek fire (about 35,000, Treadgold). Thomas: most of the Asian themes, the Kibyrrhaiot and Aegean fleets, many Slavs of Thrace and Macedonia, with Arab, Armenian, Iberian and Abasgian recruits (a claimed 80,000).
greek_note: The themes named on both sides (Opsikion, Armeniakon, the Asian and naval themes) were mostly Greek-speaking; the chroniclers stress the many foreign peoples with Thomas, but Lemerle thinks their list exaggerated.
sources: Genesios 2; Theophanes Continuatus 2.11-19; Michael II's letter to Louis the Pious; Lemerle, Thomas le Slave; en.wikipedia Thomas the Slav
note: All assaults failed; in spring 822 a sortie at Blachernae and the imperial fleet beat Thomas by land and sea. Earlier in 821 Thomas had defeated the Armeniakon army, and Olbianos ambushed his adopted son Constantius.

name: Byrida
place: the anchorage of Byrida, near Constantinople (site unknown)
commanders_b: unknown (fleet of the themes of Greece)
roman_force: The imperial fleet with Greek fire against rebel squadrons from the themes of Greece, allegedly 350 ships.
greek_note: Both fleets were manned from the Greek-speaking capital, islands and coasts; the rebel ships came from the themes of Greece (Theophanes Continuatus).
sources: Genesios 2; Theophanes Continuatus 2.16; en.wikipedia Thomas the Slav
note: Most of the rebel ships were burned or captured, giving Michael command of the sea.

name: Kedouktos
place: plain of Kedouktos, near Herakleia (Perinthos, Marmara Ereglisi)
borderline: The Roman side here is Thomas' rebel army; the Bulgars fought as Michael II's allies.
roman_force: Thomas the Slav's rebel field army, drawn mainly from the Asian themes, with Slavic and other volunteers, as it came back from the siege of Constantinople.
greek_note: Thomas' army was built on the Asian themes, Greek-speaking for the most part, with Slavs, Armenians and Caucasians.
sources: Genesios 2; Theophanes Continuatus 2.17; George the Monk; en.wikipedia Thomas the Slav
note: Disputed result: the later chronicles say Thomas was routed, George the Monk that he killed many Bulgars; most modern scholars (Bury excepted) think Thomas won at heavy cost. His fleet in the Golden Horn surrendered to Michael meanwhile.

name: Diabasis
place: plain of Diabasis, about 40 km west of Constantinople
borderline: Little or no fighting: when Michael II advanced, most of Thomas' men surrendered or fled.
roman_force: Michael II's tagmata with the Opsikion and Armeniakon troops under Katakylas and Olbianos and fresh troops from Asia Minor, against Thomas' remaining army.
greek_note: The named units on both sides were themes of Asia Minor, mostly Greek-speaking.
sources: Genesios 2; Theophanes Continuatus 2.18; en.wikipedia Thomas the Slav
note: Thomas' feigned retreat turned into a real one as his men surrendered or fled to Arkadiopolis and other towns.

name: Arkadiopolis (siege)
borderline: A blockade without assaults.
roman_force: Michael II's army blockading the town behind a ditch, against Thomas and his last loyal troops.
greek_note: Both armies were drawn mainly from the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor.
sources: Genesios 2; Theophanes Continuatus 2.19; en.wikipedia Thomas the Slav
note: After five months the starving defenders handed Thomas over for a pardon; he was executed in October 823. Bizye, Panion and Herakleia submitted later.

name: Mazara
roman_force: The loyal army of the theme of Sicily under Balata; no numbers are given.
greek_note: The army of the theme of Sicily was recruited on an island that was largely Greek-speaking by the 9th century.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; al-Nuwayri; Vasiliev (1935), vol. I; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Sicily
note: The Aghlabids landed in support of the rebel Euphemius, whose followers were kept apart from the battle; Balata fled to Enna and then Calabria.

name: Syracuse (siege)
commanders_a: unknown (garrison); Giustiniano Participazio, doge of Venice
commanders_b: Asad ibn al-Furat (died), Muhammad ibn Abi'l-Jawari
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Syracuse, relieved in 828 by an imperial fleet from the East; a Venetian squadron under the doge also came to help.
greek_note: Syracuse, the capital of the theme, was a Greek-speaking city, and the relief fleet came from the Greek-speaking East.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; John the Deacon (Venice); en.wikipedia Siege of Syracuse (827-828); en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Sicily
note: Disease killed Asad and many of his men; the Arabs lifted the siege, burned their ships when the imperial fleet blocked their retreat, and marched to Mineo.

name: Crete
commanders_b: Photeinos (strategos of the Anatolikon), Damianos (komes tou staulou, killed)
borderline: A defeat of an expedition, not a separately named battle.
roman_force: An expedition under Photeinos, strategos of the Anatolikon, and Damianos, count of the imperial stable; no numbers are given.
greek_note: The expedition was led by the strategos of the Anatolikon and drawn from Greek-speaking Anatolia and the fleet.
sources: Genesios 2; Theophanes Continuatus 2.21-22; en.wikipedia Emirate of Crete
note: The first attempt to recover Crete from the Andalusian exiles who had landed in 824 or 827/828.

name: Crete
borderline: An expedition, not a separately named battle.
roman_force: A fleet of 70 ships under Krateros, strategos of the Kibyrrhaiots, with its marines.
greek_note: The Kibyrrhaiot fleet, named in the sources, was manned from the Greek-speaking southern Anatolian coast.
sources: Genesios 2; Theophanes Continuatus 2.22; en.wikipedia Emirate of Crete
note: Krateros won a first battle but his camp was routed in a night attack; he fled to Kos, was caught and crucified.

name: Thasos
commanders_a: unknown (fleet of the Emirate of Crete)
roman_force: The imperial fleet, rebuilt after the revolt of Thomas, including the new marines (tessarakontarioi) raised by Ooryphas; numbers not given.
greek_note: The imperial fleet was manned from the Greek-speaking capital, islands and coasts.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus 2.21-26; en.wikipedia Battle of Thasos
note: Almost the whole fleet was lost, opening the Aegean to Cretan raids (Mount Athos was deserted).

name: Enna
borderline: A field battle described in the Arab chronicles, without a standard name.
roman_force: A fresh army and fleet sent by Michael II under Theodotos, with the Sicilian troops; no numbers are given.
greek_note: The reinforcements came from the Greek-speaking East and joined the largely Greek-speaking army of Sicily.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Vasiliev (1935), vol. I; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Sicily
note: Theodotos lost the battle but saved most of his men in Enna; soon after Muhammad's death he routed the Arabs (about 1,000 killed) and blockaded them in Mineo.

name: Mineo
commanders_a: Asbagh ibn Wakil (Andalusian fleet) and the Aghlabid commanders
borderline: The relief of a blockade; no pitched battle is described.
roman_force: Theodotos' army blockading the Arab remnant in Mineo; no numbers are given.
greek_note: The army of Sicily with reinforcements from the East, mostly Greek-speaking.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Vasiliev (1935), vol. I; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Sicily
note: Andalusian and Ifriqiyan reinforcements broke Theodotos' blockade; Theodotos was killed later in 830 while pursuing the Arabs after the siege of Calloniana.

name: Palermo (siege)
roman_force: The garrison of Palermo under the spatharios Symeon; no numbers are given.
greek_note: The garrison belonged to the army of the theme of Sicily, largely Greek-speaking by this time.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Cambridge Chronicle; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Sicily
note: After about a year Symeon surrendered for safe conduct; the Arab chroniclers say the population had fallen from 70,000 to 3,000. Palermo became the Arab capital of Sicily.

name: Charsianon
roman_force: The thematic troops of the kleisoura of Charsianon reinforced with detachments of the tagmata, perhaps under Theophilos in person.
greek_note: Charsianon and the tagmata, named in the sources, were mostly Greek-speaking, with a strong Armenian element in Charsianon.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus 3.23; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Battle of Charsianon (831); en.wikipedia Abbasid invasion of Asia Minor (831)
note: The raiders were crushed (25,000 captured, an exaggeration) and the prisoners paraded in the Hippodrome; later in 831 al-Abbas ibn al-Ma'mun defeated Theophilos after taking Tyana.

name: Loulon (siege)
place: Loulon, north of the Cilician Gates (near Hasangazi)
roman_force: The garrison of Loulon, which held out about 100 days and captured Ujayf by a ruse, and the relief army led by Theophilos, which was defeated.
greek_note: The garrison and the field army came from the Anatolian themes, mostly Greek-speaking with Armenians.
sources: al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Capture of Loulon
note: After the relief army was beaten and its camp plundered, the garrison surrendered for safe departure and the release of Ujayf.

name: Enna (siege)
borderline: The lower town was taken but the citadel held, and the siege ended with a ransom.
roman_force: The garrison and townspeople of Enna, the main Roman stronghold of central Sicily after the fall of Palermo; no numbers are given.
greek_note: The troops of the theme of Sicily and the towns of central and eastern Sicily were largely Greek-speaking by the 9th century.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Vasiliev, vol. I (the Amorian dynasty); en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Sicily
note: The Arabs found an unguarded path and took the lower town; the citadel held out and paid a large ransom for their withdrawal. Earlier in 837 an Arab attack on Enna had been beaten and its commander Abd al-Salam ibn Abd al-Wahhab captured.

name: Sozopetra (siege)
roman_force: Theophilos' great expedition from the eastern themes and the tagmata (under Manuel), with the Khurramite auxiliaries under Theophobos; al-Tabari's 70,000 soldiers and 30,000 servants is probably inflated.
greek_note: The themes and tagmata named in the sources were mostly Greek-speaking; the Khurramite Persians and Armenians were large minorities.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus 3.29; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Siege of Sozopetra (837)
note: The garrison refused terms and the town was stormed with ladders and burned; its sack provoked al-Mu'tasim's Amorion campaign of 838.

name: Arsamosata (siege)
roman_force: The same expeditionary army of thematic and tagmatic troops with Khurramite auxiliaries; detachments beat two relief forces.
greek_note: Thematic and tagmatic troops, mostly Greek-speaking, with Khurramite Persians and Armenians.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus 3.29; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Siege of Arsamosata (837)
note: The town was stormed and burned; a relief force from Melitene with Tayy tribesmen was routed (4,000 killed) and Ujayf's force from Baghdad was crushed near Melitene. Melitene then bought peace.

name: Anzen
commanders_a: Afshin Khaydhar ibn Kawus; Umar al-Aqta (emir of Melitene)
roman_force: Theophilos' field army: the tagmata, the Anatolian (and perhaps some European) themes, and the 'Persian' corps of Khurramite refugees under Theophobos; 25,000 (Haldon) to 40,000 (Treadgold).
greek_note: The tagmata and Anatolian themes named in the sources were mostly Greek-speaking, but the Khurramite Persians and many Armenians formed a large minority.
sources: Genesios 3; Theophanes Continuatus 3.31-33; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Battle of Anzen
note: The Romans had the better of the morning until Afshin's Turkish horse-archers and a rain storm turned the battle; the emperor's guard was surrounded and barely escaped.

name: Amorion (siege)
commanders_a: al-Mu'tasim; Afshin, Ashinas, Itakh, Ja'far ibn Dinar
commanders_b: Aetios (strategos of the Anatolikon); Theodore Krateros, Constantine Baboutzikos; Boiditzes
roman_force: The garrison of Amorion, capital of the Anatolikon, under its strategos Aetios, reinforced from the tagmata of the Exkoubitoi and the Vigla (the 30,000 sometimes given is doubted).
greek_note: The Anatolikon theme and the tagmata, named in the sources, were recruited mainly among Greek speakers.
sources: Genesios 3; Theophanes Continuatus 3.30-35; al-Tabari; Michael the Syrian; en.wikipedia Sack of Amorium
note: The wall was breached at a weak point betrayed to the caliph, and Boiditzes let the Arabs in; the city was razed. The captured officers became the 42 martyrs of Amorion.

name: Cefalù
borderline: The relief of a besieged town.
roman_force: A large army sent from the East by Theophilos under Alexios Mousele; no numbers are given.
greek_note: The army came from the Greek-speaking East under an Armenian commander and joined the Sicilian troops.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Theophanes Continuatus 3; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Sicily
note: Mousele forced the Arabs to raise the siege and won several skirmishes with raiding parties before being recalled.

name: Messina
roman_force: The garrison of Messina; no numbers are given.
greek_note: North-eastern Sicily was the most Greek-speaking part of the island.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Sicily
note: The Arabs took the city with the help of the duchy of Naples (nominally imperial, here allied to the Arabs), opening the way to Calabria.

name: Crete
borderline: An expedition, not a separately named battle.
roman_force: A large expedition under the regent Theoktistos; the new theme of the Aegean Sea was created the same year; no numbers are given.
greek_note: The fleet and landing army came from the Greek-speaking capital, islands and coasts.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus 4.1; Genesios 4; en.wikipedia Emirate of Crete
note: Theoktistos occupied much of the island but hurried home on a false rumour; the troops he left behind were destroyed.

name: Mauropotamos
place: the Mauropotamos ('Black River'), probably a tributary of the Sangarios in Bithynia (or of the Halys in Cappadocia)
commanders_a: Abu Sa'id Muhammad ibn Yusuf; probably Umar al-Aqta (emir of Melitene)
roman_force: An army led by the logothete Theoktistos; many senior officers went over to the Arabs (Theophanes Continuatus). The units are not named.
greek_note: The field army of the 840s was made up of the tagmata and Anatolian themes, mostly Greek-speaking.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus 4.16; al-Tabari; Vasiliev (1935), vol. I; en.wikipedia Battle of Mauropotamos
note: Arab troops from Qaliqala and Tarsus and from Melitene took part; a truce and exchange of prisoners followed in 845.

name: Butera
commanders_a: al-Abbas ibn al-Fadl (under the governor al-Fadl ibn Ja'far)
roman_force: The army of Sicily reinforced by troops of the kleisoura of Charsianon sent from the East; it was crushed, losing about 10,000 men.
greek_note: The Arab chroniclers name the men of Charsianon, an eastern Anatolian command, beside the Greek-speaking Sicilian army.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Vasiliev (1935), vol. I; en.wikipedia Battle of Butera; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Sicily
note: One of the heaviest Roman defeats in Sicily; Modica had fallen earlier that year.

name: Damietta
borderline: A raid and sack with little fighting, since the garrison was away.
roman_force: One of three imperial squadrons, 85 ships with about 5,000 men (al-Tabari).
greek_note: The fleet was manned from the Greek-speaking capital and naval themes.
sources: al-Tabari; Theophanes Continuatus 4.34; en.wikipedia Emirate of Crete
note: The port was a supply base for the Emirate of Crete; the Romans burned it, carried off captives and weapons and withdrew.

name: Enna
borderline: A surprise night capture through a culvert shown by a prisoner.
roman_force: The garrison of Enna, the main Roman stronghold of inner Sicily; no numbers are given.
greek_note: The garrison belonged to the largely Greek-speaking army of the theme of Sicily.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; al-Nuwayri; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Sicily
note: The garrison was massacred; the fall of Enna left Syracuse and Taormina as the main Roman strongholds.

name: Samosata (siege)
borderline: Disputed result.
roman_force: Michael III's field army; the sources do not describe it.
greek_note: The field army of the 850s was made up of the tagmata and Anatolian themes, mostly Greek-speaking.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus 4.24; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Siege of Samosata (859)
note: Greek sources tell of a sortie on the third day (a Sunday) that routed the army and captured the camp, with 100 officers taken by Karbeas; al-Tabari reports only a Roman raid with 500 prisoners, and Vasiliev thinks the Greek story exaggerated or invented to blacken Michael III.

name: Syracuse (sea)
roman_force: The fleet of the expedition sent by Michael III under Constantine Kontomytes, reported at 300 ships; about a third were lost.
greek_note: The fleet came from the capital and the naval themes, manned by Greek speakers.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Vasiliev (1935), vol. I; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Sicily
note: Fought soon after the fleet arrived at Syracuse.

name: Cefalù
roman_force: The large army brought from the East by Constantine Kontomytes, with Sicilian troops; no numbers are given.
greek_note: The expeditionary army came from the Greek-speaking themes of the East.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Vasiliev (1935), vol. I; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Sicily
note: After the defeat the Romans withdrew to Syracuse.

name: Constantinople (siege)
place: Constantinople, the Bosporus and the Princes' Islands
commanders_a: Ooryphas (eparch of the city); Michael III (returning from the east)
commanders_b: unknown (Askold and Dir in the Russian Primary Chronicle)
borderline: No pitched battle is recorded; the Rus' (about 200 ships) ravaged the suburbs and islands and withdrew undefeated.
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of the capital under the eparch Ooryphas; Michael III and the field army were away against the Arabs and the fleet was absent.
greek_note: The defenders were the garrison and people of the Greek-speaking capital.
sources: Photios, Homilies 3-4; Brussels Chronicle; Russian Primary Chronicle; en.wikipedia Siege of Constantinople (860)
note: Scored for Rome by the siege rule because the city was not taken; Wikipedia's infobox calls it a Rus' victory, since the Rus' (about 200 ships) plundered the suburbs and the Princes' Islands and left undefeated. The Rus' were led by Scandinavians and are grouped here with the Slavs.

name: Faruriyyah
place: the fortress of Faruriyyah, in the Taurus frontier zone near Tarsus (site uncertain)
borderline: A minor fortress capture; the fighting is not described in detail.
roman_force: The garrison of a frontier fortress; the sources give no units or numbers.
greek_note: The garrisons of the Taurus frontier were drawn from the Anatolian themes and kleisourai, mostly Greek-speaking with Armenians.
sources: al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Capture of Faruriyyah
note: Wasif's campaign, planned by al-Muntasir as a large offensive, went ahead after the caliph's death (June 862) but was cut short; Wasif was back in Samarra by 863. Wikipedia lists it among the empire's battles.

name: Lalakaon
place: on the Lalakaon river, at the place called Poson (Porson), near the Halys
commanders_a: Petronas (domestic of the Schools); Nasar (strategos of the Boukellarion)
commanders_b: Umar al-Aqta (emir of Melitene, killed); perhaps Karbeas (Paulicians)
roman_force: Three converging armies: the Armeniakon, Boukellarion, Koloneia and Paphlagonia themes from the north; the Anatolikon, Opsikion and Cappadocia themes with the kleisourai of Seleukeia and Charsianon from the south; and the Macedonian, Thracian and Thrakesion themes with the imperial tagmata from the west under Petronas.
greek_note: The sources name nearly every Anatolian and Thracian theme and the tagmata, recruited mainly among Greek speakers, with strong Armenian elements in the eastern themes.
sources: Genesios 4; Theophanes Continuatus 4.25; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Battle of Lalakaon
note: Umar's army was surrounded and destroyed, his son captured. The site is uncertain (most put it about 130 km south-east of Amisos). Later in 863 another Roman army killed Ali ibn Yahya al-Armani in Armenia.

name: Bishop's Meadow
place: Marj al-Usquf, a highland near Malakopeia, north of Nazianzos
roman_force: Michael III's army, probably the southern group of themes (Anatolikon, Opsikion, Cappadocia, and the kleisourai of Seleukeia and Charsianon) that later shadowed the Arabs.
greek_note: The central Anatolian themes were mostly Greek-speaking, with Armenians strong in Cappadocia and Charsianon.
sources: al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Battle of Lalakaon
note: A bloody battle with heavy losses on both sides (al-Tabari says only 1,000 of Umar's men survived); Umar broke away north and sacked Amisos.

name: Ragusa (siege)
commanders_b: Sawdan of Bari, Saba of Taranto, Kalfun the Berber
roman_force: The citizens of Ragusa, who held out for fifteen months, relieved by an imperial fleet of 100 ships under Niketas Ooryphas sent by Basil I (De administrando imperio 29).
greek_note: The defenders were the Romance-speaking Ragusans; the relief fleet named by Constantine VII was Greek-manned.
sources: Constantine VII, De administrando imperio 29; Theophanes Continuatus 5.53; en.wikipedia Siege of Ragusa (866-868)
note: The Aghlabid fleet of 36 ships first plundered Budva, Risan and Kotor; the besiegers withdrew when deserters reported the approach of the imperial fleet, so there was no battle with the relief. The Ragusans' Romance speech is entered as 'Latin'.

name: Melite (siege)
date: 870; the city fell on 29 August 870 (28 August in the Kitab al-'Uyun)
commanders_a: Halaf al-Hadim, an engineer (killed); then Sawada ibn Muhammad, sent by Muhammad ibn Khafaja, governor of Sicily
borderline: The course of the siege is known only from late Arabic sources; some say the Roman relief fleet withdrew without a fight.
roman_force: The garrison and people of Melite, who at first held out with the help of reinforcements whose origin and numbers are not given (al-Himyari; Ibn al-Athir).
greek_note: Malta belonged to the theme of Sicily, whose imperial troops were mainly Greek-speaking; the language of the island's own people at this time is uncertain.
sources: al-Himyari, Kitab al-Rawd al-Mi'tar; Ibn al-Athir; the Greek chronicle of Cassano; en.wikipedia Siege of Melite (870)
note: An Aghlabid fleet under Ahmad ibn Umar had attacked the island in 869. Other dates in the sources: 868 (Ibn Khaldun), 875 (Ibn al-Khatib). The town was plundered and its walls razed.

name: Bari
date: February 871 (the end of a blockade begun in 867-869)
war: Wars of Louis II against the Emirate of Bari
commanders_a: Louis II, emperor in Italy; Niketas Ooryphas commanded the Roman fleet sent in 869
borderline: The Roman part was naval and indirect; en.wikipedia calls the De Administrando Imperio's claim of a major imperial role 'probably a concoction'. The victory belonged to Louis II.
roman_force: A Roman fleet of about 400 ships (Annales Bertiniani) under Niketas Ooryphas came in 869, but the joint attack failed; a Ragusan fleet carrying Croats and other Slavs of imperial Dalmatia served in the siege (Constantine VII), and Louis II's final assault used a Slavic fleet.
greek_note: The Roman contribution that stayed to the end was mainly the Slavic and Dalmatian squadrons of imperial Dalmatia; the Greek-manned imperial fleet had gone home.
sources: Annales Bertiniani; Constantine VII, De Administrando Imperio 29; letter of Louis II to Basil I; en.wikipedia Emirate of Bari
note: Bari passed to imperial rule in 876, when the strategos Gregory occupied it.

name: Tephrike
borderline: A failed campaign against Tephrike that ended in the defeat of the emperor's army; not usually listed as a named battle.
roman_force: The emperor's field army, the tagmata with the eastern themes, led by Basil I in person (Theophanes Continuatus; Genesios).
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus; Genesios; en.wikipedia Battle of Bathys Ryax (background)
note: Basil I narrowly escaped. Tephrike was taken and razed in 878 (Treadgold: 879).

name: Bathys Ryax
place: Bathys Ryax (the 'Deep Stream'), the Kalinirmak pass west of Sivas
commanders_a: Christopher, Domestic of the Schools; the strategoi of Armeniakon and Charsianon
roman_force: The Domestic Christopher's field army; its advance force of 4,000-5,000 men from the themes of Armeniakon and Charsianon, of whom 600 picked men made the dawn attack (Theophanes Continuatus; Genesios).
greek_note: The sources name the themes of Armeniakon and Charsianon, Greek-speaking provinces of northern and central Anatolia with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus; Genesios; Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Battle of Bathys Ryax
note: Dated 872 (Vasiliev, Lemerle, Whittow, Treadgold) or 878 (Garsoian, Haldon). Chrysocheir was struck down by Poulades, a former captive, and beheaded; the battle ended the Paulicians as a military power.

name: Kardia (sea)
place: off Kardia, in the Gulf of Saros (Thrace)
commanders_a: Niketas Ooryphas, droungarios of the Fleet
commanders_b: Photios, a renegade, sent by Shu'ayb, emir of Crete
roman_force: The Imperial Fleet of Constantinople under its droungarios, armed with Greek fire; the Cretan fleet of over 50 ships (27 koumbaria) lost 20 ships (Theophanes Continuatus; Skylitzes).
greek_note: The imperial and thematic fleets were manned mainly from Constantinople and the Greek-speaking coasts and islands of the Aegean.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus; Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Battle of Kardia
note: Dated 872 (Eickhoff, Tsougarakis) or c. 873 (Treadgold; Pryor and Jeffreys). The Cretan raiders had reached the Propontis.

name: Gulf of Corinth (sea)
place: the Gulf of Corinth, near Corinth
commanders_a: Niketas Ooryphas, droungarios of the Fleet
roman_force: The Imperial Fleet under Niketas Ooryphas; the sources say he had his ships hauled across the Isthmus of Corinth to surprise the raiders.
greek_note: The imperial and thematic fleets were manned mainly from Constantinople and the Greek-speaking coasts and islands of the Aegean.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus; Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Battle of the Gulf of Corinth
note: The portage across the Isthmus is doubted by Pettegrew as a literary echo of Philip V in 217 BCE.

name: Syracuse
commanders_a: Ja'far ibn Muhammad, governor of Sicily; his son Abu Ishaq
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Syracuse, with Mardaites from the Peloponnese; the relief fleet under Adrianos was held at Monemvasia by contrary winds (Theodosios the Monk; Theophanes Continuatus).
greek_note: Syracuse was a Greek-speaking city, defended by its own citizens and imperial troops from the Peloponnese.
sources: Theodosios the Monk, letter on the fall of Syracuse; Theophanes Continuatus; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Siege of Syracuse (877-878)
note: The Aghlabids breached the seaward wall and stormed the city on 21 May 878; Theodosios says over 4,000 notables were killed.

name: Cephalonia (sea)
roman_force: The Imperial Fleet under Nasar, refilled at Methone with troops of the theme of the Peloponnese after many oarsmen deserted (Theophanes Continuatus; Skylitzes).
greek_note: The sources name the imperial fleet and the troops of the Peloponnese, a mainly Greek-speaking theme with Slavic settlers.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus; Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Battle of Cephalonia
note: A night attack on an Aghlabid fleet of about 60 ships (Skylitzes) whose crews were raiding ashore.

name: Stelai (sea)
place: off southern Calabria (Punta Stilo, or Stylis near Rhegion)
commanders_b: al-Husayn ibn Rabah, Aghlabid governor of Sicily (Ibn Idhari)
roman_force: The Imperial Fleet under Nasar, 140 ships according to Ibn Idhari, against 45 Aghlabid ships (Vita Eliae iunioris).
greek_note: The imperial and thematic fleets were manned mainly from Constantinople and the Greek-speaking coasts and islands of the Aegean.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus; Ibn Idhari; Vita Eliae iunioris; en.wikipedia Battle of Stelai
note: Site disputed: Punta Stilo ('Stelai', Theophanes Continuatus), Stylis on the toe of Italy (Kislinger), or Milazzo ('Mylas', Cambridge Chronicle); also called the First Battle of Milazzo.

name: Taranto
borderline: The recovery of Taranto is recorded briefly; the fighting is not described.
roman_force: The expeditionary army of the protovestiarios Prokopios and Leo Apostyppes, with the troops of the themes of Thrace and Macedonia (Theophanes Continuatus).
greek_note: The western themes of Thrace and Macedonia were mainly Greek-speaking, with Armenian and Slavic settlers.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus; Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Battle of Stelai (aftermath)
note: Taranto had been in Arab hands since the 840s; its recovery restored the land link between Calabria and Bari. Prokopios fell in a battle in Calabria shortly before.

name: Chrysoboullon
commanders_b: Kesta Styppiotes, Domestic of the Schools (killed); the strategoi of Anatolikon and Cappadocia (killed)
roman_force: The field army of the East with the themes of Anatolikon, Cappadocia and Koron, said to be about 100,000 strong (an exaggeration), surprised in its camp at night (al-Tabari; Theophanes Continuatus).
greek_note: The sources name the themes of Anatolikon and Cappadocia, Greek-speaking provinces of central Anatolia with an Armenian element.
sources: al-Tabari; Theophanes Continuatus; en.wikipedia Kesta Styppiotes
note: The name comes from en.wikipedia's link 'Battle of Chrysoboullon (883)'. Arab chroniclers claim 70,000 dead. Andrew the Scythian was reappointed Domestic.

name: Euripos (siege)
roman_force: The troops of the theme of Hellas gathered by its strategos, with stone-throwers on the walls and ships that sallied with Greek fire against a fleet of 30 koumbaria (Skylitzes).
greek_note: The defenders were the levies of the theme of Hellas in central Greece.
sources: Skylitzes; Theophanes Continuatus; en.wikipedia Siege of Euripos
note: Land assault and naval fighting; a final sortie routed the besiegers. Skylitzes' claim that Yazaman fell there is an error (he died in 891).

name: Milazzo
roman_force: A squadron of the Imperial Fleet of Constantinople; Arabic sources say 5,000 drowned and 7,000 were killed.
greek_note: The imperial and thematic fleets were manned mainly from Constantinople and the Greek-speaking coasts and islands of the Aegean.
sources: Cambridge Chronicle; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Battle of Milazzo (888)
note: Known only from Arabic sources; it ended large imperial naval operations off Italy for decades.

name: Boulgarophygon
commanders_b: Leo Katakalon, Domestic of the Schools; the protovestiarios Theodosios (killed)
roman_force: The whole field army: the themes and tagmata of Asia Minor, brought to Europe after a truce with the Arabs (Theophanes Continuatus; Skylitzes).
greek_note: The sources name the Anatolian themes and the tagmata, raised mainly in Greek-speaking Asia Minor with an Armenian element.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus; Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Battle of Boulgarophygon
note: Almost the whole army was lost; peace followed with an annual tribute to Bulgaria.

name: Taormina
date: July 902; the town surrendered on 1 August 902
commanders_b: Eustathios, droungarios of the Fleet; Michael Charaktos; Constantine Karamallos, commandant of Taormina
roman_force: The imperial forces in Sicily and Calabria with a naval squadron, who chose to fight before the walls; the main fleet did not come (Continuator of George the Monk).
greek_note: The last imperial forces in Sicily were drawn from the Greek-speaking population of eastern Sicily and Calabria.
sources: Continuator of George the Monk; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Siege of Taormina (902)
note: A pitched battle before the walls, then the surrender of the town; the fall of Taormina ended imperial Sicily except for a few enclaves.

name: Thessalonica
commanders_b: Leo Chitzilakes and Niketas, strategoi; Petronas, protospatharios
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Thessalonica; appeals to the surrounding Slavic tribes and provinces brought little help, and the fleet under Himerios did not engage (John Kaminiates).
greek_note: Thessalonica was a Greek-speaking city defended mainly by its own citizens (Kaminiates was one of them).
sources: John Kaminiates, The Capture of Thessalonica; Theophanes Continuatus; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Sack of Thessalonica (904)
note: The raiders had 54 ships and stormed the low seaward walls; about 22,000 captives were carried off. The day of the fall is given as 29 or 31 July.

name: Chandax
roman_force: Himerios' expedition of 177 ships and about 43,000 men: the Imperial Fleet, the naval themes, troops of the European themes, Mardaites and 700 Rus' (Constantine VII, De Ceremoniis 2.44).
greek_note: The muster list in De Ceremoniis names the naval themes of the Aegean and southern Greece, which furnished most of the crews and soldiers; the 700 Rus' were a small fraction.
sources: Constantine VII, De Ceremoniis 2.44; Theophanes Continuatus; en.wikipedia Himerios (admiral); en.wikipedia Siege of Chandax (background)
note: Himerios raised the siege on news that Leo VI was dying.

name: Chios
commanders_a: Leo of Tripoli; Damian of Tarsus
roman_force: The fleet returning from the Cretan expedition (177 ships at the start).
greek_note: The same expedition whose muster list (De Ceremoniis 2.44) names the Aegean naval themes.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus; Mas'udi; en.wikipedia Himerios (admiral)
note: The imperial fleet was annihilated and Himerios barely escaped.

name: Garigliano
date: June - August 915 (siege, then the final battle in August)
war: Arab raids in Italy: the Garigliano colony
place: the Saracen fortified camp on the Garigliano, near Minturnae
commanders_a: Pope John X; Nicholas Picingli, strategos of Longobardia; Alberic I of Spoleto; Guaimar II of Salerno; Landulf I of Benevento and Capua; John I of Gaeta; Gregory IV of Naples
roman_force: A strong contingent from Calabria and Apulia (Longobardia) under the strategos Nicholas Picingli (Liudprand; Leo of Ostia).
greek_note: Calabria was largely Greek-speaking, while Apulia (Longobardia) was mostly Lombard and Latin-speaking.
sources: Liudprand, Antapodosis; Leo of Ostia, Chronicle of Montecassino; en.wikipedia Battle of Garigliano (915)
note: Spoleto, Gaeta and Naples also fought in the Christian league. The Muslims of the Garigliano were an independent colony, sometimes described as Fatimid subjects.

name: Acheloos
place: on the river Acheloos near Anchialos (Pomorie)
commanders_b: Leo Phokas the Elder, Domestic of the Schools; John Bogas; Romanos Lekapenos commanded the fleet
roman_force: The tagmata, the European themes and the themes of Asia Minor brought over for the campaign, with the fleet under Romanos Lekapenos at the Danube mouth; estimates range from 30,000 to about 60,000 (Theophanes Continuatus; Skylitzes).
greek_note: The sources name the tagmata and the Anatolian themes, raised mainly in Greek-speaking Asia Minor with Armenians, besides the European thematic troops.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus; Skylitzes; Leo the Deacon; en.wikipedia Battle of Achelous (917)
note: Magyar and Pecheneg participation on the Bulgarian side, reported only in the Miracula Sancti Georgii, is disputed.

name: Katasyrtai
roman_force: The last troops in the capital, gathered by Leo Phokas after Acheloos (Skylitzes).
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Skylitzes; Theophanes Continuatus; en.wikipedia Battle of Katasyrtai
note: A night battle; the imperial army was routed.

name: Pegae
place: Pegae ('the Spring'), outside the Land Walls of Constantinople
commanders_b: Pothos Argyros, Domestic of the Schools; Leo Argyros; Alexios Mosele, droungarios of the Fleet (drowned); John the Rhaiktor
roman_force: Troops of the tagmata, the Hetaireia (imperial guard) and sailors of the fleet (Theophanes Continuatus; Skylitzes).
greek_note: The tagmata and the fleet of the capital were recruited mainly from Greek-speaking Anatolia, Thrace and the Aegean; the Hetaireia also had foreign guardsmen.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus; Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Battle of Pegae
note: The list of battles on en.wikipedia dates it 922; the battle article and the sources give March 921.

name: Thermopolis
commanders_b: Michael, son of Moroleon (mortally wounded), sent by Pothos Argyros
borderline: A small ambush known by its place name only.
roman_force: A detachment of the field army of Pothos Argyros, Domestic of the Schools (Theophanes Continuatus).
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus; Skylitzes; en.wikipedia, the article on the war of 913-927 with Bulgaria
note: The site is placed near Burgas in en.wikipedia; its order relative to Pegae (March 921) is not certain.

name: Constantinople
commanders_b: Saktikios, a commander of the tagmata (mortally wounded)
roman_force: Units of the tagmata sent out by Romanos I against the Bulgarian camp (Theophanes Continuatus; Skylitzes).
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus; Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Battle of Constantinople (922)
note: Saktikios took the lightly held camp but was driven back when the main Bulgarian army returned.

name: Lemnos
commanders_a: John Rhadenos, patrikios and droungarios of the Fleet
roman_force: The Imperial Fleet of Constantinople under its droungarios (Skylitzes).
greek_note: The imperial and thematic fleets were manned mainly from Constantinople and the Greek-speaking coasts and islands of the Aegean.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus; Skylitzes (tr. Wortley, p. 211); en.wikipedia Leo of Tripoli
note: Most of Leo's fleet was destroyed and he disappears from the sources. en.wikipedia (after the PmbZ) dates it 921/922.

name: Adrianople
borderline: A siege ended by famine; the fighting is only briefly reported.
roman_force: The garrison of Adrianople under Moroleon (Theophanes Continuatus).
greek_note: The Thracian garrisons were recruited mainly from the Greek-speaking population, with Armenian settlers.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus; Skylitzes
note: Moroleon held out until hunger forced the surrender. Simeon had already taken Adrianople by treachery in 914 (no battle).

name: Melitene
