commanders_a: John Kourkouas, Domestic of the Schools; Theophilos Kourkouas; Melias (the Armenian contingent)
borderline: A storming of the lower town; the citadel held and the emir accepted tributary status, so the result was partial.
roman_force: John Kourkouas' eastern field army with his brother Theophilos and an Armenian contingent under Melias, which stormed the lower city.
greek_note: The sources name an Armenian contingent; the rest of the army came from the mainly Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor.
sources: en.wikipedia John Kourkouas
note: Melitene was finally annexed in 934 (separate entry).

name: Dvin
place: Dvin, the old capital of Armenia
commanders_b: John Kourkouas, Domestic of the Schools
roman_force: The eastern field army of John Kourkouas (Ibn al-Athir; Armenian historians).
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia John Kourkouas
note: The siege failed and Kourkouas withdrew.

name: Theodosiopolis
commanders_a: John Kourkouas; Theophilos Kourkouas, strategos of Chaldia
roman_force: The eastern field army of John Kourkouas with the troops of Chaldia under his brother Theophilos.
greek_note: The army of the East and the Pontic theme of Chaldia were mainly Greek-speaking, with many Armenians.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia John Kourkouas
note: Some date the siege to 928-929. The city became tributary, revolted in 939, and was taken again in 949.

name: Melitene
date: spring 934; the city surrendered on 19 May 934
commanders_a: John Kourkouas, Domestic of the Schools; Theophilos Kourkouas
roman_force: About 50,000 men under John Kourkouas, the eastern themes with Armenian troops; Armenians under Melias, later strategos of Lykandos, had fought at Melitene in 926.
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Conquest of Melitene (934); en.wikipedia John Kourkouas
note: The lower city had been stormed in 926 and later attacks failed; in 934 the city resisted fiercely and then surrendered through famine, the first major Muslim city annexed by the empire.

name: Charpete
place: near Charpete (Hisn Ziyad, Harput), above Elazig
commanders_b: John Kourkouas, Domestic of the Schools
roman_force: A detachment of John Kourkouas' eastern field army, given as 20,000 men, defeated while separated from the main army.
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Vasiliev, Byzance et les Arabes II; Runciman, The Emperor Romanus Lecapenus; Treadgold; en.wikipedia Battle of Charpete (938); en.wikipedia John Kourkouas
note: Sayf al-Dawla took the fort of Charpete; Arabic sources claim 70 patrikioi captured. en.wikipedia's article on Sayf al-Dawla says the imperial advance was not halted.

name: Hieron
place: off Hieron, at the Black Sea mouth of the Bosporus
roman_force: Fifteen old chelandia fitted with Greek-fire siphons, manned in the capital while the main fleet was away against the Arabs (Liudprand; Theophanes Continuatus).
greek_note: The imperial and thematic fleets were manned mainly from Constantinople and the Greek-speaking coasts and islands of the Aegean.
sources: Liudprand, Antapodosis; Theophanes Continuatus; Skylitzes; Russian Primary Chronicle; en.wikipedia, the article on the Rus' war of 941
note: The surviving Rus' raided Bithynia until Bardas Phokas and John Kourkouas, with the eastern army, hemmed them in; their remaining fleet was destroyed by Theophanes off Thrace in September 941.

name: Theodosiopolis
borderline: Recorded briefly; a siege that ended with the city's capture.
roman_force: The troops of Chaldia and the neighbouring eastern themes under Theophilos Kourkouas.
greek_note: Chaldia (Pontus) was a Greek-speaking theme; the eastern armies also had many Armenians.
sources: Theophanes Continuatus; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia John Kourkouas

name: Crete
place: the camp of the expedition near Chandax, Crete
borderline: Not usually given a battle name; the defeat of an expedition in a surprise attack on its camp.
roman_force: An expedition of about 128 ships with the naval themes and tagmatic troops, whose muster lists survive in De Ceremoniis 2.45.
greek_note: The muster lists name the naval themes of the Aegean and the tagmata, mainly Greek-speaking.
sources: Constantine VII, De Ceremoniis 2.45; Theophanes Continuatus; en.wikipedia Siege of Chandax (background)

name: Darb al-Kankarun
place: the pass of Darb al-Kankarun, between Lykandos and Germanikeia, near Elbistan
commanders_a: Leo Phokas the Younger, strategos of Cappadocia
roman_force: The troops of the theme of Cappadocia and the neighbouring frontier themes under Leo Phokas, strategos of Cappadocia, who ambushed the returning raiders in a pass.
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Yahya of Antioch; Theophanes Continuatus; en.wikipedia Battle of Darb al-Kankarun; en.wikipedia Sayf al-Dawla
note: Arabic sources call the campaign ghazwat al-musiba, 'the dreadful expedition'. The battle article gives about 5,000 Arabs killed and 3,000 captured; the article on Sayf al-Dawla says about 8,000 lost. Earlier in the campaign Sayf al-Dawla had beaten Bardas Phokas the Elder at Batn al-Luqan.

name: Gerace
commanders_a: al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Kalbi, emir of Sicily
commanders_b: the patrikios Malakenos (killed); Paschalios, strategos of Calabria; Makroioannes commanded the fleet
roman_force: A large army, larger than the Kalbid force, sent under the patrikios Malakenos with a fleet under Makroioannes and joined by the troops of the theme of Calabria.
greek_note: Calabria was largely Greek-speaking, and the expeditionary troops came from the eastern themes.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Cambridge Chronicle; en.wikipedia Battle of Gerace
note: The Kalbid army had been reinforced with 7,000 horse and 5,000 foot from Ifriqiya; after the rout the emperor asked for a truce and the tribute continued.

name: Marash
commanders_b: Bardas Phokas the Elder, Domestic of the Schools (wounded); Constantine Phokas (captured)
roman_force: The Domestic's field army of the East, much larger than Sayf al-Dawla's force (600 horsemen according to his panegyrists).
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Yahya of Antioch; Ibn al-Athir; Abu Firas; en.wikipedia Battle of Marash (953)
note: The patrikios Leo Maleinos fell; Constantine Phokas died a prisoner in Aleppo.

name: Hadath
place: al-Hadath (Adata), which Sayf al-Dawla was refortifying
commanders_b: Bardas Phokas the Elder, Domestic of the Schools; Nikephoros Phokas (wounded); Theodoulos Parsakoutenos (captured)
roman_force: Bardas Phokas' field army, about 50,000 men according to Arab sources, which name Rus', Bulgarians and Armenians in it (al-Mutanabbi; Yahya of Antioch).
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: al-Mutanabbi, ode on al-Hadath; Yahya of Antioch; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Battle of Hadath (954); en.wikipedia Sayf al-Dawla
note: A charge of 500 ghulam horsemen broke the imperial army; about 3,000 fell. Sayf al-Dawla completed the new walls on 12 November 954.

name: Hadath
commanders_a: the Hamdanid garrison of al-Hadath (Sayf al-Dawla)
commanders_b: Nikephoros Phokas (Yahya of Antioch names Bardas Phokas the Elder)
roman_force: The eastern field army, described in the Arabic sources as Greeks, Slavs, Bulgarians and Rus'; it blocked the roads and began to mine the walls.
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Yahya of Antioch; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Siege of Hadath (955); en.wikipedia Sayf al-Dawla
note: The besiegers withdrew when Sayf al-Dawla approached, and the garrison sallied and took the abandoned siege engines.

name: Arghana
place: a defile near Arghana (Ergani), on the road north of Amida
roman_force: John Tzimiskes' army of the eastern frontier, which tried to block Sayf al-Dawla's return and lost about 4,000 men in a battle fought in torrential rain.
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Vasiliev, Byzance et les Arabes II; en.wikipedia Battle of Arghana (956); en.wikipedia Sayf al-Dawla
note: Sayf al-Dawla entered Amida (Diyarbakir) the next day, 25 May 956.

name: Samosata
commanders_a: John Tzimiskes; Basil Lekapenos, parakoimomenos (brought reinforcements)
borderline: The storming is recorded briefly; the fighting is not described.
roman_force: John Tzimiskes' eastern army, reinforced in June by troops brought by Basil Lekapenos.
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Raban; en.wikipedia Sayf al-Dawla
note: Tzimiskes also took the fortress of Raban; the battle of Raban against Sayf al-Dawla's relief army followed in the autumn. The old site is now under the Ataturk reservoir.

name: Amida
commanders_b: Naja (Nadja), a Circassian ghulam of Sayf al-Dawla
borderline: Not given a battle name of its own; known by the place.
roman_force: John Tzimiskes' eastern army in its spring invasion of the Jazira, in which Dara was also taken.
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Raban (background); en.wikipedia Sayf al-Dawla; en.wikipedia, the article on the conquest of Cilicia
note: Naja led about 10,000 men, half of whom are said to have fallen. en.wikipedia's article on the conquest of Cilicia places the victory at Dara.

name: Raban
place: near the fortress of Raban (Araban), south of al-Hadath
roman_force: The eastern field army under John Tzimiskes, reinforced by Basil Lekapenos; the army reformed by Nikephoros Phokas after 955 with many Armenians.
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Yahya of Antioch; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Battle of Raban
note: Over 1,700 Hamdanid horsemen were captured and paraded in Constantinople.

name: Andrassos
place: the pass of Kylindros at Andrassos, in the Taurus between Cilicia and Cappadocia (site unidentified)
commanders_a: Leo Phokas the Younger, Domestic of the West; Constantine Maleinos, strategos of Cappadocia
roman_force: The troops of the frontier provinces left in Anatolia, among them the theme of Cappadocia under Maleinos, while the best troops were in Crete (Leo the Deacon; Theophanes Continuatus).
greek_note: The sources name the thematic troops of Cappadocia and the neighbouring provinces, Greek-speaking with a strong Armenian element.
sources: Leo the Deacon; Theophanes Continuatus; Yahya of Antioch; en.wikipedia Battle of Andrassos
note: Sayf al-Dawla escaped with a few hundred horsemen; the site and the Hamdanid numbers (3,000 to 30,000) are disputed.

name: Chandax
commanders_a: Nikephoros Phokas, Domestic of the Schools; Nikephoros Pastilas, strategos of Thrakesion (killed)
commanders_b: the emir Abd al-Aziz ibn Shu'ayb (Kouroupas) and his son al-Nu'man (Anemas), both captured
roman_force: The army of Asia Minor, themes and tagmata, carried by a large fleet of Greek-fire dromons and transports; one modern estimate is about 34,000 men (Leo the Deacon; Theophanes Continuatus).
greek_note: The sources name the army of the Asian themes (Thrakesion among them), mainly Greek-speaking, with Armenians.
sources: Leo the Deacon; Theophanes Continuatus; Theodosios the Deacon, The Capture of Crete; en.wikipedia Siege of Chandax
note: Includes the landing battle, the ambush of Pastilas, the night destruction of a relief army (40,000, Leo the Deacon) and the winter blockade; the wall was mined and the city stormed on 6 March 961.

name: Taormina
date: spring - 25 December 962 (a siege of more than nine months)
commanders_a: Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Kalbi, emir of Sicily
roman_force: The garrison and townsmen of Taormina, one of the last imperial strongholds in Sicily.
greek_note: Eastern Sicily's Christian population was Greek-speaking.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Cambridge Chronicle; en.wikipedia Battle of the Straits (background)
note: Taken on Christmas Day 962 and razed.

name: Aleppo
commanders_a: Nikephoros Phokas, Domestic of the East; John Tzimiskes
roman_force: Nikephoros Phokas' field army of the East, said by Arabic sources to number 70,000.
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Leo the Deacon; Yahya of Antioch; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Sayf al-Dawla
note: The improvised army before the walls was routed and the city sacked; the citadel held out.

name: Rometta
commanders_a: al-Hasan ibn Ammar al-Kalbi; Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Kalbi
roman_force: The Greek garrison and townsmen of Rometta, the last imperial fortress in Sicily.
greek_note: The defenders were the Greek-speaking Christians of the Val Demone.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Cambridge Chronicle; en.wikipedia Siege of Rometta
note: Rometta fell in May 965, completing the Muslim conquest of Sicily.

name: Adana
commanders_a: John Tzimiskes, Domestic of the East
commanders_b: the Arabs of Adana and Tarsus
roman_force: Tzimiskes' eastern field army.
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Leo the Deacon; Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Sayf al-Dawla; en.wikipedia, the article on the conquest of Cilicia
note: Leo the Deacon: about 5,000 Arabs fell on a hill afterwards called the Hill of Blood. Tzimiskes then attacked Mopsuestia without success.

name: Rometta
commanders_a: al-Hasan ibn Ammar al-Kalbi; al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Kalbi
roman_force: Nikephoros II's Sicilian expedition, said to number about 40,000, many of them veterans of Crete, with cavalry under Manuel Phokas.
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Cambridge Chronicle; Leo the Deacon; en.wikipedia Siege of Rometta
note: A relief battle inside the siege of Rometta; more than a quarter of the army is said to have fallen.

name: Mopsuestia
date: siege abandoned in 964; the city was stormed on 13 July 965
commanders_b: the garrison and people of Mopsuestia
roman_force: Nikephoros II's field army of the East with its siege train; the walls were undermined (Leo the Deacon).
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Leo the Deacon; Yahya of Antioch; en.wikipedia Sayf al-Dawla
note: en.wikipedia (conquest of Cilicia) says spring 965; Yahya of Antioch gives 13 July. The inhabitants were deported.

name: Tarsus
date: summer 965; the city surrendered on 16 August 965
commanders_b: the garrison and people of Tarsus
roman_force: Nikephoros II's field army (about 40,000 in the campaign of 964, the tagmata and the Anatolian themes), which defeated the Tarsiots in a pitched battle before the walls in spring 965 and then blockaded the city (Leo the Deacon).
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Leo the Deacon; Yahya of Antioch; en.wikipedia Sayf al-Dawla
note: Tarsus surrendered on terms; Cilicia became imperial.

name: Straits of Messina
commanders_a: Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Kalbi, emir of Sicily
roman_force: The fleet of the Sicilian expedition, carrying the survivors of Rometta.
greek_note: The imperial and thematic fleets were manned mainly from Constantinople and the Greek-speaking coasts and islands of the Aegean.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Cambridge Chronicle; en.wikipedia Battle of the Straits
note: Also called the Battle of the Straits. Fatimid divers fixed Greek-fire pots to the rudders; about 1,000 prisoners were taken.

name: Antioch
commanders_a: Michael Bourtzes; Peter, stratopedarches; Sachakios Brachamios
roman_force: A blockading force from the fort of Baghras under Michael Bourtzes, who with Brachamios and 300 men scaled the Kallas towers at night; Peter's army arrived three days later (Leo the Deacon; Skylitzes).
greek_note: The eastern armies under Nikephoros II were mainly Greek-speaking, with many Armenians (Brachamios was one).
sources: Leo the Deacon; Skylitzes; Yahya of Antioch; en.wikipedia Siege of Antioch (968-969)
note: The garrison was about 1,000 foot and 500 horse. Antioch was then held by local rulers nominally under the Hamdanids.

name: Bovino
war: Otto I's war in southern Italy (967-970)
commanders_a: the strategos of Longobardia (probably the patrikios Eugenios)
commanders_b: Pandulf Ironhead, prince of Capua and Benevento (captured)
roman_force: The imperial forces of the theme of Longobardia (Apulia), reinforced from the East in 968-969.
greek_note: Imperial troops sent from the East served beside Lombard and Latin-speaking Apulian levies.
sources: Leo of Ostia; Lupus Protospatharius; en.wikipedia Pandulf Ironhead; en.wikipedia Landulf IV of Benevento
note: Pandulf fought as Otto I's vassal; he was held in Constantinople until 970. The Roman commander is not certain.

name: Aleppo
borderline: The city was taken and the citadel capitulated by treaty (the Treaty of Safar, 969/970).
roman_force: Peter's army of the East, which had just taken Antioch.
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Yahya of Antioch; Kamal al-Din; en.wikipedia Peter (stratopedarches)

name: Arcadiopolis
commanders_a: Bardas Skleros, magistros; Peter, stratopedarches; John Alakaseus
roman_force: 10,000-12,000 men under Bardas Skleros, the troops of the West (the tagmata of Thrace and Macedonia under Peter), in three bodies, two hidden in woods (Leo the Deacon; Skylitzes).
greek_note: The western armies of Thrace and Macedonia were mainly Greek-speaking, with Armenian and Slavic settlers.
sources: Leo the Deacon; Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Battle of Arcadiopolis (970)
note: A feigned retreat drew the Pecheneg contingent into an ambush. The Primary Chronicle claims a Rus' victory; the Greek accounts are preferred.

name: Capua
war: Otto I's war in southern Italy (967-970)
commanders_a: the Capuans, in the captivity of Pandulf Ironhead; the relieving army of Otto I
commanders_b: Eugenios, patrikios and strategos of Bari (Longobardia); Marinus II of Naples
borderline: The fighting before the walls is not described; the siege was given up when Otto I's army approached.
roman_force: The imperial forces of Longobardia under Eugenios, reinforced from the East in 968-969, with the Neapolitans of Marinus II, who ravaged the land around Capua.
greek_note: Imperial troops sent from the East served beside Lombard and Latin-speaking Apulian and Neapolitan contingents.
sources: Leo of Ostia; en.wikipedia Pandulf Ironhead; en.wikipedia Landulf IV of Benevento; en.wikipedia Marinus II of Naples
note: Eugenios also took Avellino and threatened Benevento. Naples, nominally an imperial duchy, is not counted as Rome here.

name: Preslav
date: April 971; the city was stormed on 13 April
roman_force: John I's army of 30,000-40,000: the Immortals (a new guard cavalry), about 15,000 picked infantry and 13,000 cavalry with a siege train, while 300 ships went to the Danube (Leo the Deacon).
greek_note: The tagmata and the eastern and western themes were mainly Greek-speaking, with many Armenians.
sources: Leo the Deacon; Skylitzes; en.wikipedia, the article on Sviatoslav's invasion of Bulgaria
note: A battle before the walls was followed by the storming of the city; Tsar Boris II was captured.

name: Dorostolon
date: late April - July 971 (a siege of about three months, with three pitched battles)
commanders_a: John I Tzimiskes; Bardas Skleros; Peter, stratopedarches
commanders_b: Sviatoslav I of Kiev (wounded); Sphangel and Ikmor (both killed)
roman_force: John I's army of 28,000-30,000 (15,000 infantry and 13,000 cavalry, with the Immortals), Peter and Skleros guarding the walls with the western and eastern troops, and 300 ships with Greek fire on the Danube (Leo the Deacon).
greek_note: The tagmata and themes of East and West, mainly Greek-speaking with many Armenians.
sources: Leo the Deacon; Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Siege of Dorostolon
note: The Rus' were starved into a treaty and left Bulgaria; Dorostolon was renamed Theodoropolis.

name: Alexandretta
commanders_a: Nicholas, patrikios, a eunuch of John I's household
commanders_b: Aras; Ibn al-Zayyat, former emir of Tarsus
roman_force: A small force sent to relieve Antioch, which lured a Fatimid detachment of about 4,000 into a deserted camp (Leo the Deacon; Ibn al-Dawadari).
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Leo the Deacon; Skylitzes; Ibn al-Dawadari; en.wikipedia Battle of Alexandretta
note: A battle within the Fatimid siege of Antioch.

name: Antioch
date: 971 (the siege was lifted in early July 971)
commanders_a: the garrison of Antioch; a relief force under the patrikios Nicholas
roman_force: The imperial garrison installed in 969, helped by the small relief force that won at Alexandretta.
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Yahya of Antioch; Leo the Deacon; en.wikipedia Battle of Alexandretta
note: The Fatimid army, mostly Kutama Berbers, withdrew when the Qarmatians advanced into southern Syria; some put the start of the siege in late 970.

name: Nisibis
commanders_b: the Hamdanid emir Abu Taghlib of Mosul (garrison)
borderline: The fighting is not described; the town may have been taken with little resistance.
roman_force: John I's eastern field army, which crossed the Euphrates in October 972.
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Yahya of Antioch; Matthew of Edessa; en.wikipedia, the article on the Syrian campaigns of John Tzimiskes
note: Abu Taghlib then agreed to pay tribute; the siege of Mayyafariqin that followed was abandoned.

name: Amida
date: July 973 (the Hamdanid army arrived on 4 July; the battle was fought the next day)
commanders_a: Abu'l-Qasim Hibat Allah, brother of the Hamdanid emir Abu Taghlib of Mosul
commanders_b: Melias (Mleh), Domestic of the Schools of the East (captured)
roman_force: The eastern field army under the Domestic Melias (Mleh), an Armenian, which was attacking Amida after John I's campaign of 972.
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Yahya of Antioch; Stephen of Taron; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Melias (Domestic of the Schools); en.wikipedia, the article on the Syrian campaigns of John Tzimiskes
note: The en.wikipedia battle article is titled 'Amida (972)' and the campaign article says winter 972/973; the article on Melias gives July 973. Melias died a prisoner, probably in 974.

name: Baalbek
war: Roman-Fatimid wars: John I's Syrian campaign of 975
borderline: A siege with little recorded detail.
roman_force: John I's field army of the East, led by the emperor (Leo the Deacon; John I's letter to Ashot III in Matthew of Edessa).
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Leo the Deacon; Matthew of Edessa; en.wikipedia, the article on the Syrian campaigns of John Tzimiskes
note: Byblos, Balanea and Gabala were also taken in 975; Tripoli was not.

name: Lapara
place: before the rebel-held fortress of Lapara, on the borders of Lykandos
roman_force: Rebels: the eastern frontier armies under Skleros, with Armenian and Arab supporters; loyalists: the army of Anatolia under Peter and Eustathios Maleinos (Skylitzes; Leo the Deacon).
greek_note: Both armies were imperial forces raised mainly in Greek-speaking Asia Minor, with many Armenians, especially in the eastern frontier armies.
sources: Skylitzes; Leo the Deacon; Yahya of Antioch; en.wikipedia Peter (stratopedarches)
note: Skleros surprised the loyalists while they besieged Lapara; the survivors withdrew to Kotyaion.

name: Rhageai
roman_force: Rebels: Skleros' eastern armies; loyalists: the regrouped army of Anatolia under the eunuch Leo.
greek_note: Both armies were imperial forces raised mainly in Greek-speaking Asia Minor, with many Armenians, especially in the eastern frontier armies.
sources: Skylitzes; Yahya of Antioch; en.wikipedia Peter (stratopedarches)
note: The loyalists had earlier beaten Skleros' subordinates Michael Bourtzes and Romanos Taronites; many loyalist commanders fell.

name: Pankaleia
place: the plain of Pankaleia, north-east of Amorion
roman_force: Rebels: Skleros' eastern armies; loyalists: the forces gathered in Anatolia by Bardas Phokas, recalled from exile.
greek_note: Both armies were imperial forces raised mainly in Greek-speaking Asia Minor, with many Armenians, especially in the eastern frontier armies.
sources: Leo the Deacon; Yahya of Antioch; en.wikipedia Battle of Pankaleia
note: Modern scholars, following Leo the Deacon and Yahya, treat this as a defeat for Phokas; Skylitzes gives the name Pankaleia to the decisive battle of 979.

name: Abydos
commanders_a: Bardas Parsakoutenos, magistros, commander of the Imperial Fleet
roman_force: Loyalists: the Imperial Fleet with Greek fire, whose men then landed and beat the rebels ashore; rebels: the fleet that Skleros had raised in the Aegean (Leo the Deacon).
greek_note: The imperial and thematic fleets were manned mainly from Constantinople and the Greek-speaking coasts and islands of the Aegean.
sources: Leo the Deacon; Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Bardas Parsakoutenos
note: Skylitzes credits a naval victory over the rebel fleet of Michael Kourtikios to Theodore Karantenos; it may be the same action. Abydos was recaptured.

name: Nicaea
borderline: A siege ended by agreement: Manuel hid his lack of food with a ruse and left with his men under terms.
roman_force: Rebels: Skleros' main army; loyalists: the garrison and townsmen of Nicaea under Manuel Erotikos Komnenos (Skylitzes).
greek_note: Both armies were imperial forces raised mainly in Greek-speaking Asia Minor, with many Armenians, especially in the eastern frontier armies.
sources: Skylitzes

name: Basilika Therma
roman_force: Rebels: Skleros' eastern armies; loyalists: Phokas' Anatolian forces before the Iberian reinforcement.
greek_note: Both armies were imperial forces raised mainly in Greek-speaking Asia Minor, with many Armenians, especially in the eastern frontier armies.
sources: Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Battle of Pankaleia

name: Sarvenis
place: Sarvenis (Aquae Saravenae, Kirsehir), north of Caesarea, after the Georgian sources; Skylitzes calls it Pankaleia
commanders_a: Bardas Phokas the Younger; John Tornikios (the Iberian contingent)
roman_force: Loyalists: Phokas' Anatolian forces with 12,000 Iberian horsemen sent by David III of Tao under John Tornikios (Skylitzes); rebels: Skleros' eastern armies.
greek_note: Both armies were imperial forces raised mainly in Greek-speaking Asia Minor, with many Armenians, especially in the eastern frontier armies.
sources: Skylitzes; Leo the Deacon; Yahya of Antioch; Psellos; en.wikipedia Battle of Pankaleia
note: Phokas wounded Skleros in single combat and the rebel army fled; Skleros escaped to the Hamdanid Abu Taghlib and then Baghdad. Skylitzes names this battle Pankaleia; Leo the Deacon gives that name to the first battle (978), which Phokas lost. Some (Forsyth, Tarchnichvili) see Skylitzes' account as a blend of the two. Skylitzes calls this decisive battle of 979 Pankaleia; modern scholars (Tarchnichvili, Forsyth) place it at Sarvenis (Aquae Saravenae, Kirsehir), with Pankaleia the first battle of June 978.

name: Gates of Trajan
place: the pass of the Gates of Trajan (Trayanovi Vrata), near Ihtiman
commanders_b: Basil II; Stephen Kontostephanos, Domestic of the West; Leo Melissenos
roman_force: Basil II's army of the West and the tagmata, perhaps 15,000-20,000 men, of whom an elite Armenian infantry unit cut its way out and saved the emperor (Leo the Deacon; Skylitzes).
greek_note: The tagmata and western themes were mainly Greek-speaking; the sources single out an Armenian infantry unit.
sources: Leo the Deacon; Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Battle of the Gates of Trajan
note: Leo the Deacon was present. The imperial insignia and baggage were captured. Some give 16 August.

name: Larissa (siege)
date: fell in 986 after a long blockade (some date the capture 983)
commanders_b: the garrison and townsmen of Larissa
borderline: A blockade ended by famine; little fighting is recorded.
roman_force: The garrison and people of Larissa, the chief town of the theme of Hellas in Thessaly.
greek_note: Larissa was a Greek-speaking town; Kekaumenos records Vlachs in its district.
sources: Skylitzes; Kekaumenos, Strategikon; en.wikipedia Samuel of Bulgaria; en.wikipedia Battle of the Gates of Trajan
note: The siege is variously dated from 977 or 983; Zlatarski and Cholpanov date the capture to 983. The inhabitants were deported.

name: Serdica
roman_force: Basil II's army of the West and the tagmata, perhaps 15,000-20,000 men, with siege engines; the eastern armies stayed facing the Arabs (Leo the Deacon, an eyewitness).
greek_note: The tagmata and western themes were mainly Greek-speaking; an Armenian infantry unit is named in the retreat.
sources: Leo the Deacon; Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Battle of the Gates of Trajan
note: Sorties burned the siege engines; Basil lifted the siege and retreated.

name: Chrysopolis
commanders_b: Kalokyros Delphinas (captured and executed); Nikephoros Phokas Barytrachelos
roman_force: Loyalists: Basil II's troops from the capital with the 6,000 Rus' warriors (Varangians) sent by Vladimir of Kiev; rebels: a detachment of Bardas Phokas' Anatolian army (Skylitzes; Yahya of Antioch).
greek_note: The sources name the Rus' contingent; the rest of both armies were imperial troops raised mainly in Greek-speaking Anatolia and Thrace.
sources: Skylitzes; Yahya of Antioch; Psellos; en.wikipedia, the article on the rebellion of Bardas Phokas the Younger
note: Basil crossed the Bosporus by night and surprised the rebel camp.

name: Chersonesos
commanders_b: the citizens and garrison of Cherson
borderline: Whether Cherson then held for Basil II or for the rebel Phokas, and so whether Vladimir was fighting the emperor, is disputed.
roman_force: The citizens and garrison of Cherson, the empire's city in the Crimea.
greek_note: Cherson was a Greek-speaking city defended by its own citizens.
sources: Russian Primary Chronicle; Leo the Deacon; Yahya of Antioch
note: The Primary Chronicle tells of a siege of several months, ended when the water supply was cut; modern scholars (Poppe) date it 989.

name: Abydos
commanders_b: Bardas Phokas (died on the field); Leo Melissenos
borderline: The battle barely began: Phokas died, of a seizure or poison, as he rode at the emperor's line, and his army broke up.
roman_force: Loyalists: Basil II's army with the Varangians; rebels: Phokas' Anatolian army, with Caucasian troops from David III of Tao, besieging Abydos (Psellos; Skylitzes).
greek_note: Both armies were mainly imperial thematic and tagmatic troops; the sources name the Rus' and the Iberian contingents.
sources: Psellos; Skylitzes; Yahya of Antioch; en.wikipedia Bardas Phokas the Younger
note: Some give 16 April 989.

name: Orontes
place: the fords of the Orontes near Apamea
roman_force: The forces of the duchy of Antioch under Michael Bourtzes, with the Hamdanid troops of Aleppo as allies.
greek_note: The army of the duchy of Antioch mixed Greek-speaking tagmata with many Armenians and local Syrian Christians.
sources: Yahya of Antioch; Ibn al-Qalanisi; en.wikipedia Battle of the Orontes
note: About 5,000 of the imperial army fell. Basil II relieved Aleppo by a forced march in 995 without a battle.

name: Thessalonica
commanders_b: Gregory Taronites, doux of Thessalonica (killed); his son Ashot (captured)
roman_force: The garrison and forces of the duchy of Thessalonica under Gregory Taronites, an Armenian prince in imperial service.
greek_note: The garrison of Thessalonica was drawn from the Greek-speaking population of Macedonia, under Armenian commanders.
sources: Skylitzes; Stephen of Taron; en.wikipedia Battle of Thessalonica (995)
note: An ambush; Skylitzes' account implies 996, but John Chaldos was already doux in 995/996.

name: Spercheios
commanders_a: Nikephoros Ouranos, Domestic of the West
roman_force: A large army given by Basil II to Nikephoros Ouranos as commander of the West, which forded the flooded river by night (Skylitzes).
greek_note: The armies of the West were raised mainly in Greek-speaking Thrace, Macedonia and Greece, with Armenians.
sources: Skylitzes; Yahya of Antioch; en.wikipedia Battle of Spercheios
note: en.wikipedia gives 16 July 997 in the battle article and 19 July 996 in the article on Samuel. Yahya: 1,000 heads and 12,000 captives.

name: Tyre
commanders_a: the Fatimid fleet and army sent by the regent Barjawan
borderline: A naval action in support of a rebel city; few details survive.
roman_force: A squadron of imperial ships sent to help Tyre, which had rebelled against the Fatimids under the sailor Allaqa (Yahya of Antioch).
greek_note: The imperial and thematic fleets were manned mainly from Constantinople and the Greek-speaking coasts and islands of the Aegean.
sources: Yahya of Antioch; Ibn al-Qalanisi; en.wikipedia Battle of Apamea (background)
note: The Fatimids beat off the imperial ships and retook Tyre.

name: Apamea
place: the plain of al-Mudiq near Apamea
roman_force: The army of the duchy of Antioch under Damian Dalassenos, with Georgian and Armenian officers such as the patrikios Tchortovanel (captured) (Yahya of Antioch).
greek_note: The army of the duchy of Antioch mixed Greek-speaking tagmata with many Armenians and Georgians.
sources: Yahya of Antioch; Ibn al-Qalanisi; en.wikipedia Battle of Apamea
note: 5,000-10,000 of the imperial army fell and about 2,000 were captured. Basil II's campaign of 999 followed.

name: Servia
borderline: A siege recorded briefly by Skylitzes.
roman_force: Basil II's field army of the Balkan war (Skylitzes).
greek_note: The armies of the West, raised mainly in Greek-speaking Thrace, Macedonia and Greece, with Armenians and eastern veterans moved to the Balkans.
sources: Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Samuel of Bulgaria
note: Some date it 1002 and credit Basil's generals.

name: Vodena
borderline: A siege recorded briefly by Skylitzes.
roman_force: Basil II's field army of the Balkan war (Skylitzes).
greek_note: The armies of the West, raised mainly in Greek-speaking Thrace, Macedonia and Greece, with Armenians and eastern veterans moved to the Balkans.
sources: Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Samuel of Bulgaria
note: The town fell after a long siege; its garrison was resettled.

name: Vidin
roman_force: Basil II's field army of the Balkan war with its siege train (Skylitzes).
greek_note: The armies of the West, raised mainly in Greek-speaking Thrace, Macedonia and Greece, with Armenians and eastern veterans moved to the Balkans.
sources: Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Samuel of Bulgaria; en.wikipedia Battle of Skopje
note: Some date it 1003. Samuel raided Adrianople on 15 August 1003 while Basil was at Vidin.

name: Bari
commanders_a: Gregory Tarchaneiotes, catepan of Italy; Pietro II Orseolo, doge of Venice
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Bari under the catepan; a Venetian fleet broke the blockade (John the Deacon).
greek_note: The catepan's garrison was imperial, but Bari's citizens were mostly Lombard and Latin-speaking.
sources: John the Deacon, Chronicle of Venice; Lupus Protospatharius
note: The siege lasted several months and was raised after the Venetian relief.

name: Skopje
roman_force: Basil II's field army, which forded the Vardar and attacked Samuel's camp at night (Skylitzes).
greek_note: The armies of the West, raised mainly in Greek-speaking Thrace, Macedonia and Greece, with Armenians and eastern veterans moved to the Balkans.
sources: Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Battle of Skopje
note: Skopje was then surrendered by its governor Romanos.

name: Pernik
roman_force: Basil II's field army of the Balkan war (Skylitzes).
greek_note: The armies of the West, raised mainly in Greek-speaking Thrace, Macedonia and Greece, with Armenians and eastern veterans moved to the Balkans.
sources: Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Samuel of Bulgaria
note: Basil withdrew with heavy losses.

name: Kreta
place: near the village of Kreta, east of Thessalonica
roman_force: Basil II's field army of the Balkan war.
greek_note: The armies of the West, raised mainly in Greek-speaking Thrace, Macedonia and Greece, with Armenians and eastern veterans moved to the Balkans.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kreta; en.wikipedia Samuel of Bulgaria
note: Little is known of this battle.

name: Bari
roman_force: A large army gathered by the new catepan Basil Mesardonites, who brought reinforcements in March 1010.
greek_note: Imperial troops sent from the East served beside local Apulian levies.
sources: Lupus Protospatharius; Annales Barenses; en.wikipedia Melus of Bari; en.wikipedia Norman conquest of southern Italy
note: The rebels were Lombard citizens of Bari; the city negotiated its surrender and the catepan entered on 11 June 1011.

name: Kleidion
place: the Kleidion pass (Klyuch), between the Belasitsa and Ograzhden mountains
commanders_a: Basil II; Nikephoros Xiphias, strategos of Philippopolis
roman_force: Basil II's main Balkan field army, veterans of many campaigns, with the flanking force under Nikephoros Xiphias that crossed the Belasitsa to take the Bulgarian wall from the rear (Skylitzes).
greek_note: The armies of the West, raised mainly in Greek-speaking Thrace, Macedonia and Greece, with Armenians and eastern veterans moved to the Balkans.
sources: Skylitzes; Kekaumenos; en.wikipedia Battle of Kleidion
note: Skylitzes says 15,000 prisoners were blinded (8,000 in the Bulgarian translation of Manasses). Samuel died on 6 October 1014.

name: Thessalonica
place: the fields west of Thessalonica (or by the Galikos river)
commanders_a: Theophylaktos Botaneiates, doux of Thessalonica; his son Michael
roman_force: The forces of the duchy of Thessalonica under Theophylaktos Botaneiates, with cavalry under his son Michael.
greek_note: The duchy of Thessalonica's troops came from Greek-speaking Macedonia.
sources: Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Battle of Thessalonica (1014)
note: A Bulgarian diversion before Kleidion; Botaneiates then joined Basil.

name: Strumitsa
place: a gorge near Strumitsa (perhaps the Kosturino gorge)
roman_force: A detachment of Basil II's army under Theophylaktos Botaneiates, sent to clear the passes towards Thessalonica (Skylitzes).
greek_note: The armies of the West, raised mainly in Greek-speaking Thrace, Macedonia and Greece, with Armenians and eastern veterans moved to the Balkans.
sources: Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Battle of Strumica
note: Basil lifted the siege of Strumitsa and withdrew.

name: Moglena
commanders_a: Basil II; Nikephoros Xiphias; Constantine Diogenes
borderline: A siege recorded briefly by Skylitzes.
roman_force: Basil II's field army; the river was diverted and the walls undermined (Skylitzes).
greek_note: The armies of the West, raised mainly in Greek-speaking Thrace, Macedonia and Greece, with Armenians and eastern veterans moved to the Balkans.
sources: Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Battle of Bitola (1015)

name: Bitola
roman_force: A large detachment left in Pelagonia under George Gonitsiates and Orestes to ravage the country and guard Basil's rear (Skylitzes).
greek_note: The armies of the West, raised mainly in Greek-speaking Thrace, Macedonia and Greece, with Armenians and eastern veterans moved to the Balkans.
sources: Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Battle of Bitola (1015)
note: The detachment was ambushed and destroyed.

name: Pernik
roman_force: Basil II's field army with its siege train (Skylitzes).
greek_note: The armies of the West, raised mainly in Greek-speaking Thrace, Macedonia and Greece, with Armenians and eastern veterans moved to the Balkans.
sources: Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Battle of Setina (background)
note: Basil withdrew to Mosynopolis after heavy losses.

name: Arenula
commanders_a: Melus of Bari; Gilbert Buatere and the Normans
commanders_b: Leo Passianos (sent by the catepan Leo Tornikios Kontoleon)
roman_force: The forces of the catepanate of Italy under Leo Passianos.
greek_note: The catepanate's army combined imperial troops from the Balkans and Anatolia with Lombard and Latin-speaking Apulian levies.
sources: William of Apulia; Leo of Ostia; Amatus of Montecassino; en.wikipedia Norman conquest of southern Italy; en.wikipedia Melus of Bari
note: William of Apulia calls it indecisive; Leo of Ostia and Amatus a victory for Melus.

name: Civita
place: Civita, near San Paolo di Civitate
commanders_b: Leo Tornikios Kontoleon, catepan of Italy
roman_force: The catepan's army of the catepanate of Italy.
greek_note: The catepanate's army combined imperial troops from the Balkans and Anatolia with Lombard and Latin-speaking Apulian levies.
sources: William of Apulia; Leo of Ostia; Lupus Protospatharius; en.wikipedia Norman conquest of southern Italy
note: Most sources give Melus the victory; Lupus Protospatharius and the Annals of Bari record an imperial victory.

name: Kastoria
borderline: A failed siege; the fighting is not described.
roman_force: Basil II's army of 1017, which included Rus' mercenaries (Skylitzes).
greek_note: The armies of the West, raised mainly in Greek-speaking Thrace, Macedonia and Greece, with Armenians and eastern veterans moved to the Balkans.
sources: Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Battle of Setina
note: Basil withdrew on news of Bulgarian negotiations with the Pechenegs.

name: Setina
roman_force: Basil II's army of 1017, which included Rus' mercenaries; the units under Constantine Diogenes were ambushed and rescued by the emperor (Skylitzes).
greek_note: The armies of the West, raised mainly in Greek-speaking Thrace, Macedonia and Greece, with Armenians and eastern veterans moved to the Balkans.
sources: Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Battle of Setina
note: About 200 Bulgarians were taken prisoner (Skylitzes).

name: Vaccarizza
commanders_b: the catepan's commanders (Leo Tornikios Kontoleon's army)
roman_force: The army of the catepanate of Italy.
greek_note: The catepanate's army combined imperial troops from the Balkans and Anatolia with Lombard and Latin-speaking Apulian levies.
sources: William of Apulia; Leo of Ostia; en.wikipedia Norman conquest of southern Italy
note: A decisive victory for Melus: the land from the Fortore to Trani came under his control, and Tornikios was replaced by Basil Boioannes.

name: Dyrrhachium
commanders_a: Niketas Pegonites, strategos of Dyrrhachium; David Areianites
roman_force: The garrison of Dyrrhachium under its strategos, whose sortie broke the besiegers (Skylitzes).
greek_note: Dyrrhachium was an imperial Greek-speaking stronghold; its garrison came from the empire.
sources: Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Battle of Dyrrhachium (1018)
note: Ivan Vladislav's death ended Bulgarian resistance; the Chronicle of the Priest of Duklja tells another version.

name: Cannae
roman_force: The catepan Basil Boioannes' army, with a detachment of the Varangian Guard sent by Basil II at his request.
greek_note: The catepanate's army combined imperial troops from the Balkans and Anatolia, Apulian levies and a Varangian detachment.
sources: William of Apulia; Amatus of Montecassino; Leo of Ostia; en.wikipedia Battle of Cannae (1018)
note: Amatus says the Normans numbered 250 and only ten survived. Melus fled to the Papal States and then to Henry II.

name: Garigliano tower
place: a fortified tower on the Garigliano, in the territory of Gaeta
commanders_a: Basil Boioannes, catepan of Italy; Pandulf IV of Capua
borderline: The capture of a single tower; a small action.
roman_force: The catepan's army, helped by Pandulf IV of Capua; Dattus held the tower with papal troops.
greek_note: The catepanate's army combined imperial troops with Apulian levies.
sources: Leo of Ostia; Annales Barenses; en.wikipedia Norman conquest of southern Italy
note: Dattus was executed at Bari on 15 June 1021 by the poena cullei.

name: Shirimni
commanders_b: George I of Georgia; Rati Baghuashi and Khursi (both killed)
roman_force: Basil II's field army of the East, led in person; its make-up is not detailed, but Varangians are reported in the Georgian campaign of 1021-1022.
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Skylitzes; Aristakes of Lastivert; Kartlis Tskhovreba; en.wikipedia Battle of Shirimni
note: Sometimes dated 1022; the war ended in 1022 after a second victory at Svindax. en.wikipedia lists an Armenian ally of Georgia.

name: Svindax
roman_force: Basil II's field army of the East, led in person.
greek_note: The army of this period was raised mainly in the Greek-speaking themes of Asia Minor and the tagmata of Constantinople, with a substantial Armenian element.
sources: Kartlis Tskhovreba; Aristakes of Lastivert; en.wikipedia Battle of Svindax
note: George I then made peace, ceding the disputed lands of Tao.

name: Troia
commanders_a: the citizens and garrison of Troia
commanders_b: Henry II, emperor in the West
roman_force: The settlers and garrison of Troia, a frontier city founded by Basil Boioannes, which had Norman mercenaries in imperial pay.
greek_note: Troia's settlers were mostly Lombard and Latin-speaking Apulians, with Norman soldiers; few Greek speakers are likely.
sources: Raoul Glaber; Leo of Ostia; Amatus of Montecassino; en.wikipedia Norman conquest of southern Italy
note: Troia did not fall; Raoul Glaber says the townsmen finally made a nominal submission, and Henry withdrew.

name: Lemnos
commanders_a: David of Ohrid, strategos of Samos; Nikephoros Kabasilas, doux of Thessalonica
roman_force: The fleets of Samos and of the Kibyrrhaiotai and the troops of Nikephoros Kabasilas from Thessalonica (Skylitzes).
greek_note: The sources name the naval theme of the Kibyrrhaiotai, the squadron of Samos and the troops of Thessalonica, all Greek-speaking provinces.
sources: Skylitzes; en.wikipedia Battle of Lemnos (1024)
note: Chrysocheir's 800 Rus' had forced the Hellespont; the imperial commanders feigned negotiations and then destroyed them.

name: Kldekari (siege)
place: Kldekari fortress, in the Trialeti range
commanders_a: Liparit IV of Kldekari, for Bagrat IV
commanders_b: the parakoimomenos ('Parakimanos' of the Georgian chronicle), sent by Constantine VIII
borderline: Known only from the Georgian chronicle; the Wikipedia articles say the fortress was 'fiercely defended' and the Romans forced to retreat, without detail of the fighting.
roman_force: The army that Constantine VIII sent into Georgia under his parakoimomenos, which overran Artaani and threatened Kldekari; the sources give no units or numbers. Probably the eastern tagmata with the troops of the theme of Iberia (inferred).
greek_note: An expedition sent from Constantinople would have included the Greek-speaking tagmata, beside Armenian and Georgian troops of the Iberian frontier themes.
sources: Georgian Chronicles (Chronicle of Kartli); en.wikipedia Kldekari Fortress; en.wikipedia, the article on the war with Georgia of 1028
note: The same campaign met a successful local defence in Shavsheti organized by Bishop Saba of Tbeti (not entered). Peace followed under Romanos III (1030/31).

name: Qaybar
war: Wars with the Mirdasids of Aleppo
place: Qaybar, near the frontier of Antioch and Aleppo
commanders_b: officers of Michael Spondyles, doux of Antioch
borderline: Known only as the place where a Roman force was destroyed by the Kilab; no separate article.
roman_force: A detachment of the army of the doux of Antioch; the sources give no units or numbers.
greek_note: The ducate of Antioch drew on Greek, Armenian and Syrian Christian soldiers of the frontier.
sources: Yahya of Antioch; en.wikipedia Battle of Azaz (1030) (background)
note: The defeat led Romanos III to march on Aleppo in 1030.

name: Azaz
war: Wars with the Mirdasids of Aleppo
commanders_a: Shibl al-Dawla Nasr, Mirdasid emir of Aleppo
roman_force: The emperor's field army, about 20,000 by modern estimate, with the Exkoubitoi under Leo Choirosphaktes, the Hetaireia and Armenian and other foreign mercenaries; routed by 700-2,000 Bedouin horsemen of the Kilab and Numayr.
greek_note: The tagmata were recruited mainly in Anatolia and Thrace, but the army 'contained many foreign mercenaries', Armenians among them.
sources: Skylitzes, Romanos III 4; Yahya of Antioch; Psellos, Chronographia 3.7-11; en.wikipedia Battle of Azaz (1030)
note: The Arabs took the whole baggage train but could not exploit the victory.

name: Edessa
commanders_b: Marwanid and Numayrid commanders (Nasr al-Dawla, Shibl al-Dawla)
borderline: A purchased citadel followed by fighting for the town, not a pitched battle.
roman_force: The garrison troops of Teluch and the Euphrates frontier under Maniakes, who occupied the citadel sold by Ibn Utayr and held it against the Muslim troops in the town.
greek_note: The frontier commands of the Euphrates were manned by Greek and Armenian soldiers with local Syrian Christians.
sources: Skylitzes, Romanos III 10; Matthew of Edessa 1.50; en.wikipedia George Maniakes, Numayrids
note: Dated 1031 or 1032; the Muslim inhabitants were killed or expelled and Edessa stayed Roman until 1086.

name: Edessa
commanders_a: the Roman garrison of the citadel
commanders_b: Shabib ibn Waththab (Numayrid), with Marwanid and Uqaylid troops
borderline: Siege of uncertain scale; the town was taken and looted but the citadel held.
roman_force: The Roman garrison of the citadel of Edessa; no numbers are given.
greek_note: The frontier garrisons of the 1030s were Greek and Armenian.
sources: Skylitzes, Michael IV; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Numayrids
note: The attackers withdrew when the Seljuks threatened Harran; peace in 1037 confirmed Edessa as Roman.

name: Messina
place: beach near the Strait of Messina, possibly Pelorus (Torre Faro)
commanders_a: George Maniakes, Katakalon Kekaumenos, Harald Sigurdsson, Stephen (fleet)
roman_force: At least 10,000 men: eastern thematic units (Kekaumenos led the Armeniakon contingent), up to 1,000 Varangians under Harald, and up to 2,000 Italian recruits including 300-500 Normans under Arduin and Rainulf, landed by Stephen's fleet.
greek_note: Skylitzes names thematic contingents from Anatolia (the Armeniakon) as the core of the army, with Varangian and Italian-Norman mercenaries.
sources: Skylitzes, Michael IV 20; Kekaumenos, Strategikon; Malaterra 1.7; en.wikipedia Capture of Messina (1038)
note: An opposed landing; Messina then surrendered without a siege.

name: Rometta
place: Rometta, in the hills west of Messina
commanders_a: George Maniakes, Katakalon Kekaumenos, Harald Sigurdsson, Basil Pediadites
roman_force: 10,000-15,000 men (modern estimate): Anatolian thematic and tagmatic troops, 1,000 Varangians, 2,000 Italian recruits and auxiliaries including 300-500 Normans, perhaps some Sicilian Christians.
greek_note: The army was built round thematic troops from Anatolia; the Varangians and Italians were a few thousand at most.
sources: Skylitzes, Michael IV 20; Malaterra 1.7; en.wikipedia Battle of Rometta (1038)
note: Fought against a combined Kalbid-Zirid army; Rometta was taken.

name: Syracuse (siege)
commanders_a: George Maniakes, Katakalon Kekaumenos, Harald Sigurdsson, William Iron Arm, Arduin, Stephen
roman_force: Maniakes' expeditionary army of 10,000-15,000: Anatolian thematic troops, 1,000 Varangians, 2,000 Italian recruits with 300-500 Normans, and the fleet.
greek_note: The thematic contingents from Anatolia formed the bulk; Varangians, Lombards and Normans were mercenaries.
sources: Skylitzes, Michael IV 20; Malaterra 1.7; Amatus 2.8; en.wikipedia Campaign for Syracuse (1038-1040)
note: The garrison was defeated in a battle under the walls (William Iron Arm killed its commander in single combat) and the city taken in 1040.

name: Dranginai (Troina)
commanders_a: George Maniakes, Harald Sigurdsson, Arduin, William Iron Arm, Drogo of Hauteville
roman_force: A large army with 1,000 Varangians in the centre under Harald, 300-500 Norman horse on the wings under William Iron Arm, and the Roman heavy cavalry that Maniakes sent in to decide the battle.
greek_note: Skylitzes' account has the Roman cavalry and thematic troops as the main force, with Varangians and Normans as named mercenary units.
sources: Skylitzes, Michael IV 20; Malaterra 1.7; en.wikipedia Battle of Dranginai (1040)
note: Troina is the usual identification. Malaterra's 60,000 Zirids and Skylitzes' 50,000 dead are not credible.

name: Thessalonica
borderline: Skylitzes describes Michael IV leaving Thessalonica as the rebels approached rather than a pitched battle.
roman_force: The emperor's escort and the troops with him at Thessalonica; the sources give no units or numbers.
greek_note: The tagmata and the troops of Thessalonica were mainly Greek-speaking.
sources: Skylitzes, Michael IV 24; en.wikipedia Battle of Thessalonica (1040); en.wikipedia Uprising of Peter Delyan
note: Not a double of 1040-thessalonica-siege: English Wikipedia has two articles, this one (Delyan 'surprised and defeated' Michael IV at Thessalonica, after which the emperor fled and his officer Manuel Ivats went over to Delyan) and 'Battle of Thessalonica (2nd 1040)', Alusian's failed attack in the autumn. Delyan's rebels were former Roman subjects of the Bulgarian lands, counted here as Bulgaria.

name: Thebes
roman_force: The thematic army of Hellas; no numbers are given.
greek_note: The theme of Hellas was raised in Boeotia and Attica.
sources: Skylitzes, Michael IV 24; en.wikipedia Uprising of Peter Delyan

name: Thessalonica (siege)
commanders_a: the garrison of Thessalonica (the patrikios Constantine)
roman_force: The garrison and the tagma stationed at Thessalonica, which sallied and routed Alusian's besieging army (said to be 40,000, with 15,000 killed).
greek_note: The defenders were the Greek-speaking garrison and citizens of Thessalonica.
sources: Skylitzes, Michael IV 26; en.wikipedia Battle of Thessalonica (2nd 1040); en.wikipedia Uprising of Peter Delyan
note: The sortie was credited to Saint Demetrios; the rebel figures are Skylitzes'.

name: Olivento
place: on the Olivento river, near Venosa
commanders_a: William Iron Arm, Rainulf Drengot, Arduin
roman_force: Several thousand men: units of the Opsikion and Thrakesion and Varangians (Harald Hardrada among them), against 300 Norman knights and 600 foot.
greek_note: Skylitzes names the Opsikion and Thrakesion units, Anatolian Greek-speaking troops, as Dokeianos' army.
sources: Skylitzes, Michael IV 28; William of Apulia 1; Amatus 2.21; en.wikipedia Battle of Olivento
note: Some accounts give 16 March. Many Romans drowned in the river.

name: Montemaggiore
commanders_a: William Iron Arm, Drogo and Humphrey of Hauteville, Rainulf Drengot
roman_force: 'Several thousand' (18,000 in the Annals of Bari): fresh troops from Asia Minor, soldiers back from Sicily and the Varangian Guard from Bari, in two lines.
greek_note: The army was mainly Anatolian thematic troops brought over from Asia and from Sicily, with the Varangians.
sources: Skylitzes, Michael IV 28; Annales Barenses; William of Apulia 1; en.wikipedia Battle of Montemaggiore
note: Many of the fleeing Romans drowned in the Ofanto.

name: Montepeloso
place: Monte Siricolo, near Montepeloso (Irsina), on the Bradano
commanders_a: William Iron Arm, Atenulf of Benevento
roman_force: The catepan's army with the Varangian Guard and troops brought from the Balkan themes (Skylitzes speaks of Macedonians); no numbers are given.
greek_note: Boioannes' army was reinforced from the Balkan themes; Apulian levies were Lombard.
sources: William of Apulia 1; Amatus 2.26; Skylitzes, Michael IV 28; en.wikipedia Battle of Montepeloso
note: The last pitched battle between Normans and Romans on the Italian mainland.

name: Messina
borderline: A defence of the city with a sortie; named only as the defence of Messina.
roman_force: The garrison of Messina, Kekaumenos' Armeniakon contingent of about 500 horse and 300 foot by Skylitzes' account.
greek_note: The defenders were the Armeniakon thematic troops left with Kekaumenos.
sources: Skylitzes, Michael IV 20; en.wikipedia Katakalon Kekaumenos
note: The figures for Kekaumenos' men are from Skylitzes; Messina was the last Roman foothold in Sicily, held until 1042-43.

name: Ostrovo
roman_force: The emperor's field army of the tagmata and western themes, with about 500 Varangians under Harald Hardrada, to whom the Norse sagas give a decisive part.
greek_note: The army was raised from the tagmata and the western themes; the Varangians were a few hundred.
sources: Skylitzes, Michael IV 28; Psellos, Chronographia 4.40-48; Heimskringla, Harald's saga; en.wikipedia Uprising of Peter Delyan
note: Ostrovo is usually identified with Arnissa in Greek Macedonia; Delyan was captured or killed.

name: Ani
commanders_a: Vahram Pahlavuni, for Gagik II of Ani
borderline: Known mainly from Armenian sources; date 1042 or 1044.
roman_force: An army of the eastern themes sent to claim Ani under the will of Hovhannes-Smbat; Armenian sources call it 100,000, which is not credible.
greek_note: The eastern armies drew on both Greek-speaking Anatolia and the Armenian provinces.
sources: Aristakes Lastivertc'i 10; Matthew of Edessa 1.66; en.wikipedia Siege of Ani (list of sieges)
note: Ani was ceded to the empire in 1045 by negotiation.

name: Sasireti
war: Georgian civil war (revolt of Liparit IV)
place: near Sasireti, Shida Kartli, near Kaspi
borderline: The Romans were auxiliaries of one side in a Georgian civil war.
roman_force: Roman auxiliaries sent to support Liparit, of unknown number, beside Liparit's Georgians and an army from Kakheti.
greek_note: The sources say only that a Roman force supported Liparit; it probably came from the theme of Iberia, recruited largely among Armenians and Georgians.
sources: Georgian Chronicles (Life of Bagrat IV); en.wikipedia Battle of Sasireti
note: Some lists date it to 1047. Bagrat's side included about 1,000-2,000 Varangians of Ingvar's expedition.

name: Bar
place: the mountains between Bar (Antivari) and Crmnica
commanders_a: Stefan Vojislav of Duklja and five of his sons
commanders_b: Michael (Michaelus Anastasii), governor of Dyrrhachium; Curcilius, toparch (killed); Ljutovid of Zahumlje (killed)
roman_force: The army of the theme of Dyrrhachium with its local Slav vassals, 60,000 according to Skylitzes, and allies paid in gold: Ljutovid of Zahumlje, the zupan of Raska and the ban of Bosnia (Chronicle of the Priest of Duklja).
greek_note: The western themes of Dyrrhachium and Nikopolis mixed Greek, Slav and Albanian soldiers.
sources: Skylitzes, Constantine IX 5; Kekaumenos, Strategikon; Chronicle of the Priest of Duklja 38; en.wikipedia Battle of Bar
note: Also called the battle of Tudjemili; dated 1042 or 1043. Kekaumenos says the Romans lost over 40,000; the figures are inflated.

name: Ostrovo
place: Ostrovo, on the road from Dyrrhachium to Thessalonica
roman_force: Loyalist: the field army sent from Constantinople under Stephen. Rebel: Maniakes' army from Italy, with Varangians and Italian (Lombard and Norman) troops he had brought across from Apulia.
greek_note: Both armies were built on the regular tagmata and themes; Maniakes added the Italian and Varangian soldiers of his command.
sources: Skylitzes, Constantine IX 3; Psellos, Chronographia 6.84-86; en.wikipedia George Maniakes
note: Maniakes was winning when he was mortally wounded; his army then surrendered.

name: Constantinople (sea)
place: off the northern mouth of the Bosporus, near Pharos
commanders_a: Constantine IX, Basil Theodorokanos, Katakalon Kekaumenos
roman_force: The imperial fleet of dromons with Greek fire, the remnants of which had been gathered in the capital; Varangians were in the city. A pursuing squadron of 14 or 24 ships was lost, and Kekaumenos defeated the Rus' who came ashore.
greek_note: The imperial fleet was crewed by Greek-speaking oarsmen and marines of the capital and the Aegean themes.
sources: Psellos, Chronographia 6.90-95; Skylitzes, Constantine IX 6; Russian Primary Chronicle s.a. 1043; en.wikipedia, the article on the Rus' war of 1043
note: The Slavonic chronicles blame a storm. About 800 captives were reportedly blinded.

name: Taranto
borderline: Unnamed engagement near Taranto, known from one sentence of the Wikipedia overview (from the south Italian annals); named here from its site.
roman_force: Argyros' forces from Bari and the imperial troops left in Apulia; no units or numbers are recorded.
greek_note: As at Siponto (1053), Argyros' army was mainly Apulian Lombards with a small Greek-speaking imperial element.
sources: en.wikipedia Norman conquest of southern Italy
note: Argyros, the Lombard of Bari, had gone over to Constantine IX in 1042.

name: Dvin
commanders_a: Abu'l-Aswar Shavur, Shaddadid emir of Dvin
commanders_b: Michael Iasites, the magistros Constantine the Alan
borderline: A failed attack on Dvin; not a standard named battle.
roman_force: A large army of the eastern themes 'including many Armenians', sent after the annexation of Ani; caught on the plain the emir had flooded and shot down by his archers.
greek_note: Skylitzes notes that many of the soldiers were Armenians.
sources: Skylitzes, Constantine IX 15; Aristakes 12; en.wikipedia Abu'l-Aswar Shavur ibn Fadl
note: The Shaddadids were a Kurdish dynasty, counted here with the Muslim emirates under 'Arabs'.

name: Taranto
borderline: Unnamed engagement near Taranto, known from one sentence of the Wikipedia overview (from the south Italian annals); named here from its site.
roman_force: The field army of the catepan Eustathios Palatinos; no units or numbers are recorded.
greek_note: A catepan's army combined imperial units sent from the east with Apulian levies; the Taranto region was partly Greek-speaking.
sources: en.wikipedia Norman conquest of southern Italy
note: In the same year Humphrey of Hauteville forced Bari to make a treaty with the Normans.

name: Ganja
borderline: Known only from a short Wikipedia article that names no primary source; the Roman part (an army sent by Constantine IX under Liparit) is unverified.
roman_force: An army sent to the Caucasus by Constantine IX under the Georgian duke Liparit IV of Kldekari, with his own Georgian troops; no units or numbers are given.
greek_note: The imperial forces on the Caucasus frontier in the 1040s were drawn largely from the Armenian and Iberian themes, and Liparit's own men were Georgians.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Ganja (1046)
note: Ganja was the seat of the Shaddadid emirs. The article also lists Ibrahim Yinal among the Seljuk commanders. Two years later Liparit was captured at Kapetron.

name: Constantinople
roman_force: Rebels: the Macedonian tagmata and western troops raised at Adrianople. Loyalists: a few soldiers, Saracen prisoners, armed citizens and released convicts; the eastern army was away in Iberia.
greek_note: Psellos and Attaleiates describe the rebel army as the Macedonians of Adrianople and the defenders as the citizens of the capital.
sources: Psellos, Chronographia 6.99-123; Attaleiates 4; Skylitzes, Constantine IX 9; en.wikipedia Leo Tornikios
note: A sortie of citizens was routed and two assaults were repulsed; Tornikios withdrew in early October.

name: Rhaidestos
borderline: A repulsed attack on a town, minor.
roman_force: Loyal townsmen and garrison of Rhaidestos against the rebel Macedonian army.
greek_note: Both sides were Thracian and Macedonian Greek-speaking troops.
sources: Attaleiates 4; Skylitzes, Constantine IX 9; en.wikipedia Leo Tornikios
note: After the failure Tornikios' men deserted and he was captured at Boulgarophygon.

name: Chelidonion
borderline: A siege abandoned when the army was recalled against Tornikios; fighting not described.
roman_force: The army of Ani-Iberia and the East, which took Surmari, Anberd and Khor Virap before besieging Chelidonion.
greek_note: The eastern armies of the 1040s combined Anatolian Greek and local Armenian soldiers.
sources: Skylitzes, Constantine IX; en.wikipedia Abu'l-Aswar Shavur ibn Fadl
note: A treaty followed in which Abu'l-Aswar recognised the emperor's authority.

name: Kapetron
place: plain of Kapetron, near Pasinler (Hasankale), east of Erzurum
commanders_a: Aaron, Katakalon Kekaumenos, Liparit IV of Kldekari (captured)
roman_force: The troops of the katepanates of Vaspurakan (Aaron) and Ani-Iberia (Kekaumenos), with Liparit's Georgian army in the centre; the tagmata were in the Balkans after Tornikios' revolt. Ibn al-Athir's 50,000 and Aristakes' 60,000 are exaggerated.
greek_note: With the tagmata absent, the army was mainly local Armenian troops and Liparit's Georgians under Roman commanders.
sources: Skylitzes, Constantine IX 16; Aristakes 12; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Battle of Kapetron
note: Indecisive: the Roman wings won, but Liparit was captured and Ibrahim escaped with his booty. Some date it 1049.

name: Stragna River
place: the Stragna river (perhaps the upper Great Zab), Vaspurakan
commanders_a: Aaron, katepano of Vaspurakan; Katakalon Kekaumenos, katepano of Ani and Iberia
roman_force: The troops of the katepanates of Vaspurakan and Ani-Iberia, smaller than the Turkish raiders (20,000 according to Skylitzes).
greek_note: The eastern katepanates were garrisoned largely by local Armenian and Georgian soldiers under Roman officers.
sources: Skylitzes, Constantine IX 16; en.wikipedia Battle of the Stragna River
note: The Turks were ambushed in their camp and most were killed.

name: Dampolis
commanders_a: Tyrach, Selte and other Pecheneg chiefs
roman_force: The western army of Thrace and Macedonia under Arianites; after beating small bands he was defeated by the main Pecheneg host and fell back on Adrianople.
greek_note: The western tagmata and Thracian-Macedonian themes were Greek-speaking with Bulgarian elements.
sources: Skylitzes, Constantine IX 17; en.wikipedia Pecheneg revolt

name: Diakene
commanders_b: the rhaiktor Nikephoros (or Constantine), Katakalon Kekaumenos (wounded), Herve Frankopoulos
borderline: Site unidentified; the name Diakene is from Skylitzes.
roman_force: The armies of the East brought over to Europe, with Herve's Frankish mercenaries; Kekaumenos was badly wounded and left among the dead.
greek_note: Skylitzes names the eastern tagmata and Herve's Franks.
sources: Skylitzes, Constantine IX 17; en.wikipedia Pecheneg revolt, Katakalon Kekaumenos

name: Adrianople
commanders_b: the hetaireiarches Constantine, Samuel Bourtzes, Constantine Arianites (mortally wounded), Michael Dokeianos (captured and killed), Niketas Glabas
roman_force: Units of the western and eastern tagmata under the hetaireiarches Constantine; the Scholai under Niketas Glabas saved the camp.
greek_note: The sources name the tagmata of East and West and the Scholai, regular Roman regiments.
sources: Skylitzes, Constantine IX 17; Attaleiates 7; en.wikipedia Pecheneg revolt
note: Bourtzes attacked before the signal; the Romans lost the field but the Pechenegs failed to storm the camp.

name: Arcadiopolis
commanders_a: an imperial commander, perhaps Demetrios Katakalon
roman_force: Roman cavalry of the western army, which broke and pursued the 'innumerable' Pechenegs (Attaleiates).
greek_note: A regular Roman cavalry force of the Thracian command.
sources: Attaleiates 7; Skylitzes, Constantine IX 17; en.wikipedia Pecheneg revolt

name: Rentakion
commanders_a: the commander of the victory at Arcadiopolis
borderline: Minor and the site is unknown.
roman_force: The same western army that won at Arcadiopolis.
greek_note: Regular troops of the Thracian command.
sources: Attaleiates 7; en.wikipedia Pecheneg revolt
note: The Pechenegs, joined by another raiding column, were scattered into the forests.

name: Toplitzos
place: the Pecheneg encampment at Toplitzos, in Thrace (site unknown)
borderline: One of several small victories of the counter-raiding campaign (others at Goloe and near Charioupolis); site unknown.
roman_force: A mobile force of Varangians, Franks and other westerners under the Varangian captain Michael Akolouthos, with Bryennios' Roman cavalry.
greek_note: The sources stress the Varangians and Franks; the Roman horse of Bryennios made up the rest.
sources: Skylitzes, Constantine IX 17; en.wikipedia Pecheneg revolt
note: A victory at Goloe and the destruction of a Pecheneg band near Charioupolis belong to the same campaign.

name: Preslav
place: the Pecheneg palisaded camp near Preslav
commanders_b: Michael Akolouthos, the doux Basil (Basil the synkellos)
roman_force: A regular field army with Akolouthos' Varangians and Franks.
greek_note: Regular western and eastern regiments with the Varangian-Frankish corps.
sources: Skylitzes, Constantine IX 20; en.wikipedia Pecheneg revolt, Battle of Zygos Pass
note: The Romans could not take the palisade and withdrew when supplies ran short.

name: Zygos Pass
place: the Zygos pass over the Haemus (Balkan Mountains), south of Preslav
commanders_b: Michael Akolouthos, Basil the synkellos (killed), Nikephoros Botaneiates
roman_force: The army withdrawing from Preslav, regular regiments with Varangians and Franks; Botaneiates rallied the cavalry and led a 12-day fighting retreat to Adrianople.
greek_note: Regular Roman cavalry and infantry with the western mercenary corps.
sources: Skylitzes, Constantine IX 20; Attaleiates 7; en.wikipedia Battle of Zygos Pass
note: Peace followed soon after (c. 1053).

name: Siponto
commanders_a: Norman leaders of Apulia (Humphrey of Hauteville)
commanders_b: Argyros, catepan and doux of Italy (wounded)
borderline: Named only in the Italian chronicles; the Romans did not fight at Civitate.
roman_force: Argyros' army of Apulian levies and the few imperial troops in Italy, marching to join Pope Leo IX against the Normans.
greek_note: Argyros was a Lombard of Bari and his army was mainly Apulian Lombards with a small Roman element.
sources: William of Apulia 2; Annales Barenses s.a. 1053
note: Civitate (18 June 1053) itself is excluded: Argyros' army never joined the papal army.

name: Manzikert
roman_force: The garrison of Manzikert under Basil Apokapes, including Latin mercenaries (one of whom burned the sultan's great siege engine with Greek fire).
greek_note: The garrisons of the Armenian frontier were largely local Armenians under Roman officers, with some Latin mercenaries.
sources: Attaleiates 9; Aristakes 15; Matthew of Edessa 1.88; en.wikipedia Siege of Manzikert (1054)
note: Tughril raised the siege after about 30 days.

name: Petroe
place: plain of Hades (Petroe, Polemon), near Nicaea
commanders_a: Isaac Komnenos, Katakalon Kekaumenos, Romanos Skleros, Nikephoros Botaneiates
commanders_b: the proedros Theodore, Aaron, Basil Tarchaneiotes, Randolf the Frank
roman_force: Rebels: the regiments of the Armeniakon, two Frankish and one Rus' mercenary unit, the units of Koloneia and Chaldia and Anatolian troops. Loyalists: the western regiments with the Anatolikon and Charsianon units and Frankish mercenaries.
greek_note: The sources name thematic regiments from Anatolia and the West on both sides, with a few Frankish and Rus' units.
sources: Skylitzes, Michael VI 6-8; Psellos, Chronographia 7.8-11; Attaleiates 10; en.wikipedia Battle of Petroe
note: Michael VI abdicated; Isaac I was crowned on 1 September 1057.

name: Reggio
borderline: A siege ending in surrender; scale of fighting uncertain.
roman_force: The imperial garrison and citizens of Reggio, the capital of Roman Calabria.
greek_note: Southern Calabria was Greek-speaking.
sources: Malaterra 1.34-35; William of Apulia 2; en.wikipedia Norman conquest of southern Italy
note: The garrison withdrew to Squillace, which also fell.

name: Ani
commanders_b: Bagrat Vkhkatsi and the Roman commanders of Ani
roman_force: The garrison of the katepanate of Ani, with Armenian and Georgian troops under Roman command.
greek_note: Ani's defenders were mainly Armenian townsmen and soldiers under Roman governors.
sources: Aristakes 24; Matthew of Edessa 2.11; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Siege of Ani
note: The city was stormed after about 25 days and sacked.

name: Caesarea
commanders_a: Afshin and other emirs of Alp Arslan
borderline: Listed as a battle in the Wikipedia list but essentially a raid and sack; whether imperial troops fought is unclear.
roman_force: The citizens and local garrison of Caesarea; no field army was present.
greek_note: Cappadocia was mainly Greek-speaking with a large Armenian settlement.
sources: Attaleiates 13; Matthew of Edessa 2.20; en.wikipedia List of battles of the Roman Empire (East) ('Battle of Caesarea')
note: The shrine of Saint Basil was plundered.

name: Bari (siege)
commanders_b: Michael Maurex Avartuteles, Stephen Pateranos (catepans), Argyritzos
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Bari with reinforcements and supply fleets from Constantinople (20 ships in 1071); a Roman field army sent in 1069 was beaten in Apulia.
greek_note: Bari's citizens were Lombard Italians; the imperial troops were a minority.
sources: William of Apulia 2-3; Amatus 5; Lupus Protospatharius; en.wikipedia Siege of Bari
note: Bari surrendered on 15 or 16 April 1071, ending Roman rule in Italy.

name: Hierapolis
commanders_b: Mirdasid emir of Aleppo (Mahmud ibn Nasr), with Turkmen
borderline: A capture with fighting and a battle outside against the Aleppines.
roman_force: Romanos IV's field army of the eastern and western tagmata, thematic levies, Frankish and other mercenaries.
greek_note: Attaleiates, who served in it, describes an army of regular regiments and mercenaries raised in Anatolia and the Balkans.
sources: Attaleiates 14-15; Skylitzes Continuatus; en.wikipedia Romanos IV Diogenes
note: The city was taken and fortified; the engagements with the Aleppines and Turks were indecisive.

name: Iconium
roman_force: Units of Romanos IV's eastern army; no numbers.
greek_note: The eastern regiments of the late 1060s were recruited in Anatolia and Armenia.
sources: Attaleiates 16; en.wikipedia Battle of Iconium (1069)
note: Accounts differ: Attaleiates has the Turks sack Iconium in 1069 and escape through Cilicia; the Wikipedia article counts a Roman victory near the city.

name: Sebasteia
roman_force: The eastern army entrusted to Manuel Komnenos while Romanos IV stayed in the capital.
greek_note: Recruited in the Anatolian and Armenian themes.
sources: Attaleiates 17; Bryennios 1.11; en.wikipedia Romanos IV Diogenes
note: Khroudj then defected to Romanos, provoking Alp Arslan's campaign of 1071.

name: Manzikert
commanders_b: Romanos IV Diogenes (captured), Nikephoros Bryennios, Theodore Alyates, Andronikos Doukas
roman_force: About 40,000 at the start, perhaps half present: the tagmata of East and West (Scholai, Hetaireia, Stratelatai, about 5,000 from each half of the empire), thematic levies and archontic retinues, part of the Varangian Guard, about 500 Franks under Roussel, Uz and Pecheneg horse, Armenian infantry, Georgians and Bulgarians.
greek_note: Attaleiates names the regular Roman tagmata and themes beside a large mercenary and Armenian element; many Turkic mercenaries changed sides.
sources: Attaleiates 20; Psellos, Chronographia 7b; Bryennios 1.13-17; Skylitzes Continuatus; Aristakes 25; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Battle of Manzikert
note: Andronikos Doukas withdrew the reserve; the emperor was captured but released on terms.

name: Bari (sea)
roman_force: A relief squadron of about 20 ships sent by Romanos IV, commanded by the Norman exile Gocelin.
greek_note: The squadron came from Dyrrhachium and the Adriatic commands, with Italian sailors.
sources: William of Apulia 3; Malaterra 2.43; en.wikipedia Siege of Bari
note: Gocelin's ship was captured; Pateranos reached Bari, which surrendered soon after.

name: Belgrade (siege)
commanders_a: King Solomon, Duke Geza, Duke Ladislaus
roman_force: The garrison of Belgrade under Niketas, including Muslim ('Saracen') units that made sorties; a Pecheneg relief force under Kazar was destroyed by the ispan of Sopron.
greek_note: A frontier garrison of Roman troops with Muslim mercenaries and local Slavs.
sources: Chronicon Pictum; en.wikipedia, the article on the Hungarian war of 1071-1072
note: The siege opened with the Roman flotilla throwing 'sulphurous fires' at the Hungarian boats crossing the Sava, which the Hungarians nevertheless got across (formerly entered separately as 1071-sava). The town was sacked and the garrison surrendered the citadel to Geza; the Romans may have retaken Belgrade by a stratagem in 1072.

name: Dokeia
borderline: Not a standard named battle; named here from its site.
roman_force: Doukas army: troops raised for Michael VII, with Frankish mercenaries. Romanos' army: the survivors of Manzikert and eastern levies.
greek_note: Both sides were regular Roman regiments of Anatolia, with Frankish mercenaries on the Doukas side.
sources: Attaleiates 21; Psellos, Chronographia 7b; Bryennios 1.20-21
note: Romanos withdrew to Tyropoion and then Cilicia.

name: Paun (Taonios)
roman_force: The army under Saronites that had retaken Skopje; no units or numbers are given.
greek_note: A western Roman army of the period, probably with Frankish mercenaries.
sources: Skylitzes Continuatus; Bryennios 1.7; en.wikipedia Uprising of Georgi Voiteh
note: Nikephoros Bryennios suppressed the remaining rebels in 1073.

name: Cilicia
borderline: No conventional name.
roman_force: Doukas army with Crispin's Frankish heavy cavalry against Romanos' army raised in Cilicia and Antioch, largely Armenian.
greek_note: Romanos' last army came from the Armenian-dominated south-east; the Doukas army was regular Roman troops and Franks.
