sources: Attaleiates 21; Bryennios 1.22; en.wikipedia Romanos IV Diogenes
note: Romanos surrendered at Adana and was blinded at Kotyaion on 29 June 1072.

name: Skopje
roman_force: An army sent from Constantinople to the doux of Skopje; no numbers.
greek_note: The western armies were Greek-speaking with Bulgarian and other Balkan soldiers.
sources: Skylitzes Continuatus; Bryennios 1.7; en.wikipedia Uprising of Georgi Voiteh
note: The rebels were Bulgarian nobles joined by Serbs of Duklja under Bodin, proclaimed tsar as Peter III.

name: Kastoria
commanders_a: the imperial commanders at Kastoria (with the loyal Bulgarian noble Boris David)
roman_force: The garrison and local troops of Kastoria; no numbers.
greek_note: Local Greek and Bulgarian troops loyal to the empire.
sources: Skylitzes Continuatus; en.wikipedia Uprising of Georgi Voiteh
note: Petrilo had taken Ohrid and Devol before he was beaten here.

name: Zompos Bridge
place: the Zompos bridge over the Sangarios
commanders_b: the Caesar John Doukas (captured), Nikephoros Botaneiates, Andronikos Doukas (captured)
roman_force: An army raised in the capital and the western provinces under the Caesar, with Frankish mercenaries under Papas who stood by the emperor, against Roussel's 3,000 Franks.
greek_note: Regular Roman troops with a Frankish contingent; Botaneiates' eastern rearguard fled.
sources: Attaleiates 23; Bryennios 2.14-16; Psellos, Chronographia 7c
note: Dated 1073 or 1074. Roussel then proclaimed the captured Caesar emperor.

name: Constantinople
borderline: A demonstration and attack on the suburbs rather than a full siege.
roman_force: Rebels: the Macedonian and Thracian regiments of Bryennios' western army. Defenders: the Varangians and the troops in the capital.
greek_note: The rebels were the Macedonian tagmata of the West.
sources: Attaleiates 26; Bryennios 3.11-12
note: John Bryennios burned the suburbs and withdrew.

name: Kalavrye
place: Kalavrye (Yolcati), by the Halmyros river between Herakleia and Selymbria
commanders_b: Nikephoros Bryennios (captured), John Bryennios, Tarchaneiotes Katakalon
roman_force: Alexios' army of 5,500-6,500 (Haldon; 8,000-10,000 Birkenmeier): a few hundred Frankish knights from Italy, the newly raised Athanatoi, 2,000 Chomatenoi from Asia Minor and 2,000 Turkish horse-archers sent by Sulayman. Bryennios' army of about 12,000: 3,000 Macedonians from Thrace and Macedonia, Thessalian cavalry and infantry, the Hetaireia, Frankish mercenaries and an allied Pecheneg detachment.
greek_note: Bryennios the Younger names the western tagmata (Greek-speaking) on the rebel side and Franks, Turks and new native units on Alexios' side.
sources: Bryennios 4.4-15; Anna Komnene, Alexiad 1.4-6; Attaleiates 33; en.wikipedia Battle of Kalavrye
note: The Pechenegs on Bryennios' side turned to plunder his camp.

name: Vardar
roman_force: Alexios' small army of Chomatenoi, Franks and Turks against Basilakes' army from Dyrrhachium of Romans, Franks and Bulgarians; Alexios won by a night attack on Basilakes' camp.
greek_note: Anna and Bryennios list Roman, Frankish and Bulgarian troops for Basilakes and native and Turkish troops for Alexios.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 1.7-9; Bryennios 4.18-27; Attaleiates 35
note: Basilakes fled to Thessalonica and was handed over.

name: Dyrrhachium (siege)
roman_force: The garrison of Dyrrhachium under George Palaiologos, with the Venetian fleet at sea (victorious over the Norman fleet in July 1081).
greek_note: The garrison was Roman troops with local Albanian-Illyrian and Amalfitan-Venetian townsmen.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 3.12, 4.1-8, 5.1; William of Apulia 4; Malaterra 3.24-27; en.wikipedia Battle of Dyrrhachium (1081)
note: The city was betrayed to the Normans in February 1082. The Venetian naval victory off the city is not entered separately: no Roman ships are said to have fought.

name: Dyrrhachium
commanders_b: Alexios I Komnenos, Nabites (Varangians), Gregory Pakourianos, Nikephoros Melissenos, Constantine Bodin (did not engage)
roman_force: Perhaps 20,000 (modern estimate): the Varangian Guard (largely English), the Exkoubitoi and Vestiaritai, Macedonian and Thessalian units, the Paulician 'Manichaeans' under Xantas and Kouleon, the Frankish guard of Humbertopoulos, Turkish horse sent by Sulayman, and the Serbs of Bodin, who stood aside.
greek_note: Anna names native Macedonian and Thessalian units and the old tagmata beside the Varangians, Paulicians, Turks and Franks.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 4.4-7; William of Apulia 4; Malaterra 3.27; Orderic Vitalis 7; en.wikipedia Battle of Dyrrhachium (1081)
note: The Varangians broke the Norman right but were cut off and destroyed at a church.

name: Ioannina
roman_force: The new army Alexios raised after Dyrrhachium from the survivors, new native recruits, Paulician and Turkish troops, with light wagons fitted with poles to break the Norman charge.
greek_note: After the loss of the Varangians the army was rebuilt mainly from native recruits of the Balkan provinces, with Turkish mercenaries.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 5.4; William of Apulia 5
note: Bohemond avoided the wagons and attacked the flanks; the Roman infantry suffered heavily.

name: Arta
roman_force: The same rebuilt field army as at Ioannina; Alexios scattered caltrops before his centre, but Bohemond again attacked the wings.
greek_note: Native recruits of the Balkan provinces with Turkish and Paulician contingents.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 5.4; en.wikipedia, the article on the Norman wars of the empire
note: Bohemond had besieged Arta; the siege was lifted when Alexios approached.

name: Larissa
place: Larissa and the plain around it
commanders_a: Alexios I Komnenos, Nikephoros Melissenos, Basil Kourtikios, Leo Kephalas (defender)
roman_force: The garrison of Larissa under Leo Kephalas, and a relief army of native troops and 7,000 Turks sent by Sulayman under Kamyres; Alexios drew Bohemond off with a feigned flight of his main body under the imperial standards and struck the Norman camp.
greek_note: Anna describes a native army with a large Seljuk contingent.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 5.5-7; en.wikipedia, the article on the Norman wars of the empire
note: One entry for the six-month siege and the relief battle (spring or July 1083); the Normans fell back to Trikala and Kastoria.

name: Kastoria
roman_force: Alexios' field army with siege engines; troops were ferried across the lake to attack the town from behind.
greek_note: Mainly native troops of the Balkan provinces.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 6.1
note: The Norman garrison surrendered after the assault.

name: Corfu (sea)
commanders_b: the Venetian commanders; the Roman squadron
borderline: Three engagements; the Romans were a secondary ally of the Venetians.
roman_force: A Roman squadron fighting beside the Venetian fleet; no numbers.
greek_note: The Roman ships were crewed from the Aegean naval themes; the Venetians were the main force.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 6.5; William of Apulia 5; Dandolo
note: The Venetians and Romans won the first two actions; Guiscard destroyed their fleet in the third.

name: Beliatoba
place: Beliatoba, in the region of Philippopolis
commanders_a: Pecheneg chiefs, with the Paulician rebel Traulos
borderline: Site unidentified.
roman_force: The western field army under the domestic of the West, Gregory Pakourianos.
greek_note: The army of the West, with Pakourianos' Georgian and Armenian retainers.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 6.14

name: Dristra
commanders_b: Alexios I Komnenos, George Palaiologos, Nikephoros Melissenos
roman_force: Alexios' field army, including the new regiment of Archontopouloi (sons of fallen officers, 300 of whom were killed), the Varangians and Frankish mercenaries.
greek_note: Anna stresses the native Archontopouloi beside the foreign guards.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 7.3; en.wikipedia Battle of Dristra
note: The emperor barely escaped.

name: Oinousses Islands
place: off the Oinousses islands, between Chios and the Anatolian coast
roman_force: An imperial fleet under Niketas Kastamonites; no numbers.
greek_note: The imperial fleet was manned in the capital and the Aegean islands.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 7.8; en.wikipedia Tzachas
note: Tzachas' emirate of Smyrna is counted under 'Turkish beyliks'.

name: Chios
roman_force: A fleet and landing force under Dalassenos, with troops under Opos; no numbers.
greek_note: The fleet and marines were raised in the Aegean themes.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 7.8; en.wikipedia Tzachas
note: A siege of the citadel with a fight against Tzachas' relieving fleet; the main arm was the landing force.

name: Choirobakchoi
borderline: A small action; named only from its site.
roman_force: A small force of the emperor's household troops and the men he could gather in the capital.
greek_note: Troops of the capital and the imperial household.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 8.1-2

name: Levounion
place: the hill of Levounion near the mouth of the Hebros, by Ainos
commanders_a: Alexios I Komnenos, George Palaiologos, Constantine Dalassenos, Constantine Humbertopoulos, Monastras, Ouzas, Tugorkhan and Boniak (Cumans)
roman_force: About 13,000 Roman troops (infantry in the centre, cavalry wings under Alexios, George Palaiologos and Constantine Dalassenos), about 5,000 volunteers from the mountains (Vlachs and Bulgarians), 500 Flemish knights sent by Robert of Flanders and Latin horse under Humbertopoulos, and Turkic units under Monastras and Ouzas; the Cuman host (10,000-40,000) fought beside them as a separate allied army.
greek_note: Anna names the native army, the hill volunteers and the Flemings; the Cumans were a separate allied army.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 8.4-6; en.wikipedia Battle of Levounion
note: The Pechenegs were annihilated as a people; the survivors were settled as a tagma in Moglena.

name: Mytilene
roman_force: John Doukas' land army and Dalassenos' fleet; no numbers.
greek_note: The fleet and army of the Aegean command.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 9.1-3; en.wikipedia Tzachas
note: After three months Tzachas gave up the fortress; Dalassenos then attacked and nearly destroyed his fleet.

name: Adrianople
borderline: A defended siege of 48 days; not a standard named battle.
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Adrianople under Bryennios.
greek_note: A Thracian town garrison.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 10.3-4
note: The Cuman invasion ended with the capture of the pretender and a Roman victory near Taurokomos.

name: Nis
roman_force: The garrison of Nis under Niketas, with Pecheneg and other mercenaries.
greek_note: A Balkan frontier garrison of Roman troops and Turkic mercenaries.
sources: Albert of Aachen 1.10-12; en.wikipedia People's Crusade
note: The fighting broke out after Germans burned mills; the crusaders lost heavily and their baggage.

name: Constantinople
place: before the walls of Constantinople, by Blachernai
borderline: A clash on Holy Thursday rather than a named battle.
roman_force: Archers on the walls under Bryennios and a sortie of household troops.
greek_note: The defenders were the imperial household troops and garrison.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 10.9; Albert of Aachen 2.12-14
note: Godfrey took the oath soon after.

name: Rodosto
commanders_b: the army of Raymond IV of Toulouse
borderline: A clash with Raymond's Provencal army while he was in the capital; minor.
roman_force: Imperial troops of Thrace with Pecheneg mercenaries.
greek_note: Thracian regulars and Pecheneg horse.
sources: Raymond of Aguilers 2; Gesta Francorum 2

name: Nicaea (siege)
commanders_a: Godfrey of Bouillon, Bohemond, Raymond of Toulouse, Adhemar of Le Puy; Tatikios, Manuel Boutoumites
commanders_b: Kilij Arslan I (relief army); the Turkish garrison
roman_force: About 2,000 peltasts under Tatikios beside the crusaders, and boats hauled overland to Lake Askania under Manuel Boutoumites, who negotiated the surrender.
greek_note: Tatikios' peltasts were native light infantry; Turcopoles served with him.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 11.1-2; Gesta Francorum 2; en.wikipedia Siege of Nicaea
note: Kilij Arslan's relief army was beaten off on 16 or 21 May; the city surrendered to the Romans, not the crusaders.

name: Dorylaeum
commanders_a: Bohemond, Godfrey of Bouillon, Raymond of Toulouse, Adhemar; Tatikios
borderline: Tatikios' Roman detachment marched with the vanguard (Bohemond's division) that bore the Turkish attack, but its part in the fighting is not recorded.
roman_force: Tatikios' small Roman detachment of guides and soldiers marching with the crusader army.
greek_note: Tatikios' men were imperial troops, some of them Turcopoles.
sources: Gesta Francorum 3; Fulcher of Chartres 1.11; Anna Komnene, Alexiad 11.3; en.wikipedia Siege of Nicaea

name: Antioch (siege)
commanders_a: Bohemond, Raymond of Toulouse, Godfrey of Bouillon, Adhemar; Tatikios (to February 1098)
borderline: Tatikios left in February 1098; the Romans took no part in the capture (3 June) or the defeat of Kerbogha (28 June).
roman_force: Tatikios' Roman detachment, present for the first four months of the siege.
greek_note: Tatikios' small corps of imperial soldiers and Turcopoles.
sources: Gesta Francorum 5-9; Raymond of Aguilers; Anna Komnene, Alexiad 11.4-6
note: Alexios turned back at Philomelion in June 1098 without fighting.

name: Ephesus
war: Campaign of John Doukas in western Asia Minor
borderline: Known from Anna only; part of a campaign of recovery rather than a famous battle.
roman_force: John Doukas' army and fleet, which took Smyrna and then routed the Turks near Ephesus.
greek_note: An army of the Aegean and western Anatolian commands.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 11.5
note: The same campaign recovered Sardis, Philadelphia, Laodicea and Choma and ended with a victory at Polybotos.

name: Rhodes (sea)
borderline: Known from Anna; the Pisan crusade fleet is counted as Crusaders.
roman_force: An imperial fleet whose ships carried bronze fire-throwing heads at the prows; Landulph was a Latin in imperial service.
greek_note: The imperial fleet was crewed from the Aegean themes.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 11.10

name: Mersivan
commanders_a: Kilij Arslan I, Danishmend Gazi, Ridwan of Aleppo
commanders_b: Raymond of Toulouse, Stephen of Blois, Stephen of Burgundy, Conrad; Tzitas (Roman contingent)
borderline: The Roman contingent was small and left the field.
roman_force: A Roman contingent under Tzitas with Pecheneg horse, who deserted during the battle.
greek_note: The sources describe the imperial contingent as Pechenegs under a Roman officer.
sources: Albert of Aachen 8.18-23; Anna Komnene, Alexiad 11.8; en.wikipedia Battle of Mersivan
note: About four-fifths of the crusader army was lost.

name: Dyrrhachium (siege)
commanders_a: Alexios I Komnenos, Alexios Komnenos (doux of Dyrrhachium), Isaac Kontostephanos, Marianos Maurokatakalon (fleet)
roman_force: The garrison of Dyrrhachium, the fleet that cut Bohemond off from Italy, and Alexios' field army of native troops with Turkish, Pecheneg and Cuman mercenaries holding the passes.
greek_note: Alexios' later armies combined native regiments and Turkic mercenaries.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 12.9, 13.2-12; en.wikipedia List of battles of the Roman Empire (East)
note: Bohemond's army, starving and blockaded, accepted the Treaty of Devol.

name: Nicaea
place: Nicaea and the country west of it toward Poimanenon
commanders_b: Turkish emirs sent by the sultan Malik Shah
roman_force: The garrison of Nicaea and Alexios' field army, which caught the raiders on their return.
greek_note: Native regiments with Turkic mercenaries.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 14.5; en.wikipedia List of battles of the Roman Empire (East)
note: The Turks failed to take Nicaea and were defeated as they withdrew with their plunder.

name: Philomelion
roman_force: Alexios' field army in his new marching formation (the parataxis), infantry and archers enclosing the baggage and refugees, with cavalry on the wings.
greek_note: The army of Alexios' last years was largely native recruits drilled by the emperor, with mercenaries.
sources: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 15.4-6; en.wikipedia Battle of Philomelion
note: Sometimes dated 1117. Malik Shah sued for peace.

name: Laodicea
borderline: A capture with fighting; not a standard named battle.
roman_force: John II's field army; no units are named.
greek_note: The Komnenian field army was native regiments plus mercenaries.
sources: Choniates, Historia (John II); Kinnamos 1.2

name: Sozopolis
borderline: A capture by ruse with fighting outside the walls.
roman_force: John II's army; a cavalry detachment under Paktiarios drew the garrison out by a feigned flight.
greek_note: Komnenian native and mercenary cavalry.
sources: Choniates, Historia (John II); Kinnamos 1.2

name: Beroia
roman_force: The field army brought over from Asia Minor; the Varangian Guard, axe-bearing and largely English, broke the Pecheneg wagon laager.
greek_note: Choniates and Kinnamos stress the Varangians; the rest was native and mercenary horse.
sources: Choniates, Historia (John II); Kinnamos 1.3; en.wikipedia Battle of Beroia
note: Sometimes dated 1121. The emperor instituted a feast of the Pechenegs to mark the victory.

name: Corfu (siege)
borderline: A siege known mainly from Venetian sources; scale of fighting uncertain.
roman_force: The garrison of the citadel of Corfu; no numbers.
greek_note: An island garrison of the western themes.
sources: Kinnamos 6.10; Andrea Dandolo, Chronicle; Historia ducum Veneticorum
note: The doge raised the siege and sailed to the Holy Land; Venetian raids on Rhodes, Chios, Samos and Kefalonia followed.

name: Haram
place: Haram (Banatska Palanka), at the confluence of the Karas and the Danube
commanders_b: Setephel (Stephen II was ill and absent)
roman_force: John II's field army with Lombard ('Ligurian') mercenary knights sent to threaten an upstream crossing, Turkish horse-archers, and a Danube flotilla with bolt-throwers and incendiaries.
greek_note: Choniates and Kinnamos describe the native army with Lombard and Turkish contingents and the river fleet.
sources: Choniates, Historia (John II); Kinnamos 1.4; en.wikipedia Battle of Haram
note: Date disputed (1128; or 1125-26, or 1127-29); the Hungarians had sacked Belgrade, Branicevo and Nis in 1127.

name: Frangochorion
borderline: A siege and occupation of the district; many fleeing Hungarians died when a bridge over the Karas collapsed.
roman_force: John II's army after Haram, with Lombard and Turkish mercenaries.
greek_note: The same Komnenian field army as at Haram.
sources: Kinnamos 1.4; Choniates, Historia (John II); en.wikipedia, the article on the Hungarian war of 1127-1129

name: Branicevo
commanders_a: Stephen II, with Bohemian troops under Vaclav of Olomouc
roman_force: The garrison of Branicevo under Kourtikios.
greek_note: A Danube frontier garrison.
sources: Kinnamos 1.4; Choniates, Historia (John II); en.wikipedia, the article on the Hungarian war of 1127-1129
note: The fort was stormed and destroyed; John II rebuilt it and blamed Kourtikios.

name: Zdrelo
place: the Zdrelo gorge of the Mlava
borderline: A rearguard defeat recorded mainly by Kinnamos and the Hungarian chronicles.
roman_force: The rearguard of John II's army withdrawing up the Mlava valley.
greek_note: Part of the Komnenian field army.
sources: Kinnamos 1.4; en.wikipedia, the article on the Hungarian war of 1127-1129
note: Peace followed in October 1129 (Makk), with Branicevo, Belgrade and Zemun left to the empire.

name: Kastamon
commanders_b: the Danishmend garrison of Gazi Gumushtigin
borderline: A capture celebrated with a triumph; scale of fighting not recorded.
roman_force: John II's field army with siege engines.
greek_note: Native regiments with mercenaries.
sources: Choniates, Historia (John II); Kinnamos 1.5; en.wikipedia John II Komnenos
note: The Turks retook Kastamon soon after and John recaptured it in 1134-35.

name: Gangra
borderline: A siege ending in surrender after a winter blockade and bombardment.
roman_force: John II's army with siege engines; no units named.
greek_note: Native regiments and mercenaries of the Komnenian army.
sources: Choniates, Historia (John II); Kinnamos 1.5
note: Gangra was lost again soon after.

name: Antioch
war: Cilician and Syrian campaigns of John II
commanders_b: Raymond of Poitiers, prince of Antioch
borderline: A short siege with bombardment ending in Raymond's submission.
roman_force: John II's expeditionary army with siege engines.
greek_note: Native regiments with Pecheneg and Varangian contingents.
sources: Kinnamos 1.8; Choniates, Historia (John II); William of Tyre 14.30
note: The Principality of Antioch is counted under 'Crusaders'.

name: Anazarbus
war: Cilician and Syrian campaigns of John II
commanders_b: the garrison of Leo I, Rubenid lord of Cilicia
roman_force: John II's expeditionary army with siege engines; the sources mention Macedonian and Pecheneg contingents in this campaign.
greek_note: The army of the 1137-38 expedition combined native regiments (Macedonians) with Pechenegs, Varangians and Latins.
sources: Choniates, Historia (John II); Kinnamos 1.7; Gregory the Priest
note: Taken after a siege of about 37 days; Tarsus, Adana and Mopsuestia fell earlier in the campaign.

name: Shaizar (siege)
war: Cilician and Syrian campaigns of John II
commanders_a: John II Komnenos, Raymond of Poitiers, Joscelin II of Edessa
roman_force: John II's army with a siege train of trebuchets, drawn up in three divisions by nation: Macedonians (native Romans), 'Kelts' (Normans and other Franks) and Pechenegs; the emperor led the assaults while the Latin princes sat dicing.
greek_note: The sources name a Macedonian (native) division beside the Frankish and Pecheneg divisions.
sources: Kinnamos 1.8; Choniates, Historia (John II); Usama ibn Munqidh, Kitab al-Itibar; Ibn al-Qalanisi; en.wikipedia Siege of Shaizar
note: The lower town fell but not the citadel; the emir paid an indemnity and became tributary, so the result is entered as a draw rather than a defender's win.

name: Buza'a
war: Cilician and Syrian campaigns of John II
commanders_a: John II Komnenos, Raymond of Poitiers, Joscelin II of Edessa
borderline: A seven-day siege ending in capitulation.
roman_force: John II's expeditionary army with siege engines, with the Antiochene and Edessene allies.
greek_note: Native regiments with Pecheneg and Varangian contingents.
sources: Kinnamos 1.8; Ibn al-Qalanisi; Kemal ad-Din
note: Buza'a belonged to Zengi's Aleppo.

name: Neocaesarea (siege)
commanders_b: John II Komnenos, Manuel Komnenos, John Komnenos (deserted to the Turks)
roman_force: John II's field army with Latin heavy cavalry; it lost many horses in the winter.
greek_note: Native regiments with Latin and Turkic mercenaries.
sources: Kinnamos 1.6; Choniates, Historia (John II)
note: The young Manuel distinguished himself in a rescue; the siege was abandoned.

name: Antioch
war: War with the Principality of Antioch
place: the coast and country of Antioch
commanders_a: John and Andronikos Kontostephanos, Prosouch, Demetrios Branas (fleet)
borderline: A punitive campaign with fighting on land and sea, not a single named battle.
roman_force: An army under the Kontostephanos brothers and Prosouch with a fleet under Demetrios Branas, which retook the Cilician forts, ravaged the land round Antioch and burned Raymond's ships.
greek_note: Native regiments and fleet crews with Turkish troops of Prosouch.
sources: Kinnamos 2.3; en.wikipedia Manuel I Komnenos
note: Raymond came to Constantinople and submitted in 1145.

name: Akroinon
roman_force: Manuel's field army on its march to Konya; no units named.
greek_note: Native regiments with Latin and Turkic mercenaries.
sources: Kinnamos 2.5-7; Choniates, Historia (Manuel I); en.wikipedia Manuel I Komnenos
note: Manuel then destroyed Philomelion, was nearly trapped in a charge near Konya, held off an attack on his camp at Tzibrelitzemani and withdrew without besieging Konya.

name: Constantinople
commanders_b: a division of Conrad III's German army (Conrad not present)
roman_force: A smaller imperial force drawn up with infantry in front, heavy cataphracts behind them, lighter koursores next and Cuman, Turkish and Roman archers in the rear.
greek_note: Kinnamos describes Roman infantry and cataphracts with Cuman and Turkish archers.
sources: Kinnamos 2.15; en.wikipedia Battle of Constantinople (1147)
note: The Germans lost heavily and agreed to be ferried across the Bosporus.

name: Corfu (siege)
commanders_a: Manuel I Komnenos, Stephen Kontostephanos (killed), John Axouch
commanders_b: the Sicilian garrison of Roger II
roman_force: Manuel's army and a large fleet (Kinnamos and Choniates give hundreds of ships), with the Venetian fleet as allies; the assaults by ladder failed and the garrison surrendered after a long blockade.
greek_note: The fleet and much of the army were raised in the Aegean and Balkan provinces.
sources: Kinnamos 2.19, 3.2; Choniates, Historia (Manuel I) 2
note: Roger II had seized Corfu in 1147; the fleet took part in the siege, but the main arm was the land assault.

name: Tara
commanders_a: Manuel I Komnenos, John Kantakouzenos (wounded), John Doukas Komnenos
commanders_b: Uros II, grand zupan of Raska; Bagyon (Bakchinus), Hungarian commander (captured)
roman_force: Manuel's field army, native regiments with Latin and Turkic mercenaries; the emperor fought Bakchinus hand to hand.
greek_note: The Komnenian field army of native and mercenary troops.
sources: Kinnamos 3.7-8; Choniates, Historia (Manuel I); en.wikipedia Battle of Tara
note: The exact site on the Tara (or Drina) is uncertain. Uros II submitted.

name: Zemun
commanders_a: Theodore Vatatzes (siege), Manuel I Komnenos (raiding Srem)
commanders_b: the Hungarian garrison of Geza II
roman_force: Part of Manuel's field army with siege engines under Theodore Vatatzes, while the emperor raided Srem.
greek_note: Native regiments with mercenaries.
sources: Kinnamos 3.11; en.wikipedia, the article on the Hungarian war of 1149-1155
note: Some date it to mid-1152. Over 10,000 people were carried off from Srem.

name: Mopsuestia
commanders_a: Thoros II, Rubenid lord of Cilicia
borderline: A sally of Thoros routed the besieging army; not a standard named battle.
roman_force: The imperial army of Cilicia under Andronikos; no units named.
greek_note: The Cilician command mixed Roman regulars with local Greek and Armenian troops.
sources: Kinnamos 4.17; Gregory the Priest
note: Rubenid Cilicia is counted under 'Armenia'.

name: Branicevo (siege)
commanders_a: the garrison of Branicevo (Manuel I marching to relieve it)
commanders_b: Geza II, Ban Boric of Bosnia
roman_force: The garrison of Branicevo; Manuel's relief army was delayed at Pelagonia.
greek_note: A Danube frontier garrison.
sources: Kinnamos 3.18-19; en.wikipedia Siege of Branicevo
note: Geza, with Bohemian, Saxon and Bosnian troops and Cuman or Pecheneg horse, lifted the siege when Andronikos Komnenos' plot was discovered.

name: Belgrade
place: on the road to Belgrade (near Svilajnac or Paracin by some accounts)
borderline: Site uncertain.
roman_force: A pursuing force under Basil Tzintziloukes, with a Hungarian exile contingent under Stephen, son of Geza, which was beaten first.
greek_note: Roman cavalry with a Hungarian exile unit.
sources: Kinnamos 3.19; en.wikipedia Siege of Branicevo
note: Peace was made on the Danube in 1155 on the status quo.

name: Bari
war: Norman war of 1147-1158 (Italian expedition of Manuel I)
commanders_a: Michael Palaiologos, John Doukas, Robert of Loritello
commanders_b: the Sicilian garrison of William I
roman_force: A small Roman force sent with money, Italian mercenaries hired on the spot and the rebel barons of Robert of Loritello; the citizens rose and the citadel was stormed.
greek_note: Kinnamos says the Romans were few and relied on hired Italians and rebel Norman barons.
sources: Kinnamos 4.1-5; Romuald of Salerno; Hugo Falcandus
note: Trani, Giovinazzo and other towns followed.

name: Andria
war: Norman war of 1147-1158 (Italian expedition of Manuel I)
roman_force: John Doukas' small Roman force with hired Italians, Pechenegs and the knights of the rebel barons.
greek_note: Kinnamos says the Roman element was small and the army mostly hired or rebel Latins.
sources: Kinnamos 4.6-7; Romuald of Salerno
note: Andria surrendered afterwards.

name: Brindisi
war: Norman war of 1147-1158 (Italian expedition of Manuel I)
roman_force: The Roman force besieging the citadel of Brindisi with a fleet in the harbour; its hired Italian mercenaries deserted when their pay was refused, leaving a few hundred Roman soldiers and the ships.
greek_note: After the mercenaries left, the remaining force was the Roman contingent and fleet crews.
sources: Kinnamos 4.13; Choniates, Historia (Manuel I) 2; Romuald of Salerno; en.wikipedia, the article on the Norman wars of the empire
note: A combined land and sea defeat that ended the Roman venture in Italy.

name: Harim
commanders_b: Bohemond III of Antioch, Raymond III of Tripoli, Joscelin III, Hugh VIII of Lusignan; Konstantinos Kalamanos (doux of Cilicia); Thoros II
borderline: The Romans were a secondary allied contingent.
roman_force: The troops of the doux of Cilicia, Konstantinos Kalamanos, who was captured; the whole Christian army was about 600 knights and 12,000 foot.
greek_note: The Cilician command held imperial troops with local Greek and Armenian soldiers.
sources: William of Tyre 19.9; Michael the Syrian; Ibn al-Athir
note: Ibn al-Athir claims 10,000 Christian dead; Bohemond III, Raymond III and Kalamanos were imprisoned at Aleppo.

name: Zemun (siege)
commanders_b: the Hungarian garrison of Stephen III
roman_force: Manuel's field army and Danube flotilla with siege engines; no numbers.
greek_note: Native regiments with Latin and Turkic mercenaries.
sources: Kinnamos 5.8; Choniates, Historia (Manuel I) 4
note: Stormed after a hard siege; Sirmium and Dalmatia were then occupied.

name: Sirmium
place: near Sirmium (Sremska Mitrovica), between the Sava and the Danube
commanders_a: Andronikos Kontostephanos, Andronikos Lapardas, Joseph Bryennios
roman_force: About 15,000, two-thirds native and one-third foreign: Turkish and Cuman horse-archers in the screen; the Varangians, the Hetaireia, the imperial oikeioi, Lombard lancers and 500 armoured Serbian infantry in the centre; native taxiarchies under the Branas brothers, Tatikios Aspietes and Kogh Vasil on the left; elite Roman units, German mercenaries and Turks on the right; native infantry and archers in reserve.
greek_note: Choniates' order of battle shows native Roman regiments making up about two-thirds of the army.
sources: Choniates, Historia (Manuel I) 5; Kinnamos 6.7; en.wikipedia Battle of Sirmium
note: A Danube flotilla cut down the fleeing Hungarians; Hungary ceded Srem, Bosnia, Dalmatia and Croatia south of the Krka.

name: Pantino
place: Pantino, on the Sitnica near Zvecan
commanders_b: Tihomir (drowned in the Sitnica), Stracimir, Miroslav
borderline: A Serbian dynastic war in which the Romans were the allies of one side.
roman_force: An imperial army assembled at Skopje to restore Tihomir (its commander is not named), with Greeks, Franks and Turks among the foreigners serving on Tihomir's side.
greek_note: The Lives of Nemanja describe the imperial army as Greeks with Frankish and Turkish soldiers.
sources: Stefan Nemanjic, Life of Simeon; Domentijan; en.wikipedia Battle of Pantino
note: Dated 1166, 1167 or 1168. Nemanja was then recognised as ruler of all Serbia.

name: Damietta (siege)
commanders_b: Andronikos Kontostephanos (megas doux), Amalric I of Jerusalem
roman_force: A fleet of about 230 ships (150 galleys, 60 horse transports, 10-20 large dromons) with an army aboard under Kontostephanos, besieging the city beside Amalric's army.
greek_note: Choniates describes the fleet and its marines, raised in the Aegean provinces; the army included Latin and Turkic mercenaries.
sources: Choniates, Historia (Manuel I) 5; Kinnamos 6.9; William of Tyre 20.15-17
note: The allies quarrelled and the siege was given up; much of the Roman fleet was lost in storms on the way home.

name: Myriokephalon
place: the Tzivritze pass near the fort of Myriokephalon, west of Konya (site debated)
commanders_b: Manuel I Komnenos, Andronikos Kontostephanos, Baldwin of Antioch (killed), John Kantakouzenos (killed), Theodore Mavrozomes, Andronikos Lapardas, Constantine Makrodoukas; Ampud and Leustach Ratot (Hungarians)
roman_force: 25,000-40,000 (Haldon 25,000-30,000; Birkenmeier about 35,000, of whom about 25,000 Romans) with a long siege train for Konya: the eastern and western tagmata in mixed divisions, a right wing of Antiochenes and other Westerners under Baldwin, Hungarians sent by Bela III and Serbian tributary troops.
greek_note: The eastern and western tagmata formed the main divisions; modern estimates make native Romans about 25,000 of some 35,000.
sources: Choniates, Historia (Manuel I) 6; Manuel I's letter to Henry II (in Roger of Hoveden); Michael the Syrian; en.wikipedia Battle of Myriokephalon
note: The army was ambushed in the pass; Manuel extracted a truce and the army survived, but the campaign against Konya was abandoned.

name: Neocaesarea
commanders_a: the Seljuk commanders of Kilij Arslan II
borderline: Not a standard named battle.
roman_force: A northern army drawn from Paphlagonia and Pontus, sent to support the Danishmend prince Dhu'l-Nun.
greek_note: Raised in the Paphlagonian and Pontic provinces.
sources: Choniates, Historia (Manuel I) 6; Kinnamos 7.1
note: Vatatzes' head was sent to the sultan.

name: Hyelion and Leimocheir
place: the crossings of the Meander at Hyelion and Leimocheir
commanders_a: John Komnenos Vatatzes, Constantine Doukas, Michael Aspietes (killed)
roman_force: An army that marched from Constantinople under John Vatatzes and picked up provincial reinforcements on the way; it split into two corps on either side of the river, with light troops on the heights, against a Turkish army of 20,000-24,000.
greek_note: Troops of the capital and of the western Anatolian provinces.
sources: Choniates, Historia (Manuel I) 6; en.wikipedia Battle of Hyelion and Leimocheir
note: The Turkish raiding army was almost destroyed.

name: Charax
place: Charax (Hereke), on the Gulf of Nicomedia
borderline: A minor engagement; the Romans withdrew and the Turks drove off the flocks.
roman_force: A Roman army of Bithynia; no units named.
greek_note: Local Bithynian forces.
sources: Choniates, Historia (Manuel I) 7

name: Claudiopolis
borderline: A relieved siege; the Turks withdrew on Manuel's approach.
roman_force: The garrison of Claudiopolis and a relief force led by Manuel in person by forced marches.
greek_note: Garrison and relief troops of the capital and Bithynia.
sources: Choniates, Historia (Manuel I) 7

name: Philadelphia
war: Revolt of John Komnenos Vatatzes against Andronikos I
commanders_a: John Komnenos Vatatzes, with his sons Manuel and Alexios
borderline: No battle article or list entry; an engagement known from Choniates.
roman_force: Both armies were imperial troops: the rebels had the substantial army John Komnenos Vatatzes raised in the Thrakesion region, which he arrayed from a litter, being mortally ill; Andronikos I sent a large force under Andronikos Lapardas (Choniates). No numbers are given.
greek_note: Both armies were raised in the Thrakesion and neighbouring Anatolian districts, a Greek-speaking region, with the usual foreign mercenaries.
sources: Choniates, Historia (reign of Andronikos I); en.wikipedia John Komnenos Vatatzes
note: Lapardas's army was routed and pursued; Vatatzes died on 16 May 1182 and the revolt collapsed, his sons being captured and blinded.

name: Nicaea (siege)
faction_b: Rebels of Nicaea (Isaac Angelos, Theodore Kantakouzenos)
borderline: Siege narrated by Choniates; no separate article or list entry.
roman_force: Andronikos I led the imperial field army with siege engines (on one of which he placed Euphrosyne Kastamonitissa, Isaac Angelos's mother, as a shield); the city was defended by its citizens and the rebels' followers (Choniates).
greek_note: Imperial army of the Angelan-Komnenian type, largely native troops of Anatolia and the Balkans, against the Greek townsmen of Nicaea.
sources: Choniates, Historia (Andronikos I); en.wikipedia Andronikos I Komnenos
note: Theodore Kantakouzenos was killed in a sortie; the city then surrendered on terms and Isaac Angelos was spared.

name: Prusa (siege)
borderline: Siege narrated by Choniates; no separate article or list entry.
roman_force: Andronikos I's field army, which went on from Nicaea and took Prusa by storm; the defenders were the townsmen and the rebels' followers (Choniates).
greek_note: Native imperial troops against Greek townsmen of Bithynia.
sources: Choniates, Historia (Andronikos I); en.wikipedia Andronikos I Komnenos
note: Choniates reports harsh reprisals on the defenders after the city fell.

name: Thessalonica (siege)
commanders_a: Count Baldwin, Richard of Acerra, Tancred of Lecce
commanders_b: David Komnenos (governor), John Maurozomes, Theodore Choumnos
roman_force: The garrison under the governor David Komnenos with Alan and Georgian mercenaries and the armed citizens; relief forces under John Maurozomes and Theodore Choumnos were sent by Andronikos I (Eustathios of Thessalonica; Choniates).
greek_note: Eustathios describes the defence by the Greek citizens and garrison, with Alan and Georgian mercenaries.
sources: Eustathios of Thessalonica, The Capture of Thessaloniki; Choniates; en.wikipedia Sack of Thessalonica (1185)
note: The Normans undermined the eastern wall and stormed the city, which was sacked; 7,000-8,000 dead are reported. The infobox figure of 80,000 men and 200 ships for the Norman army is not reliable.

name: Demetritzes
place: Demetritzes, on the Strymon north-west of Serres
roman_force: The field army of Alexios Branas, reinforced by Anatolian volunteers whom Isaac II armed and paid (4,000 lb of gold were sent for pay and donative), with Alan troops (Choniates).
greek_note: Choniates names the Anatolian volunteers sent by Isaac II and Alan mercenaries; the core was the native Balkan field army.
sources: Choniates, Historia (Isaac II); en.wikipedia Battle of Demetritzes
note: More than 4,000 Norman prisoners were sent to Constantinople; Thessalonica was abandoned by the Normans, and Dyrrhachium was recovered in 1186.

name: Mosynopolis
borderline: Prelude to Demetritzes, described in its article; no separate article.
roman_force: Alexios Branas's field army, reinforced by Anatolian volunteers armed and paid by Isaac II, routed the Norman advance guard, defeated it outside the walls and stormed the town (Choniates).
greek_note: The reinforcements were Anatolian volunteers paid by Isaac II; Alan troops also served in this army.
sources: Choniates, Historia (Isaac II); en.wikipedia Battle of Demetritzes

name: Cyprus
war: Revolt of Isaac Komnenos of Cyprus
commanders_a: Isaac Komnenos, Margaritus of Brindisi (Sicilian admiral)
borderline: Isaac Komnenos was a self-proclaimed emperor ruling a breakaway Roman province; the engagement has no name in the lists.
roman_force: Isaac II sent 70 ships with an expeditionary army under John Kontostephanos and Alexios Komnenos; after the troops landed, Margaritus of Brindisi seized the fleet and the landed force was defeated by Isaac Komnenos's Cypriot troops (Choniates).
greek_note: The imperial expedition came from Constantinople; Isaac Komnenos's troops were Cypriot Greeks and Armenians.
sources: Choniates, Historia (Isaac II); en.wikipedia Isaac Komnenos of Cyprus
note: Combined action: the Sicilian fleet took the ships while the troops ashore were defeated; the commanders were taken to Sicily.

name: Constantinople
place: Before the land walls of Constantinople
commanders_a: Isaac II Angelos, Conrad of Montferrat
roman_force: Isaac II's troops in the capital, led out by Conrad of Montferrat with Latin knights and heavy infantry, against the large field army that Branas had been given for the war against the Vlachs and Bulgarians and that proclaimed him at Adrianople (Choniates).
greek_note: Branas's army was the Balkan field army, recruited mainly in Thrace and Macedonia; Isaac's sortie was spearheaded by Conrad's Latins.
sources: Choniates, Historia (Isaac II); en.wikipedia Alexios Branas
note: Branas was unhorsed by Conrad and beheaded; many survivors joined Asen and Peter. Some date the revolt to late 1186.

name: Lovech (siege)
roman_force: Isaac II's field army of the Balkan and Anatolian provinces with foreign mercenaries; the sources give no composition or numbers.
greek_note: The Angelan field army was recruited chiefly in Anatolia, Thrace and Macedonia, with Latin, Alan and Turkic mercenaries.
sources: Choniates, Historia (Isaac II); en.wikipedia Siege of Lovech
note: The siege failed after three months, though an imperial ambush captured Asen's wife; Isaac accepted a truce that tacitly recognised the restored Bulgarian state.

name: Philadelphia (siege)
borderline: Siege known from Choniates only; the extent of the fighting is unclear.
roman_force: Isaac II's field army, led by the emperor in person, against the Philadelphians and the local following of the rebel Theodore Mangaphas, who had taken the imperial title and minted coins; there were skirmishes before the siege (Choniates).
greek_note: Both sides were raised in western Asia Minor and the imperial heartland.
sources: Choniates, Historia (Isaac II); en.wikipedia Theodore Mangaphas
note: Hurried by Frederick Barbarossa's approach, Isaac pardoned Mangaphas, who gave up the imperial insignia and hostages but kept Philadelphia as governor; he held it again as an independent lord in 1204-05.

name: Prousenos
war: Third Crusade (Frederick Barbarossa's march through the empire)
borderline: A clash rather than a named battle; described in the Third Crusade article.
roman_force: About 2,000 horsemen under the protostrator Manuel Kamytzes, lying in wait for the crusaders' supply train, met 5,000 German cavalry and were routed (Choniates, an eyewitness).
greek_note: The cavalry of the western army under Kamytzes was largely native Balkan troops, with mercenaries.
sources: Choniates, Historia (Isaac II); en.wikipedia Third Crusade
note: An earlier skirmish near Philippopolis on 29 August 1189 (about fifty killed) is not entered separately.

name: Tryavna
commanders_b: Isaac II Angelos, John Doukas, Manuel Kamytzes
roman_force: Isaac II's field army marching back from the siege of Tarnovo, with vanguard, main body and a long baggage train; the emperor's guard cut a way out of the rout; the soldiers' pay was in arrears (Choniates).
greek_note: The army was the regular Angelan field army of the Balkan and Anatolian provinces with foreign guards and mercenaries.
sources: Choniates, Historia (Isaac II); en.wikipedia Battle of Tryavna
note: The Bulgarians captured the imperial treasure and the imperial cross. Some date it to 1189 or 1191.

name: Limassol
war: Third Crusade (Richard I's conquest of Cyprus)
borderline: Isaac Komnenos ruled Cyprus as a breakaway self-proclaimed Roman emperor (1184-91), not a recognised successor state; no separate battle article.
roman_force: Isaac Komnenos's Cypriot troops and household guard opposing the English landing on the beach at Limassol; Richard followed with a dawn attack on Isaac's camp near Kolossi (Itinerarium Peregrinorum; Ambroise). No figures.
greek_note: Isaac's army was raised among the Greek population of Cyprus, with Armenians and some Latin mercenaries.
sources: Itinerarium Peregrinorum et Gesta Regis Ricardi 2.31-41; Ambroise, Estoire de la guerre sainte; en.wikipedia Conquest of Cyprus by Richard I
note: Richard landed against opposition and took Limassol; Wikipedia's article gives the conquest only in outline.

name: Tremetousia
war: Third Crusade (Richard I's conquest of Cyprus)
commanders_a: Richard I of England, Guy of Lusignan
borderline: Breakaway regime of Isaac Komnenos (see Limassol); the battle is named in narrative histories of the Third Crusade but has no Wikipedia article.
roman_force: Isaac Komnenos's remaining field force of Cypriot troops, deserted by most of the island's magnates; no figures in the sources.
greek_note: Raised among the Greek population of Cyprus, with Armenians.
sources: Itinerarium Peregrinorum 2.37-40; Ambroise; en.wikipedia Conquest of Cyprus by Richard I
note: Isaac fled and surrendered at the end of May 1191 near Cape Apostolos Andreas; the island passed to the Lusignans in 1192.

name: South Morava
roman_force: A large, well-prepared army that Isaac II gathered at Constantinople (Choniates); no composition is given.
greek_note: The army was raised from the Thracian, Macedonian and Anatolian provinces, as other Angelan field armies were.
sources: Choniates, Historia (Isaac II); en.wikipedia Battle of South Morava (1191)
note: Nemanja withdrew to the mountains; a peace treaty followed, sealed by the marriage of Stefan Nemanjic to Eudokia Angelina.

name: Arcadiopolis
roman_force: The two field armies of the empire: the eastern (Anatolian) army under Alexios Gidos and the western (Balkan) army under the domestic of the Schools Basil Vatatzes (Choniates).
greek_note: Choniates names the armies of the East and the West, recruited in Anatolia and in Thrace and Macedonia.
sources: Choniates, Historia (Isaac II); en.wikipedia Battle of Arcadiopolis (1194)
note: Both armies were destroyed; Gidos fled and Vatatzes fell.

name: Serres
roman_force: A field army under the sebastokrator Isaac Komnenos, son-in-law of Alexios III, whose cavalry was drawn into an ambush and surrounded (Choniates).
greek_note: The western field army of the 1190s was raised in Macedonia and Thrace, with mercenaries.
sources: Choniates, Historia (Alexios III); en.wikipedia Battle of Serres (1196)
note: Asen was murdered by his cousin Ivanko on his return to Tarnovo.

name: Prosek (siege)
place: Prosek (Prosakos), on the Vardar near Demir Kapija
borderline: Chrysos, a Vlach by birth (Choniates), was a rebel imperial commander of Strumica who made himself independent of both the empire and Kaloyan; siege known from Choniates, no article.
roman_force: Alexios III's field army, led by the emperor, besieged the rock fortress for two months with siege engines and failed assaults (Choniates); no figures.
greek_note: Imperial field army of the Balkan and Anatolian provinces.
sources: Choniates, Historia (Alexios III); en.wikipedia Dobromir Chrysos
note: After the failed campaign Alexios III recognised Chrysos's lands between the Strymon and the Vardar, including Strumica and Prosek.

name: Varna (siege)
roman_force: A large garrison that included western (Latin) mercenaries, 'the bravest in the army' (Choniates).
greek_note: The garrison of a Greek coastal city with a Latin mercenary contingent; their proportions are not given.
sources: Choniates, Historia (Alexios III); Akropolites 13; en.wikipedia Siege of Varna (1201)
note: Kaloyan's siege tower bridged the moat and the city was stormed on the third day, Easter Saturday; the defenders were thrown into the moat and buried alive.

name: Constantinople (siege)
place: Constantinople: Galata, the Golden Horn and the walls of Blachernae
commanders_a: Boniface of Montferrat, Baldwin of Flanders, Enrico Dandolo
roman_force: The Varangian Guard (mostly English and Danes), Pisan and other Latin mercenaries, the garrison of the Galata tower and the city troops; Alexios III led about 17 divisions out of the Gate of St Romanos but withdrew without fighting (Villehardouin; Choniates); about 15,000 men and 20 ships are estimated.
greek_note: The walls were held chiefly by the Varangians and Pisans, but the field army and the city militia were Greek.
sources: Villehardouin, Conquest of Constantinople; Robert of Clari; Choniates; en.wikipedia Siege of Constantinople (1203)
note: The crusaders landed at Galata on 5-6 July and took the tower holding the chain; after the assault of 17 July Alexios III fled and Isaac II was restored with Alexios IV as co-emperor (1 August).

name: Athens (siege)
borderline: Fighting between a local magnate and a city of the empire; no article or list entry.
roman_force: The Athenians held the Acropolis under their metropolitan Michael Choniates against Sgouros, lord of Nauplia, Argos and Corinth, who brought siege engines and had earlier raided Attica with pirates from Salamis and Aigina (Michael and Niketas Choniates).
greek_note: Both sides were Greek provincials of central Greece and the Peloponnese.
sources: Niketas Choniates, Historia; Michael Choniates, letters; en.wikipedia Leo Sgouros
note: Sgouros took and burned the lower town but could not take the Acropolis and moved on to Thebes and Thessaly. Some date it to early 1204.

name: Philea
place: Near Philea (Karaburun), on the Black Sea coast north-west of Constantinople
borderline: A skirmish named in crusade histories; no article.
roman_force: Alexios V's mounted force from the capital ambushed Henry of Flanders's foraging column on its way back from Philea and was routed (Villehardouin; Choniates). No figures.
greek_note: Imperial troops from the capital under Alexios V.
sources: Villehardouin 225-228; Robert of Clari; Choniates
note: Alexios V lost the imperial standard and an icon of the Virgin carried before the army.

name: Constantinople (siege)
place: Constantinople: the sea walls of the Golden Horn
commanders_a: Boniface of Montferrat, Baldwin of Flanders, Enrico Dandolo
roman_force: The Varangian Guard, which fought hard on the walls against the Venetians, with other mercenaries, the city garrison and militia under Alexios V; no reliable numbers.
greek_note: The Varangians bore the brunt of the fighting, but most defenders were the Greek troops and citizens of the capital.
sources: Villehardouin; Robert of Clari; Choniates; en.wikipedia Siege of Constantinople (1204)
note: The first assault (9 April) failed; on 12 April the Venetian ships reached the towers and Alexios V fled; the city was sacked for three days and the Latin Empire founded.

name: Poimanenon
place: Poimanenon, south of Cyzicus, near Lake Manyas
commanders_a: Peter of Bracieux, Payen of Orleans
roman_force: The army Theodore Laskaris had gathered from the towns of Bithynia and Mysia in the months after the fall of Constantinople; Villehardouin speaks only of great numbers of Greeks.
greek_note: The first Nicaean army was raised among the Greek population of north-western Asia Minor.
sources: Villehardouin 310-311; Choniates; en.wikipedia Theodore I Laskaris
note: After the victory the Latins took most of the Bithynian forts, though not Prusa.

name: Adramyttion
commanders_a: Henry of Flanders, Thierry de Loos
roman_force: A large army that Theodore Laskaris gathered around Nicaea and sent under his brother Constantine (Villehardouin); Choniates names Theodore Mangaphas, whose cavalry fled and left the infantry to be cut down.
greek_note: Raised in Bithynia and western Asia Minor; Mangaphas brought the men of Philadelphia.
sources: Villehardouin 321-322; Choniates; en.wikipedia Battle of Adramyttion (1205)
note: Villehardouin and Choniates describe different actions; modern historians assume two attempts to dislodge Henry in early 1205. Mangaphas then held Philadelphia as an independent lord allied with Laskaris.

name: Nicomedia
borderline: Unnamed engagement in a pass near Nicomedia; no article.
roman_force: Laskaris's Nicaean troops outflanked and surprised the army that David Komnenos had sent west under his young general Synadenos (Choniates); David's forces had been raised with Georgian troops and local mercenaries.
greek_note: Nicaea's troops were Bithynian Greeks; David's army mixed Pontic and Paphlagonian Greeks with Georgians.
sources: Choniates, Historia; en.wikipedia David Komnenos; en.wikipedia Theodore I Laskaris
note: Latin troops under Thierry de Loos then occupied Nicomedia, halting Laskaris's pursuit. Laskaris's general Andronikos Gidos later destroyed about 300 Frankish auxiliaries of David in the passes near Nicomedia (not entered separately).

name: Olive Grove of Kountouras
place: Olive grove of Kountouras, north-eastern Messenia
commanders_a: William of Champlitte, Geoffrey I of Villehardouin
borderline: The Greek army was local Moreote resistance; its leader Michael is identified with Michael I of Epirus by older scholarship but doubted by Loenertz. Counts only if that identification holds.
roman_force: 4,000 (Chronicle of the Morea) or over 5,000 (Villehardouin) foot and horse: contingents of the Greeks of Nikli, Veligosti and Lakedaimonia, most of the infantry being Melingoi Slavs from Taygetos.
greek_note: The Chronicle of the Morea says most of the infantry were Melingoi Slavs; the archontic contingents and cavalry were Greek.
sources: Chronicle of the Morea; Villehardouin 325-326; en.wikipedia Battle of the Olive Grove of Kountouras
note: About 500-700 Franks routed the Greeks; the victory founded the Principality of Achaea.

name: Trebizond (siege)
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Trebizond, with the people of the Pontic Alps who harassed the Seljuks in the passes; the new state had been founded in 1204 with Georgian troops sent by Queen Tamar.
greek_note: The defenders were Pontic Greeks, with Laz and Georgian elements in the Trapezuntine forces.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Siege of Trebizond (1205-1206)
note: Theodore Laskaris is said to have encouraged the sultan's attack.

name: Acrocorinth (siege)
commanders_a: Boniface of Montferrat (1205), Geoffrey I of Villehardouin, Otto de la Roche
commanders_b: Leo Sgouros (died 1208), then a Theodore, usually identified with Theodore Komnenos Doukas
borderline: Defended 1205-08 by Leo Sgouros, an independent Greek lord, not a listed successor state; Epirus applies only to the last phase if the defender Theodore was Theodore Komnenos Doukas. No siege article.
roman_force: The garrison of Leo Sgouros, lord of Nauplia, Argos and Corinth, which made energetic sorties against the Frankish siege forts; after Sgouros's death in 1208 the defence was led by a Theodore.
greek_note: Sgouros's men were Greeks of the Argolid and Corinthia.
sources: Villehardouin; Chronicle of the Morea; en.wikipedia Leo Sgouros
note: The citadel fell in 1210 to the Achaeans and Otto de la Roche of Athens; Nauplia and Argos held out until 1211-12.

name: Herakleia Pontike (siege)
borderline: No article or list entry.
roman_force: Laskaris's Nicaean field army besieged David Komnenos's city; David's ally Henry of Flanders crossed to Nicomedia and forced Laskaris to lift the siege, and the Nicaeans lost about 1,000 men crossing the flooded Sangarios (Choniates; Villehardouin's continuation).
greek_note: Both sides' forces were Greeks of north-western and northern Asia Minor.
sources: Choniates, Historia; en.wikipedia David Komnenos; en.wikipedia Theodore I Laskaris
note: Dated 1208 in the article on David Komnenos and 1206 in that on Theodore I. Laskaris took Herakleia and Amastris without resistance in 1214.

name: Antioch on the Maeander
place: Antioch on the Maeander, near Yamalak (Kuyucak)
commanders_b: Kaykhusraw I (killed); the former emperor Alexios III Angelos (captured)
roman_force: About 2,000 men (Akropolites, Gregoras; 3,000 in George of Pelagonia), of whom some 800 were Latin mercenary cavalry, most of whom fell; the rest were Nicaean Greek troops.
greek_note: About 800 of the 2,000 were Latin mercenaries; the remaining 1,200 or so were Nicaean Greeks.
sources: Akropolites 9-10; Gregoras 1.8; Choniates, Orations; en.wikipedia Battle of Antioch on the Meander
note: Laskaris is said to have killed the sultan in single combat; the victory was costly. Alexios III fought on the Seljuk side but does not make the battle civil.

name: Rhyndakos
roman_force: A Nicaean army larger than the Latins' 260 knights but with only a handful of Latin mercenaries, most having fallen at Antioch on the Maeander; it lay in ambush at the river and was scattered in a day-long fight (Henry's letter).
greek_note: With the Latin mercenaries lost at Antioch, the army was almost wholly Nicaean Greek.
sources: Henry of Flanders, letter of 1212; Akropolites 15; en.wikipedia Battle of the Rhyndacus (1211)
note: Henry advanced unopposed to Nymphaion; the Treaty of Nymphaion (1214) fixed the border.

name: Sinope (siege)
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Sinope, Greeks and some western Europeans; Alexios I, marching to relieve the city, was captured with a hunting party of about 500 men (Ibn Bibi).
greek_note: Ibn Bibi describes the defenders as Greeks with some Franks.
sources: Ibn Bibi; en.wikipedia Siege of Sinope
note: After a blockade by sea under Behram, the city surrendered to obtain Alexios's release; Trebizond became tributary to the Seljuks.

name: Dyrrhachium
place: Dyrrhachium (Durrës) and the mountain road east towards Thessalonica
commanders_b: Peter II of Courtenay (captured), Cardinal Giovanni Colonna (captured)
borderline: The siege and the ambush are not a named battle in the lists; entered as one engagement.
roman_force: Theodore Komnenos Doukas's Epirote army held Dyrrhachium against Peter of Courtenay's 160 knights and 5,500 men and then ambushed his column in the Albanian mountains; no figures are given for Theodore's troops.
greek_note: The Epirote army was raised in Epirus and Albania: Greeks with Albanian and Vlach highlanders.
sources: Akropolites 14; Richard of San Germano; en.wikipedia Theodore Komnenos Doukas; en.wikipedia Peter II of Courtenay
note: Most accounts say the siege of Dyrrhachium failed (others that the city fell and was quickly retaken); Peter was captured after accepting Theodore's offer of safe conduct and died in captivity.

name: Trebizond (siege)
place: Trebizond (Trabzon) and the passes to the south
commanders_a: Andronikos I Gidos, Theodore Polemarches, George Tornikes (killed)
roman_force: Armoured cavalry (an initial force of 500 horse), the watch of the Narrow Pass under Theodore Polemarches, Laz horsemen and light-armed Matzoukan highlanders, with the citizens of Trebizond (John Lazaropoulos).
greek_note: Lazaropoulos names the Matzoukan highlanders and the citizens, both Pontic Greek, and Laz horsemen.
sources: John Lazaropoulos, Synopsis of the Miracles of St Eugenios; Panaretos; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Siege of Trebizond (1222-1223)
note: The main account is hagiographic and its details may be embellished; the Seljuk prince was captured at Kouratoreion and released on terms ending Trebizond's vassalage. A Trapezuntine naval raid on Sinope preceded the siege.

name: Serres
place: On the road from Serres towards Constantinople
borderline: An interception rather than a named battle; no article.
roman_force: Epirote troops of Theodore Komnenos Doukas intercepted the Latin army that had lifted its siege of Serres on news of Poimanenon and killed or captured most of it (Akropolites).
greek_note: Theodore's army was raised in Epirus, Thessaly and western Macedonia.
sources: Akropolites 24; en.wikipedia Theodore Komnenos Doukas

name: Thessalonica (siege)
commanders_b: Guy Pallavicini (regent), Oberto II of Biandrate
roman_force: Theodore Komnenos Doukas's Epirote army, recruited in Epirus, Thessaly and western Macedonia; no figures in the sources.
greek_note: The Epirote army drew on the Greek towns and countryside of Epirus and Thessaly, with Albanians, Vlachs and Slavs.
sources: Akropolites 21, 24; en.wikipedia Theodore Komnenos Doukas
note: The city surrendered about December 1224 after a long blockade; Theodore was crowned emperor there (1225-27), founding the Empire of Thessalonica. A relief crusade under William VI of Montferrat (1225) failed.

name: Poimanenon
commanders_b: Alexios and Isaac Laskaris (captured), Nicholas of Mainvault (killed), Thierry of Walcourt
roman_force: John III Vatatzes's Nicaean field army; Akropolites says only that he won 'by storm'. No figures.
greek_note: The army of Nicaea was raised in western Anatolia, with Latin and Cuman mercenaries.
sources: Akropolites 22; Gregoras 2.2; en.wikipedia Battle of Poimanenon
note: The Laskaris brothers, rivals of Vatatzes, fought with the Latins and were blinded after capture; the Latins lost almost all of Asia Minor (treaty of 1225).

name: Klokotnitsa
commanders_b: Theodore Komnenos Doukas (captured), Manuel Komnenos Doukas
roman_force: A large army of the Empire of Thessalonica, raised in Macedonia, Thessaly and Epirus, with western (Latin) mercenaries (Akropolites); the infobox figures are unreliable.
greek_note: Theodore's army came from the Greek lands of Epirus, Thessaly and Macedonia, with Latin mercenaries.
sources: Akropolites 25; en.wikipedia Battle of Klokotnitsa
note: Theodore was captured and later blinded; Ivan Asen released the prisoners and took Thrace and Macedonia; Thessalonica passed to Manuel as a Bulgarian vassal. Some accounts give April 1230.

name: Gallipoli
borderline: The capture opened the 1235 campaign; how much fighting there was is not clear in the Wikipedia account.
roman_force: John III Vatatzes's army, ferried across the Hellespont, took the Venetian-held town (Akropolites).
greek_note: The Nicaean field army of western Anatolia.
sources: Akropolites 33; en.wikipedia Siege of Constantinople (1235)

name: Constantinople (siege)
war: Nicaean-Bulgarian war against the Latin Empire
commanders_a: John of Brienne, Geoffrey II of Villehardouin
commanders_b: John III Doukas Vatatzes, Ivan Asen II
roman_force: John III's Nicaean army and fleet, alongside Ivan Asen II's Bulgarians; the fleet tried to force the Golden Horn and lost 24 ships to a Venetian squadron of 25 galleys. A source's 50,000 for the allied army is exaggerated.
greek_note: The Nicaean contingent and fleet were raised in western Anatolia and the islands, with Latin and Cuman mercenaries.
sources: Akropolites 34-37; Philippe Mouskes; en.wikipedia Siege of Constantinople (1235)
note: Pisan ships also helped the defence. The siege was renewed in 1236 before Ivan Asen changed sides. The naval defeat is counted within this entry.

name: Brescia (siege)
war: Wars of the Guelphs and Ghibellines (Frederick II against the Lombard League)
borderline: A small allied contingent far from Roman lands; the Wikipedia infobox lists the Empire of Nicaea as a belligerent beside Frederick II.
roman_force: Nicaean troops sent by John III Vatatzes, which joined Frederick II's army at Verona in April 1238; their size and role are not recorded.
greek_note: Troops sent from Nicaea would have been Nicaean Greeks or the empire's mercenaries; no details survive.
sources: en.wikipedia John III Doukas Vatatzes; en.wikipedia Siege of Brescia (1238)
note: A successful sortie by the Brescians in early October forced Frederick to lift the siege.

name: Tzurulum (siege)
borderline: Siege mentioned only in passing in Wikipedia; no article.
roman_force: The Nicaean garrison of Tzurulum, placed there in the 1235 campaign; no figures.
greek_note: A garrison of the Nicaean army in Thrace.
sources: Akropolites 37; en.wikipedia Siege of Constantinople (1235)
note: Taken by Baldwin II with the western knights of his crusade of 1239, who then dispersed; Vatatzes recovered the town in 1247.

name: Thessalonica (siege)
roman_force: Vatatzes's Nicaean army, without heavy siege engines, with a fleet; the defenders were the garrison and citizens of Thessalonica (Akropolites).
greek_note: Nicaean Anatolian troops against the Greek garrison and citizens of Thessalonica.
sources: Akropolites 40; en.wikipedia Theodore Komnenos Doukas
note: The city held and the siege was broken off on news of the Mongol invasion of Asia Minor, but after 40 days of talks John Komnenos Doukas renounced the imperial title and became a Nicaean vassal despot, so politically Nicaea gained its aim.

name: Köse Dağ
place: Köse Dağ mountain, between Erzincan and Sivas
borderline: The Roman part was a small allied contingent; the battle article's infobox omits it, and Greek mercenaries in Seljuk pay would not count.
roman_force: A Trapezuntine army sent by Manuel I of Trebizond, then a Seljuk vassal, is recorded with the sultan's army; numbers unknown. Kaykhusraw II's treaty with John III Vatatzes is not known to have produced Nicaean troops, and Greek nobles serving as Seljuk mercenaries do not count.
greek_note: Contingents of Trebizond and Nicaea, both Greek-speaking states.
sources: Ibn Bibi; Bar Hebraeus; en.wikipedia Manuel I of Trebizond; en.wikipedia Battle of Köse Dağ
note: Georgian troops fought on both sides. Trebizond submitted to the Mongols after the battle.

name: Tzurulum (siege)
borderline: No article or list entry.
roman_force: John III Vatatzes's Nicaean field army with siege engines, which took Tzurulum and Vizye from the Latins (Akropolites).
greek_note: The Nicaean army of the 1240s was raised in western Anatolia, with Cuman settlers and Latin mercenaries.
sources: Akropolites 47
note: The capture left the Latins only the immediate surroundings of Constantinople.

name: Rhodes (siege)
commanders_b: William II of Villehardouin, Hugh IV of Burgundy (Achaean relief)
roman_force: A small army, perhaps only the Thrakesian troops of the pinkernes and doux John Kantakouzenos, with a fleet, reinforced by the protosebastos Theodore Kontostephanos with 300 horse from Smyrna; they destroyed the 100 Achaean knights left to help the Genoese and besieged the city again (Akropolites).
greek_note: The troops were those of the Thrakesion theme and Smyrna in western Anatolia.
sources: Akropolites 48; en.wikipedia Genoese occupation of Rhodes
note: The Genoese seized Rhodes by a night attack in 1248; the Nicaean blockade (late 1248-1249) was interrupted when William of Villehardouin arrived in May 1249, and the Genoese surrendered for safe passage in late 1249 or early 1250.

name: Thessalonica
commanders_b: Michael II Komnenos Doukas, Theodore Komnenos Doukas
borderline: An attack rather than a siege; the extent of fighting is not recorded.
roman_force: The Nicaean garrison and citizens of Thessalonica repelled the Epirote army of Michael II, urged on by the blind Theodore Komnenos Doukas (Akropolites).
greek_note: Greek garrison and citizens against an Epirote army of Greeks and Albanians.
sources: Akropolites 49; en.wikipedia Theodore Komnenos Doukas
note: Michael II then took Prilep and Veles; Vatatzes's counter-campaign of 1252 forced him to terms.

name: Sinope
borderline: Recapture recorded briefly; whether there was real fighting is unknown.
roman_force: Manuel I's Trapezuntine forces, probably with the fleet; the sources give no details.
greek_note: The army of Trebizond was Pontic Greek with Laz and Georgian elements.
sources: Panaretos; en.wikipedia Manuel I of Trebizond
note: Trebizond held Sinope until about 1265.

name: Adrianople
borderline: Akropolites describes a counter-offensive in which the Bulgarians withdrew rather than a set battle; the Wikipedia article is a stub.
roman_force: Theodore II's field army, assembled with difficulty and led by the emperor in person, which caught the Bulgarians unprepared and drove them out of Thrace (Akropolites).
greek_note: Theodore II favoured native Anatolian troops, with Cuman and Latin mercenaries.
sources: Akropolites 54; en.wikipedia Battle of Adrianople (1254)
note: The article gives 1,000-3,000 Bulgarian losses.

name: Tzepaina
place: Passes below the fortress of Tzepaina (Tsepina), western Rhodopes
borderline: Akropolites describes a rout with little or no fighting; no article.
roman_force: A Nicaean detachment under Alexios Strategopoulos and a Tornikes sent against Tzepaina, which fled in panic, abandoning its baggage and horses (Akropolites).
greek_note: A detachment of the Nicaean field army.
sources: Akropolites 58; en.wikipedia Alexios Strategopoulos; en.wikipedia Theodore II Laskaris
note: Theodore II dismissed both commanders. His own attempt on Tzepaina in late 1255 was stopped by the snow-bound passes.

name: Edessa
borderline: Named only as a place-battle in the Theodore II article, which does not name the victor; no article.
roman_force: A newly raised Nicaean army of Anatolian peasants was routed near Edessa by the forces of Michael II (Akropolites).
greek_note: Akropolites calls the Nicaean levies Anatolian peasants; the Epirote side was Greeks with Albanians.
sources: Akropolites 70; en.wikipedia Theodore II Laskaris
note: The victors are taken to be Michael II's Epirotes, whose offensive of 1257 it belongs to; Serbian troops of Stefan Uros I also defeated a Nicaean force near Prilep in the same war (not entered).

name: Prilep (siege)
borderline: No article or list entry.
roman_force: Michael II's Epirote army besieged and took Prilep, held for Nicaea by a garrison under the governor George Akropolites, after the Nicaean field army under Michael Palaiologos had been ordered to withdraw (Akropolites).
greek_note: Both sides' forces were Greek-speaking, the Epirotes with Albanian contingents.
sources: Akropolites 70-71; en.wikipedia Theodore II Laskaris
note: Akropolites was freed after Pelagonia in 1259.

name: Pelagonia
war: Pelagonia campaign (Nicaea against the Epirote-Achaean-Sicilian league)
place: Plain of Pelagonia, probably near Vevi between Florina and Kaimakchalan
commanders_a: John Palaiologos (sebastokrator), Alexios Strategopoulos, Nikephoros Rimpsas
commanders_b: William II of Villehardouin (captured), Geoffrey of Briel (captured); Michael II Komnenos Doukas (withdrew)
borderline: Epirus was a principal of the coalition but its army fled the night before the battle and John Doukas went over to Nicaea; entered as not civil, but could be treated as civil.
roman_force: John Palaiologos's army of 27 allagia (Chronicle of the Morea): Greek contingents from Asia Minor, Macedonia and Thrace with 300 German knights, 1,500 Hungarian mounted archers, 600 Serbian horse, Bulgarian cavalry, 1,500 Turkish and 2,000 Cuman horsemen; John Doukas's Thessalians changed sides to Nicaea.
greek_note: The Chronicle of the Morea lists some 6,000 foreign horsemen beside the native Greek contingents, whose number is not given.
sources: Akropolites 79-81; Pachymeres 1.30-31; Gregoras 3.5; Chronicle of the Morea; en.wikipedia Battle of Pelagonia
note: Also called the battle of Kastoria. The Duchy of Athens, the triarchs of Euboea and the Duchy of the Archipelago also sent troops to the league. Date July (Nicol) or September (Geanakoplos).

name: Trikorphon
roman_force: Michael II, returning from Cephalonia with his sons and Italian mercenaries and joined by the local population, routed the Nicaean occupation army of Alexios Strategopoulos (Pachymeres).
greek_note: Both armies were mainly Greek: the Epirote levies of Aetolia-Acarnania with Italian mercenaries, and the Nicaean army of Anatolia and Macedonia.
sources: Pachymeres 2.11; en.wikipedia Alexios Strategopoulos
note: Michael II retook Arta; Strategopoulos was released after a few months and recovered Constantinople in July 1261.

name: Constantinople (siege)
date: 1260 (Michael VIII crossed into Thrace in January; truce in August)
place: Galata, across the Golden Horn from Constantinople
roman_force: Michael VIII's army, with siege engines and miners, attacked Galata after a plot to open a gate failed; Akropolites thought the force too small for a serious assault, while other chroniclers describe a large operation. No figures.
greek_note: The Nicaean army of Anatolia and Thrace, with Cuman and Latin mercenaries.
sources: Akropolites 81; Pachymeres 2.31; Gregoras; en.wikipedia Siege of Constantinople (1260)
note: The defenders of Galata, reinforced by boat from the city, held; Michael accepted a one-year truce. Outlying places such as Selymbria were taken in the same campaign.

name: Reconquest of Constantinople
war: Wars of Nicaea against the Latin Empire
place: Constantinople, the land walls near the Gate of the Spring (Pege)
commanders_b: Baldwin II (in the city, not at the walls)
borderline: A surprise entry with only a short fight at the walls; the Latin garrison and the Venetian fleet were away raiding Daphnousia.
roman_force: About 800 soldiers, most of them Cumans, under Alexios Strategopoulos, guided by local Greek farmers (thelematarioi) who led a detachment through a passage under the walls to open the gate (Akropolites, Pachymeres).
greek_note: Most of the 800 were Cuman mercenaries, but the Nicaean officers and the thelematarioi who opened the gate were Greek.
sources: George Akropolites 85-88; Pachymeres book 2; Gregoras book 4; en.wikipedia Reconquest of Constantinople
note: Michael VIII entered the city on 15 August 1261.

name: Prinitza
war: War of Michael VIII against the Principality of Achaea (1262-1267)
place: the defile of Prinitza, near Ancient Olympia, Elis
roman_force: The expeditionary army of the Morea under Constantine Palaiologos: Turkish (Seljuk) mercenaries (about 1,500 by modern reckoning), Greek troops from Anatolia under John Makrenos, and local recruits from the Tsakonians, Kinsterna and the Slavs of Taygetos; the Chronicle of the Morea's 15,000-20,000 is much exaggerated.
greek_note: Besides the Turkish mercenaries the army included some 2,000 Anatolian Greeks under Makrenos and Greek-speaking Tsakonian and Laconian levies.
sources: Chronicle of the Morea; Pachymeres; Gregoras (briefly); Marino Sanudo Torsello; en.wikipedia Battle of Prinitza
note: The Achaean force was only about 300 men; the Chronicle of the Morea, the only detailed account, is hostile to the imperial side.

name: Settepozzi
war: War of Saint Sabas (Venice against Genoa and Michael VIII)
place: off Settepozzi (Spetses), at the mouth of the Argolic Gulf
borderline: The principal belligerent was Genoa, fighting as Michael VIII's ally and in his pay; direct participation of imperial ships is not securely attested.
roman_force: A Genoese fleet of 38 galleys and 10 saettiae in Michael VIII's pay under the Treaty of Nymphaeum (1261), sailing from the imperial base at Monemvasia; only about 14 galleys engaged.
greek_note: Martino da Canal says one of the two admirals who stayed out of the fight was a Greek; the crews were essentially Genoese.
sources: Annales Ianuenses; Martino da Canal; Pachymeres; en.wikipedia Battle of Settepozzi
note: Venice took four Genoese galleys; the defeat led Michael VIII to dismiss the Genoese fleet.

name: Makryplagi
war: War of Michael VIII against the Principality of Achaea (1262-1267)
place: the pass of Makryplagi, near Gardiki, between Messenia and the Megalopolis basin
commanders_a: William II of Villehardouin, Ancelin de Toucy
commanders_b: Alexios Philes and John Makrenos (both captured)
roman_force: The imperial army of the Morea, chiefly Greek troops from Asia Minor, after its unpaid Turkish mercenaries (over 1,000 horse under Melik and Salik) had gone over to the Achaeans.
greek_note: With the Turks gone over to William, the army that fought was mostly the Anatolian Greek contingent and local levies.
sources: Chronicle of the Morea; Pachymeres; en.wikipedia Battle of Makryplagi
note: Date 1263 or 1264. Constantine Palaiologos had left; the megas konostaulos Michael Kantakouzenos was killed earlier in a skirmish at Saint Nicholas of Mesiskli (not listed separately). The Turkish deserters fought on the Achaean side.

name: Neopatras
war: Michael VIII's war against Thessaly and the Latins of Greece
commanders_a: John I Doukas; John I de la Roche, Duke of Athens
commanders_b: the despot John Palaiologos, Alexios Kaballarios (killed)
borderline: Thessaly (John I Doukas, son of Michael II of Epirus) is treated here as an Epirote, Roman successor principality, making the battle civil; if Thessaly is not counted as Roman, this is an imperial defeat by Thessaly and Athens.
roman_force: Imperial side: a large, mostly mercenary army of mixed peoples under the despot John Palaiologos (Pachymeres' 40,000 with the fleet is exaggerated), including Cumans who changed sides in the battle. Thessalian side: John Doukas's men, with 300-500 Latin horse from Athens.
greek_note: Pachymeres stresses the mercenary, many-peopled imperial army (Cumans among them); the Thessalian force was Greek, with Latin cavalry from Athens.
sources: Pachymeres; Gregoras; en.wikipedia Battle of Neopatras
note: Dated 1271 (Poussines), 1272/73 (Failler, ODB) or late 1274/early 1275 (Geanakoplos, Nicol). Fought just before the sea battle of Demetrias. roman_state gives the imperial side; the other side is Thessaly.

name: Demetrias
war: Michael VIII's war against Thessaly and the Latins of Greece
place: off Demetrias, near Volos, Pagasetic Gulf
commanders_a: Alexios Doukas Philanthropenos (wounded); the despot John Palaiologos
commanders_b: Guglielmo II da Verona (killed), Filippo Sanudo (captured)
roman_force: Michael VIII's fleet of 50-80 ships (Gregoras 'over 50', Sanudo 80), in this period manned by Gasmouloi, Tzakones and Prosalentai (Pachymeres), reinforced during the battle by the despot John Palaiologos with troops brought from Neopatras.
greek_note: Pachymeres names the Gasmouloi (Greek-Latin, Greek-speaking), the Laconian Tzakones and the Prosalentai as the crews of Michael VIII's navy.
sources: Pachymeres; Gregoras; Marino Sanudo Torsello; en.wikipedia Battle of Demetrias
note: Dated 1271, 1272/73 (Failler, ODB) or 1275 (Geanakoplos, Nicol, Fine). The Lombard triarchs of Negroponte with Venetian ships from Crete and Euboea (Venice officially neutral); all but two Latin ships were taken.

name: Devina
war: Michael VIII's intervention in the Bulgarian rising of Ivailo (1277-1280)
place: near the fortress of Devina, at the Kotel pass, Balkan Mountains
roman_force: An army of about 10,000 sent by Michael VIII under Murin to support Ivan Asen III (Pachymeres); its composition is not recorded. Michael VIII's field armies normally combined Greek soldiers of Thrace and Macedonia with Cuman, Turkish and Latin mercenaries.
greek_note: Inferred from the make-up of Michael VIII's Balkan field armies, raised mainly in Thrace and Macedonia.
sources: Pachymeres; en.wikipedia Battle of Devina
note: A few weeks later Ivailo destroyed a second imperial army of about 5,000 under Aprenos before it reached the Balkan passes (not listed separately: no name).

name: Vatondas
war: Licario's campaigns in Euboea and the Aegean
commanders_b: Giberto II da Verona (killed or captured), John I de la Roche, Duke of Athens (captured)
roman_force: Licario's imperial forces on Euboea, which included Spanish and Catalan mercenaries and former followers of Manfred of Sicily (Marino Sanudo); the rest of the force is not described.
greek_note: Only the Latin mercenaries are named; the imperial garrisons Licario raised on Euboea were presumably largely local Greeks.
sources: Marino Sanudo Torsello, Istoria del Regno di Romania; Gregoras; en.wikipedia Licario
note: Licario then besieged Negroponte without success. Gregoras says Giberto da Verona died in Constantinople on seeing Licario; Sanudo says he was killed.

name: Berat (siege)
commanders_a: Michael Tarchaneiotes (megas domestikos), John Synadenos, Michael Komnenos Doukas, Andronikos Eonopolites
roman_force: The garrison of Berat and a relief army sent by Michael VIII under Michael Tarchaneiotes, including Turkish mercenaries who ambushed and captured Hugh of Sully; troops from the citadel joined the attack. The Angevins had about 2,000 knights and 6,000 foot.
greek_note: The relief army was the western field army of Michael VIII, raised mostly in Macedonia and Thrace, with a Turkish mercenary contingent named in the sources.
sources: Pachymeres; Gregoras; en.wikipedia Siege of Berat (1280-1281)
