note: The Angevin army fled toward Valona after Sully's capture and lost its siege train; Sully was paraded in triumph in Constantinople.

name: Trebizond (siege)
commanders_a: the defenders of Trebizond (John II was away in Constantinople)
commanders_b: David VI Narin, king of Imereti
borderline: No details of the fighting at the walls are recorded.
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Trebizond; the sources give no details. The army of Trebizond in this period was raised from the Greek archons and towns of the Pontus with Laz troops.
greek_note: The defenders were the people of the capital, a Greek-speaking city, perhaps with Laz (Kartvelian) troops.
sources: Miller, Trebizond (1926) 30; Rayfield, Edge of Empires (2012) 132; en.wikipedia Siege of Trebizond (1282)
note: The city held, but the Georgians occupied several provinces, including Chaneti (Lazia).

name: Demetrias (siege)
commanders_a: Michael Tarchaneiotes (died of disease); fleet under Alexios Raoul and John Synadenos
commanders_b: the garrison of John I Doukas
borderline: Thessaly treated as a Roman (Epirote) successor principality, so civil; little is recorded of the fighting.
roman_force: Imperial side: a land army under Michael Tarchaneiotes supported by a fleet under Alexios Raoul and John Synadenos; Thessalian side: John Doukas's garrison. Composition otherwise not recorded.
greek_note: Both armies were raised mainly in Greek lands (Macedonia, Thrace, Thessaly), with mercenaries in unknown numbers.
sources: Pachymeres; en.wikipedia Andronikos II Palaiologos; en.wikipedia Michael Tarchaneiotes
note: The town was taken, but an epidemic killed Tarchaneiotes and much of the army, which withdrew from Thessaly. roman_state gives the imperial side; the other side is Thessaly.

name: Mount Armenia (Ermeni Beli)
war: Wars of Osman with the Roman lords of Bithynia
place: the Ermeni Beli pass (Mount Armenia), in the hills of the Bithynian frontier near İnegöl
commanders_b: the tekfurs (Roman lords) of Bursa and of İnegöl (Aya Nikola)
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
borderline: Known only from fifteenth-century Ottoman chronicles; no Roman source mentions it.
roman_force: The retainers and garrison troops of the local Roman lords of Bursa and İnegöl, according to the Ottoman chronicles; no numbers.
greek_note: The Bithynian lordships were Greek-speaking frontier districts of the empire.
sources: Aşıkpaşazade; Neşri; en.wikipedia Osman I; en.wikipedia Siege of Kulaca Hisar
note: An ambush of Osman's band; he withdrew with losses (his nephew Bayhoca was killed). No clear winner.

name: Tralles (siege)
war: Turkish conquest of the Maeander valley
borderline: A siege known from Pachymeres' narrative, without a battle article; the fighting is not described in detail.
roman_force: The garrison and the settlers of Tralles, rebuilt from 1278 by Michael Tarchaneiotes for the young Andronikos II as Andronikopolis and repopulated with 36,000 people from the region; no relief came (Pachymeres).
greek_note: The 36,000 settlers were brought from the Greek population of the surrounding districts.
sources: Pachymeres; Vryonis, The Decline of Medieval Hellenism in Asia Minor (1971); en.wikipedia Aydın; en.wikipedia Michael Tarchaneiotes
note: Beylik: Menteşe. Short of supplies and water, the city was taken; many inhabitants were massacred and over 20,000 sold as slaves. Nyssa fell about the same time.

name: Kulaca Hisar (siege)
war: Wars of Osman with the Roman lords of Bithynia
place: the fort of Kulaca Hisar, near İnegöl
commanders_a: Osman, Turgut Alp, Konur Alp, Akçakoca, Abdurrahman Gazi
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
borderline: Known only from Ottoman tradition; a night attack on a fort rather than a siege.
roman_force: The garrison of a small fort belonging to the Roman lord of İnegöl (Ottoman tradition; the figure of 1,000 defenders is unverified).
greek_note: A local Bithynian garrison of the frontier lordships.
sources: Aşıkpaşazade; Neşri; en.wikipedia Siege of Kulaca Hisar
note: Called in Ottoman tradition the first castle taken by the Ottomans.

name: Domaniç (İkizce)
war: Wars of Osman with the Roman lords of Bithynia
commanders_b: Aya Nikola, lord of İnegöl; the lord of Karacahisar; Kalanoz (killed)
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
borderline: Known only from Ottoman chronicles, whose versions differ.
roman_force: The combined forces of the Roman lords of İnegöl and Karacahisar, according to the Ottoman chronicles; no numbers.
greek_note: Local Greek-speaking frontier troops of the Bithynian lordships.
sources: Aşıkpaşazade; Neşri; Oruç Bey; İnalcık, TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi 'Osman I'; en.wikipedia Battle of Domaniç
note: Also called the battle of İkizce (Ekizce); the date is not fixed (1286-1291).

name: Karacahisar (siege)
war: Wars of Osman with the Roman lords of Bithynia
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
borderline: Ottoman tradition only; the date and whether the fort was then held by a Roman lord are disputed.
roman_force: The garrison of the fort, a Roman frontier lordship according to the Ottoman tradition; nothing more is known.
greek_note: A local Greek-speaking frontier garrison, if the tradition is right that the fort was Roman.
sources: Aşıkpaşazade; Neşri; en.wikipedia Osman I; en.wikipedia Battle of Domaniç (campaign box)
note: The Osman I article places it after a battle between Bilecik and İnegöl in which Osman's brother Savcı and the Roman commander 'Pilatos' fell; this may be the same tradition as Domaniç.

name: Ioannina (siege)
commanders_a: Nikephoros I Komnenos Doukas; Florent of Hainaut, Prince of Achaea; Count Riccardo Orsini of Cephalonia
borderline: The imperial army withdrew when the Achaean army approached; how much fighting there was is unclear.
roman_force: Imperial side: an army sent by Andronikos II (commander and size not recorded), while a hired Genoese fleet with imperial soldiers raided the coast near Arta. Epirote side: the garrison of Ioannina, relieved by Achaean and Cephalonian troops.
greek_note: Both the imperial army and the Epirote defenders were raised mainly in Greek lands; the Achaean relief force was Frankish.
sources: Pachymeres; Chronicle of the Morea; en.wikipedia Andronikos II Palaiologos; en.wikipedia Nikephoros I Komnenos Doukas
note: roman_state gives the Epirote (winning) side; the other side is the restored empire. A Genoese fleet hired by Andronikos II raided near Arta at the same time.

name: Bapheus
place: the plain of Bapheus (Koyunhisar), near Nicomedia
roman_force: About 2,000 men under George Mouzalon, half of them newly hired Alan mercenaries, who did not join the fighting but covered the retreat to Nicomedia; the rest were imperial troops (Pachymeres).
greek_note: Pachymeres makes the Alans half of the force; the other half were Roman soldiers, presumably Greek-speaking.
sources: Pachymeres; en.wikipedia Battle of Bapheus
note: Dated 27 July 1302 after Pachymeres (Failler) and most modern scholars; the en.wikipedia article's infobox now gives 27 July 1299 (Gibbon, Treiyer 2017), and some put it in 1301. Osman had about 5,000 light horse. It followed Osman's blockade of Nicaea (1301).

name: Kerasous
war: Wars of Trebizond with the Turkmen
borderline: A victory recorded by Panaretos and modern histories of Trebizond, but without a battle article.
roman_force: The army of Alexios II of Trebizond; the sources give no details. Trebizond's armies were raised from its Greek archons and towns, with Laz troops and Georgian mercenaries (attested under Alexios II).
greek_note: Inferred from the recruitment of the Trapezuntine army in the Greek coastal towns of the Pontus.
sources: Michael Panaretos; Miller, Trebizond (1926); en.wikipedia Alexios II of Trebizond
note: Turkmen invaders who had taken Chalybia; no beylik is named. Alexios captured their leader and afterwards built a sea fort at Kerasous.

name: Cyzicus
war: Campaign of the Catalan Company in Anatolia (1303-1304)
place: near Cape Artake (Erdek), on the Cyzicus peninsula
borderline: The details come from Muntaner and later Catalan accounts; the casualty figures (3,000 horse, 10,000 foot) are surely exaggerated.
roman_force: The Catalan Company in imperial service: Catalan and Aragonese almogavar infantry and cavalry (Muntaner gives the Company about 1,500 horse and 4,000 almogavars on arrival; Gregoras far fewer), in a surprise attack on a Turkish camp.
greek_note: Muntaner describes the attack as made by the Company alone ('other' = Aragonese).
sources: Ramon Muntaner, Chronicle; Pachymeres; Moncada, Expedición de los catalanes (1623); en.wikipedia Battle of the Cyzicus
note: Beylik: probably Karasi.

name: Dimbos
place: the Dimbos pass, on the road from Bursa to Yenişehir
commanders_b: the tekfurs (Roman lords) of Bursa, Kite, Kestel, Adranos and Ulubat; the lord of Kite captured and executed
doubt: Its historicity is doubted: see the note.
borderline: Known only from later Ottoman tradition with legendary elements; Aşıkpaşazade may have transferred Bapheus to Dimbos.
roman_force: A host of the local garrisons of Adranos, Bidnos, Kestel and Kite gathered at Bursa (Ottoman tradition).
greek_note: Local Greek-speaking garrison troops of the Bithynian towns.
sources: Aşıkpaşazade; Spandounes; İnalcık (2003), in İznik throughout History; en.wikipedia Battle of Dimbos
note: Kestel and Ulubat were then taken.

name: Germe
war: Campaign of the Catalan Company in Anatolia (1303-1304)
borderline: A defeat of a Turkish rearguard known only from Muntaner.
roman_force: The Catalan Company in imperial service, with the Alan mercenaries (about 1,000) who joined the 1304 campaign.
greek_note: The 1304 army was the Company with Alans and some imperial troops under Marulles.
sources: Ramon Muntaner, Chronicle; en.wikipedia Catalan Company
note: Beylik not named (Karasi or Germiyan).

name: Tire
war: Campaign of the Catalan Company in Anatolia (1303-1304)
borderline: Known only from Muntaner.
roman_force: The Catalan Company in imperial service, sallying from Tire, which had a Greek garrison.
greek_note: The fighting was done by the Company; Muntaner says the Turks expected to meet only the Greek garrison.
sources: Ramon Muntaner, Chronicle; en.wikipedia Catalan Company
note: Beyliks: Menteşe, with survivors of Aulax (Aydın). The Turks lost about 700 horse but escaped.

name: Ania
war: Campaign of the Catalan Company in Anatolia (1303-1304)
commanders_a: the Catalan Company (Roger de Flor's army; Bernat de Rocafort had just joined)
borderline: Known only from Muntaner; the figures are exaggerated.
roman_force: The Catalan Company in imperial service, reinforced by Bernat de Rocafort's 200 horse and 1,000 almogavars.
greek_note: Muntaner describes an almogavar charge by the Company alone ('other' = Aragonese).
sources: Ramon Muntaner, Chronicle; en.wikipedia Catalan Company
note: Beylik: Aydın. Placed by Muntaner after Tire.

name: Kibistra
war: Campaign of the Catalan Company in Anatolia (1303-1304)
place: near Kibistra (Herakleia Kybistra, Ereğli), at the 'Iron Gate' of the Taurus
commanders_a: Roger de Flor (horse); Bernat de Rocafort and Marulles (foot)
borderline: Known only from Muntaner; the site and the scale (20,000 foot and 10,000 horse) are doubted, and some historians doubt the Company went so far east.
roman_force: The Catalan Company in imperial service, with the imperial officer Marulles; Muntaner gives no other contingents.
greek_note: Apart from Marulles and his men the force was the Catalan Company.
sources: Ramon Muntaner, Chronicle; en.wikipedia Catalan Company
note: Beylik not named (Karaman, or the Turks of the Taurus frontier).

name: Magnesia (siege)
war: Campaign of the Catalan Company in Anatolia (1303-1304)
place: Magnesia ad Sipylum (Manisa), in the Hermos valley
commanders_a: the townsmen and garrison of Magnesia
borderline: The Company was still nominally in imperial service, and the siege was lifted on the emperor's order; how much fighting there was is not well recorded.
roman_force: The townsmen and imperial garrison of Magnesia, who had killed the Catalan garrison Roger de Flor left there and seized the Company's treasure; no numbers are recorded.
greek_note: Magnesia was a Greek city of the Hermos valley defended by its own people.
sources: Pachymeres; en.wikipedia Catalan Company
note: Roger de Flor gave up the siege when Andronikos II recalled the Company to Europe; the Company then wintered at Gallipoli.

name: Philadelphia (siege)
war: Campaign of the Catalan Company in Anatolia (1303-1304)
place: Philadelphia (Alaşehir); the relief battle at Aulax nearby
commanders_a: Roger de Flor, Corbaran d'Alet; the metropolitan Theoleptos (in the city)
commanders_b: Yakub I of Germiyan (Yakub bin Ali Şir), Mehmed of Aydın
roman_force: The Catalan Company (Muntaner about 6,500: horse under Roger de Flor and almogavar foot under Corbaran d'Alet) with Alan and Greek horse in the cavalry division, relieving the city's own defenders organised by the metropolitan Theoleptos.
greek_note: Muntaner places Alan and Greek contingents in the cavalry, and the defence of the city itself was Greek, led by its bishop.
sources: Ramon Muntaner, Chronicle; Pachymeres; en.wikipedia First Siege of Philadelphia; en.wikipedia Catalan Company
note: Beyliks: Germiyan and Aydın (about 8,000 horse and 12,000 foot in Muntaner). The relief battle is called the battle of Aulax; it is one entry with the siege.

name: Skafida
place: on the Skafida river, near Sozopolis (Sozopol)
roman_force: Michael IX's field army of Thrace; its composition is not recorded. The Thracian armies of the time were Greek soldiers with Alan and Turkish (Tourkopouloi) mercenaries.
greek_note: Inferred from the recruitment of Michael IX's Thracian army.
sources: Pachymeres; Gregoras; en.wikipedia Battle of Skafida
note: Many of the pursuing imperial troops drowned when the bridge over the Skafida collapsed.

name: Gallipoli (siege)
commanders_a: Ramon Muntaner (captain of Gallipoli), Bernat de Rocafort
borderline: The details of the sally come mainly from Muntaner.
roman_force: The imperial army that blockaded the Company in Gallipoli after the murder of Roger de Flor (April 1305): Greek troops with Alans and Turcopoles (Muntaner).
greek_note: Muntaner names Greeks, Alans and Turcopoles in the besieging army.
sources: Ramon Muntaner, Chronicle; Pachymeres; en.wikipedia Catalan Company
note: The besiegers were routed with heavy loss, a few weeks before Apros.

name: Apros
place: near Apros (Kermeyan), between Rhaidestos and Kypsela
commanders_b: Michael IX Palaiologos; the Bulgarian Vojsil (wings)
roman_force: Michael IX's army of about 6,000 or more, mostly horse: Roman (Greek) troops of Thrace and Macedonia, with Alan cavalry and Turcopoles (Tourkopouloi) on the wings under the Bulgarian Vojsil; the Alans withdrew and the Turcopoles deserted to the Catalans.
greek_note: The sources (Pachymeres, Muntaner; Bartusis) name the Alan and Turcopole wings; the rest of the army was Roman troops of Thrace and Macedonia.
sources: Pachymeres; Gregoras; Ramon Muntaner, Chronicle; Bartusis (1997) 79-82; en.wikipedia Battle of Apros
note: The Catalans (about 2,500) had Turkish mercenaries from Anatolia; Michael IX was unhorsed and carried from the field.

name: Rhodes (siege)
place: the city of Rhodes and the castles of the island (Filerimos, Lindos, Feraklos)
commanders_a: Foulques de Villaret (grand master), Vignolo de' Vignoli
commanders_b: unknown local commanders; relief fleets sent by Andronikos II
borderline: The assaults of 1306 and the siege of 1307 failed; the city surrendered in 1310 rather than being stormed.
roman_force: The imperial garrisons of Rhodes, including about 300 Turkish soldiers at Filerimos, with relief fleets of 8 and then 20 galleys sent by Andronikos II in 1307.
greek_note: The defenders of the city were the Greek population and garrison (about 80 Greeks fell in 1307); the garrison of Filerimos was Turkish.
sources: Pachymeres; biographies of Clement V; Templar of Tyre; Luttrell in Setton (ed.), A History of the Crusades III (1975); en.wikipedia Hospitaller conquest of Rhodes
note: The year of the city's fall is disputed (1306-1310); 15 August 1310 is the usual date. Filerimos was betrayed in November 1306 and its Turkish garrison massacred.

name: Philadelphia (siege)
borderline: Mainly a blockade, ended by a negotiated peace.
roman_force: The garrison of Philadelphia under the governor Manuel Tagaris, with the citizens; no relief came from Constantinople.
greek_note: An isolated Greek city defended by its own garrison and people.
sources: Gregoras; Theoleptos of Philadelphia; en.wikipedia Second Siege of Philadelphia
note: Beylik: Germiyan. The walls were not breached; the siege ended in spring 1311 with a peace that probably included tribute.

name: Gallipoli
war: War with the Turks of Halil in Thrace (1311-1313)
place: the fortified Turkish camp on the Gallipoli peninsula
commanders_a: Michael IX Palaiologos (per modern accounts); Serbian cavalry sent by Stefan Milutin
roman_force: An imperial army with 2,000 cavalry sent by Stefan Milutin of Serbia (Serbian or Cuman horse; the sources disagree), while a Genoese fleet blockaded the Turks by sea.
greek_note: The imperial troops of Thrace were mainly Greek; the Serbian (or Cuman) horse and the Genoese crews were allies.
sources: Gregoras book 7; Manuel Philes (poem); Nicol (1993) 139; Bartusis (1997) 83; en.wikipedia Battle of Gallipoli (1312)
note: Halil's band (fewer than 2,000 Turks and Turcopoles) had served with the Catalan Company; not a beylik. Earlier in 1312 the protostrator Philes Palaiologos had defeated part of them in Thrace (Gregoras).

name: Manolada
place: Manolada, on the plain of Elis, northeast of Glarentza
commanders_a: Louis of Burgundy; troops sent by Michael Kantakouzenos, the imperial governor of Mystras
borderline: The Roman contingent from Mystras is stated in the English Wikipedia article without a citation; its presence and role in the battle are not securely attested.
roman_force: A contingent of imperial troops from the province of the Morea, sent by its governor Michael Kantakouzenos to reinforce Louis of Burgundy's Burgundian and Achaean army; its size is not recorded.
greek_note: The imperial province of the Morea raised its soldiers among the Greek-speaking Moreots of Laconia and Arcadia.
sources: Ramon Muntaner, Chronicle; en.wikipedia Battle of Manolada
note: Fought between Louis of Burgundy, husband of Matilda of Hainaut, and the Infante Ferdinand of Majorca, claimant through his wife Isabella of Sabran; Ferdinand's death ended the Majorcan claim. 'Majorca' stands for Ferdinand's Catalan and Majorcan troops with his Achaean partisans (new short name).

name: Bursa (siege)
borderline: A long blockade that ended in surrender, with little recorded fighting.
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Prusa, cut off by Ottoman forts and never relieved during the civil war of 1321-28.
greek_note: A Greek city of Bithynia defended by its own garrison.
sources: Gregoras; Chalkokondyles 1; Aşıkpaşazade; en.wikipedia Siege of Bursa
note: Start dated 1317 (Wikipedia article), 1320 (Wikipedia list) or even c. 1302 in Ottoman tradition.

name: Saint George
war: Wars of the imperial province of the Morea against Achaea
place: below the castle of Saint George in Skorta, Arcadia
commanders_a: Andronikos Asen (governor of the Morea at Mystras)
commanders_b: Frederick Trogisio (bailli); Bartholomew II Ghisi (captured); James, Bishop of Olena (captured); the commanders of the Teutonic Knights (killed) and of the Hospitallers in Achaea
roman_force: The forces of the imperial province of the Morea under Andronikos Asen; the sources give no composition. The Morea's armies were raised from its Greek archons and Tsakonians, with mercenaries.
greek_note: Inferred from the recruitment of the Mystras province's troops among the Peloponnesian Greeks.
sources: Chronicle of the Morea (French and Aragonese versions); Topping in Setton (ed.), A History of the Crusades III (1975) 117-118; Bon, La Morée franque (1969); en.wikipedia Battle of Saint George
note: Asen took the castle (its Greek castellan surrendered) and kept the Achaean banners flying to ambush the relief army. Imperial Morea before the despotate of 1349.

name: Philadelphia (siege)
borderline: How much fighting there was is unclear; Gregoras credits the relief largely to Philanthropenos's reputation among the Turks.
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Philadelphia; the blind Alexios Philanthropenos, sent from Constantinople with few men, raised the siege (Gregoras).
greek_note: An isolated Greek city defended by its own people, under a Greek general.
sources: Gregoras book 8; en.wikipedia Second Siege of Philadelphia (on the third siege)
note: Beylik: Germiyan.

name: Philippopolis (siege)
war: War with Bulgaria (George Terter II and Michael Shishman), 1322-1324
commanders_a: Ivan the Russian, his deputy Inas; the Alan chiefs Itil and Temir
commanders_b: Andronikos III; the Bulgarian despot Voysil of Kopsis (ally)
roman_force: Andronikos III's army, with the Bulgarian despot Voysil of Kopsis as an ally and German specialists who built a siege engine from which crossbowmen shot at the defenders (Kantakouzenos).
greek_note: Andronikos III's army of the civil-war years was raised in Thrace; the sources name only the Bulgarian ally and the German engineers as foreign elements.
sources: Kantakouzenos book 1; Gregoras book 8; en.wikipedia Ivan the Russian
note: The defenders had about 1,000 Alan horse and 2,000 foot, with Bulgarian (perhaps also Hungarian) troops. The siege failed, but the city was taken soon afterwards when pro-imperial citizens opened the gates to a hidden detachment as the garrison was being relieved (no battle).

name: Nicaea (siege)
commanders_b: unknown; Andronikos III led the relief attempt of 1329
borderline: A blockade that ended in surrender; the main fighting was the relief battle of Pelekanon (separate entry).
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Nicaea, supplied for a time across the lake; the relief army of 1329 is the Pelekanon entry.
greek_note: A Greek city of Bithynia defended by its own garrison.
sources: Kantakouzenos; Gregoras; en.wikipedia Siege of Nicaea (1328-1331)
note: The inhabitants who wished were allowed to leave.

name: Pelekanon
place: Pelekanon, near Philokrene, on the road from Chalcedon to Nicomedia
commanders_b: Andronikos III, the megas domestikos John Kantakouzenos
roman_force: About 4,000 men, the largest force Andronikos III could gather: about 2,000 from Constantinople and somewhat fewer from Thrace (Kantakouzenos).
greek_note: Kantakouzenos describes an army raised in Constantinople and Thrace, with no foreign contingents named.
sources: Kantakouzenos book 2; Gregoras; en.wikipedia Battle of Pelekanon
note: Pelekanon is placed by Wikipedia at modern Maltepe, by others near Darıca/Eskihisar on the Gulf of Nicomedia; the coordinates are a compromise. The army broke when the wounded emperor was rumoured dead; it was the last imperial field campaign in Asia.

name: Rusokastro
commanders_b: Andronikos III, John Kantakouzenos, Alexios Tzamplakon, Manuel Asen
roman_force: About 3,000 men (Kantakouzenos; other figures up to 8,000) in 16 units, the field army of Thrace under the emperor; no foreign contingents are named.
greek_note: The imperial army of the 1330s was raised mainly from the Greek pronoia soldiers of Thrace and Macedonia.
sources: Kantakouzenos book 2; Gregoras; en.wikipedia Battle of Rusokastro
note: Ivan Alexander had about 8,000 Bulgarians with 2,000 Tatar (Golden Horde) mercenaries, and 3,000 more horse joined him the night before. The imperial army withdrew into Rusokastro, which was then besieged until a peace was agreed.

name: Nicomedia (siege)
borderline: A blockade that ended in surrender, with no recorded assaults.
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Nicomedia, supplied by sea for some years; Andronikos III visited in 1333 and paid tribute to Orhan.
greek_note: A Greek city of Bithynia defended by its own garrison.
sources: Kantakouzenos; Gregoras; en.wikipedia Siege of Nicomedia
note: The garrison, short of food, surrendered and the inhabitants were allowed to leave for Constantinople.

name: Saint Eugenios (Trebizond)
place: The fortified monastery of Saint Eugenios, inside the walls of Trebizond
commanders_a: Empress Irene Palaiologina; the megas doux John the Eunuch
roman_force: Irene's party: the Amytzantarioi, her mercenaries from Constantinople and the men of the megas doux John the Eunuch from Limnia, who brought siege engines; against them the native archons holding the monastery. Two months of daily skirmishing preceded the assault.
greek_note: Panaretos describes a fight between Trapezuntine noble factions and the empress's mercenaries from Constantinople.
sources: Panaretos; en.wikipedia Irene Palaiologina of Trebizond
note: The monastery was almost destroyed; Tzanichites was sent to Limnia and executed about a year later.

name: Arta (siege)
place: Arta, with the nearby fortress of Rogoi
commanders_b: Epirote archons in the name of Nikephoros II Orsini
borderline: The revolt was put down mainly by blockade and negotiation; the scale of fighting at Arta and Rogoi is not well recorded.
roman_force: Imperial side: the field army that Andronikos III and Kantakouzenos brought into Epirus in 1340 (the sources give no numbers; in the Albanian campaign of 1337 the army had included 2,000 Turks sent by Umur of Aydin). Rebel side: the townsmen and archons of Arta and Rogoi, who had seized the governor Theodore Synadenos.
greek_note: The rebels were the Greek archons and townsmen of Epirus; the imperial army was raised in Thrace and Macedonia.
sources: Kantakouzenos 2.37-38; Gregoras; Nicol, The Despotate of Epiros 1267-1479 (1984); en.wikipedia Nikephoros II Orsini; en.wikipedia Despotate of Epirus
note: The revolt broke out in late 1338 or 1339 at the instigation of Catherine of Valois; Arta and Rogoi submitted to the emperor in 1340 before the siege of Thomokastron.

name: Thomokastron (siege)
place: Thomokastron (Riniasa), on the Ionian coast of Epirus
borderline: Ended in a negotiated surrender (Kantakouzenos guaranteed Nikephoros's safety); fighting is not described in detail.
roman_force: Imperial side: Andronikos III's army in Epirus; rebel side: the young despot Nikephoros II and the Epirote garrison of Thomokastron, backed by Catherine of Valois (Angevin Achaea). No numbers are given.
greek_note: Both armies were drawn from the Greek-speaking provinces of the empire and of Epirus.
sources: Kantakouzenos 2.38; Gregoras; Nicol, The Despotate of Epiros (1984); en.wikipedia Nikephoros II Orsini
note: Nikephoros surrendered the fortress, married Maria Kantakouzene and was made panhypersebastos.

name: Trebizond
war: Wars of Trebizond with the Turkmen
roman_force: The army of Trebizond under Irene's regime, demoralized by the civil strife; the sources give no numbers.
greek_note: Trebizond's levies were Greek-speaking Pontic townsmen and archons' retinues, with some Laz.
sources: Panaretos; en.wikipedia Irene Palaiologina of Trebizond; en.wikipedia Aq Qoyunlu
note: Panaretos's 'Turks of Amida' are usually identified with Tur Ali Beg's Aq Qoyunlu, who had raided the Bayburt district in 1340. An earlier attack had been beaten off on the Parcharia; this one burned much of the city, which was not taken.

name: Didymoteicho (siege)
commanders_a: Irene Kantakouzene (in the city); Umur Bey of Aydin (relief)
roman_force: Defenders: Kantakouzenos's partisans in Didymoteicho under his wife Irene; relief: Umur of Aydin, who came up the Evros with about 300 ships and 29,000 men (Kantakouzenos's figure; Turkish sources 15,000). Besiegers: the regency's Thracian forces.
greek_note: The garrison and the besiegers were Thracian Romans; the relieving army was Umur's Turks.
sources: Kantakouzenos 3; Gregoras; Enveri, Düsturname; en.wikipedia, the article on the civil war of 1341-47
note: Ivan Alexander of Bulgaria's troops came, clashed with the regency's forces but pillaged the countryside instead of helping the city. Umur raised the siege and plundered Thrace before withdrawing at the onset of winter.

name: Serres (siege)
borderline: The siege was abandoned because of disease; the amount of fighting is not recorded.
roman_force: Kantakouzenos's Greek-Serbian army (by now about 2,000 men, half of them Serbs) against the town's regency garrison and citizens; an epidemic forced Kantakouzenos to retreat into Serbia with about 500 men.
greek_note: The defenders were the Greek citizens of Serres; about half of Kantakouzenos's army was Serbian.
sources: Kantakouzenos 3; Gregoras; en.wikipedia, the article on the civil war of 1341-47

name: Thessalonica (siege)
commanders_b: John VI Kantakouzenos, Umur Bey of Aydin
roman_force: Defenders: the Zealot regime and the people of Thessalonica, for the regency; Apokaukos's fleet fled before Umur's navy, which carried about 6,000 men. Besiegers: Kantakouzenos's Macedonian partisans with Umur's Turks.
greek_note: The defenders were the citizens of Thessalonica; the besieging army was largely Umur's Turks.
sources: Kantakouzenos 3; Gregoras; en.wikipedia, the article on the civil war of 1341-47; en.wikipedia Zealots of Thessalonica
note: The siege failed and Kantakouzenos turned back to Thrace. The Zealots held the city until 1349-50.

name: Komotini
borderline: An attack on a camp that is not usually given a name.
roman_force: Momchil, then holding imperial titles and siding with the regency, attacked with 1,000 horsemen; Kantakouzenos was guarded by about 60 horsemen, was unhorsed and barely escaped.
greek_note: Momchil's men were Bulgarian and Greek highlanders of the Rhodope; Kantakouzenos's guard was Greek.
sources: Kantakouzenos 3; Gregoras; en.wikipedia Momchil
note: Momchil had earlier sunk three of fifteen Turkish (Aydinid) ships at Porto Lagos and beaten a Turkish force near Peritheorion.

name: Peritheorion
place: Before the walls of Peritheorion (Anastasioupolis), on Lake Vistonida
commanders_a: John VI Kantakouzenos, Umur Bey of Aydin, John Asen
borderline: Momchil, a Bulgarian brigand-lord of the Rhodope, held the titles sebastokrator (from Kantakouzenos) and despot (from the regency) but was by 1345 virtually independent; if he is not counted as Roman the battle is a victory over a Bulgarian force.
roman_force: Kantakouzenos's army with Umur's Aydinid Turks, over 20,000 in all; Umur held the right wing and the Roman noble John Asen the left. Momchil had about 5,000 infantry and 300 cavalry.
greek_note: Kantakouzenos's own Roman troops fought beside a larger Turkish contingent from Aydin.
sources: Kantakouzenos 3; Gregoras; Fine, The Late Medieval Balkans (1987); en.wikipedia Battle of Peritheorion
note: The citizens of Peritheorion shut their gates on Momchil; his cavalry was destroyed by Turkish archers and he was killed fighting on foot.

name: Serres (siege)
war: Civil war of 1341-47 (Serbian conquest of Macedonia)
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Serres, loyal to the regency; no numbers are given.
greek_note: A Greek city of eastern Macedonia defended by its own garrison and townsmen.
sources: Kantakouzenos 3; Gregoras; en.wikipedia, the article on the civil war of 1341-47
note: Dušan was crowned emperor of the Serbs and Romans in 1346, after the fall of Serres.

name: Chios (siege)
commanders_b: Kaloioannes Tzybos, governor of the citadel
roman_force: The imperial garrison of the citadel under the governor Kaloioannes Tzybos and the Greek islanders, who refused the first summons with the cry 'Death to the Genoese'; no help came from Constantinople, then in civil war. The Genoese came with a private fleet of 29 galleys.
greek_note: The defenders were the Greek inhabitants of Chios.
sources: Gregoras; Kantakouzenos 3; Argenti, The Occupation of Chios by the Genoese (1958); en.wikipedia Simone Vignoso
note: The Genoese landed on 15 June and took most of the island within a week; the citadel held out until 12 September 1346, when Tzybos and the archons capitulated on lenient terms. Vignoso then occupied Old and New Phokaia. The island passed to the Genoese Maona.

name: Constantinople
borderline: The city did not resist; the only fighting was a limited storming of part of the palace.
roman_force: Kantakouzenos entered by the disused Golden Gate with 1,000 men; the regency's palace guards held Blachernae until part of the complex was stormed.
greek_note: Kantakouzenos's Thracian troops against the palace guard of Constantinople.
sources: Kantakouzenos 3-4; Gregoras; en.wikipedia, the article on the civil war of 1341-47
note: John V persuaded his mother to accept a settlement; Kantakouzenos became senior emperor.

name: Trebizond (siege)
war: Wars of Trebizond with the Turkmen
commanders_b: Tur Ali Beg (Aq Qoyunlu) or Bayram of Chalybia with allied beys
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Trebizond during the civil wars and the Black Death; the sources give no numbers.
greek_note: A Greek city defended by its townsmen and archons.
sources: Panaretos; en.wikipedia Aq Qoyunlu; en.wikipedia Empire of Trebizond
note: The Turkmen invasion was defeated in a three-day battle (en.wikipedia Michael of Trebizond, after Miller); en.wikipedia (Emirate of Chalybia) names Bayram of Chalybia and other beys as the besiegers, so the attackers may not be the Aq Qoyunlu. The Turks had taken Oinaion in 1347-48; in the same years the Genoese seized Kerasous.

name: Golden Horn
place: Off Galata, at the mouth of the Golden Horn
roman_force: A newly built fleet of about nine large ships and some 100 smaller craft, paid for by private loans and crewed by inexperienced Constantinopolitans, with the emperor's land army attacking Galata at the same time.
greek_note: Kantakouzenos and Gregoras describe the crews as the citizens of Constantinople.
sources: Kantakouzenos 4; Gregoras; Nicol (1993); en.wikipedia, the article on the Genoese war of 1348-49
note: The imperial crews panicked and abandoned their ships, which the Genoese captured; the land attack also broke. In the following weeks the Romans burned Galata's wharves, and peace was made in spring 1349 on terms favourable to Genoa.

name: Trebizond
borderline: A naval defeat known from brief notices; not usually given a name as a battle.
roman_force: The small fleet of Trebizond under the megas doux John Kabazites; no numbers are recorded.
greek_note: The fleet was manned in Trebizond, a Greek-speaking city.
sources: Miller, Trebizond (1926) 54, after Panaretos; en.wikipedia Michael of Trebizond
note: The Trapezuntine fleet was destroyed, and the people of Trebizond then killed the Westerners in the city; in the peace that followed the Genoese received Leontokastron and gave back Kerasous, which they had seized in 1348.

name: Galata
place: Off Galata (Pera), at the mouth of the Golden Horn
commanders_b: unknown (the fleet of John VI Kantakouzenos)
roman_force: The imperial fleet of Constantinople, which with a Venetian squadron had blockaded Pera, left alone when the Venetians withdrew to Negroponte on news of the approach of Paganino Doria's Genoese fleet.
greek_note: The imperial fleet was manned in Constantinople.
sources: Gregoras; Kantakouzenos 4; en.wikipedia War of the Straits
note: A sea fight, not a joint attack on Pera: after the Venetian squadron abandoned the blockade, the imperial fleet 'was defeated by the Genoese of Pera on 28 July' 1351 (en.wikipedia War of the Straits). John VI had joined Venice and Aragon against Genoa in May 1351.

name: Heraclea
place: Heraclea (Perinthos, Marmara Ereğlisi) on the Sea of Marmara
borderline: A landing for supplies that turned into a fight with the townsmen and a sack; not usually called a battle.
roman_force: The townsmen and garrison of Heraclea, ordered by Kantakouzenos to strengthen their defences.
greek_note: A Greek town of Thrace defended by its inhabitants.
sources: Gregoras; Kantakouzenos 4; en.wikipedia War of the Straits
note: In November 1351 the Genoese also sacked Sozopolis on the Black Sea.

name: Bosporus
place: The Bosporus, from the Princes' Islands to the narrows at Diplokionion (Beşiktaş)
commanders_b: Niccolò Pisani, Pancrazio Giustinian (killed), Pons de Santapau; Constantine Tarchaneiotes (imperial squadron)
borderline: The imperial squadron apparently did not engage; Rome was a minor allied belligerent.
roman_force: Fourteen imperial galleys under Constantine Tarchaneiotes in an allied fleet of 89-90 (45 Venetian, 30 Aragonese); the imperial ships withdrew before the main fighting.
greek_note: The imperial squadron was manned in Constantinople; the Roman share of the whole allied fleet was small.
sources: Gregoras; Kantakouzenos 4; Venetian and Genoese chronicles; en.wikipedia Battle of the Bosporus
note: Tactically indecisive (allies lost 23 galleys, Genoa 16) and fought largely at night in a storm, but the Genoese held the field. Kantakouzenos made peace with Genoa on 6 May 1352.

name: Demotika
borderline: Fought by the foreign allies of the two Roman factions; no Roman troops are recorded in the battle itself.
roman_force: Kantakouzenos's side was represented by about 10,000 Ottoman horsemen sent by Orhan under his son Süleyman; John V's side by 4,000-6,000 Serbian cavalry sent by Stefan Dušan, perhaps with Bulgarians.
greek_note: The sources describe only Ottoman troops on Kantakouzenos's side; any Roman participation was small.
sources: Kantakouzenos 4; Gregoras; Fine, The Late Medieval Balkans (1987); en.wikipedia Battle of Demotika
note: Kantakouzenos claimed about 7,000 Serbs killed, Gregoras about 4,000. Often called the first Ottoman victory in Europe; John V fled to Tenedos.

name: Adrianople (siege)
commanders_a: Matthew Kantakouzenos (in the citadel), John VI Kantakouzenos (relief)
borderline: Details of the fighting are scant.
roman_force: Matthew held the citadel after the townsmen let John V in; John VI relieved him with about 10,000 Ottoman troops lent by Orhan. John V had Venetian money, Serbian troops and hired Turkish mercenaries.
greek_note: Matthew's garrison was Roman; the relief army was mostly Ottoman.
sources: Kantakouzenos 4; Gregoras; Nicol, The Reluctant Emperor (1996); en.wikipedia, the article on the civil war of 1352-57; en.wikipedia Battle of Demotika
note: The Ottomans then plundered the Thracian towns that had declared for John V.

name: Constantinople
borderline: A failed coup attempt; little fighting is recorded.
roman_force: John V sailed from Tenedos with a few ships and his partisans, hoping for a rising in the capital; Kantakouzenos's garrison held the city.
greek_note: A clash between the two imperial factions in the capital.
sources: Kantakouzenos 4; Gregoras; en.wikipedia, the article on the civil war of 1352-57
note: John V finally entered the capital with Genoese help (Francesco Gattilusio) in November 1354, without a recorded battle, and Kantakouzenos abdicated.

name: Gallipoli
borderline: An occupation of a town ruined by an earthquake, not a battle; included because standard lists treat the fall of Gallipoli as a named event.
roman_force: The surviving inhabitants and garrison of Gallipoli, whose walls had been thrown down by the earthquake of 2 March 1354.
greek_note: A Greek town of the Thracian Chersonese.
sources: Kantakouzenos 4; Gregoras; en.wikipedia, the list of battles of the Roman Empire (East); en.wikipedia, the article on the civil war of 1352-57
note: Süleyman settled Turks there and refused Kantakouzenos's offers to buy it back; it was the first permanent Ottoman base in Europe.

name: Kerasous
war: Trapezuntine civil war (Alexios III against Niketas Scholares)
place: Kerasous (Giresun), with the later siege of Kenchrina
borderline: The fighting at Kerasous and Kenchrina is barely recorded; possibly no real battle.
roman_force: Alexios III sailed with his own fleet and took the town while Niketas was absent; his cavalry then obtained the surrender of Kenchrina, the last rebel fortress.
greek_note: Both sides were Trapezuntine Greeks.
sources: Panaretos; en.wikipedia Alexios III of Trebizond
note: In March 1355 Niketas's seaborne attack on Trebizond had been abandoned without a fight; Niketas was captured and died in Trebizond in 1360.

name: Cheriana
war: Wars of Trebizond with the Turkmen
place: Cheriana (Şiran), south of the Pontic mountains
roman_force: The army of Trebizond under Alexios III, with the chronicler Michael Panaretos, who barely escaped with his life; no numbers are given.
greek_note: Trebizond's army was raised from the Greek-speaking archons and their retinues of Pontus.
sources: Panaretos; en.wikipedia Michael Panaretos; en.wikipedia Alexios III of Trebizond
note: The Turkmen are not identified; Cheriana lay on the frontier with the Turkmen of the Kelkit valley.

name: Serres
roman_force: Matthew Kantakouzenos, still claiming the imperial title, led about 5,000 Turkish troops; no Roman contingent is described.
greek_note: Matthew's army was almost entirely hired Turks.
sources: Kantakouzenos 4; Gregoras; Nicol, The Reluctant Emperor (1996); en.wikipedia Matthew Kantakouzenos
note: Matthew's attack on Serbian Serres failed; he was captured and John V paid Vojihna to hand him over, after which Matthew renounced the throne.

name: Achelous
commanders_a: Karl Thopia (per Wikipedia) and the Albanian clan chiefs
roman_force: The despot Nikephoros II's Epirote army, which had recovered Thessaly and Epirus in 1356, with a band of Turkish corsairs hired after they had raided Thessaly; no numbers are given.
greek_note: Nikephoros's support came from the Greek nobility and towns of Epirus and Thessaly, with Turkish mercenaries.
sources: Kantakouzenos 4; Nicol, The Despotate of Epiros (1984); en.wikipedia Battle of Achelous (1359); en.wikipedia Nikephoros II Orsini
note: Nikephoros's army was destroyed; the Albanian clans divided Aetolia-Acarnania (despotates of Arta and Angelokastron), and only Ioannina stayed under Greek rule.

name: Blue Waters
war: Lithuanian wars with the Golden Horde
place: The Syniukha river (Blue Waters), a tributary of the Southern Bug
commanders_b: the Tatar princes Khaçi Bey, Kutlu Buga and Dmitri (Demetrios)
borderline: The identification of the Tatar prince Dmitri with a Greek prince of Theodoro is a modern hypothesis; no Theodorite force is securely attested.
roman_force: If the prince Demetrios of the sources is the first known lord of Theodoro, he would have led a contingent of his Crimean subjects (Greeks, Goths and Alans) beside the Golden Horde's Tatar princes; nothing is known of its size.
greek_note: The presence and makeup of any Theodorite force are conjectural.
sources: Russian and Lithuanian chronicles; Vasiliev, The Goths in the Crimea (1936); en.wikipedia Principality of Theodoro; en.wikipedia Battle of Blue Waters
note: Lithuania won and took Podolia and Kiev from the Horde.

name: Gallipoli
commanders_a: Amadeus VI of Savoy; Francesco I Gattilusio, lord of Lesbos
borderline: A crusade fought on John V's behalf; any imperial participation in the assault is uncertain. Included because the list of battles of the Roman Empire (East) counts it.
roman_force: The Savoyard crusade's fifteen ships, joined at the Dardanelles by the flotilla of Francesco Gattilusio, John V's brother-in-law and vassal; the Savoyard chronicles also mention a Roman detachment under the patriarch of Constantinople.
greek_note: The assault force was Savoyard and Italian; the Roman element, if present, was small.
sources: Chronicles of Savoy; Cox, The Green Count of Savoy (1967); en.wikipedia Savoyard crusade; en.wikipedia, the list of battles of the Roman Empire (East)
note: The walls were assaulted on 22 August; the Turks left overnight and the townsmen opened the gates. Gallipoli was handed to the empire on 13 June 1367 and returned to the Ottomans in 1376/77.

name: Adrianople
place: Sazlıdere, southeast of Adrianople (Edirne), and the city
borderline: The battle at Sazlıdere is known only from later Ottoman sources; the city may have fallen to independent akıncı bands.
roman_force: The Roman governor's garrison and townsmen of Adrianople; the sources give no numbers.
greek_note: Adrianople was a Greek city of Thrace defended by its own garrison.
sources: Greek short chronicles; Ottoman chronicles (Aşıkpaşazade, Neşri); en.wikipedia Battle of Adrianople (1365)
note: Most modern scholars date the fall to 1369 (the metropolitan's poem shows the city still Roman at Christmas 1366); Wikipedia's article is titled 1365. After his defeat the tekfur fled by boat; the city surrendered.

name: Gardiki
war: Wars of the Despotate of the Morea with Achaea
commanders_a: Francis of San Severino, bailli of Achaea; Andronikos Asen and Martino Zaccaria
commanders_b: Manuel Kantakouzenos, despot of the Morea
roman_force: About 1,000 cavalry and 2,000 infantry of the despotate, raised from the Moreot archons and their followers; Achaea had about 300 cavalry and 600 infantry.
greek_note: Manuel's army was raised in the Greek despotate, which had begun to settle Albanians but still drew mostly on Greek archons and Tsakonians.
sources: Chronicle of the Morea (Aragonese version); Bon, La Morée franque (1969); en.wikipedia Battle of Gardiki
note: The charge of the newly dubbed Latin knights drove the despot from the field, but the castle held out and the bailli raised the siege.

name: Constantinople (siege)
borderline: The details and scale of the fighting are poorly recorded.
roman_force: Andronikos IV, freed with Genoese help, came with a mixed force of Ottoman cavalry and infantry from Murad I and the support of the Genoese of Galata; John V's loyalists held the city for about a month.
greek_note: Andronikos's own following was Roman, but his striking force was Ottoman and his base Genoese Galata.
sources: Chalkokondyles 1; Doukas; short chronicles; Barker, Manuel II Palaeologus (1969); en.wikipedia Andronikos IV Palaiologos
note: Andronikos was crowned in 1377 and imprisoned John V and Manuel; he gave Tenedos to Genoa, whose governor handed it to Venice instead, starting the War of Chioggia.

name: Galata (siege)
commanders_a: John V Palaiologos, Manuel II Palaiologos
borderline: The fighting around Galata, part of the Venetian-Genoese War of Chioggia, is poorly recorded; the recapture of the capital in July 1379 may have met little resistance.
roman_force: John V and Manuel, escaped to Murad, regained the capital with Venetian ships and Ottoman soldiers; Andronikos IV held out in Galata with the Genoese, keeping his mother Helena and John VI Kantakouzenos as hostages.
greek_note: The loyalists of John V in the capital were Roman; the Venetian and Ottoman contingents were auxiliary.
sources: Chalkokondyles 1; Doukas; short chronicles; Barker, Manuel II Palaeologus (1969); en.wikipedia Andronikos IV Palaiologos; en.wikipedia, the article on the civil war of 1373-79
note: Ended by agreement in May 1381: Andronikos was restored as heir and given Selymbria.

name: Serres (siege)
commanders_a: Çandarlı Hayreddin Pasha (Kara Halil), with Evrenos
borderline: The length of the siege and the extent of fighting are uncertain.
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Serres, which Manuel II had recovered from the Serbs after 1371; no numbers are given.
greek_note: A Greek city of eastern Macedonia.
sources: Short chronicles; Dennis, The Reign of Manuel II Palaeologus in Thessalonica (1960); en.wikipedia Siege of Thessalonica (1383-1387)
note: The population was enslaved; the Ottomans reached Thessalonica in October 1383.

name: Thessalonica (siege)
roman_force: Manuel II's garrison and the citizens of Thessalonica, supplied by sea; no outside help came, and the townsmen, fearing massacre, forced Manuel out.
greek_note: The defenders were the Greek citizens and garrison of Thessalonica.
sources: Manuel II, Discourse of Counsel to the Thessalonians; Kydones, letters; short chronicles; Dennis (1960); en.wikipedia Siege of Thessalonica (1383-1387)
note: Mostly a blockade. Manuel left on 6 April 1387 and the city opened its gates on 9 April on terms (a tax and a small garrison).

name: Chortiatis
place: Chortiatis (Chortaites), the mountain east of Thessalonica
borderline: Known from brief notices; not described in the English Wikipedia articles consulted.
roman_force: Manuel II's small army from Thessalonica, raised from the city's archons and townsmen; no numbers are given.
greek_note: Manuel's forces in Thessalonica were drawn from the city and its hinterland.
sources: Short chronicles; Dennis, The Reign of Manuel II Palaeologus in Thessalonica (1960); Nicol (1993)
note: A Roman defeat outside Thessalonica just before the Ottoman siege began; the exact date and course are uncertain.

name: Constantinople
place: Constantinople (the Charisian Gate and the Golden Gate fortress)
commanders_a: Manuel II Palaiologos, John V Palaiologos
borderline: John VII's entry was unopposed; the fighting of Manuel's recapture is poorly recorded.
roman_force: John VII, backed by Bayezid I and the Genoese, entered on 14 April when citizens opened the Charisian Gate; John V held out in the fortress of the Golden Gate. Manuel II returned from Lemnos with his own ships and galleys of the Knights Hospitaller and forced his way in on 17 September.
greek_note: Both factions drew on the citizens of Constantinople; the Hospitaller and Ottoman contingents were small.
sources: Short chronicles; Ignatius of Smolensk; Barker, Manuel II Palaeologus (1969); en.wikipedia John VII Palaiologos; en.wikipedia Manuel II Palaiologos
note: 'Crusaders' here stands for the Knights Hospitaller of Rhodes.

name: Philadelphia (siege)
commanders_a: Bayezid I (with Manuel II and John VII as vassals)
borderline: The fighting is not described; Romans also served on the attacking side as Ottoman vassals.
roman_force: The citizens of Philadelphia, the last Roman city in Anatolia, autonomous but loyal to the emperor; it refused to submit and was reduced by Bayezid's army, in which Manuel II and John VII had to serve as vassals.
greek_note: A Greek city of Lydia that had defended itself for decades.
sources: Chalkokondyles 2; Doukas; short chronicles; en.wikipedia, the list of battles of the Roman Empire (East); en.wikipedia Manuel II Palaiologos
note: Some date the fall to 1378/79; 1390 is the usual date.

name: Constantinople (siege)
commanders_a: Manuel II Palaiologos; John VII Palaiologos (regent from December 1399); Jean II Le Maingre, Marshal Boucicaut; Jean de Châteaumorand
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Constantinople, reinforced in 1399 by Boucicaut's French expedition (about 1,200 men) and then by Châteaumorand's garrison of about 100 men-at-arms with their valets and crossbowmen; Venetian and Genoese galleys helped keep the sea open.
greek_note: The defence rested on the city's own population, with small French and Italian reinforcements.
sources: Doukas; Chalkokondyles 2; Livre des faits de Boucicaut; Barker, Manuel II Palaeologus (1969); en.wikipedia Siege of Constantinople (1394-1402)
note: Mostly a land blockade, with Anadoluhisarı built to control the Bosporus. Bayezid's defeat by Timur at Ankara (20 July 1402) ended it; the Nicopolis crusade (1396), to which Manuel sent ten ships, is not counted as a Roman battle.

name: Akova (siege)
war: Wars of the Despotate of the Morea with Achaea
commanders_a: Evrenos Bey; Pedro de San Superano
roman_force: The despotate's garrison of Akova, held by the Romans since 1320; no numbers are given.
greek_note: A castle garrisoned by the despotate's Greek troops.
sources: Venetian documents; Topping in Setton (ed.), A History of the Crusades III (1975); en.wikipedia Pedro de San Superano; en.wikipedia Theodore I Palaiologos
note: Evrenos and the Navarrese prince met at Leontari and together besieged and took Akova.

name: Morea (4 June 1395)
war: Wars of the Despotate of the Morea with Achaea
commanders_b: Pedro de San Superano, Andronikos Asen Zaccaria (both captured)
borderline: An unnamed engagement whose site is unknown.
roman_force: The forces of the despotate under Theodore I; no details are recorded.
greek_note: Theodore I's army was Greek, with Albanian settlers he had begun to bring into the Morea.
sources: Venetian documents; en.wikipedia Andronikos Asen Zaccaria; en.wikipedia Pedro de San Superano
note: After Evrenos returned to Thessaly the Navarrese prince and his constable were defeated and captured by the Greeks; Venice paid 50,000 hyperpyra for their release in December 1395.

name: Constantinople (siege)
commanders_a: Manuel II Palaiologos (with Mehmed Çelebi's troops)
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Constantinople, with troops of Mehmed Çelebi admitted to the city at Manuel's request; their sorties failed.
greek_note: The defence rested on the city's own population, with an allied Ottoman contingent.
sources: Doukas; Chalkokondyles 4; Kastritsis, The Sons of Bayezid (2007); en.wikipedia Siege of Constantinople (1411); en.wikipedia Ottoman Interregnum
note: Musa besieged the city to punish Manuel's support of Süleyman; he also attacked Thessalonica and Selymbria. The siege was lifted and Mehmed, Manuel's ally, defeated Musa at Çamurlu (5 July 1413).

name: İnceğiz
place: İnceğiz, near Çatalca, west of Constantinople
borderline: An Ottoman civil-war battle with only a small Roman contingent.
roman_force: A few Roman troops fought under Mehmed Çelebi, Manuel II's ally, whose army was otherwise Anatolian Turks, Tatars and Turcomans (Doukas).
greek_note: Doukas mentions only a few Roman soldiers in Mehmed's army.
sources: Doukas; Kastritsis (2007); en.wikipedia Battle of İnceğiz
note: Musa's 7,000 kapıkulu decided it; Mehmed fell back on Constantinople and crossed to Anatolia. side_a is Musa's faction, side_b Mehmed's.

name: Glarentza (siege)
war: Wars of the Despotate of the Morea with Achaea
commanders_a: Theodore II Palaiologos, John VIII Palaiologos
roman_force: The imperial army that Manuel II had led to the Morea in 1415, under the despot Theodore II and the young co-emperor John VIII; it overran Messenia and Elis before besieging Centurione in Glarentza.
greek_note: The army combined troops from Constantinople with the Moreot levies, Greek and Albanian.
sources: Sphrantzes; Chalkokondyles; Zakythinos, Le Despotat grec de Morée (1932); en.wikipedia Centurione II Zaccaria
note: Centurione fled by sea in spring 1418 and Venice, from Navarino, mediated a truce; Glarentza itself was not taken (it soon passed to Oliverio Franco and then Carlo Tocco). The campaign won most of Messenia and Elis.

name: Gallipoli (siege)
commanders_a: Mustafa Çelebi, Junayd of Aydin; Demetrios Laskaris Leontares
borderline: The Roman role was as an allied force of an Ottoman pretender. side_a 'Ottomans' is Mustafa's faction, side_b Murad II's.
roman_force: The pretender Mustafa and his Turkish followers, released from Lemnos and carried by imperial galleys, with a Roman force under Demetrios Laskaris Leontares, in return for a promise to cede Gallipoli.
greek_note: Mustafa's army was Turkish; the Roman contingent and fleet under Leontares were a minority.
sources: Doukas; Sphrantzes; Chalkokondyles 5; en.wikipedia Demetrios Laskaris Leontares
note: Mustafa took Gallipoli but then refused to hand it over; Leontares was rebuffed when he demanded it, and Murad II defeated Mustafa in early 1422.

name: Constantinople (siege)
commanders_a: Manuel II Palaiologos, John VIII Palaiologos
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Constantinople, short of soldiers, defending their own walls (John Kananos); both sides had small cannon.
greek_note: Kananos's eyewitness account describes the Constantinopolitans defending their own walls; no foreign contingent is named.
sources: John Kananos; Doukas; Sphrantzes; short chronicles; en.wikipedia Siege of Constantinople (1422)
note: The general assault of 24 August was beaten off (credited by the Romans to an apparition of the Theotokos); Murad lifted the siege to deal with the revolt of his brother Küçük Mustafa, funded by the emperor.

name: Thessalonica (siege)
commanders_a: Burak Bey (1422); Murad II and Sinan Pasha (1430); Hamza Bey
commanders_b: Despot Andronikos Palaiologos (to 1423); Metropolitan Symeon; Venetian governors (Bernardo Loredan, Jacopo Dandolo, Paolo Contarini, Andrea Donato); Antonio Diedo (1430)
borderline: The city was Roman only until September 1423; Venice was the principal defender for the rest of the siege.
roman_force: The despot Andronikos's citizens until September 1423, when he handed the city to Venice; then Venetian officials, galley crews and garrison troops (150-200 soldiers sent in 1424, 200 from Padua in 1425, about 700 crossbowmen on the walls in 1426), the Greek citizens with their council of twelve nobles, the locally recruited Tzetarioi guard and mercenaries paid in wheat.
greek_note: Anagnostes and the Venetian records show the Greek citizens forming most of the defenders, with a Venetian garrison and galley crews from 1423.
sources: John Anagnostes; Symeon of Thessalonica; Doukas; Sphrantzes; Venetian senate records; en.wikipedia Siege of Thessalonica (1422-1430)
note: An assault by about 30,000 Ottomans failed in about 1426. The final assault on 29 March 1430 broke through the eastern walls; the sack lasted three days and Anagnostes reports 7,000 captives.

name: Hexamilion
place: The Hexamilion wall across the Isthmus of Corinth
borderline: The wall was breached with little recorded resistance.
roman_force: The garrison of the Hexamilion, rebuilt by Manuel II in 1415, drawn from the despotate's Greek and Albanian subjects; no numbers are given.
greek_note: The wall was manned by Moreot levies, Greek and Albanian.
sources: Sphrantzes; Chalkokondyles 5; en.wikipedia Turahan Bey; en.wikipedia Hexamilion wall
note: Turahan's cavalry ravaged the interior unopposed and attacked Mystras, Leontari, Gardiki and Davia; the raid was probably a reconnaissance.

name: Echinades
place: Off the Echinades islands, at the mouth of the Gulf of Patras
commanders_a: Leontares (probably Demetrios Laskaris Leontares); John VIII and Constantine Palaiologos in the Morea
commanders_b: Torno Tocco, illegitimate son of Carlo I Tocco
roman_force: The imperial fleet from Constantinople and the Morea under Leontares; Tocco's fleet drew ships from his Ionian islands and Epirus and from Marseille.
greek_note: The imperial fleet was manned in Constantinople and the Morea.
sources: Sphrantzes; Chalkokondyles 5; en.wikipedia Battle of the Echinades (1427)
note: Most of Tocco's ships were taken and over 150 men captured; Torno barely escaped. It was the last naval victory of the empire. 'Tocco' is the Italian house that ruled Epirus and Cephalonia.

name: Glarentza (siege)
commanders_a: John VIII Palaiologos, Constantine Palaiologos, Theodore II Palaiologos
borderline: Ended by treaty rather than by storm.
roman_force: The forces of the despotate under the emperor John VIII and his brothers, besieging the town by land while the imperial fleet blockaded it by sea.
greek_note: Moreot levies, Greek and Albanian, with troops and ships from Constantinople.
sources: Sphrantzes; Chalkokondyles 5; en.wikipedia Battle of the Echinades (1427); en.wikipedia Constantine XI Palaiologos
note: After the defeat at the Echinades Tocco ceded his Moreot lands as the dowry of his niece Maddalena (Theodora), who married Constantine; Glarentza was handed over on 1 May 1428.

name: Patras (siege)
commanders_b: the officers of Archbishop Pandolfo Malatesta
roman_force: Constantine's Moreot army, with Sphrantzes; in the fighting Constantine's horse was killed under him and Sphrantzes was captured (freed on 23 April).
greek_note: Sphrantzes, an eyewitness, describes Constantine's Moreot troops.
sources: Sphrantzes; Chalkokondyles 5; en.wikipedia Constantine XI Palaiologos
note: Patras belonged to its Latin archbishop rather than to the prince of Achaea; 'Principality of Achaea' stands for the Latin Morea. The town accepted Constantine on 4 June 1429; the archbishop's castle held out until July 1430 (Venice tried to intervene).

name: Chalandritsa (siege)
commanders_b: Centurione II Zaccaria, prince of Achaea
roman_force: The despot Thomas's Moreot army; no numbers are given.
greek_note: Moreot levies, Greek and Albanian.
sources: Sphrantzes; Chalkokondyles 5; en.wikipedia Centurione II Zaccaria
note: Centurione resisted for a time, then surrendered; his daughter Catherine married Thomas, who became heir to Achaea (annexed on Centurione's death in 1432).

name: Hexamilion
place: The Hexamilion wall across the Isthmus of Corinth
borderline: A breach and raid; the fighting is not described.
roman_force: The garrison of the Hexamilion; no details are recorded.
greek_note: The wall was manned by Moreot levies, Greek and Albanian.
sources: Chalkokondyles 5; en.wikipedia Turahan Bey; en.wikipedia Hexamilion wall
note: Turahan breached and destroyed the wall again.

name: Cembalo
borderline: A rebellion by which Theodoro took the port; no battle is described.
roman_force: The Greek inhabitants of Cembalo, who rose against the Genoese and handed the castle to Prince Alexios of Theodoro, with Alexios's forces.
greek_note: The rising was by the Greek townsmen of Cembalo; Theodoro's own subjects were Greeks, Goths and Alans.
sources: Genoese records of Caffa; Vasiliev, The Goths in the Crimea (1936); en.wikipedia Principality of Theodoro
note: Alexios had already fought the Genoese in 1422-23. Cembalo revolted again in 1439.

name: Cembalo (siege)
roman_force: Theodoro's garrison and the Greek townsmen of Cembalo; the Genoese came with a large expedition from Genoa.
greek_note: The defenders were the Greek townsmen and the troops of Theodoro.
sources: Genoese records; Vasiliev, The Goths in the Crimea (1936); en.wikipedia Principality of Theodoro
note: The Genoese retook Cembalo and plundered abandoned Kalamita, but were then destroyed by the Crimean Tatars of Hacı Giray near Solkhat; Theodoro recovered Kalamita. Theodorite participation at Solkhat is not attested, so that battle is not counted.

name: Constantinople (siege)
borderline: The scale of the fighting is not recorded.
roman_force: John VIII's garrison held the city; Demetrios, champion of the anti-unionists, attacked with an army raised with Murad II's support, including Ottoman troops. Constantine, summoned from the Morea, was held up on Lemnos by an Ottoman fleet.
greek_note: The defenders were the citizens of Constantinople; Demetrios's army included Ottoman troops.
sources: Sphrantzes; Chalkokondyles 6; en.wikipedia Demetrios Palaiologos; en.wikipedia Matthew Palaiologos Asen
note: Demetrios was repulsed and briefly imprisoned; he and Matthew Asen escaped to Galata.

name: Trebizond
borderline: High surf hampered the landing; the fighting is barely described.
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Trebizond; no numbers are given.
greek_note: A Greek city defended by its own people.
sources: Chalkokondyles; en.wikipedia Empire of Trebizond; en.wikipedia John IV of Trebizond
note: The Ottoman fleet plundered the coasts and Trebizond's Crimean dependencies, failed before the city, and was partly wrecked by a storm on the way back.

name: Thebes
war: Constantine Palaiologos's campaign in central Greece (1444-46)
commanders_a: Constantine Palaiologos, despot of the Morea
borderline: The capture of Thebes and Athens is reported without a description of fighting.
roman_force: Constantine's Moreot army, later joined by 300 Burgundian soldiers sent by Philip the Good; his governor Constantine Kantakouzenos also took Lidoriki from the Ottomans.
greek_note: Moreot levies, Greek and Albanian, with a small Burgundian company.
sources: Chalkokondyles 6; Sphrantzes; en.wikipedia Constantine XI Palaiologos; en.wikipedia, the article on the Ottoman conquest of the Morea
note: Nerio II, an Ottoman vassal, had to pay tribute to Constantine; Constantine's men raided north to the Pindus Vlachs in 1445. Murad II's revenge came in 1446.

name: Hexamilion
place: The Hexamilion wall across the Isthmus of Corinth
roman_force: Up to about 20,000 Moreots, Greeks and Albanians, under the despots Constantine and Thomas, holding the wall rebuilt in 1444; Murad brought perhaps 50,000-60,000 men with heavy cannon.
greek_note: The despotate's army combined Greek archons and townsmen with numerous Albanian settlers.
sources: Chalkokondyles 7; Sphrantzes; en.wikipedia Hexamilion wall; en.wikipedia Constantine XI Palaiologos
note: The cannon reduced the wall to rubble and it was stormed on 10 December; most defenders were killed or captured (some 60,000 Moreots are said to have been enslaved) and the despots became Ottoman tributaries.

name: Hexamilion
place: The Hexamilion wall across the Isthmus of Corinth
commanders_b: the despots Thomas and Demetrios Palaiologos
borderline: Little resistance is recorded.
roman_force: The despots' forces at the ruined wall; no details are recorded.
greek_note: Moreot levies, Greek and Albanian.
sources: Chalkokondyles 8; Sphrantzes; en.wikipedia Turahan Bey
note: Mehmed II sent Turahan to keep the despots from helping Constantinople; his army wintered in the peninsula.

name: Dervenakia
place: The pass of Dervenakia, between Corinth and Argos
roman_force: Moreot troops under Matthew Asen, the despot Demetrios's brother-in-law, who lured the Ottomans into a narrow defile; most of the Turks fell.
greek_note: Moreot levies, Greek and Albanian.
sources: Chalkokondyles 8; Sphrantzes; en.wikipedia Turahan Bey; en.wikipedia Matthew Palaiologos Asen
note: The article on Turahan places the ambush at Dervenakia, that on Matthew Asen near Leontari. Ahmed was held at Mystras and released in 1453/54.

name: Constantinople
place: Constantinople: the land walls (Mesoteichion and Lykos valley), the Golden Horn and the sea walls
commanders_a: Mehmed II; Zagan Pasha, Karaca Pasha, Ishak Pasha, Halil Pasha; Süleyman Baltoğlu (fleet)
commanders_b: Constantine XI Palaiologos (killed); Giovanni Giustiniani Longo (mortally wounded); Loukas Notaras; Theophilos Palaiologos; Demetrios Kantakouzenos; Nikephoros Palaiologos; Girolamo Minotto; Gabriele Trevisan; Alvise Diedo; Maurizio Cattaneo; the Bocchiardi brothers; Pere Julià; Cardinal Isidore; Orhan Çelebi
roman_force: Sphrantzes counted 4,773 Greeks fit to fight and some 200 foreigners, joined by about 2,000-3,000 Latins, under 8,000 in all: Giustiniani's 700 Genoese (400 from Genoa, 300 from Chios), the Venetians of the bailo Minotto, Trevisan and the Contarini, Venetian and Genoese sailors, the Bocchiardi brothers at the Myriandrion, about 200 Catalans of the consul Pere Julià, 200 archers (Naples and Chios) with Cardinal Isidore, Cretan crews who held three towers, the Castilian Francisco de Toledo, the engineer Johannes Grant, and about 600 Turks of the Ottoman pretender Orhan; 26 ships (about 10 imperial, 5 Venetian, 3 from Venetian Crete, 5 Genoese, 1 each from Ancona, Aragon and France).
greek_note: Sphrantzes's census gives about 4,800 Greek defenders against some 2,000-3,000 foreigners, mostly Genoese and Venetians.
sources: Sphrantzes; Doukas; Chalkokondyles 8; Kritoboulos 1; Nicolò Barbaro; Leonardo of Chios; Tetaldi; en.wikipedia Fall of Constantinople
note: The Ottomans had about 50,000-80,000 men (5,000-10,000 Janissaries, 1,500 Serbian horse sent by Đurađ Branković) and 110-126 ships, with Urban's great cannon. Therapia and the Stoudion fort were stormed early; ships were dragged overland into the Golden Horn on 22 April; a fire-ship attack failed on 28 April; Grant's counter-mines destroyed the Ottoman tunnels (16-25 May). The final assault after midnight on 29 May broke through when Giustiniani was wounded; the Catalans, the Cretans and Orhan's Turks fought on after the walls fell.

name: Golden Horn (20 April 1453)
place: Off the Acropolis point, at the entrance of the Golden Horn
borderline: A naval action within the siege, described at length by the sources but rarely given a separate name.
roman_force: Three Genoese ships hired by the pope with arms and men, and an imperial transport carrying grain from Sicily under its captain Phlatanelas; they fought off the Ottoman fleet for hours and entered the Golden Horn at nightfall.
greek_note: One of the four ships was imperial and Greek-crewed; the other three were Genoese.
sources: Nicolò Barbaro; Doukas; Sphrantzes; Kritoboulos 1; en.wikipedia Fall of Constantinople
note: Mehmed rode into the sea to urge on his ships; Baltoğlu was wounded in the eye, dismissed and punished.

name: Kapanion
date: c. 1456 (proposed dates range from the 1430s to 1456-58)
war: Wars of Trebizond with the Turkmen
place: Kapanion, in the hinterland of Trebizond
commanders_b: John IV Megas Komnenos; his pansebastos (killed)
roman_force: John IV's land army under his pansebastos, with the fleet meant to land in Junayd's rear; contrary winds prevented the landing.
greek_note: Trebizond's army was raised from the Greek-speaking archons and townsmen of Pontus.
sources: Chalkokondyles 9; Bryer, 'Ludovico da Bologna and the Georgian and Anatolian embassy' (1965); en.wikipedia John IV of Trebizond
note: 'Safavids' stands for the Turkmen ghazis of the Safaviyya order led by Junayd. After the rout Junayd besieged Trebizond for three days and ravaged Mesochaldia; John escaped by sea.

name: Trebizond
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Trebizond, weakened by plague; no numbers are given.
greek_note: A Greek city defended by its own people.
sources: Chalkokondyles 9; Doukas; en.wikipedia John IV of Trebizond; en.wikipedia Empire of Trebizond
note: Hızır attacked by land and sea, raided the countryside and the marketplace and took about 2,000 captives; John IV agreed to pay 2,000 (later 3,000) gold pieces a year. One account says Hızır was beaten off before the city.

name: Corinth (siege)
commanders_a: Mehmed II; Turahanoğlu Ömer Bey; Hamza Bey
commanders_b: Matthew Palaiologos Asen; Nikephoros Loukanes; the despot Demetrios Palaiologos (relief army)
roman_force: The garrison of Acrocorinth under Nikephoros Loukanes, reinforced by Matthew Asen, who slipped in at night with 70 men and supplies, with some Venetian help; Demetrios's relief army of 6,000 cavalry was lured out and beaten. The Ottomans had about 40,000 men (20,000 cavalry) and four great cannon.
greek_note: Kritoboulos and Chalkokondyles describe a Greek garrison under Greek commanders.
sources: Kritoboulos 3; Chalkokondyles 9; Sphrantzes; en.wikipedia Battle of Corinth (1458); en.wikipedia, the article on the Ottoman conquest of the Morea
note: Asen surrendered on terms on 6 August; Ömer Bey became governor. On the same campaign Tarsos and the citadel of Patras yielded after short sieges, Phlius was stormed and its garrison massacred, and Vostitsa was taken.

name: Phlius (siege)
borderline: A minor siege of the campaign, not usually named as a battle (as Akova and Mouchli, which are listed).
roman_force: The garrison of Phlius under Doxas, which held out until the Ottomans cut its water supply.
greek_note: The castles of the despotate were held by Moreot Greeks, with Albanian settlers in the countryside.
sources: Kritoboulos 3; Chalkokondyles 9; en.wikipedia, the article on the Ottoman conquest of the Morea
note: While terms were being discussed the Ottomans entered through an unguarded section and massacred the garrison. Already mentioned in the note of Corinth (siege, 1458).

name: Akova (siege)
borderline: A minor siege of the campaign, not usually named as a battle.
roman_force: The local garrisons and inhabitants, Greek and Albanian; no numbers are given.
greek_note: Moreot garrisons of Greeks and Albanians.
sources: Kritoboulos 3; Chalkokondyles 9; en.wikipedia, the article on the Ottoman conquest of the Morea
note: Akova and Roupeli resisted until the sultan almost gave up the siege.

name: Mouchli (siege)
borderline: A minor siege of the campaign, not usually named as a battle.
roman_force: The garrison of Mouchli; no numbers are given.
greek_note: A Moreot hill town garrisoned by its Greek and Albanian inhabitants.
sources: Kritoboulos 3; Chalkokondyles 9; en.wikipedia, the article on the Ottoman conquest of the Morea
note: Taken after a three-day siege once its water supply was cut.

name: Patras
war: Thomas Palaiologos's revolt against the Ottomans (1459-60)
roman_force: Thomas's Moreot troops and Albanian lords, with about 300 Italian infantry paid by the pope and the duchess of Milan (under Gianone da Cremona).
greek_note: Thomas's army combined Greek and Albanian Moreots with a small Italian company.
sources: Sphrantzes; Chalkokondyles 9; Kritoboulos 3; en.wikipedia, the article on the Ottoman conquest of the Morea; en.wikipedia Thomas Palaiologos
note: The lower town fell but the citadel held; Thomas withdrew when an Ottoman relief force approached. He did take Kalavryta.

name: Leontari
war: Thomas Palaiologos's revolt against the Ottomans (1459-60)
roman_force: Thomas's army of Greek and Albanian Moreots with his Italian mercenaries.
greek_note: Thomas's army combined Greek and Albanian Moreots with a small Italian company.
sources: Chalkokondyles 9; Sphrantzes; en.wikipedia, the article on the Ottoman conquest of the Morea
note: The Ottoman cavalry broke Thomas's lines and his men fled into Leontari castle; plague in the Ottoman camp then forced the Ottomans to withdraw.

name: Leontari (siege)
commanders_b: Demetrios Palaiologos; Manuel Bochalis and his father-in-law
roman_force: Demetrios's partisans under Manuel Bochalis took Leontari, calling on the Ottoman governors for help; Thomas came up with his army and forced them out with many casualties.
greek_note: Both despots' forces were Moreot Greeks and Albanians.
sources: Sphrantzes; Chalkokondyles 9; en.wikipedia Manuel Bochalis; en.wikipedia Demetrios Palaiologos; en.wikipedia, the article on the Ottoman conquest of the Morea
note: After Hamza Zenevisi's Ottomans withdrew from Leontari, Demetrios besieged the castle, but Thomas relieved it and Demetrios's army retreated to Mystras (en.wikipedia, the article on the Ottoman conquest of the Morea); in the Manuel Bochalis article Bochalis and his father-in-law take the town and abandon it with heavy losses when Thomas arrives. In the same civil war Thomas besieged Demetrios's Kalamata and Mantineia and took Kalamata, Zarnata, Leuktron and the Mani; Demetrios withdrew to Monemvasia.

name: Kastritsi (siege)
roman_force: The garrison and inhabitants of the fortress, who beat off the Janissaries' attacks until their water and food ran out.
greek_note: A Moreot fortress held by its Greek and Albanian inhabitants.
sources: Kritoboulos 3; Chalkokondyles 9; en.wikipedia, the article on the Ottoman conquest of the Morea
note: The garrison was executed and the women and children enslaved; the town was destroyed. The site is uncertain (Chalkokondyles's Kastritzion, between Vordonia and Leontari).

name: Gardiki (siege)
roman_force: The people of Leontari and the district, who had fled to the castle, under Manuel Bochalis.
greek_note: Refugees from Leontari and the countryside, Greek and Albanian.
sources: Kritoboulos 3; Chalkokondyles 9; Sphrantzes; en.wikipedia Manuel Bochalis
note: The castle surrendered after one day of assault; about 6,000 were then massacred, though Bochalis was spared through Mahmud Pasha.

name: Palaia Achaia
war: Thomas Palaiologos's revolt against the Ottomans (1459-60)
place: The castle of Palaia Achaia, west of Patras
borderline: A failed siege, abandoned on the approach of Zagan Pasha.
roman_force: Thomas's Moreot army, with a cannon that did little damage.
greek_note: Moreot levies, Greek and Albanian.
sources: Chalkokondyles 9; en.wikipedia, the article on the Ottoman conquest of the Morea

name: Salmeniko (siege)
commanders_a: Mehmed II; Zagan Pasha; Hamza Bey
roman_force: The garrison of Salmeniko under Graitzas Palaiologos, after the town below had surrendered.
greek_note: A Moreot garrison under a Palaiologan officer.
sources: Sphrantzes; Kritoboulos 3; Chalkokondyles 9; en.wikipedia Despotate of the Morea; en.wikipedia, the article on the Ottoman conquest of the Morea
note: The last resistance of the despotate: Graitzas and his men held the castle until July 1461 and then escaped to Venetian territory. Mystras had been surrendered without a fight on 29/30 May 1460; Monemvasia was never besieged.

name: Trebizond (siege)
commanders_a: Mehmed II; Mahmud Pasha Angelović; Kasım Pasha (fleet)
roman_force: The garrison and citizens of Trebizond behind their walls and ravines; the sources give no numbers. Uzun Hasan of the Aq Qoyunlu, David's ally, made a separate peace and sent no help.
greek_note: Trebizond was a Greek city defended by its own people; the Genoese and Venetian quarters lay outside the walls.
sources: Kritoboulos 4; Chalkokondyles 9; Doukas; Konstantin Mihailović; en.wikipedia Siege of Trebizond (1461)
note: Kasım Pasha's fleet and men besieged the walls for 32 days, and Doukas says the daily assaults made no headway; one estimate gives the Ottomans 80,000 infantry, 60,000 cavalry and 200 galleys. David surrendered on terms on 15 August 1461 when he learned that Uzun Hasan would not come; he and his sons were executed in 1463.

name: Mangup (siege)
place: Mangup (Theodoro), the cave-town fortress of the principality
roman_force: The people of Theodoro (Greeks, with Goths and Alans) under Prince Alexander, who had seized power with the support of Stephen the Great of Moldavia, and 300 Moldavian ('Wallachian') soldiers sent by Stephen.
greek_note: Theodoro's population was largely Greek-speaking Orthodox, with Crimean Goths and Alans; the Moldavians were a small contingent.
sources: Ottoman chronicles; Genoese and Moldavian letters; Vasiliev, The Goths in the Crimea (1936); en.wikipedia Principality of Theodoro; en.wikipedia Siege of Mangup
note: The Ottoman fleet had taken Genoese Caffa in June 1475. Mangup withstood five major assaults (Vasiliev) and surrendered to famine at the end of December 1475; Alexander was beheaded in Constantinople. The last battle of a Roman successor state.
